NEET unit notes · review

Physics · Unit 1: Physics and Measurement

This unit sets up the language of physics: how physical quantities are measured, expressed in standard units, reported with correct precision, and checked for consistency using dimensions. In NEET it reliably gives 1 to 2 quick questions, mostly on dimensions of constants, error propagation, significant figures and instrument least count. Its tools are also reused in every other unit.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q37

Units of measurement and systems of units

Measuring a physical quantity means comparing it with a fixed, internationally accepted reference standard called a unit. Every measured quantity is written as a numerical value times a unit, $Q = nu$. Because the quantity itself does not change, the numerical value is inversely proportional to the size of the unit, so a bigger unit gives a smaller number. A system of units is a complete set of base units plus the units derived from them. The common systems are CGS (centimetre, gram, second), FPS (foot, pound, second), MKS (metre, kilogram, second) and SI, the modern extension of MKS with seven base units. Some practical units are used for very large or very small lengths and masses. Astronomical distances use the light year, the astronomical unit and the parsec. Atomic scales use the angstrom, the fermi and the atomic mass unit.

  • Physical quantity = numerical value times unit; $n \propto \frac{1}{u}$
  • CGS, FPS and MKS are older systems; SI is the internationally accepted system
  • A good unit is well defined, reproducible, invariable and easily accessible
  • 1 light year $= 9.46 \times 10^{15}$ m
  • 1 AU $\approx 1.496 \times 10^{11}$ m
  • 1 parsec $\approx 3.08 \times 10^{16}$ m $\approx 3.26$ light years
  • 1 angstrom $= 10^{-10}$ m and 1 fermi $= 10^{-15}$ m
  • 1 u $= 1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg and 1 barn $= 10^{-28}$ $m^2$
  • Light year and parsec are units of distance, not time

$Q = n_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2$ Magnitude of a quantity is the same in any unit system; use it to convert numerical values

$1\ \text{parsec} = \frac{1\ \text{AU}}{1''}$ Distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of one arcsecond

NEET tip: Expect direct conversions or ordering questions on practical units such as light year, parsec, AU and fermi.

SI units, fundamental and derived units

SI has seven base (fundamental) units, which are mutually independent. They are the metre (length), the kilogram (mass), the second (time), the ampere (electric current), the kelvin (thermodynamic temperature), the mole (amount of substance) and the candela (luminous intensity). The radian (plane angle) and the steradian (solid angle) were earlier called supplementary units and are dimensionless. All other units are derived units, obtained by multiplying or dividing base units. Examples are the newton ($kg\,m\,s^{-2}$), joule, watt, pascal, coulomb ($A\,s$), volt, ohm, farad, weber, tesla and henry. When writing SI units, a unit named after a person has a capital symbol (N, J, W) but a lowercase full name (newton). Symbols are never pluralised and are not followed by a full stop. Standard prefixes scale units in powers of ten, such as milli $10^{-3}$, micro $10^{-6}$, nano $10^{-9}$, pico $10^{-12}$, kilo $10^{3}$, mega $10^{6}$ and giga $10^{9}$.

  • 7 base units: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd
  • Radian and steradian are dimensionless; the full sphere subtends $4\pi$ sr
  • The kilogram is the only base unit that carries a prefix
  • Derived units come from base units through defining equations
  • $1\,N = 1\,kg\,m\,s^{-2}$, $1\,J = 1\,N\,m$, $1\,W = 1\,J\,s^{-1}$ and $1\,Pa = 1\,N\,m^{-2}$
  • $1\,T = 1\,Wb\,m^{-2}$, $1\,V = 1\,J\,C^{-1}$ and $1\,\Omega = 1\,V\,A^{-1}$
  • Write 10 kg, not 10 kgs or 10 Kg

$\theta = \frac{l}{r}$ Plane angle in radian: arc length $l$ divided by radius $r$

$d\Omega = \frac{dA}{r^2}$ Solid angle in steradian: area $dA$ on a sphere divided by the square of the radius $r$

NEET tip: NEET asks which unit is fundamental or derived, which units are equivalent, or the SI unit of a given constant.

Least count and significant figures

Least count (LC) is the smallest value an instrument can measure. A metre scale has LC 1 mm. A vernier caliper has $LC = 1\,MSD - 1\,VSD$, where MSD and VSD are the values of one main scale division and one vernier scale division. A screw gauge has LC equal to the pitch divided by the number of circular scale divisions. Zero error must be subtracted from the observed reading, with its sign. Significant figures are the reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit. All non-zero digits are significant. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. Leading zeros are never significant. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. In addition and subtraction, keep the least number of decimal places. In multiplication and division, keep the least number of significant figures. When rounding, a dropped digit greater than 5 raises the preceding digit and one less than 5 leaves it unchanged. A dropped digit of exactly 5 raises the preceding digit only if that digit is odd.

  • Smaller least count means a more precise instrument
  • A zero error is positive when the zero of the vernier or circular scale lies ahead of the main scale zero
  • 0.00450 has 3 significant figures; 4.050 has 4
  • Changing units does not change the number of significant figures: 2.30 m = $2.30 \times 10^{2}$ cm (or 230. cm). Writing 230 cm without a decimal point is ambiguous about the trailing zero.
  • Exact numbers such as the 2 in $2\pi r$ have infinite significant figures
  • In scientific notation $a \times 10^{b}$, only the digits of $a$ count
  • Order of magnitude is the power of 10 when the number is written as $a \times 10^b$ with $a$ between 0.5 and 5

$LC_{vernier} = 1\,MSD - 1\,VSD = \frac{s}{n}$ Vernier least count when $n$ VSD equal $(n-1)$ MSD, where $s$ is the value of one MSD

$LC_{screw} = \frac{\text{pitch}}{N}$ Screw gauge least count, where $N$ is the number of circular scale divisions

$\text{Reading} = MSR + (VSR \times LC) - \text{zero error}$ Corrected reading for a vernier or screw gauge; MSR is the main scale reading and VSR is the coinciding vernier or circular scale division

NEET tip: Typical questions ask you to count significant figures, round off the result of an operation, or find a corrected vernier or screw gauge reading.

Errors in measurements

Error is the difference between the measured value and the true value. Systematic errors act in one direction and come from the instrument (such as zero error), from the method or from personal habits. They can be reduced by better technique. Random errors fluctuate irregularly and are reduced by taking the mean of many readings. Gross errors come from carelessness. Accuracy is closeness to the true value, while precision is the resolution or repeatability of a measurement. For readings $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$, the mean is taken as the true value. The absolute error of each reading is $|a_{mean} - a_i|$, and their average is the mean absolute error. Relative error is the mean absolute error divided by the mean, and multiplying it by 100 gives percentage error. When quantities are combined, absolute errors add in sums and differences. Relative errors add in products and quotients, and a power $n$ multiplies the relative error by $n$.

  • Errors always add, never subtract, even when the quantities are subtracted
  • In $Z = \frac{A^p B^q}{C^r}$ the percentage error is $p\%A + q\%B + r\%C$
  • The contribution of each quantity is (power) × (its relative error). For similar relative errors, the quantity with the highest power contributes the most.
  • Random error is reduced by repeating observations; systematic error is not
  • Without other information, the maximum error in a single reading is taken as the least count
  • A measurement can be precise but not accurate, and the reverse is also possible

$a_{mean} = \frac{1}{n}\sum a_i$ Mean value of $n$ readings, taken as the true value

$\Delta a_{mean} = \frac{1}{n}\sum |\Delta a_i|$ Mean absolute error, where $\Delta a_i = a_{mean} - a_i$

$\delta a = \frac{\Delta a_{mean}}{a_{mean}}$ Relative (fractional) error; multiply by 100 for percentage error

$\Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B$ Maximum absolute error for $Z = A + B$ or $Z = A - B$

$\frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = \frac{\Delta A}{A} + \frac{\Delta B}{B}$ Maximum relative error for $Z = AB$ or $Z = \frac{A}{B}$

$\frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = n\frac{\Delta A}{A}$ Relative error for $Z = A^n$

NEET tip: The most common question gives a formula with powers, such as $g = \frac{4\pi^2 l}{T^2}$, and asks for the maximum percentage error.

Dimensions of physical quantities

The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers to which the base quantities must be raised to represent it. The base quantities are mass [M], length [L], time [T], current [A], temperature [K], amount of substance [mol] and luminous intensity [cd]. The expression, for example $[MLT^{-2}]$ for force, is the dimensional formula. Pure numbers, ratios of similar quantities, angles, strain, refractive index, relative density and the arguments of $\sin$, $\log$ and $\exp$ are dimensionless. Several different quantities share the same dimensions. Work, energy and torque are one such group. Impulse and momentum are another. Pressure, stress, modulus of elasticity and energy density form a third, and Planck's constant and angular momentum a fourth. A quick way to find the dimensions of a constant is to start from a defining relation. For example, $\sigma$ comes from $P/A = \sigma T^4$, $k_B$ from $E = k_B T$ and $b$ from $\lambda_m T = b$.

  • Force $[MLT^{-2}]$, energy $[ML^2T^{-2}]$ and power $[ML^2T^{-3}]$
  • Pressure, stress and Young's modulus all have dimensions $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$
  • Surface tension and spring constant share $[MT^{-2}]$
  • Frequency, angular velocity and velocity gradient share $[T^{-1}]$
  • Planck constant and angular momentum share $[ML^2T^{-1}]$
  • Charge $[AT]$, potential $[ML^2T^{-3}A^{-1}]$ and resistance $[ML^2T^{-3}A^{-2}]$
  • Magnetic field B $[MT^{-2}A^{-1}]$ and magnetic flux $[ML^2T^{-2}A^{-1}]$
  • $\frac{L}{R}$, $RC$ and $\sqrt{LC}$ all have dimensions of time
  • A dimensionless quantity may still have a unit, for example the radian

$[G] = [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$ Gravitational constant, from $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$

$[\sigma] = [MT^{-3}K^{-4}]$ Stefan-Boltzmann constant, from power per area $= \sigma T^4$

$[k_B] = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$ Boltzmann constant (energy per kelvin); the gas constant R has $[ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}mol^{-1}]$

$[b] = [LK]$ Wien constant, from $\lambda_m T = b$

$[\epsilon_0] = [M^{-1}L^{-3}T^4A^2]$ Permittivity of free space, from Coulomb's law

$[\mu_0] = [MLT^{-2}A^{-2}]$ Permeability of free space

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} = c$ The combination has the dimensions of velocity $[LT^{-1}]$

NEET tip: NEET often combines two or three constants, such as $\sigma$, $k_B$, $b$, $h$ or $G$, and asks for the dimensions of the product or ratio.

Dimensional analysis and its applications

Dimensional analysis uses the principle of homogeneity: every term in a physically valid equation must have the same dimensions. It has three main applications. First, it checks whether an equation is dimensionally correct. A correct equation passes this check, but passing does not prove the equation is right, because dimensionless factors are not tested. Second, it converts a numerical value from one system of units to another using $n_2 = n_1 [M_1/M_2]^a [L_1/L_2]^b [T_1/T_2]^c$. Third, it derives the form of a relation, for example $T \propto \sqrt{l/g}$ for a simple pendulum, by equating the powers of M, L and T. The method has limits. It cannot find dimensionless constants such as $2\pi$. It cannot derive relations with more than three unknown dependencies in mechanics. It cannot handle relations involving $\sin$, $\log$ or exponential functions, or relations that are sums of terms. It also cannot tell whether a quantity is a scalar or a vector.

  • Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated
  • In $y = A\sin(\omega t - kx)$ both $\omega t$ and $kx$ are dimensionless, so $[k] = [L^{-1}]$
  • In $P = \frac{a}{b}e^{-bx}$, the product $bx$ is dimensionless
  • In $(P + \frac{a}{V^2})$, the term $\frac{a}{V^2}$ must have the dimensions of P
  • A dimensionally correct equation may still be physically wrong
  • For derivations, write $Q = k\,x^a y^b z^c$, equate powers of M, L and T, then solve for a, b and c

$n_2 = n_1\left[\frac{M_1}{M_2}\right]^a\left[\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right]^b\left[\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right]^c$ Converts the numerical value of a quantity with dimensions $[M^aL^bT^c]$ from system 1 to system 2

$T = k\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$ Simple pendulum time period derived dimensionally; $k$ ($= 2\pi$) cannot be found this way

NEET tip: Questions ask you to find the dimensions of unknown constants in a given equation, to convert units such as $1\,J$ into a new system, or to identify the dimensionally correct option.

Formula sheet

$Q = n_1u_1 = n_2u_2$ Numerical value $n$ is inversely proportional to the size of unit $u$

$LC_{vernier} = 1\,MSD - 1\,VSD$ Vernier least count from one main scale division (MSD) and one vernier scale division (VSD)

$LC_{screw} = \frac{\text{pitch}}{N}$ Screw gauge least count; $N$ is the number of circular scale divisions

$\text{True reading} = \text{observed reading} - \text{zero error}$ Zero error correction, applied with sign

$a_{mean} = \frac{1}{n}\sum a_i$ Mean of $n$ readings $a_i$

$\Delta a_{mean} = \frac{1}{n}\sum|a_{mean} - a_i|$ Mean absolute error

$\text{Percentage error} = \frac{\Delta a_{mean}}{a_{mean}} \times 100$ Relative error expressed as a percentage

$Z = A \pm B \Rightarrow \Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B$ Absolute errors add for sum and difference

$Z = AB \text{ or } \frac{A}{B} \Rightarrow \frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = \frac{\Delta A}{A} + \frac{\Delta B}{B}$ Relative errors add for product and quotient

$Z = \frac{A^pB^q}{C^r} \Rightarrow \frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = p\frac{\Delta A}{A} + q\frac{\Delta B}{B} + r\frac{\Delta C}{C}$ General error rule for powers; each relative error is multiplied by its power

$\theta = \frac{l}{r},\ d\Omega = \frac{dA}{r^2}$ Radian (arc length $l$ over radius $r$) and steradian (area $dA$ over $r^2$)

$1\,\text{ly} = 9.46 \times 10^{15}\,m,\ 1\,\text{pc} = 3.08 \times 10^{16}\,m$ Light year (ly) and parsec (pc), both units of distance

$[F] = [MLT^{-2}],\ [E] = [ML^2T^{-2}],\ [P] = [ML^2T^{-3}]$ Force, energy and power

$[p] = [ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$ Pressure, stress, Young's modulus and energy density

$[h] = [ML^2T^{-1}]$ Planck constant, same as angular momentum

$[G] = [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$ Universal gravitational constant

$[\sigma] = [MT^{-3}K^{-4}]$ Stefan-Boltzmann constant

$[k_B] = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$ Boltzmann constant

$[b] = [LK]$ Wien displacement constant

$[\epsilon_0] = [M^{-1}L^{-3}T^4A^2],\ [\mu_0] = [MLT^{-2}A^{-2}]$ Permittivity and permeability of free space

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} = c$ Speed of light; the combination has dimensions $[LT^{-1}]$

$[\frac{L}{R}] = [RC] = [\sqrt{LC}] = [T]$ Time constants of RL and RC circuits, and the inverse of the LC angular frequency

$n_2 = n_1\left[\frac{M_1}{M_2}\right]^a\left[\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right]^b\left[\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right]^c$ Unit conversion by dimensional analysis

Common traps

  • Subtracting errors when the quantities are subtracted: in $Z = A - B$ the maximum error is $\Delta A + \Delta B$.
  • Counting leading zeros as significant: 0.0025 has only 2 significant figures, while 2.500 has 4.
  • Applying the significant figure rule to addition: in addition and subtraction, the answer keeps the least number of decimal places, not the least number of significant figures.
  • Adding zero error instead of subtracting it: corrected reading = observed reading minus zero error, so a negative zero error effectively adds.
  • Treating light year as a unit of time: light year and parsec are units of distance.
  • Assuming a dimensionally correct equation is correct: dimensional analysis cannot detect wrong numerical factors such as $\frac{1}{2}$ or $2\pi$.
  • Confusing Boltzmann constant with the gas constant: $k_B$ has $[ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$, while R has an extra $mol^{-1}$.
  • Calling dimensionless quantities unitless: angle has the unit radian but no dimensions, and strain has neither.

Quick revision

  • SI base units are m, kg, s, A, K, mol and cd; radian and steradian are dimensionless.
  • The numerical value of a quantity is inversely proportional to the size of its unit.
  • Vernier LC = 1 MSD minus 1 VSD; screw gauge LC = pitch divided by circular divisions.
  • Leading zeros are never significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point always are.
  • Use the least decimal places for addition and subtraction, and the least significant figures for multiplication and division.
  • When rounding off a dropped digit of exactly 5, round up only if the preceding digit is odd.
  • Absolute errors add in sums and differences; relative errors add in products and quotients.
  • A power n on a quantity multiplies its percentage error by n.
  • Arguments of sin, log and exp must be dimensionless.
  • $[\sigma] = [MT^{-3}K^{-4}]$, $[k_B] = [ML^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$, $[b] = [LK]$ and $[G] = [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$.
  • Same dimensions: work and torque; Planck constant and angular momentum; pressure and energy density.
  • Dimensional analysis cannot find numerical constants or handle trigonometric and exponential relations.

Physics · Unit 2: Kinematics

Kinematics describes motion (position, velocity and acceleration) without asking what causes it. It covers motion in one dimension, the vector tools needed for two dimensions, projectile motion and uniform circular motion. In NEET it usually gives 1-2 direct questions, and its ideas (graphs, vectors, relative motion) are used throughout mechanics, electrostatics and magnetism.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q6

Frame of reference and motion in a straight line

Motion is always described relative to a frame of reference. A frame is a reference point (origin) with coordinate axes and a clock to measure time. A body is at rest or in motion only with respect to a chosen frame, so rest and motion are relative. In rectilinear (straight-line) motion, position is given by a single coordinate $x$ with a sign. Displacement $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ is the change in position. It is a vector: it can be positive, negative or zero, and it depends only on the initial and final positions. Distance, or path length, is the total length of the actual path covered. It is a scalar, never negative, and never less than the magnitude of displacement. In the point-object approximation, a body is treated as a point when its size is negligible compared with the distance it moves.

  • Rest and motion are relative to the chosen frame of reference
  • Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path
  • Path length is greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement; they are equal only for straight-line motion without reversal
  • For a closed path, displacement is zero but path length is not
  • In 1D motion, the sign of a quantity shows its direction along the chosen axis

$\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$ Displacement in 1D motion; the sign gives the direction

NEET tip: Expect conceptual questions comparing distance and displacement, for example for a particle completing a full or half circle.

Position-time and velocity-time graphs

Graphs are a very high-yield area. In a position-time ($x$-$t$) graph, the slope at any point gives the instantaneous velocity. A straight line means uniform velocity, a line parallel to the time axis means rest, and a curved graph means acceleration. An upward-curving graph (concave up) means positive acceleration. In a velocity-time ($v$-$t$) graph, the slope gives acceleration. The area under the graph gives displacement, taking area below the time axis as negative. The total area counted as positive gives distance. A horizontal $v$-$t$ line means uniform velocity. A straight sloping line means uniform acceleration. In an acceleration-time graph, the area gives the change in velocity. Two practical rules: an $x$-$t$ graph can never show two positions at the same instant, and time can never run backwards.

  • Slope of the $x$-$t$ graph gives velocity; slope of the $v$-$t$ graph gives acceleration
  • Area under the $v$-$t$ graph gives displacement; the sum of absolute areas gives distance
  • Area under the $a$-$t$ graph gives the change in velocity
  • For uniform acceleration, the $x$-$t$ graph is a parabola and the $v$-$t$ graph is a straight line
  • Velocity changes sign where the $v$-$t$ graph crosses the time axis

$v = \frac{dx}{dt}$ Velocity as the slope of the position-time graph

$a = \frac{dv}{dt}$ Acceleration as the slope of the velocity-time graph

$\Delta x = \int v\,dt$ Displacement as the area under the velocity-time graph

NEET tip: NEET often gives one graph and asks for the matching graph or quantity, or asks you to identify a physically impossible graph.

Speed and velocity; uniform and non-uniform motion

Speed is the rate of covering path length. It is a scalar and is never negative. Velocity is the rate of change of displacement. It is a vector, with both magnitude and direction. Uniform motion means a body covers equal displacements in equal intervals of time, however small. Its velocity is therefore constant, its acceleration is zero and its $x$-$t$ graph is a straight line. Non-uniform motion means the velocity changes in magnitude, in direction, or in both, so the body has acceleration. A body moving with constant speed can still be accelerating if its direction changes, as in uniform circular motion. However, constant velocity always implies constant speed and zero acceleration.

  • Speed is a scalar and never negative; velocity is a vector
  • Uniform motion has constant velocity and zero acceleration
  • Constant speed does not necessarily mean constant velocity
  • A change in direction alone produces acceleration
  • SI unit of both speed and velocity is $m\,s^{-1}$; $1\ km\,h^{-1} = \frac{5}{18}\ m\,s^{-1}$

$1\ km\,h^{-1} = \frac{5}{18}\ m\,s^{-1}$ Unit conversion used frequently in numericals

NEET tip: Statement-type questions ask whether constant speed implies zero acceleration; it does not.

Average speed and instantaneous velocity

Average speed is the total path length divided by the total time. Average velocity is the net displacement divided by the total time. Since path length is at least as large as the magnitude of displacement, average speed is at least as large as the magnitude of average velocity. They are equal only for straight-line motion with no reversal. Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval tends to zero, so $v = \frac{dx}{dt}$. Its magnitude equals the instantaneous speed. For motion given as $x(t)$, first find where $v = 0$ inside the interval. If the particle reverses direction there, compute the distance in separate pieces before averaging. For two equal distances covered at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$, the average speed is the harmonic-type mean, not the arithmetic mean.

  • Average speed is greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity
  • Average velocity is zero for a round trip, but average speed is not
  • Instantaneous speed equals the magnitude of instantaneous velocity
  • Always check for reversal by solving $v(t) = 0$ before finding distance
  • Equal distances at $v_1$ and $v_2$ give average speed $\frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$
  • Equal time intervals at $v_1$ and $v_2$ give average speed $\frac{v_1+v_2}{2}$

$v_{avg} = \frac{\text{total path length}}{\text{total time}}$ Average speed (scalar)

$\vec{v}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}$ Average velocity (vector)

$v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}$ Instantaneous velocity

$v_{avg} = \frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$ Average speed for two equal distances covered at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$

NEET tip: NEET gives polynomial $x(t)$ and asks for average speed; the trap is a turning point inside the interval, where average velocity can even be zero.

Uniformly accelerated motion and its relations

When acceleration $a$ is constant, the kinematic equations apply. These are $v = u + at$, $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ and $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$. All quantities are signed, so fix one positive direction and use it consistently. Free fall is a special case with $a = g$ directed downward, neglecting air resistance. A body thrown up with speed $u$ rises a maximum height $\frac{u^2}{2g}$ in time $\frac{u}{g}$. Time up equals time down, and it returns with the same speed. The distance covered in the $n$th second follows a separate formula. For a body starting from rest, the distances in successive equal time intervals are in the ratio $1:3:5:\dots$ (Galileo's law of odd numbers). Stopping distance is proportional to $u^2$. If acceleration varies with time or position, use calculus instead of these equations.

  • The kinematic equations are valid only for constant acceleration
  • Use a consistent sign convention for all vector quantities
  • Starting from rest, distances in successive equal intervals are in the ratio $1:3:5:7\dots$
  • Stopping distance is $\frac{u^2}{2a}$, so doubling the speed makes it four times larger
  • At the highest point of vertical motion, $v = 0$ but $a = g$
  • For variable acceleration, use $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ or integrate directly

$v = u + at$ Final velocity after time $t$

$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ Displacement in time $t$

$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ Relation without time

$s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1)$ Displacement in the $n$th second

$H = \frac{u^2}{2g},\ t = \frac{u}{g}$ Maximum height and time of ascent for vertical projection

$a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ Acceleration when velocity is given as a function of position

NEET tip: Common questions use the $n$th-second formula, the ratio of distances in successive seconds, stopping distance, and balls dropped or thrown from towers.

Scalars and vectors

A scalar has only magnitude and combines by ordinary algebra. Examples are mass, time, speed, distance, work, energy and temperature. A vector has both magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle (parallelogram) law of addition. Examples are displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum. Having a direction is not enough to be a vector. Electric current has direction but adds algebraically, so it is a scalar. Equal vectors have the same magnitude and the same direction. A negative vector has the same magnitude but the opposite direction. A null (zero) vector has zero magnitude and an arbitrary direction. Multiplying a vector by a scalar $\lambda$ scales its magnitude by $|\lambda|$ and reverses its direction if $\lambda < 0$.

  • A vector needs both magnitude and direction and must obey the triangle law
  • Current, pressure, work and energy are scalars
  • Displacement, velocity, force and momentum are vectors
  • A null vector has zero magnitude and indeterminate direction
  • A vector can be shifted parallel to itself without changing it

NEET tip: Classification questions often test whether electric current is a scalar or a vector; it is a scalar.

Vector addition and subtraction

Vectors are added geometrically using the triangle law (head-to-tail) or the parallelogram law. If two vectors of magnitudes $A$ and $B$ have an angle $\theta$ between them, the resultant magnitude is $\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$. Its direction from $\vec{A}$ is given by $\tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}$. The resultant is maximum, $A+B$, at $\theta = 0$ and minimum, $|A-B|$, at $\theta = 180^\circ$. Vector addition is commutative and associative. Subtraction means adding the negative: $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta}$. For two equal vectors of magnitude $A$, the resultant is $2A\cos\frac{\theta}{2}$, and it equals $A$ when $\theta = 120^\circ$. Three vectors can give a zero resultant only if they can form a closed triangle.

  • The resultant always lies between $|A-B|$ and $A+B$
  • Vector addition is commutative; subtraction is not
  • For equal vectors of magnitude $A$, $R = 2A\cos\frac{\theta}{2}$
  • Two equal vectors at $120^\circ$ give a resultant equal to either vector
  • Three forces in equilibrium must be able to form a closed triangle
  • The change in velocity is $\Delta \vec{v} = \vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1$, a vector subtraction

$R = \sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$ Magnitude of $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$ with angle $\theta$ between the vectors

$\tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}$ Angle of the resultant measured from $\vec{A}$

$|\vec{A}-\vec{B}| = \sqrt{A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta}$ Magnitude of the difference of two vectors

NEET tip: Questions ask for the angle when $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}| = |\vec{A}-\vec{B}|$ (answer $90^\circ$) or for possible resultant values of given forces.

Scalar and vector products

The scalar (dot) product is $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$. It is commutative and is zero for perpendicular vectors. It is used for work ($W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}$), for power, and for finding the angle between vectors. The vector (cross) product is $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$, where the direction of $\hat{n}$ follows the right-hand rule. It is anticommutative: $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = -\vec{B}\times\vec{A}$. It is zero for parallel or antiparallel vectors. The product is perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by them, and half of that gives the triangle's area. Use it for torque, angular momentum and the magnetic force on a moving charge. The cyclic rules are $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k} = \hat{i}$ and $\hat{k}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}$, while $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i} = 1$ and $\hat{i}\times\hat{i} = \vec{0}$.

  • Dot product is zero when the vectors are perpendicular
  • Cross product is zero when the vectors are parallel or antiparallel
  • $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$
  • Cross product is anticommutative; dot product is commutative
  • $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = A^2$ and $\vec{A}\times\vec{A} = \vec{0}$
  • The magnitude of the cross product gives the area of a parallelogram

$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$ Scalar product; gives work and the angle between vectors

$\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{AB}$ Angle between two vectors

$|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$ Magnitude of the cross product, equal to the area of the parallelogram

$\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = \hat{i}(A_yB_z-A_zB_y)-\hat{j}(A_xB_z-A_zB_x)+\hat{k}(A_xB_y-A_yB_x)$ Component (determinant) form of the cross product

NEET tip: Typical questions: find the angle when $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}| = \sqrt{3}\,\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$ (answer $60^\circ$), find a value making two vectors perpendicular, or find the area of a parallelogram.

Unit vector and resolution of a vector

A unit vector has magnitude 1 and only specifies direction: $\hat{A} = \frac{\vec{A}}{A}$. It has no units. The unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ point along the x, y and z axes. Resolving a vector means splitting it into components along chosen directions, usually perpendicular axes. A vector of magnitude $A$ at angle $\theta$ to the x-axis has components $A_x = A\cos\theta$ and $A_y = A\sin\theta$. Conversely, $A = \sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = \frac{A_y}{A_x}$. In 3D, $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i}+A_y\hat{j}+A_z\hat{k}$. The direction cosines are $\cos\alpha = \frac{A_x}{A}$, $\cos\beta = \frac{A_y}{A}$ and $\cos\gamma = \frac{A_z}{A}$, and the squares of the three sum to 1. A rectangular (perpendicular) component of a vector can never exceed the vector's magnitude.

  • A unit vector is dimensionless and has magnitude exactly 1
  • Rectangular components are $A\cos\theta$ and $A\sin\theta$
  • Add vectors component-wise for quick algebra
  • The squares of the direction cosines sum to 1
  • The component of $\vec{A}$ along $\vec{B}$ is $\frac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{B}$

$\hat{A} = \frac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$ Unit vector along $\vec{A}$

$A = \sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2+A_z^2}$ Magnitude from the components

$\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma = 1$ Property of direction cosines

$A_{\parallel B} = \vec{A}\cdot\hat{B}$ Projection (component) of $\vec{A}$ along $\vec{B}$

NEET tip: Questions ask for the unit vector along a given vector or a resultant, or test whether an expression such as $0.5\hat{i}+0.5\hat{j}$ is a unit vector (it is not).

Relative velocity

The velocity of A relative to B is $\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$, which is A's velocity as seen by an observer moving with B. In 1D, bodies moving in the same direction have a relative speed equal to the difference of their speeds. Bodies moving in opposite directions have a relative speed equal to the sum. For rain and a moving person, the rain's velocity relative to the person is $\vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_m$, and the umbrella should be held along this relative velocity. For river crossing with swimmer speed $v$ in still water and river speed $u$, the shortest time comes from swimming perpendicular to the flow. That gives $t = \frac{d}{v}$ with drift $\frac{ud}{v}$. The shortest path (zero drift) comes from heading upstream at angle $\theta$ to the perpendicular to the river flow, with $\sin\theta = \frac{u}{v}$ (equivalently, at $90^\circ + \theta$ to the direction of flow), which requires $v > u$, giving $t = \frac{d}{\sqrt{v^2-u^2}}$.

  • $\vec{v}_{AB} = -\vec{v}_{BA}$
  • Relative speed is the difference for the same direction and the sum for opposite directions
  • Hold the umbrella along the velocity of rain relative to the person
  • Minimum crossing time: head perpendicular to the flow
  • Zero drift is possible only if the swimmer's speed exceeds the river's speed
  • Relative acceleration is zero for two bodies in free fall, so their relative motion is uniform

$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B$ Velocity of A relative to B

$t_{min} = \frac{d}{v},\ x = \frac{ud}{v}$ Shortest crossing time and downstream drift (river width $d$, swimmer speed $v$, river speed $u$)

$\sin\theta = \frac{u}{v},\ t = \frac{d}{\sqrt{v^2-u^2}}$ Upstream heading angle (measured from the perpendicular to the flow) and time for crossing along the shortest path

NEET tip: Classic NEET problems cover trains overtaking, rain and umbrella angles, and boat or river crossing.

Motion in a plane

In 2D motion, position is $\vec{r} = x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}$, velocity is $\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$ and acceleration is $\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$. Instantaneous velocity is always tangent to the path. The x and y motions are independent of each other and can be treated as two separate 1D problems sharing the same time $t$. For constant acceleration in a plane, the vector forms are $\vec{v} = \vec{v}_0 + \vec{a}t$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{r}_0 + \vec{v}_0t + \frac{1}{2}\vec{a}t^2$. Each of these splits into separate x and y equations. To find the path equation $y(x)$, eliminate $t$ between $x(t)$ and $y(t)$. Acceleration need not be along the velocity. The component of acceleration along $\vec{v}$ changes the speed, and the component perpendicular to $\vec{v}$ changes the direction.

  • Perpendicular components of motion are independent
  • Velocity is always tangential to the trajectory
  • Constant-acceleration equations hold component-wise
  • Eliminate $t$ to get the trajectory equation
  • The tangential component of acceleration changes speed; the normal component changes direction

$\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = v_x\hat{i}+v_y\hat{j}$ Velocity in 2D

$\vec{v} = \vec{v}_0+\vec{a}t$ Velocity under constant acceleration in a plane

$\vec{r} = \vec{r}_0+\vec{v}_0t+\frac{1}{2}\vec{a}t^2$ Position under constant acceleration in a plane

NEET tip: NEET gives $\vec{r}(t)$ or $x(t)$, $y(t)$ and asks for the velocity, acceleration or path at a given instant.

Projectile motion

A projectile launched with speed $u$ at angle $\theta$, neglecting air resistance, has constant horizontal velocity $u\cos\theta$ and constant vertical acceleration $g$ downward. Its path is a parabola. The time of flight is $T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, the maximum height is $H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ and the range is $R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$. Maximum range, $\frac{u^2}{g}$, occurs at $45^\circ$. Complementary angles ($\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$) give the same range. At the top, the velocity is $u\cos\theta$ (horizontal, minimum, but not zero) and the acceleration is still $g$. Two useful relations are $\frac{H}{R} = \frac{\tan\theta}{4}$ and $R = 4H$ at $\theta = 45^\circ$; $R = H$ when $\tan\theta = 4$, i.e. $\theta \approx 76^\circ$. For horizontal projection from height $h$, the time is $\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$ (independent of $u$) and the range is $u\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$.

  • Horizontal velocity is constant; vertical motion is free fall
  • At the highest point, $v = u\cos\theta$, $a = g$, and $\vec{v}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$
  • Complementary angles give equal ranges; their times of flight satisfy $T_1T_2 = \frac{2R}{g}$
  • The range is maximum at $45^\circ$, where the height reached is $H = \frac{u^2}{4g} = \frac{R_{max}}{4}$; the greatest possible height for a given $u$ is $\frac{u^2}{2g} = \frac{R_{max}}{2}$, reached at $90^\circ$
  • The time of fall for horizontal projection does not depend on the horizontal speed
  • Kinetic energy at the top is $K\cos^2\theta$, where $K$ is the initial kinetic energy

$T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ Time of flight on level ground

$H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ Maximum height

$R = \frac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$ Horizontal range; maximum value $\frac{u^2}{g}$ at $45^\circ$

$y = x\tan\theta-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ Equation of trajectory (a parabola)

$\frac{H}{R} = \frac{\tan\theta}{4}$ Ratio of maximum height to range

$t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}},\ R = u\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$ Time and range for horizontal projection from height $h$

NEET tip: Expect ratio questions (H/R, ranges at complementary angles), velocity or kinetic energy at the top, and horizontal projection from a cliff.

Uniform circular motion

In uniform circular motion, a body moves on a circle of radius $r$ with constant speed $v$. Its velocity keeps changing direction, so it is accelerated. The centripetal acceleration $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$ is always directed towards the centre. Its magnitude is constant, but its direction changes continuously, so it is not a constant vector. Angular velocity $\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt}$ is related to speed by $v = \omega r$. Also $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi\nu$, where $T$ is the time period and $\nu$ the frequency. The velocity is tangential and perpendicular to the acceleration. As a result, the centripetal force does no work and kinetic energy stays constant. Over half a revolution, the change in velocity has magnitude $2v$. Over a full revolution, both the displacement and the average velocity are zero.

  • Speed is constant, but velocity and acceleration change in direction
  • Centripetal acceleration points towards the centre and is perpendicular to the velocity
  • Work done by the centripetal force is zero
  • $v = \omega r$; $\omega$ is the same for all points of a rotating rigid body
  • The change in velocity after an angle $\theta$ has magnitude $2v\sin\frac{\theta}{2}$
  • If the speed also changes, the net acceleration is $\sqrt{a_t^2+a_c^2}$

$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$ Centripetal acceleration magnitude

$v = \omega r$ Relation between linear and angular speed

$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi\nu$ Angular speed from the time period $T$ or frequency $\nu$

$|\Delta\vec{v}| = 2v\sin\frac{\theta}{2}$ Magnitude of the change in velocity after turning through angle $\theta$

$a = \sqrt{a_t^2+a_c^2}$ Net acceleration in non-uniform circular motion ($a_t$ tangential, $a_c$ centripetal)

NEET tip: Common questions: centripetal acceleration of a stone on a string given revolutions per minute, statements on constant quantities in UCM, and the change in velocity after a given angle.

Formula sheet

$v_{avg} = \frac{\text{path length}}{\text{time}},\ \vec{v}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta\vec{r}}{\Delta t}$ Average speed (scalar) and average velocity (vector)

$v = \frac{dx}{dt},\ a = \frac{dv}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ Instantaneous velocity and acceleration

$v = u+at$ Velocity under constant acceleration $a$; $u$ is initial velocity, $t$ is time

$s = ut+\frac{1}{2}at^2$ Displacement $s$ under constant acceleration

$v^2 = u^2+2as$ Velocity-displacement relation for constant acceleration

$s_n = u+\frac{a}{2}(2n-1)$ Displacement in the $n$th second

$v_{avg} = \frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$ Average speed for equal distances covered at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$

$R = \sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$ Resultant of two vectors with angle $\theta$ between them

$\tan\alpha = \frac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}$ Direction of the resultant relative to $\vec{A}$

$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$ Scalar product

$|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$ Magnitude of the vector product; direction by the right-hand rule

$\hat{A} = \frac{\vec{A}}{A}$ Unit vector along $\vec{A}$

$A_x = A\cos\theta,\ A_y = A\sin\theta$ Rectangular components; $\theta$ is measured from the x-axis

$\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A-\vec{v}_B$ Relative velocity of A with respect to B

$t_{min} = \frac{d}{v},\ \sin\theta = \frac{u}{v}$ River crossing: minimum time, and upstream angle to the perpendicular to the flow for zero drift ($d$ width, $v$ swimmer speed, $u$ river speed)

$\vec{r} = \vec{r}_0+\vec{v}_0t+\frac{1}{2}\vec{a}t^2$ Position in 2D motion with constant acceleration

$T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$ Time of flight of a projectile

$H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$ Maximum height of a projectile

$R = \frac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$ Range of a projectile; maximum $\frac{u^2}{g}$ at $\theta = 45^\circ$

$y = x\tan\theta-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ Trajectory equation of a projectile

$t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}},\ R = u\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$ Horizontal projection from height $h$

$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2r,\ v = \omega r$ Uniform circular motion: centripetal acceleration and linear speed

$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi\nu$ Angular speed from time period $T$ or frequency $\nu$

Common traps

  • Taking average speed equal to the magnitude of average velocity when the particle reverses direction. Find where $v = 0$ and add the distances piece by piece.
  • Using the arithmetic mean $\frac{v_1+v_2}{2}$ for equal distances. That is correct only for equal time intervals; for equal distances use $\frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$.
  • Applying $v = u+at$ and the other equations when acceleration varies with time. They hold only for constant acceleration; otherwise integrate.
  • Thinking velocity and acceleration are both zero at the top of vertical motion. Velocity is zero but acceleration remains $g$; for a projectile the speed at the top is $u\cos\theta$, not zero.
  • Believing uniform circular motion has zero or constant acceleration. The magnitude $\frac{v^2}{r}$ is constant, but the direction changes, so acceleration is not constant.
  • Mixing up the sign conventions in vertical motion. Choose upward or downward as positive once and give $g$ the correct sign.
  • Holding the umbrella along the actual direction of the rain. It must be held along the velocity of rain relative to the person.
  • Treating $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}$ and $\vec{B}\times\vec{A}$ as equal. They are opposite in direction.

Quick revision

  • Slope of $x$-$t$ gives $v$, slope of $v$-$t$ gives $a$, area under $v$-$t$ gives displacement, and area under $a$-$t$ gives the change in velocity.
  • Average speed is at least the magnitude of average velocity; they are equal only for unidirectional straight-line motion.
  • Starting from rest with uniform acceleration, distances in successive equal intervals are in the ratio $1:3:5:7$.
  • Stopping distance is proportional to $u^2$.
  • The resultant of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ lies between $|A-B|$ and $A+B$; equal vectors at $120^\circ$ give a resultant of equal magnitude.
  • The dot product is zero means perpendicular; the cross product is zero means parallel; $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|$ is the parallelogram area.
  • $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}$, in cyclic order.
  • Relative velocity: $\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A-\vec{v}_B$; for minimum crossing time head perpendicular to the flow, for zero drift head upstream at $\theta$ to the perpendicular to the flow with $\sin\theta = \frac{u}{v}$.
  • Projectile: $T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, $H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, $R = \frac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$; maximum range at $45^\circ$, and complementary angles give equal ranges.
  • At the top of a projectile path, $v = u\cos\theta$, $a = g$, and kinetic energy is $K\cos^2\theta$.
  • Horizontal projection: the fall time $\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$ is independent of the horizontal speed.
  • UCM: $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2r$ towards the centre, $v = \omega r$, $\omega = 2\pi\nu$; the centripetal force does no work.

Physics · Unit 3: Laws of Motion

Laws of Motion explains why bodies move the way they do, using Newton's three laws, momentum, friction and the dynamics of circular motion. NEET asks 2-3 questions from this unit almost every year. These are usually numericals on connected bodies, impulse, friction, conservation of momentum and banked roads, and they require clean free-body diagrams and correct vector reasoning.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q23, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q41

Force and inertia; Newton's first law of motion

Force is an external push or pull that changes, or tends to change, the state of rest or uniform motion of a body. Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or uniform motion along a straight line. Mass is the quantitative measure of linear inertia. Newton's first law states that every body continues in its state of rest or uniform straight-line motion unless an external net force acts on it. The first law therefore defines force and defines inertial frames, which are frames in which the law holds. Familiar examples are passengers jerking backward when a bus starts, jerking forward when it brakes suddenly, and dust leaving a carpet when it is beaten. Galileo's inclined plane experiments first suggested that motion needs no force to continue; force is needed only to change velocity.

  • Net force zero means acceleration zero: the body is at rest or moves with constant velocity
  • Inertia of rest, inertia of motion and inertia of direction are its three types
  • Greater mass means greater inertia
  • The first law defines inertial frames; an accelerating frame is non-inertial
  • A body moving with constant speed along a curve is NOT free of force, because its velocity direction changes

$\vec{F}_{net} = 0 \Rightarrow \vec{a} = 0,\ \vec{v} = \text{constant}$ Condition stated by the first law; equally the condition for translational equilibrium

NEET tip: Usually tested through conceptual statements, such as identifying inertia examples or recognising that uniform circular motion needs a net force.

Momentum, Newton's second law and impulse

Linear momentum is $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$. It is a vector along the velocity and its SI unit is kg m/s. Newton's second law states that the rate of change of momentum equals the applied net external force and occurs in the direction of that force. For constant mass this reduces to $F = ma$. The law is a vector law, so it applies component-wise, and it is local, meaning the force at an instant fixes the acceleration at that instant. Impulse is the product of force and time, or more generally the integral of force over time. It equals the change in momentum and is the area under the F-t graph. Impulsive forces are large forces acting for a very short time, as when a bat hits a ball. Catching a ball with the hands drawn back increases the contact time, which reduces the force.

  • One newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of $1\ m/s^2$
  • Impulse and momentum have the same unit: N s = kg m/s
  • Area under the F-t graph gives impulse, which equals the change in momentum
  • For a ball rebounding normally with the same speed, $|\Delta p| = 2mv$
  • Draw a free-body diagram for each body when solving connected-body problems
  • Apparent weight in a lift is $m(g+a)$ when accelerating upward and $m(g-a)$ when accelerating downward; it is zero in free fall

$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ Linear momentum of a body

$\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = m\vec{a}$ Second law; the second form holds for constant mass

$\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt = \vec{F}_{avg}\Delta t = \Delta \vec{p}$ Impulse-momentum theorem

$F = v\frac{dm}{dt}$ Force needed for variable mass, e.g. a conveyor belt or rocket thrust

$a = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2},\ T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$ Atwood machine with an ideal pulley, where $m_1 > m_2$

NEET tip: Expect numericals on impulse from F-t graphs, ball-rebound momentum change, lift problems, and the acceleration and tension in pulley-block systems.

Newton's third law of motion

Newton's third law states that to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces always occur in pairs. If A exerts $\vec{F}_{AB}$ on B, then B exerts $\vec{F}_{BA} = -\vec{F}_{AB}$ on A, at the same instant. Action and reaction act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel each other. A book resting on a table illustrates this. Its weight (Earth pulls book) and the normal force (table pushes book) balance each other because of the first law, not the third law. Their actual third-law partners are book pulls Earth and book pushes table. Applications include walking (the foot pushes the ground back, the ground pushes the foot forward), rocket propulsion, swimming and gun recoil. The third law, combined with the second, leads directly to conservation of momentum.

  • Action and reaction are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and simultaneous
  • They act on different bodies and are of the same nature (both gravitational, both contact, and so on)
  • Weight and normal force on a resting body are NOT an action-reaction pair
  • Internal forces of a system cancel in pairs, so only external forces change the system's momentum
  • Contact force between blocks pushed together on a smooth surface is $F_{contact} = \frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}F$ on the front block $m_2$ (the block not directly pushed), when F pushes $m_1$

$\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}$ Mutual forces between two interacting bodies

NEET tip: NEET checks whether you can correctly identify action-reaction pairs and find contact forces between blocks in contact.

Law of conservation of linear momentum and its applications

If the net external force on a system is zero, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant. Internal forces cannot change total momentum, because they cancel in third-law pairs. Momentum is a vector, so the total is the vector sum of the individual momenta. Two bodies with equal momentum magnitudes moving in different directions have a resultant that depends on the angle between them: it is maximum when they move parallel and zero when they move antiparallel. Applications include gun recoil, rocket propulsion, explosion of a shell into fragments and collisions. In a collision, momentum is always conserved, while kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions. Momentum can also be conserved along one direction when the external force has no component along that direction.

  • Conservation holds only when the net external force is zero, either overall or along a chosen axis
  • Gun recoil: $mv = MV$, so the recoil speed is $V = \frac{mv}{M}$
  • A body at rest that explodes has zero total momentum, so the fragments' momenta add vectorially to zero
  • In a two-piece explosion, the fragments move in opposite directions with KE in the inverse ratio of their masses
  • Magnitude of the resultant of two momenta $p$ at angle $\phi$ is $2p\cos(\phi/2)$
  • Momentum is conserved in all collisions, but KE is conserved only in elastic collisions

$m_1\vec{u}_1 + m_2\vec{u}_2 = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2$ Momentum conservation for two bodies with no net external force

$V_{recoil} = -\frac{m v}{M}$ Recoil velocity of a gun of mass M firing a bullet of mass m with speed v

$K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$ Kinetic energy in terms of momentum; useful for explosion problems

$|\vec{p}_1 + \vec{p}_2| = \sqrt{p_1^2 + p_2^2 + 2p_1p_2\cos\phi}$ Resultant momentum of two bodies whose momenta make angle $\phi$

NEET tip: Expect recoil and explosion numericals, plus conceptual questions on the vector total momentum of symmetric systems, such as particles moving on a circle in opposite directions.

Equilibrium of concurrent forces

Concurrent forces are forces whose lines of action pass through a single point. A particle, or a body acted on by concurrent forces, is in equilibrium when the vector sum of the forces is zero. Equivalently, the sum of components along each of x, y and z is zero. For three concurrent forces in equilibrium, the forces can be represented by the three sides of a closed triangle taken in order, so any one force is equal and opposite to the resultant of the other two. Lami's theorem gives a handy relation: each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two. Typical problems include a mass hung by two strings at different angles, a string-pulley junction, and a body held on a smooth incline by a horizontal force.

  • The equilibrium condition is $\sum \vec{F} = 0$, i.e. $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$
  • Three forces in equilibrium must be coplanar and form a closed triangle
  • Lami's theorem applies only to three concurrent forces in equilibrium
  • Resolve forces along convenient perpendicular axes
  • For a weight W hung symmetrically by two strings each at angle $\theta$ to the vertical, $T = \frac{W}{2\cos\theta}$

$\vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2 + \vec{F}_3 = 0$ Equilibrium of three concurrent forces

$\frac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \frac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$ Lami's theorem; $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ are the angles opposite to $F_1$, $F_2$, $F_3$ respectively

$R = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2F_1F_2\cos\theta}$ Resultant of two forces at angle $\theta$

NEET tip: NEET asks for string tensions in hanging-mass systems or the force needed to keep a body in equilibrium, solved by resolving components or by Lami's theorem.

Static and kinetic friction, laws of friction, rolling friction

Friction opposes relative motion, or impending relative motion, between surfaces in contact. Static friction is self-adjusting: it equals the applied force up to a maximum value, called limiting friction, given by $\mu_s N$. Once sliding starts, kinetic friction $\mu_k N$ acts. It is nearly constant and slightly less than limiting friction, since $\mu_k < \mu_s$. The laws of friction are as follows. Limiting friction is proportional to the normal reaction. It is independent of the apparent area of contact. It depends on the nature of the surfaces. Kinetic friction is roughly independent of speed. The angle of friction $\lambda$ satisfies $\tan\lambda = \mu_s$, and the angle of repose of an incline equals the angle of friction. Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings are used. Friction is necessary for walking and for vehicles to move.

  • Static friction lies in the range $0 \le f_s \le \mu_s N$; do not automatically write $\mu_s N$
  • Rolling friction is much smaller than kinetic friction, which is smaller than limiting friction
  • Pulling a body at an angle reduces the normal force N and hence the friction; pushing at an angle increases them
  • On an incline, $N = mg\cos\theta$ if no other force acts perpendicular to the surface
  • Friction on the driven wheels of a car and on a walking person's foot acts forward
  • To keep a block pressed against a vertical wall from sliding, $\mu F \ge mg$

$f_s \le \mu_s N,\ f_k = \mu_k N$ Static (up to limiting) and kinetic friction

$\tan\lambda = \mu_s = \tan\alpha_{repose}$ Angle of friction equals angle of repose

$a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$ Acceleration of a block sliding down a rough incline

$a = g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)$ Retardation of a block moving up a rough incline

$F_{min} = \frac{\mu mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}}$ Minimum pull to move a block on a rough horizontal surface, applied at angle $\tan^{-1}\mu$ above the horizontal

NEET tip: Common questions find the friction actually acting (static vs limiting), the acceleration on rough inclines, the ratio of times to slide down rough vs smooth inclines, and block-on-block motion.

Dynamics of uniform circular motion: centripetal force

In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the velocity direction changes continuously. The body therefore has a centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$ directed towards the centre, which requires a net force $mv^2/r$ towards the centre. Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is the role played by some real force or combination of forces: tension for a stone whirled on a string, gravity for a planet or satellite, friction for a car on a level turn, and the normal force component for banked roads. Because this force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it does no work and kinetic energy remains constant. If the force disappears, the body moves off along the tangent, not radially outward. A conical pendulum is another standard case, in which the horizontal component of tension supplies the centripetal force.

  • Centripetal acceleration is $\frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$, directed towards the centre
  • Work done by the centripetal force is zero
  • Speed and kinetic energy are constant, but velocity and momentum change direction
  • When the string breaks, the body flies off along the tangent
  • Centrifugal force is a pseudo force that appears only in the rotating, non-inertial frame
  • For a conical pendulum, $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$

$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$ Net inward force needed for circular motion of radius r

$v = \omega r,\ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi n$ Relation between linear speed, angular speed, period T and frequency n

$T\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r},\ T\cos\theta = mg$ Conical pendulum with the string at angle $\theta$ to the vertical

NEET tip: NEET tests identifying which real force provides the centripetal force, the vector nature of momentum in circular motion, and maximum speeds before a string breaks or a body slips.

Vehicle on a level circular road and on a banked road

On a level circular road, only static friction can supply the centripetal force. Safe turning requires $mv^2/r \le \mu_s mg$, giving $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}$, which is independent of the vehicle's mass. Banking the road at an angle $\theta$ lets the horizontal component of the normal reaction provide part, or all, of the centripetal force. At the optimum speed $v_0 = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$, no friction is needed, so wear and tear on the tyres is minimum. Above this speed, friction acts down the slope. Below it, friction acts up the slope. With friction included, the maximum safe speed on a banked road is $\sqrt{rg\frac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}}$. A cyclist turning must lean inward by an angle $\theta$ with $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$. This is the same expression as the banking condition.

  • Level road: the maximum speed $\sqrt{\mu_s r g}$ does not depend on mass
  • Banked road with no friction: $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$, and tyre wear is minimum
  • The normal reaction on a banked road exceeds mg, being $N = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$ at the optimum speed
  • Friction direction on a banked road depends on whether v is above or below $v_0$
  • Railway tracks are banked by raising the outer rail; for small $\theta$, $\tan\theta \approx \sin\theta = \frac{h}{l}$, where h is the height of the outer rail and l the distance between rails
  • If $\mu_s \ge \tan\theta$, a vehicle can stay at rest on the banked road without sliding

$v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}$ Maximum safe speed on a level curved road

$v_0 = \sqrt{r g \tan\theta}$ Optimum speed on a banked road, at which no friction is needed

$v_{max} = \sqrt{r g \frac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s \tan\theta}}$ Maximum safe speed on a rough banked road

$v_{min} = \sqrt{r g \frac{\tan\theta - \mu_s}{1 + \mu_s \tan\theta}}$ Minimum speed below which the vehicle slides down a rough banked road

$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$ Banking angle, or a cyclist's lean angle from the vertical

NEET tip: Directly asked as finding the banking angle for minimum tyre wear, the maximum speed on level or banked roads, or a cyclist's lean angle.

Formula sheet

$\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ Linear momentum, where m is mass and v is velocity

$\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = m\vec{a}$ Newton's second law, with F the net external force and a the acceleration

$\vec{J} = \vec{F}_{avg}\Delta t = \Delta\vec{p}$ Impulse, equal to the change in momentum and to the area under the F-t graph

$F = v\frac{dm}{dt}$ Thrust or force for a variable-mass system ejecting or adding mass at rate dm/dt with relative speed v

$\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}$ Third law: forces of interaction between two bodies A and B

$m_1\vec{u}_1 + m_2\vec{u}_2 = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2$ Conservation of linear momentum, with u the initial and v the final velocities

$V = \frac{mv}{M}$ Recoil speed of a gun of mass M firing a bullet of mass m at speed v

$K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$ Kinetic energy K of a body of mass m and momentum p

$R_{lift} = m(g \pm a)$ Apparent weight in a lift with acceleration a, using + for upward and - for downward acceleration

$a = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1+m_2},\ T = \frac{2m_1m_2 g}{m_1+m_2}$ Atwood machine: acceleration a and tension T for masses $m_1 > m_2$

$\frac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \frac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$ Lami's theorem for three concurrent forces in equilibrium, with each angle opposite the corresponding force

$f_s \le \mu_s N,\ f_k = \mu_k N$ Static and kinetic friction, with N the normal reaction and $\mu$ the coefficient of friction

$\tan\lambda = \mu_s$ Angle of friction $\lambda$, which equals the angle of repose

$a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$ Acceleration down a rough incline of inclination $\theta$

$t_{rough} = \frac{t_{smooth}}{\sqrt{1 - \mu_k\cot\theta}}$ Time to slide down a rough incline compared with a smooth incline of the same length

$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$ Centripetal force for speed v or angular speed $\omega$ on radius r

$v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}$ Maximum speed on a level circular road

$v_0 = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$ Optimum speed on a road banked at angle $\theta$, giving minimum tyre wear

$v_{max} = \sqrt{rg\frac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}}$ Maximum safe speed on a rough banked road

$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$ Cyclist's lean angle from the vertical, or the banking angle for the optimum speed

Common traps

  • Writing static friction as $\mu_s N$ in every case. Static friction only equals the applied force needed to prevent motion, and reaches $\mu_s N$ only at the point of slipping.
  • Treating weight and normal reaction as an action-reaction pair. They act on the same body; the true third-law pairs act on different bodies.
  • Adding momenta as scalars. Momentum is a vector, so two equal momenta in opposite directions give a total of zero, and at an angle they must be added vectorially.
  • Thinking the body flies radially outward when a whirling string breaks. It moves along the tangent, because no outward real force exists.
  • Taking $N = mg$ on inclines, banked roads or when a force is pulled at an angle. Resolve forces properly; for example, N = mg cos θ on a simple incline and N = mg/cos θ on a frictionless banked turn.
  • Assuming friction on a banked road always acts down the slope. It acts down only when v exceeds $\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$ and acts up the slope when v is below it.
  • Believing a constant-speed circular motion has no net force. A centripetal force of $mv^2/r$ is always required, even though it does no work.
  • Ignoring the sign of velocity in impulse problems. For a rebound with the same speed, the change in momentum is 2mv, not zero.

Quick revision

  • Mass is the measure of inertia, and the first law defines force and inertial frames.
  • $F = dp/dt$ is the general form of the second law, and $F = ma$ applies only for constant mass.
  • Impulse equals the change in momentum and the area under the F-t graph; increasing the contact time reduces the force.
  • Action and reaction are equal, opposite and simultaneous, and act on different bodies.
  • With zero net external force, total momentum is conserved as a vector, which explains gun recoil, explosions and rockets.
  • Equilibrium of concurrent forces requires zero vector sum; for three forces, use a closed triangle or Lami's theorem.
  • Static friction is self-adjusting up to $\mu_s N$; kinetic friction is $\mu_k N$, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$; rolling friction is the least.
  • Angle of repose equals angle of friction, with $\tan\theta = \mu_s$.
  • Centripetal force $mv^2/r$ is supplied by a real force such as tension, friction, gravity or a normal-force component.
  • On a level road $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu r g}$, and on a frictionless banked road $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$ gives minimum tyre wear.
  • A lift accelerating up increases apparent weight, and in free fall apparent weight is zero.
  • In every problem, draw a free-body diagram, choose axes, and apply $\sum F = ma$ along each axis.

Physics · Unit 4: Work, Energy and Power

This unit links force and motion through the scalar ideas of work, energy and power. It introduces the work-energy theorem, conservation of mechanical energy, conservative forces, vertical circular motion and collisions. NEET asks 2-3 questions from it almost every year, mostly variable-force work, F-x graphs, spring problems, vertical circle conditions and collision calculations, and these ideas recur throughout mechanics.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q1, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q44

Work done by a constant force and a variable force

Work measures energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement. For a constant force, work is the dot product $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = Fd\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between force and displacement. Work is a scalar. It is positive when $0 \le \theta < 90^\circ$ (force aids motion), zero when $\theta = 90^\circ$ (centripetal force, normal force on a horizontal surface, a coolie walking horizontally with a load) and negative when $90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$ (friction opposing motion, gravity on a rising body). For a variable force, divide the path into small elements so that $W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx$. Graphically, this is the area under the F-x curve, with area below the axis counted negative. In three dimensions, $W = \int (F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz)$. The SI unit is the joule (1 J = 1 N m = $10^7$ erg), and its dimensions are $[ML^2T^{-2}]$.

  • Work is a scalar but can be positive, negative or zero
  • No displacement or perpendicular force means zero work
  • Variable force: integrate, or take the area under the F-x graph
  • Area below the x-axis on an F-x graph counts as negative work
  • For a position-dependent friction coefficient, integrate $\mu(x) mg\,dx$
  • $1\ \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ and $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6\ \text{J}$

$W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = Fd\cos\theta$ Work by a constant force; $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{d}$

$W = F_x d_x + F_y d_y + F_z d_z$ Work from vector components of a constant force and displacement

$W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx$ Work by a variable force along a straight line; equals the area under the F-x graph

NEET tip: Expect integration of a position-dependent force (such as friction with variable $\mu$) or area under an F-x graph.

Kinetic and potential energies

Kinetic energy is energy of motion, $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$. It is always non-negative and independent of the direction of velocity. Potential energy is energy stored due to position or configuration. It can be defined only for conservative forces, and only changes in potential energy are physically meaningful, so the reference level is arbitrary. Near the Earth's surface, $U = mgh$, with $h$ measured from the chosen reference. The force is related to potential energy by $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$, so the force points towards decreasing potential energy. Equilibrium occurs where $\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$. It is stable at a minimum of $U$ ($\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} > 0$), unstable at a maximum ($\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} < 0$) and neutral where $U$ is constant. For equal momentum, the lighter body has more kinetic energy.

  • Kinetic energy is never negative; potential energy can be negative
  • $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$, so at equal momentum $K \propto \frac{1}{m}$
  • If $p$ increases by 100%, $K$ becomes 4 times (a 300% increase)
  • Potential energy is defined only for conservative forces
  • Force is the negative slope of the U-x graph
  • Stable equilibrium is a minimum of U; unstable is a maximum

$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$ Kinetic energy in terms of speed or momentum

$U = mgh$ Gravitational potential energy near the Earth's surface, $h \ll R_E$

$F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$ Conservative force from a potential energy function

NEET tip: NEET tests the percentage change of K with p, and reading force or equilibrium type from U-x graphs.

Work-energy theorem

The work-energy theorem states that the work done by the net force on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{net} = K_f - K_i$. It follows from Newton's second law, since $\int m v\,\frac{dv}{dx}\,dx = \Delta(\frac{1}{2}mv^2)$. It holds for constant and variable forces and for conservative and non-conservative forces alike. You add the work of every force, including gravity, friction, tension, normal force and applied force. It is the fastest route to speeds or stopping distances without finding acceleration or time. Example: a body sliding to rest on a rough floor satisfies $\mu mg s = \frac{1}{2}mu^2$, giving $s = \frac{u^2}{2\mu g}$. For a bullet stopped in a block, the average resistive force is $\frac{mu^2}{2s}$.

  • Total work by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy
  • Valid for all forces, including friction and variable forces
  • Stopping distance $s = \frac{u^2}{2\mu g}$ on a rough horizontal surface
  • Stopping distance is proportional to $u^2$ for the same retarding force
  • Bodies with equal K and equal retarding force stop in equal distance regardless of mass

$W_{net} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2$ Work-energy theorem

$W_{all} = W_c + W_{nc} = \Delta K$ Splitting net work into conservative and non-conservative parts

NEET tip: Used for speed after variable-force work, stopping distance, and bullet penetration problems.

Power

Power is the rate of doing work. Average power is $P_{avg} = \frac{W}{t}$, and instantaneous power is $P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$. Power is a scalar. The SI unit is the watt ($1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J s}^{-1}$), with dimensions $[ML^2T^{-3}]$, and $1\ \text{hp} = 746\ \text{W}$. The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power. Typical cases: for a body moving at constant velocity against a resistive force, $P = Fv$; for a pump or lift raising mass, $P = \frac{mgh}{t}$; and for a liquid ejected with speed $v$, $P = \frac{1}{2}\frac{dm}{dt}v^2$. If an engine delivers constant power from rest, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = Pt$, so $v \propto t^{1/2}$ and $s \propto t^{3/2}$. Efficiency is output power divided by input power.

  • Power is a scalar: $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$
  • kWh is energy: $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6\ \text{J}$
  • $1\ \text{hp} = 746\ \text{W}$
  • Constant power from rest: $v \propto \sqrt{t}$ and $s \propto t^{3/2}$
  • Under a constant force from rest, $P \propto t$
  • The area under a P-t graph gives work done

$P_{avg} = \frac{W}{t}$ Average power over time t

$P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = Fv\cos\theta$ Instantaneous power

$P = \frac{mgh}{t}$ Power needed to lift mass m through height h in time t (pumps, lifts)

$P = \frac{1}{2}\frac{dm}{dt}v^2$ Power to eject fluid at mass rate $\frac{dm}{dt}$ with speed v

NEET tip: Common items are motor or pump power, lift problems with friction, and power at an instant for an accelerating body.

Potential energy of a spring

An ideal spring obeys Hooke's law, $F_s = -kx$, where x is the extension or compression from the natural length and k is the spring constant (N/m). The spring force is a variable, restoring and conservative force. The work done by an external agent in slowly stretching the spring from 0 to x is $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$, and this is stored as elastic potential energy $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$. The same energy is stored for equal compression or extension. The work done by the spring force from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is $-\frac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2)$. The U-x graph is a parabola, and the F-x graph is a straight line through the origin with slope $-k$. A block of speed v hitting a spring on a smooth surface has maximum compression $x_{max} = v\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$. A spring cut into pieces has a larger k for each piece, with $k \propto \frac{1}{\text{length}}$.

  • Spring force is restoring: $F = -kx$
  • Stored energy is $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$, identical for compression and extension
  • Energy also equals $\frac{F^2}{2k}$ in terms of the force
  • Stretching from $x_1$ to $x_2$ needs $\frac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2)$, not $\frac{1}{2}k(x_2 - x_1)^2$
  • Maximum compression from $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}kx_{max}^2$

$F = -kx$ Hooke's law; k is the spring constant

$U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{F^2}{2k}$ Elastic potential energy of a spring with deformation x

$W_{ext} = \frac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2)$ External work to stretch a spring from $x_1$ to $x_2$

$x_{max} = v\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$ Maximum compression when mass m with speed v hits a spring on a smooth surface

NEET tip: Watch for extra work when stretching from $x_1$ to $x_2$, and maximum compression or speed of a block-spring system.

Conservation of mechanical energy

If only conservative forces do work on a system, its total mechanical energy $E = K + U$ remains constant, so $K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$. Kinetic and potential energy interconvert but their sum is fixed. For a body falling freely from height h, the speed just before hitting the ground is $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, independent of mass. For a simple pendulum released from angle $\theta_0$, the speed at the lowest point is $v = \sqrt{2gL(1 - \cos\theta_0)}$. On smooth surfaces of any shape, the final speed depends only on the height drop, not on the path. When non-conservative forces such as friction act, mechanical energy is not conserved: $W_{nc} = \Delta E_{mech}$, and the lost energy appears as heat or sound. The total energy of an isolated system, including all forms, is always conserved.

  • $K + U$ is constant when only conservative forces do work
  • Speed after falling height h is $\sqrt{2gh}$, independent of mass and path on smooth surfaces
  • Free fall: at height $\frac{h}{2}$, $K = U$ (taking the ground as reference)
  • With friction, $W_{friction} = E_f - E_i$, which is negative
  • Total energy of an isolated system is always conserved

$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$ Conservation of mechanical energy (conservative forces only)

$v = \sqrt{2gh}$ Speed after falling a height h from rest

$v = \sqrt{2gL(1-\cos\theta_0)}$ Speed of a pendulum bob at the lowest point when released from angle $\theta_0$

$W_{nc} = \Delta K + \Delta U$ Work by non-conservative forces equals the change in mechanical energy

NEET tip: Used in pendulum, incline, roller-coaster and spring-plus-gravity problems, often combined with collisions.

Conservative and non-conservative forces

A force is conservative if the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path. Equivalently, its work around any closed path is zero, and it can be written as $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$. Examples include gravitational, electrostatic and ideal spring forces. For a conservative force, $W_c = -\Delta U$. A non-conservative force does path-dependent work, and its work around a closed loop is not zero. Friction, viscous drag and air resistance are examples; they dissipate mechanical energy as heat, and no potential energy can be defined for them. Kinetic friction always does negative work on a sliding body relative to the surface, and this work grows with path length. Note that work by a conservative force is reversible: it can be recovered as kinetic energy.

  • Conservative force: path-independent work, zero work over a closed loop
  • Conservative examples: gravity, spring force, electrostatic force
  • Non-conservative examples: friction, air drag, viscous force
  • Potential energy exists only for conservative forces
  • Work done by friction depends on path length
  • $W_c = -\Delta U$

$\oint \vec{F}_c\cdot d\vec{r} = 0$ Closed-loop work of a conservative force is zero

$W_c = -\Delta U = U_i - U_f$ Work by a conservative force in terms of potential energy change

NEET tip: Usually a conceptual statement-type question on path independence, closed-loop work, or identifying conservative forces.

Motion in a vertical circle

A bob of mass m on a string of length L moving in a vertical circle has non-uniform speed, because gravity changes its kinetic energy. Use energy conservation between points and Newton's second law radially. With $\theta$ measured from the lowest point, the tension is $T = \frac{mv^2}{L} + mg\cos\theta$. At the top, the string must stay taut ($T \ge 0$), so $v_{top} \ge \sqrt{gL}$. This requires $v_{bottom} \ge \sqrt{5gL}$, and then $T_{bottom} - T_{top} = 6mg$. If $v_{bottom} \le \sqrt{2gL}$, the bob oscillates below the horizontal. If $\sqrt{2gL} < v_{bottom} < \sqrt{5gL}$, the string slackens somewhere above the horizontal and the bob follows a projectile path. For a rod or a bead on a ring, which can push as well as pull, the minimum top speed is zero, so $v_{bottom} \ge \sqrt{4gL}$. In general, $v^2 = u^2 - 2gL(1 - \cos\theta)$.

  • String: $v_{top,min} = \sqrt{gL}$ and $v_{bottom,min} = \sqrt{5gL}$
  • Rod or ring: $v_{top,min} = 0$ and $v_{bottom,min} = \sqrt{4gL}$
  • With $v_{bottom} = \sqrt{5gL}$: speed at horizontal position is $\sqrt{3gL}$
  • In that critical case, tensions are 6mg (bottom), 3mg (horizontal), 0 (top)
  • $T_{bottom} - T_{top} = 6mg$ for any speed, provided the circle is completed
  • Tension is maximum at the bottom, so a string is most likely to break there

$T = \frac{mv^2}{L} + mg\cos\theta$ String tension at angle $\theta$ from the lowest point

$v^2 = u^2 - 2gL(1-\cos\theta)$ Speed at angle $\theta$, given speed u at the bottom

$v_{bottom} \ge \sqrt{5gL}$, $v_{top} \ge \sqrt{gL}$ Condition to complete a vertical circle with a string

$T_{bottom} - T_{top} = 6mg$ Tension difference between the lowest and highest points

NEET tip: Asks for minimum speed, tension ratios at different points, or where the string slackens.

Elastic and inelastic collisions in one and two dimensions

In every collision, linear momentum is conserved if external impulse is negligible. In an elastic collision, total kinetic energy is also conserved.
