In an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy is lost. In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and the loss is maximum. In one-dimensional elastic collisions, the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach. The coefficient of restitution is $e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$: $e = 1$ for elastic, $0 < e < 1$ for inelastic and $e = 0$ for perfectly inelastic collisions. In a 1D elastic collision between equal masses, the bodies exchange velocities. When a heavy body hits a light one at rest, the light body moves off at about $2u_1$. When a light body hits a heavy one at rest, it rebounds with nearly the same speed. In two dimensions, conserve momentum separately along x and y. For an elastic oblique collision of equal masses with one at rest, the two velocities after collision are perpendicular.

  • Momentum is conserved in all collisions; kinetic energy only in elastic ones
  • Equal masses, 1D elastic: velocities are exchanged
  • Perfectly inelastic: common velocity, maximum KE loss
  • Fraction of KE transferred to a stationary target (elastic) is $\frac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1+m_2)^2}$, maximum when $m_1 = m_2$
  • 2D: momentum is conserved separately along x and y
  • Equal masses, elastic, target at rest: velocities after collision are at $90^\circ$
  • Ball dropped from h with restitution e rebounds to height $e^2h$

$m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$ Momentum conservation in 1D

$v_1 = \frac{(m_1-m_2)u_1 + 2m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$ Velocity of body 1 after a 1D elastic collision

$v_2 = \frac{(m_2-m_1)u_2 + 2m_1u_1}{m_1+m_2}$ Velocity of body 2 after a 1D elastic collision

$e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$ Coefficient of restitution: separation speed divided by approach speed

$\Delta K = \frac{m_1m_2(u_1-u_2)^2}{2(m_1+m_2)}$ KE lost in a perfectly inelastic collision

$m_1u_1 = m_1v_1\cos\theta_1 + m_2v_2\cos\theta_2$, $0 = m_1v_1\sin\theta_1 - m_2v_2\sin\theta_2$ 2D collision with body 2 initially at rest

NEET tip: Frequent combination: elastic collision of equal masses followed by the bob rising, $h = \frac{v^2}{2g}$, or a ballistic pendulum.

Formula sheet

$W = Fd\cos\theta$ Work by a constant force F over displacement d at angle $\theta$

$W = \int F(x)\,dx$ Work by a variable force; area under the F-x graph

$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$ Kinetic energy; m is mass, v speed, p momentum

$U = mgh$ Gravitational potential energy at height h near the Earth's surface

$F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$ Conservative force from potential energy U

$W_{net} = \Delta K$ Work-energy theorem

$P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$ Instantaneous power

$P = \frac{mgh}{t}$ Power to raise mass m through height h in time t

$1\ \text{hp} = 746\ \text{W}$, $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6\times10^6\ \text{J}$ Unit conversions for power and energy

$U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ Spring potential energy; k is spring constant, x deformation

$W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2)$ External work to stretch a spring from $x_1$ to $x_2$

$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$ Conservation of mechanical energy

$W_{nc} = \Delta E_{mech}$ Work by non-conservative forces such as friction

$v = \sqrt{2gh}$ Speed after falling height h from rest

$T = \frac{mv^2}{L} + mg\cos\theta$ Tension in a vertical circle; $\theta$ measured from the lowest point

$v_{bottom} = \sqrt{5gL}$, $v_{top} = \sqrt{gL}$ Minimum speeds to complete a vertical circle with a string of length L

$v_{bottom} = \sqrt{4gL}$ Minimum bottom speed for a rod or bead on a ring

$T_{bottom} - T_{top} = 6mg$ Tension difference in a complete vertical circle

$v_1 = \frac{(m_1-m_2)u_1 + 2m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$ Final velocity of body 1 in a 1D elastic collision

$v_2 = \frac{(m_2-m_1)u_2 + 2m_1u_1}{m_1+m_2}$ Final velocity of body 2 in a 1D elastic collision

$e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$ Coefficient of restitution

$v = \frac{m_1u_1 + m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$ Common velocity after a perfectly inelastic collision

$\Delta K = \frac{m_1m_2(u_1-u_2)^2}{2(m_1+m_2)}$ KE loss in a perfectly inelastic collision

$\frac{\Delta K}{K} = \frac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1+m_2)^2}$ Fraction of KE transferred to a stationary target in a 1D elastic collision

Common traps

  • Writing spring work from $x_1$ to $x_2$ as $\frac{1}{2}k(x_2 - x_1)^2$; the correct value is $\frac{1}{2}k(x_2^2 - x_1^2)$.
  • Using $W = Fd$ for a position-dependent force such as friction with variable $\mu$; you must integrate, for example $\int_0^L (\mu_0 - \alpha x) mg\,dx$.
  • Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision; only momentum is always conserved, and KE is conserved only in elastic collisions.
  • Using $\sqrt{5gL}$ as the minimum bottom speed for a rod; for a rod or ring it is $\sqrt{4gL}$, because the minimum top speed is zero.
  • Treating kWh as a unit of power; it is energy, equal to $3.6\times10^6$ J.
  • Thinking zero work means zero force; a centripetal force or the normal force on a horizontal surface does zero work while acting.
  • Applying mechanical energy conservation during an inelastic impact, such as a bullet embedding in a block; use momentum conservation for the impact, then energy conservation for the subsequent swing.
  • Ignoring the sign of area below the axis in F-x graphs; that area represents negative work.

Quick revision

  • $W = Fd\cos\theta$; for a variable force, $W = \int F\,dx$ or the area under the F-x graph.
  • Work-energy theorem: $W_{net} = \Delta K$, valid for all types of force.
  • $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$; doubling p makes K four times larger.
  • $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$; stable equilibrium at a minimum of U, unstable at a maximum.
  • $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$; under constant power from rest, $v \propto t^{1/2}$ and $s \propto t^{3/2}$.
  • Spring: $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$; maximum compression $x = v\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$.
  • Conservative force: path-independent work and zero closed-loop work; friction is non-conservative.
  • Vertical circle with a string: minimum speeds $\sqrt{5gL}$ at bottom and $\sqrt{gL}$ at top; $T_{bottom} - T_{top} = 6mg$.
  • Bob oscillates if $v \le \sqrt{2gL}$; string slackens if $\sqrt{2gL} < v < \sqrt{5gL}$.
  • 1D elastic collision of equal masses: velocities are exchanged.
  • Perfectly inelastic: bodies share a common velocity and KE loss is maximum; e = 0.
  • 2D elastic collision of equal masses with one at rest: velocities after collision are perpendicular.

Physics · Unit 5: Rotational Motion

This unit extends Newtonian mechanics from point particles to extended rigid bodies. It covers the centre of mass, torque, angular momentum, moment of inertia, equilibrium and the dynamics of rotation including rolling. NEET usually asks 2-3 questions from it, mostly moment of inertia calculations with the axis theorems, conservation of angular momentum, rolling on an incline and torque or equilibrium problems.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q27, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q31

Centre of mass of a two-particle system and of a rigid body

The centre of mass (COM) is the point where the entire mass of a system can be treated as concentrated when describing its translational motion. For two particles it lies on the line joining them and divides that line in the inverse ratio of the masses, so it sits closer to the heavier mass. For a rigid body it is a fixed point relative to the body, and it may lie outside the material, as in a ring. External forces alone change the motion of the COM, because internal forces cancel in pairs. If the net external force is zero, the COM moves with constant velocity, or stays at rest if it started at rest. For symmetric uniform bodies the COM lies at the geometric centre. Standard results for semicircular and hemispherical shapes should be memorised.

  • For two particles separated by d, the COM lies at $r_1 = \frac{m_2 d}{m_1+m_2}$ from $m_1$ and at $r_2 = \frac{m_1 d}{m_1+m_2}$ from $m_2$
  • $m_1 r_1 = m_2 r_2$, so the COM is nearer the heavier mass
  • Internal forces (explosions, collisions) cannot shift the COM
  • COM of a uniform semicircular ring is at $\frac{2R}{\pi}$ and of a semicircular disc at $\frac{4R}{3\pi}$, measured from the centre
  • COM of a solid hemisphere is at $\frac{3R}{8}$ and of a hollow hemisphere at $\frac{R}{2}$, measured from the centre
  • COM of a solid cone is at $\frac{h}{4}$ from the base
  • In a uniform gravitational field the centre of gravity coincides with the COM

$x_{cm} = \frac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}$ COM position of a two-particle system along a line

$\vec{r}_{cm} = \frac{\sum m_i\vec{r}_i}{M}$ COM of a system of particles; M is the total mass

$\vec{r}_{cm} = \frac{1}{M}\int \vec{r}\,dm$ COM of a continuous rigid body

$\vec{v}_{cm} = \frac{\sum m_i\vec{v}_i}{M}$ Velocity of the COM; total momentum equals $M\vec{v}_{cm}$

$M\vec{a}_{cm} = \vec{F}_{ext}$ Only the net external force accelerates the COM

NEET tip: Expect COM of composite or cut-out bodies (treat the removed part as negative mass) and questions where the COM stays at rest, such as a person walking on a boat.

Basic concepts of rotational motion

A rigid body is one in which the distance between any two particles does not change. Its motion can be pure translation, pure rotation about a fixed axis, or a combination of the two, as in rolling. In rotation about a fixed axis, every particle moves in a circle in a plane perpendicular to the axis, with its centre on the axis. All particles share the same angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration, but their linear speeds grow with distance from the axis. Angular velocity is a vector along the axis, with direction given by the right-hand rule. For constant angular acceleration, the rotational kinematic equations have the same form as the linear ones.

  • In fixed-axis rotation $\theta$, $\omega$ and $\alpha$ are the same for every particle; $v$ is proportional to $r$
  • The direction of $\vec{\omega}$ follows the right-hand thumb rule, along the axis
  • Tangential acceleration $a_t = \alpha r$ and centripetal acceleration $a_c = \omega^2 r$ act at right angles
  • Net acceleration of a particle is $\sqrt{a_t^2 + a_c^2}$
  • Rolling is translation of the COM combined with rotation about the COM
  • Units: rad, rad/s and rad/s²; 1 rev = $2\pi$ rad

$\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt},\ \alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt}$ Definitions of angular velocity and angular acceleration

$\vec{v} = \vec{\omega}\times\vec{r},\ v = \omega r$ Linear velocity of a particle at distance r from the axis

$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$ Rotational kinematics at constant $\alpha$

$\theta = \omega_0 t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$ Angular displacement at constant $\alpha$

$\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$ Time-independent relation at constant $\alpha$

NEET tip: Typical questions ask for revolutions completed while a wheel decelerates uniformly, or for the net acceleration of a point on a wheel that is speeding up.

Moment of a force and torque

Torque, or moment of a force, is the turning effect of a force about a point or axis. It is the cross product of the position vector (from the reference point to the point of application) and the force. Its magnitude equals the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the reference point to the line of action. A force whose line of action passes through the reference point produces zero torque. Torque is an axial vector, perpendicular to the plane of $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$, and is conventionally positive for anticlockwise turning. A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, non-collinear forces. It produces pure rotation, and its torque is the same about every point.

  • Torque depends on the chosen reference point, except for a couple
  • SI unit is N m; dimensions are $[ML^2T^{-2}]$, the same as work, but torque is a vector
  • Torque is maximum when $\theta = 90^\circ$ and zero when the force is parallel to $\vec{r}$
  • A couple has zero net force, so it causes no translation
  • Gravity produces no torque about the centre of gravity

$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$ Torque of force F about a point

$\tau = rF\sin\theta = F\,r_{\perp}$ Magnitude; $r_{\perp}$ is the perpendicular distance (moment arm)

$\tau_{couple} = F\,d$ Torque of a couple; d is the perpendicular distance between the two forces

NEET tip: Vector cross-product torque calculations, such as finding $\vec{r}\times\vec{F}$ with given unit vectors, are very common.

Angular momentum, its conservation and applications

The angular momentum of a particle about a point is the moment of its linear momentum. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the component along the axis is $L = I\omega$. Net external torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum. If the net external torque is zero, the total angular momentum stays constant. Applications include a skater or diver pulling in the arms (I decreases, so $\omega$ increases), Kepler's second law (constant areal velocity under a central force) and a person on a rotating stool. A particle moving uniformly in a straight line has constant angular momentum about any point. For a rotating body whose centre of mass is at rest, total linear momentum is zero, so the angular momentum is the same about every point.

  • Angular momentum is conserved when $\tau_{ext} = 0$, even if internal forces change I
  • When I changes at constant L, the rotational kinetic energy $\frac{L^2}{2I}$ changes; it increases when I decreases, because internal forces do work, and decreases when I increases. Kinetic energy is not conserved, but total energy still is
  • A central force produces zero torque about the centre, so L is conserved and areal velocity is constant
  • For straight-line uniform motion, $L = mvd$, where d is the perpendicular distance of the line from the point
  • If the total linear momentum of the body is zero (COM at rest), L is independent of the reference point
  • Total angular momentum is L about the COM plus $\vec{r}_{cm}\times M\vec{v}_{cm}$

$\vec{L} = \vec{r}\times\vec{p}$, $L = mvr\sin\theta$ Angular momentum of a particle

$L = I\omega$ Angular momentum of a rigid body about its fixed rotation axis

$\vec{\tau}_{ext} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}$ Rotational form of Newton's second law

$I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$ Conservation of angular momentum when external torque is zero

$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{L}{2m}$ Areal velocity of a planet; constant because L is conserved

$K = \frac{L^2}{2I}$ Rotational KE in terms of angular momentum

NEET tip: NEET often tests a rotating disc that gains mass or a person moving on a turntable (find the new $\omega$ and the fractional KE change), and asks whether L depends on the reference point.

Moment of inertia and radius of gyration

Moment of inertia (I) is the rotational counterpart of mass. It measures how strongly a body resists changes in its rotational motion about a given axis. It depends on the total mass, on how that mass is distributed relative to the axis, and on the position and orientation of the axis. It does not depend on angular velocity. Mass placed farther from the axis contributes more, which is why flywheels carry most of their mass on the rim. The radius of gyration K is the distance from the axis at which the whole mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia. K is a property of both the body and the axis.

  • SI unit is kg m²; dimensions are $[ML^2]$
  • I is not a fixed property of a body; it changes with the axis
  • For a given mass, the farther the mass lies from the axis, the larger I is
  • Flywheels have mass concentrated at the rim to give large I and smooth rotation
  • K is the root-mean-square distance of the mass elements from the axis
  • For a solid sphere about a diameter, $K = \sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}R$; for a ring about its axis, $K = R$

$I = \sum m_i r_i^2$ MOI of discrete particles; $r_i$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis

$I = \int r^2\,dm$ MOI of a continuous body

$I = MK^2,\ K = \sqrt{\frac{I}{M}}$ Radius of gyration

NEET tip: Questions compare I or K for bodies of the same mass and radius, or ask for the MOI of point masses at the corners of a polygon.

Moments of inertia of simple geometrical objects

These standard results must be at your fingertips. For a ring, all the mass is at distance R from its central axis, so $I = MR^2$. A disc has mass spread from the centre to R, so $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$. A hollow cylinder behaves like a ring and a solid cylinder like a disc about the central axis, because length along the axis does not matter. A thin spherical shell has $\frac{2}{3}MR^2$ and a solid sphere $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$. A thin rod has $\frac{ML^2}{12}$ about a perpendicular axis through its centre and $\frac{ML^2}{3}$ about one end. For the same M and R, the order is ring = hollow cylinder > spherical shell > disc = solid cylinder > solid sphere.

  • Ring about its axis: $MR^2$; about a diameter: $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$
  • Disc about its axis: $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$; about a diameter: $\frac{1}{4}MR^2$
  • Thin rod: $\frac{ML^2}{12}$ about the centre and $\frac{ML^2}{3}$ about an end, both for perpendicular axes
  • Solid sphere: $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$; hollow sphere: $\frac{2}{3}MR^2$ (about a diameter)
  • Solid cylinder: $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$; hollow thin cylinder: $MR^2$ (about the central axis)
  • Rectangular plate about a perpendicular axis through the centre: $\frac{M(a^2+b^2)}{12}$
  • Solid cylinder about a perpendicular axis through its centre: $M\left(\frac{R^2}{4}+\frac{L^2}{12}\right)$

$I_{ring} = MR^2,\ I_{disc} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$ About the central axis perpendicular to the plane

$I_{rod,c} = \frac{ML^2}{12},\ I_{rod,end} = \frac{ML^2}{3}$ Thin rod, axis perpendicular to its length

$I_{solid\,sphere} = \frac{2}{5}MR^2,\ I_{shell} = \frac{2}{3}MR^2$ About a diameter

$I_{plate} = \frac{M(a^2+b^2)}{12}$ Rectangular lamina with sides a and b, axis perpendicular through the centre

NEET tip: Direct recall questions, ratio problems such as a solid sphere against a hollow sphere of the same mass and radius, and bodies melted or recast into a new shape at the same density are all common.

Parallel and perpendicular axes theorems and their applications

The parallel axis theorem applies to any body. The MOI about an axis equals the MOI about a parallel axis through the COM plus $Md^2$, where d is the distance between the two axes. One of the two axes must pass through the COM. It follows that I about a centroidal axis is the minimum among all parallel axes. The perpendicular axis theorem applies only to planar (laminar) bodies. The MOI about an axis perpendicular to the plane equals the sum of the MOIs about two mutually perpendicular axes lying in the plane and meeting at the same point. In composite systems, such as spheres joined together, apply the parallel axis theorem to each part separately and then add.

  • The parallel axis theorem requires one axis through the COM; never shift directly between two non-COM axes
  • The perpendicular axis theorem is valid only for laminae, never for spheres or cylinders
  • Ring about a tangent in its plane: $\frac{3}{2}MR^2$; about a tangent perpendicular to its plane: $2MR^2$
  • Disc about a tangent in its plane: $\frac{5}{4}MR^2$; about a tangent perpendicular to its plane: $\frac{3}{2}MR^2$
  • Solid sphere about a tangent: $\frac{7}{5}MR^2$; hollow sphere about a tangent: $\frac{5}{3}MR^2$
  • Square plate: the MOI about any in-plane axis through the centre is $\frac{Ma^2}{12}$
  • For a composite body, $I_{total} = \sum (I_{cm,i} + m_i d_i^2)$

$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$ Parallel axis theorem; d is the distance between the COM axis and the parallel axis

$I_z = I_x + I_y$ Perpendicular axis theorem for a planar body; x and y lie in the plane, z is perpendicular

$I_2 - I_1 = M(d_2^2 - d_1^2)$ Relating two parallel axes, both measured from the COM

NEET tip: NEET favours composite bodies, such as joined spheres, rods forming a frame, or a disc with a hole, where the parallel axis theorem is applied to each part separately.

Equilibrium of rigid bodies

A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium when it has neither linear nor angular acceleration. Translational equilibrium requires the vector sum of external forces to be zero. Rotational equilibrium requires the vector sum of external torques to be zero. Once the net force is zero, the net torque is zero about every point if it is zero about any one point, so choose the point that eliminates the most unknown forces. A body may be in translational equilibrium but not rotational, as under a couple, or the reverse. The principle of moments for a lever states that load × load arm = effort × effort arm. Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load to effort. Ladder, beam and see-saw problems use both conditions.

  • Conditions for equilibrium: $\sum\vec{F} = 0$ and $\sum\vec{\tau} = 0$
  • Take torques about the point where unknown forces act to eliminate them
  • A couple gives rotational non-equilibrium with translational equilibrium
  • In a uniform field, the weight of a body acts at its centre of gravity (= COM)
  • A body suspended from a point comes to rest with its centre of gravity vertically below that point
  • Mechanical advantage = effort arm / load arm; it exceeds 1 when the effort arm is longer

$\sum\vec{F}_{ext} = 0$ Translational equilibrium

$\sum\vec{\tau}_{ext} = 0$ Rotational equilibrium about any point

$F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2$ Principle of moments for a lever

$M.A. = \frac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}} = \frac{d_{effort}}{d_{load}}$ Mechanical advantage of a lever

NEET tip: Expect a loaded beam on two supports (find the reactions), a balanced metre rule with masses, or a ladder against a wall.

Rigid body rotation and equations of rotational motion

For rotation about a fixed axis, net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration ($\tau = I\alpha$), the analogue of $F = ma$. Rotational KE is $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. The work done by a torque is $\int\tau\,d\theta$ and power is $\tau\omega$. The work-energy theorem gives the change in rotational KE. In rolling without slipping, $v_{cm} = \omega R$. The contact point is momentarily at rest and the top point moves at $2v_{cm}$. Total KE is $\frac{1}{2}mv^2(1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2})$. Down an incline, a smaller $\frac{K^2}{R^2}$ means larger acceleration and a quicker descent. The solid sphere therefore wins, followed by the disc and then the ring. In pure rolling, static friction does no work, so mechanical energy is conserved.

  • $\frac{K^2}{R^2}$ values: ring 1, disc or solid cylinder $\frac{1}{2}$, hollow sphere $\frac{2}{3}$, solid sphere $\frac{2}{5}$
  • Fraction of KE that is rotational in rolling: $\frac{K^2/R^2}{1+K^2/R^2}$; for a disc this is $\frac{1}{3}$
  • In pure rolling the contact point has zero velocity, the centre has $v$ and the top has $2v$
  • On a smooth (frictionless) incline there is no rolling, so all bodies slide with $g\sin\theta$
  • Static friction is needed for rolling on an incline, but it does no work
  • For a mass hanging from a rope wound on a pulley, $a = \frac{mg}{m + I/R^2}$

$\tau = I\alpha$ Equation of rotational motion about a fixed axis

$K_{rot} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ Rotational kinetic energy

$W = \int\tau\,d\theta,\ P = \tau\omega$ Work and power in rotation

$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1+\frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)$ Total KE in rolling without slipping

$a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1+K^2/R^2}$ Acceleration of a body rolling down an incline

$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+K^2/R^2}}$ Speed at the bottom after rolling down a height h

NEET tip: Ranking bodies by time taken or speed at the bottom of an incline, the ratio of rotational to total KE, and $\tau = I\alpha$ with a falling mass on a pulley are high-frequency questions.

Comparison of linear and rotational motions

Rotational motion about a fixed axis mirrors linear motion term by term, which makes rotational formulas easy to recall. Displacement x corresponds to $\theta$, velocity v to $\omega$, and acceleration a to $\alpha$. Mass m corresponds to moment of inertia I, force F to torque $\tau$, and linear momentum p to angular momentum L. Newton's second law $F = ma$ becomes $\tau = I\alpha$, and $F = \frac{dp}{dt}$ becomes $\tau = \frac{dL}{dt}$. Kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ becomes $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$, work $\int F dx$ becomes $\int\tau d\theta$, and power $Fv$ becomes $\tau\omega$. Conservation of linear momentum when the net force is zero corresponds to conservation of angular momentum when the net torque is zero. One key difference is that mass is intrinsic and constant, whereas I depends on the choice of axis.

  • x, v, a, m, F, p correspond to $\theta$, $\omega$, $\alpha$, I, $\tau$, L
  • The kinematic equations have identical form
  • $KE = \frac{p^2}{2m}$ corresponds to $KE = \frac{L^2}{2I}$
  • Impulse $\int F dt = \Delta p$ corresponds to angular impulse $\int\tau dt = \Delta L$
  • Mass is the same for every axis, but I varies with the axis

$F = ma \leftrightarrow \tau = I\alpha$ Second law analogues

$p = mv \leftrightarrow L = I\omega$ Momentum analogues

$P = Fv \leftrightarrow P = \tau\omega$ Power analogues

$\int\tau\,dt = \Delta L$ Angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum

NEET tip: Usually tested indirectly through analogy-based statements or by converting a linear problem into its rotational counterpart.

Formula sheet

$\vec{r}_{cm} = \frac{\sum m_i\vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}$ Centre of mass; $m_i$ are the masses and $\vec{r}_i$ their position vectors

$M\vec{a}_{cm} = \vec{F}_{ext}$ Motion of the COM; M is the total mass and $\vec{F}_{ext}$ the net external force

$v = \omega r,\ a_t = \alpha r,\ a_c = \omega^2 r$ Linear-angular relations; r is the distance from the axis

$\omega = \omega_0+\alpha t,\ \theta = \omega_0 t+\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2,\ \omega^2 = \omega_0^2+2\alpha\theta$ Rotational kinematics at constant angular acceleration $\alpha$

$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F},\ \tau = rF\sin\theta$ Torque; $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$

$\vec{L} = \vec{r}\times\vec{p},\ L = I\omega$ Angular momentum of a particle; of a rigid body about its fixed axis

$\vec{\tau}_{ext} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}$ Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum

$I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$ Conservation of angular momentum when $\tau_{ext} = 0$

$I = \sum m_i r_i^2 = \int r^2 dm$ Moment of inertia; r is the perpendicular distance from the axis

$K = \sqrt{\frac{I}{M}}$ Radius of gyration; M is the total mass

$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$ Parallel axis theorem; d is the distance from the parallel axis through the COM

$I_z = I_x + I_y$ Perpendicular axis theorem, valid for planar bodies only

$I_{ring} = MR^2,\ I_{disc} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$ About the central axis perpendicular to the plane; R is the radius

$I_{rod} = \frac{ML^2}{12}$ (centre), $\frac{ML^2}{3}$ (end) Thin rod of length L, axis perpendicular to the rod

$I_{solid\,sphere} = \frac{2}{5}MR^2,\ I_{hollow\,sphere} = \frac{2}{3}MR^2$ About a diameter

$\tau = I\alpha$ Rotational form of Newton's second law

$K_{rot} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{L^2}{2I}$ Rotational kinetic energy

$W = \int\tau\,d\theta,\ P = \tau\omega$ Work done by a torque and rotational power

$K_{rolling} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1+\frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)$ KE of a body rolling without slipping; v is the COM speed

$a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1+K^2/R^2}$ Acceleration rolling down an incline of angle $\theta$

$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+K^2/R^2}}$ Speed after rolling down a vertical height h

$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{L}{2m}$ Areal velocity under a central force; m is the mass of the orbiting body

$\sum\vec{F} = 0,\ \sum\vec{\tau} = 0$ Conditions for equilibrium of a rigid body

Common traps

  • Applying the parallel axis theorem between two axes that do not pass through the COM. Always go through $I_{cm}$ first.
  • Using the perpendicular axis theorem for 3D bodies such as spheres or cylinders. It holds only for planar laminae.
  • Assuming kinetic energy is conserved when a skater pulls in the arms. Angular momentum is conserved, but KE increases because work is done by internal forces.
  • Thinking angular momentum always depends on the reference point. If the body's total linear momentum is zero, as for a disc rotating about its fixed centre, L is the same about every point.
  • Assuming heavier bodies roll down faster. The time depends only on $\frac{K^2}{R^2}$, not on mass or radius.
  • Measuring r in $I = \sum mr^2$ from the origin instead of as the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation.
  • Believing the COM must lie inside the material. For a ring or a hollow sphere it lies in empty space.
  • Assuming friction does work in pure rolling. Static friction acts at the instantaneously stationary contact point, so it does no work.

Quick revision

  • The COM divides the line between two masses in the inverse ratio of the masses, and only external forces move it.
  • In fixed-axis rotation all particles share the same $\omega$ and $\alpha$, while $v = \omega r$ varies.
  • Torque is $\vec{r}\times\vec{F}$, equal to force times perpendicular distance; a couple's torque is the same about every point.
  • $\tau = \frac{dL}{dt}$; if $\tau_{ext} = 0$ then $I\omega$ is constant.
  • I depends on mass distribution and axis; $K = \sqrt{I/M}$.
  • Ring $MR^2$, disc $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$, rod $\frac{ML^2}{12}$ or $\frac{ML^2}{3}$, solid sphere $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$, hollow sphere $\frac{2}{3}MR^2$.
  • Parallel axis: $I = I_{cm}+Md^2$. Perpendicular axis: $I_z = I_x+I_y$, for laminae only.
  • Tangent axes: ring $\frac{3}{2}MR^2$ (in plane) and $2MR^2$ (perpendicular); disc $\frac{5}{4}MR^2$ and $\frac{3}{2}MR^2$; solid sphere $\frac{7}{5}MR^2$.
  • Equilibrium requires both net force and net torque to be zero; take torques about the unknown force.
  • Rolling: $v = \omega R$, KE $= \frac{1}{2}mv^2(1+K^2/R^2)$, and the solid sphere reaches the bottom first.
  • Analogues: m to I, F to $\tau$, p to L, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ to $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$, Fv to $\tau\omega$.

Physics · Unit 6: Gravitation

Gravitation explains how every mass attracts every other mass and uses this one law to describe falling bodies, planetary orbits and artificial satellites. In NEET this unit appears almost every year, usually as short ratio or proportionality questions on $g$, escape speed, orbital speed, time period and energy. These can be solved in seconds if the scaling relations are clear.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q13, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q14

Universal law of gravitation

Newton's universal law of gravitation states that every point mass attracts every other point mass. The force acts along the line joining them. It is directly proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. $G$ is a universal constant, unlike $g$, which varies from place to place. Gravitational force is always attractive and is a central force. It is conservative, so work done by it is path independent. It does not depend on the medium between the masses. For several masses, the net force is the vector sum of individual forces (superposition principle). A uniform spherical shell or solid sphere attracts an external point mass as if all its mass were concentrated at its centre. A uniform shell exerts zero net force on a mass placed anywhere inside it. Gravity is the weakest of the fundamental forces but dominates at astronomical scales.

  • $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}$, dimensions $[M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$
  • Force is always attractive, central and conservative
  • Forces between two bodies are equal and opposite (action-reaction pair)
  • Net force from many masses is found by vector addition (superposition)
  • A uniform sphere acts like a point mass at its centre for external points
  • Net gravitational force inside a uniform spherical shell is zero
  • Force is independent of the intervening medium

$F = \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$ Magnitude of gravitational force between point masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ separated by distance $r$

$\vec{F}_{12} = -\frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}\hat{r}_{12}$ Vector form of the force on $m_2$ due to $m_1$; the minus sign shows attraction, with $\hat{r}_{12}$ the unit vector from $m_1$ to $m_2$

NEET tip: Expect superposition questions (net force on a mass at the centre or vertex of a symmetric arrangement) and questions on the dimensions or nature of $G$.

Acceleration due to gravity and its variation with altitude and depth

Acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface is $g = GM/R^2$. This value is independent of the mass of the falling body. Writing $M = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho$ gives $g = \frac{4}{3}\pi G \rho R$. Above the surface, $g$ falls off as the inverse square of the distance from the centre. For small heights ($h \ll R$) this reduces to $g(1 - 2h/R)$. Below the surface, only the mass inside radius $(R-d)$ attracts. This makes $g$ decrease linearly with depth until it becomes zero at the centre. So $g$ is maximum at the surface and decreases on going either up or down. For small $h$, going up by $h$ reduces $g$ about twice as much as going down by the same $h$.

  • $g$ does not depend on the mass of the falling body
  • $g$ is maximum at the Earth's surface
  • Above the surface, $g \propto 1/r^2$; below the surface, $g \propto r$ (distance from centre)
  • At the centre of the Earth, $g = 0$
  • For small heights, the decrease in $g$ at height $h$ equals the decrease at depth $d = 2h$
  • Weight $mg$ changes with location, but mass does not

$g = \frac{GM}{R^2} = \frac{4}{3}\pi G \rho R$ Acceleration due to gravity at the surface of a planet of mass $M$, radius $R$ and density $\rho$

$g_h = \frac{g}{(1 + h/R)^2} = \frac{gR^2}{(R+h)^2}$ Exact value at height $h$ above the surface

$g_h \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$ Approximate value at height $h$, valid only for $h \ll R$

$g_d = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$ Value at depth $d$; exact for a uniform Earth

NEET tip: NEET asks for the height or depth at which $g$ becomes a given fraction of its surface value, or for ratios of $g$ on planets with different $M$, $R$ or $\rho$.

Kepler's laws of planetary motion

Kepler's first law (law of orbits) states that every planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus. The second law (law of areas) states that the line joining the Sun and the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. This is a consequence of conservation of angular momentum, because gravity is a central force. As a result, a planet moves fastest at perihelion (nearest point) and slowest at aphelion (farthest point). The third law (law of periods) states that the square of the time period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of the orbit. For a circular orbit, the semi-major axis is simply the radius. This law follows from equating the gravitational force to the required centripetal force, and it is the basis of most period-radius ratio questions.

  • Law of orbits: elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus
  • Law of areas: areal velocity is constant, which follows from conservation of angular momentum
  • Speed is maximum at perihelion and minimum at aphelion
  • Law of periods: $T^2 \propto a^3$, so $T \propto R^{3/2}$ for circular orbits
  • The constant in $T^2/a^3$ depends only on the mass of the central body
  • Semi-major axis $a = \frac{r_{min} + r_{max}}{2}$

$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{L}{2m} = \text{constant}$ Areal velocity, where $L$ is the angular momentum of a planet of mass $m$

$v_p r_p = v_a r_a$ Angular momentum conservation between perihelion ($p$) and aphelion ($a$)

$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} a^3$ Kepler's third law; $M$ is the mass of the central body and $a$ is the semi-major axis

$\frac{T_1^2}{T_2^2} = \frac{a_1^3}{a_2^3}$ Ratio form used to compare two planets orbiting the same star

NEET tip: The favourite question is $T \propto R^{3/2}$ in ratio form. Also expect speed ratios at perihelion and aphelion using $v_p r_p = v_a r_a$.

Gravitational potential energy and gravitational potential

Gravitational potential energy of two masses is the work done in bringing them from infinity to a separation $r$. Zero potential energy is taken at infinity, so $U = -GMm/r$. The value is negative because the force is attractive and the system is bound. Gravitational potential at a point is the potential energy per unit mass, $V = -GM/r$. Potential is a scalar, so contributions from several masses simply add algebraically. Near the surface, for $h \ll R$, the change in potential energy reduces to $mgh$. Inside a uniform shell, the potential is constant and equals its surface value. For a uniform solid sphere, the potential is most negative at the centre. The gravitational field is the negative gradient of the potential.

  • $U$ and $V$ are zero at infinity and negative everywhere else
  • Potential is a scalar and adds algebraically; the field is a vector
  • $\Delta U = mgh$ is valid only when $h \ll R$
  • Inside a uniform shell, $V$ is constant ($-GM/R$) and the field is zero
  • At the centre of a uniform solid sphere, $V = -\frac{3GM}{2R}$, which is 1.5 times the surface value
  • SI unit of potential is $J\,kg^{-1}$

$U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ Gravitational potential energy of masses $M$ and $m$ separated by $r$

$V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ Gravitational potential at distance $r$ from mass $M$ (for $r \geq R$ in the case of a sphere)

$\Delta U = \frac{mgh}{1 + h/R}$ Exact work needed to raise mass $m$ from the surface to height $h$

$V_{in} = -\frac{GM(3R^2 - r^2)}{2R^3}$ Potential inside a uniform solid sphere at distance $r < R$ from the centre

$E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ Gravitational field intensity obtained from potential

NEET tip: NEET tests work done in lifting a body to height $h = R$ (answer $\frac{1}{2}mgR$) and potential energy of systems of point masses, such as three masses at the vertices of a triangle.

Escape velocity

Escape velocity is the minimum speed with which a body must be projected from a planet's surface so that it never returns. To find it, set the total energy equal to zero: $\frac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - \frac{GMm}{R} = 0$. This gives $v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{2gR}$, which is about 11.2 km/s for Earth. Escape velocity does not depend on the mass of the projected body. It also does not depend on the direction of projection, provided air resistance is neglected. It does depend on the mass, radius and density of the planet. For a fixed mass, $v_e \propto 1/\sqrt{R}$. For fixed density, $v_e \propto R$. The Moon has no atmosphere because its escape velocity (about 2.4 km/s) is comparable to the speeds of gas molecules.

  • On Earth, $v_e \approx 11.2$ km/s
  • Independent of the mass of the body and the angle of projection
  • For a fixed planet mass, $v_e \propto R^{-1/2}$
  • For a fixed planet density, $v_e \propto R$
  • $v_e = \sqrt{2}\,v_o$ for a satellite orbiting close to the surface
  • Low escape velocity explains why the Moon has no atmosphere

$v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}$ Escape velocity from the surface of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$

$v_e = R\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G\rho}{3}}$ Escape velocity in terms of the planet's density $\rho$

$v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R+h}}$ Escape velocity from height $h$ above the surface

NEET tip: Expect ratio questions in which planet mass, radius or density changes. Check which quantity is held constant before scaling.

Motion of a satellite: orbital velocity, time period and energy

A satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r = R + h$ is held in orbit because gravity supplies the centripetal force. Setting $GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r$ gives the orbital velocity $v_o = \sqrt{GM/r}$, which is independent of the satellite's mass. Near the surface, $v_o = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.9$ km/s and the period is about 84 minutes. The time period follows Kepler's third law: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}$. The kinetic energy of the satellite is $GMm/2r$ and its potential energy is $-GMm/r$. So the total energy is $-GMm/2r$, which is negative, showing a bound system. The energy needed to free the satellite is its binding energy, $+GMm/2r$. A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator with a period of 24 h, moving in the same direction as Earth's rotation, at a height of about 36,000 km. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they and the satellite are in free fall together.

  • $v_o \propto r^{-1/2}$ and $T \propto r^{3/2}$; both are independent of the satellite's mass
  • Total energy $E = -KE$ and $U = 2E$, so $KE : U : E = 1 : -2 : -1$
  • Binding energy $= GMm/2r$
  • Near-Earth satellite: $v_o \approx 7.9$ km/s and $T \approx 84$ min
  • Geostationary satellite: $T = 24$ h, equatorial orbit, height about 36,000 km, used for communication
  • Polar satellites have low orbits passing over the poles and are used for remote sensing and weather
  • Weightlessness in orbit is due to free fall, not to the absence of gravity

$v_o = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R+h}} = \sqrt{\frac{gR^2}{R+h}}$ Orbital velocity at height $h$ above a planet of radius $R$

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(R+h)^3}{GM}}$ Time period of a satellite in a circular orbit

$KE = \frac{GMm}{2r},\ U = -\frac{GMm}{r},\ E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$ Energies of a satellite of mass $m$ in an orbit of radius $r$

$W = \frac{GMm}{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right)$ Energy needed to shift a satellite from orbit radius $r_1$ to a larger radius $r_2$

NEET tip: NEET asks ratios of $v_o$, $T$ or energies for orbits of different radii, and the $KE : PE : E$ relationship.

Formula sheet

$F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ Gravitational force; $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}$, $r$ is the separation

$g = \frac{GM}{R^2}$ Surface gravity of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$

$g = \frac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$ Surface gravity in terms of the planet's density $\rho$

$g_h = \frac{gR^2}{(R+h)^2}$ Gravity at height $h$ (exact)

$g_h \approx g(1 - 2h/R)$ Gravity at height $h$ for $h \ll R$

$g_d = g(1 - d/R)$ Gravity at depth $d$ below the surface

$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{L}{2m}$ Constant areal velocity (Kepler's second law); $L$ is angular momentum

$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{GM}$ Kepler's third law; $a$ is the semi-major axis, $M$ the central mass

$v_p r_p = v_a r_a$ Speeds and distances at perihelion and aphelion

$U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ Gravitational potential energy, zero at infinity

$V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ Gravitational potential (potential energy per unit mass)

$E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ Gravitational field from potential

$\Delta U = \frac{mgh}{1+h/R}$ Work done to lift mass $m$ to height $h$; reduces to $mgh$ for $h \ll R$

$V_{centre} = -\frac{3GM}{2R}$ Potential at the centre of a uniform solid sphere

$v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}$ Escape velocity from the surface (11.2 km/s for Earth)

$v_e = R\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G\rho}{3}}$ Escape velocity in terms of density $\rho$

$v_o = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ Orbital velocity at orbit radius $r = R + h$

$v_o = \sqrt{gR}$ Orbital velocity of a satellite near the surface (about 7.9 km/s)

$v_e = \sqrt{2}\,v_o$ Relation between escape velocity and near-surface orbital velocity

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ Time period of a satellite in an orbit of radius $r$

$E_{total} = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$ Total energy of an orbiting satellite; $KE = GMm/2r$, $U = -GMm/r$

$BE = \frac{GMm}{2r}$ Binding energy, the minimum energy needed to free the satellite from orbit

Common traps

  • Using $r = h$ instead of $r = R + h$ in orbital formulas. All distances are measured from the centre of the planet.
  • Applying $g(1 - 2h/R)$ when $h$ is comparable to $R$. Use the exact form $gR^2/(R+h)^2$ when $h$ is not small.
  • Assuming escape velocity depends on the mass or launch direction of the body. It depends only on the planet's $M$ and $R$.
  • Scaling escape velocity without checking what is held constant. At constant mass, $v_e \propto R^{-1/2}$; at constant density, $v_e \propto R$.
  • Thinking $g$ increases inside the Earth. It decreases linearly with depth and becomes zero at the centre.
  • Taking satellite total energy as positive or equal to $KE$. Total energy $E = -KE$ and $U = 2E$, so a higher orbit has more (less negative) total energy but lower $KE$.
  • Believing astronauts are weightless because there is no gravity in orbit. Gravity there is substantial; they appear weightless because they are in free fall.
  • Confusing $G$ with $g$. $G$ is a universal constant, while $g$ varies with height, depth and the planet considered.

Quick revision

  • $F \propto m_1m_2/r^2$: always attractive, central and conservative; $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ SI units.
  • $g = GM/R^2 = \frac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$; it is maximum at the surface and zero at the centre.
  • Height: $g_h \approx g(1 - 2h/R)$. Depth: $g_d = g(1 - d/R)$. For small $h$, the effect of height $h$ equals that of depth $2h$.
  • Kepler's laws: elliptical orbits, equal areas in equal times (angular momentum conservation), and $T^2 \propto a^3$.
  • $T \propto R^{3/2}$ and $v_o \propto R^{-1/2}$ for circular orbits about the same central mass.
  • $U = -GMm/r$ and $V = -GM/r$; both are zero at infinity and negative elsewhere.
  • Work done to lift a body to height $h = R$ is $\frac{1}{2}mgR$.
  • $v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{2gR} \approx 11.2$ km/s, independent of the body's mass and direction of projection.
  • $v_o = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.9$ km/s near Earth, and $v_e = \sqrt{2}\,v_o$.
  • Satellite energies: $KE : U : E = 1 : -2 : -1$; binding energy is $GMm/2r$.
  • Geostationary satellite: $T = 24$ h, equatorial, height about 36,000 km. Polar satellites are low-orbit and pass over the poles.
  • Inside a uniform shell, the field is zero and the potential is constant, equal to $-GM/R$.

Physics · Unit 7: Properties of Solids and Liquids

This unit covers the mechanical and thermal properties of matter. It includes elasticity of solids, fluid statics and dynamics (pressure, viscosity, Bernoulli's principle), surface tension, and thermal phenomena such as expansion, calorimetry, latent heat and heat transfer. NEET asks 2-4 questions from this unit almost every year, mostly formula-based numericals and graph interpretation, so exact formulas and limiting cases matter.

PYQs (3): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q10, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q12, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q24

Elastic behaviour, stress-strain relationship and Hooke's law

Elasticity is the property of a body to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed. Plasticity is the tendency to retain the deformation. When a force acts, internal restoring forces develop. The restoring force per unit area is called stress, and the fractional change in dimension is called strain. Hooke's law states that, for small deformations (up to the proportional limit), stress is directly proportional to strain. On the stress-strain curve, the initial straight portion obeys Hooke's law up to the proportional limit. Beyond the yield point the material deforms plastically. The maximum stress is the ultimate tensile strength, and beyond it the material reaches the fracture point. Ductile materials, such as metals, have a large plastic region. Brittle materials fracture soon after the elastic limit. Elastomers, such as rubber or the aorta, stretch a lot without obeying Hooke's law.

  • Stress = restoring force / area; SI unit $N\,m^{-2}$ (Pa), same unit as pressure
  • Strain is dimensionless; it can be longitudinal, volumetric or shear
  • Three types of stress: tensile/compressive (longitudinal), shearing (tangential) and hydraulic (volume)
  • Hooke's law is valid only within the proportional limit
  • Large gap between elastic limit and fracture point means ductile; small gap means brittle
  • Rubber has no well-defined plastic region; its stress-strain curve is non-linear

$\text{Stress} = \frac{F}{A}$ Restoring force per unit area

$\text{Longitudinal strain} = \frac{\Delta L}{L}$ Fractional change in length

$\text{Stress} = E \times \text{Strain}$ Hooke's law; $E$ is the modulus of elasticity

NEET tip: NEET asks you to identify regions on the stress-strain curve and to judge which material is ductile or brittle from given graphs.

Young's modulus, bulk modulus and modulus of rigidity

A modulus of elasticity is the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit. Young's modulus applies to change in length, bulk modulus to change in volume, and modulus of rigidity (shear modulus) to change in shape. A larger modulus means the material is more elastic, that is, harder to deform. Steel is therefore more elastic than rubber. Solids possess all three moduli. Liquids and gases have only a bulk modulus. The reciprocal of the bulk modulus is the compressibility. Poisson's ratio is lateral strain divided by longitudinal strain. Energy is stored in a stretched wire, and the energy per unit volume equals half of stress times strain. For a wire under its own weight, $\Delta L = \rho g L^2/(2Y)$, so $\Delta L \propto L^2$ and is independent of radius. Under an external load $F$, $\Delta L \propto L/r^2$. A given load produces more extension in a thinner, longer wire.

  • Moduli have the same unit as stress, Pa
  • Young's modulus of a material is independent of the wire's length and radius
  • For most materials $G \approx Y/3$
  • Bulk modulus: solids > liquids > gases; gases are the most compressible
  • The negative sign in $B$ appears because volume decreases when pressure increases
  • Poisson's ratio is dimensionless; its theoretical range is $-1$ to $0.5$
  • If the same wire is stretched, $\Delta L \propto L^2$ when volume is constant

$Y = \frac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}$ Young's modulus from load $F$, original length $L$, area $A$ and extension $\Delta L$

$B = -\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V}$ Bulk modulus; compressibility $k = 1/B$

$G = \frac{F/A}{\theta}$ Modulus of rigidity; $\theta = \Delta x/L$ is the shear strain

$u = \frac{1}{2}\,\text{stress}\times\text{strain} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{(\text{stress})^2}{Y}$ Elastic potential energy per unit volume

$U = \frac{1}{2}F\,\Delta L$ Total elastic energy stored in a stretched wire

NEET tip: Expect ratio problems comparing extensions of wires of different radius and length under the same load, and energy-stored questions.

Pressure due to a fluid column; Pascal's law and its applications

Pressure is the normal force per unit area. It is a scalar quantity. In a fluid at rest, the pressure at depth $h$ below the free surface is $P = P_a + \rho g h$. It depends only on depth, not on the shape of the vessel; this is the hydrostatic paradox. Gauge pressure, $P - P_a = \rho g h$, is what a pressure gauge or manometer reads. Atmospheric pressure is measured with a mercury barometer and equals 76 cm of Hg, about $1.013\times10^5$ Pa. Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the container walls. Applications include the hydraulic lift, hydraulic press and hydraulic brakes. All of these multiply force: a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston. Energy is conserved, so the larger piston moves through a smaller distance.

  • Pressure at the same horizontal level in a continuous static fluid is the same
  • Pressure depends on depth only, not on vessel shape or base area
  • $1\,atm = 1.013\times10^5\,Pa$; $1\,bar = 10^5\,Pa$; $1\,torr = 1\,mm$ of Hg
  • A hydraulic machine multiplies force but not work
  • Open-tube manometer: the difference in levels gives gauge pressure

$P = P_a + \rho g h$ Absolute pressure at depth $h$ in a liquid of density $\rho$

$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$ Pascal's law for a hydraulic lift; $F_2 = F_1 A_2/A_1$

$A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2$ Equal volume displaced; the large piston moves less

NEET tip: NEET tests hydraulic lift force ratios and U-tube problems with two immiscible liquids balanced at a common level.

Effect of gravity on fluid pressure

The variation of pressure with depth is entirely a consequence of gravity. Consider a fluid element in equilibrium: the difference in pressure on its top and bottom faces must support its weight, which gives $dP/dh = \rho g$. Hence pressure increases linearly with depth for an incompressible liquid. In the atmosphere, air is compressible, so pressure and density both decrease with altitude, roughly exponentially. If the effective gravity changes, the pressure difference changes too. In a lift accelerating upward, $P = P_a + \rho (g+a) h$. In free fall or in an orbiting spacecraft, the effective $g = 0$, so there is no depth-dependent pressure and no buoyancy. The buoyant force, given by Archimedes' principle, is itself the net upward force from this gravity-induced pressure difference.

  • Without gravity there is no hydrostatic pressure gradient
  • Accelerating upward: $g_{eff} = g + a$; accelerating downward: $g_{eff} = g - a$
  • In a horizontally accelerating container, the free surface tilts at $\tan\theta = a/g$
  • Buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced = $V \rho_{fluid} g$
  • A floating body has the same fraction submerged inside an accelerating lift, because both the weight and the buoyancy scale with $g_{eff}$

$P_2 - P_1 = \rho g (h_2 - h_1)$ Pressure difference between two depths

$P = P_a + \rho (g \pm a) h$ Pressure in a container accelerating vertically up (+) or down (-)

$F_B = V \rho_{fluid} g$ Buoyant force on a submerged volume $V$

NEET tip: NEET asks conceptual questions on pressure or buoyancy in an accelerating lift, in free fall, or in a horizontally accelerated tank.

Viscosity, Stokes' law and terminal velocity

Viscosity is the internal friction between adjacent fluid layers in relative motion. By Newton's law of viscosity, the viscous force is $F = \eta A\, dv/dx$, where $\eta$ is the coefficient of viscosity. The SI unit of $\eta$ is Pa s (poiseuille); the CGS unit is the poise, and 1 Pa s = 10 poise. For a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid, Stokes' law gives the drag $F = 6\pi\eta r v$. A falling sphere accelerates until weight equals buoyancy plus viscous drag; it then moves at a constant terminal velocity. The terminal velocity is proportional to $r^2$ and to $(\sigma - \rho)$. If the sphere's density is less than the fluid's, it rises; an air bubble in water is an example. The viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature, while that of gases increases.

  • Dimensions of $\eta$: $[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]$
  • Terminal velocity $v_t \propto r^2$, so a larger raindrop falls faster
  • $v_t \propto (\sigma - \rho)$; for $\sigma < \rho$ the body moves upward
  • For a fixed radius, a plot of $v_t$ against $\sigma/\rho$ is linear, with zero value at $\sigma/\rho = 1$
  • When $n$ identical drops merge into one big drop, the new terminal velocity is $n^{2/3}$ times the old
  • In the velocity-time graph of a falling sphere, $v$ rises exponentially and saturates at $v_t$

$F = \eta A \frac{dv}{dx}$ Viscous force between layers; $dv/dx$ is the velocity gradient

$F = 6\pi\eta r v$ Stokes' drag on a sphere of radius $r$ moving with speed $v$

$v_t = \frac{2 r^2 (\sigma - \rho) g}{9\eta}$ Terminal velocity; $\sigma$ is the sphere's density, $\rho$ the fluid's density

NEET tip: Very frequent: terminal velocity ratios, merging-drops problems, and graphs of $v_t$ against radius or density ratio.

Streamline and turbulent flow; critical velocity

In streamline (laminar) flow, the velocity of the fluid at any given point does not change with time. Fluid particles follow smooth paths called streamlines, and two streamlines never cross. Beyond a certain speed, called the critical velocity, the flow becomes turbulent: irregular, with eddies, and dissipating energy. The nature of the flow is predicted by the dimensionless Reynolds number $R_e = \rho v D/\eta$. As a rough guide, $R_e < 1000$ gives streamline flow, $R_e > 2000$ gives turbulent flow, and values in between are unsteady. Critical velocity is low for less viscous, denser fluids and wider pipes. For steady incompressible flow, mass conservation gives the equation of continuity, $A v = \text{constant}$. The fluid therefore speeds up where the pipe narrows.

  • Crowded streamlines indicate higher speed
  • Volume flow rate $Q = Av$ is constant along a tube
  • $R_e$ is the ratio of inertial force to viscous force
  • High viscosity favours streamline flow
  • Turbulence is caused by high speed, large diameter and low viscosity

$R_e = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta}$ Reynolds number; $D$ is the pipe diameter

$v_c = \frac{R_e\,\eta}{\rho D}$ Critical velocity for the onset of turbulence

$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ Equation of continuity for an incompressible fluid

NEET tip: Continuity is usually combined with Bernoulli; direct questions ask how critical velocity depends on $\eta$, $\rho$ and $D$.

Bernoulli's principle and its applications

Bernoulli's principle applies the work-energy theorem to steady, incompressible, non-viscous, irrotational flow along a streamline. It states that $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h$ is constant, so the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume is constant. In a horizontal pipe, a higher speed means a lower pressure. Applications include the following. A venturimeter measures flow rate from the pressure difference between the wide and narrow sections. Torricelli's law gives the speed of efflux from a hole at depth $h$ as $\sqrt{2gh}$. Dynamic lift on aircraft wings arises from faster flow above the wing. The Magnus effect explains the swing of a spinning ball. Other examples are atomizers and sprayers, and roofs blown off during storms. Combining Bernoulli with continuity solves most pipe-flow problems.

  • Bernoulli is invalid for viscous or turbulent flow
  • Every term has the dimension of pressure (energy per unit volume)
  • Efflux speed $\sqrt{2gh}$ equals the speed of free fall from height $h$
  • Horizontal range of a jet from a hole at depth $h$ in a tank of liquid height $H$: $R = 2\sqrt{h(H-h)}$, maximum at $h = H/2$
  • Pressure difference in a venturimeter: $\Delta P = \frac{1}{2}\rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2)$

$P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}$ Bernoulli's equation along a streamline

$v = \sqrt{2gh}$ Torricelli's speed of efflux from depth $h$

$Q = A_1 A_2\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta P}{\rho (A_1^2 - A_2^2)}}$ Venturimeter flow rate from pressure difference $\Delta P$ between areas $A_1$ and $A_2$

NEET tip: NEET regularly gives the areas and pressure difference in a horizontal pipe and asks for the flow rate (continuity plus Bernoulli).

Surface energy, surface tension and angle of contact

Molecules on a liquid surface experience a net inward cohesive pull, so the surface behaves like a stretched membrane with extra energy. Surface tension $S$ is the force per unit length acting perpendicular to an imaginary line on the surface. It equals the surface energy per unit area, that is, the work done to increase the surface area isothermally by one unit. A soap film has two surfaces, so the work is $2S\Delta A$. Surface tension decreases with temperature and becomes zero at the critical temperature. Detergents reduce it, while highly soluble impurities such as NaCl increase it. The angle of contact $\theta$ is the angle between the solid surface and the tangent to the liquid surface, measured inside the liquid. If adhesion exceeds cohesion, $\theta$ is acute and the liquid wets the solid, as water does glass. If cohesion dominates, $\theta$ is obtuse, as for mercury on glass.

  • Unit: $N\,m^{-1}$ or $J\,m^{-2}$; dimensions $[MT^{-2}]$
  • Water-glass: $\theta \approx 0^\circ$; mercury-glass: $\theta \approx 140^\circ$
  • Waterproofing agents increase $\theta$; detergents decrease $\theta$ and $S$
  • Liquid drops are spherical because a sphere has minimum surface area for a given volume
  • Surface tension is independent of the area of the surface

$S = \frac{F}{l}$ Surface tension as force per unit length

$W = S\,\Delta A$ Work to increase area of a single surface; use $2S\Delta A$ for a film

NEET tip: NEET checks whether you count two surfaces for a film or bubble, and asks how temperature or impurities affect surface tension.

Excess pressure across a curved surface

Surface tension makes the pressure on the concave side of a curved liquid surface greater than on the convex side. For a spherical liquid drop of radius $R$, which has one surface, the excess pressure inside is $2S/R$. A soap bubble in air has two surfaces, inner and outer, so its excess pressure is $4S/R$. An air bubble inside a liquid has only one liquid-air surface, so its excess pressure is $2S/R$. The pressure inside an air bubble at depth $h$ is $P_a + \rho g h + 2S/R$. Excess pressure is inversely proportional to radius, so smaller bubbles have higher internal pressure. When two bubbles of different sizes are connected, air flows from the smaller bubble into the larger one. For a cylindrical surface the excess pressure is $S/R$.

  • Pressure is always greater on the concave side
  • Drop: $2S/R$; soap bubble: $4S/R$; air bubble in liquid: $2S/R$
  • Smaller bubble means larger excess pressure
  • Two soap bubbles coalescing isothermally in vacuum: $R^2 = R_1^2 + R_2^2$
  • Double bubble interface radius: $r = \frac{r_1 r_2}{r_2 - r_1}$

$\Delta P = \frac{2S}{R}$ Excess pressure inside a drop or an air bubble in a liquid

$\Delta P = \frac{4S}{R}$ Excess pressure inside a soap bubble (two surfaces)

$P_{in} = P_a + \rho g h + \frac{2S}{R}$ Pressure inside an air bubble at depth $h$

NEET tip: Ratio questions on excess pressure for bubbles of different radii, and the drop versus soap bubble distinction, are common.

Applications of surface tension: drops, bubbles and capillary rise

In a narrow capillary tube, a liquid rises (or falls) because of surface tension and the angle of contact. Balancing the upward surface-tension force against the weight of the liquid column gives $h = 2S\cos\theta/(\rho g r)$. Water, with acute $\theta$, rises and forms a concave meniscus. Mercury, with obtuse $\theta$, is depressed and forms a convex meniscus. For a given liquid, $hr$ is constant; this is Jurin's law. If the tube is shorter than $h$, the liquid does not overflow; the meniscus radius increases until $R' h' = Rh$. Splitting one drop into $n$ droplets increases surface area and requires energy. Merging droplets into one drop releases energy, which may appear as heating. Everyday examples include wicks, the rise of sap, towels absorbing water and the action of soaps.

  • Capillary rise $h \propto 1/r$; a narrower tube gives a higher rise
  • In a freely falling lift ($g_{eff} = 0$), the liquid rises to the full length of the tube
  • Rise is greater at lower temperature because $S$ is larger
  • Work done by surface tension in capillary rise is $2\pi r S h$ when $\theta = 0$; half of it is stored as potential energy and half lost as heat
  • One drop of radius $R$ split into $n$ drops: each droplet has radius $r = R n^{-1/3}$

$h = \frac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$ Capillary rise in a tube of radius $r$

$W = 4\pi R^2 S (n^{1/3} - 1)$ Energy needed to split a drop of radius $R$ into $n$ equal droplets

$hR = \text{constant}$ Jurin's law; also used for an insufficient tube length

NEET tip: NEET asks capillary rise ratios, the insufficient-length concept, and energy released or absorbed when drops merge or split.

Heat, temperature and thermal expansion

Temperature measures the hotness of a body and decides the direction of heat flow. Heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference. The temperature scales are related by $\frac{C}{100} = \frac{F - 32}{180} = \frac{K - 273.15}{100}$. Most substances expand on heating. Linear, area and volume expansion follow $\Delta L = \alpha L \Delta T$, $\Delta A = \beta A \Delta T$ and $\Delta V = \gamma V \Delta T$, with $\beta = 2\alpha$ and $\gamma = 3\alpha$ for isotropic solids. For an ideal gas at constant pressure, $\gamma = 1/T$. Water shows anomalous expansion: it contracts when heated from 0 to 4 degrees Celsius and has maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius. This is why lakes freeze from the top while aquatic life survives below. A rod clamped between rigid supports develops thermal stress $Y\alpha\Delta T$ when heated.

  • A hole or cavity expands as if it were made of the surrounding material
  • $-40^\circ C = -40^\circ F$
  • Expansion of a sphere: $\Delta V = 3\alpha \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \Delta T = 4\pi R^3 \alpha \Delta T$
  • Bimetallic strip bends towards the metal with the smaller $\alpha$
  • Density decreases on heating: $\rho' \approx \rho (1 - \gamma \Delta T)$
  • Pendulum clock loses time in summer: $\frac{\Delta T_p}{T_p} = \frac{1}{2}\alpha \Delta \theta$, where $T_p$ is the period and $\Delta\theta$ the temperature rise

$\Delta L = \alpha L \Delta T$ Linear expansion

$\Delta V = \gamma V \Delta T,\ \gamma = 3\alpha,\ \beta = 2\alpha$ Volume and area expansion coefficients related to $\alpha$

$\text{Thermal stress} = Y\alpha\Delta T$ Stress in a rod prevented from expanding

$\frac{C}{5} = \frac{F - 32}{9}$ Celsius-Fahrenheit conversion

NEET tip: NEET favours $\gamma = 3\alpha$ applications (volume change of a sphere or cube), thermal stress, and scale conversions.

Specific heat capacity and calorimetry

Heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of a body by 1 K. Specific heat capacity $c$ is the heat needed per unit mass per kelvin, so $Q = mc\Delta T$. Molar specific heat is the heat needed per mole per kelvin. Water has a very high specific heat, $4186\,J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}$, which is why it is used as a coolant and why it moderates coastal climates. Calorimetry is based on conservation of energy: in an isolated system, heat lost by hot bodies equals heat gained by cold bodies. The water equivalent of a container is the mass of water that would absorb the same heat as the container for the same temperature rise; it equals $mc/c_w$. For gases, $C_p > C_v$, and Mayer's relation gives $C_p - C_v = R$.

  • $1\,cal = 4.186\,J$
  • Specific heat of water is $1\,cal\,g^{-1}\,^\circ C^{-1}$; ice and steam have about half of this value
  • Specific heat is infinite for an isothermal process and zero for an adiabatic process
  • Mixture temperature: $T = \frac{m_1 c_1 T_1 + m_2 c_2 T_2}{m_1 c_1 + m_2 c_2}$ when no phase change occurs
  • Always check whether a phase change happens before using the mixture formula

$Q = mc\Delta T$ Heat for a temperature change without phase change

$Q = nC\Delta T$ Using molar heat capacity $C$ for $n$ moles

$\sum Q_{lost} = \sum Q_{gained}$ Principle of calorimetry

NEET tip: NEET asks for the final temperature of mixtures, including water equivalent, and checks whether some ice remains unmelted.

Change of state and latent heat

During a change of state such as melting, boiling or sublimation, heat is absorbed or released without any change in temperature. This heat changes intermolecular potential energy, not kinetic energy. Latent heat $L$ is the heat per unit mass required for the phase change, so $Q = mL$. For water, the latent heat of fusion is $3.33\times10^5\,J\,kg^{-1}$ (80 cal/g) and the latent heat of vaporisation is $22.6\times10^5\,J\,kg^{-1}$ (540 cal/g). A temperature-time heating curve shows sloped regions, where the slope is inversely proportional to specific heat, and flat plateaus, where the plateau length is proportional to latent heat. Boiling point rises with pressure, as in a pressure cooker. The melting point of ice falls with pressure, which explains regelation. The triple point of water is 273.16 K at 0.006 atm. Dry ice sublimes at ordinary pressure.

  • Temperature remains constant during a phase change
  • A burn from steam at 100 degrees Celsius is worse than from water at 100 degrees Celsius, because of latent heat
  • On the heating curve, plateau length is proportional to $L$ and slope is proportional to $1/c$
  • Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals the external pressure
  • Phase diagram: the fusion curve of water has a negative slope
  • Ice at 0 degrees Celsius cools better than water at 0 degrees Celsius

$Q = mL$ Heat for phase change of mass $m$

$m L_f + m c_w (T - 0) = M c_w (T_0 - T)$ Typical ice-water mixing balance: ice of mass $m$ melts and warms to $T$ while water of mass $M$ cools from $T_0$

NEET tip: Ice-water-steam mixing problems and heating-curve interpretation (finding the ratio of latent heats or specific heats) are classic NEET items.

Heat transfer: conduction, convection and radiation

Heat is transferred in three ways. Conduction is transfer through a medium without bulk motion of matter. The rate of conduction is $H = KA\Delta T/L$, where $K$ is the thermal conductivity. Thermal resistance $R = L/(KA)$ combines like electrical resistance: added directly in series, and as reciprocals in parallel. Convection involves bulk motion of fluid. It may be natural (driven by density differences) or forced; sea breezes and trade winds are examples. Radiation needs no medium and travels as electromagnetic waves. Stefan-Boltzmann law: the power radiated is $e\sigma A T^4$. Wien's law: $\lambda_m T = b$, about $2.9\times10^{-3}\,m\,K$. A perfect blackbody has $e = 1$. Good absorbers are good emitters. Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of cooling is proportional to the excess temperature over the surroundings, for small differences. The greenhouse effect traps infrared radiation.

  • Junction temperature of two slabs in series: equate the heat currents
  • Equivalent conductivity, equal lengths in series: $K = \frac{2K_1K_2}{K_1+K_2}$; equal areas in parallel: $K = \frac{K_1+K_2}{2}$
  • Net radiation loss: $P = e\sigma A (T^4 - T_0^4)$
  • Hotter body: peak wavelength shifts to shorter values
  • Average form of Newton's cooling: $\frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k\left(\frac{T_1+T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$
  • Unit of $K$: $W\,m^{-1}K^{-1}$

$H = \frac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}$ Rate of heat conduction through a slab

$P = e\sigma A T^4$ Stefan-Boltzmann law; $\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}\,W\,m^{-2}K^{-4}$

$\lambda_m T = b$ Wien's displacement law, $b \approx 2.9\times10^{-3}\,m\,K$

$\frac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_0)$ Newton's law of cooling

NEET tip: NEET loves Stefan's $T^4$ ratio problems, Wien's law from graphs, Newton's cooling time calculations and junction temperature of composite slabs.

Formula sheet

$Y = \frac{FL}{A\Delta L}$ Young's modulus; $F$ is load, $L$ length, $A$ area, $\Delta L$ extension

$B = -\frac{V\Delta P}{\Delta V}$ Bulk modulus; compressibility $k = 1/B$

$G = \frac{F}{A\theta}$ Modulus of rigidity; $\theta$ is the shear strain

$u = \frac{1}{2}\,\text{stress}\times\text{strain}$ Elastic energy per unit volume

$P = P_a + \rho g h$ Pressure at depth $h$; $\rho$ is liquid density, $P_a$ atmospheric pressure

$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$ Pascal's law, hydraulic lift

$F_B = V\rho g$ Buoyant force; $V$ is the submerged volume

$F = \eta A \frac{dv}{dx}$ Viscous force; $\eta$ is the coefficient of viscosity

$F = 6\pi\eta r v$ Stokes' law for a sphere of radius $r$

$v_t = \frac{2r^2(\sigma - \rho)g}{9\eta}$ Terminal velocity; $\sigma$ is body density, $\rho$ fluid density

$R_e = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta}$ Reynolds number; $D$ is pipe diameter

$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ Equation of continuity

$P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{const}$ Bernoulli's equation

$v = \sqrt{2gh}$ Torricelli's speed of efflux

$S = \frac{F}{l} = \frac{W}{\Delta A}$ Surface tension, equal to surface energy per unit area

$\Delta P = \frac{2S}{R}$ (drop), $\frac{4S}{R}$ (soap bubble) Excess pressure inside curved surfaces

$h = \frac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$ Capillary rise; $\theta$ is angle of contact, $r$ tube radius

$\Delta L = \alpha L\Delta T,\ \gamma = 3\alpha,\ \beta = 2\alpha$ Thermal expansion coefficients

$Q = mc\Delta T$ Heat for a temperature change; $c$ is specific heat

$Q = mL$ Latent heat for a phase change

$H = \frac{KA\Delta T}{L}$ Heat conduction rate; $K$ is thermal conductivity

$P = e\sigma A T^4$ Stefan-Boltzmann law; $e$ is emissivity, $T$ absolute temperature

$\lambda_m T = b$ Wien's displacement law

$\frac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_0)$ Newton's law of cooling; $T_0$ is the surrounding temperature

Common traps

  • Using $4S/R$ for an air bubble inside water: an air bubble in a liquid has one surface, so the excess pressure is $2S/R$. Only a soap bubble in air uses $4S/R$.
  • Thinking a larger modulus means more stretchable: a larger Young's modulus means less strain for the same stress, so steel is more elastic than rubber.
  • Forgetting buoyancy in terminal velocity: the factor is $(\sigma - \rho)$, not $\sigma$. Terminal velocity is zero when the densities are equal, and the body rises when $\sigma < \rho$.
  • Assuming liquid overflows from a short capillary tube: it never overflows. The meniscus radius adjusts so that $hR$ stays constant.
  • Using Celsius in Stefan's law: radiation formulas need absolute temperature in kelvin.
  • Writing $\Delta V = \alpha V \Delta T$ for solids: the volume coefficient is $\gamma = 3\alpha$, so a sphere gains $4\pi R^3\alpha\Delta T$ in volume.
  • Applying the mixture formula blindly in ice-water problems: first check whether the available heat is enough to melt all the ice. If not, the final temperature is 0 degrees Celsius.
  • Applying Bernoulli between different streamlines or to viscous flow: it holds along a streamline for ideal, steady, incompressible flow.

Quick revision

  • Hooke's law: stress is proportional to strain up to the proportional limit; moduli are $Y$, $B$ and $G$, all in Pa.
  • Liquids and gases have only a bulk modulus; for most solids $G \approx Y/3$.
  • Hydrostatic pressure $\rho g h$ is independent of vessel shape; Pascal's law is the basis of hydraulic machines.
  • In free fall $g_{eff} = 0$: no hydrostatic pressure gradient, no buoyancy, and full capillary rise.
  • Terminal velocity $v_t \propto r^2(\sigma - \rho)/\eta$; when $n$ drops merge, $v_t$ grows by $n^{2/3}$.
  • Reynolds number below about 1000 means laminar flow, above about 2000 turbulent; $Av$ = constant.
  • Bernoulli: faster flow means lower pressure; efflux speed is $\sqrt{2gh}$; maximum range is from a hole at $H/2$.
  • Surface tension decreases with temperature; excess pressure is $2S/R$ for a drop and $4S/R$ for a soap bubble.
  • Capillary rise $h = 2S\cos\theta/(\rho g r)$; mercury shows depression because $\theta > 90^\circ$.
  • Expansion: $\beta = 2\alpha$, $\gamma = 3\alpha$; water has maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius; thermal stress is $Y\alpha\Delta T$.
  • Temperature is constant during a phase change; for water $L_f = 80$ cal/g and $L_v = 540$ cal/g.
  • Radiated power is proportional to $T^4$; $\lambda_m T = 2.9\times10^{-3}\,m\,K$; slabs in series add thermal resistances.

Physics · Unit 8: Thermodynamics

This unit applies energy conservation to systems that exchange heat and work, mainly ideal gases. It introduces temperature through the zeroth law, energy bookkeeping through the first law, process analysis using P-V diagrams, and the limits on converting heat into work through the second law and the Carnot engine. NEET usually asks 2-3 questions from this unit, mostly short numericals on work in adiabatic or isothermal processes, cyclic processes, first-law sign conventions, and engine or refrigerator efficiency.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q17, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q39

Thermal equilibrium, zeroth law and the concept of temperature

Two systems are in thermal equilibrium when no net heat flows between them after thermal contact. Their macroscopic variables, such as pressure, volume and temperature, then stop changing. The zeroth law states that if systems A and B are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This law defines temperature: temperature is the property that has the same value for all systems in thermal equilibrium with one another. It is also the working principle of a thermometer, because the thermometer acts as system C. Heat flows spontaneously from higher to lower temperature until the temperatures become equal. Gas laws and all thermodynamic equations use absolute temperature, measured in kelvin.

  • Thermal equilibrium means no net heat flow and steady macroscopic variables
  • The zeroth law introduces temperature as a physical quantity
  • Systems in thermal equilibrium have equal temperatures
  • A thermometer works because of the zeroth law
  • Temperature is an intensive state variable
  • A change of 1 degree Celsius equals a change of 1 K

$T(K) = t(^{\circ}C) + 273.15$ Converts Celsius temperature to absolute temperature, which must be used in all gas and thermodynamic formulas

NEET tip: Usually asked as a statement-based question identifying the law that defines temperature, which is the zeroth law.

Heat, work and internal energy

Internal energy U is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of the molecules, measured in the centre of mass frame. U is a state function, so its change depends only on the initial and final states. For an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature. Heat and work are two ways of transferring energy, and neither is a property of the system. Heat is transferred because of a temperature difference. Work is transferred by other means, such as a piston moving against pressure. Both heat and work are path functions, so their values depend on the process followed. On a P-V diagram, the work done by a gas equals the area under the curve. This work is positive for expansion and negative for compression. For a cyclic process, the net work equals the area enclosed by the loop. It is positive when the cycle runs clockwise and negative when it runs anticlockwise.

  • Internal energy is a state function, while heat and work are path functions
  • For an ideal gas, the change in internal energy depends only on the change in temperature
  • Work done by a gas is positive in expansion and negative in compression
  • Work equals the area under the P-V curve
  • Net work in a cycle equals the area enclosed by the loop
  • No work is done when the volume stays constant
  • Degrees of freedom f decide the molar heat capacity at constant volume: $C_v = \frac{f}{2}R$

$W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,dV$ Work done by a gas as its volume changes from $V_1$ to $V_2$

$\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T$ Change in internal energy of an ideal gas in any process, where n is the number of moles and $C_v$ is the molar heat capacity at constant volume

$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$ Internal energy of an ideal gas with f degrees of freedom: f = 3 for a monatomic gas and f = 5 for a diatomic gas

NEET tip: NEET often gives a P-V diagram and asks for work as an area, or uses the fact that the change in internal energy is the same for different paths between the same two states.

First law of thermodynamics

The first law of thermodynamics is the law of conservation of energy: $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$. Here $\Delta Q$ is the heat supplied to the system and $\Delta W$ is the work done by the system. Heat absorbed is taken as positive, and work done by the gas is taken as positive. In an isochoric (constant volume) process, W = 0, so all the heat changes the internal energy. In an isobaric (constant pressure) process, $W = P\Delta V$ and $Q = nC_p\Delta T$. In a cyclic process, $\Delta U = 0$, so the net heat supplied equals the net work done, which is the enclosed area. In free expansion into a vacuum, Q = 0 and W = 0, so $\Delta U = 0$. Applying the first law to an ideal gas gives Mayer's relation, $C_p - C_v = R$.

  • The first law expresses energy conservation, not the direction of a process
  • Use the convention: heat absorbed is positive and work done by the gas is positive
  • In an isochoric process, $Q = \Delta U$
  • In an isobaric process, $Q = nC_p\Delta T$ and $W = nR\Delta T$
  • In a cyclic process, $Q_{net} = W_{net}$, which equals the area of the loop
