  • Monatomic gas: $C_v = \frac{3}{2}R$ and $C_p = \frac{5}{2}R$
  • Diatomic gas: $C_v = \frac{5}{2}R$ and $C_p = \frac{7}{2}R$
  • For isobaric heating of a monatomic gas, $\Delta U : W : Q = 3 : 2 : 5$

$\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$ First law of thermodynamics, with heat absorbed and work done by the system taken as positive

$C_p - C_v = R$ Mayer's relation between the molar heat capacities of an ideal gas

$W = P(V_2 - V_1) = nR\Delta T$ Work done by a gas in an isobaric process

$Q = nC_p\Delta T$ Heat supplied in an isobaric process

$Q = nC_v\Delta T$ Heat supplied in an isochoric process

NEET tip: For a rectangular or triangular cycle on a P-V diagram, the total heat supplied equals the enclosed area, with the sign set by the direction of the cycle.

Isothermal and adiabatic processes

In an isothermal process the temperature stays constant, so PV is constant and, for an ideal gas, $\Delta U = 0$. All the heat supplied is therefore converted into work, Q = W. Such a process must be slow and must take place in a container with conducting walls in contact with a reservoir. In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged, Q = 0, so $W = -\Delta U$. Such a process is fast or takes place in an insulated container. In adiabatic expansion the gas cools, and in adiabatic compression it heats up. The process equation is $PV^\gamma$ = constant, where $\gamma = C_p/C_v$. The work done by the gas is $W = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}$, which simplifies to $nC_v(T_1 - T_2)$. On a P-V diagram, an adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal curve by a factor of $\gamma$. For the same expansion, the work done is greater in the isothermal process than in the adiabatic one.

  • Isothermal process: $\Delta T = 0$, $\Delta U = 0$ and Q = W
  • Adiabatic process: Q = 0 and $W = -\Delta U$
  • Adiabatic expansion causes cooling
  • Ratio of specific heats: $\gamma$ = 5/3 for a monatomic gas, 7/5 for a diatomic gas and 4/3 for a polyatomic gas
  • The slope of an adiabatic curve is $\gamma$ times the slope of an isothermal curve
  • For the same expansion, $W_{isothermal} > W_{adiabatic}$
  • The molar heat capacity is infinite for an isothermal process and zero for an adiabatic process
  • Isothermal bulk modulus = P, and adiabatic bulk modulus = $\gamma P$

$W = nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} = 2.303\,nRT\log_{10}\frac{V_2}{V_1}$ Work done in an isothermal process at absolute temperature T

$W = nRT\ln\frac{P_1}{P_2}$ Isothermal work written in terms of pressures

$PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$ Adiabatic process equation, where $\gamma = C_p/C_v$

$TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}$ Adiabatic relation between temperature and volume

$P^{1-\gamma}T^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$ Adiabatic relation between pressure and temperature

$W = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1}$ Work done by a gas in an adiabatic process; it is positive when the gas cools

NEET tip: NEET frequently asks for adiabatic work from a given temperature drop, using $W = \frac{nR\Delta T}{\gamma-1}$, or asks you to compare the slopes of isothermal and adiabatic curves.

Second law of thermodynamics

The first law allows any process that conserves energy, but the second law sets limits on which processes can actually occur. The Kelvin-Planck statement says that no process is possible whose sole result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and its complete conversion into work. This means no heat engine can have 100 percent efficiency. The Clausius statement says that no process is possible whose sole result is the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter body. This means a refrigerator always needs external work. A heat engine takes heat $Q_1$ from a hot source, does work W and rejects heat $Q_2$ to a sink. Its efficiency is $\eta = W/Q_1$. A refrigerator extracts heat $Q_2$ from a cold body using work W and rejects heat $Q_1$ to the surroundings. Its coefficient of performance is $\beta = Q_2/W$. The two statements of the second law are equivalent.

  • The second law gives the direction of natural processes
  • Kelvin-Planck statement: a perfect heat engine is impossible
  • Clausius statement: a perfect refrigerator is impossible
  • Efficiency of a heat engine is always less than 1
  • The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator can be greater than 1
  • Energy balance for both a heat engine and a refrigerator: $Q_1 = W + Q_2$
  • Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements are equivalent

$\eta = \frac{W}{Q_1} = 1 - \frac{Q_2}{Q_1}$ Efficiency of a heat engine; $Q_1$ is the heat absorbed from the source and $Q_2$ is the heat rejected to the sink

$\beta = \frac{Q_2}{W} = \frac{Q_2}{Q_1 - Q_2}$ Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator; $Q_2$ is the heat extracted from the cold reservoir

$\beta = \frac{1 - \eta}{\eta}$ Relation between a refrigerator and an engine working between the same reservoirs in reverse

NEET tip: Expect statement-based questions on the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements, and short numericals on efficiency or coefficient of performance.

Reversible and irreversible processes

A reversible process is one that can be retraced so that both the system and its surroundings return exactly to their original states. It must be quasi-static, meaning extremely slow and always in equilibrium, and it must involve no dissipative effects such as friction, viscosity or resistance. All real processes are irreversible. Examples include free expansion, heat flow through a finite temperature difference, mixing of gases and friction. The Carnot engine is an ideal reversible engine. Its cycle has four steps: isothermal expansion at $T_1$, adiabatic expansion from $T_1$ to $T_2$, isothermal compression at $T_2$, and adiabatic compression back to $T_1$. Carnot's theorem states that no engine working between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a Carnot engine. Its efficiency, $1 - T_2/T_1$, depends only on the reservoir temperatures and not on the working substance.

  • A reversible process must be quasi-static and free of dissipation
  • All natural processes are irreversible
  • Heat transfer through a finite temperature difference is irreversible
  • Carnot cycle order: isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression
  • In a Carnot engine, $\frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{T_2}{T_1}$
  • Carnot efficiency is independent of the working substance
  • Efficiency becomes 100 percent only if $T_2 = 0$ K, which is unattainable
  • All reversible engines working between the same two temperatures have equal efficiency

$\eta_{Carnot} = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$ Maximum possible efficiency of an engine between a source at $T_1$ and a sink at $T_2$, both in kelvin

$\frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{T_2}{T_1}$ Ratio of heat rejected to heat absorbed in a reversible Carnot cycle

$\beta_{Carnot} = \frac{T_2}{T_1 - T_2}$ Coefficient of performance of a Carnot refrigerator, with temperatures in kelvin

NEET tip: Carnot efficiency numericals, often involving a change in source or sink temperature, are very common; always convert temperatures to kelvin first.

Formula sheet

$\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$ First law: heat supplied equals the change in internal energy plus the work done by the system

$W = \int P\,dV$ Work done by a gas, equal to the area under the P-V curve

$\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T$ Change in internal energy of an ideal gas in any process; n is the number of moles

$C_v = \frac{f}{2}R, \; C_p = \left(\frac{f}{2}+1\right)R$ Molar heat capacities of an ideal gas with f degrees of freedom

$C_p - C_v = R$ Mayer's relation for an ideal gas

$\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$ Ratio of specific heats: 5/3 for a monatomic gas, 7/5 for a diatomic gas, 4/3 for a polyatomic gas

$W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$ Work done in an isobaric process

$Q = nC_p\Delta T$ Heat supplied at constant pressure

$W = 0, \; Q = nC_v\Delta T$ Work and heat in an isochoric process

$W = nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$ Work in an isothermal process, where $\Delta U = 0$ and Q = W

$PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$ Adiabatic process equation

$TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}$ Adiabatic relation between temperature and volume

$P^{1-\gamma}T^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$ Adiabatic relation between pressure and temperature

$W = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1}$ Work done by a gas in an adiabatic process

$\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{adiabatic} = \gamma \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{isothermal}$ An adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal curve

$W_{cycle} = Q_{net} = \text{area enclosed}$ Cyclic process, where $\Delta U = 0$; work is positive for a clockwise cycle on a P-V diagram

$\eta = \frac{W}{Q_1} = 1 - \frac{Q_2}{Q_1}$ Efficiency of a heat engine

$\eta_{Carnot} = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$ Efficiency of a Carnot engine; $T_1$ is the source temperature and $T_2$ the sink temperature, in kelvin

$\beta = \frac{Q_2}{W} = \frac{Q_2}{Q_1 - Q_2}$ Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator

$\beta_{Carnot} = \frac{T_2}{T_1 - T_2}$ Coefficient of performance of a Carnot refrigerator

$\beta = \frac{1-\eta}{\eta}$ Relation between engine efficiency and refrigerator coefficient of performance for the same reservoirs

Common traps

  • Using Celsius temperatures in Carnot efficiency or gas formulas is wrong; always convert to kelvin.
  • Assuming that Q = 0 means the temperature is constant is wrong; in an adiabatic process the temperature changes, while in an isothermal process Q is not zero.
  • Using $\Delta U = nC_p\Delta T$ in an isobaric process is wrong; $\Delta U$ is always $nC_v\Delta T$ for an ideal gas, and only Q uses $C_p$.
  • Mixing sign conventions causes errors; with $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$, work done by the gas is positive and heat absorbed is positive.
  • Taking the net work of an anticlockwise P-V cycle as positive is wrong; it is negative, and the net heat is rejected.
  • Using $\gamma = 5/3$ for diatomic gases like oxygen and nitrogen is wrong; use 7/5 unless stated otherwise.
  • Believing that the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator cannot exceed 1 is wrong; it usually does exceed 1, unlike efficiency.
  • Assuming free expansion does work is wrong; against a vacuum W = 0 and Q = 0, so $\Delta U = 0$ and the temperature of an ideal gas stays the same.

Quick revision

  • The zeroth law defines temperature, and systems in thermal equilibrium have equal temperatures.
  • Internal energy is a state function and depends only on T for an ideal gas; heat and work are path functions.
  • First law: $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$, with work done by the gas taken as positive.
  • Work equals the area under the P-V curve, and net work in a cycle equals the enclosed area.
  • Isochoric: W = 0. Isobaric: $W = nR\Delta T$. Cyclic: $\Delta U = 0$.
  • Isothermal: $\Delta U = 0$ and $W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$.
  • Adiabatic: Q = 0, $PV^\gamma$ = constant and $W = nR(T_1 - T_2)/(\gamma - 1)$.
  • An adiabatic curve is $\gamma$ times steeper than an isothermal curve on a P-V diagram.
  • $\gamma$ = 5/3 for monatomic, 7/5 for diatomic and 4/3 for polyatomic gases; $C_p - C_v = R$.
  • Kelvin-Planck rules out a perfect engine, and Clausius rules out a perfect refrigerator.
  • Carnot engine efficiency is $1 - T_2/T_1$, independent of the working substance, and is the maximum possible.
  • Real processes are irreversible; reversible processes are quasi-static and free of friction.

Physics · Unit 9: Kinetic Theory of Gases

Kinetic Theory of Gases explains macroscopic gas properties such as pressure, temperature and heat capacity in terms of the random motion of molecules. NEET usually asks 2-3 questions from this unit, mostly numericals on RMS speed, degrees of freedom, $\gamma$ for gases and mixtures, and mean free path. The formulas are short, so accuracy with ratios and units is what earns marks.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q2, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q45

Equation of state of a perfect gas

A perfect (ideal) gas has negligible molecular size and no intermolecular forces except during collisions. It obeys $PV = nRT$ exactly. This single equation combines Boyle's law ($PV$ constant at fixed $T$), Charles' law ($V \propto T$ at fixed $P$), Gay-Lussac's law ($P \propto T$ at fixed $V$) and Avogadro's law. Written per molecule it becomes $PV = Nk_BT$. Using density, it becomes $P = \frac{\rho RT}{M}$. Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature, where molecules are far apart. For a mixture of non-reacting gases, Dalton's law of partial pressures gives $P = P_1 + P_2 + \dots$. Temperature must always be in kelvin.

  • Ideal gas: point molecules with no intermolecular attraction.
  • Real gases behave ideally at low $P$ and high $T$.
  • $R = 8.314\ J\ mol^{-1}K^{-1}$ and $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ J\ K^{-1}$.
  • For a fixed mass of gas, $\frac{PV}{T}$ is constant.
  • Dalton's law: total pressure equals the sum of partial pressures.
  • Always convert temperature to kelvin: $T = t + 273$.

$PV = nRT = Nk_BT$ Ideal gas equation; $n$ = number of moles, $N$ = number of molecules.

$P = \frac{\rho RT}{M}$ Density form; $\rho$ = density, $M$ = molar mass in kg/mol.

$\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$ Combined gas law for a fixed amount of gas.

$P = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 + \dots$ Dalton's law for a mixture of non-reacting ideal gases.

NEET tip: Expect ratio-based questions on density or pressure change when $T$ or $P$ changes, and questions on mixtures using Dalton's law.

Work done on compressing a gas

When a gas expands or is compressed, work is exchanged with its surroundings. The work done by the gas is $W = \int P\,dV$, which equals the area under the P-V curve. Work done on the gas has the same magnitude with opposite sign, so it is positive during compression. In an isothermal compression from $V_1$ to $V_2$, the work done on the gas is $nRT\ln\frac{V_1}{V_2}$. At constant pressure, the work is $P\Delta V$. At constant volume, no work is done. In an adiabatic compression, the work done on the gas is $\frac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{\gamma - 1}$. For the same compression ratio, adiabatic compression needs more work than isothermal compression because the gas also heats up.

  • Work equals the area under the P-V curve.
  • Work by the gas is positive in expansion and negative in compression.
  • Isochoric process: $W = 0$.
  • For the same volume reduction, adiabatic compression requires more work than isothermal compression.
  • In a cyclic process, net work equals the area enclosed by the loop.

$W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,dV$ General expression for work done by the gas.

$W_{on} = nRT\ln\frac{V_1}{V_2} = 2.303\,nRT\log\frac{P_2}{P_1}$ Work done on the gas in isothermal compression.

$W = P(V_2 - V_1)$ Work done by the gas at constant pressure.

$W_{on} = \frac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{nR(T_2 - T_1)}{\gamma - 1}$ Work done on the gas in adiabatic compression.

NEET tip: NEET tests the sign convention, area under P-V graphs, and comparison of isothermal versus adiabatic work.

Kinetic theory of gases: assumptions and the concept of pressure

Kinetic theory rests on a set of assumptions. A gas consists of a very large number of identical molecules in random motion. Molecular size is negligible compared with the separation between molecules. There are no forces between molecules except during collisions. Collisions are perfectly elastic and of negligible duration, and Newton's laws apply. Pressure arises from molecular collisions with the walls. A molecule striking a wall changes momentum by $2mv_x$. Averaging over all molecules and using $\overline{v_x^2} = \frac{1}{3}\overline{v^2}$ (isotropy) gives $P = \frac{1}{3}nm\overline{v^2}$. Here $n$ is the number density. So pressure equals two-thirds of the translational kinetic energy per unit volume.

  • Molecules are point masses in random motion.
  • Collisions are elastic, and no forces act between collisions.
  • Momentum change per wall collision is $2mv_x$.
  • Isotropy gives $\overline{v_x^2} = \overline{v_y^2} = \overline{v_z^2} = \frac{1}{3}\overline{v^2}$.
  • Pressure is the same in all directions, by Pascal's law.
  • Pressure equals $\frac{2}{3}$ of the translational KE per unit volume.

$P = \frac{1}{3}nm\overline{v^2} = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{rms}^2$ Kinetic theory expression for pressure; $n$ = number density, $\rho$ = density.

$PV = \frac{1}{3}Nm\overline{v^2}$ Kinetic gas equation for $N$ molecules.

$P = \frac{2}{3}E$ $E$ = translational kinetic energy per unit volume.

NEET tip: Questions ask how pressure changes when molecular mass, speed or number density changes, or ask you to identify an incorrect assumption.

Kinetic interpretation of temperature; RMS speed of gas molecules

Comparing $PV = \frac{1}{3}Nm\overline{v^2}$ with $PV = Nk_BT$ gives the average translational KE per molecule, $\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$. Temperature is therefore a measure of the average translational KE of the molecules. This KE depends only on $T$, not on the nature of the gas. The RMS speed is $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$, so $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$ and $v_{rms} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}$. Two other characteristic speeds are the average speed $\sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}$ and the most probable speed $\sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$. They are ordered $v_{rms} > v_{avg} > v_{mp}$, in the ratio about $1.73 : 1.60 : 1.41$. At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster. This explains why hydrogen escapes Earth's atmosphere.

  • Average translational KE per molecule is $\frac{3}{2}k_BT$, independent of the gas.
  • Translational KE per mole is $\frac{3}{2}RT$.
  • $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T/M}$.
  • Doubling $T$ multiplies $v_{rms}$ by $\sqrt{2}$.
  • Speed order: $v_{rms} > v_{avg} > v_{mp}$.
  • At absolute zero, classical kinetic theory predicts zero molecular KE.

$\overline{KE} = \frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$ Average translational KE per molecule.

$v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{3k_BT}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{3P}{\rho}}$ RMS speed; $M$ = molar mass in kg/mol, $m$ = mass of one molecule.

$v_{avg} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}$ Mean speed of the molecules.

$v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$ Most probable speed (peak of the Maxwell distribution).

NEET tip: Ratio problems on $v_{rms}$ for different gases or temperatures are very common. Remember to use $M$ in kg/mol.

Degrees of freedom

Degrees of freedom ($f$) are the number of independent ways a molecule can store energy. For a system of $N$ particles with $k$ constraints, $f = 3N - k$. A monatomic gas has 3 translational degrees of freedom. A rigid diatomic molecule has 3 translational and 2 rotational, so $f = 5$; rotation about its own axis is negligible. At high temperature a diatomic molecule also vibrates. One vibrational mode contributes 2 degrees of freedom (one for KE, one for PE), giving $f = 7$. A rigid non-linear polyatomic molecule has 3 translational and 3 rotational, so $f = 6$. A rigid linear polyatomic molecule such as $CO_2$ has $f = 5$. Each vibrational mode adds 2 more terms.

  • Monatomic (He, Ar): $f = 3$.
  • Rigid diatomic ($O_2$, $N_2$): $f = 5$.
  • Diatomic with vibration: $f = 7$.
  • Rigid non-linear polyatomic ($H_2O$, $NH_3$): $f = 6$.
  • Each vibrational mode adds 2 (KE and PE).
  • Vibrational modes are usually frozen at room temperature.

$f = 3N - k$ Degrees of freedom for $N$ particles with $k$ independent constraints.

$f = f_{trans} + f_{rot} + 2f_{vib}$ Total energy terms when $f_{vib}$ vibrational modes are active.

NEET tip: NEET often gives the number of vibrational modes and asks for $\gamma$, or the reverse. Count each vibrational mode as 2.

Law of equipartition of energy and specific heat capacities of gases

The law of equipartition states that in thermal equilibrium, each quadratic energy term (degree of freedom) gets an average energy of $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$ per molecule. Hence the internal energy of $n$ moles is $U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$. This gives $C_V = \frac{f}{2}R$, and Mayer's relation gives $C_P = C_V + R$. The ratio is $\gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$. Typical values are $\frac{5}{3}$ for monatomic, $\frac{7}{5}$ for rigid diatomic and $\frac{4}{3}$ for rigid non-linear polyatomic gases (e.g. $H_2O$, $NH_3$). Rigid linear polyatomic gases such as $CO_2$ have $\gamma = \frac{7}{5}$. For mixtures, $C_V$ is the mole-weighted average. For solids, each atom acts as a 3D oscillator with energy $3k_BT$, so $C = 3R$ (Dulong-Petit law). Classical theory fails at low temperatures, where specific heats fall because modes freeze; this needs quantum theory.

  • Each degree of freedom carries $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$ per molecule, or $\frac{1}{2}RT$ per mole.
  • Each vibrational mode carries $k_BT$.
  • $\gamma$ decreases as $f$ increases, and always $1 < \gamma \le \frac{5}{3}$.
  • Monatomic: $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$, $C_P = \frac{5}{2}R$.
  • Rigid diatomic: $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$, $C_P = \frac{7}{2}R$.
  • Solids: molar heat capacity $\approx 3R \approx 25\ J\ mol^{-1}K^{-1}$.
  • Water: about $9R$ per mole, because each molecule has 3 atoms.

$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$ Internal energy of $n$ moles of an ideal gas.

$C_V = \frac{f}{2}R$ Molar heat capacity at constant volume.

$C_P - C_V = R$ Mayer's relation for an ideal gas.

$\gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$ Ratio of specific heats in terms of degrees of freedom.

$C_{V,mix} = \frac{n_1C_{V1} + n_2C_{V2}}{n_1 + n_2}$ Molar $C_V$ of a gas mixture.

$\frac{\gamma_{mix}}{\gamma_{mix} - 1} = \frac{\frac{n_1\gamma_1}{\gamma_1 - 1} + \frac{n_2\gamma_2}{\gamma_2 - 1}}{n_1 + n_2}$ Effective $\gamma$ of a mixture (equivalent to $\gamma_{mix} = \frac{C_{P,mix}}{C_{V,mix}}$).

NEET tip: Most frequent question type: find $\gamma$, $C_P$ or $C_V$ from $f$ (including vibrational modes), or for a mixture of gases.

Mean free path

Mean free path ($\lambda$) is the average distance a molecule travels between two successive collisions. A molecule of diameter $d$ collides with any molecule whose centre lies within a cylinder of radius $d$ around its path. Accounting for the relative motion of the other molecules gives $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$, where $n$ is the number density. Using $n = \frac{P}{k_BT}$, this becomes $\lambda = \frac{k_BT}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$. At constant pressure, $\lambda \propto T$. At constant temperature, $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{P}$. In a closed rigid container, $n$ is fixed, so $\lambda$ does not depend on temperature. The collision frequency is the mean speed divided by $\lambda$. At STP, $\lambda$ is about $10^{-7}\ m$.

  • $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{nd^2}$.
  • Doubling the diameter reduces $\lambda$ by a factor of 4.
  • $\lambda \propto T$ at constant $P$, and $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{P}$ at constant $T$.
  • At constant volume (fixed $n$), $\lambda$ is independent of $T$.
  • $\lambda$ is much larger than the molecular size, which justifies treating molecules as point particles.

$\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$ Mean free path; $d$ = molecular diameter, $n$ = number density.

$\lambda = \frac{k_BT}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$ Mean free path in terms of pressure and temperature.

$\nu = \frac{\bar{v}}{\lambda}$ Collision frequency; $\bar{v}$ = average speed.

$\tau = \frac{\lambda}{\bar{v}}$ Mean time between successive collisions.

NEET tip: Expect ratio questions linking $\lambda$, $d$ and $n$ for two gases, or how $\lambda$ changes with $P$ and $T$.

Avogadro's number

Avogadro's hypothesis states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules. Avogadro's number, $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ mol^{-1}$, is the number of particles in one mole of any substance. One mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP (273 K, 1 atm). Avogadro's number links the molar gas constant to the Boltzmann constant through $k_B = \frac{R}{N_A}$. This lets us move between per-mole and per-molecule quantities. The number of molecules in a sample is $N = nN_A = \frac{m}{M}N_A$. The number of molecules per unit volume at STP, $2.69 \times 10^{25}\ m^{-3}$, is called the Loschmidt number.

  • $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$ per mole.
  • Molar volume at STP is $22.4\ L = 22.4 \times 10^{-3}\ m^3$.
  • $k_B = \frac{R}{N_A}$ links molar and molecular forms.
  • Mass of one molecule: $m = \frac{M}{N_A}$.
  • Loschmidt number $\approx 2.69 \times 10^{25}\ m^{-3}$ at STP.

$k_B = \frac{R}{N_A}$ Boltzmann constant from the gas constant and Avogadro's number.

$N = nN_A = \frac{m}{M}N_A$ Number of molecules in a sample of mass $m$ and molar mass $M$.

$n_v = \frac{P}{k_BT}$ Number of molecules per unit volume.

NEET tip: Used mainly as a tool: counting molecules, finding the mass of one molecule, or converting $R$ to $k_B$ inside larger numericals.

Formula sheet

$PV = nRT = Nk_BT$ Ideal gas equation; $n$ = moles, $N$ = molecules, $R = 8.314\ J\ mol^{-1}K^{-1}$.

$P = \frac{\rho RT}{M}$ Ideal gas equation in terms of density $\rho$ and molar mass $M$.

$W = \int P\,dV$ Work done by the gas, equal to the area under the P-V curve.

$W_{on} = nRT\ln\frac{V_1}{V_2}$ Work done on the gas in isothermal compression from $V_1$ to $V_2$.

$W_{on} = \frac{nR(T_2 - T_1)}{\gamma - 1}$ Work done on the gas in adiabatic compression.

$P = \frac{1}{3}nm\overline{v^2} = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{rms}^2$ Kinetic pressure; $n$ = number density, $m$ = molecular mass.

$P = \frac{2}{3}E$ Pressure in terms of translational KE per unit volume $E$.

$\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$ Average translational KE per molecule.

$v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{3P}{\rho}}$ RMS speed; $M$ in kg/mol.

$v_{avg} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}$ Average (mean) speed.

$v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$ Most probable speed.

$f = 3N - k$ Degrees of freedom; $N$ = particles, $k$ = constraints.

$E_{per\ dof} = \frac{1}{2}k_BT$ Equipartition: energy per degree of freedom per molecule.

$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$ Internal energy of $n$ moles of an ideal gas with $f$ degrees of freedom.

$C_V = \frac{f}{2}R,\ C_P = \left(\frac{f}{2} + 1\right)R$ Molar heat capacities of an ideal gas.

$C_P - C_V = R$ Mayer's relation.

$\gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$ Ratio of specific heats: $\frac{5}{3}$ monatomic, $\frac{7}{5}$ diatomic, $\frac{4}{3}$ rigid non-linear polyatomic ($\frac{7}{5}$ for rigid linear polyatomic such as $CO_2$).

$C_{V,mix} = \frac{n_1C_{V1} + n_2C_{V2}}{n_1 + n_2}$ Molar $C_V$ of a mixture of ideal gases.

$C = 3R$ Dulong-Petit law: molar heat capacity of solids.

$\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n} = \frac{k_BT}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$ Mean free path; $d$ = molecular diameter, $n$ = number density.

$\nu = \frac{\bar{v}}{\lambda}$ Collision frequency of a molecule.

$k_B = \frac{R}{N_A} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ J\ K^{-1}$ Boltzmann constant; $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ mol^{-1}$.

$N = \frac{m}{M}N_A$ Number of molecules in mass $m$ of a substance of molar mass $M$.

Common traps

  • Using temperature in degrees Celsius in $PV = nRT$ or $v_{rms}$ formulas; always convert to kelvin.
  • Using molar mass in g/mol instead of kg/mol in $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$, which makes the answer wrong by a factor of $\sqrt{1000}$.
  • Counting a vibrational mode as 1 degree of freedom; each vibrational mode contributes 2 (KE and PE), so it carries energy $k_BT$.
  • Thinking the average KE per molecule depends on the gas; at the same $T$ all ideal gases have the same average translational KE, $\frac{3}{2}k_BT$, though their speeds differ.
  • Treating mean free path as proportional to $\frac{1}{d}$; it is proportional to $\frac{1}{d^2}$, so doubling the diameter reduces $\lambda$ four times.
  • Assuming $\lambda$ always increases with temperature; it increases with $T$ only at constant pressure, and stays constant in a closed rigid container where $n$ is fixed.
  • Finding $\gamma$ of a mixture by averaging the $\gamma$ values directly; instead average $C_V$ (and $C_P$) weighted by moles, then take the ratio.
  • Writing the work in compression with the wrong sign; work done by the gas is negative in compression, while work done on the gas is positive.

Quick revision

  • $PV = nRT = Nk_BT$; real gases behave ideally at low $P$ and high $T$.
  • Work equals the area under the P-V curve; isothermal work done by the gas is $nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$, and work done on the gas is $nRT\ln\frac{V_1}{V_2}$.
  • Kinetic pressure: $P = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{rms}^2 = \frac{2}{3}E$.
  • Average translational KE per molecule is $\frac{3}{2}k_BT$, independent of the nature of the gas.
  • $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$, so $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T/M}$.
  • Speed order: $v_{rms} > v_{avg} > v_{mp}$, in the ratio $\sqrt{3} : \sqrt{8/\pi} : \sqrt{2}$.
  • Degrees of freedom: monatomic 3, rigid diatomic 5, rigid non-linear polyatomic 6; each vibrational mode adds 2.
  • Equipartition gives $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$ per degree of freedom, so $U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$.
  • $C_V = \frac{f}{2}R$, $C_P = C_V + R$, $\gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$.
  • $\gamma$ values: $\frac{5}{3}$ (monatomic), $\frac{7}{5}$ (diatomic), $\frac{4}{3}$ (rigid non-linear polyatomic), $\frac{7}{5}$ (rigid linear polyatomic such as $CO_2$); solids have $C = 3R$.
  • Mean free path $\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n}$, so $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{d^2}$ and $\lambda \propto \frac{1}{n}$.
  • $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ mol^{-1}$, $k_B = \frac{R}{N_A}$, and the molar volume at STP is 22.4 L.

Physics · Unit 10: Oscillations and Waves

This unit covers repetitive motion, from simple harmonic motion of springs and pendulums to mechanical waves on strings and in air columns, including superposition, standing waves and beats. NEET asks 2-3 questions from it almost every year, mostly on SHM equations and energy, time periods of oscillating systems, wave equations, organ pipe and string harmonics, and beats. Questions are formula-driven but often hide a conceptual twist.

PYQs (3): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q4, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q25, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q28

Periodic motion: time period, frequency, displacement as a function of time

A motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time is periodic motion. Examples are the Earth's revolution, a clock's hands and a swinging pendulum. If a body moves to and fro about a fixed mean (equilibrium) position, the periodic motion is called oscillatory or vibratory. Every oscillation is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory; uniform circular motion is periodic but not to and fro. The time period $T$ is the smallest interval after which the motion repeats, measured in seconds. Frequency $\nu$ is the number of repetitions per second, with unit hertz (Hz). Angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi\nu$ in rad/s. The state of the body at any instant is described by its displacement $x(t)$ from the mean position. Displacement may be linear, angular, a pressure change or an electric field, depending on the system.

  • Periodic motion repeats after a fixed time T.
  • Oscillatory motion is periodic motion about a mean position.
  • All oscillations are periodic; the converse is not true.
  • Unit of frequency is Hz, equal to $s^{-1}$.
  • Displacement is measured from the equilibrium position, not from the extreme position.

$\nu = \frac{1}{T}$ Frequency from time period

$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi\nu$ Angular frequency in rad/s

NEET tip: Expect statement-type questions that separate periodic motion from oscillatory motion, or simple T, ν, ω conversions.

Periodic functions

A function $f(t)$ is periodic if $f(t+T) = f(t)$ for the smallest positive $T$, which is its period. The simplest periodic functions are $\sin\omega t$ and $\cos\omega t$, each with period $2\pi/\omega$. A linear combination $a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t$ is also periodic and is itself a simple harmonic function, with amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. Any periodic function can be expressed as a superposition of sines and cosines of different time periods with suitable coefficients. $\sin^2\omega t = \frac{1-\cos2\omega t}{2}$ is periodic with period $\pi/\omega$. It represents SHM about the mean value 1/2, with angular frequency $2\omega$. $\sin\omega t + \sin2\omega t$ is periodic but not SHM. Functions such as $e^{-\omega t}$ and $\log\omega t$ are non-periodic.

  • The condition for periodicity is $f(t+T)=f(t)$.
  • $\sin\omega t$ and $\cos\omega t$ both have period $2\pi/\omega$.
  • $a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t$ is SHM with amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.
  • $\sin^2\omega t$ and $\cos^2\omega t$ have period $\pi/\omega$.
  • A sum of sinusoids with different ω is periodic but not simple harmonic.
  • Exponential and logarithmic functions are non-periodic.

$a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\sin(\omega t+\phi),\ \tan\phi=\frac{b}{a}$ Combining two sinusoids of the same ω into a single SHM

NEET tip: NEET lists functions and asks which are periodic, which are SHM, or what their period is.

Simple harmonic motion, its equation and phase

In simple harmonic motion (SHM), the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from the mean position and always directed towards it: $a = -\omega^2 x$. Its solution is $x = A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$. Here $A$ is the amplitude, the maximum displacement. $(\omega t+\phi)$ is the phase, which fixes position and direction of motion at time t. $\phi$ is the phase constant (initial phase). SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter. Velocity is $v = -A\omega\sin(\omega t+\phi)$, with magnitude $\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$. Velocity is maximum ($A\omega$) at the mean position and zero at the extremes. Acceleration is maximum ($A\omega^2$) at the extremes and zero at the mean position. Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$, and acceleration leads displacement by $\pi$.

  • Defining condition: $a \propto -x$, or $F = -kx$.
  • Phase determines the state of motion; phase constant is the phase at t = 0.
  • $v_{max} = A\omega$ at the mean position; $a_{max} = A\omega^2$ at the extremes.
  • The v-x graph is an ellipse; the a-x graph is a straight line of negative slope.
  • Time from mean to extreme is T/4; time from mean to A/2 is T/12.
  • Velocity and displacement are $90^\circ$ out of phase; acceleration and displacement are $180^\circ$ out of phase.

$x = A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ Displacement in SHM

$v = \omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$ Speed at displacement x

$a = -\omega^2 x$ Acceleration in SHM

$\frac{x^2}{A^2}+\frac{v^2}{A^2\omega^2}=1$ Ellipse in the x-v plane; it becomes a circle when $\omega = 1$

NEET tip: Frequently tested items are the ratios $v_{max}/a_{max} = 1/\omega$, time to travel between two positions, and phase relations.

Oscillations of a spring: restoring force and force constant

A mass m attached to an ideal spring experiences a restoring force $F = -kx$ (Hooke's law). The spring (force) constant $k$, in N/m, measures stiffness. This gives $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, independent of amplitude. For a vertical spring, gravity only shifts the mean position, so T is unchanged and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\Delta l/g}$, where $\Delta l$ is the static extension. For springs in series, $1/k = 1/k_1+1/k_2$; in parallel, $k = k_1+k_2$. When a spring is cut, $k \propto 1/l$, so each piece is stiffer. The general rule for any system is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\text{inertia factor}/\text{restoring force per unit displacement}}$. For example, a floating cylinder of length L and density $\rho_c$ in a liquid of density $\rho_l$ has $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\rho_c/(\rho_l g)}$, so $T \propto 1/\sqrt{\rho_l}$.

  • Restoring force is $F = -kx$; k has unit N/m.
  • T is independent of amplitude and of g for a spring-mass system.
  • Series combination gives a softer spring; parallel gives a stiffer one.
  • Cutting a spring into n equal parts makes each part's constant nk.
  • A floating body, liquid in a U-tube, and a ball in a tunnel through the Earth are all SHM by the same method.

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$ Period of a spring-mass system

$k_{series} = \frac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}$, $k_{parallel} = k_1+k_2$ Effective spring constants

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\Delta l}{g}}$ Vertical spring with static extension $\Delta l$

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}$ Floating body, where h is the depth submerged at equilibrium

NEET tip: Expect spring combinations, cut springs, and the 'derive T for an unusual system' type (cork in a liquid, U-tube).

Energy in SHM: kinetic and potential energies

In SHM, kinetic energy is $K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(A^2-x^2)$ and potential energy is $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$. The total energy $E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$ stays constant when there is no damping. K is maximum at the mean position; U is maximum at the extremes. Both K and U oscillate with frequency $2\nu$, that is, with period T/2, while the total stays fixed. Averaged over a cycle, $\langle K\rangle = \langle U\rangle = E/2$. K equals U at $x = A/\sqrt{2}$. The energy-position graphs are parabolas: U opens upward, K opens downward, and their sum is a horizontal line. Energy is proportional to the square of both the amplitude and the frequency.

  • Total energy is proportional to $A^2$ and to $\omega^2$.
  • K and U vary with period T/2.
  • K = U at $x = \pm A/\sqrt{2}$.
  • At x = A/2, K = 3E/4 and U = E/4.
  • Time-averaged K and U each equal E/2.
  • In the x-v plane the curve is an ellipse; it is a circle only if $\omega = 1$, that is, k = m numerically.

$K = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2-x^2)$ Kinetic energy at displacement x

$U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ Potential energy at displacement x

$E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$ Total mechanical energy

NEET tip: Standard questions ask the fraction of energy as kinetic at a given x, the position where K = U, or the frequency of energy oscillation.

Simple pendulum and its time period

A simple pendulum is a point mass hanging from a light, inextensible string of length l. The restoring torque is $-mgl\sin\theta$. For small angles, $\sin\theta \approx \theta$, so the motion is angular SHM with $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$. T is independent of the bob's mass and, for small amplitudes, of the amplitude. Here l is measured from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob. A seconds pendulum has T = 2 s and $l \approx 1$ m (about 0.99 m). In non-inertial frames, replace g by $g_{eff}$. In a lift accelerating up, $g_{eff} = g+a$; accelerating down, $g-a$; in free fall, $g_{eff} = 0$, so the pendulum does not oscillate. In a car accelerating horizontally, $g_{eff} = \sqrt{g^2+a^2}$. Raising temperature lengthens l, so the pendulum clock loses time. On the Moon, T is larger.

  • Valid only for small angular amplitude.
  • $T \propto \sqrt{l}$ and $T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}$; independent of mass.
  • Seconds pendulum: T = 2 s, l is about 1 m.
  • Use $g_{eff}$ in a lift, an accelerating car or a liquid medium.
  • A girl standing up on a swing raises the centre of mass, so l decreases and T decreases.

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$ Period of a simple pendulum for small oscillations

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g_{eff}}}$ Period in accelerating frames

$\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta l}{l}$ Fractional change in period for a small change in length

NEET tip: Common angles are g_eff in a lift or car, percentage change in T when l changes, and effect of mass or amplitude (none).

Wave motion: longitudinal and transverse waves

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy and momentum through a medium without net transport of matter. Each particle only oscillates about its mean position. Mechanical waves need a medium with elasticity and inertia. Electromagnetic waves need no medium. In a transverse wave, particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation, forming crests and troughs; examples are waves on a stretched string and EM waves. Transverse mechanical waves need shear rigidity, so they travel in solids and along strings but not through the bulk of fluids. In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate along the direction of propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions; sound in air is the example. Longitudinal waves travel in solids, liquids and gases. Ripples on a water surface are a combination of both types.

  • Waves transport energy, not matter.
  • Transverse waves have crests and troughs; longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions.
  • Sound in gases is purely longitudinal.
  • Transverse mechanical waves cannot travel through the bulk of gases or liquids.
  • Polarisation is possible only for transverse waves.
  • Sound cannot travel in vacuum; light can.

NEET tip: Assertion-reason or statement questions test the medium requirement, the nature of sound, and polarisation applying only to transverse waves.

Speed of a travelling wave

Wave speed is $v = \nu\lambda$. It depends on the medium's elastic and inertial properties, not on the source. When a wave passes into another medium, its frequency stays the same while speed and wavelength change. For a transverse wave on a string, $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$, where T is tension and $\mu$ is mass per unit length. For longitudinal waves, $v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$ in fluids and $v = \sqrt{Y/\rho}$ in thin rods. Newton assumed isothermal compressions, $v = \sqrt{P/\rho}$, which gave about 280 m/s for air. Laplace corrected this to adiabatic compressions, $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$, giving about 331 m/s at STP. At constant temperature, changing pressure does not change v, because $P/\rho$ stays constant. In gases, $v \propto \sqrt{T}$ and $v \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$. Humidity increases v, since moist air is less dense. In general, $v_{solid} > v_{liquid} > v_{gas}$.

  • Frequency is set by the source; speed is set by the medium.
  • String: $v \propto \sqrt{T}$.
  • Laplace correction: compressions in sound are adiabatic.
  • Pressure has no effect on v at constant temperature.
  • $v \propto \sqrt{T}$ (absolute temperature); speed rises about 0.61 m/s per $^\circ C$ near room temperature.
  • Speed of sound is greater in moist air.

$v = \nu\lambda = \frac{\omega}{k}$ Wave speed

$v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ Transverse wave on a string: T tension, $\mu$ mass per unit length

$v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}$ Speed of sound in a gas (Laplace)

$v = \sqrt{\frac{Y}{\rho}}$ Longitudinal wave in a solid rod

NEET tip: Typical questions use the ratio of speeds in two gases or at two temperatures, and string speed when tension or diameter changes.

Displacement relation for a progressive wave

A sinusoidal wave travelling along +x is $y(x,t) = a\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)$. Here a is amplitude, $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the angular wave number, and $\omega = 2\pi\nu$ is the angular frequency. If x and t have the same sign, as in $(kx+\omega t)$, the wave travels along -x. Wave speed is $v = \omega/k$, the ratio of the coefficient of t to the coefficient of x. Particle velocity is $\partial y/\partial t$, with maximum value $a\omega$; this is different from wave speed. Particle velocity also equals $-v$ times the slope $\partial y/\partial x$. Two points separated by a path difference $\Delta x$ have phase difference $\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$. Two instants separated by $\Delta t$ at the same point have phase difference $\frac{2\pi}{T}\Delta t$. Intensity is proportional to $a^2\omega^2$.

  • $kx-\omega t$ means motion along +x; $kx+\omega t$ means motion along -x.
  • $v = \omega/k$ = coefficient of t divided by coefficient of x.
  • Maximum particle speed is $a\omega$, not v.
  • Phase difference = $(2\pi/\lambda) \times$ path difference.
  • Intensity is proportional to $a^2\omega^2$.

$y = a\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)$ Progressive wave along +x

$k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$ Angular wave number

$v_p = -v\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}$ Particle velocity in terms of wave speed and slope

$\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$ Phase difference from path difference

NEET tip: NEET gives a wave equation and asks for v, λ, ν, direction, maximum particle speed, or phase difference between two points.

Principle of superposition and reflection of waves

Principle of superposition: when two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic (vector) sum of the individual displacements, $y = y_1+y_2$. Each wave then continues unaffected. For two waves of the same frequency with amplitudes $a_1$ and $a_2$ and phase difference $\phi$, the resultant amplitude is $A = \sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+2a_1a_2\cos\phi}$. Constructive interference occurs at $\phi = 2n\pi$, giving $A = a_1+a_2$. Destructive interference occurs at $\phi = (2n+1)\pi$, giving $A = |a_1-a_2|$. On reflection from a rigid boundary (fixed end, or a denser medium), the wave suffers a phase change of $\pi$, so the pulse is inverted. On reflection from a free end (rarer medium), there is no phase change. Frequency never changes on reflection. For an incident wave $y_i = a\sin(kx-\omega t)$ reflected at a rigid end at x = 0, the reflected wave is $y_r = a\sin(kx+\omega t)$, so that $y_i + y_r = 2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$ with a node at x = 0. NCERT writes $y_r = a\sin(kx+\omega t+\pi)$ only to illustrate the $\pi$ phase change.

  • Superposition holds for small, linear disturbances.
  • Intensity is proportional to $A^2$; $I_{max}/I_{min} = \left(\frac{a_1+a_2}{a_1-a_2}\right)^2$.
  • Rigid end or denser medium: phase change $\pi$ (path change $\lambda/2$).
  • Free end or rarer medium: no phase change.
  • Reflection changes direction, and possibly phase, but not frequency or speed.

$A = \sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+2a_1a_2\cos\phi}$ Resultant amplitude of two superposed waves

$I = I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi$ Resultant intensity

NEET tip: Expect resultant amplitude or intensity ratio questions, and phase change on reflection at fixed or free ends.

Standing waves in strings and organ pipes; fundamental mode and harmonics

Two identical waves moving in opposite directions superpose to form a standing wave, $y = 2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$. Nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (amplitude 2a) alternate. Adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart, and a node and the next antinode are $\lambda/4$ apart. No net energy is transported. For a string fixed at both ends, the ends are nodes, so $L = n\lambda/2$ and $\nu_n = nv/2L$; all harmonics are present. For an open pipe, both ends are displacement antinodes, so $\nu_n = nv/2L$ and all harmonics are present. For a closed pipe, the closed end is a node and the open end an antinode, so $\nu = (2n-1)v/4L$ and only odd harmonics are present. The lowest frequency is the fundamental, or first harmonic; the fundamental of a closed pipe is half that of an open pipe of the same length. End correction is $e = 0.3d$ (0.6r) per open end.

  • Node-to-node distance is $\lambda/2$; node-to-antinode is $\lambda/4$.
  • String and open pipe: all harmonics, in the ratio 1:2:3.
  • Closed pipe: only odd harmonics, in the ratio 1:3:5.
  • In the pth harmonic of an open pipe there are p displacement nodes.
  • In the pth (odd) harmonic of a closed pipe there are (p+1)/2 nodes, counting the closed end.
  • A string fixed at both ends in the nth harmonic has n+1 nodes (including the ends) and n antinodes.
  • Pressure nodes are located at displacement antinodes, and vice versa.

$y = 2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$ Standing wave equation

$\nu_n = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ Harmonics of a string fixed at both ends, n = 1, 2, 3, ...

$\nu_n = \frac{nv}{2(L+2e)}$ Open organ pipe with end correction

$\nu = \frac{(2n-1)v}{4(L+e)}$ Closed organ pipe, odd harmonics only

NEET tip: Very high-yield: harmonic number, node/antinode counting, and comparing open and closed pipes (for example, the third harmonic of a closed pipe equal to the fundamental of an open pipe).

Beats

When two sound waves of slightly different frequencies $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ superpose, the loudness rises and falls periodically. This is called beats. The resultant is $y = 2a\cos(\pi\Delta\nu\, t)\sin(2\pi\nu_{av}t)$. The tone heard has frequency $\nu_{av} = (\nu_1+\nu_2)/2$, and its amplitude varies at the beat frequency $|\nu_1-\nu_2|$. The ear can distinguish beats only up to about 10 per second. Beats are used to find an unknown frequency and to tune instruments. Loading a tuning fork with wax lowers its frequency, while filing its prongs raises it. If loading the unknown fork reduces the beat count, it was the higher-frequency fork. If loading increases the beat count, it was the lower-frequency fork. Strings can be tuned the same way by changing tension.

  • Beat frequency = $|\nu_1-\nu_2|$.
  • Beat period = $1/|\nu_1-\nu_2|$.
  • Beats are audible only if the difference is about 10 Hz or less.
  • Waxing lowers a fork's frequency; filing raises it.
  • The unknown frequency is $\nu = \nu_{known} \pm b$; the sign is decided by the wax or file test.

$\nu_{beat} = |\nu_1-\nu_2|$ Number of beats per second

$\nu_{av} = \frac{\nu_1+\nu_2}{2}$ Frequency of the sound actually heard

NEET tip: NEET tests the wax/file sign decision, beats between two pipes or strings, and beat frequency from two given wave equations.

Formula sheet

$\omega = 2\pi\nu = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ Angular frequency ω, frequency ν, period T

$x = A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ SHM displacement: A amplitude, φ phase constant

$v = \omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$ Speed in SHM at displacement x

$a = -\omega^2x$ Acceleration in SHM

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$ Spring-mass period: m mass, k spring constant

$\frac{1}{k_s} = \frac{1}{k_1}+\frac{1}{k_2},\ k_p = k_1+k_2$ Springs in series and in parallel

$E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$ Total energy of SHM

$K = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2-x^2),\ U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ Kinetic and potential energy at displacement x

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g_{eff}}}$ Simple pendulum: l length, $g_{eff}$ effective gravity

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}$ Floating body: h submerged depth at equilibrium

$v = \nu\lambda = \frac{\omega}{k}$ Wave speed: λ wavelength, k wave number

$v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ Wave on a string: T tension, μ mass per unit length

$v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}$ Speed of sound in a gas: γ ratio of specific heats, P pressure, ρ density, M molar mass, T absolute temperature

$v = \sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}},\ v = \sqrt{\frac{Y}{\rho}}$ Longitudinal waves in a fluid (bulk modulus B) and in a rod (Young's modulus Y)

$y = a\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)$ Progressive wave along +x

$\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x$ Phase difference from path difference Δx

$A = \sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+2a_1a_2\cos\phi}$ Resultant amplitude on superposition

$y = 2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$ Standing wave; nodes $\lambda/2$ apart

$\nu_n = \frac{nv}{2L}$ String fixed at both ends, or open pipe; all harmonics n = 1, 2, 3, ...

$\nu = \frac{(2n-1)v}{4L}$ Closed pipe; odd harmonics only

$e = 0.3d = 0.6r$ End correction at each open end: d diameter, r radius

$\nu_{beat} = |\nu_1-\nu_2|$ Beat frequency

Common traps

  • Confusing particle velocity with wave velocity: maximum particle speed is $a\omega$, while wave speed is $\omega/k$. These are different quantities, linked by $v_p = -v\,\partial y/\partial x$, so $v_{p,max}/v = ak$ (the maximum slope of the wave).
  • Taking the frequency of KE or PE oscillation as ν: energies in SHM oscillate at $2\nu$, with period T/2.
  • Thinking the period of a spring-mass system changes with g or on the Moon: it depends only on m and k, whereas a pendulum's period depends on g.
  • Assuming a closed pipe has all harmonics: it has only odd harmonics, and its 'second overtone' is the 5th harmonic, not the 3rd.
  • Believing pressure changes the speed of sound: at constant temperature $P/\rho$ is constant, so v depends only on temperature, molar mass and humidity.
  • Counting nodes wrongly: in pipes, the open end is a displacement antinode and the closed end is a node; draw the pattern before counting.
  • Getting the wax/file logic backwards: wax lowers frequency, filing raises it; check whether the beat count increases or decreases.
  • Forgetting the small-angle condition for $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, or measuring l only up to the top of the bob instead of to its centre.

Quick revision

  • SHM condition: $a = -\omega^2x$; $v_{max} = A\omega$, $a_{max} = A\omega^2$.
  • Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$; acceleration leads displacement by $\pi$.
  • $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ for a spring and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ for a pendulum; neither depends on amplitude.
  • K = U at $x = A/\sqrt{2}$; energies oscillate at twice the motion's frequency.
  • The x-v graph of SHM is an ellipse, becoming a circle when $\omega = 1$.
  • Seconds pendulum: T = 2 s, l is about 1 m; use $g_{eff}$ in accelerating frames.
  • Sound in air is longitudinal; transverse mechanical waves need rigidity.
  • $v_{string} = \sqrt{T/\mu}$; $v_{sound} = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$, proportional to $\sqrt{T}$.
  • In $y = a\sin(kx-\omega t)$, $v = \omega/k$ and the wave moves along +x.
  • Fixed end: phase change $\pi$; free end: no phase change.
  • Open pipe and string: all harmonics, $nv/2L$; closed pipe: odd harmonics, $(2n-1)v/4L$.
  • Beats = $|\nu_1-\nu_2|$, audible only up to about 10 per second; wax lowers frequency, filing raises it.

Physics · Unit 11: Electrostatics

Electrostatics studies charges at rest: the forces between them, the electric field and potential they create, and how conductors, dielectrics and capacitors store charge and energy. It is one of the highest-weightage units in NEET Physics, usually giving 2-4 questions every year. Questions centre on Gauss's law, potential and work, behaviour of conductors, and capacitor combinations and energy.

PYQs (4): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q9, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q21, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q33, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q34

Electric charges and conservation of charge

Electric charge is an intrinsic property of matter and comes in two kinds, positive and negative. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charge is additive, so the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of the individual charges. It is quantized: any charge is an integer multiple of the elementary charge, $q = ne$ with $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,C$. Charge is conserved, so it can neither be created nor destroyed, only transferred. In pair production and annihilation the net charge stays the same. Bodies get charged by friction, conduction or induction, and charging always involves a transfer of electrons. A body that gains electrons becomes negative and gains a tiny amount of mass. Charge is also relativistically invariant: its value does not depend on the speed of the body.

  • SI unit is the coulomb (C). 1 C corresponds to about $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.
  • Quantization: $q = \pm ne$, where n is an integer. Quarks have fractional charge but are never found free.
  • Conservation holds in every process, including nuclear reactions and pair production.
  • Charging by induction gives a charge opposite to that of the inducing body, and the inducing body loses no charge.
  • Only electrons are transferred in ordinary charging. Protons stay bound in the nucleus.
  • Charge is a scalar and is additive.

$q = ne$ Quantization: n is the number of electrons transferred and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,C$.

NEET tip: Expect quick conceptual items on quantization, such as checking whether a given charge is possible or finding the number of electrons, and on conservation in nuclear or pair-production processes.

Coulomb's law and the superposition principle

Coulomb's law gives the force between two stationary point charges. The force is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, and it acts along the line joining them. In vacuum $F = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$, where $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\,N\,m^2\,C^{-2}$. In a medium of dielectric constant K the force falls to $F/K$. The force is a central, conservative force and obeys Newton's third law. The superposition principle says that the net force on a charge is the vector sum of the forces exerted by each other charge individually. Each pair interaction is unaffected by the presence of the other charges. Equilibrium and symmetry problems, such as charges at polygon corners or a third charge placed between two charges, rely on this principle.

  • $\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\,C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}$.
  • In a medium the permittivity becomes $\epsilon = K\epsilon_0$, and the force is reduced by a factor of K.
  • The force is a vector. Add forces vectorially, never as plain magnitudes.
  • For two like charges q and 4q a distance r apart, a third charge is in equilibrium at r/3 from q. Find the null point near the smaller charge.
  • Touching two identical conducting spheres makes each carry $(q_1+q_2)/2$.
  • Two equal forces F at angle $\theta$ give a resultant of $2F\cos(\theta/2)$.

$\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}^2}\hat{r}_{12}$ Vector form of Coulomb's law: the force on charge 1 due to charge 2, where $\hat{r}_{12}$ points from q2 to q1. Equivalently, $\vec{F}_{21} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\hat{r}_{21}$ is the force on q2 due to q1.

$F_{medium} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0 K}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$ Force inside a medium of dielectric constant K.

$\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2 + ... + \vec{F}_n$ Superposition principle for a system of charges.

NEET tip: NEET often asks how the force changes when charges are shared, the distance is changed or a medium is inserted, and where a third charge must sit to be in equilibrium.

Forces due to continuous charge distribution

When charge is spread continuously rather than located at points, divide it into small elements dq. Treat each element as a point charge and integrate their contributions vectorially. Three densities are used. Linear density $\lambda = dq/dl$ applies to wires and rings. Surface density $\sigma = dq/dA$ applies to sheets and shells. Volume density $\rho = dq/dV$ applies to solid spheres. The force on a test charge $q_0$ is $\vec{F} = \frac{q_0}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{dq}{r^2}\hat{r}$. Symmetry is essential: components that cancel in pairs can be dropped before integrating. A standard result is the field on the axis of a uniformly charged ring. It is zero at the centre and reaches its maximum at $x = R/\sqrt{2}$.

  • $dq = \lambda\,dl$, $\sigma\,dA$ or $\rho\,dV$, depending on the geometry.
  • Use symmetry to cancel perpendicular components before you integrate.
  • Ring on its axis: E = 0 at the centre, maximum at $x = R/\sqrt{2}$, and point-charge-like for $x \gg R$.
  • A small charge on the axis of a ring, displaced slightly, executes SHM if its sign is opposite to that of the ring.
  • For a uniform distribution, total charge = density times length, area or volume.

$\vec{F} = \frac{q_0}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \frac{dq}{r^2}\hat{r}$ Force on a test charge $q_0$ due to a continuous charge distribution.

$E_{axis} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Qx}{(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}}$ Field at distance x on the axis of a ring of charge Q and radius R.

NEET tip: Ring-axis field, the position of maximum field and symmetry-based cancellation are the usual angles of attack.

Electric field due to a point charge; electric field lines

The electric field at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed there: $\vec{E} = \vec{F}/q_0$, with the test charge taken to be vanishingly small. For a point charge, $E = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}$, directed radially outward for positive q and inward for negative q. The field is a vector, so fields due to several charges add by superposition. Field lines are imaginary curves whose tangent at any point gives the direction of E. They start on positive charges and end on negative charges, or at infinity. Two field lines never intersect, because the field has only one direction at each point. Lines crowd together where the field is strong. Electrostatic field lines never form closed loops. They meet a conductor's surface at right angles.

  • SI unit of E is N/C, which is the same as V/m.
  • The force on a charge is $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$. A negative charge feels a force opposite to E.
  • Uniform field lines are parallel and equally spaced.
  • There are no field lines inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.
  • The number of lines leaving a charge is proportional to its magnitude.
  • A charged particle in a uniform field moves with constant acceleration $qE/m$, so its path is parabolic if it enters perpendicular to the field.

$\vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$ Definition of the electric field.

$E = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}$ Field of a point charge q at distance r.

NEET tip: Common questions ask you to identify valid field-line diagrams (closed loops or crossing lines are wrong) or to find the field at the centre of symmetric charge arrangements.

Electric dipole and the field due to a dipole

An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges, +q and -q, separated by a small distance 2a. The dipole moment is $\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$, directed from -q to +q, and is measured in C m. The net charge is zero, but the field is not. For a short dipole ($r \gg a$) the field falls off as $1/r^3$, unlike the $1/r^2$ field of a point charge. On the axial line, $E = \frac{2kp}{r^3}$ along $\vec{p}$. On the equatorial line, $E = \frac{kp}{r^3}$ opposite to $\vec{p}$. At the same distance, the axial field is therefore twice the equatorial field. At a general angle $\theta$, $E = \frac{kp}{r^3}\sqrt{1+3\cos^2\theta}$. Polar molecules such as $H_2O$ carry permanent dipole moments.

  • The direction of $\vec{p}$ is from the negative charge to the positive charge.
  • $E_{axial} : E_{equatorial} = 2 : 1$ at equal distance.
  • The equatorial field is antiparallel to $\vec{p}$, while the axial field is parallel to it.
  • A dipole's field varies as $1/r^3$ and its potential as $1/r^2$.
  • The field is perpendicular to $\vec{p}$ where $\tan\theta = \sqrt{2}$, that is, $\theta \approx 54.7^\circ$.

$p = q \times 2a$ Dipole moment magnitude, where 2a is the separation.

$E_{axial} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{2p}{r^3}$ Field on the axis of a short dipole.

$E_{eq} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{p}{r^3}$ Field on the equatorial line of a short dipole.

$E = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{p}{r^3}\sqrt{1+3\cos^2\theta}$ Field at a general point at angle $\theta$ from the dipole axis.

NEET tip: Ratio questions comparing axial and equatorial fields, or asking how E scales with distance ($1/r^3$), are frequent.

Torque on a dipole in a uniform electric field

In a uniform electric field the two charges of a dipole feel equal and opposite forces, so the net force is zero. These forces form a couple, giving a torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$ with magnitude $pE\sin\theta$. The torque tends to align $\vec{p}$ with $\vec{E}$. The dipole has stable equilibrium at $\theta = 0^\circ$ and unstable equilibrium at $\theta = 180^\circ$, with zero torque in both cases. The torque is maximum, equal to pE, at $90^\circ$. The work needed to rotate the dipole from $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$ is $W = pE(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$. In a non-uniform field the dipole experiences both a torque and a net force, and is pulled toward the region of stronger field when aligned with it. A dipole slightly disturbed from stable equilibrium oscillates with angular SHM.

  • Uniform field: net force zero, torque generally non-zero.
  • Non-uniform field: both net force and torque can be non-zero.
  • Maximum torque, pE, occurs at $\theta = 90^\circ$.
  • Rotating from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$ requires work 2pE.
  • The time period of small oscillations is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(pE)}$.

$\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E},\ \tau = pE\sin\theta$ Torque on a dipole in a uniform field.

$W = pE(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$ Work done by an external agent in rotating a dipole from $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$.

NEET tip: Questions test zero net force but non-zero torque in a uniform field, stable versus unstable orientations, and the work needed to rotate a dipole.

Electric flux and Gauss's law

Electric flux measures the number of field lines crossing a surface. It is defined as $\Phi = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}$, which reduces to $EA\cos\theta$ for a uniform field. The area vector points along the normal, outward for a closed surface. Flux is a scalar with unit N m^2/C, equivalent to V m. Gauss's law states that the total flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by $\epsilon_0$: $\Phi = q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$. The flux does not depend on the shape or size of the surface or on where the charge sits inside it. Charges outside the surface contribute zero net flux. However, the field E at points on the surface does depend on all charges, inside and outside. Symmetry tricks follow directly: a charge at the centre of a cube sends $q/6\epsilon_0$ through each face.

  • Outgoing flux is positive and incoming flux is negative.
  • Zero net flux does not mean zero field on the surface.
  • A uniform field gives zero net flux through any closed surface.
  • Charge at the centre of a cube gives $q/(6\epsilon_0)$ per face.
  • Charge at a cube corner gives $q/(8\epsilon_0)$ through the whole cube. This is $q/(24\epsilon_0)$ through each of the 3 faces not containing the corner, and zero through the 3 faces that meet at the corner. Charge at the centre of a face gives $q/(2\epsilon_0)$.
  • Gauss's law is valid for any closed surface but useful for finding E only when symmetry exists.

$\Phi = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A} = EA\cos\theta$ Flux of a uniform field through a flat area A.

$\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{enc}}{\epsilon_0}$ Gauss's law for any closed surface.

NEET tip: Cube, hemisphere and cylinder flux problems that depend on the position of the charge and on symmetry are classic NEET items.

Applications of Gauss's law: infinite line charge, infinite plane sheet, thin spherical shell

Gauss's law with a suitable Gaussian surface gives E quickly for symmetric charge distributions. For an infinite line charge with density $\lambda$, a coaxial cylinder gives $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$, so E varies as $1/r$. For an infinite plane sheet with density $\sigma$, a pillbox gives $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$, independent of distance. For a thin spherical shell of charge Q and radius R, the field outside is $E = \frac{kQ}{r^2}$, as if all the charge sat at the centre. The field anywhere inside the shell is zero. The same method extends to a uniformly charged solid (insulating) sphere. Outside it, $E = kQ/r^2$. Inside it, $E = \frac{kQr}{R^3} = \frac{\rho r}{3\epsilon_0}$, which grows linearly with r and is maximum at the surface.

  • Line charge: E is proportional to 1/r. Plane sheet: E is independent of r. Point or sphere outside: E is proportional to $1/r^2$.
  • Between two oppositely charged parallel sheets, E = $\sigma/\epsilon_0$. Outside them, E = 0.
  • Just outside a charged conductor's surface, E = $\sigma/\epsilon_0$, twice the field of an isolated sheet.
  • For a shell, E is discontinuous at r = R, jumping from 0 to $kQ/R^2$.
  • For a solid sphere, E is continuous and peaks at r = R.
  • In terms of $\rho$, $kQ = \frac{\rho R^3}{3\epsilon_0}$ for a solid sphere.

$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$ Field at distance r from an infinite line charge.

$E = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$ Field of an infinite plane sheet (non-conducting).

$E = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r^2}\ (r \ge R),\ E = 0\ (r < R)$ Field of a thin spherical shell.

$E_{inside} = \frac{\rho r}{3\epsilon_0}$ Field inside a uniformly charged solid sphere at distance r from its centre.

NEET tip: Expect graph-based questions (E versus r for a shell and a solid sphere) and multi-sheet field problems.

Electric potential due to a point charge, a dipole and a system of charges

The electric potential at a point is the work done by an external agent in bringing a unit positive charge slowly from infinity to that point. For a point charge, $V = \frac{kq}{r}$. Potential is a scalar, so for a system of charges the individual potentials add algebraically: $V = k\sum q_i/r_i$. For a short dipole, $V = \frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}$. This is maximum on the axis and zero everywhere on the equatorial plane, even though E is not zero there. For a spherical shell, V = kQ/r outside and V = kQ/R, a constant, inside. For a uniformly charged solid sphere, $V_{inside} = \frac{kQ(3R^2 - r^2)}{2R^3}$. At the centre this equals 1.5 times the surface value.

  • SI unit is the volt, where 1 V = 1 J/C.
  • Potential is a scalar and carries the sign of the charge.
  • Dipole equatorial plane: V = 0 but E is not zero.
  • Shell: inside, V is constant and equals the surface value while E = 0.
  • Solid sphere: $V_{centre} = \frac{3}{2}V_{surface}$.
  • At points where V = 0, E need not be zero, and vice versa.

$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}$ Potential of a point charge.

$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}$ Potential of a short dipole at distance r and angle $\theta$.

$V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\sum_i \frac{q_i}{r_i}$ Potential due to a system of point charges.

$V_{in} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Q(3R^2 - r^2)}{2R^3}$ Potential inside a uniformly charged solid sphere.

NEET tip: Potential at the centre of symmetric arrangements, and points where V = 0 but E is not zero, are tested repeatedly.

Potential difference and equipotential surfaces

The potential difference between two points is the work done by an external agent per unit charge in moving a charge slowly between them: $V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l}$. The electrostatic field is conservative, so this work depends only on the end points and not on the path. A charge can be dragged through a tube or along any curved route and the work is still $q(V_B - V_A)$. The field is related to potential by $E = -dV/dr$, so E points in the direction of steepest decrease of V. An equipotential surface is one on which V is constant everywhere. No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface, and E is always perpendicular to it. Equipotentials are concentric spheres for a point charge and parallel planes for a uniform field. They crowd together where the field is strong.

  • The work done by external agent equals $q(V_B - V_A)$ for slow movement, and is path independent.
  • $E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$. In a uniform field, V = Ed.
  • E points from high potential to low potential.
  • Two equipotential surfaces never intersect.
  • The surface and interior of a conductor in equilibrium form one equipotential volume.
  • Around any closed loop, $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0$.

$V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l}$ Potential difference from the field.

$W_{A \to B} = q(V_B - V_A)$ Work by an external agent in moving charge q slowly from A to B.

$\vec{E} = -\nabla V,\ E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ Field from potential. Use it to find E when V(x) is given.

NEET tip: NEET exploits path independence (complex paths with simple end points) and the perpendicularity of equipotentials to field lines.

Electrical potential energy of a system of two point charges and of a dipole

The potential energy of a system of charges is the work done in assembling them from infinity. For two point charges, $U = \frac{kq_1q_2}{r}$. U is positive for like charges and negative for unlike charges. For three or more charges, add the energies of all distinct pairs. A charge q placed at a point where the external potential is V has energy qV. Energy conservation, $\Delta K = -\Delta U = -q\Delta V$, gives speeds of charges released in a field. A dipole in a uniform field has $U = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E} = -pE\cos\theta$. This energy is minimum, -pE, at $\theta = 0$ (stable) and maximum, +pE, at $\theta = 180^\circ$ (unstable). It is zero at $90^\circ$, which is taken as the reference orientation.

  • Count each pair once: three charges have 3 pairs and four charges have 6 pairs.
  • Negative U means a bound system that needs external work to separate.
  • Released charge: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = q(V_{initial} - V_{final})$, keeping the signs.
  • Dipole: U is minimum when aligned with E and maximum when anti-aligned.
  • The 1 eV energy unit equals $1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,J$.

$U = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{r}$ Potential energy of two point charges.

$U = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\sum_{i<j}\frac{q_iq_j}{r_{ij}}$ Potential energy of a system of point charges.

$U = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E} = -pE\cos\theta$ Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field.

NEET tip: Energy conservation problems, such as finding the speed of a charge falling toward a charged sphere, together with the configuration energy of triangles and squares, appear often.

Conductors and insulators

Conductors contain free charge carriers, while insulators have none. In electrostatic equilibrium a conductor has the following properties. E is zero everywhere inside the material. Any excess charge resides on the outer surface. E just outside is normal to the surface, with magnitude $\sigma/\epsilon_0$. The whole conductor is an equipotential. Surface charge density is greater where the radius of curvature is smaller, which is why charge leaks from sharp points (corona discharge). If a charge Q is placed inside a cavity, -Q is induced on the cavity wall and +Q on the outer surface. The field inside the cavity is non-zero because it is produced by Q. The outer surface charge redistributes uniformly on a sphere regardless of where the cavity or charge sits. The outside field is therefore symmetric and depends only on the net outer charge. Electrostatic shielding: the field inside a charge-free cavity of a conductor is zero, whatever the external charges or fields. A charge placed inside the cavity is not shielded from the outside unless the conductor is earthed.

  • Inside the conducting material, E = 0 and V = constant, equal to the surface value.
  • A charge in a cavity induces -Q on the inner wall and +Q on the outer surface of an isolated neutral conductor.
  • The outer field of a spherical conductor is unaffected by the position of the charge in the cavity.
  • $\sigma \propto 1/r$ for connected spheres, so charges divide in the ratio of the radii and the potentials become equal.
  • Outside charges cannot create a field inside an empty cavity (shielding).
  • Insulators hold charge where it is placed and do not redistribute it.

$E_{surface} = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$ Field just outside a charged conductor, directed normal to the surface.

$\frac{q_1}{q_2} = \frac{r_1}{r_2},\ \frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2} = \frac{r_2}{r_1}$ Two conducting spheres joined by a wire.

NEET tip: Cavity-charge conductor questions (field inside the cavity, in the material and outside) are a recent NEET favourite.

Dielectrics and electric polarization

Dielectrics are insulators that become polarized in an electric field. In non-polar molecules such as $O_2$ and $N_2$, the field induces dipoles by displacing the charge centres. In polar molecules such as $H_2O$ and HCl, the field partially aligns permanent dipoles that are otherwise randomly oriented. Polarization $\vec{P}$ is the dipole moment per unit volume. For linear dielectrics, $\vec{P} = \chi_e\epsilon_0\vec{E}$, where $\chi_e$ is the electric susceptibility. Polarization produces bound surface charges that set up an opposing field inside. The net field is therefore reduced, $E = E_0/K$, where the dielectric constant is $K = 1 + \chi_e = \epsilon/\epsilon_0$. K equals 1 for vacuum, is very large for water (about 80), and is effectively infinite for a metal.

  • Dielectric constant (relative permittivity) is $K = \epsilon/\epsilon_0 \ge 1$ and is dimensionless.
  • The field, force and potential due to given charges are reduced by a factor of K in a medium.
  • Polar molecules have permanent dipoles. Non-polar molecules have only induced dipoles.
  • Induced (bound) charge on a dielectric surface is $q_b = q(1 - 1/K)$.
  • Dielectric strength is the maximum field a dielectric can withstand without breakdown. For air it is about $3 \times 10^6\,V/m$.

$\vec{P} = \chi_e\epsilon_0\vec{E}$ Polarization of a linear dielectric.

$K = 1 + \chi_e = \frac{\epsilon}{\epsilon_0}$ Dielectric constant related to susceptibility.

$E = \frac{E_0}{K}$ Reduced field inside a dielectric.

NEET tip: Conceptual questions on polar versus non-polar molecules, the reduction of field by a factor of K, and induced charge on a dielectric slab are common.

Capacitors and capacitance; series and parallel combinations

A capacitor consists of two conductors carrying equal and opposite charges, ±Q, with a potential difference V between them. Capacitance is defined as $C = Q/V$. It depends only on geometry and the medium, not on Q or V. The SI unit is the farad (F), and practical values are in $\mu F$ or pF. An isolated sphere has $C = 4\pi\epsilon_0R$. In a series combination every capacitor carries the same charge, the voltages add, and $1/C_{eq} = \sum 1/C_i$. The equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest individual value. In a parallel combination every capacitor has the same voltage, the charges add, and $C_{eq} = \sum C_i$. In circuit problems, redraw the network carefully and identify which capacitors share the same pair of nodes. For a bridge circuit, use symmetry or the balanced condition.

  • Series: same Q, voltage divides as $V_i \propto 1/C_i$.
  • Parallel: same V, charge divides as $Q_i \propto C_i$.
  • Two capacitors in series: $C_{eq} = \frac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}$.
  • n identical capacitors: C/n in series and nC in parallel.
  • The capacitance of the Earth is only about 711 $\mu F$, which shows that 1 F is a huge unit.
  • In steady DC conditions no current flows through a capacitor branch.

$C = \frac{Q}{V}$ Definition of capacitance.

$C = 4\pi\epsilon_0 R$ Capacitance of an isolated conducting sphere of radius R.

$\frac{1}{C_s} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + ...$ Series combination.

$C_p = C_1 + C_2 + ...$ Parallel combination.

NEET tip: Mixed series-parallel networks asking for the charge, voltage or energy of a particular capacitor are the most common question type.

Parallel plate capacitor with and without a dielectric

A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area A separated by distance d. The field between the plates is uniform, $E = \sigma/\epsilon_0$, and $C_0 = \epsilon_0A/d$. Filling the gap completely with a dielectric of constant K gives $C = KC_0$. A slab of thickness t < d gives $C = \frac{\epsilon_0A}{d - t + t/K}$, and a metal slab ($K \to \infty$) gives $\frac{\epsilon_0A}{d-t}$. Two cases must be distinguished. If the battery stays connected, V is constant, so inserting a dielectric raises Q to KQ and U to KU, while E stays the same. If the battery is disconnected, Q is constant, so V falls to V/K, E falls to E/K and U falls to U/K. Dielectrics arranged side by side act as capacitors in parallel. Dielectric layers stacked across the gap act as capacitors in series.

  • Capacitance is proportional to A and K, and inversely proportional to d.
  • Battery connected: V is fixed, while Q and U increase by a factor of K.
  • Battery disconnected: Q is fixed, while V, E and U all decrease by a factor of K.
  • A slab of thickness t reduces the effective separation to $d - t + t/K$.
  • Side-by-side dielectric fillings combine in parallel. Layered fillings combine in series.
  • Force of attraction between the plates: $F = \frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0A}$.

$C_0 = \frac{\epsilon_0A}{d}$ Parallel plate capacitor with vacuum or air.

$C = \frac{K\epsilon_0A}{d}$ Gap completely filled with a dielectric.

$C = \frac{\epsilon_0A}{d - t + \frac{t}{K}}$ Dielectric slab of thickness t partially filling the gap.

$F = \frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon_0A}$ Attractive force between the plates.
