NEET tip: Questions on how C, Q, V, E and U change when a dielectric is inserted with the battery connected or disconnected are near-certain.

Energy stored in a capacitor

Charging a capacitor requires work against the field already built up between its plates. This work is stored as electrostatic energy, $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}QV$. The energy resides in the field, with energy density $u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2$ in vacuum and $\frac{1}{2}K\epsilon_0E^2$ in a dielectric. A battery charging a capacitor supplies energy QV, but only half of it is stored. The other half is dissipated as heat, whatever the resistance. When two capacitors at different potentials are connected, charge flows until their potentials become equal. The common potential is $V = \frac{C_1V_1 + C_2V_2}{C_1+C_2}$, and some energy is always lost. In combinations, use $\frac{1}{2}CV^2$ for parallel elements (same V) and $\frac{Q^2}{2C}$ for series elements (same Q). This makes energy-ratio questions simple.

  • Energy in series: $U \propto 1/C$, so the smaller capacitor stores more energy.
  • Energy in parallel: $U \propto C$, so the larger capacitor stores more energy.
  • The battery supplies QV and the capacitor stores QV/2. The rest is lost as heat.
  • Energy loss on sharing charge is $\frac{C_1C_2(V_1-V_2)^2}{2(C_1+C_2)}$.
  • Total charge is conserved on sharing, but energy is not.
  • Energy density depends only on the local field: $u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2$.

$U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}QV$ Energy stored in a capacitor.

$u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2$ Energy per unit volume of an electric field.

$V_{common} = \frac{C_1V_1 + C_2V_2}{C_1 + C_2}$ Common potential after two charged capacitors are connected.

$\Delta U = \frac{C_1C_2(V_1 - V_2)^2}{2(C_1 + C_2)}$ Energy lost when two capacitors share charge.

NEET tip: Ratio of the energy in one capacitor to the total energy of a network, and energy loss on sharing charge, are the favourite angles.

Formula sheet

$q = ne$ Quantization of charge. n is an integer and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,C$.

$F = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$ Coulomb force between point charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ separated by r. $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9$ SI units.

$E = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^2}$ Electric field of a point charge q at distance r.

$E_{ring} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Qx}{(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}}$ Field on the axis of a ring of charge Q and radius R at distance x from its centre.

$p = q(2a)$ Dipole moment. 2a is the separation, and p points from -q to +q.

$E_{axial} = \frac{2kp}{r^3},\ E_{eq} = \frac{kp}{r^3}$ Short dipole fields on the axial and equatorial lines, with $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}$.

$\tau = pE\sin\theta$ Torque on a dipole p at angle $\theta$ to a uniform field E.

$U = -pE\cos\theta$ Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field.

$\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{enc}}{\epsilon_0}$ Gauss's law. $q_{enc}$ is the charge enclosed by the closed surface.

$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$ Infinite line charge with linear density $\lambda$, at distance r.

$E = \frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$ Infinite plane sheet with surface density $\sigma$. Near a conductor's surface the field is $\sigma/\epsilon_0$.

$E_{shell} = \frac{kQ}{r^2}\ (r \ge R),\ 0\ (r<R)$ Thin spherical shell of charge Q and radius R.

$E_{solid,in} = \frac{kQr}{R^3} = \frac{\rho r}{3\epsilon_0}$ Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere with volume density $\rho$.

$V = \frac{kq}{r}$ Potential of a point charge. Add algebraically for several charges.

$V_{dipole} = \frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}$ Potential of a short dipole at angle $\theta$ from its axis.

$V_{solid,in} = \frac{kQ(3R^2 - r^2)}{2R^3}$ Potential inside a uniformly charged solid sphere. It equals 1.5 times the surface value at the centre.

$E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ Field as the negative potential gradient.

$W = q(V_B - V_A)$ External work to move charge q slowly from A to B, independent of the path.

$U = \frac{kq_1q_2}{r}$ Potential energy of two point charges. Sum over all pairs for a system.

$C = \frac{Q}{V},\ C_{sphere} = 4\pi\epsilon_0R$ Definition of capacitance, and the capacitance of an isolated sphere.

$C = \frac{K\epsilon_0A}{d}$ Parallel plate capacitor with plate area A, separation d and dielectric constant K.

$C = \frac{\epsilon_0A}{d - t + t/K}$ Parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric slab of thickness t.

$\frac{1}{C_s} = \sum\frac{1}{C_i},\ C_p = \sum C_i$ Series and parallel combinations.

$U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$ Energy stored in a capacitor.

$u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2$ Energy density of an electric field in vacuum.

Common traps

  • Assuming zero flux through a closed surface means zero field on it. Zero flux only means zero net enclosed charge. Outside charges still create a field on the surface.
  • Thinking the work in moving a charge depends on the path, such as through a tube or a curved route. The electrostatic field is conservative, so only the potentials at the end points matter.
  • Believing the field inside a cavity of a conductor is always zero. It is zero only if the cavity contains no charge. A charge inside the cavity produces a non-zero field there, while the outer field depends only on the outer surface charge.
  • Using the shell formula inside a solid charged sphere. For a uniformly charged insulating sphere, E inside is proportional to r and V inside is $kQ(3R^2 - r^2)/(2R^3)$, not kQ/R.
  • Confusing battery-connected and battery-disconnected cases on dielectric insertion. Connected means V is constant and Q and U rise by K. Disconnected means Q is constant and V, E and U fall by K.
  • Treating V = 0 as implying E = 0. On a dipole's equatorial line V = 0 but E is not zero. Inside a charged shell E = 0 but V is not zero.
  • Forgetting that the battery supplies energy QV while the capacitor stores only QV/2, and that energy is lost when charged capacitors are connected even though charge is conserved.
  • Taking the direction of the dipole moment as + to -. It points from -q to +q, and the equatorial field is opposite to $\vec{p}$.

Quick revision

  • Charge is quantized, additive, conserved and invariant, with $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,C$.
  • Coulomb force varies as $1/r^2$ and is reduced by a factor of K in a medium. Use vector superposition for multiple charges.
  • Distance dependence of E: point charge $1/r^2$, dipole $1/r^3$, line charge $1/r$, sheet independent of r.
  • A dipole in a uniform field feels zero net force and torque $pE\sin\theta$. Its energy is $-pE\cos\theta$, minimum when aligned.
  • Gauss's law: flux = $q_{enc}/\epsilon_0$. A cube with a central charge has $q/6\epsilon_0$ per face.
  • Shell: E = 0 inside and V constant inside. Solid sphere: E is proportional to r inside and V at the centre is 1.5 times the surface value.
  • Work = $q\Delta V$ and is path independent. Equipotentials are perpendicular to field lines and no work is done along them.
  • Released charge: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = |q\Delta V|$. Use V outside a sphere = kQ/r.
  • Conductor: E = 0 inside, charge on the surface, equipotential, surface field $\sigma/\epsilon_0$, and $\sigma$ largest at sharp points.
  • Series combination has the same Q and $C_{eq}$ smaller than the smallest capacitor. Parallel combination has the same V and $C_{eq}$ equal to the sum.
  • $C = K\epsilon_0A/d$. With a slab, use $d - t + t/K$. A metal slab reduces the separation to $d - t$.
  • $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = Q^2/2C$. Energy density is $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2$. Sharing charge always loses energy.

Physics · Unit 12: Current Electricity

Current Electricity covers how charges move steadily through conductors and how currents, voltages, resistances, cells and networks are analysed using Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's rules. It is one of the highest-weightage units in NEET Physics. It typically gives 2-4 direct questions on resistance combinations, temperature dependence, cells, power and bridge circuits, and its tools are reused in magnetism and semiconductor problems.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q36

Electric current, drift velocity and mobility

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge through a cross-section, $I = \frac{dq}{dt}$. Its SI unit is the ampere. Current has a direction but is a scalar, because it does not obey vector addition. In a metal, free electrons move randomly at high thermal speeds of about $10^5$ m/s, so their average velocity is zero. When an electric field $E$ is applied, each electron is accelerated between collisions. This gives a small net average velocity opposite to $E$, called the drift velocity, $v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m}$, where $\tau$ is the relaxation time (mean time between collisions). Drift velocity is very small, about $10^{-4}$ m/s. Current is related to drift velocity by $I = neAv_d$, where $n$ is the free-electron density. Mobility $\mu$ is the drift velocity per unit electric field. Current density $J$ is current per unit area normal to the flow; it is a vector.

  • Conventional current flows opposite to electron flow.
  • Drift velocity is about $10^{-4}$ m/s, yet a bulb glows almost instantly because the electric field is set up in the wire at nearly the speed of light.
  • For a given current, $v_d \propto \frac{1}{A}$, so drift velocity is larger at the narrower part of a wire.
  • For a wire of length $l$ across a voltage $V$, $E = \frac{V}{l}$, so $v_d \propto \frac{V}{l}$.
  • Mobility has SI unit $m^2V^{-1}s^{-1}$.
  • When temperature increases, $\tau$ decreases, so both $v_d$ and $\mu$ decrease.
  • Current density $J$ is a vector, while current $I$ is a scalar.

$I = \frac{dq}{dt}$ Instantaneous current. For steady current, $I = \frac{q}{t}$.

$v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m}$ Drift speed of electrons; $\tau$ is relaxation time and $m$ is electron mass.

$I = neAv_d$ Current in terms of electron density $n$, cross-sectional area $A$ and drift velocity $v_d$.

$\mu = \frac{v_d}{E} = \frac{e\tau}{m}$ Mobility: drift velocity per unit electric field.

$J = \frac{I}{A} = nev_d$ Current density (current per unit area).

NEET tip: NEET asks for ratios of drift velocity when length, area, voltage or temperature change, and for numerical values of $v_d$ using $I = neAv_d$.

Ohm's law and electrical resistance

Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, provided temperature and other physical conditions stay constant. So $V = IR$, where the constant $R$ is the resistance, measured in ohm ($\Omega$). Resistance arises because drifting electrons collide with lattice ions and lose energy. For a uniform wire, $R = \frac{\rho l}{A}$. Resistance depends on the material, the dimensions and the temperature. A frequent NEET type involves stretching a wire. The volume stays constant, so $lA$ is constant. Hence $R \propto l^2$ or $R \propto \frac{1}{A^2}$, which also gives $R \propto \frac{1}{r^4}$ for radius $r$. Conductance is $G = \frac{1}{R}$; its unit is siemens (S, also called mho).

  • Ohm's law holds only at constant temperature and physical conditions.
  • Resistance depends on dimensions; resistivity does not.
  • If a wire is stretched to $n$ times its length, $R' = n^2R$.
  • If the radius is reduced to $\frac{1}{n}$ of its value at constant volume, $R' = n^4R$.
  • Cutting a wire into $n$ equal parts gives each part resistance $\frac{R}{n}$.
  • The microscopic form of Ohm's law is $J = \sigma E$.

$V = IR$ Ohm's law; $R$ is constant for ohmic conductors.

$R = \frac{\rho l}{A}$ Resistance of a uniform conductor of length $l$, area $A$ and resistivity $\rho$.

$\frac{R_2}{R_1} = \left(\frac{l_2}{l_1}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\right)^2$ Change in resistance when a wire is stretched at constant volume.

$G = \frac{1}{R}$ Conductance, in siemens.

NEET tip: Expect stretching-wire ratio questions, such as finding $R'$ when length is doubled or the percentage change in $R$ for a 0.1% stretch (answer 0.2%).

V-I characteristics of ohmic and non-ohmic conductors

For ohmic conductors such as metals at constant temperature, the V-I graph is a straight line through the origin. The slope is constant: in a V-I graph the slope equals $R$, and in an I-V graph the slope equals $\frac{1}{R}$. Non-ohmic devices break this linearity in different ways. The relation may be non-linear, as in a filament bulb, where heating raises $R$. It may depend on the sign of $V$, as in a p-n junction diode. It may be non-unique, as in GaAs, where the same current can occur at more than one voltage. A water voltameter shows a non-linear graph that does not pass through the origin. For non-ohmic devices, the dynamic resistance is defined as $r_d = \frac{dV}{dI}$.

  • An ohmic conductor gives a straight-line V-I graph through the origin with constant slope.
  • Non-ohmic examples: diode, transistor, thyristor, GaAs, filament lamp and electrolytes.
  • In a V-I graph, a steeper line means larger resistance. In an I-V graph, a steeper line means smaller resistance.
  • For a metal wire plotted at two temperatures, the line with smaller slope in the I-V graph is the higher-temperature line.
  • A negative slope region, called negative resistance, occurs in GaAs.

$R = \frac{V}{I}$ Static resistance at a given operating point.

$r_d = \frac{dV}{dI}$ Dynamic resistance, used for non-linear devices.

NEET tip: Graph-based questions ask you to compare resistances or temperatures from slopes, or to identify which device is non-ohmic.

Electrical energy and power

When charge $q$ moves through a potential difference $V$, it loses energy $qV$. In a resistor this energy appears as heat; this is Joule heating. The electrical power is $P = VI$. For a resistor, this can also be written as $P = I^2R$ or $P = \frac{V^2}{R}$. Choose the form based on what is common to the resistors being compared. In series the current is common, so use $I^2R$: the larger resistance dissipates more power. In parallel the voltage is common, so use $\frac{V^2}{R}$: the smaller resistance dissipates more power. A bulb rated $P$ watt at $V$ volt has resistance $R = \frac{V^2}{P}$. When bulbs are joined in series, the lower-wattage bulb glows brighter. Power is transmitted at high voltage to reduce the $I^2R$ loss in the lines. The commercial unit of energy is the kWh, equal to $3.6 \times 10^6$ J.

  • Heat produced is $H = I^2Rt$ (Joule's law of heating).
  • Rated bulbs in series: the lower-wattage bulb has higher $R$, so it glows brighter.
  • Rated bulbs in parallel: the higher-wattage bulb glows brighter.
  • Bulbs in series: $\frac{1}{P_{total}} = \frac{1}{P_1} + \frac{1}{P_2}$. Bulbs in parallel: $P_{total} = P_1 + P_2$.
  • If supply voltage drops to a fraction $f$ of the rated value, power becomes $f^2$ times the rated power, assuming $R$ stays constant.
  • 1 kWh $= 3.6 \times 10^6$ J; this is the 'unit' on electricity bills.

$P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$ Power dissipated in a resistor.

$W = VIt = I^2Rt = \frac{V^2t}{R}$ Electrical energy consumed, or heat produced, in time $t$.

$R = \frac{V_{rated}^2}{P_{rated}}$ Resistance of an appliance from its rating.

$P_{loss} = \frac{P^2R_c}{V^2}$ Line loss when power $P$ is sent at voltage $V$ through cables of resistance $R_c$.

NEET tip: NEET frequently asks about brightness of rated bulbs in series or parallel, power at reduced voltage, and cost of energy in kWh.

Electrical resistivity and conductivity

Resistivity $\rho$ is the resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area. It is a property of the material and temperature only, not of the shape. From the free-electron model, $\rho = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau}$, so resistivity depends on the electron density $n$ and the relaxation time $\tau$. Conductivity is $\sigma = \frac{1}{\rho}$, with SI unit $\Omega^{-1}m^{-1}$ (S/m). Ohm's law in vector form is $\vec{J} = \sigma\vec{E}$. Typical resistivities are: metals $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-6}\ \Omega$m, semiconductors in between, and insulators $10^{14}$ to $10^{16}\ \Omega$m. Alloys such as nichrome, manganin and constantan have high resistivity and a very low temperature coefficient. Manganin and constantan are therefore used in standard resistors, potentiometer wires and metre-bridge wires. Nichrome is used in heater elements because of its high $\rho$ and high melting point.

  • Unit of $\rho$ is $\Omega$m; unit of $\sigma$ is S/m.
  • $\rho$ does not change when a wire is stretched or cut.
  • Silver has the lowest resistivity among common metals; copper and aluminium are used for wiring.
  • Resistivity of an alloy is generally greater than that of its constituent metals.
  • Resistivity decreases if $n$ or $\tau$ increases.

$\rho = \frac{RA}{l} = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau}$ Resistivity from measurements and from the microscopic model.

$\sigma = \frac{1}{\rho} = \frac{ne^2\tau}{m}$ Conductivity of a material.

$J = \sigma E$ Microscopic (vector) form of Ohm's law.

$\sigma = ne\mu$ Conductivity in terms of mobility.

NEET tip: Conceptual questions test whether resistivity changes with dimensions (it does not) and which material is used for heaters versus standard resistors.

Series and parallel combinations of resistors

In a series combination, the same current flows through every resistor. The voltages add, and the equivalent resistance is $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \dots$, which is larger than the largest resistor. In a parallel combination, the potential difference across each resistor is the same. The currents add, and $\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots$, which is smaller than the smallest resistor. Two useful results follow. In series, voltage divides in proportion to resistance. In parallel, current divides in inverse proportion to resistance. For $n$ identical resistors $R$, series gives $nR$, parallel gives $\frac{R}{n}$, and the ratio of series to parallel resistance is $n^2$. For complex networks, use symmetry, identify points at equal potential, or redraw the circuit between the two terminals.

  • Series: same current. Parallel: same voltage.
  • $R_{series} \geq n^2R_{parallel}$ for $n$ resistors, with equality when all are equal.
  • Two resistors in parallel: $R_{eq} = \frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}$.
  • A wire bent into a circle: the resistance between diametrically opposite points is $\frac{R}{4}$.
  • Any resistor connected between two points at equal potential carries no current and can be removed.
  • Connecting a zero-resistance wire across a resistor shorts it out.

$R_s = R_1 + R_2 + \dots + R_n$ Equivalent resistance in series.

$\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{R_n}$ Equivalent resistance in parallel.

$V_1 = \frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}V$ Voltage divider rule for two series resistors.

$I_1 = \frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}I$ Current divider rule for two parallel resistors.

NEET tip: Expect equivalent resistance of symmetric networks (cube, triangle, ring) and current or voltage division in mixed circuits.

Temperature dependence of resistance

For metals, resistivity rises approximately linearly with temperature: $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$. Here $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient of resistivity, and it is positive for metals. The physical reason is that the relaxation time $\tau$ decreases as temperature rises. Over small ranges, the resistance follows the same rule, $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$. In semiconductors and insulators, $\alpha$ is negative: rising temperature frees more charge carriers, so $n$ increases sharply and $\rho$ falls. Alloys such as manganin have a very small $\alpha$. Some materials become superconductors below a critical temperature, where $\rho = 0$. When resistors with positive and negative $\alpha$ are combined, find the total resistance as a function of $\Delta T$. Then decide how the circuit current changes; terms in $\alpha^2$ may matter.

  • Metals: $\alpha > 0$; for copper, $\alpha \approx 4 \times 10^{-3}$ $K^{-1}$.
  • Semiconductors (Si, Ge, carbon, thermistors): $\alpha < 0$.
  • Manganin and constantan: $\alpha \approx 0$, so their resistance is nearly independent of temperature.
  • Equal $R_0$ with $+\alpha$ and $-\alpha$ in series: the total stays $2R_0$, independent of $\Delta T$.
  • The same pair in parallel: $R_{eq} = \frac{R_0(1-\alpha^2\Delta T^2)}{2}$, which decreases slightly with temperature.
  • Use $\frac{R_2}{R_1} = \frac{1+\alpha T_2}{1+\alpha T_1}$ when the reference resistance at $0^\circ C$ is unknown.

$\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$ Temperature dependence of resistivity.

$R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$ Resistance at a temperature $\Delta T$ above the reference.

$\alpha = \frac{R_T - R_0}{R_0\Delta T}$ Temperature coefficient from measured resistances.

$\alpha_{eq} = \frac{R_1\alpha_1 + R_2\alpha_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ Effective temperature coefficient of two resistors in series.

NEET tip: NEET tests how current in series or parallel circuits changes when resistors with opposite temperature coefficients are heated, and numericals using $R_T = R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T)$.

Internal resistance, potential difference and emf of a cell

The emf $\varepsilon$ of a cell is the work done per unit charge by the non-electrostatic (chemical) force in moving charge from the negative to the positive terminal inside the cell. It equals the terminal voltage when no current is drawn. Internal resistance $r$ is the opposition offered by the electrolyte and electrodes. When the cell delivers current $I$ to an external resistance $R$, the current is $I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r}$ and the terminal voltage is $V = \varepsilon - Ir$, which is less than $\varepsilon$. When the cell is being charged, $V = \varepsilon + Ir$. On a short circuit ($R = 0$), $I_{max} = \frac{\varepsilon}{r}$ and $V = 0$. Maximum power is delivered to $R$ when $R = r$, and this maximum power is $\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4r}$. Internal resistance increases with the age of the cell and with the distance between the electrodes. It decreases with larger electrode area and higher temperature.

  • Emf is not a force; it is energy per unit charge, measured in volt.
  • Open circuit: $V = \varepsilon$.
  • Discharging: $V < \varepsilon$. Charging: $V > \varepsilon$.
  • Maximum power transfer condition: $R = r$. The efficiency at that point is only 50%.
  • Efficiency of power delivery is $\eta = \frac{V}{\varepsilon} = \frac{R}{R+r}$.
  • The V-I graph of a cell is a straight line with intercept $\varepsilon$ on the V-axis and slope $-r$.

$I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r}$ Current drawn from a cell of internal resistance $r$.

$V = \varepsilon - Ir$ Terminal voltage while discharging. Use $V = \varepsilon + Ir$ while charging.

$r = R\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{V} - 1\right)$ Internal resistance from measured $\varepsilon$, $V$ and $R$.

$P_{max} = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4r}$ Maximum power delivered to an external load, reached when $R = r$.

NEET tip: NEET asks for $r$ from terminal-voltage data, terminal voltage during charging, and the maximum power transfer condition.

Combination of cells in series and parallel

For cells in series, the emfs add when the cells are joined in the same sense and subtract when one is reversed. The internal resistances always add. So $n$ identical cells in series give $I = \frac{n\varepsilon}{R + nr}$. If $m$ cells out of $n$ are reversed, the net emf becomes $(n - 2m)\varepsilon$. For two cells in parallel with like terminals joined, $\varepsilon_{eq} = \frac{\varepsilon_1r_2 + \varepsilon_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2}$ and $r_{eq} = \frac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}$. For $m$ identical cells in parallel, $I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + \frac{r}{m}}$. Series is preferred when $R \gg r$ and parallel when $R \ll r$. In a mixed grouping of $n$ cells per row and $m$ rows, the current is $I = \frac{n\varepsilon}{R + \frac{nr}{m}}$. This current is maximum when $R = \frac{nr}{m}$, that is, when the external resistance equals the total internal resistance.

  • Series: emfs add with sign; internal resistances always add.
  • Parallel identical cells: emf is unchanged and internal resistance becomes $\frac{r}{m}$.
  • Reversing $m$ cells out of $n$ in series gives net emf $(n-2m)\varepsilon$, but the internal resistance is still $nr$.
  • Mixed grouping gives maximum current when $\frac{nr}{m} = R$.
  • In parallel with unequal emfs, a current circulates inside the cells even with no external load.

$\varepsilon_{eq} = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2,\ r_{eq} = r_1 + r_2$ Two cells in series, same sense.

$\varepsilon_{eq} = \frac{\varepsilon_1r_2 + \varepsilon_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2}$ Equivalent emf of two cells in parallel.

$\frac{1}{r_{eq}} = \frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}$ Equivalent internal resistance of cells in parallel.

$I = \frac{n\varepsilon}{R + \frac{nr}{m}}$ Current for a mixed grouping of $m$ rows, each with $n$ cells in series.

NEET tip: Typical questions: wrongly connected cells in series, the equivalent emf of parallel cells, and the arrangement that gives maximum current.

Kirchhoff's laws and their applications

Kirchhoff's first law (the junction rule, KCL) states that the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a junction is zero. Equivalently, the current entering a junction equals the current leaving it. This follows from conservation of charge. Kirchhoff's second law (the loop rule, KVL) states that the algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero. This follows from conservation of energy, because the electrostatic field is conservative. Use a consistent sign convention when going around a loop. Crossing a resistor in the direction of the assumed current gives a change of $-IR$, and against it $+IR$. Crossing a cell from the negative to the positive terminal gives $+\varepsilon$, and the reverse gives $-\varepsilon$. First assign currents using KCL so that the number of unknowns is minimal. Then write KVL for independent loops. A negative answer simply means the actual current flows opposite to the assumed direction.

  • KCL is based on conservation of charge; KVL is based on conservation of energy.
  • Both laws apply to DC and to quasi-static AC circuits.
  • Number of independent loop equations = branches minus junctions plus 1.
  • The node (potential) method is often faster: take one point as 0 V and apply KCL at the other nodes.
  • Potential difference between two points = the sum of potential changes along any path between them.

$\sum I = 0$ Junction rule at any node.

$\sum \varepsilon = \sum IR$ Loop rule: sum of emfs equals sum of $IR$ drops around a closed loop.

$\sum \Delta V = 0$ Total potential change around any closed loop is zero.

NEET tip: NEET gives two- or three-loop circuits with multiple cells and asks for the current in a branch or the potential difference between two points.

Wheatstone bridge

A Wheatstone bridge has four resistors $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ arranged in a quadrilateral. A cell is connected across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection, which happens when $\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$. At balance, the two ends of the galvanometer are at equal potential. The balance condition does not depend on the cell's emf or internal resistance, or on the galvanometer's resistance. Interchanging the cell and the galvanometer does not disturb the balance. In circuit problems, a balanced bridge lets you remove the central resistor, or replace it by a wire, to simplify the circuit. The bridge is most sensitive when all four resistances are of the same order. It measures medium resistances accurately but is not suited to very low or very high resistances.

  • Balance condition: $PS = QR$.
  • At balance, the galvanometer current is zero and the middle arm can be ignored.
  • Balance is unaffected by interchanging the cell and the galvanometer.
  • Highest sensitivity is obtained when $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ are comparable.
  • Its practical applications are the metre bridge, the post office box and the carey foster bridge.

$\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$ Balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge.

$S = \frac{QR}{P}$ Unknown resistance from a balanced bridge.

NEET tip: NEET hides a balanced bridge inside a network and asks for the equivalent resistance or the galvanometer current. Always check the ratio first.

Metre bridge

The metre bridge, or slide wire bridge, is a practical Wheatstone bridge. It uses a 1 m uniform wire of manganin or constantan stretched between thick copper strips. A known resistance $R$ goes in one gap and the unknown $S$ in the other. A jockey slides along the wire to find the null point at length $l$ cm from the end next to $R$. Because the wire is uniform, its resistance is proportional to length, so $\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l}{100 - l}$. To reduce errors, choose $R$ so that the null point lies near the middle of the wire. This also reduces end-correction errors from the strips and joints. Repeat the reading with $R$ and $S$ interchanged and take the mean. The thick copper strips have negligible resistance. The jockey should be pressed gently and not slid along the wire.

  • The wire is made of manganin or constantan for high $\rho$ and low $\alpha$, and must have uniform cross-section.
  • The null point is most accurate near the 50 cm mark.
  • Interchanging $R$ and $S$ shifts the null point from $l$ to $(100 - l)$.
  • Changing the cell emf or the galvanometer does not shift the null point.
  • Any resistance added in series with the cell does not shift the null point.
  • If $S$ is heated, its resistance rises, so $l$ (measured from the $R$ end) decreases and the null point shifts towards $R$.
  • Shunting $S$ reduces its resistance, so $l$ increases and the null point shifts towards $S$.

$\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l}{100 - l}$ Balance condition of a metre bridge, with $l$ in cm measured from the $R$ side.

$S = R\frac{(100 - l)}{l}$ Unknown resistance from the balancing length.

$\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l + \alpha_1}{100 - l + \alpha_2}$ Balance with end corrections $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ expressed as equivalent wire lengths.

NEET tip: Expect shift-of-null-point questions when a resistance is added in series or parallel with one arm, or when the two resistors are interchanged.

Formula sheet

$I = \frac{dq}{dt}$ Electric current; $q$ is charge, $t$ is time.

$I = neAv_d$ Current; $n$ is free-electron density, $e$ is electron charge, $A$ is area, $v_d$ is drift velocity.

$v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m}$ Drift velocity; $E$ is field, $\tau$ is relaxation time, $m$ is electron mass.

$\mu = \frac{v_d}{E} = \frac{e\tau}{m}$ Mobility of charge carriers.

$J = \frac{I}{A} = nev_d = \sigma E$ Current density; $\sigma$ is conductivity.

$V = IR$ Ohm's law; $V$ is potential difference, $R$ is resistance.

$R = \frac{\rho l}{A}$ Resistance; $\rho$ is resistivity, $l$ is length, $A$ is cross-sectional area.

$\rho = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau},\ \sigma = \frac{1}{\rho} = ne\mu$ Resistivity and conductivity from the free-electron model.

$R' = n^2R$ Resistance after stretching a wire to $n$ times its length at constant volume.

$P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$ Electrical power dissipated.

$H = I^2Rt$ Joule heat produced in time $t$.

$1\ kWh = 3.6 \times 10^6\ J$ Commercial unit of electrical energy.

$R_s = \sum R_i,\ \frac{1}{R_p} = \sum \frac{1}{R_i}$ Series and parallel equivalent resistance.

$R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$ Temperature dependence; $\alpha$ is temperature coefficient, $\Delta T$ is temperature rise.

$I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r}$ Circuit current; $\varepsilon$ is emf, $r$ is internal resistance, $R$ is external load.

$V = \varepsilon - Ir$ (discharging), $V = \varepsilon + Ir$ (charging) Terminal voltage of a cell.

$r = R\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{V} - 1\right)$ Internal resistance from terminal voltage $V$ across load $R$.

$P_{max} = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4r}$ at $R = r$ Maximum power transfer to the load.

$I = \frac{n\varepsilon}{R + nr}$ $n$ identical cells in series.

$I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + \frac{r}{m}}$ $m$ identical cells in parallel.

$\varepsilon_{eq} = \frac{\varepsilon_1r_2 + \varepsilon_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2},\ r_{eq} = \frac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}$ Two unequal cells in parallel.

$I = \frac{n\varepsilon}{R + \frac{nr}{m}}$, maximum when $R = \frac{nr}{m}$ Mixed grouping of $m$ rows with $n$ cells per row.

$\sum I = 0,\ \sum \Delta V = 0$ Kirchhoff's junction and loop rules.

$\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$ Wheatstone bridge balance condition.

$S = R\frac{100 - l}{l}$ Metre bridge; $l$ is balancing length in cm from the known-resistance side.

Common traps

  • Thinking that stretching a wire changes its resistivity. Resistivity depends only on material and temperature; only $R$ changes, as $R \propto l^2$ at constant volume.
  • Saying the higher-wattage bulb always glows brighter. In series, the lower-wattage bulb, which has higher $R$, glows brighter because the current is common and $P = I^2R$.
  • Using $V = \varepsilon - Ir$ while a cell is being charged. During charging the terminal voltage is $V = \varepsilon + Ir$, which is greater than $\varepsilon$.
  • Subtracting internal resistance for a reversed cell in series. Only the emf subtracts; internal resistances always add.
  • Assuming the null point of a metre bridge shifts when the cell or galvanometer is changed. The balance depends only on the ratio of resistances in the four arms.
  • Treating current as a vector because it has direction. Current is a scalar, while current density $J$ is a vector.
  • Assuming all resistances increase with temperature. Semiconductors and thermistors have negative $\alpha$, and alloys like manganin have nearly zero $\alpha$.
  • Believing maximum power transfer means maximum efficiency. At $R = r$ the efficiency is only 50%.

Quick revision

  • $I = neAv_d$; drift velocity is about $10^{-4}$ m/s, and $v_d \propto \frac{1}{A}$ for a fixed current.
  • Mobility is $\mu = \frac{e\tau}{m}$; both $\mu$ and $\tau$ decrease when temperature rises in metals.
  • $R = \frac{\rho l}{A}$; stretching a wire to $n$ times its length makes $R$ become $n^2R$.
  • Ohmic conductor: straight-line V-I graph through the origin. Diode, GaAs and thyristor are non-ohmic.
  • Series: same $I$, and the larger $R$ dissipates more power. Parallel: same $V$, and the smaller $R$ dissipates more power.
  • Metals have $\alpha > 0$, semiconductors have $\alpha < 0$, and manganin and constantan have $\alpha \approx 0$.
  • Equal $R_0$ with $+\alpha$ and $-\alpha$ in series gives a constant total of $2R_0$ as temperature changes.
  • Terminal voltage is $V = \varepsilon - Ir$; short-circuit current is $\frac{\varepsilon}{r}$; maximum power is $\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4r}$ at $R = r$.
  • Mixed grouping of cells gives maximum current when the external resistance equals the total internal resistance, $\frac{nr}{m}$.
  • KCL comes from charge conservation and KVL from energy conservation; a negative current means the actual direction is reversed.
  • Balanced Wheatstone bridge: $PS = QR$, and the galvanometer arm can be removed.
  • Metre bridge: $S = R\frac{100 - l}{l}$; keep the null point near 50 cm, and interchange $R$ and $S$ to cancel end errors.

Physics · Unit 13: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism

This unit explains how moving charges and currents produce magnetic fields (Biot-Savart and Ampere's laws), how magnetic fields exert forces and torques on moving charges, currents and loops, and how these ideas apply to the galvanometer, bar magnets and magnetic materials. NEET usually asks 2-4 questions here. Field at the centre of loops and arcs, force between parallel wires, charged-particle motion, galvanometer conversion and classification of magnetic materials are tested year after year.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q11, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q15

Biot-Savart law and its application to a circular current loop

The Biot-Savart law gives the field $d\vec{B}$ produced by a small current element $I\,d\vec{l}$ at position $\vec{r}$ from it. The field is perpendicular to both $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$, and it varies as $1/r^2$. For a circular loop, every element is perpendicular to the line joining it to the centre and is at the same distance R from it. Integrating gives $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$ at the centre. A circular arc that subtends angle $\theta$ at the centre gives a fraction $\theta/2\pi$ of this value. On the axis, the components perpendicular to the axis cancel and the axial components add. Direction is found with the right-hand thumb rule: curl the fingers along the current and the thumb points along B. When current splits between two arcs of a loop, the field at the centre from each arc is proportional to $I\theta$. Because the arc lengths are proportional to $\theta$ and the resistances to arc length, $I\theta$ is the same for both branches. The two fields are opposite, so the net field at the centre is zero.

  • Element magnitude: $dB=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$, which is zero along the line of the element.
  • $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}=10^{-7}\,T\,m\,A^{-1}$.
  • Field at the centre of an N-turn coil is $\frac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}$.
  • Field at the centre of an arc is proportional to the angle subtended; for a semicircle it is $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}$.
  • Straight leads pointing radially towards the centre contribute zero field at the centre.
  • Far along the axis ($x\gg R$), the loop field falls as $1/x^3$, like a dipole.
  • Equal $I\theta$ in parallel arcs means opposite and equal fields, so the net field at the centre is zero.

$d\vec{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}$ Biot-Savart law: field due to a current element

$B=\frac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}$ Field at the centre of a circular coil of N turns and radius R

$B=\frac{\mu_0 I\theta}{4\pi R}$ Field at the centre of an arc subtending angle $\theta$ (in radians)

$B=\frac{\mu_0 NIR^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$ Field on the axis at distance x from the centre of the loop

NEET tip: NEET favours combinations of arcs and straight wires, and current dividing between two arcs, asking for the field at the centre.

Ampere's law: infinitely long straight wire and solenoid

Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of $\vec{B}$ around any closed loop equals $\mu_0$ times the net current enclosed by that loop. It is useful only when symmetry makes B constant along a chosen path. For an infinitely long straight wire, take a circle of radius r around the wire, which gives $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$; the field lines are concentric circles. Inside a solid wire carrying uniform current, B grows linearly with r. Outside the wire it falls as 1/r, and it is maximum at the surface. For a long solenoid, a rectangular Amperian loop gives a uniform field $B=\mu_0 nI$ inside, where n is the number of turns per unit length. The field outside is nearly zero. At either end of a long solenoid the field is half the central value. A toroid, which is a solenoid bent into a ring, has $B=\frac{\mu_0 NI}{2\pi r}$ inside its core and zero field both in the open space and outside.

  • Only the enclosed current counts; the sign follows the right-hand rule.
  • Long wire: $B\propto 1/r$ outside, and the field lines are concentric circles.
  • Solid wire with uniform current: $B\propto r$ inside and $B=0$ on the axis.
  • Hollow pipe: $B=0$ inside and $\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ outside.
  • Solenoid: the field is independent of radius and length, and depends only on n and I.
  • Finite straight wire: $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha+\sin\beta)$.
  • Field at the end of a long solenoid is $\frac{\mu_0 nI}{2}$.

$\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_0 I_{enc}$ Ampere's circuital law

$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ Field of an infinitely long straight wire at distance r

$B=\frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2}$ Field inside a solid wire of radius R at distance $r<R$

$B=\mu_0 nI$ Field inside a long solenoid; n is the number of turns per unit length

$B=\frac{\mu_0 NI}{2\pi r}$ Field inside a toroid of N total turns at mean radius r

NEET tip: Expect a B versus r graph for a solid or hollow wire, solenoid ratio questions, and superposition of fields from two long wires.

Force on a moving charge in uniform magnetic and electric fields

A charge q moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in electric and magnetic fields experiences the Lorentz force $\vec{F}=q(\vec{E}+\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. The magnetic part is always perpendicular to the velocity. It therefore does no work and cannot change speed or kinetic energy; it only changes direction. If $\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}$, the motion is a circle of radius $r=\frac{mv}{qB}$. The period $T=\frac{2\pi m}{qB}$ does not depend on speed or radius. If the velocity makes an angle $\theta$ with B, the path is a helix. The component $v\cos\theta$ along B stays unchanged and sets the pitch, while $v\sin\theta$ gives the circular part. A charge moving parallel to B feels no magnetic force. In crossed E and B fields (a velocity selector), a particle passes undeflected when $qE=qvB$, that is $v=E/B$, regardless of its charge or mass.

  • Magnetic force is zero when the charge is at rest or moving parallel or antiparallel to B.
  • Magnetic force does no work, so kinetic energy stays constant.
  • Radius can be written as $r=\frac{p}{qB}=\frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}=\frac{\sqrt{2mqV}}{qB}$ for a particle accelerated through potential V.
  • Period and frequency are independent of speed (cyclotron frequency).
  • Helical motion has pitch $p=v\cos\theta\,T$.
  • Positive and negative charges circulate in opposite senses.
  • Undeflected motion in crossed fields requires $v=E/B$.

$\vec{F}=q(\vec{E}+\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ Lorentz force

$F=qvB\sin\theta$ Magnitude of the magnetic force

$r=\frac{mv\sin\theta}{qB}$ Radius of the circular or helical path

$T=\frac{2\pi m}{qB},\ \nu=\frac{qB}{2\pi m}$ Period and frequency of revolution

$p=\frac{2\pi m v\cos\theta}{qB}$ Pitch of the helix

$v=\frac{E}{B}$ Speed of an undeflected particle in a velocity selector

NEET tip: NEET compares radii or periods for proton, deuteron and alpha particles, and tests the 'no work done by magnetic force' idea.

Force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field

A current-carrying conductor contains drift electrons moving in a magnetic field. The sum of the Lorentz forces on these electrons gives $\vec{F}=I\vec{l}\times\vec{B}$, where $\vec{l}$ points along the current. The magnitude is $BIl\sin\theta$; it is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to B and zero when parallel. The direction comes from Fleming's left-hand rule or the cross product. For a wire of any shape in a uniform field, the force equals the force on a straight wire joining its end points while carrying the same current. Hence any closed loop in a uniform field has zero net force, although it may experience a torque. Common equilibrium problems involve a rod suspended or resting in a field, where $BIl=mg$ or the forces are balanced on an incline.

  • The vector $\vec{l}$ is taken in the direction of conventional current.
  • Net force on a closed loop in a uniform B is zero.
  • A semicircular wire feels the same force as its diameter, $F=BI(2R)$.
  • Floating or levitation condition: $BIl=mg$, or $IB=\lambda g$ per unit length.
  • Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger for field, seCond finger for current, thuMb for motion or force.

$\vec{F}=I\vec{l}\times\vec{B}$ Force on a straight conductor in a uniform field

$F=BIl\sin\theta$ Magnitude; $\theta$ is the angle between the wire and B

$\vec{F}=I\vec{L}_{eff}\times\vec{B}$ Curved wire; $\vec{L}_{eff}$ is the straight line joining its ends

NEET tip: Questions ask for the force on bent or semicircular wires, or the current needed to balance a rod's weight.

Force between two parallel currents; definition of ampere

Each of two long parallel wires sits in the field of the other. The field of wire 1 at wire 2 is $\frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$, so the force per unit length on wire 2 is $\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$. Currents in the same direction attract and opposite currents repel, which is the reverse of the rule for like charges. The forces on the two wires are equal and opposite, obeying Newton's third law. In NCERT the ampere is defined as follows. One ampere is the steady current which, maintained in two infinitely long, straight, parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of $2\times10^{-7}$ N per metre of length on each. Since 2019 the SI ampere is formally fixed through the elementary charge. Even so, the force definition gives the same value and remains the one examined. For equilibrium problems, compare the magnetic force per unit length with the weight per unit length $\lambda g$.

  • Like (parallel) currents attract and unlike (antiparallel) currents repel.
  • Force per unit length is proportional to $I_1I_2$ and to 1/d.
  • Both wires feel equal force, even if their currents differ.
  • Ampere definition: $2\times10^{-7}\,N\,m^{-1}$ at a separation of 1 m.
  • For a wire on the floor with a fixed wire above it carrying a parallel current, the attraction must not exceed $\lambda g$.
  • Stable levitation is possible for a wire above a fixed wire carrying an antiparallel current.

$\frac{F}{l}=\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$ Force per unit length between parallel wires separated by d

$\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}=\lambda g$ Balance of magnetic force with weight per unit length $\lambda$

NEET tip: Typical questions balance the magnetic force against weight per unit length, or test the attract-versus-repel direction.

Torque on a current loop in a uniform magnetic field

A rectangular loop carrying current I in a uniform field B experiences zero net force. However, the forces on opposite sides can form a couple. The torque is $\vec{\tau}=\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$, with magnetic moment $m=NIA$ directed normal to the loop plane by the right-hand rule. Its magnitude is $\tau=NIAB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the area vector (normal) and B. Torque is maximum when the plane of the loop is parallel to B ($\theta=90^\circ$). It is zero when the plane is perpendicular to B. The result holds for a planar loop of any shape. The torque tends to align $\vec{m}$ with $\vec{B}$. The loop's potential energy is $U=-\vec{m}\cdot\vec{B}$, which is minimum (stable equilibrium) at $\theta=0$ and maximum (unstable equilibrium) at $\theta=180^\circ$.

  • Net force is zero in a uniform field, but torque can be non-zero.
  • $\theta$ is measured from the normal to the loop, not from the plane.
  • Maximum torque $NIAB$ occurs when the plane is parallel to B.
  • For a fixed wire length bent into one turn, a circle gives the maximum area and hence maximum torque.
  • This torque is the working principle of the motor and the galvanometer.

$\vec{\tau}=\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$ Torque on a current loop

$\tau=NIAB\sin\theta$ Magnitude; $\theta$ is the angle between the normal and B

$U=-\vec{m}\cdot\vec{B}$ Potential energy of the loop in the field

NEET tip: NEET checks the angle convention (plane versus normal) and the torque for a given wire length bent into a circle.

Moving coil galvanometer, its sensitivity and conversion to ammeter and voltmeter

A moving coil galvanometer (MCG) has a coil pivoted between concave pole pieces with a soft iron core. This arrangement makes the field radial, so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B and the torque is $NIAB$ at every position. A spring provides a restoring torque $k\phi$. At equilibrium $NIAB=k\phi$, giving $\phi=\frac{NAB}{k}I$, a linear scale. Current sensitivity is $\frac{\phi}{I}=\frac{NAB}{k}$. Voltage sensitivity is $\frac{\phi}{V}=\frac{NAB}{kG}$, where G is the coil resistance. Doubling N doubles both the current sensitivity and G, so the voltage sensitivity stays the same. To convert to an ammeter, connect a small shunt S in parallel. To convert to a voltmeter, connect a large resistance R in series. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance.

  • The radial field makes the deflection proportional to current.
  • The soft iron core increases B, which increases sensitivity.
  • Sensitivity increases with N, A and B, and decreases with k.
  • Increasing N does not change voltage sensitivity because G also increases.
  • Ammeter resistance is $\frac{GS}{G+S}$, which is less than S.
  • Voltmeter resistance is $G+R$.
  • An ammeter is connected in series and a voltmeter in parallel.

$NIAB=k\phi$ Equilibrium condition of the galvanometer

$\frac{\phi}{I}=\frac{NAB}{k}$ Current sensitivity

$\frac{\phi}{V}=\frac{NAB}{kG}$ Voltage sensitivity

$S=\frac{I_gG}{I-I_g}$ Shunt to convert a galvanometer of full-scale current $I_g$ into an ammeter of range I

$R=\frac{V}{I_g}-G$ Series resistance for a voltmeter of range V

NEET tip: Very frequent: calculate the shunt or series resistance, and the effect of changing N on current and voltage sensitivity.

Current loop as a magnetic dipole; magnetic dipole moment

A planar current loop behaves like a magnetic dipole with moment $\vec{m}=NI\vec{A}$, in units of $A\,m^2$. Its direction is along the area vector, given by the right-hand rule. The face where the current appears anticlockwise to the viewer acts as a north pole. Far along its axis, the loop field is $B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{x^3}$, which matches the axial field of an electric dipole with $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ replaced by $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}$. A revolving electron forms a tiny current loop of current $I=\frac{ev}{2\pi r}$. Its orbital moment is $\mu=\frac{evr}{2}=\frac{e}{2m_e}L$, so the gyromagnetic ratio is $\frac{e}{2m_e}\approx8.8\times10^{10}\,C\,kg^{-1}$. With Bohr quantisation $L=\frac{nh}{2\pi}$, the minimum value is the Bohr magneton, $\mu_B=\frac{eh}{4\pi m_e}\approx9.27\times10^{-24}\,A\,m^2$.

  • The moment depends on area, not on shape.
  • Anticlockwise current as seen by the viewer gives a north pole facing the viewer.
  • For an electron, $\vec{\mu}$ is antiparallel to $\vec{L}$ because its charge is negative.
  • A charge q rotating at angular speed $\omega$ in radius r has $m=\frac{q\omega r^2}{2}$.
  • The ratio $\mu/L=q/2m$ is the same for rotating rings and discs carrying uniform charge-to-mass ratio.

$\vec{m}=NI\vec{A}$ Magnetic moment of a current loop

$B_{axis}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{x^3}$ Far-field of a loop along its axis

$\mu_l=\frac{e}{2m_e}l$ Orbital magnetic moment of an electron with angular momentum l

$\mu_B=\frac{eh}{4\pi m_e}$ Bohr magneton, about $9.27\times10^{-24}\,A\,m^2$

NEET tip: Common questions: the magnetic moment of a revolving electron or rotating charge, and how m changes when a wire is rebent into more turns.

Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid; magnetic field lines

A bar magnet behaves like a finite solenoid. The field lines of both are identical, and a solenoid with moment $NIA$ can replace a magnet of equal moment. Treating the magnet as two poles of strength $q_m$ separated by 2l gives $m=q_m(2l)$, directed from S to N. Isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist. Cutting a magnet produces smaller magnets, each with both poles. Magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops. They run from N to S outside the magnet and from S to N inside it. The tangent at any point gives the direction of B, and the crowding of lines indicates field strength. Lines never intersect, because the field has a unique direction at each point. Since lines close on themselves, the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero; this is Gauss's law for magnetism. Electric field lines from static charges, by contrast, start and end on charges.

  • Magnetic field lines form closed loops.
  • Outside a magnet the lines run N to S; inside they run S to N.
  • Gauss's law for magnetism: $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}=0$, so no monopoles exist.
  • Cutting a magnet perpendicular to its axis halves m and keeps pole strength the same.
  • Cutting a magnet along its axis halves both pole strength and m.
  • The magnetic moment of a magnet points from S to N.
  • Field lines never cross each other.

$m=q_m\times2l$ Magnetic moment of a bar magnet of pole strength $q_m$ and magnetic length 2l

$\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}=0$ Gauss's law for magnetism

NEET tip: Assertion-type questions on closed field lines, the absence of monopoles, and cutting or bending magnets.

Magnetic field of a bar magnet along and perpendicular to its axis

The field of a bar magnet is found the same way as that of an electric dipole, with $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ replaced by $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}$. On the axial line at distance r from the centre, $B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2mr}{(r^2-l^2)^2}$. For a short magnet ($r\gg l$) this becomes $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3}$, directed along $\vec{m}$. On the equatorial (perpendicular bisector) line, $B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{(r^2+l^2)^{3/2}}$, which for a short magnet becomes $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{r^3}$, directed opposite to $\vec{m}$. At equal distances, the axial field is therefore twice the equatorial field. At a general point at angle $\theta$ from the axis, the field is $B=\frac{\mu_0 m}{4\pi r^3}\sqrt{3\cos^2\theta+1}$. Neutral points occur where the magnet's field cancels an external field.

  • Both fields vary as $1/r^3$ for a short magnet.
  • Ratio of axial to equatorial field at the same distance is $2:1$.
  • The axial field is along m; the equatorial field is opposite to m.
  • The general point formula interpolates between the axial and equatorial cases.
  • Doubling the distance reduces the field to 1/8.

$B_{ax}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3}$ Axial field of a short bar magnet

$B_{eq}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{r^3}$ Equatorial field of a short bar magnet

$B=\frac{\mu_0 m}{4\pi r^3}\sqrt{3\cos^2\theta+1}$ Field at a general point at angle $\theta$ from the axis

NEET tip: Ratio questions comparing axial and equatorial fields, and their $1/r^3$ dependence, are standard.

Torque on a magnetic dipole in a uniform magnetic field

A magnetic dipole in a uniform field B experiences zero net force but a torque $\vec{\tau}=\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$ of magnitude $mB\sin\theta$, which tries to align m with B. Its potential energy is $U=-mB\cos\theta$. This is minimum ($-mB$, stable) at $\theta=0$ and maximum ($+mB$, unstable) at $\theta=180^\circ$. The work needed to rotate the dipole from $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$ is $W=mB(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)$. For example, rotating it from $0$ to $180^\circ$ needs $2mB$ and from $0$ to $90^\circ$ needs $mB$. If slightly displaced from stable equilibrium, a freely suspended magnet performs angular SHM with period $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mB}}$, where I is its moment of inertia. This principle underlies the compass needle and lets m or B be determined from oscillation periods.

  • In a uniform field, F = 0 while $\tau$ is generally non-zero.
  • In a non-uniform field there is also a net force.
  • Work from $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$ is $W=U_2-U_1$.
  • Stable equilibrium at $0^\circ$, unstable at $180^\circ$.
  • Period of oscillation $T\propto1/\sqrt{B}$.

$\tau=mB\sin\theta$ Torque on a dipole in a uniform field

$U=-mB\cos\theta$ Potential energy of the dipole

$W=mB(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)$ Work done in rotating the dipole from $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$

$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mB}}$ Period of small oscillations of a freely suspended magnet

NEET tip: Work done in rotating a dipole and its oscillation period are the usual numericals.

Para-, dia- and ferromagnetic substances

Materials are classified by their response to an applied field. Magnetisation M is the net dipole moment per unit volume, H is the magnetic intensity, and susceptibility is $\chi=M/H$. These are related by $B=\mu_0(H+M)=\mu_0\mu_rH$, with $\mu_r=1+\chi$. Diamagnetic substances (Bi, Cu, Pb, Si, water, $N_2$, NaCl) have small negative $\chi$ and $\mu_r$ slightly less than 1. They are weakly repelled and move from stronger to weaker field regions. Superconductors are perfect diamagnets with $\chi=-1$, which expels field lines (Meissner effect). Paramagnetic substances (Al, Na, Ca, $O_2$, $CuCl_2$) have permanent atomic moments, small positive $\chi$ and $\mu_r$ slightly greater than 1. They are weakly attracted towards stronger fields. Ferromagnetic substances (Fe, Co, Ni, Gd) contain domains with aligned moments. They have very large positive $\chi$ and $\mu_r$ (up to thousands), are strongly attracted, and concentrate field lines inside them.

  • Diamagnetism is present in all materials but is masked if para- or ferromagnetism exists.
  • Diamagnetic: $-1\le\chi<0$, $0\le\mu_r<1$; field lines are expelled.
  • Paramagnetic: $0<\chi<\epsilon$ (small), $1<\mu_r<1+\epsilon$; field lines are slightly concentrated.
  • Ferromagnetic: $\chi\gg1$, $\mu_r\gg1$; field lines are strongly concentrated.
  • A diamagnetic liquid in a U-tube is depressed in the limb placed in the field; a paramagnetic liquid rises.
  • A rod hung in a field aligns perpendicular to it if diamagnetic and parallel to it if paramagnetic.
  • Ferromagnetism arises from domains, which grow and align in an applied field.

$M=\frac{m_{net}}{V}$ Magnetisation: net dipole moment per unit volume

$B=\mu_0(H+M)$ Relation between B, H and M

$\chi=\frac{M}{H}$ Magnetic susceptibility

$\mu_r=1+\chi,\ \mu=\mu_0\mu_r$ Relative permeability and permeability

NEET tip: Matching substances to classes and to the signs of $\chi$ and $\mu_r$ is asked almost every year.

Effect of temperature on magnetic properties

Temperature disturbs the alignment of atomic dipoles. Paramagnetic susceptibility follows Curie's law, $\chi=\frac{C\mu_0}{T}$: it is inversely proportional to absolute temperature, because thermal agitation opposes alignment. Diamagnetism arises from induced moments, so it is essentially independent of temperature. A ferromagnet loses its spontaneous domain alignment when heated above the Curie temperature $T_C$ and becomes paramagnetic. Above $T_C$ its susceptibility follows $\chi=\frac{C}{T-T_C}$ (the Curie-Weiss form). The Curie temperatures given in NCERT are Fe 1043 K, Co 1394 K, Ni 631 K, Gd 317 K and $Fe_2O_3$ 893 K. Cooling below $T_C$ restores ferromagnetic behaviour. Heating a permanent magnet therefore weakens it, which is why magnets must not be overheated.

  • Curie's law: $\chi\propto1/T$ for paramagnets.
  • Diamagnetic $\chi$ is independent of T.
  • Above $T_C$, a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.
  • Curie-Weiss law holds for $T>T_C$.
  • M is proportional to $B/T$ for paramagnets in weak fields, until saturation.

$\chi=\frac{C\mu_0}{T}$ Curie's law for paramagnets; C is the Curie constant

$\chi=\frac{C}{T-T_C}$ Susceptibility of a ferromagnet above the Curie temperature $T_C$

NEET tip: Questions ask for the ratio of susceptibilities at two temperatures, or what happens to a ferromagnet above $T_C$.

Formula sheet

$d\vec{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}$ Biot-Savart law; $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,T\,m\,A^{-1}$

$B=\frac{\mu_0 NI}{2R}$ Centre of a coil of N turns, radius R

$B=\frac{\mu_0 I\theta}{4\pi R}$ Centre of an arc subtending angle $\theta$ in radians

$B=\frac{\mu_0 NIR^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$ Axis of a circular coil at distance x from the centre

$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha+\sin\beta)$ Finite straight wire at perpendicular distance d; $\alpha,\beta$ are angles subtended by the ends

$\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_0 I_{enc}$ Ampere's circuital law

$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ Infinitely long straight wire at distance r

$B=\mu_0 nI$ Inside a long solenoid; n is turns per unit length

$B=\frac{\mu_0 NI}{2\pi r}$ Inside a toroid of N turns at radius r

$\vec{F}=q(\vec{E}+\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ Lorentz force on charge q with velocity v

$r=\frac{mv}{qB},\ T=\frac{2\pi m}{qB}$ Radius and period of circular motion in B

$v=\frac{E}{B}$ Velocity selector: undeflected speed in crossed fields

$\vec{F}=I\vec{l}\times\vec{B}$ Force on a current-carrying wire of length l

$\frac{F}{l}=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ Force per unit length between parallel wires separated by d

$\vec{m}=NI\vec{A},\ \vec{\tau}=\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$ Magnetic moment of a loop and the torque on it

$U=-\vec{m}\cdot\vec{B}$ Potential energy of a dipole in a field

$\frac{\phi}{I}=\frac{NAB}{k},\ \frac{\phi}{V}=\frac{NAB}{kG}$ Current and voltage sensitivity; k is the spring constant, G the coil resistance

$S=\frac{I_gG}{I-I_g}$ Shunt for an ammeter of range I

$R=\frac{V}{I_g}-G$ Series resistance for a voltmeter of range V

$\mu_l=\frac{e}{2m_e}l,\ \mu_B=\frac{eh}{4\pi m_e}$ Orbital moment of an electron and the Bohr magneton

$B_{ax}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3},\ B_{eq}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{r^3}$ Fields of a short bar magnet of moment m

$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mB}}$ Oscillation period of a magnet; I is its moment of inertia

$B=\mu_0(H+M),\ \chi=\frac{M}{H},\ \mu_r=1+\chi$ Magnetisation relations

$\chi=\frac{C\mu_0}{T}$ Curie's law for paramagnets

$\chi=\frac{C}{T-T_C}$ Ferromagnet above the Curie temperature

Common traps

  • Assuming a magnetic force can change a particle's speed: magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity, does no work, and keeps kinetic energy constant.
  • Using $\theta$ from the plane of the loop in $\tau=NIAB\sin\theta$: $\theta$ is measured from the normal (area vector), so torque is maximum when the plane is parallel to B.
  • Thinking parallel currents repel like charges do: parallel currents attract and antiparallel currents repel.
  • Believing that increasing the number of turns raises voltage sensitivity: resistance rises in the same proportion, so voltage sensitivity is unchanged.
  • Treating ammeter resistance as equal to the shunt: it is $\frac{GS}{G+S}$, which is smaller than both G and S.
  • Forgetting that field lines inside a magnet run from S to N: they are closed loops, and the net flux through any closed surface is zero.
  • Assuming every material's susceptibility depends on temperature: diamagnetic susceptibility is temperature-independent, and only paramagnets follow Curie's law.
  • Ignoring that radial straight leads give zero field at the centre, or that current dividing between two arcs of a uniform loop gives zero net field at the centre.

Quick revision

  • Centre of a loop: $\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$; an arc gives the fraction $\theta/2\pi$ of it; a long wire gives $\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$; a solenoid gives $\mu_0 nI$.
  • Field at the end of a long solenoid is half the field at its centre.
  • Lorentz force: $q(\vec{E}+\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$; radius $r=\frac{mv}{qB}$; period $\frac{2\pi m}{qB}$ is independent of speed.
  • Velocity selector condition is $v=E/B$; helix pitch is $v\cos\theta\cdot T$.
  • Any closed loop in a uniform B feels zero net force, but torque $\vec{m}\times\vec{B}$ can act.
  • Parallel wires: $\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ per metre; one ampere gives $2\times10^{-7}\,N\,m^{-1}$ at 1 m separation.
  • Galvanometer: radial field, $\phi\propto I$; ammeter uses a low shunt in parallel, voltmeter a high resistance in series.
  • Magnetic moment $m=NIA$; electron orbital moment ratio is $\frac{e}{2m_e}$; Bohr magneton is $9.27\times10^{-24}\,A\,m^2$.
  • Short magnet: axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance, and both vary as $1/r^3$.
  • Dipole energy $U=-mB\cos\theta$; work from $0$ to $180^\circ$ is $2mB$.
  • Dia: $\chi<0$, repelled. Para: small $\chi>0$, weakly attracted. Ferro: $\chi\gg1$, domains, strongly attracted.
  • Curie's law $\chi\propto1/T$ for paramagnets; above $T_C$ a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.

Physics · Unit 14: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents

This unit covers how a changing magnetic flux produces an emf (Faraday's and Lenz's laws), how coils store energy and couple through self and mutual inductance, and how alternating currents behave in resistors, inductors and capacitors, including resonance, power, generators and transformers. NEET usually sets 2-3 questions from it. The common types are direct formula applications (solenoid inductance, LCR current amplitude, transformer ratios), conceptual questions on Lenz's law and eddy currents, and graph-based questions on induced emf and power.

PYQs (4): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q3, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q5, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q30, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q32

Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction

Magnetic flux through a surface measures how many field lines pass through it: $\Phi_B = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A} = BA\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{B}$ and the area vector (the normal). Its SI unit is the weber ($1\,Wb = 1\,T\,m^2$). Faraday's law states that an emf is induced in a circuit whenever the flux linked with it changes. The magnitude of this emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage: $\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$. The flux can change in three ways: by changing $B$, by changing the area $A$, or by changing the orientation $\theta$, for example by rotating the coil. What matters is the rate of change, not the value of flux. A huge but constant flux induces no emf. If $\Phi$ versus $t$ is plotted, the emf is the negative of the slope of that graph.

  • Emf depends on the rate of change of flux, not on the flux itself
  • Flux can change through B, through A, or through the angle $\theta$
  • For N tightly wound turns the flux linkage is $N\Phi$
  • The minus sign expresses Lenz's law (direction of the emf)
  • Flux is a scalar; its SI unit is the weber ($Wb$)
  • The induced emf exists even if the circuit is open; a current needs a closed path

$\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$ Flux through a plane area A in a uniform field B; $\theta$ is the angle between B and the normal

$\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$ Faraday's law: induced emf in a coil of N turns

$\varepsilon_{avg} = -N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ Average emf over a finite time interval

NEET tip: Expect $\Phi = f(t)$ given as a polynomial or trigonometric function and a question asking for the emf at an instant, obtained by differentiating; or a $\Phi$-t graph whose slope gives the emf.

Induced emf and current; Lenz's law

Lenz's law says the induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produces it. It is a statement of energy conservation: work must be done against the opposing force, and that work appears as electrical energy. When a magnet's north pole approaches a coil, the near face of the coil becomes a north pole and repels it. A rod of length $l$ moving with speed $v$ perpendicular to $B$ develops a motional emf $Blv$. A rod rotating about one end develops $\frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$. In a closed circuit of resistance $R$, the induced current is $I=\varepsilon/R$ and the power dissipated is $\varepsilon^2/R$. The charge that flows depends only on the total flux change, not on how fast it happens. A sliding rod experiences a retarding force $B^2l^2v/R$, so an external agent must keep pushing to maintain constant speed.

  • Lenz's law follows from conservation of energy
  • Approaching magnet is repelled; receding magnet is attracted
  • Motional emf: $\varepsilon = Blv$ when B, l and v are mutually perpendicular
  • Induced charge $Q = N\Delta\Phi/R$ is independent of time taken
  • Dissipated power $P = \varepsilon^2/R$; if $\varepsilon \propto \cos t$, then $P \propto \cos^2 t$
  • Use Fleming's right-hand rule for the direction of the induced current in a moving conductor

$\varepsilon = Blv$ Motional emf in a straight conductor moving perpendicular to B

$\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}B\omega l^2$ Emf across a rod of length l rotating with angular speed $\omega$ about one end, perpendicular to B

$I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R},\ Q = \frac{N\Delta\Phi}{R}$ Induced current and total induced charge in a circuit of resistance R

$F = \frac{B^2l^2v}{R},\ P = \frac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}$ Retarding force on a sliding rod and the power needed to keep it at constant speed

NEET tip: NEET asks for the direction of induced current using Lenz's law, power-versus-time graphs (find emf, then square it), and rotating rod or sliding rod emf calculations.

Eddy currents

Eddy currents (Foucault currents) are loops of induced current that circulate inside the bulk of a conductor when the flux through it changes. By Lenz's law they oppose the motion or the change that causes them, producing damping and heating. Their useful applications include: - electromagnetic damping in moving-coil galvanometers, which makes the pointer dead-beat; - magnetic braking in electric trains; - induction furnaces, which melt metals by heating; - electric power meters. Their harmful effect is energy lost as heat in transformer cores and motor armatures. This loss is reduced by using laminated cores, or cores with slots, which increase the resistance of the eddy-current paths. A magnet dropped through a vertical copper tube falls with an acceleration less than $g$ and can reach a terminal speed. Similarly, a metal plate swinging between magnet poles is damped quickly, while a slotted plate swings much more freely.

  • Eddy currents oppose the change in flux (Lenz's law)
  • They cause heating and damping
  • They are reduced by laminating cores or cutting slots
  • Applications: magnetic braking, dead-beat galvanometer, induction furnace, power meters
  • A magnet falling through a metal tube has acceleration less than g
  • A slotted metal plate is damped less than a solid plate

NEET tip: Usually tested as a statement-based conceptual question on applications, on reducing eddy-current loss by lamination, or on a magnet falling through a conducting ring or tube with $a<g$.

Self and mutual inductance

Self-inductance $L$ is the property of a coil that opposes changes in its own current, much as inertia opposes changes in motion. It is defined by $N\Phi = LI$, and the self-induced emf is $\varepsilon = -L\frac{dI}{dt}$. For a long solenoid, $L = \mu_0 n^2 A l = \mu_0 \pi n^2 r^2 l$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length. Inserting a core of relative permeability $\mu_r$ multiplies $L$ by $\mu_r$. The energy stored in an inductor is $\frac{1}{2}LI^2$. Mutual inductance $M$ links two coils: $N_2\Phi_2 = MI_1$ and $\varepsilon_2 = -M\frac{dI_1}{dt}$. For two coaxial solenoids, $M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l$, with $r_1$ the radius of the inner one, and $M_{12}=M_{21}$. Ignoring mutual inductance, inductors in series add ($L_1+L_2$) and in parallel combine like resistors. The SI unit of inductance is the henry.

  • L depends only on geometry and the core material, not on the current
  • Solenoid: $L \propto n^2$, $L \propto N^2$, $L \propto A$
  • Energy stored in an inductor: $\frac{1}{2}LI^2$; magnetic energy density $\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$
  • $M_{12} = M_{21}$; coupling coefficient $k \le 1$
  • Series inductors: $L_1+L_2$; parallel: $\frac{L_1L_2}{L_1+L_2}$ (no mutual coupling)
  • Voltage across an inductor is $L\,dI/dt$; in parallel each inductor has the same voltage across it, so $L_1\,dI_1/dt = L_2\,dI_2/dt$ and the current divides inversely as $L$ (each carries $I/2$ only if $L_1 = L_2$)

$L = \frac{N\Phi}{I},\ \varepsilon = -L\frac{dI}{dt}$ Definition of self-inductance and the self-induced emf

$L = \mu_0 n^2 \pi r^2 l = \frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l}$ Self-inductance of a long solenoid (multiply by $\mu_r$ for a core)

$M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l$ Mutual inductance of coaxial solenoids, $r_1$ = inner radius

$U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$ Magnetic energy stored in an inductor

$M = k\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ Mutual inductance in terms of the coupling coefficient $0\le k\le 1$

NEET tip: Direct formula recall (solenoid L or M), energy stored, and series/parallel inductor emf ratios are frequent single-step questions.

Alternating current: peak and RMS values

An alternating current varies sinusoidally: $I = I_0\sin\omega t$, with $\omega = 2\pi f$. Its average over a full cycle is zero. Its average over a half cycle is $\frac{2I_0}{\pi} \approx 0.637I_0$. The root mean square (rms), or effective, value is the steady DC that would produce the same heat in a resistor in the same time. For a sinusoid, $I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707I_0$, and similarly $V_{rms}=\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$. AC ammeters and voltmeters read rms values. Indian domestic supply is 220 V rms at 50 Hz, so the peak voltage is about 311 V. The form factor is $\frac{I_{rms}}{I_{avg}} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}} \approx 1.11$. For non-sinusoidal waveforms, compute $\sqrt{\langle I^2\rangle}$ directly. For example, a square wave of height $I_0$ has $I_{rms}=I_0$.

  • The full-cycle average of sinusoidal AC is zero
  • Half-cycle average $= 2I_0/\pi$
  • rms $= I_0/\sqrt{2}$ for a sine wave only
  • AC meters read rms values
  • 220 V mains is rms; peak $\approx 311$ V
  • In $\omega = 2\pi f$, the 2000 in $\sin(2000t)$ is $\omega$, not f

$I = I_0\sin\omega t,\ \omega = 2\pi f$ Instantaneous alternating current, $I_0$ = peak value

$I_{rms} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}},\ V_{rms} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$ Effective (rms) values for sinusoidal AC

$I_{avg,\,half} = \frac{2I_0}{\pi}$ Mean current over a half cycle

$I_{rms} = \sqrt{\langle I^2 \rangle}$ General definition of rms for any waveform

NEET tip: Watch whether the question gives or asks for peak or rms values; reading $\omega$ and $V_0$ directly from $V=V_0\sin\omega t$ is a must.

Reactance and impedance

In a pure resistor, voltage and current are in phase. In a pure inductor, the voltage leads the current by $\pi/2$, and the opposition offered is the inductive reactance $X_L = \omega L$. In a pure capacitor, the current leads the voltage by $\pi/2$, and the opposition is the capacitive reactance $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$. Reactances are measured in ohms. $X_L$ grows with frequency, so an inductor blocks high frequencies. $X_C$ falls with frequency, so a capacitor blocks DC ($\omega = 0$) and passes high frequencies. Impedance $Z$ is the total opposition of an AC circuit. For a series RLC circuit it is found from phasors as $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L-X_C)^2}$, and the peak current is $I_0 = \frac{V_0}{Z}$. Phasors are rotating vectors whose projections give the instantaneous values. Adding voltage phasors vectorially, not arithmetically, is essential.

  • Resistor: V and I in phase
  • Inductor: V leads I by $90^\circ$ (mnemonic ELI)
  • Capacitor: I leads V by $90^\circ$ (mnemonic ICE)
  • $X_L \propto f$, $X_C \propto 1/f$
  • For DC, an inductor acts as a plain wire and a capacitor as an open circuit
  • Voltages in an AC series circuit add as phasors

$X_L = \omega L = 2\pi fL$ Inductive reactance in ohm

$X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi fC}$ Capacitive reactance in ohm

$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$ Impedance of a series LCR circuit

$I_0 = \frac{V_0}{Z},\ I_{rms} = \frac{V_{rms}}{Z}$ Ohm's law form for AC circuits

NEET tip: Compute $X_L$ and $X_C$ first; if they are equal, Z = R immediately, which is a common shortcut in current-amplitude questions.

LCR series circuit and resonance

In a series LCR circuit driven by $V = V_0\sin\omega t$, the current is $I = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, where $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$. The circuit is inductive if $X_L > X_C$ (current lags) and capacitive if $X_C > X_L$ (current leads). Resonance occurs when $X_L = X_C$, that is $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$. At resonance Z is minimum and equal to R, the current is maximum ($V_0/R$), $\phi = 0$ and the power factor is 1. $V_L$ and $V_C$ are equal and opposite, cancelling each other, and each may be much larger than the source voltage. Sharpness of resonance is measured by the quality factor $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$. The bandwidth is $2\Delta\omega = R/L$, so $Q = \omega_0/(2\Delta\omega)$. A smaller R gives a sharper resonance. Resonance is used in radio and TV tuning circuits. It needs both L and C to be present.

  • Resonance condition: $X_L = X_C$, $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$
  • At resonance: $Z_{min} = R$, $I_{max} = V/R$, $\phi=0$
  • $V_L = V_C$ at resonance, in antiphase; each can exceed the source voltage
  • Below $\omega_0$ the circuit is capacitive; above $\omega_0$ it is inductive
  • Q factor $= \omega_0/\text{bandwidth}$; low R gives sharp resonance
  • Resonant frequency is independent of R

$\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$ Phase angle between source voltage and current

$\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},\ f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$ Resonant angular frequency and frequency

$Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$ Quality factor (sharpness of resonance)

$2\Delta\omega = \frac{R}{L}$ Bandwidth, the separation of the half-power frequencies

NEET tip: NEET often gives L, C, R and $\omega$ that satisfy resonance; recognising $X_L = X_C$ quickly gives $I_0 = V_0/R$.

Power in AC circuits; wattless current

The average power in an AC circuit is $P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$. Here $\cos\phi$ is the power factor, equal to $\frac{R}{Z}$. Only the resistor dissipates power, so equivalently $P = I_{rms}^2R$. For a pure resistor $\cos\phi = 1$. For a pure inductor or a pure capacitor $\phi = 90^\circ$, so the average power is zero: energy is stored and returned every cycle. At resonance the power factor is 1 and the power is maximum. Resolve $I_{rms}$ into two parts. The component $I_{rms}\cos\phi$, in phase with the voltage, does the work. The component $I_{rms}\sin\phi$, in quadrature, consumes no power and is called wattless current. A low power factor means a larger current is needed for the same power, which raises transmission losses. Capacitors are therefore used to improve the power factor in industrial loads.

  • Average power $= V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$
  • Power factor $\cos\phi = R/Z$
  • Pure L or C: zero average power
  • Wattless current $= I_{rms}\sin\phi$
  • Power is maximum at resonance
  • Only the resistance dissipates energy: $P = I_{rms}^2R$

$P_{avg} = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi$ True (average) power in an AC circuit

$\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}$ Power factor of a series LCR circuit

$P_{avg} = I_{rms}^2 R$ Power dissipated, all in the resistor

$I_{wattless} = I_{rms}\sin\phi$ Current component $90^\circ$ out of phase that does no work

NEET tip: Typical questions find power from $V = V_0\sin\omega t$ and $I = I_0\sin(\omega t-\phi)$ using $\frac{V_0I_0}{2}\cos\phi$, or identify the zero-power case.

AC generator

An AC generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. A coil of N turns and area A rotates with angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform field B. The flux linked is $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$, so the emf is $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, and its peak value is $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$. The emf is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to B, where flux is zero but changing fastest. The emf is zero when the plane is perpendicular to B, where flux is maximum. The main parts are the armature coil, the field magnets, slip rings and carbon brushes. Doubling $\omega$ doubles both the peak emf and the frequency. Commercial generators in India produce 50 Hz. The mechanical energy is supplied by turbines driven by water, steam or wind.

  • Works on electromagnetic induction
  • Peak emf $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$
  • Flux maximum means emf zero; flux zero means emf maximum
  • Slip rings and brushes connect the rotating coil to the external circuit
  • Peak emf is proportional to $\omega$, N, B and A
  • Converts mechanical energy into electrical energy

$\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$ Instantaneous emf of the AC generator

$\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega = NBA(2\pi f)$ Peak emf; f is the rotation frequency

NEET tip: Expect direct calculation of peak emf from N, B, A and rpm (convert rpm to rad/s), or the phase relation between flux and emf.

Transformer

A transformer changes alternating voltage using mutual induction between primary and secondary coils wound on a common soft-iron core.
