  • Using atomic masses with $m_H$ automatically accounts for the electrons
  • $Q>0$ means energy is released; $Q<0$ means energy is absorbed
  • Converting MeV to keV means multiplying by $10^3$, so watch the units in options

$E=mc^2$ Mass-energy equivalence

$\Delta m=Zm_H+(A-Z)m_n-M_{atom}$ Mass defect calculated from atomic masses

$E_b=\Delta m\times931.5$ MeV Binding energy when $\Delta m$ is in u

$Q=(\sum m_{\text{reactants}}-\sum m_{\text{products}})\times931.5$ MeV Energy released in a nuclear reaction, with masses in u

NEET tip: Q-value and binding-energy numericals using given masses in u are very frequent; check carefully whether the answer is asked in MeV or keV.

Binding energy per nucleon and its variation with mass number

Binding energy per nucleon, $E_{bn}=E_b/A$, measures nuclear stability: the higher its value, the more stable the nucleus. On the plot of $E_{bn}$ against $A$, the curve rises steeply for light nuclei, with local peaks at $^4He$ (7.07 MeV), $^{12}C$ and $^{16}O$. It reaches a maximum of about 8.75 MeV near $A=56$ ($Fe$). It stays nearly constant at about 8 MeV for $30<A<170$, then falls to about 7.6 MeV for $^{238}U$. The flat middle region reflects the saturation property of the short-range nuclear force: each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours. Heavy nuclei have lower $E_{bn}$ because Coulomb repulsion among many protons grows. The curve explains energy release in two ways. Splitting a heavy nucleus (fission) produces fragments with higher $E_{bn}$. Joining light nuclei (fusion) also produces a nucleus with higher $E_{bn}$. In both cases the products are more tightly bound, and energy is released.

  • Peak of the curve is about 8.75 MeV per nucleon near $A=56$ (iron), the most stable region
  • $E_{bn}$ is about 8 MeV over the broad range $30<A<170$
  • $^{238}U$ has about 7.6 MeV per nucleon; deuteron has $E_b=2.22$ MeV, i.e. 1.11 MeV per nucleon
  • $^4He$ shows a sharp local peak, making it unusually stable
  • Saturation of nuclear forces explains the nearly constant middle region
  • Energy is released whenever the products have higher total binding energy than the reactants

$E_{bn}=\frac{E_b}{A}$ Binding energy per nucleon, the measure of stability

$Q=\sum (E_b)_{\text{products}}-\sum (E_b)_{\text{reactants}}$ Energy released, calculated from binding energies

NEET tip: Expect curve-based reasoning (which nucleus is most stable, why fission and fusion release energy) and energy-release calculations using $A\times E_{bn}$ values.

Nuclear fission and fusion

In fission, a heavy nucleus splits into two medium-mass fragments after absorbing a slow (thermal) neutron. A typical reaction is $^{235}_{92}U+^1_0n\to^{236}_{92}U\to^{144}_{56}Ba+^{89}_{36}Kr+3^1_0n$, which releases about 200 MeV per fission. The extra neutrons released can cause further fissions, creating a chain reaction. In a nuclear reactor, three components control this. A moderator (heavy water or graphite) slows the fast neutrons. Control rods (cadmium or boron) absorb excess neutrons. A coolant removes the heat. The multiplication factor $K$ is the ratio of neutrons in one generation to the previous one. $K=1$ is critical (steady), $K>1$ is supercritical (as in a bomb), and $K<1$ is subcritical. In fusion, light nuclei combine into a heavier one. This needs temperatures of about $10^7$ K to overcome Coulomb repulsion, so it is called thermonuclear fusion. The Sun's proton-proton cycle converts $4\,^1H$ into $^4He$ and releases 26.7 MeV.

  • Fission of $^{235}U$ releases about 200 MeV, i.e. about 0.9 MeV per nucleon
  • Slow (thermal) neutrons are the most effective in causing fission of $^{235}U$
  • Moderator slows neutrons; control rods (Cd, B) absorb neutrons
  • $K=1$ critical, $K>1$ supercritical, $K<1$ subcritical
  • Fusion requires about $10^7$ K, which is the source of stellar energy
  • Proton-proton cycle: $4\,^1H+2e^-\to\,^4He+2\nu+6\gamma+26.7$ MeV (26.7 MeV includes positron annihilation)
  • Energy released per unit mass is larger in fusion than in fission
  • D-T fusion: $^2H+^3H\to^4He+n+17.6$ MeV

$^{235}_{92}U+^1_0n\to^{144}_{56}Ba+^{89}_{36}Kr+3^1_0n+200$ MeV Typical fission reaction; both $A$ and $Z$ are conserved

$K=\frac{\text{neutrons in generation } (n+1)}{\text{neutrons in generation } n}$ Multiplication factor of a chain reaction

$4\,^1_1H+2e^-\to\,^4_2He+2\nu+6\gamma+26.7$ MeV Net proton-proton cycle in stars; 26.7 MeV includes positron annihilation

NEET tip: Questions test balancing fission equations (finding the number of neutrons or missing $A$, $Z$), the roles of moderator and control rods, and comparisons of fission with fusion.

Formula sheet

$N(\theta)\propto\frac{1}{\sin^4(\theta/2)}$ Rutherford scattering: $N$ is the number of alpha particles scattered at angle $\theta$

$r_0=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{2Ze^2}{K}$ Distance of closest approach; $K$ is the alpha kinetic energy and $Z$ the target atomic number

$b=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Ze^2\cot(\theta/2)}{K}$ Impact parameter $b$ for an alpha particle scattered through $\theta$

$\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{Ze^2}{r^2}$ Centripetal force balance for an electron of mass $m$ and speed $v$ in an orbit of radius $r$

$mvr=\frac{nh}{2\pi}$ Bohr angular momentum quantisation; $n$ is the orbit number and $h$ is Planck's constant

$r_n=0.529\frac{n^2}{Z}$ Å Radius of the $n$th Bohr orbit of a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number $Z$

$v_n=2.18\times10^6\frac{Z}{n}$ m/s Orbital speed in the $n$th orbit

$E_n=-13.6\frac{Z^2}{n^2}$ eV Total energy of the $n$th level

$K_n=-E_n,\ U_n=2E_n$ Kinetic energy $K_n$ and potential energy $U_n$ in terms of the total energy $E_n$

$T_n\propto\frac{n^3}{Z^2}$ Time period of revolution in the $n$th orbit

$2\pi r_n=n\lambda$ De Broglie condition for stationary orbits; $\lambda$ is the electron wavelength

$\frac{1}{\lambda}=RZ^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$ Wavelength of an emitted line for $n_2\to n_1$; $R=1.097\times10^7$ m$^{-1}$

$h\nu=E_{n_2}-E_{n_1}$ Photon energy (frequency $\nu$) in a transition between levels

$\lambda(\text{nm})=\frac{1240}{E(\text{eV})}$ Photon energy to wavelength conversion

$N_{lines}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ Maximum number of spectral lines from level $n$

$A=Z+N$ Mass number $A$ in terms of protons $Z$ and neutrons $N$

$R=R_0A^{1/3}$ Nuclear radius; $R_0=1.2$ fm

$\rho_{nucleus}\approx2.3\times10^{17}$ kg/m$^3$ Nuclear density, the same for all nuclei

$1\,u=1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg $\equiv931.5$ MeV/$c^2$ Atomic mass unit and its energy equivalent

$E=mc^2$ Mass-energy equivalence; $c$ is the speed of light

$\Delta m=Zm_H+(A-Z)m_n-M_{atom}$ Mass defect from the hydrogen atom mass $m_H$, neutron mass $m_n$ and atomic mass $M_{atom}$

$E_b=\Delta m\times931.5$ MeV Binding energy with $\Delta m$ in u

$E_{bn}=\frac{E_b}{A}$ Binding energy per nucleon

$Q=(\sum m_{\text{reactants}}-\sum m_{\text{products}})\times931.5$ MeV Q-value of a nuclear reaction, with masses in u

$K=\frac{N_{n+1}}{N_n}$ Neutron multiplication factor in a chain reaction

Common traps

  • Writing $N(\theta)\propto1/\sin^4\theta$. The correct dependence is on $\sin^4(\theta/2)$, and the count falls very steeply with angle, so the plot is never bell-shaped or rising.
  • Forgetting $Z$ for hydrogen-like ions. Energy scales as $Z^2$, radius as $1/Z$ and speed as $Z$, so $He^+$ has $E_1=-54.4$ eV, not $-13.6$ eV.
  • Mixing up signs of orbital energies. Kinetic energy is positive and equals $-E$, while potential energy equals $2E$. A more negative $E$ means a more tightly bound electron.
  • Assuming the series limit is the longest wavelength. The series limit ($n_2\to\infty$) is the shortest wavelength; the longest comes from $n_2=n_1+1$.
  • Thinking that a larger nucleus is denser. Since $R\propto A^{1/3}$, nuclear density is the same for all nuclei.
  • Judging stability by total binding energy. Stability depends on binding energy per nucleon, which peaks near $A=56$.
  • Mixing nuclear and atomic masses when computing mass defect. If atomic masses are given, use $m_H$ in place of $m_p$ so the electron masses cancel.
  • Answering in MeV when options are in keV, or using 931 instead of the given 931.5. Always use the conversion supplied in the question.

Quick revision

  • Geiger-Marsden experiment: most alpha particles pass undeflected and about 1 in 8000 is deflected by more than $90^\circ$, revealing a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
  • Rutherford scattering: $N(\theta)\propto1/\sin^4(\theta/2)$; smaller impact parameter gives larger deflection, and $b=0$ gives $180^\circ$.
  • Rutherford model failed to explain atomic stability and line spectra.
  • Bohr model: $r_n\propto n^2/Z$, $v_n\propto Z/n$, $E_n=-13.6Z^2/n^2$ eV, and $L=nh/2\pi$.
  • In any orbit $K:U:E=1:-2:-1$; the ionisation energy of H is 13.6 eV.
  • Spectral series by lower level: Lyman ($n_1=1$) UV, Balmer ($n_1=2$) visible, Paschen ($n_1=3$), Brackett ($n_1=4$) and Pfund ($n_1=5$) IR.
  • Maximum number of spectral lines from level $n$ is $n(n-1)/2$; $\lambda(\text{nm})=1240/E(\text{eV})$.
  • Nuclear radius $R=1.2A^{1/3}$ fm; nuclear density is about $2.3\times10^{17}$ kg/m$^3$ for every nucleus.
  • 1 u = $1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg = 931.5 MeV/$c^2$; a neutron is heavier than a proton.
  • Binding energy $E_b=\Delta m\times931.5$ MeV; $Q>0$ means the reaction releases energy.
  • BE per nucleon peaks at about 8.75 MeV near Fe-56, is about 7.6 MeV for U-238, and a flat middle region shows nuclear force saturation.
  • Fission of U-235 releases about 200 MeV; moderator slows neutrons, control rods absorb them, and $K=1$ is critical. Fusion needs about $10^7$ K, and the p-p cycle releases 26.7 MeV.

Physics · Unit 19: Electronic Devices

This unit covers semiconductor materials and the p-n junction devices built from them: rectifier diodes, LEDs, photodiodes, solar cells and Zener diodes. It ends with digital logic gates. NEET usually asks 1-2 questions from here, mostly on biasing and depletion width, Zener regulator circuits, rectifier output frequency, photon energy and band gap, and truth tables of combined gates.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q16, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q42

Semiconductors

In solids, atomic energy levels form a valence band (VB) and a conduction band (CB) separated by an energy gap $E_g$. Metals have overlapping bands. Insulators have a large gap ($E_g > 3$ eV). Semiconductors have a small gap: Si about 1.1 eV and Ge about 0.7 eV. In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, thermal energy breaks covalent bonds and creates equal numbers of free electrons and holes, so $n_e = n_h = n_i$. Doping gives extrinsic semiconductors. Adding a pentavalent impurity (P, As, Sb) gives n-type, where the donor level lies just below the CB and electrons are the majority carriers. Adding a trivalent impurity (B, Al, Ga, In) gives p-type, where the acceptor level lies just above the VB and holes are the majority carriers. A doped crystal remains electrically neutral. Resistivity of a semiconductor decreases as temperature rises, i.e. it has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance.

  • Si and Ge are tetravalent and form covalent bonds in a diamond-like lattice
  • At 0 K an intrinsic semiconductor behaves as an insulator
  • Holes act as positive charge carriers; total current is $I = I_e + I_h$
  • n-type: $n_e \gg n_h$; p-type: $n_h \gg n_e$
  • Mass action law $n_e n_h = n_i^2$ holds in thermal equilibrium
  • Both n-type and p-type materials are electrically neutral
  • Electron mobility is greater than hole mobility

$n_e n_h = n_i^2$ Mass action law; use it to find minority carrier density after doping

$\sigma = \frac{1}{\rho} = e(n_e \mu_e + n_h \mu_h)$ Conductivity of a semiconductor in terms of carrier densities and mobilities

$n_e \approx N_D$ (n-type), $n_h \approx N_A$ (p-type) The majority carrier density is approximately equal to the dopant concentration when $N_D$ (or $N_A$) is much greater than $n_i$.

NEET tip: Expect numericals on $n_e n_h = n_i^2$ to find minority carrier density, and conceptual questions on dopant type, band diagrams and the temperature dependence of resistance.

Semiconductor diode: I-V characteristics in forward and reverse bias

When p- and n-regions are joined, majority carriers diffuse across the junction. They leave behind immobile ions, which form the depletion region, and set up a barrier potential (about 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge). At equilibrium, diffusion current equals drift current. In forward bias (p connected to +), the barrier height and depletion width decrease. Current is negligible until the threshold (knee) voltage, then rises exponentially, and the current is due to majority carriers. In reverse bias (p connected to -), the barrier and depletion width increase. Only a tiny, almost voltage-independent reverse saturation current flows, in the microampere range, due to minority carriers. At the breakdown voltage the reverse current rises sharply. Dynamic resistance is $r_d = \Delta V/\Delta I$. An ideal diode has zero resistance in forward bias and infinite resistance in reverse bias.

  • Depletion region contains immobile ions and no free carriers
  • Electric field in the depletion region points from the n side to the p side
  • Depletion width order: reverse bias > unbiased (or open circuit) > forward bias
  • A diode in an open branch carries no current and behaves as an unbiased diode
  • Forward current comes from majority carriers; reverse current from minority carriers
  • Reverse saturation current increases with temperature
  • The I-V graph is non-linear, so a diode is a non-ohmic device

$r_d = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$ Dynamic (AC) resistance of a diode from the slope of its I-V curve

$I = \frac{V - V_0}{R}$ Current in a series diode-resistor circuit, where $V_0$ is the barrier (knee) voltage; take $V_0 = 0$ for an ideal diode

NEET tip: NEET checks whether you can identify the bias state of diodes in a circuit (including open branches) and rank depletion widths or currents, or use $r_d = \Delta V/\Delta I$ from a graph.

Diode as a rectifier

A rectifier converts AC to pulsating DC using the one-way conduction of a diode. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode. It conducts only during the half cycle in which it is forward biased, so the output appears only in alternate half cycles and has the same frequency as the input. A full-wave rectifier uses two diodes with a centre-tap transformer. Each diode conducts in alternate half cycles, and current through the load always flows in the same direction. As a result, the output ripple frequency is twice the input frequency. The pulsating output is smoothed with a capacitor filter placed in parallel with the load. The capacitor charges near the peaks and discharges slowly through the load, giving a nearly steady DC. A larger RC gives smaller ripple. Full-wave rectification is more efficient than half-wave.

  • Half-wave: output frequency = $f$; full-wave: output frequency = $2f$
  • For 50 Hz mains, full-wave ripple frequency is 100 Hz
  • In a centre-tap circuit, each diode receives half of the secondary voltage
  • The filter capacitor is connected in parallel with the load resistor
  • Larger time constant $R_L C$ gives a smoother output
  • Maximum efficiency is 40.6% for half-wave and 81.2% for full-wave

$V_{dc} = \frac{V_m}{\pi}$, $V_{rms} = \frac{V_m}{2}$ Average and rms output of a half-wave rectifier, where $V_m$ is the peak voltage

$V_{dc} = \frac{2V_m}{\pi}$, $V_{rms} = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}$ Average and rms output of a full-wave rectifier

$f_{out} = 2 f_{in}$ Output (ripple) frequency of a full-wave rectifier

NEET tip: Questions focus on output frequency, identifying input-output waveforms, and the role of the filter capacitor.

I-V characteristics of LED

A light emitting diode (LED) is a heavily doped p-n junction operated in forward bias. Injected minority carriers recombine with majority carriers near the junction and release energy as photons of energy roughly equal to $E_g$. Visible LEDs use a band gap of about 1.8 eV to 3 eV, for example GaAsP for red, yellow or orange light. The I-V characteristic resembles that of an ordinary diode, but the threshold voltage is higher and depends on colour. It is about 1.8 V for red and about 3 V for blue, so a shorter wavelength needs a higher threshold voltage. Light intensity increases with forward current up to a limit. The reverse breakdown voltage of an LED is low (about 5 V), so it must not be reverse biased carelessly. Compared with incandescent lamps, LEDs offer low operating voltage, low power consumption, fast switching, long life and nearly monochromatic light.

  • Operated in forward bias; light comes from radiative recombination
  • Photon energy is approximately $E_g$, so colour is set by the band gap
  • Si and Ge are not used for visible LEDs: their gaps are too small and they are indirect band gap materials
  • Threshold voltage order: red < yellow < green < blue
  • Reverse breakdown voltage is low, about 5 V

$E_g \approx h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$ Relates band gap to emitted wavelength

$\lambda(\text{nm}) \approx \frac{1240}{E_g(\text{eV})}$ Quick conversion between wavelength and photon energy

NEET tip: Typical questions ask for the wavelength or colour from the band gap, the biasing mode of an LED, or a comparison of threshold voltages of LEDs of different colours.

Photodiode and solar cell

A photodiode is a p-n junction operated in reverse bias with a window that admits light. Photons with $h\nu > E_g$ create electron-hole pairs near the depletion region. The junction field separates them, so the reverse current increases in proportion to light intensity. Reverse bias is used because the fractional change in the small minority-carrier current is large, which makes the device sensitive; it is used as a light detector. A solar cell is a large-area p-n junction that needs no external bias. Its operation has three steps: generation of electron-hole pairs, separation of the carriers by the junction field, and collection at the electrodes. This produces a photo-voltage (emf). Its I-V curve lies in the fourth quadrant and gives the open-circuit voltage $V_{oc}$ and the short-circuit current $I_{sc}$. Ideal materials have $E_g$ near 1.5 eV, high absorption and high conductivity, for example Si, GaAs, CdTe and CuInSe$_2$.

  • Photodiode: reverse biased; solar cell: unbiased (acts as a source)
  • Photocurrent in a photodiode is proportional to light intensity
  • A photon can generate a carrier only if $h\nu \ge E_g$
  • Solar cell I-V curve is drawn in the fourth quadrant
  • Solar spectrum peaks near 1.5 eV, so materials with $E_g \approx 1$ to $1.8$ eV are preferred
  • Solar cells are used in satellites, calculators and power supplies for remote areas

$\lambda_{max} = \frac{hc}{E_g}$ Longest wavelength that a photodiode or solar cell can detect or absorb

$P_{max} = (V I)_{max}$, fill factor $= \frac{V_m I_m}{V_{oc} I_{sc}}$ Maximum power output of a solar cell and a measure of its quality

NEET tip: NEET asks why a photodiode is reverse biased, for the cutoff wavelength from $E_g$, and for the quadrant or shape of the solar cell I-V curve.

Zener diode and Zener diode as a voltage regulator

A Zener diode is heavily doped on both sides, which gives a very thin depletion layer and a very strong junction field (about $5 \times 10^6$ V/m). It is designed to operate in reverse breakdown. At the Zener voltage $V_Z$, the field pulls electrons out of covalent bonds (internal field emission), and the current rises sharply while the voltage stays nearly constant at $V_Z$. In a voltage regulator, the Zener is reverse biased and connected in parallel with the load, with a series resistor $R_s$. If the input voltage or the load changes, the Zener current adjusts and the extra voltage drops across $R_s$. The load voltage therefore stays at $V_Z$. The drop across the series resistor is $V_{in} - V_Z$. If the voltage across the Zener without it, $V_{in}R_L/(R_s+R_L)$, is below $V_Z$, the Zener does not conduct and behaves like an open circuit.

  • Zener is used in reverse bias; in forward bias it acts like an ordinary diode
  • Heavier doping gives a lower breakdown voltage
  • Load is connected in parallel with the Zener; the resistor is in series with the input
  • Voltage across $R_s$ is $V_{in} - V_Z$; current through $R_s$ is $I = I_Z + I_L$
  • Breakdown is not destructive if the current is limited by $R_s$
  • Before assuming regulation, check that the voltage across the Zener without it, $V_{in}R_L/(R_s+R_L)$, is at least $V_Z$. If it is less, treat the Zener as an open circuit.

$I_s = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{R_s}$ Current through the series resistor

$I_L = \frac{V_Z}{R_L}$ Load current, since the load voltage is fixed at $V_Z$

$I_Z = I_s - I_L$ Current through the Zener diode

$P_Z = V_Z I_Z$ Power dissipated in the Zener; must stay below its rated value

NEET tip: Expect Zener regulator numericals: voltage across the series resistor, Zener current or power, and checks on whether the Zener is actually in breakdown.

Logic gates: OR, AND, NOT, NAND and NOR

Logic gates process binary signals (0 and 1). In the truth tables below, inputs are written in the order 00, 01, 10, 11. OR gate: $Y = A + B$; output is 1 if at least one input is 1 (outputs 0, 1, 1, 1). AND gate: $Y = A \cdot B$; output is 1 only if both inputs are 1 (outputs 0, 0, 0, 1). NOT gate: $Y = \overline{A}$; it inverts the single input. NAND gate is AND followed by NOT: $Y = \overline{A \cdot B}$ (outputs 1, 1, 1, 0). NOR gate is OR followed by NOT: $Y = \overline{A + B}$ (outputs 1, 0, 0, 0). NAND and NOR are universal gates because each can be used to build any other gate. Shorting both inputs of a NAND or a NOR gives a NOT gate. To find the output of a combination of gates, write the Boolean expression stage by stage and simplify it using De Morgan's theorems.

  • OR: any input 1 gives output 1
  • AND: all inputs 1 gives output 1
  • NAND: output 0 only when all inputs are 1
  • NOR: output 1 only when all inputs are 0
  • NAND and NOR are universal gates
  • NAND with inputs shorted gives NOT; NAND followed by NOT gives AND
  • NOR followed by NOT gives OR; NOT on both inputs of a NOR gives AND

$Y = A + B$, $Y = A \cdot B$, $Y = \overline{A}$ Boolean expressions for OR, AND and NOT

$Y = \overline{A \cdot B}$, $Y = \overline{A + B}$ Boolean expressions for NAND and NOR

$\overline{A + B} = \overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}$, $\overline{A \cdot B} = \overline{A} + \overline{B}$ De Morgan's theorems for simplifying gate combinations

NEET tip: Almost every year NEET gives a combination of gates and asks for the equivalent single gate or the truth table, so practise writing Boolean expressions step by step.

Formula sheet

$n_e n_h = n_i^2$ Mass action law; $n_e$ = electron density, $n_h$ = hole density, $n_i$ = intrinsic carrier density

$n_e = n_h = n_i$ Carrier densities in an intrinsic semiconductor

$\sigma = e(n_e \mu_e + n_h \mu_h)$ Conductivity; $\mu_e$ and $\mu_h$ are electron and hole mobilities, $e$ is the electronic charge

$\rho = \frac{1}{e(n_e \mu_e + n_h \mu_h)}$ Resistivity of a semiconductor

$I = I_e + I_h$ Total current is the sum of electron and hole currents

$r_d = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$ Dynamic resistance of a diode from the I-V curve

$I = \frac{V - V_0}{R}$ Current in a forward-biased diode-resistor series circuit; $V_0$ = knee voltage (0.7 V Si, 0.3 V Ge, 0 for ideal)

$V_{dc} = \frac{V_m}{\pi}$ Average output of a half-wave rectifier; $V_m$ = peak voltage

$V_{dc} = \frac{2V_m}{\pi}$ Average output of a full-wave rectifier

$V_{rms} = \frac{V_m}{2}$ (half-wave), $\frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}$ (full-wave) rms value of rectified output

$f_{out} = f_{in}$ (half-wave), $f_{out} = 2f_{in}$ (full-wave) Output ripple frequency of rectifiers

$\eta_{max} = 40.6\%$ (half-wave), $81.2\%$ (full-wave) Maximum rectification efficiency

$E_g = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$ Band gap related to the emitted (LED) or absorbed (photodiode, solar cell) wavelength

$\lambda(\text{nm}) \approx \frac{1240}{E(\text{eV})}$ Quick photon wavelength-energy conversion

$\lambda_{max} = \frac{hc}{E_g}$ Cutoff wavelength for photo-detection or absorption

$I_s = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{R_s}$ Current through the series resistor in a Zener regulator

$I_L = \frac{V_Z}{R_L}$, $I_Z = I_s - I_L$ Load current and Zener current in a regulator

$P_Z = V_Z I_Z$ Power dissipated in the Zener diode

$Y = A + B$, $Y = A \cdot B$, $Y = \overline{A}$ OR, AND, NOT gates

$Y = \overline{A \cdot B}$, $Y = \overline{A + B}$ NAND and NOR (universal gates)

$\overline{A + B} = \overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}$, $\overline{A \cdot B} = \overline{A} + \overline{B}$ De Morgan's theorems

Common traps

  • Thinking an n-type semiconductor is negatively charged. Every doped semiconductor is electrically neutral; only the majority carrier type changes.
  • Assuming a diode in an open (broken) branch is forward biased. With no current it behaves as an unbiased diode, so its depletion width lies between the forward- and reverse-biased cases.
  • Taking full-wave output frequency equal to input frequency. It is $2f$; for example, 50 Hz input gives 100 Hz ripple.
  • Saying a photodiode works in forward bias. It works in reverse bias, because the fractional change in reverse current due to light is significant.
  • Assuming the Zener always regulates. It conducts in breakdown only if the reverse voltage across it reaches $V_Z$; otherwise treat it as an open circuit.
  • Using the full input voltage across the series resistor of a Zener circuit. The drop across it is $V_{in} - V_Z$.
  • Confusing NAND with NOR outputs. NAND gives 0 only for input 11; NOR gives 1 only for input 00.
  • Believing semiconductor resistance increases with temperature as in metals. It decreases, because more carriers are generated.

Quick revision

  • Band gaps: Si about 1.1 eV, Ge about 0.7 eV; insulators above 3 eV.
  • Pentavalent dopant gives n-type with a donor level near the CB; trivalent dopant gives p-type with an acceptor level near the VB.
  • Use $n_e n_h = n_i^2$ to get the minority carrier density.
  • Depletion width: reverse bias > unbiased > forward bias.
  • Barrier potential: about 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge; reverse current is a small minority-carrier current.
  • Half-wave output frequency is $f$; full-wave is $2f$; the filter capacitor goes in parallel with the load.
  • LED: forward bias, photon energy about $E_g$, $\lambda(\text{nm}) = 1240/E_g(\text{eV})$; threshold voltage rises from red to blue.
  • Photodiode is reverse biased; solar cell is unbiased with its I-V curve in the fourth quadrant.
  • Solar cell action: generation, separation, collection; ideal $E_g$ is near 1.5 eV.
  • Zener: heavily doped, used in reverse breakdown, load in parallel; $I_s = I_Z + I_L$.
  • NAND and NOR are universal gates; shorting their inputs gives NOT.
  • Solve gate combinations by writing Boolean expressions stage by stage and applying De Morgan's theorems.

Physics · Unit 20: Experimental Skills

This unit covers the practical experiments of the NCERT Class 11 and 12 physics syllabus. It deals with instruments such as the vernier calipers, screw gauge, metre bridge, optical bench and travelling microscope, and with the procedures, graphs, errors and corrections used in each experiment. NEET usually asks 2-3 direct questions from this unit on least count, zero error, end or index correction, the shape of graphs and formula-based calculations, so it is a high-scoring and low-effort area.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q20

Vernier calipers: internal and external diameter and depth of a vessel

Vernier calipers measure lengths more finely than the main scale alone. The main scale division (MSD) is usually 1 mm. N vernier divisions coincide with (N-1) main scale divisions. The outside (lower) jaws measure the external diameter of a beaker or rod. The inside (upper) jaws measure the internal diameter. The thin depth strip at the tail measures the depth of a vessel. To take a reading, note the main scale reading (MSR) just before the vernier zero. Then find the vernier division that coincides with any main scale line (VSR). If the vernier zero lies to the right of the main scale zero when the jaws are closed, the zero error is positive. If it lies to the left, the zero error is negative. The zero error is always subtracted algebraically from the observed reading.

  • Least count = 1 MSD - 1 VSD, which is typically 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm
  • External diameter is measured with the outside jaws, internal diameter with the inside jaws, and depth with the depth strip
  • Positive zero error means the vernier zero is to the right of the main zero, so the correction is negative
  • Take readings at several orientations and use the mean to reduce random error
  • Wall thickness of a hollow cylinder = (external diameter - internal diameter)/2

$LC = 1\,MSD - 1\,VSD = \frac{1\,MSD}{N}$ Least count when N vernier divisions equal (N-1) main scale divisions

$\text{Reading} = MSR + (VSR \times LC) - (\text{zero error})$ True reading with the zero error removed algebraically

NEET tip: NEET often gives an unusual vernier design (for example 10 VSD = 9 MSD with MSD = 0.5 mm) or a negative zero error and asks for the corrected reading.

Screw gauge: thickness or diameter of a thin sheet or wire

A screw gauge (micrometer) works on the principle of a screw. The linear distance moved by the spindle is proportional to the rotation of the thimble. Pitch is the distance moved by the spindle in one complete rotation. The least count equals the pitch divided by the number of circular scale divisions, usually 0.01 mm. It is used to measure the diameter of a thin wire or the thickness of a sheet. The ratchet is used so that the object is held with uniform pressure and is not compressed. Zero error is positive when the circular scale zero lies below the reference line. It is negative when it lies above. Backlash error arises from wear of the screw threads. It is avoided by always rotating the screw in one direction.

  • Pitch = linear distance moved per rotation, and LC = pitch/number of circular divisions
  • Turn the ratchet, not the thimble, to avoid overtightening
  • Positive zero error means the circular scale zero is below the reference line
  • Backlash error is avoided by rotating in one direction only
  • For a wire, take readings at different places along it in two mutually perpendicular directions

$LC = \frac{\text{pitch}}{\text{number of circular scale divisions}}$ Least count of the screw gauge

$\text{Reading} = PSR + (CSR \times LC) - (\text{zero error})$ Corrected diameter or thickness (PSR = pitch scale reading, CSR = circular scale reading)

NEET tip: Expect calculations of least count from pitch and divisions, and corrected readings with a zero error given as a number of circular divisions above or below the line.

Simple pendulum: dissipation of energy from amplitude-squared vs time graph

A real pendulum loses energy to air resistance and friction at the support. Its amplitude therefore decreases with time. For light damping (damping force = -bv), the amplitude decays as $A = A_0 e^{-bt/2m}$. The mechanical energy is proportional to $A^2$, so it decays as $e^{-bt/m}$. In the experiment, the amplitude is noted at regular time intervals and $A^2$ is plotted against t. The curve is a falling exponential, which shows that energy is dissipated continuously. A plot of $\ln A^2$ against t is a straight line with slope -b/m. The time for the energy to fall to half its value is $(m/b)\ln 2$. The time period stays nearly the same for small damping.

  • Energy is proportional to the square of the amplitude, $E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2$
  • The $A^2$ vs t graph is an exponential decay, not a straight line
  • The $\ln A^2$ vs t graph is linear with slope -b/m
  • The energy decays twice as fast as the amplitude (exponent b/m against b/2m)
  • The time period is practically unchanged for light damping

$A(t) = A_0 e^{-bt/2m}$ Amplitude of a lightly damped oscillator

$E(t) = E_0 e^{-bt/m}$ Mechanical energy decay, since $E \propto A^2$

NEET tip: Questions ask for the graph shape or the fraction of energy left when the amplitude has fallen to a given fraction (energy fraction = square of the amplitude fraction).

Metre scale: mass of an object by the principle of moments

A metre scale balanced on a knife edge works on the principle of moments. In equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the fulcrum. First, the scale is balanced alone to find its centre of gravity G (ideally at 50 cm). A known mass is then hung on one side and the unknown mass on the other. Their positions are adjusted until the scale balances again with the fulcrum at G. The unknown mass is $m = M d_1/d_2$, where $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the distances of the known and unknown masses from the fulcrum. If the fulcrum is not at G, the weight of the scale acting at G must also be included in the moment equation. Repeat the measurement for different positions and take the mean.

  • Clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment about the fulcrum
  • Find the centre of gravity of the scale first
  • If the fulcrum is shifted from G, include the scale's own weight acting at G
  • Use thin threads for suspension and keep the scale horizontal

$m_1 d_1 = m_2 d_2$ Balance condition when the fulcrum is at the centre of gravity of the scale

$M d_1 = m d_2 + m_s d_s$ General balance condition including the scale mass $m_s$ acting at G, a distance $d_s$ from the fulcrum, on the same side as m

NEET tip: NEET typically asks for an unknown mass when the fulcrum is not at the centre of gravity, so the scale's own weight must be included.

Young's modulus of elasticity of a metallic wire

Searle's apparatus is used to find Young's modulus of a metallic wire. Two identical wires hang from the same rigid support. The reference wire carries a constant load. The experimental wire is loaded in steps. Using a reference wire cancels errors due to temperature changes and yielding of the support. The extension is read with a micrometer screw and a spirit level. The micrometer is adjusted each time to bring the bubble back to the centre. The diameter of the wire is measured with a screw gauge, and the original length with a metre scale. The load vs extension graph is a straight line within the elastic limit, and its slope gives Mg/l. Readings are taken both while loading and while unloading. The mean is used to cancel elastic lag.

  • Stress/strain = Y within the elastic limit
  • The reference wire compensates for thermal expansion and sagging of the support
  • The extension is measured with a micrometer and spirit level, and the diameter with a screw gauge
  • The load-extension graph is a straight line through the origin, so Y = (slope) × L/(πr²) if slope = Mg/l
  • The maximum error comes from the radius, since r appears squared

$Y = \frac{MgL}{\pi r^2 \, l}$ Young's modulus (M = load, L = original length, r = radius, l = extension)

$\frac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \frac{\Delta L}{L} + 2\frac{\Delta r}{r} + \frac{\Delta l}{l}$ Maximum relative error in Y

NEET tip: NEET asks for the percentage error in Y, the role of the reference wire, or the slope of the load-extension graph.

Surface tension of water by capillary rise and effect of detergents

Water rises in a clean, narrow glass capillary because the adhesion between water and glass is greater than the cohesion within water. The angle of contact is nearly zero. The rise h is found by balancing the surface tension force against the weight of the liquid column. A travelling microscope is used to measure the height of the meniscus, the level of the water in the beaker and the internal radius of the capillary. When a detergent is added, the surface tension falls, so the capillary rise decreases. This is why detergents help water to penetrate fabrics and wet them. A narrower tube gives a larger rise, since hr is constant (Jurin's law). Hot water also rises less, because surface tension decreases with temperature.

  • Height of rise is inversely proportional to the radius: hr = constant
  • The contact angle for pure water and clean glass is about 0°
  • Detergents and soaps reduce surface tension, so the rise decreases
  • The travelling microscope measures both h and r
  • Meniscus correction: use h + r/3 for an accurate value

$h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}$ Capillary rise (T = surface tension, θ = contact angle, ρ = density)

$T = \frac{r\rho g}{2}\left(h + \frac{r}{3}\right)$ Surface tension of water with θ ≈ 0 and the meniscus correction

NEET tip: NEET tests the effect of detergents or temperature on the rise, or the change in h when the radius changes.

Coefficient of viscosity by terminal velocity of a spherical body

A small steel ball falling through a viscous liquid such as glycerine first accelerates. It soon reaches a constant terminal velocity. At that point, the weight equals the buoyant force plus the viscous drag given by Stokes' law, $6\pi\eta r v$. Two marks are made on a tall jar, the upper one well below the liquid surface so the ball is already at terminal velocity there. The time taken to cross the marks gives v. Plotting v against $r^2$ for balls of different radii gives a straight line through the origin. The coefficient of viscosity is obtained from its slope. The ball should be dropped along the axis of the jar to avoid wall effects. The temperature must be noted, because viscosity of liquids decreases sharply as temperature rises.

  • Terminal velocity is proportional to $r^2$
  • The upper mark must be well below the surface so terminal velocity is reached
  • The v vs $r^2$ graph is a straight line, and η is found from its slope
  • Viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature, while that of gases increases
  • Drop the ball along the axis, away from the walls

$v_t = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$ Terminal velocity (ρ = density of the ball, σ = density of the liquid)

$\eta = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9v_t}$ Coefficient of viscosity from the measured terminal velocity

NEET tip: NEET asks for the ratio of terminal velocities for different radii, or the shape of the velocity-time graph (it rises and then becomes flat).

Speed of sound in air using a resonance tube

A resonance tube is a tube closed at one end by a water column. A vibrating tuning fork is held over the open end and the length of the air column is changed. Loud sound (resonance) is heard when the natural frequency of the air column matches the fork. The closed end is a node and the open end is an antinode. The antinode actually forms slightly above the open end, at a distance called the end correction, e = 0.3d. At the first resonance, $l_1 + e = \lambda/4$. At the second, $l_2 + e = 3\lambda/4$. Subtracting the two eliminates the end correction, giving $v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)$. The resonance length is located accurately by approaching it from both sides.

  • This is a closed pipe, so only odd harmonics are present
  • End correction e = 0.3d = 0.6r, where d is the internal diameter
  • $l_2 - l_1 = \lambda/2$ is independent of the end correction
  • $l_2 \approx 3l_1$, and $l_2$ is slightly greater than $3l_1$ because of the end correction ($l_2 = 3l_1 + 2e$)
  • The speed of sound increases with temperature and humidity

$v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)$ Speed of sound from the first two resonance lengths

$e = \frac{l_2 - 3l_1}{2}$ End correction from the resonance lengths

$v = 4f(l_1 + e)$ Speed of sound from the first resonance with the end correction

NEET tip: NEET frequently asks for v or e from the given $l_1$ and $l_2$. Note that this experiment needs an end correction, not an index correction.

Specific heat capacity of a solid and a liquid by method of mixtures

The method of mixtures is based on the principle of calorimetry: heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold body and the calorimeter, assuming no losses. For a solid, a heated sample of known mass is quickly dropped into water at a known temperature in a copper calorimeter. The water is stirred and the highest steady temperature of the mixture is noted. For a liquid, a hot solid of known specific heat is dropped into the liquid instead. The calorimeter is polished and insulated to reduce heat loss by radiation and conduction. The transfer must be quick to reduce heat loss to the surroundings.

  • Heat lost = heat gained (principle of calorimetry)
  • The copper calorimeter has low specific heat and good conductivity
  • Note the maximum temperature of the mixture
  • Polished surfaces and insulation reduce radiation and conduction losses
  • Heat loss to the surroundings makes the calculated specific heat of the solid smaller than the true value

$m_1 s_1 (T_1 - T) = (m_2 s_w + m_c s_c)(T - T_2)$ Method of mixtures: hot solid ($m_1, s_1, T_1$), water ($m_2, s_w$) and calorimeter ($m_c, s_c$) both initially at $T_2$, final temperature T

NEET tip: NEET gives masses and temperatures and asks for the specific heat or the final temperature, sometimes including the water equivalent of the calorimeter.

Resistivity of a wire using a metre bridge

A metre bridge is a practical form of the Wheatstone bridge. It uses a 1 m uniform wire with a jockey. A known resistance R from a resistance box and the unknown wire X are placed in the two gaps. The jockey is slid along the wire to find the balance point where the galvanometer shows no deflection. If R is in the left gap and the balance length l is measured from the left end, then $R/X = l/(100 - l)$. The resistivity follows from the measured length and diameter of the wire. The balance point should lie near the middle of the wire for maximum sensitivity and minimum end error. R and X are interchanged and the mean is taken to cancel end corrections.

  • This is the Wheatstone bridge principle, P/Q = R/S at balance
  • At balance, no current flows through the galvanometer
  • A null point near 50 cm gives the highest accuracy
  • Interchange the resistances to remove end error
  • The thick copper strips have negligible resistance, and the jockey should be pressed gently, never slid while pressed

$X = R\frac{100 - l}{l}$ Unknown resistance with R in the left gap and l in cm from the left end

$\rho = \frac{X\pi r^2}{L}$ Resistivity of the wire of length L and radius r

$X = R\frac{100 - l + \beta}{l + \alpha}$ With end corrections α and β at the two ends

NEET tip: NEET asks for X or the shift of the balance point when resistances change, and why the null point should be near the middle.

Resistance of a wire using Ohm's law

The resistance of a wire is found from Ohm's law, V = IR, at constant temperature. The circuit has a battery, a key, a rheostat, an ammeter in series with the wire and a voltmeter in parallel with it. The current is varied with the rheostat and the corresponding values of V and I are noted. The V-I graph for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin. The slope of V vs I gives R, while the slope of I vs V gives 1/R. A large current heats the wire and increases its resistance, so currents are kept small. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance. The resistivity is then calculated from the wire's dimensions.

  • Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the wire
  • The V-I graph is linear and the slope (V on the y-axis) gives R
  • Keep the current small to avoid heating
  • Positive terminals of the meters go towards the positive terminal of the battery
  • Resistance depends on length and area, but resistivity is a material property

$R = \frac{V}{I}$ Ohm's law, valid at constant temperature

$\rho = \frac{RA}{L} = \frac{R\pi d^2}{4L}$ Resistivity from resistance, length L and diameter d

NEET tip: NEET asks how to compare resistances from the slopes of V-I or I-V graphs, or about the correct placement of meters.

Resistance and figure of merit of a galvanometer by half deflection method

In the half deflection method, a high resistance R is connected in series with the galvanometer and a cell. R is adjusted to get an even-numbered deflection θ. A shunt S is then connected across the galvanometer and adjusted until the deflection becomes θ/2. If R is much larger than G, the main current is nearly unchanged, so the shunt carries half the current and G ≈ S. The exact formula is G = RS/(R - S). The figure of merit is the current needed for a deflection of one division. It is k = E/[(R + G)θ], with the unit ampere per division. A smaller figure of merit means a more sensitive galvanometer.

  • Keep R very large (several kΩ) compared with G
  • Choose an even deflection so that θ/2 is a whole number
  • G ≈ S when R is much larger than G
  • The figure of merit is the current per division, and sensitivity is its reciprocal
  • Use a low-resistance cell (accumulator) to keep the emf steady

$G = \frac{RS}{R - S}$ Galvanometer resistance by the half deflection method

$k = \frac{E}{(R + G)\theta}$ Figure of merit in A/div (E = emf, θ = deflection in divisions)

NEET tip: Expect a calculation of G from R and S, or the figure of merit from E, R, G and θ.

Focal length of convex mirror, concave mirror and convex lens by parallax method

On an optical bench, the image position is located by the no-parallax method. The image is located when the tip of the image pin and the tip of the image coincide and do not separate when the eye is moved sideways. The bench scale readings may not equal the actual distances between the optical element and the pins. The index correction is found with an index rod of known length: index correction = actual length - observed length. It is added to every measured distance. For a concave mirror and a convex lens, real images are located directly and u, v are used in the mirror or lens formula. A convex mirror forms only a virtual image, so a convex lens is used to form a real image that acts as a virtual object. A plot of 1/v against 1/u is a straight line with equal intercepts of 1/f on both axes.

  • No parallax means the image and the pin are at the same position
  • Index correction is needed in optical bench experiments
  • Index correction = actual distance (index rod) - observed distance
  • For a convex mirror, use an auxiliary convex lens
  • The u-v graph is a rectangular hyperbola, and the 1/u-1/v graph is a straight line with intercepts 1/f
  • At u = v = 2f, the image is the same size as the object for a concave mirror or convex lens

$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ Mirror formula for concave and convex mirrors, with sign convention

$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ Lens formula for a convex lens, with sign convention

$f = \frac{R}{2}$ For a convex mirror, R is the distance from the mirror to the point where the lens-formed image coincides with its own pin

NEET tip: NEET asks which experiment needs index correction (optical bench focal length) and for f from u-v data.

Angle of deviation vs angle of incidence for a triangular prism

Pins are fixed in front of a triangular glass prism to trace the incident ray, and the emergent ray is traced by sighting through the other face. The angle of deviation δ is measured for different angles of incidence i, usually from 30° to 60°. The δ-i graph is U-shaped but not symmetric. Its lowest point gives the angle of minimum deviation $\delta_m$. At minimum deviation, i = e and the refracted ray inside the prism travels parallel to the base, with $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$. The refractive index then follows from the prism formula. For a given δ other than $\delta_m$, there are two values of i, which are interchangeable as i and e.

  • $i + e = A + \delta$ and $r_1 + r_2 = A$
  • The δ vs i graph is U-shaped with a single minimum
  • At minimum deviation, i = e, r = A/2 and the ray inside is parallel to the base
  • δ increases with refractive index, so violet deviates more than red
  • Keep the pins vertical and widely separated (about 5 cm or more)

$\delta = i + e - A$ Angle of deviation for a prism of angle A

$n = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$ Refractive index from the angle of minimum deviation

NEET tip: NEET tests the shape of the δ-i graph, the condition i = e at minimum deviation, and n from A and $\delta_m$.

Refractive index of a glass slab using a travelling microscope

A travelling microscope with a vernier on its vertical scale is used to measure the real and apparent thickness of a glass slab. First, a mark on paper is focused and the reading $R_1$ is taken. The slab is placed over the mark, and the microscope is raised to refocus the mark seen through the glass, giving $R_2$. Finally, lycopodium powder or chalk dust sprinkled on the top surface is focused, giving $R_3$. The real thickness is $R_3 - R_1$ and the apparent thickness is $R_3 - R_2$. Their ratio gives the refractive index. The microscope must always be moved in one direction to avoid backlash error.

  • Real thickness = $R_3 - R_1$ and apparent thickness = $R_3 - R_2$
  • Normal shift = $R_2 - R_1 = t(1 - 1/n)$
  • Lycopodium powder makes the top surface visible
  • Move the microscope in one direction only to avoid backlash
  • The least count is found as in vernier calipers

$n = \frac{\text{real thickness}}{\text{apparent thickness}} = \frac{R_3 - R_1}{R_3 - R_2}$ Refractive index of the glass slab

$d = t\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)$ Apparent shift of the mark for a slab of thickness t

NEET tip: NEET gives the three microscope readings and asks for n, or gives n and t and asks for the shift.

Characteristic curves of a p-n junction diode in forward and reverse bias

A p-n junction diode is studied in forward bias with a milliammeter and in reverse bias with a microammeter, the voltage being changed with a potential divider. In forward bias (p side to positive), the current is negligible until the knee or threshold voltage is reached. This is about 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge. Beyond it, the current rises steeply, almost exponentially. In reverse bias, only a tiny, nearly constant reverse saturation current of the order of μA flows, due to minority carriers. This current increases with temperature. The forward resistance is low and the reverse resistance is very high. The dynamic resistance is the reciprocal of the slope of the I-V curve at a point.

  • Knee voltage is about 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge
  • Use a milliammeter in forward bias and a microammeter in reverse bias
  • The reverse saturation current is due to minority carriers and depends on temperature
  • The I-V curve is non-linear, so the diode is a non-ohmic device
  • Exceeding the reverse breakdown voltage of an ordinary diode damages it

$r_d = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$ Dynamic (ac) resistance of the diode from the slope of the characteristic

NEET tip: NEET asks you to identify the forward or reverse characteristic graph, the knee voltage, or the dynamic resistance from a graph.

Characteristic curves of a Zener diode and reverse breakdown voltage

A Zener diode is a heavily doped p-n junction designed to operate in the reverse breakdown region. Its forward characteristic is like that of an ordinary diode. In reverse bias, the current is negligible until the Zener voltage $V_Z$ is reached. At that point, the current rises sharply while the voltage across the diode stays almost constant. This voltage is read from the vertical part of the reverse characteristic. A series resistor limits the current to protect the diode. Because the voltage stays constant over a wide range of current, the Zener diode is used as a voltage regulator. Heavy doping makes the depletion layer very thin, so the electric field across it becomes very strong.

  • Heavily doped, with a thin depletion layer
  • Operated in reverse bias at breakdown
  • The voltage across it stays nearly constant at $V_Z$ beyond breakdown
  • A series resistor is essential to limit the current
  • Used as a voltage regulator

$R_s = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{I}$ Series resistance, where I is the total current through $R_s$ (Zener current + load current)

$I_Z = I - I_L = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{R_s} - \frac{V_Z}{R_L}$ Current through the Zener diode in a regulator circuit

NEET tip: NEET asks for the Zener current or series resistance in a regulator circuit, or for identifying the breakdown region on a graph.

Identification of diode, LED, resistor and capacitor from a mixed collection

Components are identified using a multimeter in the resistance or continuity mode. The leads are connected one way and then reversed. A resistor shows the same finite resistance in both directions and no change with time. A diode conducts (low resistance) in one direction only and shows very high resistance on reversal. An LED behaves like a diode but also glows when forward biased. A capacitor shows a deflection that starts large and gradually decays as it charges, ending at very high resistance. On reversing the leads, the same transient appears again. An integrated circuit (IC) has many terminals.

  • Resistor: same steady resistance in both directions
  • Diode: conducts in one direction only, with no light
  • LED: one-way conduction with light emission
  • Capacitor: momentary current that decays to zero in either direction
  • IC: multiple terminals

NEET tip: NEET describes the multimeter behaviour of an unknown component and asks you to identify it.

Formula sheet

$LC_{vernier} = 1\,MSD - 1\,VSD = \frac{MSD}{N}$ Least count of vernier calipers, where N vernier divisions equal (N-1) main scale divisions

$LC_{screw} = \frac{p}{N}$ Least count of a screw gauge, p = pitch, N = number of circular divisions

$\text{True reading} = \text{observed} - \text{zero error}$ Zero error is subtracted algebraically

$E = E_0 e^{-bt/m}$ Energy of a damped pendulum, $E \propto A^2$, b = damping constant, m = bob mass

$m_1 d_1 = m_2 d_2$ Principle of moments, masses times distances from the fulcrum

$Y = \frac{MgL}{\pi r^2 l}$ Young's modulus, M = load, L = length, r = radius, l = extension

$h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}$ Capillary rise, T = surface tension, r = tube radius, ρ = liquid density

$v_t = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$ Terminal velocity, ρ = ball density, σ = liquid density, η = viscosity

$v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)$ Speed of sound from a resonance tube, f = fork frequency

$e = 0.3d = \frac{l_2 - 3l_1}{2}$ End correction of the resonance tube, d = internal diameter

$m_1 s_1 (T_1 - T) = (m_2 s_w + m_c s_c)(T - T_2)$ Method of mixtures, heat lost = heat gained

$X = R\frac{100 - l}{l}$ Metre bridge with R in the left gap and balance length l cm from the left

$\rho = \frac{R\pi r^2}{L}$ Resistivity, r = wire radius, L = wire length

$R = \frac{V}{I}$ Ohm's law, the slope of the V-I graph

$G = \frac{RS}{R - S}$ Galvanometer resistance by half deflection, R = series resistance, S = shunt

$k = \frac{E}{(R + G)\theta}$ Figure of merit in A/div

$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ Mirror formula

$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ Lens formula

$\text{Index correction} = \text{actual length} - \text{observed length}$ Optical bench correction found with an index rod

$n = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$ Prism refractive index, A = prism angle, $\delta_m$ = minimum deviation

$n = \frac{R_3 - R_1}{R_3 - R_2}$ Glass slab refractive index from travelling microscope readings

$r_d = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$ Dynamic resistance of a diode

$R_s = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{I}$ Series resistor for a Zener regulator, I = total current

Common traps

  • Adding a positive zero error instead of subtracting it. The correct rule is true value = observed value - zero error, taken with its sign.
  • Confusing end correction with index correction. The resonance tube needs an end correction, while optical bench focal length experiments need an index correction.
  • Assuming the $A^2$ vs t graph of a damped pendulum is linear. It is exponential, and only $\ln A^2$ vs t is linear.
  • Using $v = 4fl_1$ without the end correction. Using $v = 2f(l_2 - l_1)$ removes the end correction automatically.
  • Thinking detergents increase capillary rise. They lower surface tension, so the rise decreases.
  • Writing G = S in the half deflection method even when R is not large. The exact formula is G = RS/(R - S).
  • Taking the prism δ-i graph as symmetric or V-shaped. It is a smooth U-shaped curve that is not symmetric, with a single minimum where i = e.
  • Expecting a Zener diode to regulate in forward bias. It regulates only in reverse breakdown and needs a series resistor.

Quick revision

  • Vernier least count is 0.1 mm and screw gauge least count is 0.01 mm. Zero error is always subtracted algebraically.
  • Backlash error occurs in the screw gauge and travelling microscope. Avoid it by rotating in one direction only.
  • Damped pendulum: $E \propto A^2$ decays as $e^{-bt/m}$, and the $\ln A^2$ vs t graph is a straight line.
  • In Searle's experiment, the reference wire cancels temperature and support-yielding errors, and the radius gives the largest error.
  • Capillary rise follows hr = constant, and detergents or a rise in temperature lower the rise.
  • Terminal velocity is proportional to $r^2$, and the v vs $r^2$ graph is a straight line.
  • Resonance tube: $l_2 - l_1 = \lambda/2$, e = 0.3d, and $l_2 \approx 3l_1$.
  • Metre bridge accuracy is best near the 50 cm null point. Interchange the resistances to cancel end error.
  • Half deflection: G = RS/(R - S), and the figure of merit has the unit A/div.
  • An optical bench needs an index correction, and the no-parallax condition locates the image.
  • Prism: at minimum deviation, i = e, r = A/2 and the ray inside is parallel to the base. Slab: n = real thickness/apparent thickness.
  • Diode knee voltage is 0.7 V (Si) or 0.3 V (Ge). A Zener diode is used in reverse breakdown. A capacitor shows a decaying deflection on a multimeter, and an LED glows in forward bias.

Chemistry · Unit 1: Some Basic Concepts in Chemistry

This unit sets up the quantitative language of chemistry: the nature and measurement of matter, Dalton's atomic theory, the laws of chemical combination, atomic and molecular masses, and the mole concept. These ideas are then used to find percentage composition, empirical and molecular formulae, and stoichiometric quantities. NEET asks 1-2 direct numerical questions from this unit every year, and mole-based reasoning is needed in almost every other physical chemistry chapter.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q51, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q63

Matter and its nature

Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It exists as solid (definite shape and volume), liquid (definite volume only) or gas (neither definite). Matter is classified as pure substances or mixtures. Pure substances are elements or compounds and have a fixed composition. Mixtures are homogeneous (uniform composition, for example air or sugar solution) or heterogeneous (non-uniform, for example sand in water). Mixtures can be separated by physical methods, but compounds need chemical methods. Properties are physical (colour, density, melting point) or chemical (reactivity, combustibility). Measurements use SI units, which have seven base units: m, kg, s, A, K, cd and mol. Every measurement carries some uncertainty, which is expressed through significant figures. Precision means closeness of repeated readings to each other, while accuracy means closeness to the true value. Rounding follows a fixed rule. If the digit to be dropped is greater than 5, the preceding digit is increased by one. If it is less than 5, the preceding digit is unchanged. If it is exactly 5, the preceding digit is increased by one only when it is odd and left unchanged when it is even.

  • Mixture: variable composition, separable by physical methods; compound: fixed composition, separable only chemically
  • Seven SI base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, candela, mole
  • All non-zero digits are significant
  • Zeros between non-zero digits are significant
  • Leading zeros are not significant, e.g. $0.0034$ has 2 significant figures
  • Trailing zeros are significant only if a decimal point is present, e.g. $0.200$ has 3 significant figures
  • Exact numbers (counted objects, defined values) have infinite significant figures
  • In scientific notation $N \times 10^n$, only the digits in $N$ are significant
  • Addition and subtraction: round the result to the least number of decimal places
  • Multiplication and division: round the result to the least number of significant figures
  • Rounding when the dropped digit is exactly 5: raise the preceding digit if odd, keep it if even

$d = \frac{m}{V}$ Density of a substance, in $g\,cm^{-3}$ or $kg\,m^{-3}$

$T(K) = t(^{\circ}C) + 273.15$ Converts Celsius to Kelvin

$^{\circ}F = \frac{9}{5}(^{\circ}C) + 32$ Converts Celsius to Fahrenheit

NEET tip: NEET asks about counting significant figures, the rounding-off rule (especially the 'dropped digit is 5' case) and classifying a substance as element, compound or type of mixture.

Dalton's atomic theory: atom, molecule, element and compound

In 1808 John Dalton proposed his atomic theory, which has four main postulates. First, matter consists of indivisible atoms. Second, all atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties, while atoms of different elements differ. Third, compounds form when atoms of different elements combine in a fixed ratio. Fourth, chemical reactions only rearrange atoms; atoms are neither created nor destroyed. The theory was able to explain the laws of conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions. Key terms follow from this picture. An atom is the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction. A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and has all its properties. An element contains only one kind of atom, for example $Na$, $H_2$, $O_3$ or $S_8$. A compound contains two or more kinds of atoms in a fixed ratio, for example $H_2O$ or $CO_2$. The theory has limitations. It cannot explain the law of gaseous volumes. Discoveries of subatomic particles showed that atoms are divisible. Isotopes showed that atoms of one element can differ in mass, and isobars showed that atoms of different elements can have the same mass.

  • Dalton's theory explains conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions
  • Dalton's theory fails to explain Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes
  • Isotopes (same element, different mass) contradict 'all atoms of an element are identical'
  • Discovery of electrons, protons and neutrons contradicts 'atoms are indivisible'
  • Monoatomic molecules: noble gases such as $He$ and $Ar$
  • Polyatomic elemental molecules: $O_3$, $P_4$, $S_8$
  • Molecules of compounds contain different atoms; atomicity of $NH_3$ is 4
  • Dalton's theory did not distinguish atoms from molecules; Avogadro's idea of molecules removed this gap

NEET tip: Expect statement-based questions on which postulate is incorrect or which law Dalton's theory could not explain.

Laws of chemical combination

Five laws govern chemical combination. The law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier) states that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The law of definite proportions (Proust) states that a given compound always contains the same elements in the same mass ratio, whatever its source. The law of multiple proportions (Dalton) states that when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio. For example, in $H_2O$ and $H_2O_2$, the oxygen masses combining with 2 g of hydrogen are 16 g and 32 g, a ratio of 1:2. Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes states that gases react, and gaseous products form, in simple whole-number volume ratios at the same temperature and pressure. For example, 2 volumes of $H_2$ react with 1 volume of $O_2$ to give 2 volumes of water vapour. Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

  • Conservation of mass: Lavoisier (1789)
  • Definite proportions: Proust
  • Multiple proportions: Dalton (1803); always compare masses for a fixed mass of the other element
  • Typical multiple-proportion pairs: $CO$/$CO_2$, $H_2O$/$H_2O_2$, the oxides of nitrogen
  • Gay-Lussac's law is a volume relationship, applicable only to gases at the same T and P
  • Gay-Lussac's law is effectively the law of definite proportions applied to volumes
  • Avogadro distinguished atoms from molecules and explained Gay-Lussac's law
  • Volume ratio of gases = mole ratio = ratio of stoichiometric coefficients (same T, P)

$\text{Total mass of reactants} = \text{Total mass of products}$ Law of conservation of mass

$V \propto n$ (constant $T$, $P$) Avogadro's law; gas volumes are proportional to number of moles

NEET tip: NEET gives mass data for two compounds of the same pair of elements and asks which law is illustrated, or matches each law with its scientist.

Atomic and molecular masses

Atomic masses are measured relative to the carbon-12 standard. One atomic mass unit (u) is defined as exactly one-twelfth of the mass of one $^{12}C$ atom, which equals $1.66056 \times 10^{-24}$ g. Most elements occur as mixtures of isotopes. The atomic mass used in calculations is therefore an average atomic mass, weighted by natural abundance. Chlorine, for example, is about 75.77% $^{35}Cl$ and 24.23% $^{37}Cl$, giving an average of about 35.45 u. The molecular mass of a covalent molecule is the sum of the atomic masses of all its atoms; for $H_2O$ it is $2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02$ u. Ionic solids such as $NaCl$ do not contain discrete molecules. For them we use the formula mass, which is the sum of atomic masses in one formula unit; for $NaCl$ it is 58.5 u.

  • $1\,u = 1\,amu = \frac{1}{12}$ of the mass of one $^{12}C$ atom $= 1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\,g$
  • The mass of one $^{12}C$ atom is exactly 12 u
  • Average atomic mass depends on isotopic abundance, so it is usually non-integral
  • Molecular mass applies to covalent molecules
  • Formula mass applies to ionic compounds
  • Atomic and molecular masses are relative masses expressed in u
  • Mass of one atom in grams = atomic mass in u multiplied by $1.66 \times 10^{-24}$ g, which equals $\frac{\text{molar mass}}{N_A}$
  • Mass spectrometry is used to determine isotopic masses and abundances

$\bar{A} = \frac{\sum (\text{abundance}_i \times m_i)}{\sum \text{abundance}_i}$ Average atomic mass from isotopic masses and abundances

$M = \sum (\text{number of atoms} \times \text{atomic mass})$ Molecular mass or formula mass

$\text{Mass of 1 atom} = \frac{\text{Molar mass}}{N_A}$ Absolute mass of a single atom or molecule in grams

NEET tip: NEET often asks for the average atomic mass from isotopic abundance data, or the absolute mass of one atom or molecule in grams.

Mole concept and molar mass

A mole is the amount of substance that contains exactly $6.02214076 \times 10^{23}$ elementary entities, such as atoms, molecules, ions or electrons. This number is the Avogadro constant, $N_A$. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in grams. It is numerically equal to the atomic, molecular or formula mass in u; for example, $H_2O$ has a molar mass of 18.02 g mol$^{-1}$. The mole links three measurable quantities: mass, number of particles and gas volume. At STP (273.15 K, 1 bar), one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.7 L. The older convention (273 K, 1 atm) uses 22.4 L, and NEET follows whichever value the question data indicate. Always specify the entity being counted. One mole of $O_2$ contains $N_A$ molecules but $2N_A$ oxygen atoms.

  • $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\,mol^{-1}$
  • 1 mole of any substance contains $N_A$ entities of that substance
  • Gram atomic mass: mass of 1 mol of atoms; gram molecular mass: mass of 1 mol of molecules
  • 1 mol of $H_2SO_4$ contains 2 mol H, 1 mol S and 4 mol O
  • Molar volume at STP: 22.7 L (1 bar) or 22.4 L (1 atm), both at 273 K
  • Number of electrons, protons or ions = moles of substance × entities per formula × $N_A$
  • The mole concept applies to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons and even photons

$n = \frac{m}{M}$ Moles from given mass and molar mass

$n = \frac{N}{N_A}$ Moles from number of particles

$n = \frac{V_{gas}}{22.7\,L}$ (or $22.4\,L$) Moles of a gas from its volume at STP

$N = n \times N_A \times \text{atomicity}$ Number of atoms in a given amount of molecules

NEET tip: NEET asks you to compare the number of atoms or molecules in different given masses, or to find the number of electrons or ions in a sample. Always convert everything to moles first.

Percentage composition

Percentage composition gives the mass percentage of each element in a compound. It can be calculated from the formula and used to check the purity of a sample or to identify a compound. Take one mole of the compound and divide the mass of each element in it by the molar mass, then multiply by 100. For ethanol, $C_2H_5OH$ (molar mass 46.07 g mol$^{-1}$), carbon is $\frac{24.02}{46.07} \times 100 = 52.14\%$. Hydrogen works out to 13.13% and oxygen to 34.73%. The percentages of all elements must add up to 100%. In experimental data, oxygen is often not given directly and is found as 100 minus the sum of the other percentages.

  • Percentage composition is based on mass, not on number of atoms
  • The sum of all elemental percentages equals 100
  • Missing oxygen % = 100 − (sum of the other elements' %)
  • Percentage composition is the same for compounds sharing an empirical formula, e.g. $C_2H_2$ and $C_6H_6$
  • Use one mole of the compound as the calculation basis
  • Percentage composition is used to derive the empirical formula (next topic)

$\%\,\text{element} = \frac{\text{atoms of element in formula} \times \text{atomic mass}}{\text{molar mass of compound}} \times 100$ Mass percent of an element in a compound

NEET tip: NEET asks for the mass percent of an element in a compound, or for the element with the highest percentage among several compounds.

Empirical and molecular formulae

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. The molecular formula shows the actual number of each kind of atom in one molecule. The two are related by $\text{Molecular formula} = n \times \text{Empirical formula}$, where n is a whole number. For example, glucose $C_6H_{12}O_6$ has the empirical formula $CH_2O$ with n = 6. To find an empirical formula from percentage composition, follow four steps. First, assume a 100 g sample, so each percentage becomes a mass in grams. Second, divide each mass by the atomic mass to get moles. Third, divide every mole value by the smallest one. Fourth, if the results are fractional (such as 1.5 or 1.33), multiply all of them by a small integer to obtain whole numbers. To get the molecular formula, divide the molar mass (from data, or from vapour density × 2) by the empirical formula mass to find n.

  • Empirical formula = simplest whole-number atomic ratio
  • Molecular formula = actual atoms per molecule
  • Same empirical formula: $CH_2O$ for formaldehyde, acetic acid and glucose
  • Same empirical formula: $CH$ for acetylene and benzene
  • Ratio near 1.5: multiply all values by 2
  • Ratio near 1.33: multiply all values by 3
  • Ratio near 1.25: multiply all values by 4
  • Molar mass of a gas or vapour = 2 × vapour density
  • For ionic compounds the empirical formula is usually the formula used, e.g. $NaCl$

$n = \frac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}}$ Multiplier relating molecular and empirical formulae

$M = 2 \times VD$ Molar mass from vapour density

$\text{Moles of element} = \frac{\%\,\text{element}}{\text{atomic mass}}$ Relative moles of each element in a 100 g sample

NEET tip: A common NEET question gives percentage composition plus molar mass (or vapour density) and asks for the molecular formula. Watch for ratios like 1.5 that need multiplying.

Chemical equations and stoichiometry

A balanced chemical equation shows reactants and products with equal numbers of each atom on both sides. Its coefficients give the mole ratios, and for gases at the same T and P they also give the volume ratios. Stoichiometry uses these ratios to relate amounts of reactants and products. The standard route is: convert the given mass or volume to moles, apply the mole ratio from the equation, then convert back to the quantity asked. For complete combustion of a hydrocarbon $C_xH_y$, each mole produces x moles of $CO_2$ and y/2 moles of $H_2O$. The limiting reagent is the reactant that is used up first, and it decides how much product forms. To find it, divide the moles of each reactant by its coefficient; the smallest value is limiting. NCERT also covers stoichiometry in solutions, which uses mass percent, mole fraction, molarity (M) and molality (m).

  • Always balance the equation before using the coefficients
  • Coefficients give mole ratios, not mass ratios
  • Limiting reagent: smallest value of (moles available ÷ coefficient)
  • The excess reagent is left over after the reaction
  • Combustion: $C_xH_y + (x + \frac{y}{4})O_2 \rightarrow xCO_2 + \frac{y}{2}H_2O$
  • Molarity depends on temperature, because volume changes with temperature
  • Molality and mole fraction are independent of temperature
  • Sum of the mole fractions of all components = 1
  • For gases at the same T and P, coefficient ratio = volume ratio
  • Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100

$C_xH_y + \left(x + \frac{y}{4}\right)O_2 \rightarrow xCO_2 + \frac{y}{2}H_2O$ General complete combustion of a hydrocarbon

$M = \frac{n_{solute}}{V_{solution}(L)}$ Molarity

$m = \frac{n_{solute}}{W_{solvent}(kg)}$ Molality

$x_A = \frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}$ Mole fraction of component A

$\text{Mass}\,\% = \frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 100$ Mass percent of a solution

$M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$ Dilution of a solution

$\%\,\text{yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$ Efficiency of a reaction

NEET tip: NEET regularly asks for the mass of product (such as $CO_2$ from combustion of a hydrocarbon) or for the limiting reagent. Write the balanced equation first, then work with moles.

Formula sheet

$1\,u = \frac{1}{12}\,m(^{12}C) = 1.66056 \times 10^{-24}\,g$ Definition of the atomic mass unit

$N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\,mol^{-1}$ Avogadro constant

$n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{N}{N_A} = \frac{V_{STP}}{22.7\,L}$ Master mole relation (use 22.4 L for 1 atm, 273 K)

$\bar{A} = \frac{\sum x_i m_i}{\sum x_i}$ Average atomic mass

$\text{Mass of one particle} = \frac{M}{N_A}$ Absolute mass of an atom or molecule

$M = 2 \times VD$ Molar mass from vapour density

$\%\,\text{element} = \frac{\text{mass of element in 1 mol}}{M} \times 100$ Percentage composition

$\text{Molecular formula} = n \times \text{Empirical formula}$ Relation between the two formulae

$n = \frac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical formula mass}}$ Formula multiplier

$C_xH_y + \left(x + \frac{y}{4}\right)O_2 \rightarrow xCO_2 + \frac{y}{2}H_2O$ Hydrocarbon combustion stoichiometry

$\text{Limiting reagent: smallest } \frac{n_{available}}{\text{coefficient}}$ Identifies the reactant that controls the amount of product

$M = \frac{n_{solute}}{V(L)}$ Molarity (temperature dependent)

$m = \frac{n_{solute}}{W_{solvent}(kg)}$ Molality (temperature independent)

$x_A + x_B = 1$ Mole fractions of a binary mixture

$M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$ Dilution equation

$d = \frac{m}{V}$ Density

$T(K) = t(^{\circ}C) + 273.15$ Temperature conversion to kelvin

$^{\circ}F = \frac{9}{5}\,^{\circ}C + 32$ Celsius to Fahrenheit

$\text{Law of multiple proportions: masses of B per fixed mass of A in simple ratio}$ Dalton; e.g. $H_2O$ and $H_2O_2$ give an oxygen ratio of 1:2

$V \propto n$ (constant $T$, $P$) Avogadro's law; gas volume ratio = mole ratio

$\%\,\text{yield} = \frac{\text{actual}}{\text{theoretical}} \times 100$ Percentage yield

Common traps

  • Rounding a terminal 5 by always raising the previous digit. The correct rule: when the dropped digit is exactly 5, raise the preceding digit only if it is odd and keep it if it is even.
  • Counting trailing zeros as significant in numbers like 2500 with no decimal point. Trailing zeros are significant only when a decimal point is present, and leading zeros are never significant.
  • Confusing molecules with atoms. One mole of $O_3$ has $N_A$ molecules but $3N_A$ atoms, so always check which entity the question counts.
  • Using mass ratios directly from equation coefficients. Coefficients give mole ratios, so convert mass to moles first.
  • Taking the reactant with the smaller mass or smaller number of moles as the limiting reagent. Instead, compare moles divided by the stoichiometric coefficient.
  • Mixing the two molar volume values. Use 22.7 L at 1 bar and 273 K, or 22.4 L at 1 atm and 273 K, as indicated by the data or options.
  • Rounding mole ratios like 1.5 or 1.33 to the nearest integer when finding an empirical formula. Multiply all the ratios by 2 or 3 instead.
  • Treating molarity as temperature independent. Molarity changes with temperature because volume changes, whereas molality and mole fraction do not.

Quick revision

  • Pure substances (elements, compounds) have fixed composition; mixtures are homogeneous or heterogeneous and separable by physical means.
  • There are seven SI base units, and the mole is the unit of amount of substance.
  • Significant figures: answers to addition and subtraction keep the least decimal places; answers to multiplication and division keep the least significant figures.
  • Dalton's theory explains the mass-based laws but not Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes; isotopes and subatomic particles contradict it.
  • The five laws: conservation of mass (Lavoisier), definite proportions (Proust), multiple proportions (Dalton), gaseous volumes (Gay-Lussac) and Avogadro's law.
  • $1\,u = 1.66 \times 10^{-24}\,g$, and the mass of one $^{12}C$ atom is exactly 12 u.
  • Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean, which is why chlorine is about 35.5 u.
  • Master relation: $n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{N}{N_A} = \frac{V}{22.7\,L}$ at STP.
  • Percentage composition is computed on a 1 mol basis, and all percentages add up to 100.
  • Empirical formula route: % → grams → moles → divide by smallest → whole numbers. Then molecular formula = n × empirical formula, with n = M ÷ empirical formula mass.
  • Stoichiometry: balance the equation, convert to moles, apply the mole ratio, then convert back. The limiting reagent decides the yield.
  • Molarity is temperature dependent; molality and mole fraction are temperature independent.

Chemistry · Unit 2: Atomic Structure

This unit explains how electrons are arranged and how they behave inside atoms. It builds from the wave and particle nature of light and matter, through the Bohr and quantum mechanical models, to quantum numbers, orbital shapes and electronic configurations. NEET asks numerical questions on Bohr relations, spectral lines, de Broglie and uncertainty, and conceptual questions on nodes, quantum numbers and configurations every year.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q88

Nature of electromagnetic radiation; photoelectric effect
