Electromagnetic radiation consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation. In vacuum all such waves travel at speed c. The electromagnetic spectrum, in order of increasing wavelength, is gamma, X-rays, UV, visible, IR, microwave and radio. Wave theory could not explain black-body radiation or the photoelectric effect. Planck proposed that energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets called quanta, with $E = h\nu$. In the photoelectric effect, electrons are ejected from a metal surface only if the frequency of light is at least the threshold frequency $\nu_0$. Ejection is instantaneous. The kinetic energy of the ejected electrons increases with frequency but does not depend on intensity. The number of electrons ejected is proportional to intensity. Einstein explained this by treating light as photons.

  • $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m $s^{-1}$ for all EM waves in vacuum
  • Wavenumber $\bar{\nu} = 1/\lambda$, usually in $cm^{-1}$ or $m^{-1}$
  • Below $\nu_0$ no electron is emitted, however intense the light
  • Intensity controls the number of photoelectrons; frequency controls their kinetic energy
  • Work function $W_0 = h\nu_0$ is lowest for alkali metals such as Cs and K
  • Energy of 1 mole of photons is $N_A h\nu$

$c = \nu\lambda$ Relates frequency and wavelength of radiation

$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$ Energy of one photon, with $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s

$h\nu = h\nu_0 + \frac{1}{2}m_e v^2$ Einstein photoelectric equation

$KE_{max} = h(\nu - \nu_0) = eV_0$ Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons; $V_0$ is the stopping potential

NEET tip: Expect numericals on photon energy, number of photons emitted by a lamp of given power, and the kinetic energy of photoelectrons from a given work function.

Spectrum of the hydrogen atom

When hydrogen gas is excited by an electric discharge, it emits a line emission spectrum rather than a continuous one. Each line comes from an electron falling from a higher level $n_2$ to a lower level $n_1$. The lines are grouped into series according to the final level $n_1$. Lyman series ($n_1 = 1$) lies in the UV region. Balmer series ($n_1 = 2$) is the only one in the visible region. Paschen ($n_1 = 3$), Brackett ($n_1 = 4$) and Pfund ($n_1 = 5$) lie in the IR region. All wavelengths obey the Rydberg formula. Within a series, the first line ($n_2 = n_1 + 1$) has the longest wavelength. The series limit ($n_2 = \infty$) has the shortest wavelength. The formula also applies to hydrogen-like species such as $He^+$ and $Li^{2+}$ when multiplied by $Z^2$.

  • Atomic spectra are line spectra and act as a fingerprint of each element
  • Lyman is UV, Balmer is visible, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund are IR
  • The first line of a series has the lowest energy and longest wavelength
  • The series limit has the highest energy and shortest wavelength
  • Maximum number of lines when an electron falls from level n to the ground state is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$
  • The longest-wavelength line of Lyman corresponds to $2 \rightarrow 1$

$\bar{\nu} = 109677\, Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right) cm^{-1}$ Rydberg formula for H-like species, with $n_2 > n_1$

$N = \frac{(n_2 - n_1)(n_2 - n_1 + 1)}{2}$ Number of spectral lines for a transition from $n_2$ down to $n_1$

NEET tip: NEET often asks which transition gives a line of the same wavelength in $He^+$ as a given line in H, or the region or count of spectral lines.

Bohr model: postulates, energy and radii relations, limitations

Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom has four main postulates. First, the electron moves in circular orbits (stationary states) of fixed energy around the nucleus. Second, the energy of an orbit does not change with time while the electron stays in it. Third, energy is absorbed or emitted only when the electron jumps between orbits, with $\Delta E = h\nu$. Fourth, angular momentum is quantised, $mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$. From these postulates, the radius, energy and velocity of each orbit follow for hydrogen and H-like ions. Energy is negative, meaning the electron is bound and is more stable than a free electron at infinity. The model has clear limitations. It fails for multi-electron atoms. It cannot explain fine structure, the Zeeman effect (magnetic field) or the Stark effect (electric field). It does not account for the dual nature of the electron or the uncertainty principle, and it cannot explain the ability of atoms to form molecules.

  • Radius varies as $n^2/Z$; energy varies as $-Z^2/n^2$; velocity varies as $Z/n$
  • Energy gap between successive levels decreases as n increases
  • Ionisation energy of H is 13.6 eV, or $2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J per atom
  • In an orbit, KE equals $-E$ and PE equals $2E$
  • Bohr's model applies only to one-electron species: H, $He^+$, $Li^{2+}$, $Be^{3+}$
  • It violates the Heisenberg principle because it assigns a definite path to the electron

$mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$ Quantisation of angular momentum

$r_n = 52.9 \frac{n^2}{Z}$ pm Radius of the nth Bohr orbit

$E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} \frac{Z^2}{n^2}$ J $= -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2}$ eV Energy of the nth orbit

$v_n = 2.18 \times 10^6 \frac{Z}{n}$ m $s^{-1}$ Velocity of the electron in the nth orbit

$\Delta E = h\nu = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_i^2} - \frac{1}{n_f^2}\right)$ J Energy of the photon for a transition between levels

NEET tip: Ratio-based questions are common, for example the radius or energy of $Li^{2+}$ or $He^+$ in a given orbit compared with H, and the KE:PE:TE relationship.

Dual nature of matter; de Broglie relationship

De Broglie proposed that matter, like radiation, has a dual nature: every moving particle has a wave associated with it. Its wavelength is $\lambda = h/mv$. For macroscopic objects the mass is so large that the wavelength is negligibly small, so wave behaviour cannot be observed. For electrons the wavelength is significant. Electron diffraction confirmed this, and the electron microscope is based on the wave nature of electrons. Applying de Broglie's idea to Bohr's model, a stable orbit is one in which a whole number of electron wavelengths fits around the circumference. This leads directly to Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum.

  • Wave nature is significant only for microscopic particles
  • Wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum
  • Orbit condition $2\pi r = n\lambda$ gives $mvr = nh/2\pi$
  • Electron microscope uses electron waves; electron diffraction is the experimental proof
  • For the same kinetic energy, a lighter particle has a longer wavelength

$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{p}$ de Broglie wavelength

$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m\,KE}}$ Wavelength from kinetic energy

$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \approx \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}$ Å Wavelength of an electron accelerated through potential V

$2\pi r = n\lambda$ Number of waves fitting in the nth Bohr orbit

NEET tip: Expect a direct calculation of $\lambda$ for an electron or a ball, or a comparison of wavelengths of particles with equal KE or equal velocity.

Heisenberg uncertainty principle

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that it is impossible to determine both the exact position and the exact momentum (or velocity) of a microscopic particle such as an electron at the same time. The product of the uncertainties is at least $h/4\pi$. The reason is that to locate an electron precisely, it must be illuminated by light of wavelength smaller than its dimensions. Such high-energy photons change its momentum on impact, so position and momentum cannot both be known exactly. The principle rules out definite orbits with fixed paths, which is a major failure of Bohr's model. Instead, we can only describe the probability of finding the electron. For macroscopic objects the uncertainties are negligible, so the principle has no practical effect on them.

  • The more precisely position is known, the less precisely momentum is known
  • The principle is significant only for microscopic particles
  • It rejects the concept of a fixed orbit and leads to the concept of probability
  • The same form applies to energy and time: $\Delta E \cdot \Delta t \geq h/4\pi$

$\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \frac{h}{4\pi}$ Uncertainty relation between position and momentum

$\Delta x \cdot \Delta v \geq \frac{h}{4\pi m}$ Uncertainty in velocity for a particle of mass m

NEET tip: NEET asks for $\Delta v$ or $\Delta x$ from given data, or for the case when $\Delta x = \Delta p$ so that $\Delta p = \sqrt{h/4\pi}$.

Quantum mechanical model of the atom

The quantum mechanical model treats the electron as a wave and describes it with the Schrödinger wave equation, $\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$, where $\hat{H}$ is the Hamiltonian (total energy operator). Solving this equation for an atom gives only certain allowed energies (quantised energy levels) and the corresponding wave functions $\psi$. These solutions automatically introduce the quantum numbers n, l and $m_l$. Main features of the model: electron energy is quantised; the exact path of an electron cannot be determined; an orbital is the region where the probability of finding the electron is maximum; and $|\psi|^2$ gives probability density. For hydrogen, energy depends only on n. For multi-electron atoms, energy depends on both n and l.

  • Based on wave-particle duality and the uncertainty principle
  • $\psi$ has no physical meaning; $\psi^2$ gives probability density
  • An orbital is a probability region, not a fixed path
  • In H, orbitals of the same n are degenerate (e.g. 2s and 2p)
  • In multi-electron atoms 2s is lower in energy than 2p because of shielding and penetration

$\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$ Schrödinger wave equation in operator form

NEET tip: Statement-based questions test the differences between an orbit and an orbital and the dependence of energy on n alone (H) versus on n + l (multi-electron atoms).

Atomic orbitals as one-electron wave functions

An atomic orbital is a one-electron wave function $\psi$ obtained by solving the Schrödinger equation for an electron in an atom. Each orbital is specified by a set of three quantum numbers n, l and $m_l$, and can hold at most two electrons. $\psi$ itself can be positive or negative and has no direct physical significance. Its square, $|\psi|^2$, gives the probability density of finding the electron at a point. A node is a region where $\psi$, and hence $\psi^2$, is zero. Radial nodes are spherical surfaces. Angular nodes are planes or cones. Boundary surface diagrams enclose about 90% of the probability and are used to represent orbital shapes.

  • Radial nodes $= n - l - 1$
  • Angular nodes $= l$
  • Total nodes $= n - 1$
  • Each orbital is defined by n, l and $m_l$ and holds a maximum of 2 electrons
  • Boundary surface diagrams represent about 90% probability of finding the electron

$\text{radial nodes} = n - l - 1$ Number of spherical nodes

$\text{angular nodes} = l$ Number of nodal planes or cones

NEET tip: Counting radial and angular nodes for orbitals like 3p, 4d or 5s is a near-certain one-mark question.

Variation of psi and psi-squared with r for 1s and 2s orbitals

For a 1s orbital, $\psi$ is maximum at the nucleus and decreases steadily with r, never becoming zero at finite r, so it has no node. $\psi^2$ also is maximum at the nucleus. For 2s, $\psi$ starts positive at r = 0, falls, becomes zero at one value of r (one radial node), turns negative and then approaches zero. $\psi^2$ is maximum at the nucleus, drops to zero at the node and rises to a second, smaller maximum. For 3s, $\psi$ crosses zero twice (two radial nodes). For s orbitals $\psi$ is non-zero at the nucleus, but for p and d orbitals $\psi$ starts from zero at r = 0. The radial probability function $4\pi r^2 \psi^2$ is zero at the nucleus. For 1s it peaks at 52.9 pm, which equals the Bohr radius.

  • Number of times $\psi$ crosses zero (excluding r = 0) equals the number of radial nodes
  • 1s has 0 radial nodes, 2s has 1, 3s has 2
  • A plot starting at a non-zero value at r = 0 indicates an s orbital
  • A plot starting at zero at r = 0 indicates a p or d orbital
  • $\psi^2$ is never negative
  • Radial probability for 1s peaks at $a_0 = 52.9$ pm

$P(r) = 4\pi r^2 \psi^2$ Radial probability density at distance r

NEET tip: NEET shows $\psi$ vs r plots and asks for the number of radial nodes. Count the zero crossings and check whether the curve starts at zero (p, d) or not (s).

Quantum numbers and their significance

Four quantum numbers completely describe an electron in an atom. The principal quantum number n (1, 2, 3, and so on) gives the shell, the size of the orbital and its main energy. The azimuthal quantum number l (0 to n−1) gives the subshell and the orbital shape: s, p, d and f for l = 0, 1, 2 and 3. The magnetic quantum number $m_l$ (−l to +l, including 0) gives the spatial orientation of the orbital. The spin quantum number $m_s$ (+1/2 or −1/2) gives the spin orientation of the electron. A shell n contains $n^2$ orbitals and up to $2n^2$ electrons. A subshell contains $2l + 1$ orbitals.

  • n determines size and energy (energy depends only on n in H)
  • l determines shape and orbital angular momentum
  • $m_l$ determines orientation; there are $2l+1$ values
  • Number of subshells in shell n equals n
  • Invalid sets such as n = 2, l = 2 or l = 1, $m_l$ = 2 are common distractors

$\text{orbitals in shell} = n^2$; $\text{electrons} = 2n^2$ Capacity of a shell

$\text{orbitals in subshell} = 2l + 1$; $\text{electrons} = 2(2l+1)$ Capacity of a subshell

$L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\frac{h}{2\pi}$ Orbital angular momentum

NEET tip: Questions test identifying a valid or invalid set of quantum numbers, or counting electrons with a given n, l or $m_l$.

Shapes of s, p and d orbitals

s orbitals (l = 0) are spherically symmetric and have no angular node. Their size increases from 1s to 2s to 3s. p orbitals (l = 1) are dumbbell shaped and come in three orientations: $p_x$, $p_y$ and $p_z$. Each p orbital has one nodal plane passing through the nucleus. For example, $p_z$ has the xy-plane as its nodal plane. d orbitals (l = 2) are five in number. $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$ and $d_{zx}$ have lobes between the axes. $d_{x^2-y^2}$ has lobes along the x and y axes. $d_{z^2}$ has two lobes along the z-axis with a doughnut-shaped ring in the xy-plane. Four d orbitals have two nodal planes each, while $d_{z^2}$ has two conical nodal surfaces. All five 3d orbitals are equivalent in energy in an isolated atom.

  • s is spherical, p is dumbbell, d is mostly cloverleaf
  • Each p orbital has 1 nodal plane; each d orbital has 2 angular nodes
  • $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2}$ have lobes along the axes
  • $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$ and $d_{zx}$ have lobes between the axes
  • $d_{z^2}$ has no nodal plane; its angular nodes are conical
  • The orbitals within each p or d set are degenerate in an isolated atom

NEET tip: Identify nodal planes, for example that the xy-plane is the nodal plane of $p_z$, $d_{xz}$ and $d_{yz}$, or which d orbital has lobes along the axes.

Electron spin and spin quantum number

Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit proposed that an electron spins about its own axis, much like the earth. This gives the electron an intrinsic spin angular momentum and a magnetic moment. The spin can have only two orientations relative to a chosen axis, described by $m_s = +1/2$ (clockwise, $\uparrow$) and $m_s = -1/2$ (anticlockwise, $\downarrow$). An orbital can hold at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins. Unpaired electrons make a species paramagnetic, while species with all electrons paired are diamagnetic.

  • Spin quantum number s = 1/2 for every electron; $m_s = \pm 1/2$
  • The spin quantum number does not come from the Schrödinger equation
  • Two electrons in one orbital have opposite spins
  • More unpaired electrons give a greater magnetic moment
  • Total spin $= n \times \frac{1}{2}$ for n unpaired electrons; spin multiplicity $= 2S + 1$

$\text{spin angular momentum} = \sqrt{s(s+1)}\frac{h}{2\pi}$ With s = 1/2 this equals $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\frac{h}{2\pi}$

$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM Spin-only magnetic moment for n unpaired electrons

NEET tip: Count unpaired electrons in an ion such as $Fe^{3+}$ or $Mn^{2+}$ to find its magnetic moment or total spin.

Aufbau principle, Pauli's exclusion principle and Hund's rule

The Aufbau principle states that electrons fill orbitals in increasing order of energy. The (n + l) rule decides this order: the lower the value of n + l, the lower the energy. If two orbitals have the same n + l, the one with lower n is filled first. This gives the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p. Pauli's exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins. Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity states that pairing of electrons in degenerate orbitals (p, d, f) does not begin until each orbital in that subshell is singly occupied with parallel spins.

  • Lower (n + l) means lower energy; for a tie, lower n means lower energy
  • 4s (n + l = 4) fills before 3d (n + l = 5)
  • Pauli's principle limits each orbital to 2 electrons
  • Hund's rule applies only to degenerate orbitals
  • Pairing in p starts with the 4th electron, in d with the 6th, in f with the 8th

$\text{energy order} \propto (n + l)$ Aufbau rule for multi-electron atoms

NEET tip: NEET asks which principle is violated by a given orbital diagram, or asks you to rank orbitals by energy using the n + l rule.

Electronic configuration of elements

Electronic configuration shows how the electrons of an atom are distributed among its orbitals, written as $nl^x$, for example $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$. A noble-gas core can be used as shorthand, such as [Ar] $3d^5 4s^1$ for Cr. Valence electrons determine chemical properties. When forming cations of transition elements, electrons are removed from the outermost ns orbital before (n−1)d. For example, $Fe^{2+}$ is [Ar] $3d^6$, not [Ar] $3d^4 4s^2$. Important exceptions in the 3d series are Cr ([Ar] $3d^5 4s^1$) and Cu ([Ar] $3d^{10} 4s^1$). Similar exceptions occur in heavier elements such as Mo, Ag and Au.

  • K and Ca: the 4s orbital fills before 3d
  • Cr is $3d^5 4s^1$ and Cu is $3d^{10} 4s^1$
  • Transition metal cations lose 4s electrons first
  • Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons (e.g. $N^{3-}$, $O^{2-}$, $F^-$, Ne, $Na^+$)
  • Unpaired electrons: Cr has 6, Mn has 5, Fe has 4, Cu has 1

NEET tip: Typical questions ask for the configuration of ions such as $Cu^{2+}$ or $Cr^{3+}$, the number of unpaired electrons, or the number of electrons with l = 1 or l = 2.

Extra stability of half-filled and completely filled orbitals

Half-filled ($p^3$, $d^5$, $f^7$) and completely filled ($p^6$, $d^{10}$, $f^{14}$) subshells have extra stability for two reasons. The first is symmetrical distribution of electrons: electrons in a half-filled or fully filled subshell shield one another relatively less, so they are more strongly attracted by the nucleus, which gives extra stability. The second, and more important, is exchange energy. Electrons with parallel spins in degenerate orbitals can exchange positions, and each such exchange releases energy and stabilises the atom. The number of possible exchanges is greatest for half-filled and fully filled arrangements. This explains why Cr is $3d^5 4s^1$ rather than $3d^4 4s^2$, and why Cu is $3d^{10} 4s^1$. It also explains why N has a higher first ionisation energy than O.

  • Exchange energy is the main reason for extra stability
  • Number of exchanges for n parallel electrons is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$
  • $d^5$ has 10 exchanges; $d^4$ has only 6
  • This explains higher IE of N than O, and of P than S
  • $Mn^{2+}$ ($d^5$) and $Fe^{3+}$ ($d^5$) are especially stable

$N_{exchange} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ Number of exchange pairs for n parallel-spin electrons in a subshell

NEET tip: NEET tests the reason for the Cr and Cu exceptions and comparisons of ionisation energy or stability involving half-filled configurations.

Formula sheet

$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$ Photon energy

$c = \nu\lambda$, $\bar{\nu} = \frac{1}{\lambda}$ Wave relations

$h\nu = h\nu_0 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ Photoelectric equation

$\bar{\nu} = R_H Z^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$, $R_H = 109677\ cm^{-1}$ Rydberg formula

$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ Maximum number of spectral lines from level n to the ground state

$mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$ Bohr quantisation of angular momentum

$r_n = 52.9\frac{n^2}{Z}$ pm Bohr radius of the nth orbit

$E_n = -13.6\frac{Z^2}{n^2}$ eV $= -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\frac{Z^2}{n^2}$ J Bohr energy of the nth orbit

$v_n = 2.18 \times 10^6 \frac{Z}{n}$ m $s^{-1}$ Electron velocity in the nth orbit

$KE = -E_n$, $PE = 2E_n$ Energy relations in a Bohr orbit

$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m\,KE}}$ de Broglie wavelength

$\lambda = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}$ Å Wavelength of an electron accelerated through V volts

$\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \frac{h}{4\pi}$ Heisenberg uncertainty principle

$\hat{H}\psi = E\psi$ Schrödinger equation

$\text{radial nodes} = n - l - 1$, $\text{angular nodes} = l$, $\text{total nodes} = n - 1$ Node counting

$n^2$ orbitals and $2n^2$ electrons per shell; $2l+1$ orbitals per subshell Shell and subshell capacity

$L = \sqrt{l(l+1)}\frac{h}{2\pi}$ Orbital angular momentum

$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM Spin-only magnetic moment

$(n + l)$ rule Order of filling of orbitals (Aufbau)

$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ exchanges Exchange energy count for n parallel spins

Common traps

  • Assuming that increasing light intensity increases the kinetic energy of photoelectrons. Intensity increases only the number of electrons; KE depends on frequency.
  • Forgetting the $Z^2$ factor in the Rydberg formula for $He^+$ or $Li^{2+}$, or using $Z$ in place of $Z^2$ for energy. Radius varies as $n^2/Z$ and energy as $Z^2/n^2$.
  • Counting the origin r = 0 as a radial node for p or d orbitals. Only zero crossings at finite r count as radial nodes.
  • Writing $Fe^{2+}$ as [Ar] $3d^4 4s^2$. Electrons leave the 4s orbital first, so it is [Ar] $3d^6$.
  • Thinking 2s and 2p differ in energy in the hydrogen atom. In H, energy depends only on n, so they are degenerate.
  • Assuming the series limit has the longest wavelength. The series limit has the shortest wavelength and the first line has the longest.
  • Thinking $d_{z^2}$ has nodal planes like the other d orbitals. Its two angular nodes are conical surfaces.
  • Applying Bohr's formulas to multi-electron species such as He or $Li^+$. They are valid only for one-electron species.

Quick revision

  • $E = h\nu$; photoemission occurs only if $\nu \geq \nu_0$; $KE_{max} = h(\nu - \nu_0)$.
  • Spectral series by $n_1$: Lyman 1 (UV), Balmer 2 (visible), Paschen 3, Brackett 4, Pfund 5 (all IR).
  • Bohr relations: $r \propto n^2/Z$, $E \propto -Z^2/n^2$, $v \propto Z/n$; ionisation energy of H is 13.6 eV.
  • de Broglie: $\lambda = h/mv$; Bohr orbit condition $2\pi r = n\lambda$.
  • Heisenberg: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq h/4\pi$; this rules out fixed orbits.
  • $\psi^2$ gives probability density; an orbital is a one-electron wave function.
  • Radial nodes $= n-l-1$; angular nodes $= l$; 1s, 2s and 3s have 0, 1 and 2 radial nodes.
  • s-orbital $\psi$ is non-zero at the nucleus; p and d $\psi$ start at zero.
  • Allowed values: l from 0 to n−1; $m_l$ from −l to +l; $m_s = \pm 1/2$; shell capacity $2n^2$.
  • Filling order uses the n + l rule; Pauli allows 2 electrons per orbital; Hund's rule requires single occupancy first.
  • Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] $3d^5 4s^1$ and Cu is [Ar] $3d^{10} 4s^1$, due to exchange energy and symmetry.
  • Spin-only magnetic moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM; $Mn^{2+}$ and $Fe^{3+}$ have 5 unpaired electrons, giving 5.92 BM.

Chemistry · Unit 3: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

This unit explains why atoms combine and how they do it. It covers ionic, covalent, coordinate, metallic and hydrogen bonds. It also uses Lewis structures, VSEPR, valence bond theory with hybridization, and molecular orbital theory to predict shape, polarity, magnetism, bond order and stability. NEET asks 3 to 4 direct questions from this unit almost every year, on shapes, hybridization, dipole moment, MO configurations, bond order and hydrogen bonding, so it is a high-yield scoring area.

PYQs (3): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q75, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q89, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q90

Kossel-Lewis approach to chemical bond formation

Kossel and Lewis proposed that atoms combine to attain a stable noble gas configuration, an octet (or a duplet for H, Li and Be). Kossel explained ionic bonding: electropositive atoms lose electrons, electronegative atoms gain them, and the ions are held by electrostatic attraction. Lewis explained covalent bonding by sharing of electron pairs, shown with Lewis dot structures. Formal charge identifies the most stable Lewis structure, which is the one with the lowest formal charges on its atoms. The octet rule has clear limitations. Some molecules have an incomplete octet ($BeCl_2$, $BF_3$, $LiCl$). Some are odd-electron molecules ($NO$, $NO_2$). Others have an expanded octet using d orbitals ($PCl_5$, $SF_6$, $H_2SO_4$). Noble gases also form compounds such as $XeF_2$ and $XeF_4$. The theory also cannot explain molecular shape or bond energy.

  • Octet rule: atoms gain, lose or share electrons to get 8 valence electrons.
  • Only valence electrons take part in bonding.
  • Incomplete octet: $BeCl_2$ (4 electrons around Be), $BF_3$ (6 electrons around B).
  • Odd-electron molecules: $NO$ and $NO_2$.
  • Expanded octet: $PF_5$ (10 electrons), $SF_6$ (12 electrons), $IF_7$ (14 electrons).
  • Formal charge is a bookkeeping charge, not a real charge on the atom.
  • Coordinate (dative) bond: both shared electrons come from one atom, as in $NH_4^+$ and $H_3O^+$.

$FC = V - L - \frac{1}{2}S$ Formal charge. V is valence electrons, L is non-bonding (lone pair) electrons, S is shared (bonding) electrons.

NEET tip: Expect formal charge on each O atom of $O_3$ (+1, 0, −1) and identification of molecules that violate the octet rule.

Ionic and covalent bonds

An ionic (electrovalent) bond forms by complete transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal. The resulting ions are held by non-directional electrostatic forces in a crystal lattice. Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points and are hard and brittle. They conduct electricity in the molten state or in aqueous solution, and are generally soluble in polar solvents. A covalent bond forms by mutual sharing of electron pairs. It can be single, double or triple, and it is directional, which gives molecules definite shapes. Covalent compounds usually have low melting points, are poor conductors and dissolve in non-polar solvents. A bond between identical atoms is non-polar. A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar covalent, with partial charges. Most real bonds are intermediate: ionic bonds have some covalent character, and covalent bonds between unlike atoms have some ionic character.

  • Ionic bonds are non-directional, so they show no isomerism.
  • Covalent bonds are directional, so they give definite geometry and can show isomerism.
  • An electronegativity difference above about 1.7 suggests predominantly ionic character.
  • A polar covalent bond carries partial charges, for example $H^{\delta+}-Cl^{\delta-}$.
  • Single bond = 1 sigma; double bond = 1 sigma + 1 pi; triple bond = 1 sigma + 2 pi.
  • Ionic solids do not conduct in the solid state because the ions are fixed in the lattice.

NEET tip: Questions usually compare properties such as conductivity, solubility and melting point of ionic and covalent compounds, or count sigma and pi bonds.

Formation of ionic bonds and factors affecting it

Ionic bond formation involves three steps: ionisation of the metal atom (needs energy), electron gain by the non-metal atom (usually releases energy), and packing of the gaseous ions into a lattice (releases lattice energy). Formation is favoured by three factors: low ionisation enthalpy of the metal, highly negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal, and high lattice enthalpy. The overall energy change is analysed by the Born-Haber cycle. For NaCl, ionisation of Na (+495.8 kJ/mol) and electron gain of Cl (−348.7 kJ/mol) together are endothermic. The large lattice enthalpy released makes the overall process exothermic. Therefore lattice enthalpy, not the octet alone, is the real driving force for ionic compound formation in the solid state. Alkali and alkaline earth metals combining with halogens and oxygen form the most typical ionic compounds.

  • Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal favours cation formation.
  • Highly negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal favours anion formation.
  • High lattice enthalpy stabilises the ionic solid.
  • In the gas phase, $Na(g) + Cl(g) \rightarrow Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g)$ is endothermic.
  • The Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to ionic compound formation.
  • Smaller ions with higher charge give stronger ionic lattices.

$\Delta_f H = \Delta_{sub}H + IE + \frac{1}{2}\Delta_{diss}H + \Delta_{eg}H - U$ Born-Haber cycle for an MX-type solid. U is the lattice enthalpy, taken as the energy needed to separate the lattice, so it is subtracted for lattice formation.

NEET tip: Asked as conceptual statements on the conditions that favour ionic bond formation and on the role of lattice enthalpy.

Lattice enthalpy

Lattice enthalpy is the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous constituent ions. For NaCl it is +788 kJ/mol. It measures the strength of the ionic lattice and the stability of the compound. It increases with the charge on the ions and decreases with the sum of their radii. So MgO has a much higher lattice enthalpy than NaCl, and LiF is higher than CsI. A high lattice enthalpy means a high melting point, greater hardness and usually lower solubility. Solubility depends on the balance between lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpy. A compound dissolves if hydration enthalpy can compensate the lattice enthalpy. It cannot be measured directly; it is obtained from the Born-Haber cycle.

  • Lattice enthalpy is proportional to the product of ionic charges.
  • It is inversely proportional to interionic distance $(r_+ + r_-)$.
  • Order: $MgO > CaO > NaF > NaCl > KCl$.
  • Among alkali halides, $LiF$ has the highest and $CsI$ the lowest lattice enthalpy.
  • A compound dissolves if hydration enthalpy is at least comparable to lattice enthalpy.
  • It is determined indirectly using the Born-Haber cycle.

$U \propto \frac{z_+ z_-}{r_+ + r_-}$ Relative lattice enthalpy from ionic charges and radii.

NEET tip: Typical questions ask you to arrange compounds by lattice enthalpy using charge first, then size.

Electronegativity

Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself. It is a relative property with no units; the Pauling scale is most common. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0), followed by O (3.5), then N and Cl (3.0). Across a period electronegativity increases, and down a group it decreases. It rises with effective nuclear charge and falls with atomic size. It also depends on hybridisation: greater s-character means higher electronegativity, so $sp > sp^2 > sp^3$ carbon. The electronegativity difference between bonded atoms decides bond polarity and percentage ionic character. Electronegativity differs from electron gain enthalpy: the latter is a measurable energy change of an isolated gaseous atom.

  • Pauling values: $F = 4.0$, $O = 3.5$, $N = Cl = 3.0$, $C = 2.5$, $H = 2.1$.
  • Trend: increases across a period and decreases down a group.
  • Cs and Fr are the least electronegative.
  • Hybridised carbon order: $C_{sp} > C_{sp^2} > C_{sp^3}$.
  • A larger electronegativity difference gives a more polar and more ionic bond.
  • Electronegativity concerns a bonded atom; electron gain enthalpy concerns an isolated atom.

$\chi_A - \chi_B = 0.208\sqrt{\Delta}$ Pauling relation. $\Delta$ (kcal/mol) is the extra bond energy of A–B over the mean of A–A and B–B.

NEET tip: Used indirectly to decide bond polarity, dipole moment direction and acidity order.

Fajan's rule

Fajans' rule explains partial covalent character in ionic bonds. A cation distorts (polarises) the electron cloud of a nearby anion, which draws electron density between the nuclei and gives the bond partial covalency. Covalent character increases in four situations. First, the cation is small. Second, the cation carries a high charge. Third, the anion is large and highly charged. Fourth, the cation has a pseudo noble gas (18-electron) configuration, as in $Cu^+$, $Ag^+$ and $Zn^{2+}$; poorly shielding d electrons make such cations more polarising than noble gas cations of similar size. Greater covalent character lowers melting point and solubility in water and raises solubility in organic solvents. Examples: $LiCl$ is more covalent than $NaCl$, and $AlCl_3$ is more covalent than $NaCl$. $CuCl$ is more covalent than $NaCl$ despite similar ionic size. Among the lithium halides, $LiI$ is the most covalent.

  • Small, highly charged cation means high polarising power.
  • Large, highly charged anion means high polarisability.
  • An 18-electron cation is more polarising than an 8-electron cation of similar size.
  • Covalent character: $LiI > LiBr > LiCl > LiF$.
  • Covalent character: $AlCl_3 > MgCl_2 > NaCl$.
  • Higher covalent character gives a lower melting point; $AgCl$ has lower water solubility than expected.

$\phi = \frac{\text{charge on cation}}{\text{radius of cation}}$ Ionic potential. A higher value means greater polarising power and more covalent character.

NEET tip: Expect ordering of covalent character or melting points among halides and oxides.

Dipole moment

Dipole moment measures the polarity of a bond or molecule. It equals the magnitude of charge multiplied by the distance between the charges. It is a vector, drawn by chemists from the positive to the negative end, and its unit is the debye. The net molecular dipole is the vector sum of bond dipoles and lone pair contributions. Symmetrical molecules have zero dipole moment even with polar bonds: $CO_2$, $BF_3$, $CH_4$, $CCl_4$, $PCl_5$, $SF_6$ and $XeF_4$. $H_2O$ (1.85 D) and $NH_3$ (1.47 D) are polar. $NH_3$ has a larger dipole than $NF_3$ (0.23 D): in $NH_3$ the lone pair moment adds to the N–H bond moments, while in $NF_3$ it opposes the N–F moments. Applications include deciding polarity and geometry, distinguishing cis and trans isomers, and calculating percent ionic character. Polarity also follows functional groups, in the sense NEET uses it (polarity as reflected by hydrogen bonding and interaction with polar media). For example, $CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3 < CH_3COCH_3 < CH_3CH_2OH < CH_3COOH$. By dipole moment alone, acetone (about 2.9 D) is higher than ethanol (about 1.7 D). Boiling points follow the same ether < ketone < alcohol < acid order.

  • $1\,D = 3.336 \times 10^{-30}\,C\,m$.
  • Zero dipole moment: $CO_2$, $BF_3$, $CH_4$, $CCl_4$, $SF_6$, $XeF_2$, $XeF_4$, trans-dichloroethene.
  • $NH_3$ (1.47 D) is more polar than $NF_3$ (0.23 D) because of the lone pair direction.
  • Dipole order: $CH_3Cl > CH_2Cl_2 > CHCl_3 > CCl_4 (= 0)$.
  • cis-isomers are generally more polar than trans-isomers.
  • p-dichlorobenzene has zero dipole moment; ortho > meta > para.

$\mu = q \times d$ Dipole moment from charge and separation.

$\%\,\text{ionic character} = \frac{\mu_{observed}}{\mu_{ionic}} \times 100$ Percent ionic character of a bond.

$\mu_R = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2 + 2\mu_1\mu_2\cos\theta}$ Resultant of two bond dipoles at angle $\theta$.

NEET tip: NEET frequently asks to pick zero-dipole molecules, order polarity, or explain $NH_3$ vs $NF_3$.

VSEPR theory and shapes of simple molecules

VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory, developed by Sidgwick, Powell, Nyholm and Gillespie, says that electron pairs around the central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion. Shape is decided by the total number of electron pairs, bond pairs plus lone pairs. Multiple bonds are treated as a single super pair. Repulsion order is lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp, so lone pairs distort shapes and reduce bond angles. Electron pair geometries are linear (2 pairs), trigonal planar (3), tetrahedral (4), trigonal bipyramidal (5), octahedral (6) and pentagonal bipyramidal (7). In trigonal bipyramidal arrangements, lone pairs occupy equatorial positions. Example shapes: $SF_4$ is see-saw, $ClF_3$ is T-shaped, $XeF_2$ and $I_3^-$ are linear. $BrF_5$ is square pyramidal and $XeF_4$ is square planar.

  • 2 bp: linear ($BeCl_2$, $CO_2$).
  • 3 bp: trigonal planar ($BF_3$). 2 bp + 1 lp: bent ($SO_2$).
  • 4 bp: tetrahedral ($CH_4$, $BF_4^-$, $NH_4^+$).
  • 3 bp + 1 lp: pyramidal ($NH_3$, 107°). 2 bp + 2 lp: bent ($H_2O$, 104.5°).
  • 5 bp: trigonal bipyramidal ($PCl_5$). 4 bp + 1 lp: see-saw ($SF_4$).
  • 3 bp + 2 lp: T-shaped ($ClF_3$). 2 bp + 3 lp: linear ($XeF_2$, $I_3^-$).
  • 6 bp: octahedral ($SF_6$). 5 bp + 1 lp: square pyramidal ($BrF_5$, $XeOF_4$).
  • 4 bp + 2 lp: square planar ($XeF_4$, $ICl_4^-$).
  • 7 bp: pentagonal bipyramidal ($IF_7$). 6 bp + 1 lp: distorted octahedral ($XeF_6$).

$\text{electron pairs} = \frac{1}{2}(V + M - c + a)$ Steric number of the central atom. V is its valence electrons, M is monovalent atoms attached, c is cationic charge, a is anionic charge.

$\text{lone pairs} = \text{electron pairs} - \text{bonded atoms}$ Gives lone pairs on the central atom to decide the shape.

NEET tip: Match-the-list questions pairing species like $PCl_5$, $BrF_5$, $BF_4^-$, $SF_4$, $XeF_4$ with geometries are very common.

Valence bond theory

Valence bond theory (Heitler, London, Pauling) says a covalent bond forms when half-filled atomic orbitals of two atoms with opposite spins overlap. The shared pair then concentrates between the nuclei. As two H atoms approach, attraction outweighs repulsion and energy falls to a minimum at 74 pm, the bond length. The 435.8 kJ/mol released is the H–H bond enthalpy. Greater overlap gives a stronger bond. Head-on (axial) overlap gives a sigma bond, through s–s, s–p or p–p overlap. Sideways (lateral) overlap of parallel p orbitals gives a pi bond. A sigma bond is stronger because the overlap is larger, and it allows free rotation. A pi bond is weaker and restricts rotation. Overlap can be positive (bonding), negative (antibonding) or zero. VBT explains directional bonds but needs hybridisation to explain shapes such as tetrahedral $CH_4$.

  • Bonding needs half-filled orbitals with opposite spins.
  • Bond strength is proportional to the extent of overlap.
  • H–H: bond length 74 pm, bond enthalpy 435.8 kJ/mol.
  • Sigma bond: axial overlap, stronger, forms first, allows free rotation.
  • Pi bond: lateral overlap, weaker, forms only after a sigma bond.
  • Overlap strength: p–p (axial) > s–p > s–s.
  • s orbitals cannot form pi bonds.

NEET tip: Statement-based questions on sigma vs pi strength, types of overlap and the energy curve of $H_2$ formation.

Hybridization involving s, p and d orbitals

Hybridisation is the intermixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies on the same atom. It produces an equal number of identical hybrid orbitals with equivalent energy and shape. Only orbitals take part, not electrons, and both half-filled and fully filled orbitals can hybridise. Hybrid orbitals form only sigma bonds or hold lone pairs; pi bonds use unhybridised orbitals. The number of electron pairs gives the hybridisation: 2 is sp, 3 is $sp^2$, 4 is $sp^3$, 5 is $sp^3d$, 6 is $sp^3d^2$ and 7 is $sp^3d^3$. In $sp^3d$ (for example $PCl_5$), the axial bonds are longer and weaker than the equatorial bonds. Inner-shell d orbitals give $dsp^2$ (square planar, $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$) and $d^2sp^3$ (octahedral inner-orbital complexes). More s-character means a shorter, stronger bond and a larger angle.

  • $sp$: 180°, linear, 50% s-character ($BeCl_2$, $C_2H_2$).
  • $sp^2$: 120°, trigonal planar, 33.3% s ($BF_3$, $C_2H_4$).
  • $sp^3$: 109°28', tetrahedral, 25% s ($CH_4$).
  • $sp^3d$: trigonal bipyramidal, using the $d_{z^2}$ orbital ($PCl_5$).
  • $sp^3d^2$: octahedral, using $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2}$ ($SF_6$).
  • $sp^3d^3$: pentagonal bipyramidal ($IF_7$).
  • $dsp^2$: square planar ($[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$, $[PtCl_4]^{2-}$).
  • $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is $sp^3$ tetrahedral; $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is $dsp^2$ square planar.
  • $PCl_5$ (solid) exists as $[PCl_4]^+[PCl_6]^-$.

$H = \frac{1}{2}(V + M - c + a)$ Hybridisation number: 2 = sp, 3 = $sp^2$, 4 = $sp^3$, 5 = $sp^3d$, 6 = $sp^3d^2$, 7 = $sp^3d^3$.

$\%\,s = \frac{1}{\text{number of orbitals mixed}} \times 100$ s-character of a hybrid orbital.

NEET tip: Identifying hybridisation and geometry of central atoms in molecules, ions and simple complexes is tested almost every year.

Resonance

When a single Lewis structure cannot explain all properties of a molecule, two or more structures (canonical forms) are written. They differ only in the position of electrons, not of atoms. The actual molecule is a resonance hybrid that is more stable than any canonical form. The canonical forms have no real existence. The energy difference between the actual molecule and the most stable canonical form is the resonance energy. Resonance averages bond lengths. In $O_3$ both O–O bonds are equal (128 pm), between single (148 pm) and double (121 pm). In $CO_3^{2-}$ all three C–O bonds are equal with bond order 4/3. In benzene all C–C bonds are 139 pm. Canonical forms must have the same number of unpaired electrons and nearly equal energy.

  • Only electrons move between canonical forms, never atoms.
  • The resonance hybrid is lower in energy than every canonical form.
  • Average bond order = total bonds between the atoms ÷ number of resonating positions.
  • Bond order 4/3 in $CO_3^{2-}$ and $NO_3^-$.
  • Bond order 1.5 in $O_3$, $NO_2^-$, $HCOO^-$ and benzene.
  • Bond order 1.25 in $PO_4^{3-}$; 1.5 in $SO_4^{2-}$ (with d-orbital participation).
  • Resonance energy measures extra stability, for example in benzene.

$\text{B.O.} = \frac{\text{total number of bonds between two atom types}}{\text{number of resonating structures}}$ Average bond order in resonating species.

NEET tip: Asked as comparisons of bond order or bond length, for example $CO$, $CO_2$ and $CO_3^{2-}$ (C–O length: $CO < CO_2 < CO_3^{2-}$).

Molecular orbital theory and LCAO

Molecular orbital theory (Hund and Mulliken) treats electrons as belonging to the whole molecule. Atomic orbitals combine to form molecular orbitals, which are polycentric and influenced by all nuclei. The number of MOs formed equals the number of AOs combined. Filling follows the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule. MOs are approximated by the Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO). Additive combination of wave functions gives a bonding MO, and subtractive combination gives an antibonding MO. Effective combination needs three conditions. The AOs must have comparable energy, for example 1s with 1s but not 1s with 2s. They must have the same symmetry about the molecular axis; with z as the axis, $2p_z$ cannot combine with $2p_x$. They must also overlap to the maximum extent. MOT successfully explains the paramagnetism of $O_2$, which VBT fails to explain.

  • Atomic orbitals are monocentric; molecular orbitals are polycentric.
  • n atomic orbitals combine to give n molecular orbitals.
  • Bonding MO: $\psi_A + \psi_B$. Antibonding MO: $\psi_A - \psi_B$.
  • Combining AOs need comparable energy, the same symmetry and maximum overlap.
  • With z as the internuclear axis, $s$ and $p_z$ can combine but $s$ and $p_x$ cannot.
  • MOT explains the paramagnetism of $O_2$ and the existence of $H_2^+$.

$\sigma = \psi_A + \psi_B$ Bonding MO by constructive interference.

$\sigma^* = \psi_A - \psi_B$ Antibonding MO by destructive interference.

NEET tip: Statement questions on LCAO conditions and on the number of MOs formed.

Bonding and antibonding orbitals; sigma and pi bonds

A bonding molecular orbital comes from constructive overlap. It concentrates electron density between the nuclei, reduces repulsion and lies lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals, so it stabilises the molecule. An antibonding molecular orbital comes from destructive overlap. It has a nodal plane between the nuclei and lies higher in energy than the parent AOs, so electrons in it destabilise the molecule. The antibonding orbital is raised slightly more than the bonding orbital is lowered. Sigma MOs, such as $\sigma 1s$, $\sigma 2s$ and $\sigma 2p_z$, are symmetrical about the internuclear axis. Pi MOs, such as $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi 2p_y$, come from sideways overlap. They have a nodal plane containing the internuclear axis and are not symmetrical about it. $\pi^*$ orbitals have an additional node between the nuclei. Pi bonding orbitals occur as a degenerate pair.

  • Bonding MO: lower energy, electron density between the nuclei.
  • Antibonding MO: higher energy, nodal plane between the nuclei, marked with *.
  • Sigma MO: cylindrically symmetrical about the internuclear axis.
  • Pi MO: a nodal plane contains the internuclear axis.
  • $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi 2p_y$ are degenerate; so are $\pi^* 2p_x$ and $\pi^* 2p_y$.
  • Electrons in antibonding MOs cancel the effect of an equal number of bonding electrons.

NEET tip: Questions ask about nodal planes, the symmetry of sigma vs pi MOs, or which combination is allowed.

MO configurations of homonuclear diatomic molecules

For molecules with up to 14 electrons ($H_2$ to $N_2$), s–p mixing raises $\sigma 2p_z$ above $\pi 2p$. The order is $\sigma 1s < \sigma^* 1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^* 2s < (\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y) < \sigma 2p_z < (\pi^* 2p_x = \pi^* 2p_y) < \sigma^* 2p_z$. For $O_2$, $F_2$ and $Ne_2$, $\sigma 2p_z$ lies below the $\pi 2p$ orbitals. $B_2$ is paramagnetic, with two unpaired electrons in the $\pi 2p$ orbitals. $C_2$ is diamagnetic and has only pi bonds, a double bond made of two pi bonds. $N_2$ has bond order 3 and is diamagnetic. $O_2$ has two unpaired electrons in $\pi^*$ orbitals, so it is paramagnetic with bond order 2. $F_2$ has bond order 1. In $Ne_2$ all MOs up to $\sigma^* 2p_z$ are filled. That orbital is the HOMO, and the bond order is zero, so $Ne_2$ does not exist. Paramagnetism arises from unpaired electrons.

  • $N_2$ (14 electrons): $KK\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^* 2s^2\,\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2\,\sigma 2p_z^2$.
  • $O_2$ (16 electrons): $KK\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^* 2s^2\,\sigma 2p_z^2\,\pi 2p^4\,\pi^* 2p_x^1 = \pi^* 2p_y^1$.
  • Paramagnetic species: $B_2$, $O_2$, $O_2^+$, $O_2^-$, $N_2^+$, $N_2^-$, $H_2^+$, $He_2^+$.
  • Diamagnetic species: $H_2$, $C_2$, $N_2$, $F_2$, $O_2^{2-}$, $CO$, $NO^+$.
  • HOMO of $N_2$ is $\sigma 2p_z$; HOMO of $O_2$ is $\pi^* 2p$; HOMO of $Ne_2$ is $\sigma^* 2p_z$.
  • $C_2$ contains two pi bonds and no sigma bond in the simple MO picture.

$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ BM$ Spin-only magnetic moment from the number of unpaired electrons n.

NEET tip: NEET asks the HOMO of a species, magnetic behaviour, or the number of unpaired electrons from MO configurations.

Bond order, bond length and bond energy

Bond order is half the difference between the numbers of electrons in bonding ($N_b$) and antibonding ($N_a$) molecular orbitals. A positive bond order means the molecule is stable. Zero bond order ($He_2$, $Be_2$, $Ne_2$) means it does not exist. A higher bond order means a shorter bond length and a higher bond dissociation energy, so the bond is stronger. Bond length is the equilibrium internuclear distance. Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of bonds of a given type in the gaseous state. Isoelectronic species have the same bond order: $N_2$, $CO$, $NO^+$ and $CN^-$ all have 3. Removing an electron from an antibonding orbital raises bond order ($O_2^+$ is 2.5). Adding an electron to one lowers it ($O_2^-$ is 1.5, $O_2^{2-}$ is 1). If bond orders are equal, the species with fewer antibonding electrons is more stable, so $H_2^+$ is more stable than $He_2^+$.

  • Bond orders: $H_2 = 1$, $H_2^+ = 0.5$, $He_2^+ = 0.5$, $He_2 = 0$.
  • Bond orders: $B_2 = 1$, $C_2 = 2$, $N_2 = 3$, $O_2 = 2$, $F_2 = 1$, $Ne_2 = 0$.
  • Bond order: $O_2^+ (2.5) > O_2 (2) > O_2^- (1.5) > O_2^{2-} (1)$.
  • Bond length follows the reverse order: $O_2^{2-} > O_2^- > O_2 > O_2^+$.
  • Bond order: $N_2 (3) > N_2^+ = N_2^- (2.5)$; $N_2^+$ is more stable than $N_2^-$.
  • Bond length order for carbon bonds: C–C > C=C > C≡C (154, 134, 120 pm).
  • Bond enthalpy of $F_2$ is lower than that of $Cl_2$ because of lone pair repulsion in small F.

$\text{B.O.} = \frac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$ Bond order from MO electron counts.

$\text{Bond length} \propto \frac{1}{\text{B.O.}}$ Qualitative relation: a higher bond order gives a shorter bond.

$\text{Bond energy} \propto \text{B.O.}$ Qualitative relation: a higher bond order gives a stronger bond.

NEET tip: Ordering bond orders, bond lengths or stabilities of $O_2$, $N_2$ and their ions is a favourite question.

Metallic bonding (elementary idea)

Metallic bonding is the force holding metal atoms together in a metallic crystal. In the electron sea (free electron) model, each metal atom loses its valence electrons and becomes a positive kernel. The kernels sit at fixed lattice points in a sea of delocalised mobile electrons, and the attraction between kernels and electrons is the metallic bond. The bond is non-directional. This model explains metallic properties. Mobile electrons give high electrical and thermal conductivity. They absorb and re-emit light, which gives lustre. Layers of kernels can slide without breaking bonds, which explains malleability and ductility. Metallic bond strength increases with the number of valence electrons and decreases with atomic size. This explains why transition metals have high melting points and alkali metals are soft with low melting points.

  • Positive kernels sit in a sea of delocalised electrons.
  • The metallic bond is non-directional.
  • Mobile electrons explain conductivity, lustre, malleability and ductility.
  • Bond strength increases with the number of valence electrons.
  • Bond strength decreases with increasing atomic size.
  • Alkali metals have weak metallic bonding and low melting points.
  • Transition metals have strong metallic bonding involving d electrons.

NEET tip: Asked conceptually: which property the electron sea model explains, or melting point trends among metals.

Hydrogen bonding and its applications

A hydrogen bond is the attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and a lone pair on another electronegative atom. It is shown by a dotted line and is weaker than a covalent bond. Intermolecular hydrogen bonds link different molecules, as in $HF$, $H_2O$, alcohols, carboxylic acids (dimers) and p-nitrophenol. These raise boiling point, viscosity and solubility in water. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds form within one molecule, as in o-nitrophenol and salicylaldehyde. They cause chelation and lower boiling point and water solubility. Applications include the anomalously high boiling point of water, the lower density of ice (open cage structure), the existence of $KHF_2$, the miscibility of ethanol with water, acetic acid dimers, and the structure of DNA and proteins.

  • Strength order: F–H···F > O–H···O > N–H···N.
  • Boiling point: $H_2O > HF > NH_3$ (water forms more H-bonds per molecule).
  • Ice has an open cage structure, so it is less dense than liquid water.
  • o-nitrophenol is steam volatile; p-nitrophenol is not (intermolecular H-bonding).
  • $HF_2^-$ exists (as in $KHF_2$), but $HCl_2^-$ does not.
  • Acetic acid shows a dimeric structure in benzene.
  • Lower alcohols and amines are soluble in water due to H-bonding.
  • H-bonds hold DNA base pairs and the protein secondary structure ($\alpha$-helix, $\beta$-sheet).

NEET tip: Common questions compare boiling points or solubility, intra- vs intermolecular H-bonding, or the polarity and boiling order of ether, ketone, alcohol and acid (ether < ketone < alcohol < acid; polarity here is as reflected by H-bonding, since by dipole moment alone acetone, about 2.9 D, is higher than ethanol, about 1.7 D).

Formula sheet

$FC = V - L - \frac{1}{2}S$ Formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure.

$U \propto \frac{z_+ z_-}{r_+ + r_-}$ Lattice enthalpy rises with ionic charge and falls with ionic size.

$\Delta_f H = \Delta_{sub}H + IE + \frac{1}{2}\Delta_{diss}H + \Delta_{eg}H - U$ Born-Haber cycle for an MX-type ionic solid.

$\chi_A - \chi_B = 0.208\sqrt{\Delta}$ Pauling electronegativity difference from extra bond energy.

$\phi = \frac{z}{r}$ Ionic potential. A higher value means more polarising and more covalent character (Fajans' rule).

$\mu = q \times d$ Dipole moment; $1\,D = 3.336 \times 10^{-30}\,C\,m$.

$\%\,\text{ionic character} = \frac{\mu_{obs}}{\mu_{ionic}} \times 100$ Percent ionic character from dipole moments.

$\mu_R = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2 + 2\mu_1\mu_2\cos\theta}$ Resultant of two bond dipoles.

$H = \frac{1}{2}(V + M - c + a)$ Steric number, which gives hybridisation and electron pair geometry.

$\text{lp} = H - \text{number of bonded atoms}$ Lone pairs on the central atom.

$\text{lp–lp} > \text{lp–bp} > \text{bp–bp}$ VSEPR repulsion order.

$CH_4\,(109.5^\circ) > NH_3\,(107^\circ) > H_2O\,(104.5^\circ)$ Bond angle decreases as the number of lone pairs increases.

$\%\,s: sp\,(50) > sp^2\,(33.3) > sp^3\,(25)$ More s-character gives a shorter bond, larger angle and more electronegative orbital.

$\sigma = \psi_A + \psi_B$, $\sigma^* = \psi_A - \psi_B$ LCAO formation of bonding and antibonding MOs.

$\text{B.O.} = \frac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$ Bond order from MO theory; zero means the molecule does not exist.

$\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y < \sigma 2p_z$ (up to 14 electrons); $\sigma 2p_z < \pi 2p$ (O_2, F_2, Ne_2) Energy order of 2p MOs for light vs heavier diatomics.

$\mu_s = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ BM$ Spin-only magnetic moment from n unpaired electrons.

$O_2^+ (2.5) > O_2 (2) > O_2^- (1.5) > O_2^{2-} (1)$ Bond order sequence; bond length follows the reverse order.

$N_2 = CO = NO^+ = CN^- = 3$ Isoelectronic species (14 electrons) with bond order 3.

$\text{B.O.}_{avg} = \frac{\text{total bonds}}{\text{resonating positions}}$ Resonance bond order, for example $CO_3^{2-} = 4/3$, $O_3 = 1.5$.

$F\cdots H > O\cdots H > N\cdots H$ Hydrogen bond strength order; boiling point $H_2O > HF > NH_3$.

Common traps

  • Assuming polar bonds always make a polar molecule. Symmetry cancels bond dipoles, so $CO_2$, $BF_3$, $CCl_4$ and $XeF_4$ have zero dipole moment.
  • Using the $N_2$-type MO order for $O_2$, $F_2$ and $Ne_2$. For these, $\sigma 2p_z$ lies below $\pi 2p$, and the HOMO of $Ne_2$ is $\sigma^* 2p_z$.
  • Confusing electron pair geometry with molecular shape. $H_2O$ is $sp^3$ with a tetrahedral electron arrangement, but its shape is bent. $XeF_4$ is $sp^3d^2$ but square planar.
  • Thinking $NF_3$ is more polar than $NH_3$ because F is more electronegative. In $NF_3$ the lone pair moment opposes the bond moments, so $NH_3$ (1.47 D) is far more polar than $NF_3$ (0.23 D).
  • Believing resonance structures interconvert or exist separately. Only the resonance hybrid exists, and atoms never change position.
  • Placing lone pairs in axial positions of a trigonal bipyramid. Lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, which gives see-saw $SF_4$, T-shaped $ClF_3$ and linear $XeF_2$.
  • Assuming intramolecular hydrogen bonding raises boiling point. It actually lowers boiling point and water solubility, so o-nitrophenol is more volatile than p-nitrophenol.
  • Assuming all $[NiX_4]^{2-}$ complexes have the same geometry. $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is $dsp^2$ square planar and diamagnetic, while $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is $sp^3$ tetrahedral and paramagnetic.

Quick revision

  • Octet rule exceptions: $BF_3$ and $BeCl_2$ (incomplete), $NO$ and $NO_2$ (odd electron), $PCl_5$ and $SF_6$ (expanded).
  • Lattice enthalpy of NaCl is +788 kJ/mol; it increases with charge and decreases with size ($MgO \gg NaCl$).
  • Fajans' rule: a small, highly charged or 18-electron cation with a large anion gives more covalent character and a lower melting point.
  • Zero dipole moment: $CO_2$, $BF_3$, $CH_4$, $CCl_4$, $PCl_5$, $SF_6$, $XeF_2$, $XeF_4$, p-dichlorobenzene.
  • Shapes: $SF_4$ see-saw, $ClF_3$ T-shaped, $XeF_2$ linear, $BrF_5$ square pyramidal, $XeF_4$ square planar, $IF_7$ pentagonal bipyramidal.
  • Hybridisation number 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 corresponds to sp, $sp^2$, $sp^3$, $sp^3d$, $sp^3d^2$, $sp^3d^3$.
  • In $PCl_5$, axial bonds are longer than equatorial bonds; solid $PCl_5$ is $[PCl_4]^+[PCl_6]^-$.
  • Sigma bonds are stronger than pi bonds; pi bonds form by lateral overlap of unhybridised p orbitals.
  • Bond orders: $N_2 = 3$, $O_2 = 2$, $F_2 = 1$, $C_2 = 2$ (two pi bonds), $B_2 = 1$; $He_2$, $Be_2$ and $Ne_2$ are 0.
  • Paramagnetic species: $O_2$, $B_2$, $O_2^+$, $O_2^-$, $NO$. Diamagnetic species: $N_2$, $C_2$, $F_2$, $CO$, $O_2^{2-}$.
  • Higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond; C–O length order is $CO < CO_2 < CO_3^{2-}$.
  • H-bond strength F > O > N; boiling point $H_2O > HF > NH_3$; ice floats; polarity (NEET sense, as reflected by H-bonding) follows ether < ketone < alcohol < carboxylic acid, the same as the boiling point order (by dipole moment alone, acetone, about 2.9 D, is higher than ethanol, about 1.7 D).

Chemistry · Unit 4: Chemical Thermodynamics

Chemical thermodynamics studies energy changes in physical and chemical processes using macroscopic properties such as internal energy, enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy. It explains why reactions release or absorb heat, which processes are spontaneous, and how the standard Gibbs energy change fixes the equilibrium constant. NEET asks 2-3 questions from this unit every year, mostly on sign conventions, work in different processes, Hess's law calculations, entropy changes and the $\Delta G$-$K$ relation.

PYQs (3): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q59, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q69, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q74

System and surroundings

The system is the part of the universe chosen for study, for example a reaction mixture in a beaker. Everything else is the surroundings, and system plus surroundings make up the universe. The real or imaginary wall that separates them is the boundary. Systems are classified by what can cross this boundary. An open system exchanges both matter and energy with the surroundings, such as reactants in an open beaker. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter, such as a sealed metal vessel. An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy, such as an ideal thermos flask. The energy of an isolated system stays constant. Only the surroundings close to the system usually take part in heat exchange.

  • Universe = system + surroundings
  • Open system: matter and energy are both exchanged
  • Closed system: only energy is exchanged
  • Isolated system: no exchange of matter or energy
  • A thermos flask is the standard example of an isolated system
  • The boundary may be real or imaginary and rigid or movable

NEET tip: Expect direct identification of open, closed or isolated systems from everyday examples such as a sealed bottle, an open beaker, a thermos or a living cell (open).

Extensive and intensive properties

An extensive property depends on the amount of matter present. Mass, volume, number of moles, internal energy, enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy and heat capacity are extensive. An intensive property does not depend on the amount of matter. Temperature, pressure, density, refractive index, viscosity, surface tension, molar heat capacity, specific heat and molar quantities are intensive. One simple test is to divide the system into two halves: an extensive property is shared between the halves, while an intensive property stays the same in each. The ratio of two extensive properties is always intensive. For example, density is mass divided by volume, and molar volume is volume divided by moles. Likewise, heat capacity C is extensive, but molar heat capacity $C_m$ and specific heat c are intensive.

  • Extensive properties: m, V, n, U, H, S, G, C
  • Intensive properties: T, p, density, viscosity, surface tension, $C_m$, specific heat
  • Extensive divided by extensive gives an intensive property
  • Molar quantities and E° (electrode potential) are intensive
  • Extensive properties are additive and intensive properties are not

$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$ Density: an intensive property formed as the ratio of two extensive properties

$C_m = \frac{C}{n}$ Molar heat capacity: intensive, obtained from the extensive heat capacity

NEET tip: NEET gives a list of properties and asks which are all intensive or all extensive; watch for the trap pair heat capacity (extensive) versus molar heat capacity (intensive).

State functions and types of processes

A state function depends only on the initial and final states of the system and not on the path followed. Examples are U, H, S, G, p, V and T. Path functions such as heat q and work w depend on how the change is carried out. For a cyclic process, the change in every state function is zero, but q and w need not be zero. Processes are classified by the condition held fixed. An isothermal process has constant T, so $\Delta U = 0$ for an ideal gas. An adiabatic process has q = 0. An isobaric process has constant p, and an isochoric process has constant V, so w = 0. A reversible process proceeds through infinitesimal steps and stays almost at equilibrium at every stage. An irreversible process occurs in a finite time and is the kind found in nature.

  • State functions: U, H, S, G, p, V, T
  • Path functions: q and w (their sum q + w is a state function)
  • Cyclic process: $\Delta U = \Delta H = \Delta S = \Delta G = 0$
  • Isothermal: $\Delta T = 0$; adiabatic: q = 0; isochoric: $\Delta V = 0$; isobaric: $\Delta p = 0$
  • Reversible work is the maximum work obtainable in expansion
  • All natural (spontaneous) processes are irreversible

$\oint dU = 0$ The change in any state function over a complete cycle is zero

NEET tip: Cyclic p-V diagrams are common; remember that for a full cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so $q = -w$, while the individual work and heat terms are non-zero.

First law: work, heat, internal energy and enthalpy

The first law states that energy can be neither created nor destroyed. Its mathematical form is $\Delta U = q + w$, using the convention that q and w are positive when heat or work enters the system. Pressure-volume work is $w = -p_{ext}\Delta V$. Expansion against zero external pressure (free expansion) gives w = 0. For reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, $w = -2.303nRT\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$, and because $\Delta U = 0$, it follows that $q = -w$. For an adiabatic process, $\Delta U = w$. The change in internal energy equals the heat exchanged at constant volume ($\Delta U = q_V$). Enthalpy is defined as H = U + pV, and its change equals the heat exchanged at constant pressure ($\Delta H = q_p$). For gaseous reactions, $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$. Here $\Delta n_g$ is the moles of gaseous products minus the moles of gaseous reactants.

  • Sign convention: work done on the system and heat absorbed are both positive
  • Free expansion of an ideal gas: w = 0, q = 0, $\Delta U = 0$, $\Delta T = 0$
  • Isothermal ideal gas: $\Delta U = 0$ and $\Delta H = 0$, so q = -w
  • Adiabatic: q = 0 and $\Delta U = w$; an adiabatic expansion cools the gas
  • $\Delta H = \Delta U$ when $\Delta n_g = 0$ or only solids and liquids are involved
  • The magnitude of reversible work exceeds irreversible work for the same expansion
  • Unit conversion: 1 L atm = 101.3 J

$\Delta U = q + w$ First law of thermodynamics

$w = -p_{ext}(V_2 - V_1)$ Irreversible work against a constant external pressure

$w_{rev} = -2.303\,nRT\log\frac{V_2}{V_1} = -2.303\,nRT\log\frac{p_1}{p_2}$ Reversible isothermal work for an ideal gas

$H = U + pV$ Definition of enthalpy

$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$ Relation between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$ for gaseous reactions

$\Delta U = nC_V(T_2 - T_1)$ Work done in an adiabatic process, since $w = \Delta U$ when q = 0

NEET tip: Common questions include free-expansion values, calculating $\Delta H - \Delta U$ from $\Delta n_g$, and reading work signs from p-V cycles of isothermal and adiabatic steps.

Heat capacity and molar heat capacity

Heat capacity C is the heat needed to raise the temperature of a substance by 1 K, so q = C$\Delta T$. Molar heat capacity $C_m$ refers to 1 mol of substance, and specific heat c refers to 1 g. For heating at constant volume, q = $\Delta U$ = n$C_V\Delta T$. For heating at constant pressure, q = $\Delta H$ = n$C_p\Delta T$. For an ideal gas, $C_p - C_V = R$, so $C_p$ is always greater than $C_V$. This is because at constant pressure part of the heat is used to do expansion work. For a monoatomic gas, $C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$, $C_p = \frac{5}{2}R$ and $\gamma = 1.67$. For a diatomic gas, $C_V = \frac{5}{2}R$, $C_p = \frac{7}{2}R$ and $\gamma = 1.4$. A bomb calorimeter works at constant volume and measures $\Delta U$. A coffee-cup calorimeter works at constant pressure and measures $\Delta H$.

  • $C_p - C_V = R$ for 1 mol of an ideal gas
  • Monoatomic gas: $\gamma = 5/3$; diatomic gas: $\gamma = 7/5$
  • For an ideal gas, $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ holds for any process, not only at constant volume
  • Bomb calorimeter measures $\Delta U$ (constant V); coffee-cup calorimeter measures $\Delta H$ (constant p)
  • Calorimeter calculation: q = $C_{cal}\Delta T$
  • Water has a high specific heat of 4.18 J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$

$q = mc\Delta T = nC_m\Delta T$ Heat absorbed or released for a temperature change

$C_p - C_V = R$ Mayer relation for an ideal gas

$\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_V}$ Ratio of heat capacities, which depends on the atomicity of the gas

$\Delta H = nC_p\Delta T$ Enthalpy change of an ideal gas

NEET tip: Typical questions are numericals on calorimeter heat and $\Delta U$/$\Delta H$ from heat capacities, and conceptual questions on why $C_p > C_V$.

Hess's law of constant heat summation

Hess's law states that if a reaction occurs in several steps, its total enthalpy change equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of the steps. This is true because enthalpy is a state function. The law lets us calculate enthalpies that cannot be measured directly. A standard example is the enthalpy of formation of CO, obtained by combining the combustion of C and the combustion of CO. Thermochemical equations can be handled like algebraic equations. Reversing a reaction changes the sign of $\Delta H$. Multiplying a reaction by a factor multiplies $\Delta H$ by the same factor. Adding reactions adds their $\Delta H$ values. Hess's law is also the basis of the Born-Haber cycle used to find lattice enthalpy.

  • Hess's law is a consequence of H being a state function
  • Reversing a reaction changes the sign of $\Delta H$
  • Multiplying a reaction by a factor multiplies $\Delta H$ by the same factor
  • The physical states of all species must match when equations are combined
  • Hess's law underlies the Born-Haber cycle for lattice enthalpy

$\Delta_r H = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3 + \dots$ Total enthalpy change for a reaction carried out in steps

$C(s) + \frac{1}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow CO(g);\ \Delta H = \Delta_c H(C) - \Delta_c H(CO)$ Classic Hess's law application to find the enthalpy of formation of CO

NEET tip: Usually tested as a numerical where 2-3 given equations must be manipulated to reach a target equation; check signs and coefficients carefully.

Enthalpies of bond dissociation, combustion, formation, atomization, sublimation, phase transition, hydration, ionization and solution

The standard enthalpy of formation, $\Delta_f H^\circ$, is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states. It is zero for elements in their reference forms, such as graphite, $O_2(g)$ and $Br_2(l)$. Combustion enthalpy ($\Delta_c H$) refers to burning 1 mol of a substance completely and is always negative. Bond dissociation enthalpy is the energy needed to break 1 mol of bonds in the gas phase. Atomization enthalpy ($\Delta_a H$) converts 1 mol of a substance into gaseous atoms. Phase transitions include fusion, vaporization and sublimation, with $\Delta_{sub}H = \Delta_{fus}H + \Delta_{vap}H$. Ionization enthalpy refers to removing an electron from a gaseous atom. Hydration enthalpy is the enthalpy released when gaseous ions become surrounded by water. Enthalpy of solution is the lattice enthalpy plus the hydration enthalpy.

  • $\Delta_f H^\circ$ = 0 for the reference form of an element (graphite, not diamond)
  • Combustion and hydration enthalpies are negative; bond dissociation, atomization, sublimation and ionization enthalpies are positive
  • Atomization of $H_2$ equals its bond dissociation enthalpy
  • For $CH_4$, $\Delta_a H$ = 4 times the average C-H bond enthalpy
  • $\Delta_{sub}H > \Delta_{vap}H$ for the same substance
  • Dissolution is endothermic when lattice enthalpy exceeds the magnitude of hydration enthalpy (for example $NH_4Cl$)
  • Lattice enthalpy is found through the Born-Haber cycle

$\Delta_r H^\circ = \sum \nu\Delta_f H^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \nu\Delta_f H^\circ(\text{reactants})$ Reaction enthalpy from enthalpies of formation

$\Delta_r H = \sum BE(\text{reactants}) - \sum BE(\text{products})$ Reaction enthalpy from bond enthalpies (gas-phase reactions)

$\Delta_{sub}H = \Delta_{fus}H + \Delta_{vap}H$ Sublimation enthalpy from fusion and vaporization enthalpies

$\Delta_{sol}H = \Delta_{lattice}H + \Delta_{hyd}H$ Enthalpy of solution of an ionic solid

NEET tip: Common questions ask which reaction represents a true $\Delta_f H^\circ$ (1 mol product from elements in standard states) and use bond-enthalpy numericals with the reactants-minus-products order.

Second law of thermodynamics and spontaneity

The first law cannot predict direction, because exothermic character alone does not make a process spontaneous. Ice melting above 273 K is spontaneous but endothermic. The second law states that the entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous process and remains constant at equilibrium. Entropy S is a state function that measures the disorder or randomness of a system. Its change is defined using reversible heat: $\Delta S = \frac{q_{rev}}{T}$. Entropy increases on melting, on vaporization, when gas moles increase, on heating and on dissolution. For an ideal gas expanding isothermally, $\Delta S = 2.303nR\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$, whatever the path. This is why free expansion still has a positive $\Delta S_{sys}$. At a phase transition, $\Delta S = \frac{\Delta H_{trans}}{T}$, where T is the transition temperature.

  • Entropy order: $S_{gas} \gg S_{liquid} > S_{solid}$
  • $\Delta S$ is positive when gas moles increase, $\Delta n_g > 0$
  • $\Delta S$ is a state function and is always calculated from a reversible path
  • Free expansion: $\Delta S_{sys} = nR\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$, $\Delta S_{surr} = 0$
  • Reversible adiabatic process: $\Delta S = 0$ (isentropic)
  • Entropy rises with temperature, and a given heat q raises entropy more at low T
  • Unit of S: J K$^{-1}$. Molar entropy (e.g. tabulated $S^\circ$) has the unit J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$

$\Delta S = \frac{q_{rev}}{T}$ Definition of entropy change

$\Delta S = 2.303\,nR\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$ Isothermal entropy change of an ideal gas, valid for both reversible and free expansion

$\Delta S_{trans} = \frac{\Delta H_{trans}}{T_{trans}}$ Entropy of fusion or vaporization at the transition temperature

$\Delta S^\circ_r = \sum S^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum S^\circ(\text{reactants})$ Standard entropy change of a reaction

NEET tip: NEET often tests the signs of $\Delta S$ for given changes and asks for $\Delta S_{sys}$ and $\Delta S_{surr}$ in free or isothermal expansion.

Entropy of the universe and Gibbs energy as criteria for spontaneity

A process is spontaneous when the total entropy change of the universe is positive: $\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} > 0$. At constant p and T, $\Delta S_{surr} = -\frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$. Combining the two gives the Gibbs energy, G = H - TS, so $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = -T\Delta S_{total}$. At constant T and p, a process is spontaneous if $\Delta G < 0$, at equilibrium if $\Delta G = 0$, and non-spontaneous if $\Delta G > 0$. When $\Delta H$ is negative and $\Delta S$ is positive, the process is spontaneous at all T. When $\Delta H$ is positive and $\Delta S$ is negative, it is never spontaneous. When both are negative, it is spontaneous at low T. When both are positive, it is spontaneous at high T. The crossover temperature is $T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$. $-\Delta G$ also equals the maximum useful (non-pV) work.

  • Spontaneous: $\Delta S_{total} > 0$ or $\Delta G < 0$
  • Equilibrium: $\Delta S_{total} = 0$ or $\Delta G = 0$
  • $\Delta H < 0, \Delta S > 0$: spontaneous at all temperatures
  • $\Delta H > 0, \Delta S < 0$: non-spontaneous at all temperatures
  • $\Delta H < 0, \Delta S < 0$: spontaneous below $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$
  • $\Delta H > 0, \Delta S > 0$: spontaneous above $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$
  • Spontaneity says nothing about the rate of a reaction

$\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr}$ Entropy criterion for spontaneity

$\Delta S_{surr} = -\frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$ Entropy change of the surroundings at constant p

$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ Gibbs-Helmholtz relation for constant T and p

$T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$ Temperature at which $\Delta G = 0$ (equilibrium or crossover point)

$-\Delta G = w_{useful,max}$ Maximum non-expansion work obtainable

NEET tip: A favourite question type gives $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ and asks for the minimum temperature for spontaneity; convert $\Delta H$ (kJ) and $\Delta S$ (J/K) to the same energy unit first.

Standard Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant

The Gibbs energy change under non-standard conditions is $\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$. At equilibrium, $\Delta_r G = 0$ and Q = K, which gives $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303RT\log K$. If $\Delta G^\circ$ is negative, then K > 1 and products are favoured. If $\Delta G^\circ$ is positive, then K < 1 and reactants are favoured. If $\Delta G^\circ = 0$, then K = 1. In that last case, $\Delta H^\circ = T\Delta S^\circ$, so $\Delta S^\circ = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{T}$. This applies, for example, when equal concentrations of N and D exist in a $N \rightleftharpoons D$ equilibrium. Combining the equations gives $-RT\ln K = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$. From this, K can be calculated from tabulated $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ values.

  • $\Delta G^\circ < 0$ means K > 1; $\Delta G^\circ > 0$ means K < 1; $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ means K = 1
  • At equilibrium $\Delta G = 0$, but $\Delta G^\circ$ is generally not zero
  • 2.303RT is about 5.7 kJ mol$^{-1}$ at 298 K
  • Each tenfold increase in K lowers $\Delta G^\circ$ by about 5.7 kJ mol$^{-1}$ at 298 K
  • Always use T in kelvin and R = 8.314 J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$

$\Delta_r G = \Delta_r G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ Gibbs energy change at any composition

$\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303RT\log K$ Link between standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant

$K = e^{-\Delta_r G^\circ/RT}$ Equilibrium constant from the standard Gibbs energy change

$-2.303RT\log K = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$ Calculates K, $\Delta H^\circ$ or $\Delta S^\circ$ from the other quantities

NEET tip: Watch for K = 1 (equal concentrations) situations, where $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ and $\Delta S^\circ = \Delta H^\circ/T$ with T in kelvin.

Formula sheet

$\Delta U = q + w$ First law (work done on the system is positive)

$w = -p_{ext}\Delta V$ Irreversible pressure-volume work

$w_{rev} = -2.303\,nRT\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$ Reversible isothermal work for an ideal gas

$w_{adiabatic} = \Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$ Work in an adiabatic process

$H = U + pV$ Definition of enthalpy

$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$ Relation between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$

$q_V = \Delta U,\ q_p = \Delta H$ Heat at constant volume and at constant pressure

$C_p - C_V = R$ Mayer relation for an ideal gas

$q = mc\Delta T = C\Delta T$ Calorimetry

$\Delta_r H^\circ = \sum \Delta_f H^\circ(P) - \sum \Delta_f H^\circ(R)$ Reaction enthalpy from formation enthalpies

$\Delta_r H = \sum BE(R) - \sum BE(P)$ Reaction enthalpy from bond enthalpies

$\Delta_{sub}H = \Delta_{fus}H + \Delta_{vap}H$ Sublimation enthalpy

$\Delta_{sol}H = \Delta_{lattice}H + \Delta_{hyd}H$ Enthalpy of solution

$\Delta S = \frac{q_{rev}}{T}$ Definition of entropy change

$\Delta S = 2.303\,nR\log\frac{V_2}{V_1}$ Isothermal entropy change of an ideal gas

$\Delta S_{trans} = \frac{\Delta H_{trans}}{T}$ Entropy of phase transition

$\Delta S_{surr} = -\frac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}$ Entropy change of the surroundings

$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ Gibbs energy criterion

$\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{total}$ Link between $\Delta G$ and the entropy of the universe

$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ Gibbs energy at any composition

$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$ Standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant

$T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$ Crossover or equilibrium temperature

Common traps

  • Treating free expansion as having $\Delta S_{sys} = 0$. In fact $\Delta S_{sys} = nR\ln(V_2/V_1) > 0$; only q, w, $\Delta U$ and $\Delta S_{surr}$ are zero.
  • Mixing up sign conventions. In current usage, work done on the system is positive and expansion work is negative ($w = -p_{ext}\Delta V$).
  • Using bond enthalpies as products minus reactants. The correct order for bond enthalpies is reactants minus products, which is the reverse of the formation-enthalpy formula.
  • Counting liquids and solids in $\Delta n_g$. Only gaseous moles are counted when converting between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$.
  • Mixing kJ and J in $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ or $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$. Convert both to the same unit, and use T in kelvin rather than $^\circ C$.
  • Assuming every exothermic reaction is spontaneous, or that a negative $\Delta G$ means a fast reaction. Spontaneity depends on both $\Delta H$ and $T\Delta S$, and it says nothing about rate.
  • Thinking $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ at every equilibrium. It is $\Delta G$ that is zero at equilibrium; $\Delta G^\circ$ is zero only when K = 1.
  • Taking diamond or $O_3$ as the reference state. $\Delta_f H^\circ$ = 0 only for the most stable form, such as graphite and $O_2(g)$.

Quick revision

  • Isolated systems exchange no matter or energy, closed systems exchange only energy, and open systems exchange both.
  • U, H, S and G are extensive state functions, while q and w are path functions.
  • $\Delta U = q + w$, $\Delta U = q_V$ and $\Delta H = q_p$.
  • For an isothermal ideal gas, $\Delta U = \Delta H = 0$ and $q = -w$. For a reversible path, $q = -w = 2.303nRT\log(V_2/V_1)$.
  • Free expansion gives w = q = $\Delta U$ = 0, but $\Delta S_{sys} > 0$.
  • $\Delta H - \Delta U = \Delta n_g RT$, and $C_p - C_V = R$.
  • Hess's law: reversing a reaction flips the sign of $\Delta H$ and multiplying a reaction scales $\Delta H$.
  • Combustion and hydration enthalpies are negative, while bond dissociation, atomization and ionization enthalpies are positive.
