  • $\Delta S_{total} > 0$ and $\Delta G < 0$ are equivalent criteria for a spontaneous process.
  • For $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, check the signs of $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ to fix the temperature range of spontaneity.
  • $\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$: when K = 1, $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ and $\Delta S^\circ = \Delta H^\circ/T$.
  • In any cyclic process, every state function change is zero, so $q_{net} = -w_{net}$.

Chemistry · Unit 5: Solutions

This unit covers how to express solution concentration, how a solute changes the vapour pressure of a solvent (Raoult's law), and how real solutions deviate from ideal behaviour. It then treats colligative properties and their use in finding molar masses, including abnormal values explained by the van't Hoff factor. NEET asks 2-3 questions from it almost every year, usually short numericals on $\Delta T_f$, $\Delta T_b$, $\pi$ and $i$, plus conceptual statement or assertion questions on ideal and non-ideal solutions.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q54, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q71

Concentration terms: molality, molarity, mole fraction and percentage

Concentration tells how much solute is present in a given amount of solution or solvent. Molarity ($M$) is moles of solute per litre of solution. It changes with temperature because volume expands or contracts on heating. Molality ($m$) is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Mole fraction ($x$) is the ratio of moles of one component to total moles. Mass percentage is grams of solute per 100 g of solution. Molality, mole fraction, mass percentage and ppm (parts per million, used for trace amounts) all depend only on mass or moles, so they are temperature independent. This is why colligative property expressions use molality. To convert between molarity and molality you need the density of the solution. In a binary mixture the mole fractions always add up to 1.

  • Molarity depends on temperature; molality, mole fraction, mass percent and ppm do not
  • The sum of mole fractions of all components equals 1
  • Molality uses mass of solvent only, not mass of solution
  • Volume percent and mass by volume percent depend on temperature
  • Converting molarity to molality requires the solution density

$M = \frac{n_B}{V_{solution}(L)}$ Molarity in mol $L^{-1}$

$m = \frac{n_B \times 1000}{w_A(g)}$ Molality in mol $kg^{-1}$, where $w_A$ is the mass of solvent

$x_A = \frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}$, $x_A + x_B = 1$ Mole fraction of component A in a binary solution

$\text{mass \%} = \frac{w_B}{w_A + w_B} \times 100$ Mass percentage of solute

$m = \frac{1000\,M}{1000\,d - M \times M_B}$ Molality from molarity; $d$ is density in g $mL^{-1}$ and $M_B$ is solute molar mass

$\text{ppm} = \frac{w_B}{w_{total}} \times 10^6$ Concentration of trace components

NEET tip: NEET asks which concentration term is temperature independent and gives quick conversions such as molarity to molality using density, or mass percent to mole fraction.

Vapour pressure of solutions and Raoult's law

In a closed vessel, a liquid's vapour reaches equilibrium with the liquid and exerts a vapour pressure. When a non-volatile solute is added, part of the surface is occupied by solute particles. Fewer solvent molecules can escape, so the vapour pressure falls. Raoult's law states that, for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component equals its mole fraction in the solution multiplied by the vapour pressure of the pure component. By Dalton's law, the total vapour pressure is the sum of the partial pressures. Total pressure varies linearly with the mole fraction of either component. In the vapour phase, the more volatile component (the one with higher $p^0$) is richer than in the liquid. For a non-volatile solute, only the solvent contributes, so $p = p_A^0 x_A$. Raoult's law can be seen as a special case of Henry's law where $K_H = p^0$.

  • Vapour pressure depends on the nature of the liquid and on temperature, not on the amount of liquid
  • A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent
  • Partial pressure is proportional to mole fraction in the liquid phase
  • Vapour phase composition is found using Dalton's law: $y_A = p_A/p_{total}$
  • The vapour is richer in the more volatile component

$p_A = p_A^0 x_A$ Raoult's law for component A

$p_{total} = p_A^0 x_A + p_B^0 x_B$ Total vapour pressure of a solution of two volatile liquids

$p_{total} = p_A^0 + (p_B^0 - p_A^0) x_B$ Linear dependence of total pressure on $x_B$

$y_A = \frac{p_A}{p_{total}}$ Mole fraction of A in the vapour phase

$\frac{1}{p_{total}} = \frac{y_A}{p_A^0} + \frac{y_B}{p_B^0}$ Total pressure from vapour phase composition

NEET tip: Expect numericals that ask for total vapour pressure, or for the vapour phase mole fraction, from given $p^0$ values and liquid composition.

Ideal and non-ideal solutions

An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the entire composition range, with $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$ and $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$. This happens because A-B interactions are nearly equal in strength to A-A and B-B interactions. Interactions are present; they are simply similar in magnitude, not absent. Examples are n-hexane + n-heptane, bromoethane + chloroethane, and benzene + toluene. Non-ideal solutions deviate from Raoult's law. Positive deviation: A-B interactions are weaker than A-A and B-B. Molecules escape more easily, so vapour pressure is higher than predicted, with $\Delta_{mix}H > 0$ and $\Delta_{mix}V > 0$. Examples are ethanol + acetone, ethanol + water, and carbon disulphide + acetone. Such solutions form minimum boiling azeotropes, such as about 95% ethanol by volume in water. Negative deviation: A-B interactions are stronger, often through hydrogen bonding. Vapour pressure is lower than predicted, with $\Delta_{mix}H < 0$ and $\Delta_{mix}V < 0$. Examples are chloroform + acetone, phenol + aniline, $HNO_3$ + water and $HCl$ + water. Such solutions form maximum boiling azeotropes, such as 68% $HNO_3$.

  • Ideal solution: $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$, $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$, $\Delta_{mix}S > 0$, $\Delta_{mix}G < 0$
  • In an ideal solution, A-B interactions are similar to A-A and B-B, not absent
  • Positive deviation: weaker A-B forces, $\Delta_{mix}H > 0$, volume expansion, minimum boiling azeotrope
  • Negative deviation: stronger A-B forces, $\Delta_{mix}H < 0$, volume contraction, maximum boiling azeotrope
  • Chloroform + acetone shows negative deviation due to H-bonding between $CHCl_3$ H and acetone $C=O$
  • Phenol + aniline shows negative deviation due to H-bonding between phenolic $-OH$ and the $-NH_2$ nitrogen
  • Ethanol + water shows positive deviation because ethanol breaks some water-water H-bonds
  • Azeotropes boil at constant composition and cannot be separated by fractional distillation

$\Delta_{mix}H = 0,\ \Delta_{mix}V = 0$ Conditions for an ideal solution

$p_A > p_A^0 x_A$ Positive deviation from Raoult's law

$p_A < p_A^0 x_A$ Negative deviation from Raoult's law

NEET tip: This is the most frequently tested area, through statement-based and assertion-reason questions on the sign of deviation for named pairs, the sign of $\Delta_{mix}H$ and $\Delta_{mix}V$, and azeotrope type.

Vapour pressure-composition plots

Vapour pressure-composition plots show $p_A$, $p_B$ and $p_{total}$ against mole fraction at constant temperature. Ideal solution: all three plots are straight lines. The total pressure line joins $p_A^0$ (at $x_A = 1$) to $p_B^0$ (at $x_B = 1$) and always lies between the two pure-component vapour pressures. Positive deviation: the curves bulge above the ideal straight lines. If the deviation is large, the total pressure curve passes through a maximum. A maximum vapour pressure means a minimum boiling point, which corresponds to a minimum boiling azeotrope. Negative deviation: the curves sag below the ideal lines. A large deviation gives a minimum in total pressure, which corresponds to a maximum boiling azeotrope. At the azeotropic composition, the liquid and vapour have identical composition. For a non-volatile solute, the plot of solution vapour pressure against $x_{solvent}$ is a straight line through the origin with slope $p_A^0$.

  • Ideal solution: partial and total pressure plots are linear
  • Positive deviation: plots lie above the ideal lines; a maximum in $p_{total}$ gives a minimum boiling azeotrope
  • Negative deviation: plots lie below the ideal lines; a minimum in $p_{total}$ gives a maximum boiling azeotrope
  • Higher vapour pressure means a lower boiling point
  • At the azeotropic point, $x_A$ (liquid) $= y_A$ (vapour)

$p_{total} = p_A^0 + (p_B^0 - p_A^0) x_B$ Equation of the straight-line total pressure plot for an ideal solution

NEET tip: NEET shows or describes a graph and asks you to identify ideal, positive or negative deviation, or the azeotrope type it produces.

Colligative properties: relative lowering of vapour pressure, depression of freezing point, elevation of boiling point, osmotic pressure

Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles in a dilute solution, not on their nature. There are four. Relative lowering of vapour pressure: equals the mole fraction of the solute. Elevation of boiling point: the solution boils at a higher temperature because its vapour pressure is lower. Here $\Delta T_b = K_b m$. Depression of freezing point: the solution freezes at a lower temperature. Here $\Delta T_f = K_f m$. $K_b$ and $K_f$ (in K kg $mol^{-1}$) depend only on the solvent. For water, $K_b = 0.52$ and $K_f = 1.86$. Osmotic pressure ($\pi$): the extra pressure that must be applied to the solution side to stop solvent from flowing through a semipermeable membrane. Here $\pi = CRT$. Solutions with equal osmotic pressure are isotonic. For example, 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) is isotonic with blood. Placed in a hypertonic solution (more than 0.9% NaCl), cells lose water and shrink. For plant cells this is called plasmolysis; for red blood cells it is crenation. In a hypotonic solution, cells swell and may burst. Applying pressure greater than $\pi$ reverses the flow; this reverse osmosis is used for desalination.

  • Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles only
  • Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the solute mole fraction
  • $K_b$ and $K_f$ are characteristic of the solvent, not the solute
  • For water, $K_f = 1.86$ K kg $mol^{-1}$ and $K_b = 0.52$ K kg $mol^{-1}$
  • Osmosis is the flow of solvent from lower to higher solute concentration through a semipermeable membrane
  • 0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood; cells shrink in hypertonic and swell in hypotonic solutions
  • Reverse osmosis requires an applied pressure greater than $\pi$ and is used for desalination
  • For solutions in the same solvent with equal molality, the one giving the most solute particles (largest $i \times m$) has the lowest freezing point and the highest boiling point

$\frac{p_A^0 - p_A}{p_A^0} = x_B$ Relative lowering of vapour pressure

$\frac{p_A^0 - p_A}{p_A^0} \approx \frac{n_B}{n_A}$ Approximation for dilute solutions

$\Delta T_b = K_b m$ Elevation of boiling point

$\Delta T_f = K_f m$ Depression of freezing point

$K_b = \frac{R M_A T_b^2}{1000\,\Delta_{vap}H}$ Ebullioscopic constant in terms of solvent properties ($M_A$ in g $mol^{-1}$)

$K_f = \frac{R M_A T_f^2}{1000\,\Delta_{fus}H}$ Cryoscopic constant in terms of solvent properties ($M_A$ in g $mol^{-1}$)

$\pi = CRT = \frac{n_B}{V} RT$ Osmotic pressure of a dilute solution

NEET tip: NEET often asks you to rank solutions by freezing point or boiling point using $i \times m$, and sets single-step numericals on $\Delta T_f$ or $\pi$.

Determination of molecular mass using colligative properties

Each colligative property is proportional to the moles of solute, so measuring it gives the molar mass of the solute. Substitute $n_B = w_B / M_B$ into the expression and rearrange. Osmotic pressure is preferred for polymers, proteins and other biomolecules. It is measured at room temperature, which avoids denaturation. Even dilute solutions give a measurable $\pi$, whereas $\Delta T_f$ or $\Delta T_b$ would be too small to measure accurately for such large molecules. Freezing point depression is generally preferred over boiling point elevation because $K_f$ is larger, giving a bigger, more measurable change. Always use consistent units: • masses in grams with the factor 1000 for molality • $R = 0.083$ L bar $mol^{-1}$ $K^{-1}$ (or 0.0821 L atm $mol^{-1}$ $K^{-1}$) for $\pi$ in bar (or atm) with $V$ in litres

  • Molar mass is obtained by substituting $n_B = w_B/M_B$ into the colligative equation
  • Osmotic pressure is the best method for macromolecules: measured at room temperature with a large measurable magnitude
  • $w_A$ is the mass of solvent and $w_B$ is the mass of solute
  • Units of $R$ must match the units of pressure and volume

$M_B = \frac{w_B M_A\, p_A^0}{w_A (p_A^0 - p_A)}$ Molar mass from relative lowering of vapour pressure (dilute solution)

$M_B = \frac{1000\, K_b\, w_B}{\Delta T_b\, w_A}$ Molar mass from elevation of boiling point

$M_B = \frac{1000\, K_f\, w_B}{\Delta T_f\, w_A}$ Molar mass from depression of freezing point

$M_B = \frac{w_B R T}{\pi V}$ Molar mass from osmotic pressure

NEET tip: Typical questions give mass of solute, mass of solvent and $\Delta T_f$ (or $\pi$) and ask for molar mass; questions on why osmotic pressure is chosen for proteins are also common.

Abnormal molar mass and van't Hoff factor

When a solute dissociates or associates in solution, the number of particles changes. The measured colligative property then differs from the expected value, giving an abnormal molar mass. Dissociation (for example KCl or $K_2SO_4$ in water) increases the number of particles. The observed colligative property is larger, so the calculated molar mass is lower than the true value. Association (for example ethanoic acid or benzoic acid dimerising through H-bonds in benzene) decreases the number of particles. The observed colligative property is smaller, so the calculated molar mass is higher. The van't Hoff factor $i$ corrects for this. For dissociation, $i > 1$; for association, $i < 1$; for non-electrolytes such as glucose or urea, $i = 1$. For complete dissociation, $i$ equals the number of ions: 2 for NaCl, 3 for $K_2SO_4$ and $CaCl_2$, and 4 for $K_3[Fe(CN)_6]$. For complete dimerisation, $i = 0.5$. The modified equations simply multiply by $i$.

  • $i > 1$ for dissociation, $i < 1$ for association, $i = 1$ for non-electrolytes
  • Dissociation lowers the observed molar mass; association raises it
  • Ethanoic acid dimerises in benzene, so $i$ approaches 0.5
  • For complete dissociation, $i$ equals the number of ions formed
  • Effective particle concentration equals $i \times m$; use this to compare $\Delta T_f$ or $\Delta T_b$
  • $i$ can be used to find the degree of dissociation or association

$i = \frac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{abnormal molar mass}}$ Definition of $i$ via molar mass

$i = \frac{\text{observed colligative property}}{\text{calculated colligative property}}$ Definition of $i$ via colligative property

$i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$ Dissociation into $n$ particles with degree $\alpha$

$i = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)\alpha$ Association of $n$ molecules with degree $\alpha$

$\Delta T_f = i K_f m$, $\Delta T_b = i K_b m$, $\pi = iCRT$ Modified colligative equations

$\frac{p_A^0 - p_A}{p_A^0} = i\, x_B$ Modified relative lowering of vapour pressure

NEET tip: NEET frequently asks you to find $i$ or $\alpha$ from $\Delta T_f$ data, or to rank electrolytes by freezing point or osmotic pressure.

Formula sheet

$M = \frac{n_B}{V(L)}$ Molarity (temperature dependent)

$m = \frac{n_B \times 1000}{w_A(g)}$ Molality (temperature independent)

$x_A = \frac{n_A}{n_A + n_B}$ Mole fraction

$m = \frac{1000M}{1000d - M M_B}$ Molarity to molality conversion

$p_A = p_A^0 x_A$ Raoult's law

$p_{total} = p_A^0 + (p_B^0 - p_A^0)x_B$ Total vapour pressure of an ideal binary solution

$y_A = \frac{p_A}{p_{total}}$ Vapour phase mole fraction

$\Delta_{mix}H = 0,\ \Delta_{mix}V = 0$ Ideal solution conditions

$\frac{p_A^0 - p_A}{p_A^0} = i\,x_B$ Relative lowering of vapour pressure

$\Delta T_b = iK_b m$ Elevation of boiling point

$\Delta T_f = iK_f m$ Depression of freezing point

$\pi = iCRT$ Osmotic pressure

$K_b = \frac{RM_A T_b^2}{1000\Delta_{vap}H}$ Ebullioscopic constant

$K_f = \frac{RM_A T_f^2}{1000\Delta_{fus}H}$ Cryoscopic constant

$M_B = \frac{1000K_f w_B}{\Delta T_f w_A}$ Molar mass from freezing point depression

$M_B = \frac{1000K_b w_B}{\Delta T_b w_A}$ Molar mass from boiling point elevation

$M_B = \frac{w_B RT}{\pi V}$ Molar mass from osmotic pressure

$i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$ van't Hoff factor for dissociation

$i = 1 - (1 - \frac{1}{n})\alpha$ van't Hoff factor for association

$i = \frac{M_{normal}}{M_{observed}}$ van't Hoff factor from molar masses

$K_f(H_2O) = 1.86$, $K_b(H_2O) = 0.52$ K kg $mol^{-1}$ Standard constants for water

Positive deviation: $\Delta_{mix}H > 0$, $\Delta_{mix}V > 0$; Negative deviation: $\Delta_{mix}H < 0$, $\Delta_{mix}V < 0$ Signs for non-ideal solutions

Common traps

  • Thinking that no interactions exist between components of an ideal solution; in fact A-B interactions are present and similar in strength to A-A and B-B interactions.
  • Assigning positive deviation to phenol + aniline or chloroform + acetone; both show negative deviation because of strong A-B hydrogen bonding.
  • Using mass of solution instead of mass of solvent when calculating molality.
  • Calling molarity temperature independent; molarity changes with temperature because volume does, while molality and mole fraction do not.
  • Forgetting the van't Hoff factor when comparing electrolytes; for example, 0.1 m $CaCl_2$ ($i = 3$) has a lower freezing point than 0.1 m NaCl ($i = 2$) or 0.1 m glucose ($i = 1$).
  • Linking positive deviation to a maximum boiling azeotrope; positive deviation gives a minimum boiling azeotrope and negative deviation gives a maximum boiling azeotrope.
  • Assuming dissociation increases the observed molar mass; it decreases the observed molar mass, while association increases it.
  • Mixing units of $R$ in osmotic pressure problems; use $R = 0.083$ L bar $mol^{-1}$ $K^{-1}$ with $V$ in litres and $T$ in kelvin.

Quick revision

  • Molality, mole fraction and mass percent are temperature independent; molarity is not.
  • Raoult's law: $p_A = p_A^0 x_A$; the vapour is richer in the more volatile component.
  • Ideal solution: obeys Raoult's law at all compositions, with $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$ and $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$; example: benzene + toluene.
  • Positive deviation pairs: ethanol + water, ethanol + acetone, $CS_2$ + acetone; these form minimum boiling azeotropes.
  • Negative deviation pairs: chloroform + acetone, phenol + aniline, $HNO_3$ + water; these form maximum boiling azeotropes.
  • Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute.
  • $\Delta T_b = iK_b m$, $\Delta T_f = iK_f m$, $\pi = iCRT$.
  • For water, $K_f = 1.86$ and $K_b = 0.52$ K kg $mol^{-1}$; these constants depend only on the solvent.
  • Osmotic pressure is the best method for finding molar masses of proteins and polymers.
  • 0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood; reverse osmosis is used for desalination.
  • $i > 1$ for dissociation, $i < 1$ for association (ethanoic acid in benzene, $i \approx 0.5$), $i = 1$ for non-electrolytes.
  • Rank colligative effects by $i \times m$: more particles mean a lower freezing point, a higher boiling point and a higher osmotic pressure.

Chemistry · Unit 6: Equilibrium

Equilibrium covers reversible physical and chemical processes that reach a dynamic balance. It includes the quantitative treatment of chemical equilibria through $K_c$, $K_p$ and Gibbs energy, and of ionic equilibria through $K_a$, $K_b$, $K_w$, pH, hydrolysis, $K_{sp}$ and buffers. NEET asks 2-4 questions from this unit almost every year, mostly short numericals on $K_p$/$K_c$, pH, $K_{sp}$ and solubility, plus Le Chatelier shift questions.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q52

Meaning of equilibrium; dynamic equilibrium

When a reversible process is carried out in a closed system, the rate of the forward process gradually falls and the rate of the reverse process rises. Eventually the two rates become equal. From then on, the observable properties stay constant: concentration, pressure, colour and density. This state is called equilibrium. It is dynamic, not static, because both processes continue at the molecular level at equal rates. Isotope (tracer) experiments prove this: if $D_2$ is added to an equilibrium $N_2$, $H_2$, $NH_3$ mixture, deuterium soon appears in ammonia. Equilibrium can be approached from either direction, and the same equilibrium state is reached. It can be established only in a closed system at constant temperature. A catalyst helps reach equilibrium faster but does not change the equilibrium position.

  • At equilibrium, rate of forward reaction = rate of backward reaction
  • Measurable properties become constant, but molecular activity continues
  • Equilibrium is attained only in a closed system at constant temperature
  • Equilibrium can be approached from either side
  • A catalyst shortens the time to reach equilibrium but does not shift it
  • The double half-arrow symbol $\rightleftharpoons$ denotes equilibrium

$r_f = r_b$ Kinetic condition of equilibrium

NEET tip: Statement-type questions test that equilibrium is dynamic, needs a closed system and is unaffected by a catalyst.

Physical equilibria: solid-liquid, liquid-gas and solid-gas

Physical equilibria involve phase changes without any chemical change. Solid-liquid: ice and water coexist at 273 K and 1 atm. The melting point is the temperature at which the rate of melting equals the rate of freezing. Liquid-gas: water in a closed vessel evaporates until the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation. The pressure then reaches a constant value, the equilibrium vapour pressure, which depends only on temperature and the nature of the liquid. The boiling point is the temperature at which vapour pressure equals the external pressure (373 K at 1.013 bar for water). Solid-gas: substances such as iodine, camphor and $NH_4Cl$ sublime, giving a solid-vapour equilibrium in a closed vessel. Dissolution of a solid in a liquid also reaches equilibrium in a saturated solution, where the rate of dissolution equals the rate of crystallisation.

  • Solid-liquid: $H_2O(s) \rightleftharpoons H_2O(l)$ at the normal melting point (273 K, 1 atm)
  • Liquid-gas: $H_2O(l) \rightleftharpoons H_2O(g)$; vapour pressure is constant at a given temperature
  • Vapour pressure depends on temperature, not on the amount of liquid or the vessel volume
  • Solid-gas: sublimation of $I_2$, camphor and $NH_4Cl$
  • Saturated solution: solid solute is in dynamic equilibrium with dissolved solute
  • Pressure increase favours the denser phase; ice melts under pressure because water is denser than ice

NEET tip: Matching-type questions pair each physical equilibrium with its example or condition, such as boiling point or sublimation.

Henry's law

Henry's law describes the equilibrium between a gas and its solution in a liquid. At constant temperature, the solubility (mole fraction) of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above the liquid. The constant $K_H$ depends on the gas, the solvent and the temperature. A higher $K_H$ means lower solubility. Gas solubility decreases as temperature increases, because dissolution of gases is usually exothermic, so $K_H$ increases with temperature. Applications include sealing soda bottles under high $CO_2$ pressure, the bends in deep-sea divers (nitrogen dissolves in blood under high pressure), diluting air with helium in scuba tanks, and anoxia at high altitude. The law holds well for gases that do not react chemically with the solvent, at low pressure.

  • Mass of gas dissolved per unit volume is proportional to its partial pressure at constant temperature
  • Higher $K_H$ means lower solubility of the gas
  • Gas solubility decreases as temperature rises
  • Applications: soda water, the bends, He-diluted scuba air, altitude anoxia
  • The law fails for gases that react with the solvent, such as $NH_3$ or $HCl$ in water

$p = K_H \, x$ Partial pressure of a gas vs its mole fraction in solution

$m \propto p$ Mass of gas dissolved is proportional to its pressure (constant T)

NEET tip: Expect a conceptual question on the effect of temperature on gas solubility or on comparing $K_H$ values of different gases.

Law of chemical equilibrium

Guldberg and Waage's law of mass action states that the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants. For a general reaction $aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$ at equilibrium, the ratio of the product of product concentrations to the product of reactant concentrations, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, is constant at a given temperature. This is the law of chemical equilibrium. The same expression with non-equilibrium concentrations is the reaction quotient $Q$. Comparing $Q$ with $K$ predicts the direction of net reaction. The value of $K$ depends on how the equation is written: reversing the reaction inverts $K$, multiplying the equation by $n$ raises $K$ to the power $n$, and adding equations multiplies their constants. Pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the expression.

  • $K_c$ depends only on temperature, not on initial concentrations, pressure or catalyst
  • If $Q < K$, the reaction moves forward; if $Q > K$, backward; if $Q = K$, the system is at equilibrium
  • Pure solids and pure liquids have activity 1 and are omitted
  • Large $K$ ($>10^3$): products predominate; small $K$ ($<10^{-3}$): reactants predominate
  • Reverse reaction: $K' = 1/K$; equation multiplied by $n$: $K' = K^n$; reactions added: $K = K_1 K_2$

$K_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$ Equilibrium constant in terms of molar concentrations

$Q_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$ (any instant) Reaction quotient; compare with $K$ to predict direction

NEET tip: Common questions ask for $K$ of a reversed, halved or combined equation from given $K$ values.

Equilibrium constants Kp and Kc

For gaseous reactions, the equilibrium constant can be written in terms of partial pressures ($K_p$) or molar concentrations ($K_c$). Since $p = cRT$, the two are related by $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$. Here $\Delta n_g$ is the moles of gaseous products minus the moles of gaseous reactants. If $\Delta n_g = 0$, as in $H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI$, then $K_p = K_c$. Use $R = 0.0821$ L atm $K^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ (or 0.0831 L bar $K^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$) consistently with the pressure unit. For heterogeneous equilibria, only gaseous species appear in $K_p$; for example, $K_p = p_{CO_2}$ for $CaCO_3(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_2(g)$. The units of $K_c$ are $(mol\,L^{-1})^{\Delta n}$. Degree of dissociation problems are solved with an ICE (initial, change, equilibrium) table.

  • $\Delta n_g$ counts only gaseous species
  • $\Delta n_g = 0$: $K_p = K_c$; $\Delta n_g > 0$: $K_p > K_c$ (when $RT > 1$)
  • Heterogeneous equilibria: solids and liquids are omitted from both $K_p$ and $K_c$
  • Units of $K_c$ are $(mol\,L^{-1})^{\Delta n}$; units of $K_p$ are $(atm)^{\Delta n}$ or $(bar)^{\Delta n}$
  • For $PCl_5 \rightleftharpoons PCl_3 + Cl_2$ with degree of dissociation $\alpha$: $K_p = \frac{\alpha^2 P}{1-\alpha^2}$

$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$ Converts between $K_c$ and $K_p$

$p_i = x_i P_{total}$ Partial pressure of a component from its mole fraction

$\alpha = \frac{D - d}{(n-1)d}$ Degree of dissociation from vapour densities ($D$ initial, $d$ equilibrium, $n$ particles formed per molecule)

NEET tip: NEET often asks for the $K_p/K_c$ ratio or the $\Delta n_g$ of a given reaction, including heterogeneous ones.

Significance of Gibbs energy in chemical equilibrium

Gibbs energy links thermodynamics to equilibrium. At any instant, $\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$. At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q = K$, giving $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303RT\log K$. A negative $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K > 1$ and the forward reaction is favoured, so products predominate. A positive $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K < 1$ and reactants predominate. If $\Delta G^\circ = 0$, then $K = 1$. Since $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$, the value of $K$ changes with temperature. A reaction proceeds spontaneously while $\Delta G < 0$ and stops at equilibrium when $\Delta G$ becomes zero. Remember that $\Delta G^\circ$ fixes the value of $K$, while the sign of $\Delta G$ (through $Q$) gives the instantaneous direction of the reaction.

  • At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$
  • $\Delta G^\circ < 0$ gives $K > 1$; $\Delta G^\circ > 0$ gives $K < 1$; $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ gives $K = 1$
  • $\Delta G < 0$: spontaneous in the forward direction; $\Delta G > 0$: the reverse is spontaneous
  • Use $R = 8.314$ J $K^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ and keep the energy units consistent

$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ Gibbs energy change at any composition

$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$ Relates standard Gibbs energy to the equilibrium constant

$K = e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}$ Calculates $K$ from $\Delta G^\circ$

NEET tip: Typical questions ask for the sign or value of $\Delta G^\circ$ from $K$ (or vice versa), or the value of $\Delta G$ at equilibrium.

Factors affecting equilibrium; Le Chatelier's principle

Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that reduces the effect of the change. Adding a reactant or removing a product shifts the equilibrium forward. Increasing pressure (by reducing volume) shifts it towards fewer gaseous moles; there is no effect if $\Delta n_g = 0$. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction. Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of $K$: for an exothermic reaction $K$ decreases with rise in temperature, and for an endothermic reaction it increases. A catalyst does not shift the equilibrium. Adding an inert gas at constant volume has no effect. Adding an inert gas at constant pressure shifts the equilibrium towards more gaseous moles. In the Haber process ($\Delta H < 0$, $\Delta n_g = -2$), high pressure and moderate temperature with an Fe catalyst are used.

  • Concentration and pressure changes shift the position of equilibrium but leave $K$ unchanged
  • Temperature changes $K$; use the van't Hoff relation for quantitative work
  • Catalyst: no shift; equilibrium is reached faster
  • Inert gas at constant V: no effect; at constant P: shift towards more gaseous moles
  • $N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3$ is favoured by high pressure and low temperature
  • $N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO$ (endothermic, $\Delta n_g = 0$): pressure has no effect, high temperature favours NO
  • Physical systems: pressure melts ice and raises the boiling point of water

$\log\frac{K_2}{K_1} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{2.303R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$ van't Hoff equation: variation of $K$ with temperature

NEET tip: Expect a question on the direction of shift for a given change, especially inert gas addition or the effect of temperature on $K$.

Weak and strong electrolytes; ionization

Substances that conduct electricity in aqueous solution by forming ions are called electrolytes. Strong electrolytes are almost completely ionised in water. Examples are strong acids ($HCl$, $HNO_3$, $H_2SO_4$), strong bases ($NaOH$, $KOH$) and most salts ($NaCl$). For these, the degree of ionisation $\alpha \approx 1$. Weak electrolytes, such as $CH_3COOH$, $NH_4OH$ and $HCN$, ionise only partially. An equilibrium exists between their unionised molecules and ions, so $\alpha \ll 1$. Ionic equilibrium is the equilibrium between ions and unionised molecules of a weak electrolyte. By Ostwald's dilution law, the degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte increases with dilution. It also generally increases with temperature, because ionisation is endothermic and $K$ rises. Faraday classified substances as electrolytes and non-electrolytes; Arrhenius then explained conduction through ionisation in solution.

  • Strong electrolytes: $\alpha \approx 1$; weak electrolytes: $\alpha \ll 1$
  • Ionic equilibrium exists only for weak electrolytes
  • $\alpha$ increases with dilution and with rise in temperature
  • Non-electrolytes such as glucose and urea give no ions
  • Ostwald's dilution law is valid only for weak electrolytes

$K = \frac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha} \approx c\alpha^2$ Ostwald's dilution law for a weak binary electrolyte

$\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{K}{c}}$ Degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte ($\alpha \ll 1$)

NEET tip: Classification of electrolytes and the effect of dilution on $\alpha$ are tested conceptually.

Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis concepts of acids and bases

Arrhenius: acids give $H^+$ (as $H_3O^+$) in water, and bases give $OH^-$. This concept is limited to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basicity of $NH_3$. Bronsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. An acid and the base formed when it loses a proton are a conjugate acid-base pair; for example, $HCl/Cl^-$ and $NH_4^+/NH_3$. A strong acid has a weak conjugate base, and vice versa. Amphoteric (amphiprotic) species, such as $H_2O$, $HCO_3^-$ and $HSO_4^-$, can both donate and accept a proton. Lewis: an acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a base is an electron-pair donor. Lewis acids include electron-deficient molecules ($BF_3$, $AlCl_3$), cations ($H^+$, $Fe^{3+}$, $Ag^+$) and molecules with vacant d-orbitals ($SiF_4$, $SnCl_4$). Lewis bases include $NH_3$, $H_2O$, $OH^-$ and $Cl^-$. Every Bronsted base is a Lewis base, but not every Lewis acid is a Bronsted acid.

  • Arrhenius concept: restricted to aqueous medium
  • Conjugate pairs differ by exactly one $H^+$
  • Stronger acid means weaker conjugate base
  • Amphiprotic species: $H_2O$, $HCO_3^-$, $HSO_4^-$, $H_2PO_4^-$
  • Lewis acids: $BF_3$, $AlCl_3$, $SO_3$, $CO_2$, metal cations
  • Lewis bases: species with lone pairs, such as $NH_3$, $H_2O$, $OH^-$
  • $BF_3$ is a Lewis acid but not a Bronsted acid

$HA + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_3O^+ + A^-$ Bronsted acid $HA$ with conjugate base $A^-$

NEET tip: Questions ask for the conjugate acid or base of a species, or ask you to identify Lewis acids from a list.

Acid-base equilibria and ionization constants

For a weak acid $HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$, the ionisation constant is $K_a = [H^+][A^-]/[HA]$; similarly $K_b$ is defined for a weak base. A larger $K_a$ (smaller $pK_a$) means a stronger acid. For dilute solutions with $\alpha \ll 1$, $[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a c}$ and $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/c}$. For a conjugate pair, $K_a K_b = K_w$, so $pK_a + pK_b = 14$ at 298 K. Polyprotic acids such as $H_2S$, $H_2CO_3$ and $H_3PO_4$ ionise stepwise, with $K_{a1} \gg K_{a2} \gg K_{a3}$, because removing $H^+$ from a negatively charged ion is harder. Acid strength of $H-X$ increases down a group as bond strength falls: $HF < HCl < HBr < HI$. Across a period it increases with electronegativity of the central atom: $CH_4 < NH_3 < H_2O < HF$. Factors increasing acid strength are bond weakness, polarity and stability of the conjugate base.

  • $pK_a = -\log K_a$; a lower $pK_a$ means a stronger acid
  • $K_a K_b = K_w$ for a conjugate acid-base pair
  • Polyprotic acids: $K_{a1} > K_{a2} > K_{a3}$; $[H^+]$ comes mainly from the first step
  • Down a group, bond strength decides acidity: $HI$ is the strongest hydrohalic acid
  • Across a period, electronegativity decides acidity

$K_a = \frac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$ Ionisation constant of a weak acid

$[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a c}$ Hydrogen ion concentration of a weak acid

$[OH^-] = \sqrt{K_b c}$ Hydroxide ion concentration of a weak base

$pK_a + pK_b = pK_w = 14$ Conjugate pair relation at 298 K

NEET tip: Short numericals on the pH or $\alpha$ of a weak acid or base from $K_a$ and $c$ are very common.

Ionization of water and the pH scale

Water self-ionises: $2H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_3O^+ + OH^-$. The ionic product $K_w = [H^+][OH^-] = 1.0\times10^{-14}$ at 298 K. In pure water, $[H^+] = [OH^-] = 10^{-7}$ M. $K_w$ increases with temperature because ionisation is endothermic. Pure water therefore has pH less than 7 at higher temperature, yet remains neutral because $[H^+] = [OH^-]$. The pH is $-\log[H^+]$. At 298 K, pH < 7 is acidic, pH = 7 is neutral and pH > 7 is basic, with pH + pOH = 14. The molarity of pure water is 55.55 M, and its degree of ionisation is about $1.8\times10^{-9}$. For very dilute strong acids such as $10^{-8}$ M HCl, the $H^+$ from water must be added, giving a pH of about 6.98, not 8. When strong acid and strong base solutions are mixed, calculate the net excess of $H^+$ or $OH^-$ over the total volume.

  • $K_w = 10^{-14}$ at 298 K and increases with temperature
  • A change of 1 pH unit is a 10-fold change in $[H^+]$
  • Neutrality means $[H^+] = [OH^-]$, not necessarily pH 7
  • Acidic solutions cannot have pH > 7 on dilution; pH approaches 7
  • $10^{-8}$ M HCl has pH about 6.98
  • Human blood pH is about 7.4; gastric juice about 1.2

$K_w = [H^+][OH^-] = 10^{-14}$ Ionic product of water at 298 K

$pH = -\log[H^+]$ Definition of pH

$pH + pOH = pK_w = 14$ Relation at 298 K

$[H^+]_{mix} = \frac{N_1V_1 - N_2V_2}{V_1+V_2}$ Mixing a strong acid with a strong base (acid in excess)

NEET tip: NEET asks the pH of mixtures of strong acids and bases, very dilute acids, or the effect of temperature on $K_w$.

Common ion effect

The common ion effect is the suppression of a weak electrolyte's ionisation, or of a sparingly soluble salt's solubility, when a strong electrolyte containing a common ion is added. It is an application of Le Chatelier's principle. Adding $CH_3COONa$ to $CH_3COOH$ lowers $[H^+]$ and raises the pH. Adding $NH_4Cl$ to $NH_4OH$ lowers $[OH^-]$. The solubility of $AgCl$ falls in a solution containing $NaCl$. If a salt $AB$ with solubility product $K_{sp}$ dissolves in a solution with a common ion concentration $c$, its solubility becomes $s \approx K_{sp}/c$. Applications include: purification of NaCl by passing HCl gas; salting out of soap with NaCl; precipitation of Group II sulphides with $H_2S$ in acidic medium (low $[S^{2-}]$); and precipitation of Group III hydroxides with $NH_4OH$ in the presence of $NH_4Cl$.

  • A common ion suppresses ionisation and decreases solubility
  • The value of $K_a$ or $K_{sp}$ does not change; only the equilibrium position shifts
  • HCl suppresses $H_2S$ ionisation, so only low-$K_{sp}$ Group II sulphides precipitate
  • $NH_4Cl$ suppresses $NH_4OH$ ionisation, so only Group III hydroxides precipitate
  • Basis of buffer action and of salting out

$s = \frac{K_{sp}}{[\text{common ion}]}$ Solubility of an AB-type salt in the presence of a common ion

$[H^+] = \frac{K_a[HA]}{[A^-]}$ $[H^+]$ of a weak acid in the presence of its salt

NEET tip: Expect a calculation of solubility in a solution containing a common ion, or questions on the qualitative-analysis applications.

Hydrolysis of salts and pH of their solutions

Salt hydrolysis is the reaction of the cation or anion of a salt with water, which changes the pH. Salts of a strong acid and a strong base (NaCl) do not hydrolyse; their pH is 7. A salt of a weak acid and a strong base ($CH_3COONa$, $Na_2CO_3$) undergoes anionic hydrolysis and gives a basic solution. A salt of a strong acid and a weak base ($NH_4Cl$, $CuSO_4$) undergoes cationic hydrolysis and gives an acidic solution. A salt of a weak acid and a weak base ($CH_3COONH_4$) undergoes both. Its pH depends on the relative $K_a$ and $K_b$ and is independent of concentration. The hydrolysis constant is $K_h = K_w/K_a$ or $K_w/K_b$, and the degree of hydrolysis is $h = \sqrt{K_h/c}$. For a weak acid and weak base salt, $h = \sqrt{K_w/(K_aK_b)}$, also independent of concentration.

  • Strong acid + strong base salt: neutral, no hydrolysis
  • Weak acid + strong base salt: basic (pH > 7)
  • Strong acid + weak base salt: acidic (pH < 7)
  • Weak acid + weak base salt: neutral if $K_a = K_b$, acidic if $K_a > K_b$, basic if $K_b > K_a$
  • Degree of hydrolysis increases with dilution and with temperature. For weak acid + weak base salts, h is independent of dilution but still increases with temperature.

$pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_a + \log c)$ Salt of weak acid and strong base

$pH = 7 - \frac{1}{2}(pK_b + \log c)$ Salt of strong acid and weak base

$pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_a - pK_b)$ Salt of weak acid and weak base

$K_h = \frac{K_w}{K_a}$, $h = \sqrt{\frac{K_h}{c}}$ Hydrolysis constant and degree of hydrolysis (weak acid + strong base salt)

NEET tip: Questions ask whether a salt solution is acidic, basic or neutral, or ask for the pH of salts such as $CH_3COONa$ and $NH_4Cl$.

Solubility and solubility product

For a sparingly soluble salt in a saturated solution, $A_xB_y(s) \rightleftharpoons xA^{y+} + yB^{x-}$. The solubility product is $K_{sp} = [A^{y+}]^x[B^{x-}]^y$, which is constant at a given temperature. If the molar solubility is $s$, then $K_{sp} = x^x y^y s^{x+y}$. Thus $K_{sp} = s^2$ for AB (AgCl), $4s^3$ for $AB_2$ or $A_2B$ ($CaF_2$, $Ag_2CrO_4$, and $Hg_2Cl_2$, which gives $Hg_2^{2+}$ + $2Cl^-$), and $27s^4$ for $AB_3$ ($Al(OH)_3$). Solubility order can be read directly from $K_{sp}$ only for salts of the same type. For different stoichiometries, calculate $s$ for each. The ionic product $Q_{sp}$ predicts precipitation: if $Q_{sp} > K_{sp}$, precipitation occurs; if $Q_{sp} = K_{sp}$, the solution is saturated; if $Q_{sp} < K_{sp}$, it is unsaturated. Solubility decreases in the presence of a common ion. It increases if an ion is removed, for example by complex formation or by acid acting on salts of weak acids.

  • $K_{sp}$ applies only to saturated solutions of sparingly soluble salts
  • Compare $K_{sp}$ directly only for salts of the same formula type
  • $Hg_2Cl_2$ dissociates as $Hg_2^{2+} + 2Cl^-$ (dimeric mercurous ion), so $K_{sp} = 4s^3$
  • Precipitation occurs when the ionic product exceeds $K_{sp}$
  • Mixing solutions dilutes each ion; use the concentrations after mixing for $Q_{sp}$
  • The salt with lower $K_{sp}$ (same type) precipitates first in selective precipitation

$K_{sp} = x^x y^y s^{x+y}$ General relation for $A_xB_y$ with molar solubility $s$

$K_{sp} = s^2$ (AB), $4s^3$ ($AB_2$), $27s^4$ ($AB_3$), $108s^5$ ($A_2B_3$) Quick relations for common salt types

$Q_{sp} > K_{sp}$ Condition for precipitation

NEET tip: NEET favours ranking the solubilities of salts with different stoichiometries from given $K_{sp}$ values, which requires calculating $s$, not comparing $K_{sp}$ directly.

Buffer solutions

A buffer solution resists changes in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added or on dilution. An acidic buffer is a weak acid with its salt of a strong base, such as $CH_3COOH + CH_3COONa$. A basic buffer is a weak base with its salt of a strong acid, such as $NH_4OH + NH_4Cl$. In an acetate buffer, added $H^+$ is consumed by $CH_3COO^-$ and added $OH^-$ by $CH_3COOH$. The pH is given by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. Buffer capacity is maximum when [salt] = [acid], where pH = $pK_a$. The effective buffer range is $pK_a \pm 1$. Diluting a buffer does not change its pH, since the ratio stays the same. A buffer can also be prepared by partially neutralising a weak acid with a strong base. For example, if moles of NaOH are half the moles of $CH_3COOH$, then pH = $pK_a$. A salt of a weak acid and weak base, $CH_3COONH_4$, also shows buffer action. Blood is buffered at pH about 7.4 by $H_2CO_3/HCO_3^-$.

  • Acidic buffer: weak acid + its conjugate base salt
  • Basic buffer: weak base + its conjugate acid salt
  • Strong acid + its salt (e.g. $HCl + NaCl$) is not a buffer
  • Maximum buffer capacity occurs at [salt]/[acid] = 1
  • Buffer pH is unchanged on dilution
  • Weak acid + strong base, with the weak acid in excess, gives a buffer
  • Blood buffer: $H_2CO_3/HCO_3^-$, pH about 7.4

$pH = pK_a + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$ Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer

$pOH = pK_b + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{base}]}$ Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a basic buffer

$\beta = \frac{\text{moles of acid or base added per litre}}{\Delta pH}$ Buffer capacity

NEET tip: Questions ask you to identify which mixture forms a buffer, or to calculate buffer pH from moles of weak acid partly neutralised by a strong base.

Formula sheet

$K_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$ Law of chemical equilibrium

$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$ Relation between $K_p$ and $K_c$

$K_{reverse} = \frac{1}{K}$; $K_{(n \times eq)} = K^n$; $K_{overall} = K_1K_2$ Manipulating equilibrium constants

$Q < K$: forward; $Q > K$: backward Predicting the direction of reaction

$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$ Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant

$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$ Gibbs energy at any instant

$\log\frac{K_2}{K_1} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{2.303R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)$ van't Hoff equation

$p = K_H x$ Henry's law

$\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{K}{c}}$ Ostwald's dilution law

$[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a c}$; $[OH^-] = \sqrt{K_b c}$ Weak acid and weak base

$K_w = [H^+][OH^-] = 10^{-14}$ (298 K) Ionic product of water

$pH + pOH = 14$ At 298 K

$K_aK_b = K_w$ Conjugate acid-base pair

$K_h = \frac{K_w}{K_a}$ or $\frac{K_w}{K_b}$ or $\frac{K_w}{K_aK_b}$ Hydrolysis constants

$pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_a + \log c)$ Salt of weak acid and strong base

$pH = 7 - \frac{1}{2}(pK_b + \log c)$ Salt of strong acid and weak base

$pH = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(pK_a - pK_b)$ Salt of weak acid and weak base

$K_{sp} = x^x y^y s^{x+y}$ Solubility product of $A_xB_y$

$s = \frac{K_{sp}}{c}$ Solubility of an AB salt with common ion concentration $c$

$pH = pK_a + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$ Acidic buffer

$pOH = pK_b + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{base}]}$ Basic buffer

$HF < HCl < HBr < HI$ Acid strength trend of hydrogen halides (bond strength)

Common traps

  • Comparing solubilities directly from $K_{sp}$ values for salts of different formula types. Convert each $K_{sp}$ to molar solubility $s$ first, using $s^2$, $4s^3$, $27s^4$ and so on.
  • Treating $Hg_2Cl_2$ as giving $2Hg^+$. The mercurous ion is dimeric, $Hg_2^{2+}$, so $Hg_2Cl_2 \rightleftharpoons Hg_2^{2+} + 2Cl^-$ and $K_{sp} = 4s^3$.
  • Including solids or liquids in $K_p$ or $K_c$, or counting them in $\Delta n_g$. Only gaseous species count in $\Delta n_g$ and in $K_p$.
  • Thinking that a catalyst, pressure or concentration changes $K$. Only temperature changes the value of the equilibrium constant.
  • Assuming inert gas addition always shifts equilibrium. At constant volume there is no shift; only at constant pressure does it shift towards more gaseous moles.
  • Writing pH = 8 for $10^{-8}$ M HCl. The $10^{-7}$ M $H^+$ from water must be added, giving a pH of about 6.98, since an acid can never be basic.
  • Assuming pure water always has pH 7. At higher temperature $K_w$ rises and pH falls below 7, but water remains neutral.
  • Taking $HCl + NaCl$ or $NaOH + NaCl$ as buffers. A buffer needs a weak acid or weak base with its conjugate partner.

Quick revision

  • Equilibrium is dynamic: $r_f = r_b$ in a closed system; a catalyst does not shift it.
  • Gas solubility is proportional to partial pressure ($p = K_Hx$); a higher $K_H$ means lower solubility, and gas solubility falls as temperature rises.
  • $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$; when $\Delta n_g = 0$, $K_p = K_c$.
  • $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$; at equilibrium $\Delta G = 0$; negative $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K > 1$.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure favours fewer gaseous moles, heat favours the endothermic side, and only temperature changes $K$.
  • Bronsted conjugate pairs differ by one $H^+$; $BF_3$, $AlCl_3$ and metal cations are Lewis acids.
  • $K_aK_b = K_w$; $pK_a + pK_b = 14$; for polyprotic acids $K_{a1} > K_{a2} > K_{a3}$.
  • $K_w = 10^{-14}$ at 298 K and increases with temperature; pH + pOH = 14.
  • A common ion suppresses ionisation and solubility (Group II and III qualitative analysis, salting out of soap).
  • Weak acid + strong base salt is basic; strong acid + weak base salt is acidic; for weak acid + weak base salts, pH is independent of concentration.
  • $K_{sp}$: AB = $s^2$, $AB_2$ = $4s^3$, $AB_3$ = $27s^4$; precipitation occurs when $Q_{sp} > K_{sp}$.
  • Buffer pH = $pK_a + \log$[salt]/[acid]; maximum capacity at pH = $pK_a$; buffer pH is unchanged on dilution; blood pH is 7.4.

Chemistry · Unit 7: Redox Reactions and Electrochemistry

This unit links electron transfer (redox) chemistry with the production and use of electricity. It covers oxidation numbers, balancing redox equations, conductance of electrolytes, galvanic and electrolytic cells, electrode potentials, the Nernst equation, the link between cell potential and Gibbs energy, and commercial cells. NEET asks 2-4 questions here every year, mostly numericals on $\Lambda_m$, Kohlrausch's law, $E^\circ$ combination, Nernst equation and $\Delta G = -nFE$, plus oxidation-number and statement-type questions.

PYQs (4): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q56, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q62, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q65, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q81

Electronic concepts of oxidation and reduction

The classical definitions describe oxidation as addition of oxygen or an electronegative element, or removal of hydrogen or an electropositive element. Reduction is the reverse. The electronic concept is more general. Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons, and the two always occur together, which is why the reaction is called redox. In $Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu$, zinc loses $2e^-$ and is oxidised, while $Cu^{2+}$ gains $2e^-$ and is reduced. The species that accepts electrons is the oxidising agent (oxidant), and it gets reduced itself. The electron donor is the reducing agent (reductant), and it gets oxidised. Each half-reaction pairs an oxidised and a reduced form, called a redox couple, for example $Zn^{2+}/Zn$. The tendency of a couple to gain electrons is measured later by its electrode potential.

  • Oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain of electrons (OIL RIG)
  • The oxidant is itself reduced; the reductant is itself oxidised
  • Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously; electrons lost = electrons gained
  • In $2Na + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2NaCl$, Na is the reductant and $Cl_2$ is the oxidant
  • A redox couple is written as oxidised form/reduced form, e.g. $Cu^{2+}/Cu$
  • Metals usually act as reducing agents; non-metals such as $F_2$, $O_2$ and $Cl_2$ act as oxidising agents

$Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-$ (oxidation); $Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu$ (reduction) Splitting a redox reaction into its two electron-transfer half-reactions

NEET tip: NEET asks you to identify the oxidant and reductant, or which element is oxidised or reduced, in a given reaction, often inside statement-type questions.

Oxidation number and rules for assigning it

Oxidation number (ON) is the charge an atom would carry if all its bonds were completely ionic.

  • Rules for assigning ON
  • The ON of an element in its free state is 0 (e.g. $O_2$, $P_4$, $S_8$)
  • For a monatomic ion, the ON equals its charge
  • F is always $-1$
  • O is $-2$, except: $-1$ in peroxides ($H_2O_2$, $Na_2O_2$), $-\frac{1}{2}$ in superoxides ($KO_2$), $+2$ in $OF_2$ and $+1$ in $O_2F_2$
  • H is $+1$ with non-metals and $-1$ in metal hydrides such as $NaH$ and $CaH_2$
  • In their compounds, alkali metals are always $+1$ and alkaline earth metals are always $+2$
  • The ONs in a neutral species add up to 0; in an ion they add up to its charge
  • An increase in ON is oxidation; a decrease in ON is reduction
  • Fractional ONs are averages: Fe in $Fe_3O_4$ is $+\frac{8}{3}$ and S in $S_4O_6^{2-}$ is $+2.5$ (two S at $+5$, two at 0)
  • Peroxide linkages give unexpected values: Cr in $CrO_5$ is $+6$ and S in $H_2SO_5$ is $+6$
  • Types of redox reaction: combination, decomposition, displacement and disproportionation
  • In disproportionation, one element is oxidised and reduced at the same time: $Cl_2 + 2OH^- \rightarrow Cl^- + ClO^- + H_2O$ and $2H_2O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O + O_2$
  • Max ON is usually the group valence: N $+5$ in $N_2O_5$, S $+6$ in $SO_3$, Cl $+7$ in $Cl_2O_7$
  • An element at its maximum ON acts only as an oxidant; at its minimum ON it acts only as a reductant

$\sum (\text{ON} \times \text{number of atoms}) = \text{net charge}$ Basic equation used to find an unknown oxidation number

NEET tip: Expect ordering questions on ONs of atoms in oxides and hydrides (e.g. $P_4O_{10}$, $N_2O_3$, $AlH_3$) and on species with peroxide linkages or fractional ONs.

Balancing of redox reactions

Redox equations are balanced by two methods.

  • Oxidation number method
  • Find the elements whose ON changes
  • Equalise the total increase and decrease in ON by multiplying with suitable coefficients
  • Balance O with $H_2O$ and H with $H^+$ (acid) or $OH^-$ (base)
  • Ion-electron (half-reaction) method
  • Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions separately
  • Balance atoms other than O and H
  • Balance O by adding $H_2O$ and H by adding $H^+$
  • Balance charge with electrons
  • Equalise the electrons in both halves and add them
  • In basic medium, add $OH^-$ to both sides to neutralise $H^+$
  • The number of electrons gained or lost per formula unit is the n-factor
  • A balanced equation must conserve both atoms and charge
  • In acid, add $H_2O$ on the oxygen-deficient side and $H^+$ on the other side
  • In base, convert $H^+$ to $H_2O$ by adding equal $OH^-$ to both sides
  • $MnO_4^-$ gains 5, 3 or 1 electron in acidic, neutral or strongly basic medium respectively
  • $Cr_2O_7^{2-}$ gains $6e^-$ per ion (2 Cr going from $+6$ to $+3$)
  • Stoichiometric shortcut: equivalents of oxidant = equivalents of reductant (moles x n-factor)

$MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O$ Permanganate in acid gains $5e^-$; mole ratio $MnO_4^-:Fe^{2+} = 1:5$

$Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 6Fe^{2+} + 14H^+ \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 6Fe^{3+} + 7H_2O$ Dichromate in acid gains $6e^-$; mole ratio 1:6

$2MnO_4^- + 5C_2O_4^{2-} + 16H^+ \rightarrow 2Mn^{2+} + 10CO_2 + 8H_2O$ Permanganate-oxalate titration; ratio 2:5

NEET tip: NEET asks for coefficients of $H^+$, $H_2O$ or electrons in a balanced equation, or mole ratios such as $KMnO_4$ : $FeSO_4$ in acidic medium.

Electrolytic and metallic conduction

In metallic (electronic) conduction, current is carried by mobile electrons. The metal undergoes no chemical change and no matter is transferred. Conductance decreases as temperature rises because increased lattice vibrations hinder electron flow. In electrolytic (ionic) conduction, current is carried by ions in molten electrolytes or solutions, and chemical changes (redox) occur at the electrodes. It depends on the nature of the electrolyte, the size and solvation of the ions, the nature and viscosity of the solvent, the concentration and the temperature. Electrolytic conductance increases with temperature because viscosity falls and ionic mobility (and dissociation for weak electrolytes) rises. Strong electrolytes such as $NaCl$, $HCl$ and $KNO_3$ dissociate almost completely. Weak electrolytes such as $CH_3COOH$ and $NH_4OH$ ionise only partially.

  • Metallic conduction: electrons carry the charge, there is no chemical change, and conductance falls as T rises
  • Electrolytic conduction: ions carry the charge, there is chemical change at the electrodes, and conductance rises as T rises
  • Heavily hydrated small ions (e.g. $Li^+$) move more slowly in water than larger ions
  • $H^+$ and $OH^-$ have unusually high ionic mobility (Grotthuss-type proton hopping)
  • Pure water is a very poor conductor because its self-ionisation is tiny

NEET tip: NEET tests the effect of temperature on metallic versus electrolytic conductance and the factors affecting ionic conductance, usually as statement questions.

Conductance and molar conductivity; variation with concentration

Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance.

  • Definitions
  • Resistance: $R = \rho \frac{l}{A}$, where $\rho$ is resistivity
  • Conductance: $G = \frac{1}{R}$, in siemens (S)
  • Conductivity (specific conductance): $\kappa = \frac{1}{\rho} = G \times G^*$, where $G^* = \frac{l}{A}$ is the cell constant
  • Molar conductivity: $\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}$, with $\kappa$ in S $cm^{-1}$ and c in mol $L^{-1}$, giving S $cm^2$ $mol^{-1}$
  • Variation with dilution
  • $\kappa$ decreases on dilution because there are fewer ions per unit volume
  • $\Lambda_m$ increases on dilution because the volume containing 1 mol of electrolyte increases
  • Strong electrolytes: $\Lambda_m$ increases slowly on dilution and decreases linearly with $\sqrt{c}$ ($\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}$)
  • Weak electrolytes: $\Lambda_m$ rises steeply at low c due to increased ionisation, so $\Lambda_m^\circ$ cannot be found by extrapolation
  • Units: $\kappa$ in S $m^{-1}$ (1 S $m^{-1}$ = 0.01 S $cm^{-1}$); $\Lambda_m$ in S $m^2$ $mol^{-1}$ (1 S $m^2$ $mol^{-1}$ = $10^4$ S $cm^2$ $mol^{-1}$)
  • The cell constant is usually found using standard KCl solutions of known $\kappa$
  • For a strong electrolyte, a plot of $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{c}$ is a straight line with slope $-A$ and intercept $\Lambda_m^\circ$
  • A depends on the solvent, the temperature and the charge type of the electrolyte ($NaCl$, $CaCl_2$, $MgSO_4$ have different A)

$G = \frac{1}{R}$, $\kappa = G \times \frac{l}{A}$ Conductivity from measured conductance and cell constant

$\Lambda_m = \frac{1000\,\kappa}{c}$ Molar conductivity in S $cm^2$ $mol^{-1}$ ($\kappa$ in S $cm^{-1}$, c in mol $L^{-1}$)

$\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}$ Debye-Huckel-Onsager equation for strong electrolytes; use the slope and one data point to get $\Lambda_m^\circ$

NEET tip: Numericals on cell constant, $\Lambda_m$ from $\kappa$, and finding $\Lambda_m^\circ$ from the slope of the $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{c}$ plot are very common.

Kohlrausch's law and its applications

Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that, at infinite dilution, each ion makes a definite contribution to the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte, independent of its partner ion. Hence $\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+\lambda_+^\circ + \nu_-\lambda_-^\circ$.

  • Application 1: Find $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of weak electrolytes from strong ones, e.g. $\Lambda^\circ(CH_3COOH) = \Lambda^\circ(CH_3COONa) + \Lambda^\circ(HCl) - \Lambda^\circ(NaCl)$
  • Application 2: Find the degree of dissociation, $\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_m^c}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$
  • Application 3: Find the dissociation constant, $K_a = \frac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$
  • Application 4: Find the solubility of sparingly soluble salts (e.g. $AgCl$, $BaSO_4$), since their saturated solution is effectively at infinite dilution, so $S = \frac{1000\,\kappa}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$
  • Application 5: Then find $K_{sp}$ from S
  • For $CaCl_2$: $\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda^\circ_{Ca^{2+}} + 2\lambda^\circ_{Cl^-}$; for $Al_2(SO_4)_3$: $2\lambda^\circ_{Al^{3+}} + 3\lambda^\circ_{SO_4^{2-}}$
  • Choose the strong-electrolyte combination so that the unwanted ions cancel
  • For a 1:1 salt, $K_{sp} = S^2$, with S in mol $L^{-1}$
  • For the solubility calculation, subtract the conductivity of water: $\kappa_{salt} = \kappa_{solution} - \kappa_{water}$

$\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+\lambda_+^\circ + \nu_-\lambda_-^\circ$ Kohlrausch's law; $\nu$ is the number of ions per formula unit

$\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_m^c}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$, $K_a = \frac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$ Degree of dissociation and dissociation constant of a weak electrolyte

$S = \frac{1000\,\kappa}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$ Solubility (mol $L^{-1}$) of a sparingly soluble salt

NEET tip: Typical questions: combine three strong-electrolyte $\Lambda^\circ$ values to get a weak acid's $\Lambda^\circ$, or find an ionic $\lambda^\circ$ after first getting $\Lambda_m^\circ$ from the Onsager equation.

Electrolytic and galvanic cells

A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy, as in the Daniell cell. An electrolytic cell uses external electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction, as in the electrolysis of molten NaCl.

  • In both cell types, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode
  • Galvanic cell: anode is negative, cathode is positive
  • Electrolytic cell: anode is positive (connected to the + terminal), cathode is negative
  • Salt bridge (KCl or $KNO_3$ in agar gel): completes the circuit and keeps each solution electrically neutral
  • Faraday's laws: $w = ZIt$ and $Q = It$; deposition of 1 mol of $M^{n+}$ needs nF
  • Product of electrolysis depends on electrode potential and overpotential
  • Aqueous NaCl gives $H_2$ at the cathode and $Cl_2$ at the anode
  • Galvanic: $\Delta G < 0$, $E_{cell} > 0$; electrolytic: driven by an external source with $E_{ext}$ greater than the cell emf
  • Electrons flow from anode to cathode through the external wire in both types
  • Without a salt bridge, charge accumulates and the current stops quickly
  • Electrolysis of aqueous $CuSO_4$ with Pt electrodes: Cu at the cathode, $O_2$ at the anode
  • 1 F = 96487 C $mol^{-1}$ = charge on 1 mol of electrons

$w = ZIt$, $Z = \frac{M}{nF}$ Mass deposited in electrolysis (Faraday's first law)

$\frac{w_1}{w_2} = \frac{E_1}{E_2}$ Faraday's second law; same charge deposits masses proportional to equivalent weights

NEET tip: Statement questions compare the sign of electrodes in galvanic and electrolytic cells, the role of the salt bridge, and electrolysis products.

Electrode potentials and standard electrode potential

When a metal dips into a solution of its ions, a potential difference called the electrode potential develops at the interface. By IUPAC convention, it is expressed as a reduction potential. The standard electrode potential $E^\circ$ is measured at 1 M concentration, 1 bar pressure and 298 K, against the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE).

  • SHE: Pt | $H_2$(1 bar) | $H^+$(1 M), with $E^\circ = 0$ by definition
  • Arranging $E^\circ$ values gives the electrochemical series
  • More positive $E^\circ$ means a stronger oxidising agent ($F_2$, +2.87 V)
  • More negative $E^\circ$ means a stronger reducing agent (Li, -3.05 V, strongest in aqueous solution)
  • A metal with lower $E^\circ$ displaces a metal with higher $E^\circ$ from its salt solution
  • Metals with negative $E^\circ$ liberate $H_2$ from dilute acids
  • $E^\circ$ is intensive: it does not change when the half-reaction is multiplied
  • To combine half-reactions, add $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$ values, not $E^\circ$ values
  • Oxidation potential = $-$(reduction potential)
  • Cu ($E^\circ$ = +0.34 V) does not liberate $H_2$ from dilute HCl; Zn (-0.76 V) does
  • Example of combining half-reactions: $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$ is found from $Fe^{3+}/Fe$ and $Fe^{2+}/Fe$ via the n-weighted formula

$E^\circ_3 = \frac{n_1E^\circ_1 - n_2E^\circ_2}{n_3}$ $E^\circ$ of a half-reaction obtained by subtracting two half-reactions (use + for adding), with $n_3 = n_1 - n_2$

NEET tip: Very common: combine two given $E^\circ$ values to get a third (e.g. $Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}$, $Cu^{2+}/Cu^+$), or rank species by oxidising or reducing power.

Half-cell and cell reactions; emf of a galvanic cell

A galvanic cell has an oxidation half-cell (anode) and a reduction half-cell (cathode). The cell reaction is their sum with the electrons cancelled.

  • Cell notation: anode | anode electrolyte || cathode electrolyte | cathode
  • Example: Daniell cell, $Zn|Zn^{2+}(1M)||Cu^{2+}(1M)|Cu$
  • The emf is the potential difference between the electrodes when no current flows
  • $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$, using reduction potentials for both
  • Daniell cell: $E^\circ = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10$ V
  • A positive $E_{cell}$ means the reaction as written is spontaneous; a negative value means the reverse is spontaneous
  • The emf exceeds the potential difference measured while current is drawn
  • Anode is on the left, cathode on the right; || denotes the salt bridge
  • Do not multiply $E^\circ$ by stoichiometric coefficients when balancing the cell reaction
  • The half-cell with higher $E^\circ$ becomes the cathode
  • Example: $Mg|Mg^{2+}||Ag^+|Ag$ has $E^\circ = 0.80 - (-2.37) = 3.17$ V

$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} = E^\circ_{right} - E^\circ_{left}$ Standard emf from standard reduction potentials

NEET tip: NEET gives cell notation or two $E^\circ$ values and asks for $E^\circ_{cell}$, the spontaneous direction, or which metal acts as the anode.

Nernst equation and its applications

The Nernst equation relates electrode or cell potential to concentration.

  • General form for a cell reaction: $E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \frac{2.303RT}{nF}\log Q$
  • At 298 K: $E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q$
  • Single electrode $M^{n+} + ne^- \rightarrow M$: $E = E^\circ - \frac{0.059}{n}\log\frac{1}{[M^{n+}]}$
  • Application 1: Find the potential at non-standard concentrations
  • Application 2: Find the equilibrium constant; at equilibrium $E_{cell} = 0$, so $E^\circ = \frac{0.059}{n}\log K_c$
  • Application 3: Find pH; a hydrogen electrode has $E = -0.059\,pH$
  • Application 4: Concentration cells, which have $E^\circ = 0$; emf arises only from a concentration difference
  • Pure solids and liquids are taken as 1 in Q; gases enter as partial pressure in bar
  • Increasing reactant concentration (or decreasing product concentration) increases $E_{cell}$
  • In a concentration cell, the more dilute side is the anode
  • A large positive $E^\circ$ gives a very large K: n = 2 and $E^\circ$ = 1.1 V give $K \approx 10^{37}$

$E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q$ Nernst equation at 298 K

$\log K_c = \frac{nE^\circ_{cell}}{0.059}$ Equilibrium constant from standard emf

$E = \frac{0.059}{n}\log\frac{c_2}{c_1}$ ($c_2 > c_1$) Emf of a concentration cell

$E_{H^+/H_2} = -0.059\,pH$ Potential of a hydrogen electrode at 1 bar $H_2$

NEET tip: Expect calculations of $E_{cell}$ for given ion concentrations, of $K_c$ from $E^\circ$, or of the pH of the solution in a hydrogen electrode.

Relationship between cell potential and Gibbs energy

The electrical work done by a reversible galvanic cell equals the decrease in Gibbs energy, so $\Delta G = -nFE_{cell}$ and $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell}$. Since $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303RT\log K$, it follows that $E^\circ_{cell} = \frac{2.303RT}{nF}\log K$. These relations connect electrochemistry with thermodynamics.

  • $E_{cell} > 0$, $\Delta G < 0$: spontaneous under the given conditions; separately, $E^\circ_{cell} > 0$, $\Delta G^\circ < 0$: $K > 1$
  • $E_{cell} = 0$, $\Delta G = 0$: equilibrium
  • $E_{cell} < 0$, $\Delta G > 0$: non-spontaneous
  • $\Delta G$ is extensive: doubling the equation doubles $\Delta G$, while $E$ remains the same
  • This relation is the basis for combining half-cell potentials through $nE^\circ$ values
  • F = 96487 C $mol^{-1}$, often taken as 96500
  • $\Delta G$ (in J) = $-nFE$, with F in C mol$^{-1}$ and E in volts
  • Daniell cell: $\Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 96500 \times 1.10 = -212.3$ kJ $mol^{-1}$

$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell}$ Standard Gibbs energy change from standard emf

$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$ Links standard Gibbs energy to the equilibrium constant

NEET tip: Direct numericals ask for $\Delta G^\circ$ in kJ from $E^\circ$ and n, or for the sign of $\Delta G$ given cell data; watch the J/kJ conversion.

Dry cell and lead accumulator

The dry cell (Leclanche cell) is a primary cell, which means it cannot be recharged.

  • Dry cell components
  • Anode: zinc container
  • Cathode: carbon (graphite) rod surrounded by powdered $MnO_2$ and carbon
  • Electrolyte: moist paste of $NH_4Cl$ and $ZnCl_2$
  • Voltage: about 1.5 V
  • Anode reaction: $Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-$
  • Cathode reaction: $MnO_2 + NH_4^+ + e^- \rightarrow MnO(OH) + NH_3$
  • $NH_3$ forms the complex $[Zn(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$
  • Lead storage battery (lead accumulator) is a secondary cell, which means it can be recharged
  • Lead accumulator anode: Pb
  • Lead accumulator cathode: lead grid packed with $PbO_2$
  • Lead accumulator electrolyte: about 38% $H_2SO_4$
  • On discharge, both electrodes become coated with $PbSO_4$ and $H_2SO_4$ is consumed
  • On charging, the reactions reverse
  • Each lead cell gives about 2 V; a 12 V battery has 6 cells in series
  • Mn changes from +4 to +3 in the dry cell cathode reaction
  • The density of the acid falls on discharge and is used to check the state of charge
  • On charging, $PbSO_4$ is converted back to Pb and $PbO_2$

$Pb + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow PbSO_4 + 2e^-$ Anode reaction of the lead accumulator during discharge

$PbO_2 + SO_4^{2-} + 4H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow PbSO_4 + 2H_2O$ Cathode reaction during discharge

$Pb + PbO_2 + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2PbSO_4 + 2H_2O$ Overall discharge reaction; it is reversed on charging

NEET tip: Questions ask for the electrode reactions, the change in ON of Mn or Pb, the electrolyte, or primary versus secondary classification.

Fuel cells

Fuel cells convert the chemical energy of fuels such as $H_2$, $CH_4$ or $CH_3OH$ directly into electricity, with reactants supplied continuously. In the $H_2$-$O_2$ fuel cell used in the Apollo space programme, the gases are bubbled through porous carbon electrodes into concentrated aqueous NaOH or KOH. Finely divided Pt or Pd catalysts are built into the electrodes. The water produced was used as drinking water by astronauts. Fuel cells are pollution-free and about 70% efficient, compared with about 40% for thermal power plants.

  • Reactants are fed continuously and products are removed; the cell is not stored or recharged
  • Electrolyte: concentrated KOH or NaOH; electrodes: porous carbon with Pt/Pd catalyst
  • Anode reaction: oxidation of $H_2$
  • Cathode reaction: reduction of $O_2$
  • The only product is water, so there is no pollution
  • Efficiency is high (about 70%) because the energy is converted directly
  • Theoretical efficiency is $\frac{\Delta G}{\Delta H}$

$2H_2 + 4OH^- \rightarrow 4H_2O + 4e^-$ Anode reaction of the $H_2$-$O_2$ fuel cell

$O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-$ Cathode reaction of the $H_2$-$O_2$ fuel cell

$2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O$; $\eta = \frac{\Delta G}{\Delta H}$ Overall reaction and thermodynamic efficiency

NEET tip: NEET asks for the electrode reactions, the electrolyte or catalyst used, or the advantages and efficiency of the $H_2$-$O_2$ fuel cell.

Formula sheet

$\sum \text{ON} = \text{net charge}$ Assigning oxidation numbers

Moles x n-factor (oxidant) = moles x n-factor (reductant) Redox stoichiometry and titrations

$MnO_4^-$: n = 5 (acid), 3 (neutral), 1 (strong base); $Cr_2O_7^{2-}$: n = 6 n-factors of common oxidants

$R = \rho\frac{l}{A}$, $G = \frac{1}{R}$ Resistance and conductance

$\kappa = G \times G^*$, $G^* = \frac{l}{A}$ Conductivity and cell constant

$\Lambda_m = \frac{1000\,\kappa}{c}$ Molar conductivity in S $cm^2$ $mol^{-1}$

$\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}$ Strong electrolytes (Debye-Huckel-Onsager)

$\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+\lambda_+^\circ + \nu_-\lambda_-^\circ$ Kohlrausch's law

$\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$, $K_a = \frac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$ Weak electrolyte dissociation

$S = \frac{1000\,\kappa}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$, $K_{sp} = S^2$ (1:1 salt) Solubility from conductance

$w = ZIt = \frac{MIt}{nF}$ Faraday's first law

$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$ Standard cell emf

$E^\circ_3 = \frac{n_1E^\circ_1 \pm n_2E^\circ_2}{n_3}$ Combining half-cell potentials

$E = E^\circ - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q$ Nernst equation at 298 K

$\log K = \frac{nE^\circ}{0.059}$ Equilibrium constant from emf

$E_{H^+/H_2} = -0.059\,pH$ pH from a hydrogen electrode

$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$ Thermodynamics of cells

$E^\circ$: Li $-3.05$ V, Zn $-0.76$ V, SHE 0, Cu $+0.34$ V, Ag $+0.80$ V, $F_2$ $+2.87$ V Key reference values of the electrochemical series

$Pb + PbO_2 + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2PbSO_4 + 2H_2O$ Lead accumulator discharge

$MnO_2 + NH_4^+ + e^- \rightarrow MnO(OH) + NH_3$ Dry cell cathode

$2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O$ (KOH, Pt/C electrodes) $H_2$-$O_2$ fuel cell

Common traps

  • Adding $E^\circ$ values directly when combining half-reactions into a new half-reaction. $E^\circ$ is intensive, so you must combine $nE^\circ$ values (via $\Delta G^\circ$) and divide by the new n.
  • Multiplying $E^\circ$ by stoichiometric coefficients when balancing a cell reaction. Electrode potential does not depend on the amount of substance.
  • Assuming the anode is always negative. It is negative in a galvanic cell but positive in an electrolytic cell; oxidation at the anode is common to both.
  • Thinking conductivity and molar conductivity both increase on dilution. On dilution $\kappa$ decreases while $\Lambda_m$ increases.
  • Forgetting the factor 1000 or the unit conversion in $\Lambda_m = \frac{1000\kappa}{c}$. Keep $\kappa$ in S $cm^{-1}$ and c in mol $L^{-1}$ to get S $cm^2$ $mol^{-1}$.
  • Taking O as $-2$ in every compound. It is $-1$ in peroxides and in the peroxo bonds of $CrO_5$ and $H_2SO_5$, so Cr and S stay at $+6$, not $+10$ or $+8$.
  • Assuming $MnO_2$ is oxidised when it is heated with a halide and concentrated $H_2SO_4$. $MnO_2$ is the oxidant: Mn goes from $+4$ to $+2$ while the halide is oxidised to the halogen.
  • Extrapolating the $\Lambda_m$ vs $\sqrt{c}$ plot of a weak electrolyte to get $\Lambda_m^\circ$. This is only valid for strong electrolytes; use Kohlrausch's law for weak ones.

Quick revision

  • Oxidation = electron loss or ON increase; reduction = electron gain or ON decrease; the oxidant gets reduced.
  • F is always $-1$; O is $-2$, except in peroxides ($-1$), superoxides ($-\frac{1}{2}$) and $OF_2$ ($+2$); H is $-1$ in metal hydrides.
  • Balance redox equations by electron equality; in acid use $H^+/H_2O$, in base add $OH^-$.
  • Metallic conductance falls with temperature; electrolytic conductance rises with temperature.
  • $\kappa$ decreases and $\Lambda_m$ increases on dilution; strong electrolytes follow $\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A\sqrt{c}$.
  • Kohlrausch's law gives $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of weak electrolytes, $\alpha$, $K_a$ and the solubility of sparingly soluble salts.
  • Higher $E^\circ$ means a stronger oxidant and the cathode; $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$; Daniell cell = 1.10 V.
  • Nernst at 298 K: $E = E^\circ - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q$; at equilibrium E = 0 and $\log K = \frac{nE^\circ}{0.059}$.
  • $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$; a positive E means the reaction is spontaneous.
  • Dry cell: Zn anode, $MnO_2$/C cathode, $NH_4Cl$ + $ZnCl_2$ paste, about 1.5 V, primary cell.
  • Lead accumulator: Pb anode, $PbO_2$ cathode, 38% $H_2SO_4$, $PbSO_4$ forms on discharge, secondary cell.
  • $H_2$-$O_2$ fuel cell: porous C electrodes with Pt/Pd, KOH electrolyte, water as product, about 70% efficient.

Chemistry · Unit 8: Chemical Kinetics

Chemical kinetics studies how fast reactions occur, the factors that control their speed, and the mechanism by which reactants change into products. NEET asks one or two questions from this unit almost every year. These are mostly numericals on rate law, units of $k$, zero and first order integrated equations, half-life and Arrhenius activation energy, plus conceptual questions on order, molecularity and collision theory.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q60, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q64

Rate of a chemical reaction

The rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. For reactants the concentration decreases, so a minus sign is used to keep the rate positive. For a general reaction $aA + bB \rightarrow cC + dD$, each concentration change is divided by its stoichiometric coefficient, so that one unique rate is obtained for the whole reaction. The average rate is measured over a finite time interval. The instantaneous rate is the slope of the concentration versus time curve at a particular instant, i.e. a tangent, as $\Delta t \rightarrow 0$. Units are $mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}$. For gaseous reactions the units can be $atm\,s^{-1}$ when partial pressures are used. The rate generally decreases with time because reactant concentration falls.

  • Rate is always reported as a positive quantity.
  • Rate of disappearance of a reactant is not equal to the rate of reaction unless its coefficient is 1.
  • The instantaneous rate is the slope of the tangent on the concentration versus time graph.
  • The average rate equals the instantaneous rate only for a zero order reaction.
  • For $N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3$: $-\frac{d[N_2]}{dt} = -\frac{1}{3}\frac{d[H_2]}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d[NH_3]}{dt}$.

$r_{av} = -\frac{\Delta[R]}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta[P]}{\Delta t}$ Average rate over the time interval $\Delta t$.

$r = -\frac{1}{a}\frac{d[A]}{dt} = -\frac{1}{b}\frac{d[B]}{dt} = \frac{1}{c}\frac{d[C]}{dt} = \frac{1}{d}\frac{d[D]}{dt}$ Instantaneous rate of reaction for $aA + bB \rightarrow cC + dD$.

NEET tip: Expect questions that relate the rate of disappearance of one species to the rate of formation of another using stoichiometric coefficients.

Factors affecting rate: concentration, temperature, pressure and catalyst

Concentration: for most reactions, rate increases with reactant concentration as dictated by the rate law. Zero order reactions are the exception, since their rate does not depend on concentration. Temperature: rate rises sharply with temperature. For many reactions, a 10 K rise roughly doubles or triples the rate constant; the ratio $k_{T+10}/k_T$ is called the temperature coefficient. Pressure: for gaseous reactions, increasing pressure decreases volume and raises concentration, so collisions become more frequent and the rate increases. Pressure has negligible effect on reactions in solids and liquids. Catalyst: a catalyst gives an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and so increases the rate. It remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction. It does not change $\Delta H$, $\Delta G$ or the equilibrium constant. It speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner. Surface area and the nature of reactants also affect the rate.

  • Temperature coefficient $= \frac{k_{T+10}}{k_T} \approx 2$ to $3$.
  • A catalyst lowers $E_a$ but cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction ($\Delta G > 0$) occur.
  • A catalyst does not alter the equilibrium position or $K$; it only shortens the time needed to reach equilibrium.
  • Increasing pressure raises the rate of gaseous reactions only, through increased concentration.
  • Rate depends on concentration, not on the total amount of reactant.

$\frac{k_{T_2}}{k_{T_1}} = \mu^{\frac{T_2 - T_1}{10}}$ Approximate rate constant at a new temperature when the temperature coefficient $\mu$ is known.

NEET tip: Statement-based questions on what a catalyst can and cannot change ($E_a$ versus $\Delta H$, $\Delta G$, $K$) are very common.

Elementary and complex reactions

An elementary reaction takes place in a single step: reactants collide and form products directly.
