The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by field strength: $I^- < Br^- < SCN^- < Cl^- < S^{2-} < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < edta^{4-} < NH_3 < en < CN^- < CO$. $\Delta_o$ also increases with higher metal oxidation state and on going from 3d to 4d to 5d metals.

  • Strongest ligands are $CO$ and $CN^-$; halides are weak-field, with $I^-$ the weakest.
  • Within ligands: $NH_3 > H_2O > F^- > Cl^-$.
  • 4d and 5d metal complexes are nearly always low spin.
  • In a square planar complex, $d_{x^2-y^2}$ is the highest-energy orbital.
  • CFT ignores covalent character, so it cannot explain why neutral $CO$ is the strongest ligand.

$CFSE_{oct} = (-0.4\,n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6\,n_{e_g})\Delta_o + mP$ Crystal field stabilisation energy for an octahedral complex; m is the number of extra electron pairs formed.

$\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ Tetrahedral splitting compared with octahedral splitting for the same metal and ligands.

NEET tip: Ligand field-strength order and high-spin versus low-spin configurations ($t_{2g}^x e_g^y$) are asked almost every year.

Colour and magnetic properties

Most transition metal complexes are coloured because of d–d transitions. An electron in $t_{2g}$ absorbs visible light and is promoted to $e_g$, and we see the complementary colour. $[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ ($d^1$) absorbs at about 498 nm (blue-green) and appears violet. Ions with $d^0$ (e.g. $Sc^{3+}$, $Ti^{4+}$) or $d^{10}$ (e.g. $Zn^{2+}$, $Cu^+$) configurations show no d–d transitions and are colourless. Intensely coloured species such as $MnO_4^-$ and $CrO_4^{2-}$ owe their colour to charge transfer, not d–d transitions. Anhydrous $CuSO_4$ is white and $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$ is blue, because there is no splitting without ligands. Replacing $H_2O$ in green $[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ with $en$ raises $\Delta_o$, so the complex absorbs at shorter wavelength and turns blue, then violet. Magnetic behaviour follows from the number of unpaired electrons, using the spin-only formula. Spin-only moments are 1.73 BM for n = 1, 2.83 for n = 2, 3.87 for n = 3, 4.90 for n = 4 and 5.92 for n = 5.

  • Larger $\Delta_o$ means higher-energy absorption, i.e. shorter wavelength absorbed.
  • Colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed.
  • $d^6$ low spin, such as $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$ and $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$, has n = 0 and is diamagnetic.
  • $d^5$ high spin, such as $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ and $[MnF_6]^{4-}$, has n = 5, the maximum.
  • Procedure: find the O.S., find the d-count, decide strong or weak field, then count unpaired electrons.

$\Delta_o = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$ (per ion), $\Delta_o = \frac{N_Ahc}{\lambda}$ (per mole) Crystal field splitting from the wavelength absorbed by a $d^1$ complex.

$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \text{BM}$ Compare paramagnetism of complexes; the highest n gives the highest $\mu$.

NEET tip: Questions ask which species has the highest spin-only moment or which is colourless; work out the d-count and spin state carefully.

Importance in qualitative analysis, extraction of metals and biological systems

Qualitative analysis uses several characteristic complexes. $Ni^{2+}$ gives a rosy-red precipitate with dimethylglyoxime (DMG). $Cu^{2+}$ gives deep blue $[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$ with excess $NH_3$. $Fe^{3+}$ gives blood-red $[Fe(SCN)(H_2O)_5]^{2+}$ with $SCN^-$, and Prussian blue $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$ with $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$. Water hardness is estimated by titrating $Ca^{2+}$ and $Mg^{2+}$ with $Na_2EDTA$. In metallurgy, Ag and Au are leached with $CN^-$ in the presence of air to form $[Ag(CN)_2]^-$ and $[Au(CN)_2]^-$, then recovered by displacement with Zn. Nickel is refined by the Mond process via volatile $[Ni(CO)_4]$. In biology, chlorophyll contains Mg, haemoglobin contains Fe, and vitamin $B_{12}$ (cyanocobalamin) contains Co. In medicine, cis-platin $cis-[PtCl_2(NH_3)_2]$ is an anticancer drug. EDTA removes Pb in lead poisoning, and D-penicillamine and desferrioxamine B remove excess Cu and Fe. Wilkinson's catalyst $[(Ph_3P)_3RhCl]$ hydrogenates alkenes, and $[Ag(S_2O_3)_2]^{3-}$ forms when photographic film is fixed with hypo.

  • Chlorophyll contains Mg; haemoglobin contains Fe; vitamin $B_{12}$ contains Co.
  • Cis-platin is the cis isomer; the trans isomer is inactive as an anticancer drug.
  • Mond process: $Ni + 4CO \rightarrow [Ni(CO)_4]$, which decomposes on heating to give pure Ni.
  • Gold and silver extraction is a cyanide process: complexation followed by Zn displacement.
  • Electroplating of Ag and Au uses $[Ag(CN)_2]^-$ and $[Au(CN)_2]^-$ baths.
  • EDTA titration is used to estimate water hardness.

$4Au + 8CN^- + 2H_2O + O_2 \rightarrow 4[Au(CN)_2]^- + 4OH^-$ Leaching of gold.

$2[Au(CN)_2]^- + Zn \rightarrow [Zn(CN)_4]^{2-} + 2Au$ Recovery of gold by displacement with zinc.

NEET tip: Usually a match-the-column question pairing a metal with a biomolecule, or a drug or catalyst with the complex involved.

Formula sheet

$\mu_s = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \text{BM}$ Spin-only magnetic moment: n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 gives 1.73, 2.83, 3.87, 4.90, 5.92 BM.

$CN = \sum(\text{ligands} \times \text{denticity})$ Coordination number.

$\text{O.S.} = \text{charge of complex} - \sum \text{ligand charges}$ Oxidation state of the central metal.

$CFSE = (-0.4\,n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6\,n_{e_g})\Delta_o + mP$ Octahedral crystal field stabilisation energy.

$\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$ Tetrahedral splitting; because $\Delta_t$ is small, tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin.

$\Delta_o = \frac{N_A hc}{\lambda}$ Splitting energy per mole from the absorbed wavelength.

$I^- < Br^- < SCN^- < Cl^- < S^{2-} < F^- < OH^- < C_2O_4^{2-} < H_2O < NCS^- < edta^{4-} < NH_3 < en < CN^- < CO$ Spectrochemical series in increasing field strength.

$\Delta_o > P \Rightarrow$ low spin; $\Delta_o < P \Rightarrow$ high spin Spin-state decision for $d^4$ to $d^7$ octahedral ions.

sp3: tetrahedral; dsp2: square planar; d2sp3: inner-orbital octahedral; sp3d2: outer-orbital octahedral VBT hybridisation and the geometry it produces.

$MA_3B_3$: fac + mer; $MA_4B_2$: cis + trans; $MA_2B_2C_2$: 5 geometrical isomers Geometrical isomer counts for octahedral complexes.

$[M(AA)_3]$: d/l pair; $cis-[M(AA)_2B_2]$: chiral; $trans-[M(AA)_2B_2]$: achiral Optical activity of chelate complexes.

$Ni^{2+} + 2\,DMG \rightarrow$ rosy-red complex Test for nickel.

$Fe^{3+} + SCN^- \rightarrow [Fe(SCN)(H_2O)_5]^{2+}$ (blood red) Test for ferric ion.

$Cu^{2+} + 4NH_3 \rightarrow [Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$ (deep blue) Test for cupric ion.

$4Fe^{3+} + 3[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} \rightarrow Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$ (Prussian blue) Confirmatory test for $Fe^{3+}$.

$Ni + 4CO \xrightarrow{330-350\,K} [Ni(CO)_4] \xrightarrow{450-470\,K} Ni + 4CO$ Mond process for refining nickel.

$4Au + 8CN^- + 2H_2O + O_2 \rightarrow 4[Au(CN)_2]^- + 4OH^-$ Cyanide leaching of gold (silver is analogous).

$AgBr + 2S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow [Ag(S_2O_3)_2]^{3-} + Br^-$ Fixing of photographic film with hypo.

$[(Ph_3P)_3RhCl]$ Wilkinson's catalyst for hydrogenation of alkenes.

$cis-[PtCl_2(NH_3)_2]$ Cis-platin, an anticancer drug.

Common traps

  • Counting ligands instead of donor atoms for the coordination number. $[Co(en)_3]^{3+}$ has CN 6, not 3.
  • Counting chlorides inside the bracket as ionisable. Only counter ions outside the sphere precipitate with $AgNO_3$ or conduct as separate ions.
  • Assuming every bis-chelate complex is chiral. $trans-[M(AA)_2B_2]$ has a mirror plane and is achiral; only the cis form and $[M(AA)_3]$ are chiral.
  • Expecting geometrical isomerism in tetrahedral complexes. All positions are equivalent, so tetrahedral complexes have no cis/trans isomers.
  • Using the neutral atom's electron configuration. Always find the oxidation state first; e.g. $Co^{3+}$ is $3d^6$, and $NH_3$ makes it low spin and diamagnetic.
  • Reversing the spectrochemical order of $H_2O$ and $NH_3$. Correct order is $CO > CN^- > en > NH_3 > H_2O > F^- > Cl^-$.
  • Alphabetising by multiplying prefixes or by symbol in names. 'tetraammine' is listed under 'a', so ammine comes before aqua and chlorido.
  • Forgetting the -ate ending and Latin roots for anionic complexes, e.g. ferrate, not ironate, in $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$.

Quick revision

  • Werner: primary valency = oxidation state (ionisable); secondary valency = coordination number (non-ionisable, directional).
  • Number of ions = complex ion + counter ions; $[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3$ is a 1:3 electrolyte.
  • EDTA is hexadentate; $NO_2^-$, $SCN^-$ and $CN^-$ are ambidentate; chelates are extra stable (chelate effect).
  • Naming: ligands alphabetical, anionic ligands end in -ido, special names aqua, ammine, carbonyl, nitrosyl; anionic complexes take -ate.
  • $MA_3B_3$ gives fac/mer; $MA_4B_2$ and $[M(AA)_2B_2]$ give cis/trans; tetrahedral complexes give no geometrical isomers.
  • $[M(AA)_3]$ and $cis-[M(AA)_2B_2]$ are optically active; trans forms are inactive.
  • VBT: d2sp3 is inner-orbital low spin; sp3d2 is outer-orbital high spin; dsp2 is square planar; sp3 is tetrahedral.
  • Octahedral splitting: $t_{2g}$ at $-0.4\Delta_o$, $e_g$ at $+0.6\Delta_o$; $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9}\Delta_o$.
  • Field strength: $CO > CN^- > en > NH_3 > H_2O > F^- > Cl^- > Br^- > I^-$.
  • $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM; $d^5$ high spin is maximum (5.92 BM); $d^6$ low spin is zero.
  • $d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions are colourless; colour seen is complementary to light absorbed; larger $\Delta_o$ means shorter wavelength absorbed.
  • Applications: Ni–DMG (red), $Fe^{3+}$–SCN (blood red), Mond process (Ni), cyanide process (Au, Ag), chlorophyll (Mg), haemoglobin (Fe), vitamin $B_{12}$ (Co), cis-platin (anticancer).

Chemistry · Unit 13: Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds

This unit covers how organic compounds are purified, how their constituent elements (N, S, P, halogens) are detected, and how the percentage of each element is determined to arrive at empirical and molecular formulae. NEET regularly asks direct questions on Lassaigne's test colours, the choice of purification technique, Kjeldahl's limitations and short percentage-composition numericals. It is a high-scoring and largely fact-based unit.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q55

Purification: crystallization, sublimation, distillation, differential extraction and chromatography

The choice of purification method depends on the nature of the compound and its impurities. Crystallisation uses the difference in solubility of the compound and its impurities in a suitable solvent; fractional crystallisation separates substances of similar solubility. Sublimation purifies solids that pass directly into vapour, such as camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid and iodine. Distillation methods depend on boiling points. Simple distillation suits liquids with very different boiling points. Fractional distillation suits close-boiling liquids, as in crude oil refining. Reduced-pressure distillation is used for liquids that decompose below their boiling points, such as glycerol from spent lye. Steam distillation suits steam-volatile, water-immiscible liquids such as aniline and essential oils. Differential extraction uses a separating funnel and an immiscible organic solvent. Chromatography separates components using a stationary phase and a mobile phase, through adsorption (column, TLC) or partition (paper).

  • Crystallisation: impure solid is dissolved in minimum hot solvent and cooled; activated charcoal removes coloured impurities
  • Sublimable solids: camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid, $I_2$
  • Simple distillation separates chloroform (b.p. 334 K) from aniline (b.p. 457 K)
  • Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column and is used for crude oil
  • Reduced-pressure distillation recovers glycerol from spent lye in the soap industry
  • Steam distillation: the liquid boils when $p_{water} + p_{organic} = p_{atm}$, so it distils below 373 K
  • Steam distillation separates o-nitrophenol (steam volatile because of intramolecular H-bonding) from p-nitrophenol
  • Differential extraction uses a separating funnel; continuous extraction is used when the compound is sparingly soluble in the organic solvent
  • Adsorption chromatography: column chromatography and TLC (silica gel or alumina as adsorbent)
  • Partition chromatography: paper chromatography, where water held in the paper is the stationary phase
  • Colourless spots are located by UV light, by an iodine chamber, or by spraying a reagent (ninhydrin for amino acids)
  • The less strongly adsorbed component moves faster and elutes first

$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance from base line}}{\text{distance moved by solvent from base line}}$ Retardation factor in TLC or paper chromatography; always less than 1

$p = p_1 + p_2$ In steam distillation the mixture boils when the sum of the vapour pressures of water and the organic liquid equals atmospheric pressure

NEET tip: Expect match-the-column or single-correct questions pairing a mixture with its purification method, plus questions on the meaning of $R_f$ and on steam distillation of aniline or o-nitrophenol.

Qualitative analysis: detection of nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and halogens

Lassaigne's test is the standard method for detecting N, S and halogens. The compound is fused with sodium metal, which converts N, S and halogens into ionic forms: $NaCN$, $Na_2S$ and $NaX$. The fused mass is extracted with water to give the sodium fusion extract (SFE). Nitrogen gives Prussian blue with $FeSO_4$ followed by conc. $H_2SO_4$. Sulphur gives a black precipitate with lead acetate and a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside. When N and S are both present, insufficient sodium gives $NaSCN$, which produces a blood-red colour with $Fe^{3+}$. Halogens are detected with $AgNO_3$ after boiling the extract with $HNO_3$. Phosphorus is detected separately: the compound is heated with $Na_2O_2$ to oxidise P to phosphate, then boiled with $HNO_3$ and ammonium molybdate to give a yellow precipitate.

  • Nitrogen: $6CN^- + Fe^{2+} \rightarrow [Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$
  • Prussian blue forms by $3[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} + 4Fe^{3+} \rightarrow Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3 \cdot xH_2O$; the $Fe^{3+}$ comes from partial oxidation of $Fe^{2+}$
  • N and S together: $Na + C + N + S \rightarrow NaSCN$; then $Fe^{3+} + SCN^- \rightarrow [Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$, which is blood red
  • With excess sodium, $NaSCN + 2Na \rightarrow NaCN + Na_2S$, so the separate tests for N and S are seen instead of blood red
  • Sulphur with lead acetate in acetic acid: $S^{2-} + Pb^{2+} \rightarrow PbS$, a black precipitate
  • Sulphur with sodium nitroprusside: $S^{2-} + [Fe(CN)_5NO]^{2-} \rightarrow [Fe(CN)_5NOS]^{4-}$, a violet colour
  • Halogens: the extract is first boiled with $HNO_3$ to decompose $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which would otherwise interfere
  • $AgCl$ is white and soluble in $NH_4OH$; $AgBr$ is pale yellow and sparingly soluble; $AgI$ is yellow and insoluble
  • Phosphorus: the compound is heated with $Na_2O_2$ to form phosphate, then boiled with $HNO_3$ and ammonium molybdate to give yellow $(NH_4)_3PO_4 \cdot 12MoO_3$
  • Hydrazine ($NH_2NH_2$) contains no carbon, so it cannot form $CN^-$ and gives a negative Lassaigne test for N
  • Diazonium salts lose $N_2$ on heating and also fail the test

NEET tip: NEET asks for colours and formulae of complexes (Prussian blue, blood red, violet) and asks which biomolecules, such as the sulphur-containing amino acids, give positive N and S tests.

Quantitative analysis (basic principles): C, H, N, halogens, S and P

Carbon and hydrogen are estimated by Liebig's combustion method. The compound is burnt with $CuO$; the water formed is absorbed in anhydrous $CaCl_2$ and the $CO_2$ in $KOH$, and each is weighed. Nitrogen is estimated by Dumas' method, where it is converted to $N_2$ gas and its volume is measured. Alternatively, Kjeldahl's method converts nitrogen to $(NH_4)_2SO_4$; the $NH_3$ released with $NaOH$ is absorbed in a known excess of acid, and the remaining acid is back-titrated. Halogens are estimated by Carius' method: heating with fuming $HNO_3$ and $AgNO_3$ precipitates $AgX$. Sulphur is oxidised to $H_2SO_4$ and weighed as $BaSO_4$. Phosphorus is oxidised to $H_3PO_4$ and weighed either as ammonium phosphomolybdate or as $Mg_2P_2O_7$. Oxygen is found by difference.

  • Liebig method: $CaCl_2$ absorbs $H_2O$ and $KOH$ absorbs $CO_2$
  • Dumas method: hot $CuO$ converts N to $N_2$; the gas is collected over $KOH$ solution, and copper gauze reduces any oxides of nitrogen
  • Kjeldahl method is unsuitable for nitro and azo compounds and for nitrogen in a ring, such as pyridine
  • Kjeldahl method is widely used for foods and fertilisers
  • Carius tube contents: fuming $HNO_3$ plus $AgNO_3$ for halogens, or plus $BaCl_2$ for sulphur
  • Molar masses to remember: $BaSO_4$ = 233, $Mg_2P_2O_7$ = 222, $(NH_4)_3PO_4 \cdot 12MoO_3$ = 1877
  • Molar masses to remember: $AgCl$ = 143.5, $AgBr$ = 188, $AgI$ = 235
  • %O = 100 minus the sum of the percentages of all other elements

$\%C = \frac{12}{44} \times \frac{m_{CO_2}}{m} \times 100$ Carbon from the mass of $CO_2$ (Liebig)

$\%H = \frac{2}{18} \times \frac{m_{H_2O}}{m} \times 100$ Hydrogen from the mass of water (Liebig)

$\%N = \frac{28}{22400} \times \frac{V_{STP}}{m} \times 100$ Dumas method, with $V$ in mL at STP

$\%N = \frac{1.4 \times N_{acid} \times V_{acid\,used}}{m}$ Kjeldahl method, using the normality and volume (mL) of acid neutralised by $NH_3$

$\%X = \frac{\text{at. mass of } X}{108 + \text{at. mass of } X} \times \frac{m_{AgX}}{m} \times 100$ Halogen by the Carius method

$\%S = \frac{32}{233} \times \frac{m_{BaSO_4}}{m} \times 100$ Sulphur by the Carius method

$\%P = \frac{62}{222} \times \frac{m_{Mg_2P_2O_7}}{m} \times 100$ Phosphorus weighed as magnesium pyrophosphate

$\%P = \frac{31}{1877} \times \frac{m_{(NH_4)_3PO_4 \cdot 12MoO_3}}{m} \times 100$ Phosphorus weighed as ammonium phosphomolybdate

NEET tip: NEET checks the absorbents in Liebig's method, the compounds for which Kjeldahl's method fails, and direct substitution into the %N, %X and %S formulae.

Calculation of empirical and molecular formulae

The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. The molecular formula is the actual number of atoms in one molecule. To find the empirical formula, divide the percentage of each element by its atomic mass to get relative moles. Then divide each value by the smallest one. If the results are fractions such as 0.5 or 0.33, multiply all values by a suitable small integer to get whole numbers. The molecular formula is n times the empirical formula, where n = molar mass divided by empirical formula mass. The molar mass is often given directly or obtained from vapour density, since molar mass = 2 × vapour density.

  • Always find %O by difference before calculating moles
  • Do not round values like 1.5 or 1.33; multiply all values by 2 or 3 instead
  • n must be a whole number
  • Glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$), acetic acid ($C_2H_4O_2$) and formaldehyde ($CH_2O$) all have the same empirical formula, $CH_2O$
  • Benzene ($C_6H_6$) and acetylene ($C_2H_2$) share the empirical formula $CH$

$\text{relative moles} = \frac{\% \text{ of element}}{\text{atomic mass}}$ First step in finding the empirical formula

$n = \frac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}$ Multiplier that converts the empirical formula to the molecular formula

$M = 2 \times VD$ Molar mass from vapour density

NEET tip: NEET usually gives percentage composition and vapour density or molar mass, and asks for the molecular formula.

Numerical problems in organic quantitative analysis

Numericals in this unit combine the estimation formulae with formula determination. In Dumas problems, correct the gas volume to STP. Subtract the aqueous tension from the observed pressure if the gas is moist, then apply the combined gas law. In Kjeldahl problems, find the acid actually neutralised by $NH_3$ by subtracting the acid neutralised by $NaOH$ in the back titration. Remember that $H_2SO_4$ is dibasic. In gravimetric problems, multiply the mass of precipitate by the mass fraction of the element in it. Worked example: 0.2475 g of a compound gives 0.4950 g of $CO_2$ and 0.2025 g of $H_2O$. Then %C = (12/44)(0.4950/0.2475)(100) = 54.5. Similarly, %H = (2/18)(0.2025/0.2475)(100) = 9.1.

  • Dumas: use $\frac{p_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{p_2V_2}{T_2}$ with $p_1 = p - \text{aqueous tension}$
  • STP values: 760 mm Hg and 273 K; 1 mol of $N_2$ (28 g) occupies 22400 mL
  • Kjeldahl: acid used by $NH_3$ = total acid minus acid neutralised by $NaOH$
  • Kjeldahl: $1\,M\,H_2SO_4 = 2\,N$
  • Fraction of the element in common precipitates: Cl in $AgCl$ = 35.5/143.5, Br in $AgBr$ = 80/188, S in $BaSO_4$ = 32/233
  • Check that all percentages, including oxygen, add up to 100

$V_{STP} = \frac{(p - f) \times V \times 273}{760 \times T}$ Converts a moist $N_2$ volume to STP; $f$ is the aqueous tension in mm Hg

$\%N = \frac{1.4 \times M \times 2(V - \frac{V_1}{2})}{m}$ Kjeldahl with $V$ mL of $M$ molar $H_2SO_4$, back-titrated with $V_1$ mL of $M$ molar $NaOH$

NEET tip: Typical NEET numericals ask for %N by Kjeldahl or Dumas, or %Br or %S by Carius, in two or three steps using standard molar masses.

Formula sheet

$R_f = \frac{d_{substance}}{d_{solvent}}$ Retardation factor in chromatography

$p_{water} + p_{organic} = p_{atm}$ Boiling condition in steam distillation, reached below 373 K

$Na + C + N \rightarrow NaCN$ Lassaigne fusion for nitrogen

$2Na + S \rightarrow Na_2S$ Lassaigne fusion for sulphur

$Na + X \rightarrow NaX$ Lassaigne fusion for halogens

$Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3 \cdot xH_2O$ Prussian blue, which confirms nitrogen

$[Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$ Blood-red colour, which shows N and S are both present

$[Fe(CN)_5NOS]^{4-}$ Violet colour from sodium nitroprusside, which confirms sulphur

$PbS$ Black precipitate with lead acetate, which confirms sulphur

$(NH_4)_3PO_4 \cdot 12MoO_3$ Yellow precipitate, which confirms phosphorus

$AgCl$ white, $AgBr$ pale yellow, $AgI$ yellow Halogen identification after boiling the extract with $HNO_3$

$\%C = \frac{12}{44} \times \frac{m_{CO_2}}{m} \times 100$ Liebig carbon estimation

$\%H = \frac{2}{18} \times \frac{m_{H_2O}}{m} \times 100$ Liebig hydrogen estimation

$\%N = \frac{28}{22400} \times \frac{V_{STP}}{m} \times 100$ Dumas nitrogen estimation

$\%N = \frac{1.4 \times N \times V}{m}$ Kjeldahl nitrogen estimation

$\%X = \frac{X}{108 + X} \times \frac{m_{AgX}}{m} \times 100$ Carius halogen estimation

$\%S = \frac{32}{233} \times \frac{m_{BaSO_4}}{m} \times 100$ Carius sulphur estimation

$\%P = \frac{62}{222} \times \frac{m_{Mg_2P_2O_7}}{m} \times 100$ Phosphorus estimation

$n = \frac{M}{EF\ mass}$ Molecular formula = n × empirical formula

$M = 2 \times VD$ Molar mass from vapour density

Common traps

  • Assuming every nitrogen compound gives Prussian blue. Hydrazine has no carbon and diazonium salts lose $N_2$, so both give a negative test.
  • Expecting blood red whenever N and S are both present. The blood-red colour appears only when $NaSCN$ survives; excess sodium decomposes it into $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which give the separate tests.
  • Adding $AgNO_3$ directly to the extract to test for halogens. $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$ must first be destroyed by boiling with $HNO_3$, or they will precipitate as $AgCN$ and $Ag_2S$.
  • Applying Kjeldahl's method to nitrobenzene, azo compounds or pyridine. Their nitrogen is not converted to $(NH_4)_2SO_4$, so the method fails for them.
  • Using the moist gas pressure directly in Dumas calculations. Subtract the aqueous tension first, then convert to STP.
  • Rounding 1.5 or 1.33 to the nearest integer in empirical formula work. Multiply all ratios by 2 or 3 instead.
  • Thinking that a higher $R_f$ means stronger adsorption. A larger $R_f$ means weaker adsorption, so the component moves farther.
  • Confusing distillation types. Glycerol needs reduced-pressure distillation, while aniline and o-nitrophenol need steam distillation.

Quick revision

  • Sublimation purifies camphor, naphthalene, anthracene, benzoic acid and iodine.
  • Steam distillation suits steam-volatile, water-immiscible liquids (aniline, essential oils, o-nitrophenol), which distil below 373 K.
  • Fractional distillation separates close-boiling liquids, as in crude oil refining.
  • Paper chromatography is partition chromatography; TLC and column chromatography are adsorption chromatography.
  • Lassaigne's test converts N, S and X into $NaCN$, $Na_2S$ and $NaX$.
  • N gives Prussian blue; N plus S gives blood red; S gives black $PbS$ or violet with nitroprusside.
  • $AgCl$ is white and dissolves in $NH_3$; $AgBr$ is pale yellow; $AgI$ is yellow and insoluble.
  • P gives a yellow ammonium phosphomolybdate precipitate.
  • Liebig method: $CaCl_2$ absorbs water and $KOH$ absorbs $CO_2$.
  • Kjeldahl: %N = 1.4NV/m; it fails for nitro, azo and ring nitrogen.
  • Carius method: $AgX$ for halogens, $BaSO_4$ (233) for S, $Mg_2P_2O_7$ (222) for P.
  • Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, with n = M/EF mass and M = 2 × VD.

Chemistry · Unit 14: Some Basic Principles of Organic Chemistry

This unit lays the foundation of organic chemistry. It covers bonding and hybridization of carbon, classification, isomerism and IUPAC nomenclature, and the electronic effects (inductive, electromeric, resonance, hyperconjugation) that control the stability of reactive intermediates and the course of reactions. NEET asks 2-4 questions every year from it, mostly on intermediate stability, electronic effects, isomer counting and IUPAC names, and these concepts underpin every later organic chapter.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q48

Tetravalency of carbon; shapes of simple molecules and hybridization

Carbon (ground state $1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$) is tetravalent. Promotion of one 2s electron gives four half-filled orbitals, so carbon forms four covalent bonds. These orbitals mix (hybridize) to give equivalent hybrid orbitals. In $sp^3$ carbon, as in $CH_4$, there are four hybrids arranged tetrahedrally at $109^{\circ}28'$. In $sp^2$ carbon, as in $C_2H_4$, three hybrids form a trigonal planar arrangement at $120^{\circ}$ and one unhybridized p orbital forms a $\pi$ bond. In $sp$ carbon, as in $C_2H_2$, two hybrids are linear at $180^{\circ}$ and two p orbitals form two $\pi$ bonds. More s-character keeps electrons closer to the nucleus. Hence an $sp$ carbon is the most electronegative, its bonds are the shortest and strongest, and $HC\equiv CH$ is weakly acidic. Hybridization therefore fixes molecular shape, bond length, bond strength and acidity.

  • $sp^3$: 25% s-character, tetrahedral, $109^{\circ}28'$ (alkanes, $CH_3^-$ pyramidal)
  • $sp^2$: 33.3% s-character, trigonal planar, $120^{\circ}$ (alkenes, benzene, $C=O$, $CH_3^+$, $CH_3^{\bullet}$)
  • $sp$: 50% s-character, linear, $180^{\circ}$ (alkynes, $C\equiv N$, $CO_2$, allenic central carbon)
  • Electronegativity of carbon: $sp > sp^2 > sp^3$
  • Bond lengths: $C-C$ 154 pm, $C=C$ 134 pm, $C\equiv C$ 120 pm; benzene $C-C$ 139 pm
  • A $\pi$ bond forms by sideways overlap and prevents free rotation about $C=C$

Steric number $= $ number of $\sigma$ bonds $+$ number of lone pairs 4 gives $sp^3$, 3 gives $sp^2$, 2 gives $sp$; use it to assign hybridization of any atom

$\%\,s = \frac{1}{\text{number of hybrid orbitals}} \times 100$ s-character: 25% ($sp^3$), 33.3% ($sp^2$), 50% ($sp$)

NEET tip: Expect questions asking for the hybridization of each carbon in a given molecule (e.g. $CH_2=C=CH_2$, $CH_3-CH=CH-C\equiv N$) or a comparison of bond lengths and acidity based on s-character.

Classification of organic compounds by functional groups

Organic compounds are first classified by structure. Acyclic (open-chain or aliphatic) compounds have straight or branched chains. Cyclic compounds are of three kinds. Alicyclic compounds are carbocyclic rings that behave like aliphatics, e.g. cyclohexane. Aromatic compounds may be benzenoid (benzene, naphthalene) or non-benzenoid (tropolone). Heterocyclic compounds contain a ring heteroatom, e.g. furan, thiophene and pyridine. Compounds are further grouped by functional group, the atom or group that decides characteristic chemical behaviour. When a molecule contains several groups, the senior one is named as the suffix and the rest become prefixes. Knowing the functional-group seniority order is therefore essential for both classification and IUPAC naming.

  • Functional groups: $-COOH$ (acid), $-SO_3H$, $-COOR$ (ester), $-COX$ (acyl halide), $-CONH_2$ (amide), $-CN$ (nitrile), $-CHO$ (aldehyde), $>C=O$ (ketone), $-OH$ (alcohol), $-NH_2$ (amine), $-O-$ (ether)
  • Seniority: $-COOH > -SO_3H > $ anhydride $> -COOR > -COX > -CONH_2 > -CN > -CHO > >C=O > -OH > -NH_2 > C=C > C\equiv C$
  • Always-prefix groups (never suffix): $-X$ (halo), $-NO_2$ (nitro), $-OR$ (alkoxy)
  • Heterocyclic aromatic examples: furan (O), thiophene (S), pyridine (N)
  • Non-benzenoid aromatic example: tropolone

NEET tip: NEET checks the seniority order indirectly, for instance by asking which group becomes the suffix in a polyfunctional IUPAC name, or by asking you to identify alicyclic, aromatic or heterocyclic compounds.

Homologous series

A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and the same general formula. Successive members differ by one $-CH_2-$ unit, which corresponds to a molecular mass difference of 14 u. Members show very similar chemical properties because they share the functional group. Their physical properties change gradually with molecular mass: boiling point rises, while solubility in water falls along the series. All members can usually be prepared by similar general methods. Examples are alkanes ($CH_4$, $C_2H_6$, $C_3H_8$), alkenes, alkynes, alkanols and alkanoic acids. The general formula lets you check whether two compounds are homologues and also calculate the degree of unsaturation.

  • Adjacent homologues differ by $CH_2$, i.e. 14 u
  • Chemical properties are similar; physical properties show a regular gradation
  • Boiling point increases with chain length; among isomers, branching lowers it
  • Same general formula and similar methods of preparation
  • Example: $CH_3OH$, $C_2H_5OH$ and $C_3H_7OH$ are homologues

$C_nH_{2n+2}$, $C_nH_{2n}$, $C_nH_{2n-2}$ Alkanes, alkenes (also cycloalkanes), alkynes (also dienes)

$C_nH_{2n+1}OH$; $C_nH_{2n}O$; $C_nH_{2n}O_2$ Alcohols (and ethers); aldehydes and ketones; carboxylic acids and esters

$DU = \frac{2C + 2 + N - H - X}{2}$ Degree of unsaturation: number of rings plus $\pi$ bonds

NEET tip: Typical asks: pick the pair that are homologues, or calculate the mass difference between members three steps apart (3 x 14 = 42 u).

Structural and stereoisomerism

Isomers have the same molecular formula but different properties. Structural isomers differ in how atoms are connected. Chain isomers differ in the carbon skeleton (n-pentane, isopentane, neopentane). Position isomers differ in the location of a group (propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol). Functional isomers have different functional groups (ethanol and methoxymethane). Metamers differ in the alkyl groups on either side of a functional group (diethyl ether and methyl propyl ether). Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement. Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism needs restricted rotation, about a $C=C$ or in a ring, with two different groups on each restricted carbon. Optical isomerism arises from chirality, usually a carbon bearing four different groups. Such molecules have non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers) that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

  • Structural isomerism types: chain, position, functional, metamerism
  • Geometrical isomerism needs a $C=C$ with $a \neq b$ on each carbon; $CH_2=CHCl$ shows none
  • cis: like groups on the same side (higher dipole); trans: opposite sides (usually higher melting point)
  • A chiral carbon carries four different groups; enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images
  • dextro (+) rotates light clockwise, laevo (-) anticlockwise; an equimolar mixture is a racemic mixture (optically inactive)
  • $C_4H_{10}$ has 2 isomers, $C_5H_{12}$ has 3, $C_4H_{10}O$ has 7 (4 alcohols and 3 ethers)

Number of stereoisomers $= 2^n$ $n$ = number of stereocentres in an unsymmetrical molecule; symmetric molecules give fewer because meso forms appear

Geometrical isomers $= 2^n$ $n$ = number of stereogenic double bonds in an unsymmetrical polyene

NEET tip: NEET asks you to name the type of isomerism shown by a given pair, count structural isomers for a formula, or spot which compound shows geometrical or optical isomerism.

Nomenclature: trivial and IUPAC

Trivial names usually reflect a compound's source: formic acid comes from ants (Latin formica), acetic acid from vinegar (acetum), and methane was called marsh gas. IUPAC names are built as prefix, then word root, then primary suffix, then secondary suffix. The word root gives the number of carbons (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct, non, dec). The primary suffix gives saturation (ane, ene, yne). The secondary suffix shows the principal functional group. The rules are applied in order. First, select the longest chain that contains the principal group and the maximum number of multiple bonds. Second, number the chain so that the principal group, then the multiple bonds, then the substituents get the lowest locants. Third, write substituent prefixes in alphabetical order, ignoring di, tri, sec and tert but counting iso and neo.

  • Lowest locant rule: compare locant sets at the first point of difference
  • If ene and yne tie in position, the double bond gets the lower number; in the name, ene is written before yne
  • Multiplying prefixes di, tri and tetra are ignored when alphabetising
  • Example: $CH_3CH(CH_3)CH_2CH_3$ is 2-methylbutane
  • Example: $CH_2=CH-CH_2-OH$ is prop-2-en-1-ol
  • Benzene derivatives: ortho = 1,2, meta = 1,3, para = 1,4
  • Carbon of $-CHO$, $-COOH$ or $-CN$ is C-1 when such a group is the principal group

Name $=$ prefix(es) $+$ word root $+$ primary suffix $+$ secondary suffix Template for assembling any IUPAC name

NEET tip: The usual NEET question gives a branched or polyfunctional structure (often with a $C=C$ or a ring) and asks for the correct IUPAC name; the distractors break the locant or alphabetical rules.

Homolytic and heterolytic bond fission

A covalent bond can break in two ways. In homolytic fission, each atom takes one electron of the shared pair, giving neutral free radicals. Homolysis is favoured by heat, UV light and peroxides, and by non-polar solvents or the gas phase; electrons are shown moving with half-headed (fish-hook) arrows. In heterolytic fission, the more electronegative atom takes both electrons, giving a cation and an anion. Heterolysis is favoured by polar solvents and a large electronegativity difference; electrons move as a pair, shown by full arrows. Heterolysis of a carbon bond gives a carbocation or a carbanion. These modes of fission produce the reactive intermediates that drive free-radical and polar (ionic) reactions respectively.

  • Homolysis gives free radicals; it occurs in free-radical (homopolar) reactions
  • Heterolysis gives ions; it occurs in polar (ionic) reactions
  • A fish-hook arrow shows one-electron movement; a full arrow shows two-electron movement
  • In heterolysis the more electronegative atom keeps the bonding pair
  • Example: $Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2Cl^{\bullet}$ is homolysis; $(CH_3)_3C-Br \rightarrow (CH_3)_3C^+ + Br^-$ is heterolysis

$A-B \rightarrow A^{\bullet} + B^{\bullet}$ Homolytic fission

$A-B \rightarrow A^+ + :B^-$ Heterolytic fission when $B$ is more electronegative

NEET tip: NEET asks which conditions favour homolysis, or which intermediate a given fission produces.

Free radicals, carbocations and carbanions; their stability

Free radicals, carbocations and carbanions are short-lived intermediates. A carbon free radical has 7 valence electrons, is roughly $sp^2$ and planar, and its stability order is $3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ} > CH_3^{\bullet}$, with benzyl and allyl radicals extra-stable through resonance. A carbocation has 6 valence electrons, is $sp^2$ and planar with an empty p orbital, and is electron-deficient. Any factor that supplies electron density stabilises it: +I effect, hyperconjugation and resonance. Its order is $3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ} > CH_3^+$, and benzylic and allylic cations are strongly stabilised. A carbanion has 8 valence electrons, is $sp^3$ and pyramidal, and has a lone pair. Electron-withdrawing groups (-I, -R) stabilise it, so its order is reversed: $CH_3^- > 1^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 3^{\circ}$. Carbanions conjugated with $\pi$ systems become $sp^2$ and are stabilised by resonance.

  • Carbocation: $sp^2$, planar, 6 electrons, electrophilic; can rearrange by 1,2-hydride or methyl shift
  • Stability: $(C_6H_5)_3C^+ > (C_6H_5)_2CH^+ > C_6H_5CH_2^+ \approx CH_2=CHCH_2^+ \approx 3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ} > CH_3^+$
  • Vinyl ($CH_2=CH^+$) and phenyl cations are very unstable because the positive charge sits on an $sp^2$ or $sp$-like carbon and there is no resonance
  • Carbanion: $sp^3$, pyramidal, 8 electrons, nucleophilic; stability $CH_3^- > 1^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 3^{\circ}$
  • Free radical: 7 electrons, neutral, paramagnetic; stability $3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ} > CH_3^{\bullet}$
  • In a benzylic or allylic carbocation, the empty p orbital overlaps the adjacent filled $\pi$ system (resonance); hyperconjugation with filled $\alpha$ $C-H$ $\sigma$ orbitals stabilises alkyl-substituted carbocations, e.g. $(CH_3)_3C^+$ with 9 $\alpha$-H, and a substituted benzylic or allylic cation carrying $\alpha$-H on an alkyl group can benefit from both

Carbocation stability $\propto$ electron donation $(+I, +R$, number of $\alpha$-H$)$ Quick rule for ranking carbocations

Carbanion stability $\propto$ electron withdrawal $(-I, -R)$ Quick rule for ranking carbanions (opposite trend)

NEET tip: The single most tested idea: rank carbocations, radicals or carbanions, or identify which orbital interactions (filled $\sigma$ or $\pi$ with an empty p) stabilise a given intermediate.

Electrophiles and nucleophiles

An electrophile ('electron-loving') is an electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid. It attacks electron-rich centres. Electrophiles may be positive, such as $H^+$, $NO_2^+$, $Br^+$, $Cl^+$ and carbocations. They may also be neutral, such as $BF_3$, $AlCl_3$, $FeCl_3$ and $SO_3$, or the carbonyl carbon. A nucleophile ('nucleus-loving') is an electron-rich species that donates an electron pair, so it is a Lewis base. It attacks electron-deficient centres. Nucleophiles may be negative, such as $OH^-$, $CN^-$, $Cl^-$, $RO^-$ and carbanions. They may also be neutral with a lone pair or $\pi$ electrons, such as $H_2O$, $NH_3$, $ROH$ and $R_3N$. Polar reactions are described as a nucleophile attacking an electrophilic centre, with curved arrows starting from the electron pair.

  • Electrophiles are Lewis acids; nucleophiles are Lewis bases
  • Neutral electrophiles: $BF_3$, $AlCl_3$, $SO_3$, $:CCl_2$ (dichlorocarbene)
  • Neutral nucleophiles: $H_2O$, $NH_3$, $ROH$, $RNH_2$
  • Ambident nucleophiles have two donor sites, e.g. $CN^-$ (C or N) and $NO_2^-$ (N or O)
  • Carbonyl carbon is electrophilic and carbonyl oxygen is nucleophilic
  • A curved arrow always starts at the electron source (nucleophile) and points to the electron sink

NEET tip: Questions ask you to classify a list of species as electrophiles or nucleophiles, especially neutral ones like $BF_3$, $AlCl_3$, $NH_3$ or $H_2O$.

Inductive effect, electromeric effect, resonance and hyperconjugation

The inductive effect is a permanent polarisation transmitted along a $\sigma$ chain. It fades rapidly with distance and is almost negligible beyond three bonds. Groups that withdraw electrons show -I (e.g. $-NO_2$, $-CN$, halogens), and alkyl groups that push electrons show +I. The electromeric effect is temporary. It is a complete shift of $\pi$ electrons in a multiple bond, occurs only when an attacking reagent is present, and disappears when the reagent is removed. Resonance is delocalisation of $\pi$ electrons or lone pairs, shown by contributing structures whose weighted average is the resonance hybrid. The hybrid is more stable than any single contributor. Hyperconjugation ('no-bond resonance') is delocalisation of $\sigma$ electrons of an $\alpha$ $C-H$ bond into an adjacent empty p orbital or $\pi$ system. It stabilises carbocations, free radicals and alkenes.

  • -I order: $-NO_2 > -CN > -COOH > -F > -Cl > -Br > -I > -OCH_3 > -C_6H_5$
  • +I order: $(CH_3)_3C- > (CH_3)_2CH- > CH_3CH_2- > CH_3-$
  • +E effect: electrons move toward the attacking electrophile (e.g. $H^+$ adding to an alkene); -E effect: electrons move away from the attacking nucleophile (e.g. $CN^-$ adding to $C=O$)
  • +R groups donate a lone pair to the ring: $-OH$, $-OR$, $-NH_2$, $-NHCOCH_3$, $-X$; -R groups withdraw: $-NO_2$, $-CN$, $-CHO$, $-COR$, $-COOH$
  • Favoured contributors: more covalent bonds, complete octets, least charge separation, negative charge on the more electronegative atom
  • Hyperconjugation is greater with more $\alpha$-H, so it is strongest for $-CH_3$ and absent for $-C(CH_3)_3$ (Baker-Nathan order)
  • Alkene stability rises with the number of $\alpha$-H: $(CH_3)_2C=C(CH_3)_2$ is the most stable

Resonance energy $= E_{\text{most stable contributor}} - E_{\text{actual hybrid}}$ Extra stability gained from delocalisation; about 150 kJ/mol for benzene

Number of hyperconjugative structures $=$ number of $\alpha$-H atoms Compare the extent of hyperconjugation in carbocations, radicals and alkenes

NEET tip: NEET asks you to name the effect responsible for a stability or acidity trend, count $\alpha$-H for hyperconjugation, or pick the most stable resonance contributor.

Types of organic reactions: substitution, addition, elimination and rearrangement

Organic reactions fall into four broad types. In substitution, one atom or group replaces another. Examples are free-radical chlorination of methane, nucleophilic substitution ($S_N1$, $S_N2$) in alkyl halides, and electrophilic substitution in benzene. In addition, a reagent adds across a multiple bond, so the product contains all atoms of both reactants. Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition (Markovnikov orientation), and carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition. In elimination, atoms or groups are lost from adjacent carbons to form a multiple bond, as in dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic $KOH$ or dehydration of alcohols with concentrated $H_2SO_4$. The more substituted alkene is the major product (Saytzeff rule). In rearrangement, atoms or groups migrate within a molecule to give a structural isomer, often via a carbocation shifting to a more stable form.

  • Substitution: free radical (alkanes, $h\nu$), nucleophilic (alkyl halides), electrophilic (arenes)
  • Addition: electrophilic to $C=C$ (Markovnikov rule), nucleophilic to $C=O$
  • Elimination: $\beta$-elimination gives the more substituted alkene as the major product (Saytzeff rule)
  • Rearrangement: 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shift converts $1^{\circ}$ or $2^{\circ}$ carbocations to more stable ones
  • Addition and elimination are reverse processes; a rearranged product has the same molecular formula as the starting material

$CH_4 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} CH_3Cl + HCl$ Free-radical substitution

$CH_3CH=CH_2 + HBr \rightarrow CH_3CHBrCH_3$ Electrophilic addition (Markovnikov)

$CH_3CH_2Br + KOH(alc) \rightarrow CH_2=CH_2 + KBr + H_2O$ Elimination (dehydrohalogenation)

$CH_3CH_2Br + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow CH_3CH_2OH + Br^-$ Nucleophilic substitution

NEET tip: NEET gives a reaction and asks you to classify it, or predict a product where a carbocation rearrangement or Markovnikov or Saytzeff orientation decides the answer.

Formula sheet

$sp^3$: $109^{\circ}28'$; $sp^2$: $120^{\circ}$; $sp$: $180^{\circ}$ Bond angles from hybridization

$\%\,s$: $sp^3 = 25$, $sp^2 = 33.3$, $sp = 50$ s-character; electronegativity and acidity of $C-H$ rise with it

$C-C$ 154 pm $> C=C$ 134 pm $> C\equiv C$ 120 pm Bond lengths; benzene $C-C$ = 139 pm (resonance)

$DU = \frac{2C + 2 + N - H - X}{2}$ Degree of unsaturation (rings plus $\pi$ bonds)

$C_nH_{2n+2}$, $C_nH_{2n}$, $C_nH_{2n-2}$ General formulas of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes

Homologues differ by $CH_2$ = 14 u Homologous series

Stereoisomers $= 2^n$ $n$ = stereocentres (unsymmetrical molecule)

$-COOH > -SO_3H > -COOR > -COX > -CONH_2 > -CN > -CHO > >C=O > -OH > -NH_2$ Functional group priority in IUPAC naming

$A-B \rightarrow A^{\bullet} + B^{\bullet}$; $A-B \rightarrow A^+ + B^-$ Homolytic and heterolytic fission

$3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ} > CH_3$ Stability of carbocations and free radicals

$CH_3^- > 1^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 3^{\circ}$ Stability of carbanions

$(C_6H_5)_3C^+ > (C_6H_5)_2CH^+ > C_6H_5CH_2^+$ Resonance-stabilised carbocations

$-NO_2 > -CN > -COOH > -F > -Cl > -Br > -I$ -I effect order

$(CH_3)_3C- > (CH_3)_2CH- > C_2H_5- > CH_3-$ +I effect order

$-CH_3 > -CH_2CH_3 > -CH(CH_3)_2 > -C(CH_3)_3$ Hyperconjugation (Baker-Nathan) order, set by the number of $\alpha$-H

Hyperconjugative structures $=$ number of $\alpha$-H Extent of hyperconjugation

Resonance energy $= E_{\text{contributor}} - E_{\text{hybrid}}$ Stabilisation by delocalisation

Markovnikov rule In $HX$ addition to an unsymmetrical alkene, $H$ adds to the carbon with more H (via the more stable carbocation)

Saytzeff rule In elimination, the more substituted alkene is the major product

$CH_4 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} CH_3Cl + HCl$ Free-radical substitution

Common traps

  • Applying the carbocation order to carbanions: carbanion stability is reversed ($CH_3^- > 1^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 3^{\circ}$) because alkyl +I groups destabilise a negative charge.
  • Counting all H atoms for hyperconjugation: only H atoms on carbons directly attached to the positive, radical or $sp^2$ centre ($\alpha$-H) count; $(CH_3)_3C^+$ has 9.
  • Treating the inductive effect as temporary: inductive is permanent and acts through $\sigma$ bonds, whereas the electromeric effect is temporary and needs an attacking reagent.
  • Believing resonance structures interconvert or exist separately: only the hybrid is real, and it is more stable than every contributor.
  • Calling all carbanions $sp^3$: benzylic or allylic carbanions become $sp^2$ to delocalise the lone pair.
  • Thinking a vinyl cation is as stable as an allyl cation: in a vinyl cation the charge is on the double-bond carbon with no resonance stabilisation, so it is very unstable.
  • Alphabetising with multiplying prefixes: di, tri, sec and tert are ignored, but iso and neo are counted (e.g. ethyl before dimethyl).
  • Assuming every alkene shows cis-trans isomerism: each doubly bonded carbon must carry two different groups, so $CH_3CH=CH_2$ shows none.

Quick revision

  • Carbon is tetravalent; hybridization $sp^3$, $sp^2$, $sp$ gives tetrahedral, trigonal and linear shapes.
  • More s-character means more electronegative carbon, shorter bonds and more acidic $C-H$.
  • Homologues differ by $CH_2$ (14 u) and share the general formula and chemical properties.
  • Structural isomerism includes chain, position, functional and metamerism; stereoisomerism includes geometrical and optical.
  • In IUPAC naming, the principal group gets the lowest locant, then multiple bonds, then substituents (alphabetical order).
  • Homolysis (light, heat, peroxide) gives radicals; heterolysis (polar solvent) gives ions.
  • Carbocation and radical stability is $3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ} > CH_3$; carbanion stability is the reverse.
  • Benzylic and allylic intermediates are stabilised by resonance; alkyl-substituted ones by +I and hyperconjugation.
  • Electrophiles are Lewis acids ($BF_3$, $NO_2^+$); nucleophiles are Lewis bases ($NH_3$, $OH^-$, $H_2O$).
  • The inductive effect is permanent and distance-dependent; the electromeric effect is temporary and reagent-dependent.
  • Hyperconjugation is no-bond resonance of an $\alpha$ $C-H$ $\sigma$ bond with an empty p orbital or $\pi$ system; more $\alpha$-H gives more stability.
  • Reaction types are substitution, addition (Markovnikov), elimination (Saytzeff) and rearrangement (hydride or methyl shift).

Chemistry · Unit 15: Hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons is the foundation of organic chemistry. It covers the classification, nomenclature, preparation and reactions of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and benzene, with emphasis on reaction mechanisms and stereochemistry. NEET regularly asks about stereochemical outcomes (syn vs anti addition, cis/trans), Markovnikov vs anti-Markovnikov products, conjugation, ozonolysis-based structure deduction, acidity of alkynes and directive effects in benzene, so precise mechanistic understanding scores directly.

PYQs (3): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q76, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q77, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q83

Classification, isomerism and IUPAC nomenclature

Hydrocarbons contain only C and H. They are classified as open-chain (aliphatic) or cyclic. Aliphatic hydrocarbons are saturated (alkanes, $C_nH_{2n+2}$) or unsaturated (alkenes $C_nH_{2n}$, alkynes $C_nH_{2n-2}$). Cyclic hydrocarbons are alicyclic (e.g. cyclohexane) or aromatic (benzenoid). Alkanes show chain isomerism from $C_4$ onwards. Alkenes and alkynes also show position isomerism, and alkenes show geometrical isomerism. IUPAC naming follows these rules: choose the longest chain containing the maximum number of multiple bonds, give the multiple bonds the lowest locants, then cite substituents alphabetically. If a double and a triple bond would get equal locants, the double bond gets the lower number. Dienes are classified by the spacing of their double bonds. In conjugated dienes the double bonds alternate with one single bond (1,3-type). In isolated dienes they are separated by two or more single bonds (1,4-type and beyond). Cumulated dienes (allenes) have adjacent double bonds.

  • Number of structural isomers: $C_4H_{10}$ = 2, $C_5H_{12}$ = 3, $C_6H_{14}$ = 5
  • Conjugated diene: $C=C-C=C$ pattern, e.g. buta-1,3-diene, hepta-1,3-diene
  • Hepta-1,4-, 1,5- and 1,6-dienes are isolated (non-conjugated)
  • Suffixes: -ane, -ene, -yne; for both double and triple bonds use -en-yne, e.g. pent-1-en-4-yne
  • Alicyclic compounds behave like aliphatic ones; aromatic compounds follow Huckel's rule

$DU = \frac{2C + 2 + N - H - X}{2}$ Degree of unsaturation (rings + $\pi$ bonds) from a molecular formula

$C_nH_{2n+2},\ C_nH_{2n},\ C_nH_{2n-2}$ General formulas of alkanes, alkenes (or cycloalkanes) and alkynes (or dienes)

NEET tip: Expect conjugated vs isolated diene identification, isomer counting, and IUPAC naming of branched or en-yne compounds.

General methods of preparation, properties and reactions

Alkanes are prepared in four main ways. Catalytic hydrogenation of alkenes or alkynes uses $Pt$, $Pd$ or $Ni$. Alkyl halides can be reduced with $Zn/H^+$. The Wurtz reaction ($2RX + 2Na$ in dry ether) gives symmetrical alkanes with an even number of carbons. Decarboxylation of sodium carboxylates with soda lime gives an alkane with one carbon fewer, while Kolbe's electrolysis gives $R-R$. Physically, boiling point rises with molecular mass and falls with branching. Alkanes undergo substitution, combustion, controlled oxidation, isomerisation, aromatisation and pyrolysis. Alkenes are prepared by partial reduction of alkynes, by dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic $KOH$ (Saytzeff product), by dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides with $Zn$, and by acidic dehydration of alcohols. Ethyne is made from $CaC_2$ and water, or from vicinal dihalides by double dehydrohalogenation. Oxidation of alkenes is also important. Cold, dilute alkaline $KMnO_4$ (Baeyer's reagent) gives a vicinal diol by syn addition. Hot acidic $KMnO_4$ cleaves the double bond to give ketones or acids.

  • Wurtz reaction is unsuitable for odd-carbon alkanes (it gives a mixture); methane cannot be made by it
  • Soda lime decarboxylation: $RCOONa + NaOH \xrightarrow{CaO,\ \Delta} RH + Na_2CO_3$
  • Aromatisation: n-hexane gives benzene with $Cr_2O_3/V_2O_5/Mo_2O_3$ at 773 K and 10-20 atm
  • Dehydrohalogenation follows Saytzeff's rule: the more substituted alkene is the major product
  • Baeyer's reagent is decolourised by alkenes; a cis alkene gives the meso diol and a trans alkene gives the racemic diol
  • Isomerisation: n-alkanes give branched alkanes with anhydrous $AlCl_3/HCl$

$2RX + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} R-R + 2NaX$ Wurtz reaction; doubles the carbon chain

$CaC_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow C_2H_2 + Ca(OH)_2$ Laboratory/industrial preparation of ethyne

$C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{conc.\ H_2SO_4,\ 443\ K} CH_2=CH_2 + H_2O$ Acidic dehydration of alcohol to an alkene

$C_nH_{2n+2} + \frac{3n+1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow nCO_2 + (n+1)H_2O$ Complete combustion of an alkane

NEET tip: NEET tests reagent-product matching (Wurtz, soda lime, Kolbe, Lindlar, Baeyer's) and boiling-point order among isomeric alkanes.

Alkanes: conformations, Sawhorse and Newman projections of ethane

Free rotation about the $C-C$ sigma bond in ethane produces infinitely many spatial arrangements called conformations. The two extremes are staggered (dihedral angle 60 degrees, hydrogens farthest apart, minimum energy) and eclipsed (dihedral angle 0 degrees, maximum torsional strain). All other arrangements are skew forms. The energy difference in ethane is only about 12.5 kJ/mol, so the conformers interconvert rapidly at room temperature and cannot be isolated. In a Sawhorse projection the $C-C$ bond is drawn as a slanted line, with the front carbon at the lower left and the rear carbon at the upper right. In a Newman projection the molecule is viewed along the $C-C$ bond. The front carbon is a point with three bonds radiating from it, and the rear carbon is a circle with bonds emerging from its edge. Torsional strain arises from repulsion between the electron clouds of bonds on adjacent carbons.

  • Stability order: staggered > skew > eclipsed
  • Conformers have the same bond lengths and bond angles; they differ only in rotation about the sigma bond
  • Conformers are not separable; the rotational barrier is about 12.5 kJ/mol for ethane
  • Newman projection: front carbon is a dot, rear carbon is a circle
  • Rotating one carbon by 60 degrees interconverts the staggered and eclipsed forms

$\Delta E_{eclipsed - staggered} \approx 12.5\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ Torsional energy barrier in ethane

NEET tip: Questions ask which conformation is more stable, or to read Newman projections to identify relative positions of groups (often mixed with stereochemistry of addition products).

Mechanism of halogenation of alkanes

Halogenation of alkanes in diffused sunlight, UV light or at high temperature proceeds by a free radical chain mechanism with three steps. In initiation, homolysis of $Cl-Cl$ (the weaker bond compared with $C-H$) produces chlorine free radicals. In propagation, $Cl^\bullet$ abstracts a hydrogen from methane to form $CH_3^\bullet$ and $HCl$. The methyl radical then attacks $Cl_2$ to give $CH_3Cl$ and regenerate $Cl^\bullet$, which continues the chain. In termination, any two radicals combine, for example $CH_3^\bullet + CH_3^\bullet \rightarrow C_2H_6$. Formation of ethane as a by-product supports the radical mechanism. With excess chlorine the reaction continues to $CH_2Cl_2$, $CHCl_3$ and $CCl_4$. Reactivity of halogens is $F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2$. Fluorination is explosive, and iodination is reversible, so it needs an oxidant such as $HIO_3$ or $HNO_3$.

  • Ease of hydrogen abstraction: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > CH_4$, because radical stability follows the same order
  • Bromination is more selective than chlorination
  • Ethane formed during chlorination of methane is evidence for the free radical mechanism
  • Excess halogen leads to polyhalogenation

$Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2Cl^\bullet$ Initiation by homolytic fission

$CH_4 + Cl^\bullet \rightarrow CH_3^\bullet + HCl;\ CH_3^\bullet + Cl_2 \rightarrow CH_3Cl + Cl^\bullet$ Chain propagation steps

$CH_4 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons CH_3I + HI;\ 5HI + HIO_3 \rightarrow 3I_2 + 3H_2O$ Iodination is reversible; an oxidant removes HI

NEET tip: NEET asks to identify initiation, propagation or termination steps, the by-product ethane, and the relative reactivity of halogens or of $1^\circ/2^\circ/3^\circ$ hydrogens.

Alkenes: geometrical isomerism

The $C=C$ double bond (one sigma and one pi bond) does not allow free rotation, because rotation would break pi overlap. Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism therefore arises when each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups. In the cis isomer, similar groups lie on the same side; in the trans isomer, they lie on opposite sides. For example, but-2-ene exists as cis and trans forms, whereas but-1-ene and propene do not, because one carbon carries two hydrogens. Cis isomers are generally more polar and have higher boiling points. For example, cis-but-2-ene boils at about 277 K and trans-but-2-ene at about 274 K, and trans-but-2-ene has zero dipole moment. Trans isomers pack better in the crystal lattice and usually have higher melting points. Geometrical isomers are diastereomers with different physical and chemical properties.

  • Condition: $abC=Cab$ or $abC=Cde$ type, i.e. $a \neq b$ on each carbon
  • Cis: higher dipole moment and higher boiling point; trans: higher melting point and greater stability
  • trans-But-2-ene and trans-1,2-dichloroethene have zero dipole moment
  • Lindlar's catalyst gives the cis alkene; $Na$/liquid $NH_3$ gives the trans alkene
  • Interconversion requires breaking the pi bond (heat or light)

NEET tip: Identify which alkene shows cis-trans isomerism, compare dipole moments or boiling points, and relate alkyne reduction method to cis or trans product.

Mechanism of electrophilic addition: hydrogen, halogens, water and hydrogen halides

Pi electrons make alkenes nucleophilic, so they undergo electrophilic addition. Hydrogen adds in the presence of $Pt$, $Pd$ or $Ni$ on the metal surface by syn addition to give the alkane. Halogens add through a cyclic halonium ion; the halide ion then attacks from the opposite face, so the overall addition is anti. Decolourisation of red-brown $Br_2$ in $CCl_4$ is a test for unsaturation. Anti addition means trans-but-2-ene gives meso-2,3-dibromobutane, while cis-but-2-ene gives racemic (±)-2,3-dibromobutane. Hydrogen halides add in two steps. $H^+$ adds first to form the more stable carbocation (the rate-determining step), and then $X^-$ attacks. Reactivity is $HI > HBr > HCl$. Water adds only in the presence of an acid catalyst (dilute $H_2SO_4$). Protonation forms a carbocation, water attacks, and deprotonation gives an alcohol with Markovnikov orientation. Rearrangement of the carbocation is possible.

  • Halogen addition is anti (via a bromonium ion); catalytic hydrogenation and $KMnO_4$ dihydroxylation are syn
  • trans-alkene + anti addition gives the meso product; cis-alkene + anti addition gives the racemic product
  • HX reactivity: $HI > HBr > HCl > HF$ (follows bond weakness)
  • Carbocation intermediates may undergo hydride or methyl shifts to more stable cations
  • Acid-catalysed hydration gives the Markovnikov alcohol (OH on the more substituted carbon); unsymmetrical alkenes usually give $2^\circ$ or $3^\circ$ alcohols, but ethene gives ethanol ($1^\circ$)

$CH_2=CH_2 + Br_2 \xrightarrow{CCl_4} BrCH_2CH_2Br$ Bromine water / $Br_2$ in $CCl_4$ test for unsaturation (anti addition)

$CH_3CH=CH_2 + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} CH_3CH(OH)CH_3$ Acid-catalysed hydration (Markovnikov)

$RCH=CH_2 + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pt/Pd/Ni} RCH_2CH_3$ Catalytic hydrogenation (syn)

NEET tip: Statement-type questions test stereochemistry of $Br_2$ addition (meso vs racemic) via Newman or Fischer projections; know syn vs anti for each reagent.

Markownikoff's rule and peroxide effect

Markovnikov's rule states that when an unsymmetrical reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part goes to the carbon carrying fewer hydrogens. The rule follows from carbocation stability ($3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$; benzylic and allylic cations are especially stable). For example, propene with $HBr$ gives 2-bromopropane. In the presence of peroxides such as benzoyl peroxide, $HBr$ adds in the anti-Markovnikov manner (peroxide or Kharasch effect) by a free radical mechanism. The peroxide forms radicals, which generate $Br^\bullet$ from $HBr$. $Br^\bullet$ adds to the terminal carbon to give the more stable carbon radical, which then abstracts $H$ from $HBr$. Propene therefore gives 1-bromopropane. The peroxide effect is shown only by $HBr$. The $H-Cl$ bond is too strong to be cleaved by radicals. With $HI$, the weak $H-I$ bond breaks easily, but iodine radicals combine to form $I_2$ instead of adding to the double bond.

  • Markovnikov orientation is controlled by carbocation stability; anti-Markovnikov orientation by radical stability
  • Peroxide effect: only $HBr$, not $HCl$ or $HI$
  • In both cases the more stable intermediate forms; only the attacking species differs ($H^+$ vs $Br^\bullet$)
  • For $Ph-CH=CH-CH_3$, $HBr$ puts Br on the benzylic carbon, while $HBr$/peroxide puts Br on the carbon next to $CH_3$
  • Symmetrical alkenes give the same product either way

$CH_3CH=CH_2 + HBr \rightarrow CH_3CHBrCH_3$ Markovnikov addition (ionic)

$CH_3CH=CH_2 + HBr \xrightarrow{(C_6H_5CO)_2O_2} CH_3CH_2CH_2Br$ Anti-Markovnikov addition (Kharasch/peroxide effect)

$(C_6H_5COO)_2 \rightarrow 2C_6H_5COO^\bullet \rightarrow 2C_6H_5^\bullet + 2CO_2$ Radical generation from benzoyl peroxide

NEET tip: Multi-step sequences combine alkyne reduction with HBr or HBr/peroxide; decide the product from the stability of the intermediate, then classify the products as position or stereo isomers.

Ozonolysis and polymerization of alkenes

Ozonolysis is the addition of ozone to an alkene to form an ozonide, followed by cleavage with $Zn$/$H_2O$ to give aldehydes and/or ketones. Each $C=C$ is replaced by two $C=O$ groups. This makes ozonolysis a tool for locating the double bond: join the carbonyl carbons of the products back with a double bond to rebuild the alkene. $Zn$ dust prevents the $H_2O_2$ formed from oxidising aldehydes to acids. For example, propene gives methanal and ethanal, and but-2-ene gives two molecules of ethanal. Polymerization is the joining of many alkene molecules under high temperature, high pressure and a catalyst or initiator. Ethene gives polythene, used for polythene bags and films. Propene gives polypropene, used for pipes, toys and bottles.

  • Terminal $=CH_2$ gives $HCHO$; internal $=CHR$ gives an aldehyde $RCHO$; $=CR_2$ gives a ketone
  • A symmetrical alkene gives one carbonyl product only
  • Number of carbons is conserved overall in reductive ozonolysis
  • Polymerisation of ethene uses high T and P with a trace of $O_2$ or peroxide initiator, or Ziegler-Natta catalyst
  • Polymers of alkenes are addition polymers; the monomer formula equals the repeat unit

$CH_3CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{(i)\ O_3\ (ii)\ Zn/H_2O} CH_3CHO + HCHO$ Reductive ozonolysis of propene

$n\,CH_2=CH_2 \xrightarrow{high\ T,\ P,\ catalyst} \left(CH_2-CH_2\right)_n$ Polymerisation of ethene to polythene

$n\,CH_3CH=CH_2 \rightarrow \left(CH(CH_3)-CH_2\right)_n$ Polypropene formation

NEET tip: Given ozonolysis products, deduce the alkene (or vice versa), including dienes giving dicarbonyl compounds.

Alkynes: acidic character, addition reactions and polymerization

In terminal alkynes, the hydrogen on the sp carbon (50% s character) is acidic, because the conjugate base carbanion is held close to the nucleus. Ethyne therefore reacts with $Na$ to form sodium acetylide and liberate $H_2$, and with $NaNH_2$ to form sodium acetylide and $NH_3$, which alkenes and alkanes cannot do. Terminal alkynes also give a white precipitate with ammoniacal $AgNO_3$ and a red precipitate with ammoniacal $Cu_2Cl_2$. Internal alkynes have no acidic hydrogen. Alkynes undergo addition reactions in which two molecules of reagent can add. They take up $H_2$ (Lindlar's catalyst gives a cis alkene, $Na$/liquid $NH_3$ gives a trans alkene, and $Pt$/$Ni$ goes all the way to the alkane). They decolourise $Br_2$ and add $HX$ by Markovnikov's rule to give gem-dihalides. Hydration with $HgSO_4$/dil. $H_2SO_4$ at 333 K proceeds via an enol to give a carbonyl compound. Linear polymerisation of ethyne gives polyacetylene, a conducting polymer. Cyclic polymerisation (red-hot iron tube, 873 K) gives benzene.

  • Acidity: $HC\equiv CH > H_2C=CH_2 > H_3C-CH_3$
  • Among alkynes: $HC\equiv CH > CH_3C\equiv CH \gg CH_3C\equiv CCH_3$ (no acidic H)
  • Hydration of ethyne gives ethanal; all other alkynes give ketones (propyne gives propanone)
  • Alkynes are less reactive than alkenes toward electrophilic addition, because the vinylic cation is less stable
  • 3 molecules of $HC\equiv CH$ give benzene (cyclic trimerisation)

$HC\equiv CH + NaNH_2 \rightarrow HC\equiv C^-Na^+ + NH_3$ Acidic nature of terminal alkyne

$HC\equiv CH + H_2O \xrightarrow{Hg^{2+},\ H_2SO_4,\ 333\ K} CH_3CHO$ Hydration of alkyne via enol tautomerism

$3HC\equiv CH \xrightarrow{red\ hot\ Fe\ tube,\ 873\ K} C_6H_6$ Cyclic polymerisation to benzene

$CH_3C\equiv CH + 2HBr \rightarrow CH_3CBr_2CH_3$ Markovnikov addition giving gem-dihalide

NEET tip: Typical questions: acidity order based on s-character, which alkyne reacts with $NaNH_2$ or ammoniacal $AgNO_3$, and the product of hydration or partial reduction.

Benzene: structure and aromaticity

Benzene, $C_6H_6$, was proposed by Kekulé as a cyclic structure with alternating single and double bonds. Its true structure is a resonance hybrid of two Kekulé forms. All six carbons are $sp^2$ hybridised and lie in a planar regular hexagon, with all $C-C$ bonds equal at 139 pm (between $C-C$ 154 pm and $C=C$ 134 pm). The unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form a delocalised cloud of six pi electrons above and below the ring. This delocalisation gives extra stability (resonance energy), so benzene prefers substitution over addition despite its high unsaturation. Aromaticity is defined by Huckel's rule. A compound is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated, and has $(4n+2)$ pi electrons ($n$ = 0, 1, 2...). Examples are benzene (6), naphthalene (10), the cyclopentadienyl anion and the tropylium cation (6 each).

  • All $C-C$ bonds in benzene are 139 pm; bond angle is 120 degrees
  • Benzene shows no isomeric 1,2-disubstituted forms, consistent with resonance
  • Huckel: $4n+2$ pi electrons with $n = 1$ gives 6 (benzene)
  • Cyclooctatetraene (8 pi electrons, non-planar tub shape) is not aromatic
  • Cyclopentadiene (with an $sp^3$ carbon) is not aromatic, but its anion is

$\pi\ electrons = 4n + 2$ Huckel's rule for aromaticity (planar, cyclic, fully conjugated)

NEET tip: NEET asks which species is aromatic, why benzene prefers substitution, and the $C-C$ bond length or hybridisation in benzene.

Electrophilic substitution: halogenation and nitration

Benzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution in three steps. First, an electrophile is generated, usually with the help of a Lewis or Brønsted acid. Second, the electrophile attacks the pi system to form a resonance-stabilised arenium ion (sigma complex), in which one carbon becomes $sp^3$. This step is slow and rate determining because aromaticity is temporarily lost. Third, a proton is removed by a base such as $AlCl_4^-$ or $HSO_4^-$, restoring aromaticity. In halogenation, benzene reacts with $Cl_2$ or $Br_2$ in the presence of anhydrous $FeCl_3$, $FeBr_3$ or $AlCl_3$ in the dark to give halobenzene. The Lewis acid polarises the halogen to generate $Cl^+$. In nitration, benzene is heated with the nitrating mixture (conc. $HNO_3$ + conc. $H_2SO_4$) at 323-333 K. $H_2SO_4$ protonates $HNO_3$, which loses water to give the nitronium ion $NO_2^+$, the electrophile. The product is nitrobenzene.

  • The arenium ion (sigma complex) is a carbocation and is non-aromatic
  • Halogenation needs a Lewis acid; in UV light benzene instead adds $Cl_2$
  • Nitronium ion $NO_2^+$ is the electrophile in nitration; $H_2SO_4$ acts as an acid
  • Excess nitrating mixture at higher temperature gives m-dinitrobenzene
  • Anhydrous conditions are essential for halogenation

$Cl_2 + AlCl_3 \rightarrow Cl^+ + AlCl_4^-$ Generation of chloronium electrophile

$HNO_3 + 2H_2SO_4 \rightleftharpoons NO_2^+ + H_3O^+ + 2HSO_4^-$ Formation of nitronium ion

$C_6H_6 + HNO_3 \xrightarrow{conc.\ H_2SO_4,\ 323-333\ K} C_6H_5NO_2 + H_2O$ Nitration of benzene

NEET tip: Identify the electrophile in a given reaction, the rate-determining step, or the role of $H_2SO_4$ and $FeCl_3$.

Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation

In Friedel-Crafts alkylation, benzene is treated with an alkyl halide and anhydrous $AlCl_3$, which generates the carbocation $R^+$ as electrophile; for example, $CH_3Cl$ gives toluene. Alkylation has two drawbacks. The alkyl group activates the ring, causing polyalkylation, and the carbocation can rearrange, so n-propyl chloride gives mainly isopropylbenzene (cumene). In Friedel-Crafts acylation, an acyl chloride or acid anhydride with anhydrous $AlCl_3$ forms the resonance-stabilised acylium ion $RC\equiv O^+$; for example, $CH_3COCl$ gives acetophenone. The acyl group deactivates the ring, so only monoacylation occurs, and acylium ions do not rearrange. Neither reaction works on strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene (which is even used as a solvent) or on rings bearing $-NH_2$. In aniline, the $-NH_2$ group forms a complex with $AlCl_3$, converting it into a deactivating group.

  • Electrophile: $R^+$ in alkylation and $RCO^+$ (acylium) in acylation
  • $AlCl_3$ must be anhydrous; in acylation it is needed in more than catalytic amount
  • Alkylation suffers polysubstitution and rearrangement; acylation suffers neither
  • Aryl and vinyl halides cannot be used as the alkylating agent
  • Nitrobenzene and aniline do not undergo Friedel-Crafts reactions

$C_6H_6 + CH_3Cl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5CH_3 + HCl$ Friedel-Crafts alkylation

$C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl$ Friedel-Crafts acylation (acetophenone)

$CH_3COCl + AlCl_3 \rightarrow CH_3CO^+ + AlCl_4^-$ Acylium ion generation

NEET tip: Expect rearranged products (n-propyl to isopropyl), identification of the electrophile, and which substrates fail Friedel-Crafts.

Directive influence of functional groups in monosubstituted benzene

An existing substituent decides both where a second group enters the ring and how fast. Ortho/para-directing activating groups donate electron density by +R or +I/hyperconjugation, raising electron density at the ortho and para positions. Examples are $-OH$, $-NH_2$, $-NHR$, $-NHCOCH_3$, $-OCH_3$, $-CH_3$ and $-C_2H_5$. Halogens are ortho/para directing but deactivating: their strong -I effect lowers overall reactivity, while +R still favours ortho and para attack. Meta-directing deactivating groups withdraw electrons by -R/-I, making the ortho and para positions most electron-deficient, so meta attack is least disfavoured. Examples are $-NO_2$, $-CN$, $-CHO$, $-COR$, $-COOH$, $-COOR$, $-SO_3H$ and $-NR_3^+$. For example, nitration of toluene gives o- and p-nitrotoluene, while nitration of nitrobenzene gives m-dinitrobenzene. The para product often exceeds the ortho product because of steric hindrance.

  • Activating groups are o/p directing; deactivating groups are m directing, except halogens (o/p but deactivating)
  • Reactivity: phenol > toluene > benzene > chlorobenzene > nitrobenzene
  • Groups with a lone pair on the atom attached to the ring are generally o/p directors
  • Groups with a pi bond to an electronegative atom, or a positive charge, on the attached atom are m directors
  • In strongly acidic nitration, aniline forms anilinium ($-NH_3^+$, meta directing), so substantial meta product forms

$C_6H_5CH_3 \xrightarrow{HNO_3/H_2SO_4} o\text{-} + p\text{-}NO_2C_6H_4CH_3$ Methyl is o/p directing and activating

$C_6H_5NO_2 \xrightarrow{HNO_3/H_2SO_4,\ \Delta} m\text{-}C_6H_4(NO_2)_2$ Nitro is meta directing and deactivating

NEET tip: NEET asks you to rank compounds by reactivity toward electrophilic substitution or to predict the major product of a second substitution.

Formula sheet

$C_nH_{2n+2},\ C_nH_{2n},\ C_nH_{2n-2}$ General formulas: alkane, alkene, alkyne

$DU = \frac{2C+2+N-H-X}{2}$ Degree of unsaturation

$2RX + 2Na \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} R-R + 2NaX$ Wurtz reaction

$RCOONa \xrightarrow{NaOH/CaO,\ \Delta} RH + Na_2CO_3$ Decarboxylation (one carbon less)

$2RCOOK + 2H_2O \xrightarrow{electrolysis} R-R + 2CO_2 + H_2 + 2KOH$ Kolbe's electrolysis (alkane at anode)

$\Delta E \approx 12.5\ kJ\ mol^{-1}$ Staggered vs eclipsed energy difference in ethane

$Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2Cl^\bullet$ Initiation in free-radical halogenation

$F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2$ Reactivity of halogens toward alkanes

$RC\equiv CR' \xrightarrow{H_2,\ Pd/C,\ quinoline\ (Lindlar)} cis\text{-}alkene$ Syn partial reduction of alkyne

$RC\equiv CR' \xrightarrow{Na/liq.\ NH_3} trans\text{-}alkene$ Anti partial reduction of alkyne

$HI > HBr > HCl$ Reactivity of HX toward alkenes

$CH_3CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{HBr,\ (C_6H_5CO)_2O_2} CH_3CH_2CH_2Br$ Peroxide (Kharasch) effect, HBr only

$C=C \xrightarrow{(i)\ O_3\ (ii)\ Zn/H_2O} C=O + O=C$ Reductive ozonolysis

$C=C \xrightarrow{cold\ dil.\ alk.\ KMnO_4} HO-C-C-OH$ Baeyer's test; syn dihydroxylation

$HC\equiv CH + H_2O \xrightarrow{HgSO_4/H_2SO_4,\ 333\ K} CH_3CHO$ Hydration of ethyne

$3HC\equiv CH \xrightarrow{Fe,\ 873\ K} C_6H_6$ Cyclic trimerisation

$HC\equiv CH > CH_2=CH_2 > CH_3CH_3$ Acidity order (s-character 50%, 33%, 25%)

$\pi\ electrons = 4n+2$ Huckel's rule for aromaticity

$HNO_3 + 2H_2SO_4 \rightleftharpoons NO_2^+ + H_3O^+ + 2HSO_4^-$ Nitronium ion formation

$C_6H_6 + RCl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5R + HCl$ Friedel-Crafts alkylation

$C_6H_6 + RCOCl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5COR + HCl$ Friedel-Crafts acylation

$C_6H_{14} \xrightarrow{Cr_2O_3/V_2O_5,\ 773\ K} C_6H_6 + 4H_2$ Aromatisation of n-hexane

Common traps

  • Assuming every dihalide addition is syn. $Br_2$ adds anti: a trans-alkene gives the meso dibromide and a cis-alkene the racemic one. Cold alkaline $KMnO_4$ adds syn, so a cis-alkene gives the meso diol.
  • Applying the peroxide effect to HCl or HI. Only HBr shows anti-Markovnikov addition with peroxides.
  • Calling hepta-1,4-diene conjugated. Conjugation needs exactly one single bond between the double bonds (1,3-pattern).
  • Thinking the products of HBr and HBr/peroxide on $Ph-CH=CH-CH_3$ are stereoisomers. They are position (structural) isomers, with Br on the benzylic carbon vs the carbon next to $CH_3$.
  • Writing n-propylbenzene as the major product of benzene + n-propyl chloride/$AlCl_3$. The carbocation rearranges, so isopropylbenzene is major.
  • Treating halogens as activating because they are o/p directing. They are deactivating (-I dominates) but o/p directing (+R).
  • Expecting internal alkynes such as but-2-yne to react with $NaNH_2$ or ammoniacal $AgNO_3$. Only terminal alkynes have an acidic hydrogen.
  • Believing staggered and eclipsed ethane can be separated. The barrier is only about 12.5 kJ/mol, so they interconvert freely.

Quick revision

  • Alkane boiling point rises with chain length and falls with branching; n-pentane > isopentane > neopentane.
  • Free-radical halogenation goes through initiation, propagation and termination; ethane by-product proves the radical path.
  • Staggered ethane is the most stable conformer (60 degree dihedral angle); eclipsed is the least stable.
  • Geometrical isomerism needs restricted rotation and two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon.
  • Lindlar's catalyst gives the cis-alkene; Na/liq. $NH_3$ gives the trans-alkene.
  • Markovnikov addition goes via the more stable carbocation; the peroxide effect (HBr only) goes via the more stable radical.
  • Ozonolysis: replace each $C=C$ with two $C=O$; terminal $=CH_2$ gives $HCHO$.
  • Terminal alkynes are acidic because of the 50% s-character carbon; hydration gives ethanal from ethyne and ketones from others.
  • Benzene has all $C-C$ bonds at 139 pm, is $sp^2$ and planar with 6 delocalised pi electrons; aromaticity requires $4n+2$ pi electrons.
  • Electrophilic substitution electrophiles: $Cl^+$ (via $FeCl_3$), $NO_2^+$ (nitrating mixture), $R^+$ and $RCO^+$ (via $AlCl_3$).
  • Friedel-Crafts fails on nitrobenzene and aniline; alkylation suffers rearrangement and polysubstitution, acylation does not.
  • o/p directors: $-OH$, $-NH_2$, $-OCH_3$, $-CH_3$, halogens. m directors: $-NO_2$, $-CN$, $-CHO$, $-COOH$, $-SO_3H$.

Chemistry · Unit 16: Organic Compounds Containing Halogens

This unit covers haloalkanes and haloarenes: how they are prepared, how the polar C–X bond controls their physical and chemical behaviour, and how they react by nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2), elimination and with metals. NEET regularly asks about reagent-based conversions, SN1 versus SN2 reactivity order, stereochemistry, Grignard reagents with active-hydrogen compounds, and the uses and environmental effects of polyhalogen compounds.

PYQs (1): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q72

General methods of preparation, properties and reactions

Haloalkanes are made from alcohols using $HX$ ($ZnCl_2$ catalyst for $HCl$), $PCl_3$, $PCl_5$ or $SOCl_2$. With $SOCl_2$ the by-products $SO_2$ and $HCl$ escape as gases, so the product is pure. They are also made from alkenes by $HX$ addition (Markovnikov; anti-Markovnikov only for $HBr$ with peroxide) and by halogen exchange (Finkelstein, Swarts). Haloarenes are made by electrophilic halogenation with a Lewis acid, or from diazonium salts (Sandmeyer, Gattermann, $KI$ for iodides). Boiling points follow $RI > RBr > RCl > RF$ and fall with branching. Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution and β-elimination (alcoholic $KOH$, Saytzeff product). They also react with metals: Wurtz coupling, and Grignard reagent formation in dry ether. Grignard reagents are destroyed by any compound with an active H ($H_2O$, $ROH$, $RNH_2$, $RCOOH$, terminal alkynes), giving the alkane $RH$. Haloarenes are o,p-directing but deactivating in electrophilic substitution.

  • Alcohol reactivity towards $HX$: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$; $HX$ reactivity: $HI > HBr > HCl$
  • $SOCl_2$ is preferred because both by-products are gases
  • Peroxide (Kharasch) effect is shown by $HBr$ only, not by $HCl$ or $HI$
  • Finkelstein: $NaI$ in dry acetone; $NaCl$ or $NaBr$ precipitates and drives the reaction forward
  • Swarts: $AgF$, $Hg_2F_2$, $CoF_2$ or $SbF_3$ give alkyl fluorides
  • $KCN$ gives nitriles, $AgCN$ gives isocyanides; $KNO_2$ gives alkyl nitrites, $AgNO_2$ gives nitroalkanes
  • p-Dichlorobenzene melts higher than its o- and m-isomers because its symmetry gives better crystal packing
  • $RMgX$ with $R'NH_2$, $H_2O$ or $ROH$ gives the alkane $RH$
  • Wurtz–Fittig: $ArX + RX + Na$ gives $Ar-R$; Fittig: $2ArX + 2Na$ gives $Ar-Ar$

$ROH + SOCl_2 \rightarrow RCl + SO_2\uparrow + HCl\uparrow$ Best method for alkyl chlorides

$RCl + NaI \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} RI + NaCl\downarrow$ Finkelstein reaction for alkyl iodides

$CH_3Br + AgF \rightarrow CH_3F + AgBr$ Swarts reaction for alkyl fluorides

$2RX + 2Na \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} R-R + 2NaX$ Wurtz reaction, giving a higher alkane
