$RMgX + R'NH_2 \rightarrow RH + R'NHMgX$ Grignard reagent is protonated by an active-H compound, giving an alkane

$ArN_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{Cu_2Cl_2/HCl} ArCl + N_2$ Sandmeyer reaction

NEET tip: Expect reagent-to-product matching ($KCN$ vs $AgCN$, $SOCl_2$, Finkelstein, Swarts) and Grignard reagents reacting with acidic-H compounds to give the alkane.

Nature of the C-X bond

Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar: the carbon carries $\delta+$ and the halogen $\delta-$. This makes the carbon an electrophilic site for nucleophiles. Down the group the halogen gets larger, so C–X bond length increases ($C-F < C-Cl < C-Br < C-I$) and bond enthalpy decreases. C–I is therefore the weakest bond, and iodides are the most reactive alkyl halides. Dipole moment order is $CH_3Cl > CH_3F > CH_3Br > CH_3I$; $CH_3F$ is lower than $CH_3Cl$ because its very short bond outweighs its higher charge separation. The C–X bond in haloarenes is shorter and stronger because of $sp^2$ hybridisation of carbon and partial double-bond character from resonance. Haloarenes are less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution for four reasons: resonance, $sp^2$ hybridisation, instability of the phenyl cation, and repulsion of the nucleophile by the electron-rich ring. Haloarenes therefore resist nucleophilic substitution unless electron-withdrawing groups such as $-NO_2$ sit at the ortho or para positions.

  • C–X bond enthalpy: $C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I$
  • Reactivity of RX towards substitution: $RI > RBr > RCl > RF$
  • Dipole moment: $CH_3Cl > CH_3F > CH_3Br > CH_3I$
  • Chlorobenzene has a smaller dipole moment than cyclohexyl chloride
  • Haloarene C–X has partial double-bond character from resonance
  • o/p-$NO_2$ groups activate haloarenes towards nucleophilic substitution; m-$NO_2$ has little effect
  • Halogen is deactivating by $-I$ effect but o,p-directing by $+R$ effect

$\overset{\delta+}{C}-\overset{\delta-}{X}$ Polarity of the C–X bond; the carbon is the electrophilic centre

NEET tip: NEET asks for orders of bond enthalpy, bond length and dipole moment, and the reasons haloarenes are less reactive towards nucleophiles.

Mechanisms of substitution reactions

SN2 is a single concerted step: the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group, passes through a pentacoordinate transition state, and the configuration inverts (Walden inversion). The rate depends on both reactants, so the reaction is second order. Steric hindrance controls SN2 reactivity, giving $CH_3X > 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$. SN1 occurs in two steps. The slow ionisation forms a planar carbocation, which the nucleophile then attacks from either face. This gives racemisation, usually with some excess of the inverted product. The rate depends only on the substrate, so the reaction is first order. Carbocation stability controls SN1 reactivity, giving $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > CH_3X$. Polar protic solvents favour SN1. Allylic and benzylic halides react fast by SN1 because their carbocations are resonance-stabilised. For both mechanisms the leaving-group order is $I^- > Br^- > Cl^- > F^-$. A chiral carbon gives optical activity; retention, inversion and racemisation describe what happens to its configuration.

  • SN2: one step, second order, inversion, favoured by primary substrates and strong nucleophiles
  • SN1: carbocation intermediate, first order, racemisation, favoured by tertiary substrates and polar protic solvents
  • SN2 reactivity: $CH_3X > 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$
  • SN1 reactivity: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > CH_3X$
  • Benzylic and allylic halides are highly reactive in SN1
  • Elimination competes with substitution; bulky bases and alcoholic $KOH$ favour elimination
  • Saytzeff rule: the more substituted alkene is the major elimination product
  • Haloarenes undergo nucleophilic substitution only under drastic conditions (Dow's process) or when activated by o/p-$NO_2$

$\text{Rate} = k[RX][Nu^-]$ SN2 rate law (second order)

$\text{Rate} = k[RX]$ SN1 rate law (first order)

$C_6H_5Cl \xrightarrow{(i)\ NaOH,\ 623\ K,\ 300\ atm;\ (ii)\ H^+} C_6H_5OH$ Dow's process: nucleophilic substitution of a haloarene under drastic conditions

NEET tip: Frequent questions: arrange halides in order of SN1 or SN2 reactivity, and predict the stereochemical outcome (inversion vs racemisation).

Uses of haloalkanes and haloarenes

Polyhalogen compounds have many industrial, agricultural and medical uses. Dichloromethane is a solvent, paint remover, aerosol propellant and metal-cleaning agent. Chloroform is a solvent for fats, alkaloids and iodine, and is used to make the refrigerant freon R-22; it was once a general anaesthetic. Iodoform was used as an antiseptic because it releases free iodine, not because of its own action. Carbon tetrachloride is used to manufacture refrigerants and propellants, as a cleaning fluid and as a solvent; it was formerly used in fire extinguishers. Freons such as $CCl_2F_2$ (freon-12) are refrigerants, air-conditioner coolants and aerosol propellants. DDT was the first chlorinated organic insecticide and was used against malaria-carrying mosquitoes and typhus-carrying lice. Among haloarenes, chlorobenzene is used to make phenol and DDT, and p-dichlorobenzene is a moth repellent.

  • $CH_2Cl_2$: solvent, paint remover, propellant
  • $CHCl_3$: solvent and starting material for freon R-22; former anaesthetic
  • $CHI_3$: antiseptic action is due to liberated $I_2$
  • $CCl_4$: manufacture of refrigerants and propellants; formerly a fire extinguisher
  • Freon-12 is $CCl_2F_2$: refrigerant and aerosol propellant
  • DDT is p,p'-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane, an insecticide
  • Chlorobenzene is the starting material for phenol and DDT

$CH_3COR + 3I_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + RCOONa + 3NaI + 3H_2O$ Iodoform reaction: gives yellow $CHI_3$ from methyl ketones (and ethanol and some secondary alcohols)

NEET tip: Match-the-column questions pair each compound with its use, for example iodoform with antiseptic and freon with refrigerant.

Environmental effects of chloroform, iodoform, freons and DDT

Chloroform vapour depresses the central nervous system, causing dizziness, fatigue and headache. Chronic exposure damages the liver and kidneys. In air and light chloroform is slowly oxidised to highly poisonous phosgene ($COCl_2$). It is therefore stored in closed, dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim, and a small amount of ethanol is added to convert any phosgene into harmless ethyl carbonate. Iodoform has an objectionable smell and has been replaced by other iodine-containing formulations. Freons are very stable and unreactive, so they drift into the stratosphere. There UV light splits off chlorine free radicals, which destroy ozone in a chain reaction, thinning the ozone layer and increasing UV exposure (skin cancer, cataract). Carbon tetrachloride also depletes ozone and can cause liver cancer. DDT is not biodegradable. Because it is fat-soluble, it is stored in fatty tissue and builds up along food chains (biomagnification). Many insects have also become resistant to it, and it was banned in many countries.

  • $CHCl_3$ in air and light gives poisonous phosgene, $COCl_2$
  • Chloroform is stored in dark bottles, filled completely, with about 1% ethanol added
  • Freons cause ozone depletion through chlorine free radicals
  • One chlorine radical can destroy many $O_3$ molecules because the radical is regenerated (chain reaction)
  • DDT is non-biodegradable and fat-soluble, so it biomagnifies; insects developed resistance; banned in the USA in 1973
  • $CCl_4$ depletes ozone and is linked to liver damage and cancer
  • Iodoform was discontinued mainly because of its objectionable smell

$2CHCl_3 + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2COCl_2 + 2HCl$ Formation of poisonous phosgene from chloroform

$CF_2Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \dot{C}l + \dot{C}F_2Cl$ Freon releases a chlorine radical in the stratosphere

$\dot{C}l + O_3 \rightarrow Cl\dot{O} + O_2$ First step of ozone destruction

$Cl\dot{O} + O \rightarrow \dot{C}l + O_2$ The chlorine radical is regenerated, so the chain continues

NEET tip: NEET asks why chloroform is stored in dark bottles, which compound forms phosgene, and why DDT and freons are environmentally harmful.

Formula sheet

$ROH + SOCl_2 \rightarrow RCl + SO_2 + HCl$ Darzens method; gives pure alkyl chloride

$3ROH + PCl_3 \rightarrow 3RCl + H_3PO_3$ Alkyl chloride from an alcohol

$ROH + PCl_5 \rightarrow RCl + POCl_3 + HCl$ Alkyl chloride from an alcohol

$RCl + NaI \xrightarrow{\text{acetone}} RI + NaCl$ Finkelstein reaction

$RBr + AgF \rightarrow RF + AgBr$ Swarts reaction

$CH_3CH=CH_2 + HBr \xrightarrow{\text{peroxide}} CH_3CH_2CH_2Br$ Anti-Markovnikov (Kharasch) addition, shown only by $HBr$

$ArN_2^+X^- \xrightarrow{Cu_2X_2/HX} ArX + N_2$ Sandmeyer reaction ($X = Cl, Br$)

$ArN_2^+X^- \xrightarrow{Cu/HX} ArX + N_2$ Gattermann reaction

$ArN_2^+Cl^- + KI \rightarrow ArI + KCl + N_2$ Preparation of iodoarene

$2RX + 2Na \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} R-R + 2NaX$ Wurtz reaction

$ArX + RX + 2Na \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} Ar-R + 2NaX$ Wurtz–Fittig reaction

$2ArX + 2Na \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} Ar-Ar + 2NaX$ Fittig reaction

$RX + Mg \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} RMgX$ Grignard reagent formation

$RMgX + HZ \rightarrow RH + Mg(Z)X$ Any active-H compound ($H_2O$, $ROH$, $RNH_2$, $RCOOH$, terminal alkyne) gives the alkane

$RX \xrightarrow{\text{alc. } KOH} \text{alkene}$ Dehydrohalogenation (β-elimination); follows Saytzeff rule

$RX + KCN \rightarrow RCN$; $RX + AgCN \rightarrow RNC$ Ambident nucleophile: $KCN$ gives nitrile, $AgCN$ gives isocyanide

$RX + KNO_2 \rightarrow R-O-N=O$; $RX + AgNO_2 \rightarrow R-NO_2$ $KNO_2$ gives alkyl nitrite, $AgNO_2$ gives nitroalkane

$\text{Rate}_{S_N2} = k[RX][Nu^-]$; $\text{Rate}_{S_N1} = k[RX]$ Kinetics of the two substitution mechanisms

$S_N2: CH_3X > 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$; $S_N1: 3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > CH_3X$ Substrate reactivity orders

$RI > RBr > RCl > RF$ Order of reactivity and boiling point of alkyl halides

$CH_3Cl > CH_3F > CH_3Br > CH_3I$ Dipole moment order

$2CHCl_3 + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2COCl_2 + 2HCl$ Phosgene formation from chloroform

$\dot{C}l + O_3 \rightarrow Cl\dot{O} + O_2$ Ozone depletion by freons

Common traps

  • Assuming $CH_3F$ has the highest dipole moment: $CH_3Cl$ is highest, because the C–F bond is very short.
  • Writing a nitrile for $AgCN$: the bond in $AgCN$ is largely covalent, so attack occurs through N and the product is an isocyanide; ionic $KCN$ gives the nitrile.
  • Treating a Grignard reagent with an amine and expecting a C–N coupled product: the amine N–H protonates $RMgX$, so the product is simply the alkane $RH$.
  • Applying the peroxide effect to $HCl$ or $HI$: only $HBr$ shows anti-Markovnikov addition with peroxide.
  • Thinking SN1 gives 100% racemisation: usually partial racemisation occurs with some excess of the inverted product.
  • Assuming chlorobenzene undergoes SN reactions as easily as alkyl chlorides: its partial double-bond character and $sp^2$ carbon make it unreactive unless conditions are drastic or o/p-$NO_2$ groups are present.
  • Calling halogens meta-directing because they deactivate the ring: they are deactivating but ortho/para-directing.
  • Thinking iodoform itself is the antiseptic: its antiseptic action comes from liberated iodine.

Quick revision

  • $SOCl_2$ gives pure alkyl chlorides because its by-products $SO_2$ and $HCl$ are gases.
  • Finkelstein uses $NaI$ in acetone; Swarts uses $AgF$, $Hg_2F_2$, $CoF_2$ or $SbF_3$.
  • C–X bond enthalpy falls from F to I, so reactivity rises from F to I.
  • SN2 is one step, second order and gives inversion; reactivity is highest for methyl halides.
  • SN1 goes through a carbocation, is first order and gives racemisation; reactivity is highest for tertiary, allylic and benzylic halides.
  • Boiling point rises with molecular mass and falls with branching; p-dichlorobenzene has the highest melting point of the three isomers.
  • Grignard reagents give the alkane with water, alcohols, amines, acids and terminal alkynes.
  • Alcoholic $KOH$ favours elimination (Saytzeff); aqueous $KOH$ favours substitution to the alcohol.
  • Haloarenes are o,p-directing but deactivating; they are converted to phenol by Dow's process at 623 K and 300 atm.
  • Chloroform forms phosgene in light, so it is stored in dark, full bottles with ethanol added.
  • Freons release chlorine radicals that destroy ozone in a chain reaction.
  • DDT is non-biodegradable and fat-soluble, so it biomagnifies along food chains.

Chemistry · Unit 17: Organic Compounds Containing Oxygen

This unit covers alcohols, phenols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids: how they are classified, the reasons behind their acidity and reactivity, and the named reactions used to convert one into another. NEET regularly asks reaction-sequence and reagent-identification questions from it, including the Etard reaction, haloform, aldol, Cannizzaro, Reimer-Tiemann, Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reactions. Acidity orders and distinguishing tests such as Lucas, Tollens', Fehling's and iodoform are also frequent, so the unit is high-yield for scoring.

PYQs (3): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q46, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q82, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q86

Alcohols: identification of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols

An alcohol is primary (1°), secondary (2°) or tertiary (3°) according to how many carbons are attached to the carbinol carbon (the C bearing OH). The Lucas test uses conc. $HCl$ with anhydrous $ZnCl_2$. The alcohol reacts by an $S_N1$-type path, and the insoluble alkyl chloride separates out as turbidity. Tertiary alcohols give turbidity immediately because they form the most stable carbocation. Secondary alcohols give turbidity within about 5 minutes. Primary alcohols give no turbidity at room temperature and react only on heating. Dehydrogenation over heated Cu at 573 K gives an aldehyde from a 1° alcohol, a ketone from a 2° alcohol and an alkene from a 3° alcohol (by dehydration). Oxidation is also diagnostic: 1° alcohols give aldehydes and then acids, 2° alcohols give ketones, and 3° alcohols resist mild oxidation.

  • Lucas reagent is conc. $HCl$ with anhydrous $ZnCl_2$; the order of reactivity is 3° > 2° > 1°
  • Turbidity in the Lucas test is caused by the insoluble alkyl chloride
  • Cu at 573 K: 1° alcohol gives aldehyde, 2° gives ketone, 3° gives alkene
  • PCC oxidises a 1° alcohol only up to the aldehyde stage
  • 3° alcohols are not oxidised by mild oxidants because the carbinol carbon has no H

$R-OH + HCl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ ZnCl_2} R-Cl + H_2O$ Lucas test reaction; speed indicates 3° > 2° > 1°

$RCH_2OH \xrightarrow{Cu,\ 573\ K} RCHO + H_2$ Dehydrogenation of 1° alcohol; a 2° alcohol gives a ketone, a 3° alcohol gives an alkene

NEET tip: Expect a match of alcohol class with Lucas test time, or with the product formed over Cu at 573 K.

Mechanism of dehydration of alcohols

Alcohols lose water on heating with protic acids. Ethanol needs conc. $H_2SO_4$ at 443 K. Secondary alcohols need 85% $H_3PO_4$ at about 440 K, and tertiary alcohols need only 20% $H_3PO_4$ at about 358 K. The mechanism (E1 for 2° and 3° alcohols) has three steps. Step 1 is fast protonation of the OH group, which converts it into a good leaving group ($H_2O$). Step 2 is the slow, rate-determining loss of water to give a carbocation. Step 3 is loss of a β-proton to give the alkene. Since carbocation stability decides the rate, the ease of dehydration is 3° > 2° > 1°. The more substituted alkene is the major product (Saytzeff rule). Carbocations may also rearrange by hydride or methyl shifts. If excess ethanol is used at 413 K, the product is diethyl ether, formed by an $S_N2$ attack of a second alcohol molecule.

  • Step 1 is protonation, step 2 (slow, rate-determining) is carbocation formation, step 3 is deprotonation
  • Ease of dehydration is 3° > 2° > 1°, the same as the order of carbocation stability
  • The more substituted alkene is the major product (Saytzeff rule)
  • Rearrangements (1,2-H or 1,2-$CH_3$ shift) can give unexpected alkenes
  • Ethanol gives an alkene with conc. $H_2SO_4$ at 443 K but an ether at 413 K
  • Acid acts as a catalyst and is regenerated at the end

$CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{conc.\ H_2SO_4,\ 443\ K} CH_2=CH_2 + H_2O$ Intramolecular dehydration of ethanol

$2C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4,\ 413\ K} C_2H_5OC_2H_5 + H_2O$ Intermolecular dehydration giving an ether

NEET tip: NEET asks for the rate-determining step, the major alkene (often after a rearrangement) or the relative ease of dehydration.

Phenols: acidic nature

Phenol ($pK_a \approx 10$) is far more acidic than ethanol ($pK_a \approx 15.9$) and water. There are two reasons. First, the OH is attached to an sp2 carbon, which is more electronegative and polarises the O–H bond. Second, and more important, the phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of its negative charge over the ring. This delocalisation is more effective than in phenol itself, where resonance requires charge separation. Phenol reacts with $Na$ and $NaOH$ but not with $NaHCO_3$, since it is weaker than carbonic acid. Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) at the ortho or para positions, such as $-NO_2$, increase acidity strongly through the -R effect. Electron-donating groups ($-CH_3$, $-OCH_3$) decrease acidity. A meta EWG acts only through the -I effect, so its influence is smaller. Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol, $pK_a \approx 0.71$ as per NCERT) is very strongly acidic.

  • Acidity order: carboxylic acid > phenol > water > ethanol
  • Phenol dissolves in $NaOH$ but gives no $CO_2$ with $NaHCO_3$
  • p-nitrophenol (7.1) > o-nitrophenol (7.2) > m-nitrophenol (8.3) > phenol (10.0) in acidity
  • o-nitrophenol is slightly weaker than the para isomer because of intramolecular H-bonding
  • Cresols are less acidic than phenol because of the +I/hyperconjugation effect of $CH_3$
  • More nitro groups at ortho/para mean higher acidity: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol is the strongest

$C_6H_5OH + NaOH \rightarrow C_6H_5ONa + H_2O$ Phenol neutralises a strong base

$pK_a = -\log K_a$ A lower $pK_a$ means a stronger acid

NEET tip: Arranging substituted phenols in order of acidity, and the NaHCO3 versus NaOH test, are favourite NEET questions.

Electrophilic substitution of phenols: halogenation, nitration and sulphonation

The OH group strongly activates the benzene ring and directs incoming electrophiles to ortho and para positions through its +R effect. Bromination in a solvent of low polarity ($CHCl_3$ or $CS_2$) at low temperature gives monobromophenols, with para as the major product. With bromine water, phenol is converted at once into 2,4,6-tribromophenol, a white precipitate, without any Lewis acid. The polar solvent increases ionisation to phenoxide, which is even more activating. Dilute $HNO_3$ at 298 K gives o- and p-nitrophenol. These are separated by steam distillation: the ortho isomer is volatile because of intramolecular H-bonding, while the para isomer is intermolecularly H-bonded and less volatile. Conc. $HNO_3$ gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid). Sulphonation with conc. $H_2SO_4$ gives mainly o-phenolsulphonic acid near room temperature (kinetic control) and p-phenolsulphonic acid at about 373 K (thermodynamic control).

  • $-OH$ is an activating, ortho/para-directing group; no Lewis acid is needed for halogenation
  • $Br_2$ in $CS_2$ at low temperature gives mono-bromination (mainly para)
  • Bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, a test for phenol
  • o-nitrophenol is steam volatile (intramolecular H-bond); p-nitrophenol is not
  • Picric acid is better prepared by sulphonation followed by nitration (higher yield)
  • Sulphonation gives ortho at low temperature and para at 373 K

$C_6H_5OH + 3Br_2(aq) \rightarrow C_6H_2Br_3OH \downarrow + 3HBr$ 2,4,6-tribromophenol, a white precipitate

$C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{conc.\ HNO_3} C_6H_2(NO_2)_3OH$ Picric acid formation

NEET tip: NEET contrasts bromine water with Br2 in CS2, and asks about steam distillation of nitrophenol isomers.

Reimer-Tiemann reaction

In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, phenol is heated with chloroform and aqueous $NaOH$ at about 340 K, followed by acidification. An -CHO group is introduced at the ortho position, giving salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde). The base removes HCl from chloroform to form dichlorocarbene ($:CCl_2$). This is an electron-deficient electrophile and attacks the electron-rich phenoxide ring, mainly at the ortho position. The intermediate is a substituted benzal chloride ($-CHCl_2$ group). Alkali hydrolyses this to the aldehyde, which exists as the phenoxide until acid is added. Using carbon tetrachloride instead of chloroform gives salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). The reaction is an electrophilic substitution on the highly activated phenoxide ion.

  • Reagents: $CHCl_3$ with aqueous $NaOH$, then $H^+$
  • The electrophile is dichlorocarbene $:CCl_2$
  • The intermediate is a benzal chloride ($-CHCl_2$) type species
  • The major product is the ortho isomer, salicylaldehyde
  • With $CCl_4$ in place of $CHCl_3$, salicylic acid is formed

$C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{CHCl_3,\ aq.\ NaOH;\ H^+} o-HOC_6H_4CHO$ Reimer-Tiemann formylation giving salicylaldehyde

$CHCl_3 + OH^- \rightarrow :CCl_2 + H_2O + Cl^-$ Generation of the dichlorocarbene electrophile

NEET tip: NEET asks to identify the electrophile (:CCl2), the intermediate, or the product when CCl4 replaces CHCl3.

Ethers: structure

In ethers (R–O–R'), the oxygen is sp3 hybridised and carries two lone pairs, giving a bent shape. The C–O–C bond angle in dimethyl ether is about 111.7°, slightly more than the tetrahedral angle. This widening is caused by repulsion between the bulky alkyl groups. The C–O bond length is about 141 pm. In aryl alkyl ethers such as anisole, the oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, which gives the Ar–O bond partial double-bond character and makes it shorter. Because of the bent shape, ethers have a net dipole moment. They cannot H-bond with each other, so their boiling points are close to those of alkanes of similar mass. They can, however, accept H-bonds from water, so their water solubility is comparable to that of alcohols. With HI, an alkyl aryl ether is cleaved to give a phenol and an alkyl iodide. The bond broken is the O–alkyl bond, because the Ar–O bond is strengthened by partial double-bond character.

  • The O atom is sp3 hybridised with a bent C–O–C geometry
  • The bond angle is about 111.7° in $CH_3OCH_3$, larger than 109.5° due to repulsion between alkyl groups
  • Ethers are polar (net dipole) but have no intermolecular H-bonding, so they have low boiling points
  • Ethers are soluble in water because they accept H-bonds
  • In anisole, the Ar–O bond has partial double-bond character
  • $C_6H_5OCH_3 + HI \rightarrow C_6H_5OH + CH_3I$

$C_6H_5OCH_3 + HI \rightarrow C_6H_5OH + CH_3I$ Cleavage of an alkyl aryl ether; phenol and alkyl iodide are formed

NEET tip: NEET asks why the C–O–C angle exceeds the tetrahedral angle, or which products form when an ether is cleaved by HI.

Aldehydes and ketones: nature of the carbonyl group

In the carbonyl group, the carbon is sp2 hybridised. It forms three sigma bonds lying in one plane at about 120°, giving a trigonal planar arrangement. The remaining unhybridised p orbital overlaps with a p orbital of oxygen to form the π bond. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polar. It is best described as a resonance hybrid of the neutral form and the dipolar form $>C^+–O^-$. The carbonyl carbon is therefore electrophilic (a Lewis acid site) and the oxygen is nucleophilic (a Lewis base site). This polarity gives aldehydes and ketones high dipole moments, larger than those of ethers. Their boiling points lie between those of hydrocarbons/ethers and alcohols of comparable mass, because of dipole-dipole attraction without H-bonding. Lower members are water soluble because they accept H-bonds. The planar geometry allows nucleophiles to attack from either face.

  • Carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised, trigonal planar, with bond angles of about 120°
  • The C=O bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond
  • Polarisation $>C^{\delta+}=O^{\delta-}$ makes the carbon electrophilic
  • Boiling point order: alcohols > aldehydes/ketones > ethers ≈ alkanes (similar molar mass)
  • Lower aldehydes and ketones are miscible with water through H-bonding with water

NEET tip: NEET asks about hybridisation, the polarity of C=O, or boiling point comparisons among carbonyl compounds, alcohols and ethers.

Nucleophilic addition to C=O: HCN, NH3 and its derivatives; Grignard reagent

In nucleophilic addition, the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon roughly perpendicular to the plane of the group. The carbon changes from sp2 to sp3, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate that is then protonated. HCN adds in the presence of a base catalyst, which generates the stronger nucleophile $CN^-$; the product is a cyanohydrin. Ammonia derivatives ($H_2N–Z$) react by addition followed by elimination of water, giving $>C=N–Z$. The pH must be weakly acidic (about 3.5), so that the carbonyl is activated without protonating the nucleophile. Hydroxylamine gives oximes, hydrazine gives hydrazones, phenylhydrazine gives phenylhydrazones, 2,4-DNP gives orange-yellow 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazones, and semicarbazide gives semicarbazones. Formaldehyde with ammonia gives hexamethylenetetramine (urotropine). Grignard reagents add $R^-$ to the carbonyl carbon. After hydrolysis, HCHO gives a 1° alcohol, other aldehydes give 2° alcohols and ketones give 3° alcohols.

  • Hybridisation changes from sp2 (planar) to sp3 (tetrahedral)
  • Addition of HCN is base catalysed because the true nucleophile is $CN^-$
  • $NH_2OH$ gives an oxime, $NH_2NH_2$ a hydrazone, $C_6H_5NHNH_2$ a phenylhydrazone, $NH_2NHCONH_2$ a semicarbazone
  • In semicarbazide, only the $NH_2$ not attached to C=O acts as the nucleophile
  • Reactions with ammonia derivatives work best at pH about 3.5
  • Grignard addition: HCHO gives a 1° alcohol, RCHO a 2° alcohol, $R_2CO$ a 3° alcohol
  • $6HCHO + 4NH_3 \rightarrow (CH_2)_6N_4 + 6H_2O$ (urotropine)

$>C=O + HCN \xrightarrow{OH^-} >C(OH)CN$ Cyanohydrin formation

$>C=O + H_2N-Z \rightarrow >C=N-Z + H_2O$ Addition-elimination with ammonia derivatives

$>C=O + RMgX \rightarrow >C(R)OMgX \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} >C(R)OH$ Grignard synthesis of alcohols

NEET tip: NEET asks you to identify the product (oxime, semicarbazone, cyanohydrin) or the type of alcohol formed from a carbonyl compound and RMgX.

Relative reactivities of aldehydes and ketones

Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition, for two reasons. The sterically smaller H atom lets the nucleophile approach the carbonyl carbon more easily. In addition, ketones have two electron-releasing alkyl groups, which reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon more than the single alkyl group of an aldehyde does. Hence HCHO > $CH_3CHO$ > $CH_3COCH_3$, and reactivity falls further as the alkyl groups become larger. Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde are less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes like propanal, because the ring donates electrons to the carbonyl group by resonance. Electron-withdrawing groups on the ring increase reactivity, while electron-donating groups decrease it. For example, p-nitrobenzaldehyde > benzaldehyde > p-tolualdehyde > p-methoxybenzaldehyde.

  • Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones for both steric and electronic reasons
  • HCHO > $CH_3CHO$ > $CH_3CH_2CHO$ > $CH_3COCH_3$ > $C_2H_5COCH_3$
  • Aliphatic aldehydes are more reactive than aromatic aldehydes (resonance in aromatic ones)
  • An EWG ($-NO_2$) on the ring increases reactivity; an EDG ($-OCH_3$, $-CH_3$) decreases it
  • Bulky groups lower reactivity, e.g. di-tert-butyl ketone is very unreactive

NEET tip: Arranging carbonyl compounds by their reactivity towards HCN or nucleophilic addition is a frequent NEET question.

Oxidation and reduction: Wolff-Kishner and Clemmensen

Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids, even by mild agents such as Tollens' reagent, Fehling's solution, $HNO_3$, $KMnO_4$ and $K_2Cr_2O_7$. Ketones are oxidised only by strong oxidants under vigorous conditions, with cleavage of C–C bonds into a mixture of acids with fewer carbons. Reduction with $NaBH_4$, $LiAlH_4$ or $H_2$/catalyst converts aldehydes into 1° alcohols and ketones into 2° alcohols. The C=O group can also be reduced completely to $CH_2$. In the Clemmensen reduction, zinc amalgam with conc. HCl is used, so it suits compounds that are stable in acid. In the Wolff-Kishner reduction, the hydrazone is first formed and then heated with KOH in ethylene glycol, releasing $N_2$; it suits compounds that are sensitive to acid but stable in base.

  • Aldehydes are oxidised by mild reagents to RCOOH; ketones need drastic conditions and undergo C–C cleavage
  • $NaBH_4$ or $LiAlH_4$ reduce aldehydes to 1° alcohols and ketones to 2° alcohols
  • $NaBH_4$ does not reduce an isolated C=C bond
  • Clemmensen reduction uses $Zn-Hg$ with conc. HCl (acidic medium)
  • Wolff-Kishner reduction uses $NH_2NH_2$, then KOH in ethylene glycol with heat (basic medium)
  • Both reductions convert C=O into $CH_2$, giving a hydrocarbon

$>C=O \xrightarrow{Zn-Hg,\ conc.\ HCl} >CH_2 + H_2O$ Clemmensen reduction (acidic)

$>C=O \xrightarrow{NH_2NH_2} >C=NNH_2 \xrightarrow{KOH,\ ethylene\ glycol,\ \Delta} >CH_2 + N_2$ Wolff-Kishner reduction (basic)

NEET tip: NEET asks which reagent converts C=O to CH2 and which method suits acid-sensitive versus base-sensitive substrates.

Acidity of alpha-hydrogen

A hydrogen on the carbon next to the carbonyl group (the α-hydrogen) is unusually acidic. The $pK_a$ is about 19–20 for acetone, compared with about 50 for an alkane. There are two reasons. The strongly electron-withdrawing C=O group polarises the α C–H bond. More importantly, the conjugate base (the enolate ion) is stabilised by resonance, with the negative charge shared between the α-carbon and the oxygen. This acidity is responsible for keto-enol tautomerism, aldol condensation, α-halogenation and the haloform reaction. A hydrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups, as in 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds, is even more acidic ($pK_a$ about 9–11). Compounds without α-hydrogens cannot form enolates and therefore do not undergo aldol condensation. Examples are HCHO, $C_6H_5CHO$, $(CH_3)_3CCHO$ and benzophenone.

  • α-H acidity arises from the -I effect of C=O and resonance stabilisation of the enolate
  • Keto-enol tautomerism requires an α-H
  • No α-H in HCHO, $C_6H_5CHO$, $(CH_3)_3CCHO$, $C_6H_5COC_6H_5$, so they cannot undergo aldol condensation
  • Acidity of α-H increases when it lies between two C=O groups
  • Always count α-H carefully: an α-carbon bearing three alkyl groups, such as $(CH_3)_3C-$ (tert-butyl), has no α-H; an isopropyl α-carbon still has one α-H

$CH_3COCH_3 + OH^- \rightleftharpoons CH_3COCH_2^- + H_2O$ Enolate formation, the basis of aldol and haloform reactions

NEET tip: NEET often hinges on spotting which carbon has α-hydrogens before predicting aldol or Cannizzaro products.

Aldol condensation, Cannizzaro reaction and haloform reaction

Aldol condensation occurs when aldehydes or ketones with at least one α-H are treated with dilute NaOH. The enolate attacks a second carbonyl molecule to give a β-hydroxy aldehyde (aldol) or β-hydroxy ketone (ketol). On heating, this loses water to give an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound. Crossed aldol between two different carbonyl compounds, each with α-H, gives four products. Claisen-Schmidt condensation is the crossed aldol of ArCHO with a ketone; the E (trans) alkene is favoured. In the Cannizzaro reaction, aldehydes without α-H react with conc. NaOH and disproportionate: one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate and another is reduced to the alcohol by hydride transfer. In crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO, the HCHO is always the molecule oxidised, to formate. In the haloform reaction, methyl ketones ($CH_3CO–$), $CH_3CHO$, ethanol and $CH_3CH(OH)R$ react with NaOX to give a haloform and a carboxylate with one carbon fewer. Any C=C bond present is not attacked. Chloroform slowly oxidises in air and light to poisonous phosgene.

  • Aldol needs an α-H and dilute base; heating gives the α,β-unsaturated product
  • Two different enolisable carbonyl compounds give four crossed aldol products
  • Claisen-Schmidt reaction: ArCHO + ketone gives an α,β-unsaturated ketone (E isomer favoured)
  • Cannizzaro needs no α-H and conc. NaOH; it is a disproportionation
  • Crossed Cannizzaro: HCHO is oxidised to $HCOO^-$ and the other aldehyde is reduced
  • Haloform: $CH_3CO-R$ gives $R-COO^- + CHX_3$; $CHI_3$ is a yellow precipitate
  • $CHCl_3$ forms phosgene ($COCl_2$) on exposure to air and light

$2CH_3CHO \xrightarrow{dil.\ NaOH} CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO \xrightarrow{\Delta} CH_3CH=CHCHO + H_2O$ Aldol condensation of ethanal giving but-2-enal

$2C_6H_5CHO + NaOH(conc.) \rightarrow C_6H_5CH_2OH + C_6H_5COONa$ Cannizzaro reaction

$RCOCH_3 + 3NaOX \rightarrow RCOONa + CHX_3 + 2NaOH$ Haloform reaction of methyl ketones

$2CHCl_3 + O_2 \xrightarrow{light} 2COCl_2 + 2HCl$ Formation of poisonous phosgene from chloroform

NEET tip: NEET builds product-prediction questions on self versus crossed aldol, crossed Cannizzaro, and haloform products such as carboxylate plus CHX3.

Chemical tests to distinguish aldehydes and ketones

Aldehydes are reducing agents, while ketones generally are not. Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) is reduced by all aldehydes, aliphatic and aromatic, giving a silver mirror. Fehling's solution and Benedict's solution (both alkaline $Cu^{2+}$ complexes) give a red-brown precipitate of $Cu_2O$ only with aliphatic aldehydes; aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde do not respond. Schiff's reagent (decolourised rosaniline dye) turns pink with aldehydes. The iodoform test ($I_2$/NaOH) gives a yellow $CHI_3$ precipitate with methyl ketones and with acetaldehyde, the only aldehyde that responds. The 2,4-DNP test gives an orange-yellow precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones, so it confirms a carbonyl group without distinguishing between them. Sodium bisulphite adds to aldehydes and to most methyl ketones. α-Hydroxy ketones such as fructose also reduce Tollens' and Fehling's reagents.

  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with all aldehydes
  • Fehling's and Benedict's solutions give red $Cu_2O$ with aliphatic aldehydes only
  • Schiff's reagent turns pink (magenta) with aldehydes
  • Iodoform test is positive for methyl ketones $CH_3COR$, $CH_3CHO$, $C_2H_5OH$ and $CH_3CH(OH)R$, but not for $CH_3COOH$ or its esters and amides
  • 2,4-DNP is positive for both aldehydes and ketones
  • Benzaldehyde is positive with Tollens' but negative with Fehling's

$RCHO + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+ + 3OH^- \rightarrow RCOO^- + 2Ag + 2H_2O + 4NH_3$ Tollens' (silver mirror) test

$RCHO + 2Cu^{2+} + 5OH^- \rightarrow RCOO^- + Cu_2O \downarrow + 3H_2O$ Fehling's test, red-brown precipitate

NEET tip: NEET asks which test distinguishes a given pair, such as benzaldehyde versus acetophenone or propanal versus propanone.

Carboxylic acids: acidic strength and factors affecting it

Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols and alcohols. The carboxylate ion is stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures, which place the negative charge equally on two oxygens. In phenoxide, the charge is delocalised onto less electronegative carbon atoms. As a result, carboxylic acids release $CO_2$ with $NaHCO_3$ (brisk effervescence), whereas phenols do not. Electron-withdrawing groups stabilise the anion and increase acidity. Acidity increases with the number of such groups, with their electronegativity, and as they move closer to the COOH group. Electron-donating groups decrease acidity. Typical $pK_a$ values are $HCOOH$ 3.75, $C_6H_5COOH$ 4.19 and $CH_3COOH$ 4.76. Directly attached sp2 or phenyl groups increase acidity. In benzoic acids, $-NO_2$ increases acidity and $-OCH_3$ at the para position decreases it. Most ortho-substituted benzoic acids are stronger than benzoic acid itself, an observation known as the ortho effect.

  • The carboxylate ion has equivalent resonance structures, so carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols
  • $RCOOH + NaHCO_3$ gives $CO_2$ effervescence; phenols do not
  • $CF_3COOH > CCl_3COOH > CHCl_2COOH > ClCH_2COOH > CH_3COOH$
  • $FCH_2COOH > ClCH_2COOH > BrCH_2COOH > ICH_2COOH$
  • 2-chlorobutanoic > 3-chlorobutanoic > 4-chlorobutanoic acid; the -I effect falls with distance
  • $HCOOH > C_6H_5COOH > CH_3COOH > (CH_3)_2CHCOOH$
  • p-nitrobenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-methoxybenzoic acid; most ortho isomers are stronger (ortho effect)

$RCOOH + NaHCO_3 \rightarrow RCOONa + H_2O + CO_2 \uparrow$ Test for the carboxylic acid group

$K_a = \frac{[RCOO^-][H_3O^+]}{[RCOOH]}$ Acid dissociation constant; larger $K_a$ means a stronger acid

NEET tip: Arranging substituted acids by pKa, or choosing the reagent (NaHCO3) that separates acids from phenols, is common in NEET.

Formula sheet

$R-OH \xrightarrow{conc.\ HCl/ZnCl_2} R-Cl$ Lucas test; turbidity appears immediately (3°), in about 5 min (2°) or not at room temperature (1°)

$CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{conc.\ H_2SO_4,\ 443\ K} CH_2=CH_2$ Acid-catalysed dehydration via a carbocation

$C_6H_5OH + 3Br_2(aq) \rightarrow C_6H_2Br_3OH$ Bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol

$C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{CHCl_3,\ NaOH;\ H^+} o-HOC_6H_4CHO$ Reimer-Tiemann reaction; the electrophile is $:CCl_2$

$C_6H_5CH_3 \xrightarrow{CrO_2Cl_2,\ CS_2;\ H_3O^+} C_6H_5CHO$ Etard reaction giving benzaldehyde

$C_6H_5COCl \xrightarrow{H_2,\ Pd/BaSO_4} C_6H_5CHO$ Rosenmund reduction of an acid chloride to an aldehyde

$C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{anhyd.\ AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3$ Friedel-Crafts acylation giving acetophenone

$>C=O + HCN \rightarrow >C(OH)CN$ Cyanohydrin formation (base catalysed)

$>C=O + H_2N-Z \rightarrow >C=N-Z$ Oxime, hydrazone, phenylhydrazone, 2,4-DNP derivative or semicarbazone formation at pH about 3.5

$>C=O + RMgX \xrightarrow{H_3O^+} >C(R)OH$ HCHO gives a 1° alcohol, RCHO a 2° alcohol, $R_2CO$ a 3° alcohol

$>C=O \xrightarrow{Zn-Hg/HCl} >CH_2$ Clemmensen reduction (acidic medium)

$>C=O \xrightarrow{NH_2NH_2;\ KOH/glycol,\ \Delta} >CH_2$ Wolff-Kishner reduction (basic medium)

$2RCH_2CHO \xrightarrow{dil.\ NaOH} RCH_2CH(OH)CH(R)CHO$ Aldol addition; needs α-H; heating gives the α,β-unsaturated product

$2ArCHO \xrightarrow{conc.\ NaOH} ArCH_2OH + ArCOO^-$ Cannizzaro reaction; needs no α-H

$RCOCH_3 + 3NaOX \rightarrow RCOONa + CHX_3 + 2NaOH$ Haloform reaction; $CHI_3$ is a yellow precipitate

$RCHO + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+ + 3OH^- \rightarrow RCOO^- + 2Ag + 2H_2O + 4NH_3$ Tollens' silver mirror test for aldehydes

$RCHO + 2Cu^{2+} + 5OH^- \rightarrow RCOO^- + Cu_2O + 3H_2O$ Fehling's test; aliphatic aldehydes only

$RCOOH + NaHCO_3 \rightarrow RCOONa + H_2O + CO_2$ Effervescence distinguishes acids from phenols

$pK_a = -\log K_a$ A lower $pK_a$ means a stronger acid

$RCOOH > C_6H_5OH > H_2O > C_2H_5OH$ Order of acidity

$HCHO > CH_3CHO > CH_3COCH_3$ Order of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition

Common traps

  • Assuming every aldehyde gives a positive Fehling's test. Benzaldehyde and other aromatic aldehydes give the Tollens' test but not the Fehling's test.
  • Thinking phenol reacts with NaHCO3. Phenol is weaker than carbonic acid, so only carboxylic acids (and very strong phenols such as picric acid) liberate CO2.
  • Using aldol conditions for aldehydes without α-H. HCHO, PhCHO and (CH3)3CCHO undergo Cannizzaro reaction with conc. NaOH instead. In crossed Cannizzaro, HCHO is always oxidised.
  • Forgetting that the iodoform test is positive for ethanol, acetaldehyde and 2° alcohols of the type CH3CH(OH)R. The haloform product acid has one carbon fewer than the methyl ketone.
  • Writing o-nitrophenol as more acidic than p-nitrophenol. Intramolecular H-bonding makes the ortho isomer slightly weaker, but also makes it steam volatile.
  • Interchanging Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl, acidic) with Wolff-Kishner (NH2NH2/KOH, basic). Choose the method by the acid or base sensitivity of the other groups present.
  • Counting α-hydrogens wrongly. A carbon adjacent to C=O that carries three alkyl groups, as in (CH3)3C–, has no α-H, so condensation can occur only at the other α-carbon.
  • Assuming 2,4-DNP distinguishes aldehydes from ketones. It is positive for both, and only confirms the presence of a carbonyl group.

Quick revision

  • Lucas test: turbidity is immediate for 3°, appears in about 5 min for 2°, and does not form at room temperature for 1°. Over Cu at 573 K, 1° alcohols give aldehydes, 2° give ketones and 3° give alkenes.
  • In dehydration, carbocation formation is the slow step. Ease is 3° > 2° > 1°, the Saytzeff product is major, and rearrangements are possible.
  • Phenol has pKa about 10 because phenoxide is resonance stabilised. EWG at ortho/para positions increase acidity and EDG decrease it.
  • Bromine water converts phenol to a white 2,4,6-tribromophenol precipitate. Dilute HNO3 gives o- and p-nitrophenol (ortho is steam volatile), and conc. HNO3 gives picric acid.
  • Reimer-Tiemann: CHCl3 with NaOH gives the :CCl2 electrophile and salicylaldehyde; using CCl4 gives salicylic acid.
  • In ethers, O is sp3 hybridised and the C–O–C angle is about 111.7°. HI cleaves anisole to phenol and CH3I.
  • The C=O carbon is sp2 and electrophilic. Nucleophilic addition reactivity is HCHO > CH3CHO > ketones, and aliphatic carbonyls are more reactive than aromatic ones.
  • With ammonia derivatives, NH2OH gives oximes, N2H4 hydrazones, PhNHNH2 phenylhydrazones and semicarbazide semicarbazones. Grignard addition gives 1°, 2° or 3° alcohols.
  • Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) and Wolff-Kishner (N2H4, KOH, glycol) both convert C=O to CH2.
  • Aldol condensation needs an α-H and dilute base. Cannizzaro needs no α-H and conc. base. The haloform reaction needs a methyl ketone (CH3CO–R) group and gives CHX3 plus RCOO–.
  • Tollens' reagent responds to all aldehydes, Fehling's only to aliphatic ones. The iodoform test detects methyl ketones and CH3CHO, and 2,4-DNP detects any carbonyl.
  • Acid strength: CF3COOH > CCl3COOH > ClCH2COOH > HCOOH > PhCOOH > CH3COOH. The -I effect falls with distance, and ortho-substituted benzoic acids are stronger (ortho effect).

Chemistry · Unit 18: Organic Compounds Containing Nitrogen

This unit covers amines and arenediazonium salts: how amines are prepared, their structure and nomenclature, why they are basic and how that basicity changes with structure, the tests that tell primary, secondary and tertiary amines apart, and how diazonium salts convert $-NH_2$ into many other groups on a benzene ring. NEET asks 1-3 questions from it every year, mostly on reagent-product matching, basicity order, distinguishing tests and conversion sequences built on NCERT reactions.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q79, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q84

General methods of preparation, properties, reactions and uses

Amines are prepared mainly by five routes. Nitro compounds are reduced with $Sn/HCl$, $Fe/HCl$ or $H_2/Pd$; $Fe/HCl$ is preferred because the $FeCl_2$ formed is hydrolysed back to $HCl$. Alkyl halides undergo ammonolysis, but this gives a mixture of 1°, 2° and 3° amines and the quaternary salt. Nitriles are reduced with $LiAlH_4$, $H_2/Ni$ or $Na/C_2H_5OH$; amides are reduced with $LiAlH_4$ followed by $H_2O$. Gabriel phthalimide synthesis gives pure 1° aliphatic amines only. Hofmann bromamide degradation gives a 1° amine with one carbon fewer than the amide. Lower amines are gases or liquids with a fishy smell. Their boiling points are lower than those of alcohols because N-H...N hydrogen bonds are weaker than O-H...O bonds. Key reactions are alkylation, acylation, benzoylation, the carbylamine reaction, reaction with $HNO_2$ and electrophilic substitution in aniline. Amines are used in dyes, drugs and polymers.

  • Reduction of nitrobenzene with $Sn/HCl$ or $Fe/HCl$ followed by neutralisation gives aniline; $NaBH_4$ does not reduce $-NO_2$ to $-NH_2$
  • $RCN \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} RCH_2NH_2$: benzonitrile gives benzylamine, not aniline
  • $RCONH_2 \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4,\ H_2O} RCH_2NH_2$: the carbon count is retained
  • Hofmann bromamide: $RCONH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow RNH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O$, so the amine has one carbon less; benzamide gives aniline
  • Gabriel synthesis cannot make aromatic 1° amines, because aryl halides do not undergo $S_N$ reaction with the phthalimide anion
  • Ammonolysis of alkyl halides gives a mixture; using excess $NH_3$ favours the 1° amine
  • Acid hydrolysis of acetanilide gives aniline, since the amide bond is cleaved
  • Boiling points follow 1° > 2° > 3° for isomeric amines; 3° amines have no N-H bond and cannot hydrogen bond among themselves
  • Bromine water converts aniline to a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline
  • Direct nitration of aniline gives a large amount of meta product (about 47%) because the anilinium ion forms in acid; acetylation first gives mainly the para product
  • Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reactions, because the $-NH_2$ group forms a salt with $AlCl_3$ and deactivates the ring
  • Sulphonation of aniline gives sulphanilic acid, which exists as a zwitterion
  • Aniline darkens on storage because it is oxidised by air

$C_6H_5NO_2 \xrightarrow{Sn/HCl\ or\ Fe/HCl} C_6H_5NH_2$ Standard preparation of aniline

$RCONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/NaOH} RNH_2$ Hofmann bromamide degradation; the product has one carbon fewer

$RC\equiv N \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4\ or\ Na/C_2H_5OH} RCH_2NH_2$ Reduction of a nitrile to a 1° amine, ascending the series by one carbon

$C_6H_5NH_2 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{pyridine} C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 + HCl$ Acetylation; pyridine removes the $HCl$ formed, driving the reaction forward. Acetylation itself moderates the activating effect of $-NH_2$, because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl group

NEET tip: NEET most often asks which reagent gives a given amine; check the carbon count (Hofmann removes one carbon, nitrile reduction adds $CH_2$) and the reagent's actual reducing ability.

Amines: nomenclature, classification and structure

Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one, two or three hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups. They are classified as primary ($RNH_2$), secondary ($R_2NH$) or tertiary ($R_3N$); $R_4N^+X^-$ is a quaternary ammonium salt. In common names, alkylamine is written as one word (methylamine). In IUPAC names, the 'e' of the alkane is replaced by 'amine' (ethanamine). Substituents on nitrogen are shown with the locant N (N-methylethanamine). Aniline, $C_6H_5NH_2$, is accepted as the IUPAC name benzenamine. In aliphatic amines, nitrogen is $sp^3$ hybridised and pyramidal, and the lone pair occupies the fourth orbital. The C-N-C angle in trimethylamine is about $108^\circ$, close to tetrahedral. In aniline, the lone pair is delocalised into the ring, which gives nitrogen partial $sp^2$ character and a flatter geometry.

  • Classification depends on the number of carbons attached to nitrogen, not on the carbon bearing $-NH_2$; tert-butylamine is a 1° amine
  • Examples of IUPAC names: $CH_3NHC_2H_5$ is N-methylethanamine and $(CH_3)_2NC_6H_5$ is N,N-dimethylbenzenamine
  • Diamines are named with the suffix diamine, for example $H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2$ is hexane-1,6-diamine
  • Benzylamine ($C_6H_5CH_2NH_2$) is an aliphatic amine (phenylmethanamine), not an aryl amine
  • Toluidines are methylanilines and anisidines are methoxyanilines
  • Aliphatic amine nitrogen is $sp^3$ and pyramidal, with bond angles of about $108^\circ$
  • The general formula of saturated acyclic amines is $C_nH_{2n+3}N$

$C_nH_{2n+3}N$ General formula of saturated aliphatic amines, used to count isomers

NEET tip: Expect questions asking you to count isomers of $C_3H_9N$ or $C_4H_{11}N$ and classify them as 1°, 2° or 3°, or to pick the correct IUPAC name.

Basic character of amines

Amines are Lewis and Brønsted bases because nitrogen carries a lone pair. Basicity is measured by $K_b$ or $pK_b$: the larger the $K_b$ (or the smaller the $pK_b$), the stronger the base. Alkyl groups raise basicity through their +I effect. In water, however, the order is also controlled by solvation through hydrogen bonding and by steric hindrance. For methyl amines the order in water is $(CH_3)_2NH > CH_3NH_2 > (CH_3)_3N > NH_3$. For ethyl amines it is $(C_2H_5)_2NH > (C_2H_5)_3N > C_2H_5NH_2 > NH_3$. In the gas phase only the inductive effect operates, so the order is 3° > 2° > 1° > $NH_3$. Aryl amines are much weaker bases ($pK_b$ of aniline is 9.38) because the lone pair is delocalised into the ring and the anilinium ion has fewer resonance structures. Electron-donating ring groups raise basicity and electron-withdrawing groups lower it.

  • Approximate $pK_b$ values: $(C_2H_5)_2NH$ 3.00, $(C_2H_5)_3N$ 3.25, $C_2H_5NH_2$ 3.29, $(CH_3)_2NH$ 3.27, $CH_3NH_2$ 3.38, $(CH_3)_3N$ 4.22, $NH_3$ 4.75, $C_6H_5NH_2$ 9.38
  • Overall order: aliphatic amines > $NH_3$ > aryl amines
  • p-Toluidine ($pK_b$ 8.92) and p-anisidine ($pK_b$ 8.70) are more basic than aniline
  • p-Nitroaniline ($pK_b$ about 13.0) is much less basic than aniline because $-NO_2$ shows -R and -I effects
  • Benzylamine is more basic than aniline because its lone pair is not delocalised into the ring
  • N-Methylaniline and N,N-dimethylaniline are slightly more basic than aniline
  • Amines form salts with mineral acids, for example $C_6H_5NH_3^+Cl^-$; treating the salt with $NaOH$ regenerates the amine
  • Amides are almost neutral because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl group

$RNH_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons RNH_3^+ + OH^-$ Base ionisation of an amine in water

$K_b = \frac{[RNH_3^+][OH^-]}{[RNH_2]}$ Base dissociation constant of an amine

$pK_b = -\log K_b$ A lower $pK_b$ means a stronger base

$pK_a + pK_b = 14$ Relation between a conjugate acid-base pair at 298 K; a weaker base has a stronger conjugate acid

NEET tip: NEET asks you to arrange amines in order of basicity (aqueous versus gas phase, or substituted anilines), often combined with a reduction or oxidation product as in the p-nitrotoluene statement questions.

Identification of primary, secondary and tertiary amines

Three tests distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines. In the Hinsberg test, the amine reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride ($C_6H_5SO_2Cl$). A 1° amine gives an N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide, which dissolves in alkali because its N-H is acidic. A 2° amine gives an N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, which has no acidic H and is insoluble in alkali. A 3° amine does not react. The carbylamine (isocyanide) test is given only by 1° amines, aliphatic or aromatic: heating with $CHCl_3$ and alcoholic $KOH$ produces a foul-smelling isocyanide. Nitrous acid ($NaNO_2 + HCl$) also distinguishes the classes. 1° aliphatic amines liberate $N_2$ gas. 1° aromatic amines give diazonium salts at 273-278 K. 2° amines give yellow oily N-nitrosamines. 3° aliphatic amines form soluble salts, while 3° aromatic amines undergo ring nitrosation at the para position.

  • Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride; p-toluenesulphonyl chloride works the same way
  • 1° amine gives a sulphonamide that is soluble in $KOH$; 2° gives one that is insoluble; 3° gives no reaction
  • The carbylamine test is positive only for 1° amines, both aliphatic and aromatic
  • 1° aliphatic amines with $HNO_2$ give effervescence of $N_2$ and a mixture of products (alcohol, alkene)
  • Aniline with $NaNO_2/HCl$ at 273-278 K gives benzenediazonium chloride without evolving $N_2$
  • 2° amines with $HNO_2$ give yellow, oily N-nitrosamines, which are carcinogenic
  • N,N-Dimethylaniline with $HNO_2$ gives p-nitroso-N,N-dimethylaniline, a green solid

$RNH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \xrightarrow{\Delta} RNC + 3KCl + 3H_2O$ Carbylamine test, positive only for 1° amines

$RNH_2 + HNO_2 \rightarrow ROH + N_2 + H_2O$ 1° aliphatic amine with nitrous acid; $N_2$ effervescence

$C_6H_5SO_2Cl + RNH_2 \rightarrow C_6H_5SO_2NHR + HCl$ Hinsberg reaction; the product dissolves in alkali

NEET tip: Typical questions ask which test distinguishes a given pair of amines, or which statement about Hinsberg or carbylamine behaviour is correct.

Diazonium salts: importance in synthetic organic chemistry

Arenediazonium salts, $ArN_2^+X^-$, are made by diazotisation: a 1° aromatic amine is treated with $NaNO_2 + HCl$ at 273-278 K. They are stable only in cold solution, and arene salts are more stable than alkyl ones because of resonance with the ring. Because $N_2$ is an excellent leaving group, the $-N_2^+$ group can be replaced by Cl, Br or CN (Sandmeyer reaction with Cu(I) salts, or Gattermann reaction with Cu/HX), by I (with $KI$), by F (heating the fluoroborate), by H (with $H_3PO_2$ or ethanol), by OH (warm water) or by $NO_2$. This makes them the standard route to fluoro- and iodobenzenes and to substitution patterns that direct substitution cannot give, such as 1,3,5-tribromobenzene. In coupling reactions the $N_2$ group is retained: with phenol in alkaline medium they give orange p-hydroxyazobenzene, and with aniline in mildly acidic medium they give yellow p-aminoazobenzene. These coloured azo compounds are used as dyes.

  • Diazotisation is carried out at 273-278 K because the salt decomposes to phenol and $N_2$ at higher temperatures
  • Sandmeyer reactions: $CuCl/HCl$ gives $ArCl$, $CuBr/HBr$ gives $ArBr$, $CuCN/KCN$ gives $ArCN$
  • Gattermann reaction: copper powder with $HCl$ or $HBr$ gives $ArCl$ or $ArBr$
  • Iodobenzene forms directly with $KI$ and no catalyst is needed
  • Fluorobenzene is made by heating $ArN_2^+BF_4^-$ (Balz-Schiemann reaction)
  • $H_3PO_2$ or $CH_3CH_2OH$ replaces $-N_2^+$ by H; this is used to remove $-NH_2$ after it has served as a directing group
  • Warming in water gives phenol, $ArOH$
  • $ArN_2^+BF_4^-$ with $NaNO_2/Cu$ on heating gives nitrobenzene
  • Coupling is electrophilic substitution, usually at the para position, and the $N_2$ group is retained
  • The sequence aniline, then $Br_2$ water, then diazotisation, then $H_3PO_2$ gives 1,3,5-tribromobenzene

$C_6H_5NH_2 + NaNO_2 + 2HCl \xrightarrow{273-278\ K} C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + NaCl + 2H_2O$ Diazotisation

$ArN_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{CuCN/KCN} ArCN + N_2$ Sandmeyer cyanation

$ArN_2^+Cl^- \xrightarrow{HBF_4} ArN_2^+BF_4^- \xrightarrow{\Delta} ArF + BF_3 + N_2$ Preparation of aryl fluorides

$ArN_2^+Cl^- + H_3PO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow ArH + N_2 + H_3PO_3 + HCl$ Replacement of the diazo group by H

$C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{OH^-} p\text{-}HOC_6H_4N{=}NC_6H_5$ Coupling with phenol gives an orange azo dye

NEET tip: NEET sets multi-step conversions (A to B to C) and reagent-product matching for Sandmeyer, Gattermann, $KI$, $HBF_4$, $H_3PO_2$ and coupling reactions.

Formula sheet

$C_6H_5NO_2 \xrightarrow{Fe/HCl} C_6H_5NH_2$ Preparation of aniline; $Fe/HCl$ is preferred

$RCONH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow RNH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O$ Hofmann bromamide degradation; product has one carbon fewer

$RCN \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} RCH_2NH_2$ Nitrile reduction; amine has one carbon more than the alkyl halide used to make the nitrile

$RCONH_2 \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} RCH_2NH_2$ Amide reduction; carbon count unchanged

$Phthalimide \xrightarrow{KOH} \xrightarrow{RX} \xrightarrow{NaOH(aq)} RNH_2$ Gabriel synthesis; pure 1° aliphatic amines only

$RNH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \rightarrow RNC + 3KCl + 3H_2O$ Carbylamine test for 1° amines

$C_6H_5SO_2Cl$ Hinsberg's reagent; product soluble in alkali (1°), insoluble (2°), no reaction (3°)

$NaNO_2 + HCl,\ 273-278\ K$ Diazotisation conditions for 1° aryl amines

$pK_b = -\log K_b$ Lower $pK_b$ means stronger base

$(C_2H_5)_2NH > (C_2H_5)_3N > C_2H_5NH_2 > NH_3$ Basicity of ethyl amines in water

$(CH_3)_2NH > CH_3NH_2 > (CH_3)_3N > NH_3$ Basicity of methyl amines in water

$3° > 2° > 1° > NH_3$ Basicity in the gas phase (inductive effect only)

$C_6H_5NH_2 + 3Br_2 \rightarrow 2,4,6\text{-}Br_3C_6H_2NH_2 + 3HBr$ Bromination of aniline gives a white precipitate

$ArN_2^+ \xrightarrow{CuCl/HCl} ArCl$ Sandmeyer chlorination; $CuBr/HBr$ gives $ArBr$

$ArN_2^+ \xrightarrow{Cu/HCl} ArCl$ Gattermann reaction

$ArN_2^+ \xrightarrow{KI} ArI$ Iodination without a catalyst

$ArN_2^+BF_4^- \xrightarrow{\Delta} ArF$ Balz-Schiemann fluorination

$ArN_2^+ \xrightarrow{H_3PO_2\ or\ C_2H_5OH} ArH$ Deamination (replacement by H)

$ArN_2^+ \xrightarrow{H_2O,\ warm} ArOH$ Preparation of phenol

$ArN_2^+ + C_6H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{H^+} p\text{-}H_2NC_6H_4N{=}NAr$ Coupling with aniline gives yellow p-aminoazobenzene

Common traps

  • Assuming benzonitrile with $LiAlH_4$ gives aniline. It gives benzylamine, $C_6H_5CH_2NH_2$, because the cyano carbon is kept.
  • Thinking $NaBH_4$ reduces nitrobenzene to aniline. $NaBH_4$ is a mild hydride reagent that does not reduce $-NO_2$; use $Sn/HCl$, $Fe/HCl$ or $H_2/Pd$.
  • Assuming 3° amines are the most basic in water. Solvation and steric effects make 2° amines the strongest; 3° amines are strongest only in the gas phase.
  • Using Gabriel synthesis to make aniline. It fails because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.
  • Expecting only o/p products from direct nitration of aniline. Protonation gives the meta-directing $-NH_3^+$ group, so about 47% of the product is meta; protect the group by acetylation first.
  • Classifying tert-butylamine as a 3° amine. It is 1° because nitrogen is bonded to only one carbon.
  • Thinking 2° or 3° amines give the carbylamine test. Only 1° amines (aliphatic and aromatic) give an isocyanide.
  • Assuming electron-withdrawing groups make both acids and amines weaker. A p-$NO_2$ group strengthens benzoic acid but weakens aniline as a base, while p-$CH_3$ makes p-toluidine more basic than aniline.

Quick revision

  • Hofmann bromamide removes one carbon; nitrile reduction adds one carbon (as $CH_2$); amide reduction keeps the carbon count.
  • Gabriel synthesis gives pure 1° aliphatic amines only, never aryl amines.
  • Boiling points: 1° > 2° > 3° amines, and all are lower than the corresponding alcohols.
  • Aqueous basicity: $(C_2H_5)_2NH > (C_2H_5)_3N > C_2H_5NH_2 > NH_3$ and $(CH_3)_2NH > CH_3NH_2 > (CH_3)_3N > NH_3$.
  • Aryl amines are weaker bases than $NH_3$; the $pK_b$ of aniline is 9.38.
  • Electron-donating groups ($-CH_3$, $-OCH_3$) raise the basicity of aniline; electron-withdrawing groups ($-NO_2$, $-Cl$) lower it.
  • Hinsberg test: 1° sulphonamide is alkali-soluble, 2° is insoluble, 3° does not react.
  • Carbylamine test (foul-smelling isocyanide) is given only by 1° amines.
  • With $HNO_2$: 1° aliphatic gives $N_2$, 1° aromatic gives a diazonium salt, 2° gives a yellow N-nitrosamine.
  • Aniline gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline with bromine water, gives sulphanilic acid on sulphonation and does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reactions.
  • Diazonium reagents: Sandmeyer uses Cu(I) salts, Gattermann uses Cu/HX, $KI$ gives $ArI$, $HBF_4$ then heat gives $ArF$, $H_3PO_2$ gives $ArH$, warm water gives $ArOH$.
  • Coupling: phenol in alkaline medium gives an orange azo dye; aniline in mildly acidic medium gives a yellow azo dye; substitution is at the para position and $N_2$ is retained.

Chemistry · Unit 19: Biomolecules

Biomolecules covers the chemistry of the organic molecules that build and run living systems: carbohydrates, proteins, enzymes, vitamins, nucleic acids and hormones. NEET asks one to three direct, mostly factual questions from this unit every year. Typical angles are glucose structure evidence, reducing versus non-reducing sugars, glycosidic linkages, protein structure levels, vitamin sources and deficiencies, and DNA versus RNA composition. Learning the NCERT lines closely is the fastest way to score here.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q50, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q80

General introduction and importance of biomolecules

Living systems are made of non-living molecules called biomolecules. They interact to sustain and reproduce life. The main classes are carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, vitamins and hormones. Carbohydrates are the chief energy source and also serve as structural material, for example cellulose in plant cell walls. Proteins form the structural basis of tissues, and as enzymes they catalyse almost every biochemical reaction. Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) store and transmit genetic information and direct protein synthesis. Vitamins are needed in small amounts for normal growth and health. Hormones act as chemical messengers that coordinate body functions. Most biomolecules are polymers of simple units: monosaccharides, amino acids and nucleotides. NEET treats this unit as largely factual, so precise NCERT terminology matters.

  • Major biomolecules: carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, vitamins, hormones
  • Monosaccharides polymerise to polysaccharides
  • Amino acids polymerise to proteins
  • Nucleotides polymerise to nucleic acids
  • Carbohydrates provide energy and structural support
  • Proteins act as structural material and as enzymes
  • Nucleic acids carry heredity
  • Vitamins and hormones regulate metabolism

NEET tip: Rarely asked on its own; it frames which monomer builds which biopolymer.

Carbohydrates: classification; aldoses and ketoses

Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give these units on hydrolysis. Many fit the formula $C_x(H_2O)_y$ (hydrates of carbon), but this definition fails both ways. Rhamnose, $C_6H_{12}O_5$, is a carbohydrate yet does not fit the formula. Acetic acid, $C_2H_4O_2$, fits the formula but is not a carbohydrate. On the basis of hydrolysis, carbohydrates fall into three classes: 1. Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further (glucose, fructose, ribose). 2. Oligosaccharides give 2 to 10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis; disaccharides include sucrose, maltose and lactose. 3. Polysaccharides give a large number of units (starch, cellulose, glycogen, gums). Sweet, crystalline, water-soluble carbohydrates are called sugars. Carbohydrates that reduce Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent are reducing sugars. All monosaccharides are reducing sugars. A monosaccharide with an aldehyde group is an aldose, and one with a keto group is a ketose. They are further named by carbon count, for example aldohexose (glucose) and ketohexose (fructose).

  • All monosaccharides, both aldoses and ketoses, are reducing sugars
  • Disaccharides are reducing only if a free hemiacetal or hemiketal group remains
  • Maltose and lactose are reducing; sucrose is non-reducing
  • Glucose is an aldohexose; fructose is a ketohexose
  • Ribose is an aldopentose; glyceraldehyde is an aldotriose
  • D or L configuration is assigned relative to glyceraldehyde
  • D-sugar: the $-OH$ on the lowest asymmetric carbon points to the right in the Fischer projection
  • D/L describes configuration, not the sign of rotation, which is shown as (+) or (-)
  • Polysaccharides are non-sugars: not sweet, generally insoluble

$C_x(H_2O)_y$ General formula of many carbohydrates; not a valid definition, since rhamnose and acetic acid are exceptions

NEET tip: Expect statement-type questions on which sugars are reducing and on classifying a sugar as an aldose or ketose with a given number of carbons.

Monosaccharides: glucose and fructose

Glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$) is prepared in two ways: 1. By boiling sucrose with dilute $HCl$ or $H_2SO_4$ in alcoholic solution. 2. Commercially, by hydrolysing starch with dilute $H_2SO_4$ at 393 K under 2 to 3 atm. The open-chain structure is proved by these reactions: 1. Prolonged heating with $HI$ gives n-hexane, so the six carbons form a straight chain. 2. Glucose forms an oxime with $NH_2OH$ and a cyanohydrin with $HCN$, so a carbonyl group is present. 3. Bromine water oxidises it to gluconic acid, so the carbonyl is an aldehyde. 4. Acetylation gives a pentaacetate, so there are five $-OH$ groups. 5. Nitric acid gives saccharic acid, so a primary alcohol group is present. The open-chain structure cannot explain everything. Glucose does not give Schiff's test or form an adduct with $NaHSO_3$, its pentaacetate does not react with $NH_2OH$, and it exists in alpha and beta forms. These facts are explained by a six-membered cyclic hemiacetal (pyranose) formed between the C5 $-OH$ and the $-CHO$ group. The alpha and beta forms are anomers that differ only at C1. Fructose is D-(-)-fructose, a ketohexose with its keto group at C2. It forms a five-membered furanose ring through its C5 $-OH$.

  • $HI$ gives n-hexane, proving a straight chain
  • Bromine water gives gluconic acid, proving an aldehyde group
  • $HNO_3$ gives saccharic acid, proving a primary alcohol group
  • Pentaacetate formation proves five $-OH$ groups
  • Glucose gives a negative Schiff's test and no $NaHSO_3$ adduct
  • Alpha-glucose melts at 419 K; beta-glucose melts at 423 K
  • Anomers differ at C1, the anomeric carbon
  • Glucose forms a pyranose (six-membered) ring
  • Fructose forms a furanose (five-membered) ring
  • Natural glucose is D-(+); natural fructose is D-(-), laevorotatory

$C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} C_6H_{12}O_6\,(\text{glucose}) + C_6H_{12}O_6\,(\text{fructose})$ Preparation of glucose from sucrose

$(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n + nH_2O \xrightarrow{H^+,\ 393\,K,\ 2-3\,atm} nC_6H_{12}O_6$ Commercial preparation of glucose from starch

$CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HI,\ \Delta} CH_3(CH_2)_4CH_3$ Proves a straight six-carbon chain

$CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH \xrightarrow{Br_2\ water} COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH$ Gluconic acid forms, proving an aldehyde group

$CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HNO_3} COOH(CHOH)_4COOH$ Saccharic acid forms, proving a primary alcohol group

NEET tip: NEET often asks which reagent proves which structural feature, or which observations the open-chain structure cannot explain.

Constituent monosaccharides of sucrose, lactose and maltose

Sucrose is made of alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-fructose. They are joined by a glycosidic linkage between C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose. Both reducing groups are used up in this bond, so sucrose is non-reducing. Sucrose itself is dextrorotatory. Its hydrolysis gives glucose ($+52.5^\circ$) and fructose ($-92.4^\circ$). The product mixture is laevorotatory, so the sign of rotation changes. This process is called inversion, and the product is invert sugar. Maltose contains two alpha-D-glucose units joined C1 to C4. Lactose, the milk sugar, contains beta-D-galactose and beta-D-glucose joined C1 of galactose to C4 of glucose. In both maltose and lactose, the second unit keeps a free hemiacetal group, so both are reducing sugars.

  • Sucrose: alpha-D-glucose + beta-D-fructose, linked C1 to C2, non-reducing
  • Maltose: alpha-D-glucose + alpha-D-glucose, linked C1 to C4, reducing
  • Lactose: beta-D-galactose + beta-D-glucose, linked C1 to C4, reducing
  • Hydrolysis of sucrose gives laevorotatory invert sugar
  • Galactose appears only in lactose among these three
  • The bond between monosaccharide units is a glycosidic (ether-type) linkage

$\text{Sucrose}\,(+) \xrightarrow{H^+\ or\ invertase} \text{D-glucose}\,(+52.5^\circ) + \text{D-fructose}\,(-92.4^\circ)$ Inversion of cane sugar; the net rotation becomes negative

$\text{Maltose} + H_2O \xrightarrow{maltase} 2\,\text{D-glucose}$ Enzymatic hydrolysis of maltose

NEET tip: Matching a disaccharide with its constituent monosaccharides and linkage, and the reason sucrose is non-reducing, are frequent questions.

Alpha-amino acids, peptide bond and polypeptides

Alpha-amino acids carry an $-NH_2$ group and a $-COOH$ group on the same (alpha) carbon. They are obtained when proteins are hydrolysed. The general formula is $R-CH(NH_2)-COOH$; glycine has $R = H$ and alanine has $R = CH_3$. By the relative number of amino and carboxyl groups, amino acids are acidic, basic or neutral. Nutritionally, essential amino acids cannot be made in the body and must come from the diet; examples are valine, leucine, lysine and phenylalanine. Non-essential amino acids are synthesised by the body. All naturally occurring alpha-amino acids except glycine are optically active, and most have the L-configuration. In aqueous solution, the acidic carboxyl group and the basic amino group give a dipolar ion called a zwitterion. This makes amino acids amphoteric, crystalline solids with high melting points. A peptide bond is an amide link, $-CO-NH-$, formed between the $-COOH$ of one amino acid and the $-NH_2$ of another with loss of water. Two amino acids form a dipeptide. More than ten form a polypeptide. A polypeptide with more than about 100 residues and molecular mass above 10000 u is a protein.

  • Glycine is the only optically inactive natural alpha-amino acid
  • Natural amino acids mostly have the L-configuration
  • Zwitterion form: $H_3N^+-CHR-COO^-$
  • Zwitterions make amino acids amphoteric
  • Amino acids have high melting points and dissolve in water
  • Essential amino acids must be taken in the diet
  • Peptide bond: $-CO-NH-$, an amide linkage
  • Glycylalanine (Gly-Ala) is a dipeptide
  • Fibrous proteins (keratin, myosin) are insoluble in water
  • Globular proteins (insulin, albumins) are soluble in water

$R-CH(NH_2)-COOH \rightleftharpoons R-CH(NH_3^+)-COO^-$ Zwitterion formation; explains amphoteric nature

$H_2N-CH_2-COOH + H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COOH \rightarrow H_2N-CH_2-CO-NH-CH(CH_3)-COOH + H_2O$ Formation of the peptide bond in glycylalanine

NEET tip: Watch for questions on the zwitterion, optical inactivity of glycine, essential amino acids, and counting peptide bonds (n amino acids give n-1 peptide bonds).

Protein structure: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary

Protein structure is described at four levels. 1. Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in the chain. A change of even one amino acid can alter the protein's function. 2. Secondary structure is the shape the chain takes, and has two common forms: (a) In the alpha-helix, the chain twists into a right-handed screw. It is held by intramolecular hydrogen bonds between the $-NH$ of one residue and the $>C=O$ of an adjacent turn. (b) In the beta-pleated sheet, chains are stretched almost to maximum extension and laid side by side. They are held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds. 3. Tertiary structure is the further folding of the chain, which gives fibrous or globular molecules. It is stabilised by hydrogen bonds, disulphide linkages, van der Waals forces and electrostatic attractions. 4. Quaternary structure is the spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits, as in haemoglobin, which has four subunits. Proteins with only tertiary structure can also be fully biologically active.

  • Primary structure: the amino acid sequence, held by peptide bonds
  • Alpha-helix: right-handed, intramolecular hydrogen bonds
  • Beta-pleated sheet: intermolecular hydrogen bonds between side-by-side chains
  • Tertiary structure: overall folding into fibrous or globular shape
  • Tertiary bonds: hydrogen bonds, $-S-S-$ bonds, van der Waals and electrostatic forces
  • Quaternary structure exists only when two or more subunits are present
  • Haemoglobin has four subunits

NEET tip: Statement questions test the handedness of the alpha-helix, intra- versus intermolecular hydrogen bonding, and which level involves subunits.

Denaturation of proteins

A protein in its natural state in a living system is called a native protein and is biologically active. Physical changes such as heat, or chemical changes such as a shift in pH, disturb the hydrogen bonds. The globules then unfold and the helices uncoil, and the protein loses its biological activity. This is denaturation. During denaturation, the secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed, but the primary structure stays intact because peptide bonds are not broken. Two common examples are the coagulation of egg white on boiling and the curdling of milk. Milk curdles because bacteria produce lactic acid, which changes the pH.

  • Causes: change of temperature or pH, and some chemicals
  • Denaturation destroys secondary and tertiary structure
  • Primary structure and peptide bonds remain intact
  • The protein loses its biological activity
  • Examples: boiled egg white, curdling of milk by lactic acid

NEET tip: Usually asked as which structural level survives denaturation (the primary structure).

Enzymes

Enzymes are biocatalysts, and most are globular proteins. They catalyse reactions under mild conditions of temperature and pH and are highly specific for their substrate and reaction. For example, maltase converts maltose to glucose, and invertase hydrolyses sucrose. Enzymes are usually named by the suffix -ase. Enzymes that catalyse oxidation of one substrate with reduction of another are called oxidoreductases. Enzymes work by lowering the activation energy. For acid hydrolysis of sucrose, the activation energy is about 6.22 kJ mol$^{-1}$; with the enzyme sucrase it is about 2.15 kJ mol$^{-1}$. The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex, which then breaks into products. This is often described by the lock-and-key model.

  • Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins
  • They are highly specific and work at optimum temperature and pH
  • They are named with the suffix -ase
  • Maltase acts on maltose; invertase (sucrase) acts on sucrose
  • Enzymes lower activation energy without changing equilibrium
  • Mechanism: an enzyme-substrate complex forms at the active site

$E + S \rightleftharpoons ES \rightarrow E + P$ Enzyme-substrate complex mechanism

NEET tip: Typical questions match an enzyme to its substrate or test that enzymes are proteins that lower activation energy.

Vitamins: classification and functions

Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts in the diet for normal growth and health. Their deficiency causes specific diseases. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in the liver and adipose tissue. Water-soluble vitamins (the B group and C) are excreted in urine and must be supplied regularly; vitamin $B_{12}$ is the exception, as it is stored in the liver. Vitamin H (biotin) is soluble in neither water nor fat. Sources and deficiency diseases: 1. A: fish liver oil, carrots, butter, milk; deficiency causes xerophthalmia and night blindness. 2. $B_1$ (thiamine): yeast, milk, green vegetables, cereals; deficiency causes beri beri. 3. $B_2$ (riboflavin): milk, egg white, liver; deficiency causes cheilosis. 4. $B_6$ (pyridoxine): yeast, milk, egg yolk, cereals; deficiency causes convulsions. 5. $B_{12}$: meat, fish, egg, curd; deficiency causes pernicious anaemia. 6. C (ascorbic acid): citrus fruits, amla, green leafy vegetables; deficiency causes scurvy. 7. D: sunlight, fish, egg yolk; deficiency causes rickets and osteomalacia. 8. E: vegetable oils such as wheat germ oil and sunflower oil; deficiency causes fragile RBCs and muscular weakness. 9. K: green leafy vegetables; deficiency causes increased blood clotting time.

  • Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K
  • Water-soluble vitamins: the B group and C
  • Vitamin $B_{12}$ is water-soluble but stored in the liver
  • Vitamin H (biotin) is soluble in neither water nor fat
  • A: carrots, fish liver oil; night blindness
  • $B_1$: beri beri
  • $B_2$: cheilosis
  • $B_6$: convulsions
  • $B_{12}$: meat, fish; pernicious anaemia
  • C: citrus fruits, amla; scurvy
  • D: sunlight; rickets
  • E: sunflower and wheat germ oil; fragile RBCs
  • K: green leafy vegetables; delayed blood clotting

NEET tip: Match-list questions pair vitamins with sources or deficiency diseases; memorise the full table.

Nucleic acids: chemical constitution of DNA and RNA

Nucleic acids are long-chain polymers of nucleotides, so they are polynucleotides. Their hydrolysis gives a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and nitrogenous bases. In DNA the sugar is beta-D-2-deoxyribose and the bases are adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine. In RNA the sugar is beta-D-ribose and uracil replaces thymine. A nucleoside is a base attached at C1' of the sugar. A nucleotide is a nucleoside with phosphoric acid esterified at C5'. Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester linkages between C5' and C3' of adjacent sugars. DNA is a double helix, as proposed by Watson and Crick. Its two strands are complementary and held by hydrogen bonds: A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds, and G pairs with C through three. RNA is usually single-stranded and occurs in three types: mRNA, rRNA and tRNA.

  • Nucleoside = base + sugar
  • Nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate
  • Nucleotides are linked by 5'-3' phosphodiester bonds
  • DNA sugar is 2-deoxyribose, which lacks the $-OH$ at C2'
  • RNA sugar is ribose
  • Purines: adenine and guanine
  • Pyrimidines: cytosine, thymine and uracil
  • DNA bases: A, G, C, T; RNA bases: A, G, C, U
  • A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds); G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds)
  • DNA is a double helix; RNA is single-stranded
  • Types of RNA: mRNA, rRNA, tRNA

$\text{Base} + \text{Sugar} \rightarrow \text{Nucleoside};\ \text{Nucleoside} + H_3PO_4 \rightarrow \text{Nucleotide}$ Building units of nucleic acids

$[A] = [T],\ [G] = [C]$ Complementary base pairing in double-stranded DNA

NEET tip: NEET asks which base or sugar is absent in DNA or RNA, nucleoside versus nucleotide, and the number of hydrogen bonds in base pairs.

Biological functions of nucleic acids

DNA is the chemical basis of heredity and the reserve of genetic information. It carries the genetic code that keeps the identity of different species over millions of years. Before cell division, DNA replicates so that each daughter cell gets an identical copy. DNA directs protein synthesis, but RNA molecules carry out the actual synthesis: 1. mRNA carries the message from DNA. 2. tRNA brings specific amino acids. 3. rRNA forms part of the ribosomes where proteins are assembled. The flow of information is from DNA to RNA to protein. The DNA sequence of a person is unique, and this is the basis of DNA fingerprinting, used in forensics and paternity testing.

  • DNA stores genetic information and is the basis of heredity
  • DNA replicates before cell division
  • RNA carries out protein synthesis
  • mRNA carries the code; tRNA carries amino acids; rRNA forms ribosomes
  • Information flows DNA to RNA to protein
  • DNA fingerprinting identifies individuals

NEET tip: Usually tested as the role of DNA versus the role of the RNA types in protein synthesis.

Hormones: general introduction

Hormones are molecules that act as intercellular messengers. They are produced by endocrine glands and released directly into the bloodstream, which carries them to target sites. Chemically, hormones fall into three groups: 1. Steroids: estrogens and androgens. 2. Polypeptides: insulin and endorphins. 3. Amino acid derivatives: epinephrine, norepinephrine and thyroxine. Hormones maintain the balance of biological activities: 1. Insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose within a narrow range. 2. Epinephrine and norepinephrine mediate responses to external stimuli. 3. Thyroxine, made in the thyroid gland, is an iodinated derivative of tyrosine. Too little causes hypothyroidism (lethargy, obesity); too much causes hyperthyroidism.
