Iodine deficiency enlarges the thyroid, giving goitre. 4. Glucocorticoids control carbohydrate metabolism and inflammation. 5. Mineralocorticoids control the excretion of water and salt by the kidney. 6. Deficiency of adrenal cortex hormones causes Addison's disease. 7. Testosterone is the male sex hormone; estradiol and progesterone are female sex hormones.

  • Hormones are secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood
  • Steroid hormones: estrogens, androgens, testosterone
  • Polypeptide hormones: insulin, endorphins
  • Amino acid derivatives: thyroxine, epinephrine, norepinephrine
  • Insulin and glucagon regulate blood glucose
  • Thyroxine is an iodinated tyrosine derivative; iodine deficiency causes goitre
  • Adrenal cortex hormone deficiency causes Addison's disease
  • Progesterone prepares the uterus for implantation

NEET tip: Expect a question classifying a hormone as steroid, polypeptide or amino acid derivative, or matching a hormone to its function.

Formula sheet

$C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} + H_2O \xrightarrow{H^+} C_6H_{12}O_6 + C_6H_{12}O_6$ Sucrose hydrolyses to glucose and fructose (invert sugar)

$(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n + nH_2O \xrightarrow{H^+,\ 393\,K,\ 2-3\,atm} nC_6H_{12}O_6$ Commercial preparation of glucose from starch

$\text{Glucose} \xrightarrow{HI,\ \Delta} n\text{-hexane}$ Straight six-carbon chain

$\text{Glucose} \xrightarrow{NH_2OH} \text{oxime};\ \xrightarrow{HCN} \text{cyanohydrin}$ Carbonyl group present

$\text{Glucose} \xrightarrow{Br_2\ water} \text{gluconic acid}$ Aldehyde group present

$\text{Glucose} \xrightarrow{(CH_3CO)_2O} \text{glucose pentaacetate}$ Five $-OH$ groups

$\text{Glucose or gluconic acid} \xrightarrow{HNO_3} \text{saccharic acid}$ Primary alcohol group present

$\text{Sucrose} = \alpha\text{-D-glucose}\,(C1) - \beta\text{-D-fructose}\,(C2)$ Glycosidic link; non-reducing

$\text{Maltose} = \alpha\text{-D-glucose}\,(C1) - \alpha\text{-D-glucose}\,(C4)$ Reducing disaccharide

$\text{Lactose} = \beta\text{-D-galactose}\,(C1) - \beta\text{-D-glucose}\,(C4)$ Milk sugar; reducing

$H_3N^+-CHR-COO^-$ Zwitterion of an alpha-amino acid

$-CO-NH-$ Peptide (amide) bond; n amino acids give (n-1) peptide bonds

$E + S \rightleftharpoons ES \rightarrow E + P$ Enzyme action through an enzyme-substrate complex

$\text{Nucleotide} = \text{base} + \text{pentose} + \text{phosphate}$ Monomer of nucleic acids

$A=T\ (2\ H\text{-bonds}),\ G\equiv C\ (3\ H\text{-bonds})$ Base pairing in DNA

$\text{DNA: 2-deoxyribose, A, G, C, T};\ \text{RNA: ribose, A, G, C, U}$ Composition difference between DNA and RNA

Common traps

  • Calling the alpha-helix left-handed. It is a right-handed helix held by intramolecular hydrogen bonds; the beta-pleated sheet uses intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
  • Assuming fructose is non-reducing because it is a ketose. All monosaccharides, including fructose, reduce Tollens' and Fehling's reagents. Sucrose is non-reducing because its C1 and C2 are both locked in the glycosidic bond.
  • Equating D/L with (+)/(-). D and L describe configuration relative to glyceraldehyde; fructose is D yet laevorotatory.
  • Thinking denaturation breaks peptide bonds. Only secondary and tertiary structures are lost; the primary structure is retained.
  • Assuming every biologically active protein has quaternary structure. Quaternary structure exists only for proteins with two or more subunits; many single-chain proteins are fully active.
  • Treating vitamin $B_{12}$ like other water-soluble vitamins. It is water-soluble but stored in the liver. Biotin (vitamin H) is soluble in neither water nor fat.
  • Mixing up nucleoside and nucleotide. A nucleoside has no phosphate; a nucleotide has a phosphate at C5'. Uracil occurs only in RNA and thymine only in DNA.
  • Assuming every compound fitting $C_x(H_2O)_y$ is a carbohydrate. Acetic acid fits the formula but is not a carbohydrate, while rhamnose ($C_6H_{12}O_5$) does not fit but is one.

Quick revision

  • Glucose structure evidence: $HI$ proves a straight chain; Br2 water proves an aldehyde; $HNO_3$ proves a primary alcohol; acetylation proves five $-OH$ groups.
  • Glucose fails Schiff's test and the $NaHSO_3$ test, which supports its cyclic pyranose structure.
  • Alpha- and beta-glucose are anomers differing at C1, with melting points 419 K and 423 K.
  • Glucose forms a pyranose (six-membered) ring; fructose forms a furanose (five-membered) ring.
  • Sucrose: alpha-glucose and beta-fructose linked C1 to C2; it is non-reducing, and its hydrolysis gives invert sugar.
  • Maltose (glucose + glucose, C1 to C4) and lactose (galactose + glucose, C1 to C4) are reducing sugars.
  • Glycine is optically inactive; amino acids exist as zwitterions and are amphoteric.
  • The alpha-helix is right-handed with intramolecular hydrogen bonds; the beta-sheet has intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
  • Quaternary structure means two or more subunits; denaturation keeps the primary structure.
  • Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble; B and C are water-soluble ($B_{12}$ is stored in the liver).
  • Key vitamin sources: A from carrots, $B_{12}$ from meat, E from sunflower oil, K from green leafy vegetables.
  • DNA contains deoxyribose and thymine; RNA contains ribose and uracil. A=T has two hydrogen bonds and G≡C has three. Hormones are steroids, polypeptides or amino acid derivatives.

Chemistry · Unit 20: Principles Related to Practical Chemistry

This unit covers the laboratory chemistry NEET expects you to know from NCERT: detecting elements and functional groups, preparing standard inorganic and organic compounds, volumetric (acid-base and redox) titrations, systematic salt analysis, simple calorimetry, colloid preparation and a clock-reaction kinetic study. NEET usually asks 1-2 direct questions from it. These test reagents, colours of precipitates, formulas of double salts, stoichiometry of $KMnO_4$ titrations and indicator choice, so careful factual recall scores easy marks.

PYQs (2): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q49, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q57

Detection of extra elements: nitrogen, sulphur and halogens

Covalent organic compounds do not ionise, so N, S and halogens are first converted to ionic sodium salts by fusing the compound with sodium metal (Lassaigne's test). The fused mass is extracted with water to give the sodium fusion extract (SFE). Nitrogen becomes $NaCN$. Boiling with $FeSO_4$ gives $Na_4[Fe(CN)_6]$, and acidifying followed by $Fe^{3+}$ gives Prussian blue $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$. Sulphur becomes $Na_2S$, which gives a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside and a black $PbS$ precipitate with lead acetate. If both N and S are present, $NaSCN$ forms and gives a blood-red colour with $Fe^{3+}$. Halogens become $NaX$. The extract is boiled with $HNO_3$ to destroy $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which would otherwise interfere. Adding $AgNO_3$ then gives AgCl (white, soluble in $NH_4OH$), AgBr (pale yellow, sparingly soluble) or AgI (yellow, insoluble).

  • Sodium fusion converts covalent N, S and X into ionic $NaCN$, $Na_2S$ and $NaX$.
  • Prussian blue $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$ confirms nitrogen.
  • Violet $Na_4[Fe(CN)_5NOS]$ with sodium nitroprusside confirms sulphur.
  • Blood-red $[Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$ means N and S are both present.
  • Boil the extract with $HNO_3$ before the $AgNO_3$ test for halogens.
  • Hydrazine has no carbon, so it cannot form $CN^-$ and does not give the Lassaigne test for N.

$Na + C + N \rightarrow NaCN$ Conversion of nitrogen during sodium fusion

$3Na_4[Fe(CN)_6] + 4Fe^{3+} \rightarrow Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3 + 12Na^+$ Prussian blue formation (test for N)

$Na_2S + Na_2[Fe(CN)_5NO] \rightarrow Na_4[Fe(CN)_5NOS]$ Violet colour (test for S)

$NaSCN + Fe^{3+} \rightarrow [Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$ Blood-red colour when both N and S are present

NEET tip: NEET asks the formula or colour of the complex formed (Prussian blue, violet or blood red) and why $HNO_3$ is added before the $AgNO_3$ test.

Detection of functional groups: hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl and amino

Alcohols: alcoholic $-OH$ releases $H_2$ with sodium metal and gives a red colour with ceric ammonium nitrate. The Lucas reagent (conc. $HCl$ + anhydrous $ZnCl_2$) gives turbidity immediately with 3°, in about 5 minutes with 2°, and not at room temperature with 1° alcohols. Phenols: phenolic $-OH$ gives a violet colour with neutral $FeCl_3$ and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol with bromine water. Carbonyl compounds: these give a yellow-orange precipitate with 2,4-DNP. Aldehydes also give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, a red $Cu_2O$ precipitate with Fehling's solution (aliphatic aldehydes only) and a pink colour with Schiff's reagent. Methyl ketones such as acetone give a red colour with sodium nitroprusside in alkali. Carboxylic acids: these give brisk effervescence of $CO_2$ with $NaHCO_3$ and a fruity ester smell when warmed with ethanol and conc. $H_2SO_4$. Amines: primary amines give the offensive-smelling isocyanide in the carbylamine test. Aromatic primary amines give an orange-red azo dye in the azo dye test.

  • The $NaHCO_3$ test distinguishes $-COOH$ from phenol, because phenol is too weak an acid to react.
  • Neutral $FeCl_3$ gives violet with phenols; alcohols do not respond.
  • 2,4-DNP reacts with both aldehydes and ketones; Tollens', Fehling's and Schiff's tests are for aldehydes.
  • Benzaldehyde gives the Tollens' test but not the Fehling's test.
  • The carbylamine test is given only by primary amines (aliphatic and aromatic).
  • The azo dye test needs diazotisation at 0-5 °C followed by coupling with alkaline $\beta$-naphthol.

$RCHO + 2[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+ + 3OH^- \rightarrow RCOO^- + 2Ag + 4NH_3 + 2H_2O$ Tollens' silver mirror test for aldehydes

$RNH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \rightarrow RNC + 3KCl + 3H_2O$ Carbylamine test for primary amines

$RCOOH + NaHCO_3 \rightarrow RCOONa + H_2O + CO_2$ Effervescence test for the carboxyl group

$RCHO + 2Cu^{2+} + 5OH^- \rightarrow RCOO^- + Cu_2O + 3H_2O$ Fehling's test: red precipitate of $Cu_2O$

NEET tip: Expect match-the-test-to-the-group questions and questions that distinguish pairs such as phenol and carboxylic acid, or aldehyde and ketone.

Preparation of inorganic compounds: Mohr's salt and potash alum

Mohr's salt, $FeSO_4\cdot(NH_4)_2SO_4\cdot6H_2O$, is ferrous ammonium sulphate. It is prepared by dissolving equimolar amounts of ferrous sulphate and ammonium sulphate in the minimum amount of water containing a little dilute $H_2SO_4$. The solution is concentrated by gentle heating and cooled slowly to give pale green crystals. Potash alum, $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot24H_2O$ (or $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot12H_2O$), is made in the same way from equimolar potassium sulphate and aluminium sulphate and crystallises as colourless octahedra. Dilute $H_2SO_4$ is added in both cases to suppress hydrolysis of $Fe^{2+}$ and $Al^{3+}$. Prolonged heating is avoided, because it oxidises $Fe^{2+}$ to $Fe^{3+}$ and makes the product yellowish. Both are double salts: in water they give all their constituent ions and retain no identity as a complex.

  • Mohr's salt contains 6 water molecules and is pale green, from $Fe^{2+}$.
  • Potash alum contains 24 water molecules per $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3$ unit.
  • In potash alum, $K^+:Al^{3+}:SO_4^{2-} = 1:1:2$.
  • Dilute $H_2SO_4$ prevents hydrolysis of $Fe^{2+}$ and $Al^{3+}$.
  • Crystals form only on slow cooling of the concentrated solution; the mixture is not evaporated to dryness.
  • Mohr's salt is a primary standard in redox titrations because $Fe^{2+}$ in it is stable to air oxidation.

$FeSO_4\cdot(NH_4)_2SO_4\cdot6H_2O$ Mohr's salt, molar mass 392 g/mol

$K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot24H_2O$ Potash alum, molar mass 948 g/mol (474 for the $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot12H_2O$ unit)

NEET tip: NEET asks the ion ratio in potash alum, the number of water molecules, the double-salt nature, or the role of dilute $H_2SO_4$.

Preparation of organic compounds: acetanilide, p-nitroacetanilide, aniline yellow and iodoform

Acetanilide: aniline is acetylated with acetic anhydride in glacial acetic acid (or with acetyl chloride) and the mixture is poured into ice water. This gives white crystals, m.p. about 114 °C. p-Nitroacetanilide: acetanilide is nitrated with a conc. $HNO_3$ + conc. $H_2SO_4$ mixture below 10 °C. Acetylation moderates the activating effect of $-NH_2$, protects it from oxidation, and directs substitution mainly to the para position because of steric hindrance at ortho. The o-isomer stays in the ethanol filtrate, while the p-isomer forms pale yellow crystals (m.p. about 214 °C). Aniline yellow (p-aminoazobenzene): aniline is diazotised with $NaNO_2$/$HCl$ at 0-5 °C and the diazonium salt is coupled with aniline. Iodoform: ethanol or acetone is warmed with $I_2$ and $NaOH$ (or with $KI$ and $NaOCl$). It forms yellow crystals with a characteristic antiseptic smell, m.p. about 119 °C.

  • Acetylation converts the strongly activating $-NH_2$ into the moderately activating $-NHCOCH_3$.
  • Nitration is kept below 10 °C to avoid polynitration and oxidation.
  • The p-nitro product is separated from the o-isomer by crystallisation from ethanol.
  • Diazotisation requires 0-5 °C because diazonium salts decompose at higher temperature.
  • Aniline yellow is p-aminoazobenzene, $C_6H_5N=NC_6H_4NH_2$.
  • The iodoform reaction is given by compounds with $CH_3CO-$ or $CH_3CH(OH)-$ groups.

$C_6H_5NH_2 + (CH_3CO)_2O \rightarrow C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 + CH_3COOH$ Preparation of acetanilide

$C_6H_5NHCOCH_3 + HNO_3 \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} p\text{-}O_2NC_6H_4NHCOCH_3 + H_2O$ Preparation of p-nitroacetanilide

$C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + C_6H_5NH_2 \rightarrow p\text{-}H_2NC_6H_4N=NC_6H_5 + HCl$ Aniline yellow by diazo coupling

$CH_3CH_2OH + 4I_2 + 6NaOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H_2O$ Iodoform from ethanol

$CH_3COCH_3 + 3I_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + CH_3COONa + 3NaI + 3H_2O$ Iodoform from acetone

NEET tip: NEET asks why acetylation precedes nitration, which compounds give iodoform, and the reagents and temperature for diazotisation.

Titrimetric exercises: acids, bases and use of indicators

In an acid-base titration, a standard solution reacts with an unknown solution until the equivalence point. The end point is shown by an indicator that changes colour within the pH jump. Phenolphthalein, a weak acid indicator (pH 8.2-10), is colourless in acid and pink in base. Methyl orange, a weak base indicator (pH 3.1-4.4), is red in acid and yellow in base. Indicators are chosen as follows. Strong acid with strong base: either indicator works, because the pH jump is large (about 3 to 11). Weak acid with strong base: phenolphthalein. Strong acid with weak base: methyl orange. Weak acid with weak base: no sharp end point, so no simple indicator is suitable. Oxalic acid dihydrate is a primary standard. $NaOH$ is not, because it is hygroscopic and absorbs $CO_2$, so it must be standardised.

  • At the equivalence point, gram equivalents of acid equal gram equivalents of base.
  • Phenolphthalein turns pink in base; methyl orange turns yellow in base and red in acid.
  • The indicator's colour-change range must lie within the steep part of the titration curve.
  • A primary standard is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic and of high molar mass.
  • Oxalic acid has n-factor 2 as an acid; $Na_2CO_3$ has n-factor 2 with methyl orange.
  • Only a few drops of indicator are used, because indicators are themselves weak acids or bases.

$N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$ Equivalence condition in a titration

$n_1M_1V_1 = n_2M_2V_2$ Same condition using molarity and n-factors

$N = M \times n$ Normality from molarity and n-factor

$M = \frac{w \times 1000}{M_m \times V(mL)}$ Molarity of a solution made by weighing mass $w$ of a solute of molar mass $M_m$

NEET tip: Indicator choice for a given acid-base pair and simple $n_1M_1V_1 = n_2M_2V_2$ calculations are the usual questions.

Oxalic acid vs KMnO4 and Mohr's salt vs KMnO4

$KMnO_4$ is a strong oxidant in acid medium ($MnO_4^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+}$, n-factor 5). It acts as its own indicator: the end point is the first permanent light pink colour. Only dilute $H_2SO_4$ is used. $HCl$ is unsuitable because it is oxidised to $Cl_2$, and $HNO_3$ is unsuitable because it is itself an oxidant. Oxalic acid solution is warmed to 60-70 °C because the reaction is slow at first. It is then autocatalysed by the $Mn^{2+}$ produced, and oxalic acid has n-factor 2. Mohr's salt is titrated at room temperature, because heating lets air oxidise $Fe^{2+}$; it has n-factor 1. $KMnO_4$ is not a primary standard, because it is not available pure and decomposes in light. It is standardised against oxalic acid or Mohr's salt.

  • $KMnO_4$ is a self-indicator, going from colourless to light pink at the end point.
  • $KMnO_4$ is taken in the burette and the reducing agent in the conical flask.
  • Only dilute $H_2SO_4$ is used to acidify the solution.
  • The oxalate reaction is slow at first, so the solution is warmed to 60-70 °C; once $Mn^{2+}$ forms, it autocatalyses the reaction.
  • Mohr's salt is titrated cold; dilute $H_2SO_4$ prevents hydrolysis and air oxidation.
  • Mole ratio: $MnO_4^-:C_2O_4^{2-} = 2:5$ and $MnO_4^-:Fe^{2+} = 1:5$.

$2MnO_4^- + 5C_2O_4^{2-} + 16H^+ \rightarrow 2Mn^{2+} + 10CO_2 + 8H_2O$ Oxalic acid (oxalate) vs $KMnO_4$

$MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O$ Mohr's salt vs $KMnO_4$

$5M_{KMnO_4}V_{KMnO_4} = 2M_{ox}V_{ox}$ Molarity relation for the oxalic acid titration

$5M_{KMnO_4}V_{KMnO_4} = M_{Fe^{2+}}V_{Fe^{2+}}$ Molarity relation for the Mohr's salt titration

$E_{KMnO_4} = \frac{158}{5} = 31.6$ Equivalent weight of $KMnO_4$ in acid medium

NEET tip: NEET gives volumes and molarity of oxalic acid or $Fe^{2+}$ and asks the molarity of $KMnO_4$ using n-factors 5, 2 and 1.

Qualitative salt analysis: cations Pb2+, Cu2+, Al3+, Fe3+, Zn2+, Ni2+, Ca2+, Ba2+, Mg2+, NH4+

Cations are separated into groups by group reagents. Group 0 ($NH_4^+$): $NH_3$ is evolved on heating with $NaOH$ and gives a brown precipitate with Nessler's reagent. Group I ($Pb^{2+}$): dilute $HCl$ gives white $PbCl_2$, which is soluble in hot water. It is confirmed by yellow $PbI_2$ with $KI$ and yellow $PbCrO_4$ with $K_2CrO_4$. Group II ($Pb^{2+}$, $Cu^{2+}$): $H_2S$ in dilute $HCl$ gives black $CuS$. $Cu^{2+}$ gives a deep blue $[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$ solution with excess $NH_4OH$ and a chocolate-brown precipitate with $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$. Group III ($Fe^{3+}$, $Al^{3+}$): $NH_4OH$ in the presence of $NH_4Cl$ gives reddish-brown $Fe(OH)_3$ and white gelatinous $Al(OH)_3$. $Fe^{3+}$ gives Prussian blue with $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$ and blood red with $KSCN$. $Al^{3+}$ gives a blue lake with litmus. Group IV ($Zn^{2+}$, $Ni^{2+}$): $H_2S$ in ammoniacal medium gives white $ZnS$ and black $NiS$. $Ni^{2+}$ gives a rosy-red precipitate with dimethylglyoxime. Group V ($Ca^{2+}$, $Ba^{2+}$): $(NH_4)_2CO_3$ gives white carbonates. Group VI ($Mg^{2+}$): $Na_2HPO_4$ gives white $MgNH_4PO_4$.

  • In acid medium (Group II), $[S^{2-}]$ is low, so only very low $K_{sp}$ sulphides precipitate.
  • $NH_4Cl$ suppresses $OH^-$ by the common-ion effect, so only Group III hydroxides precipitate.
  • Ammoniacal medium (Group IV) raises $[S^{2-}]$, so $ZnS$, $NiS$, $CoS$ and $MnS$ precipitate.
  • $Zn^{2+}$ gives a white or bluish-white precipitate with $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$.
  • $Ba^{2+}$ gives yellow $BaCrO_4$ and an apple-green flame; $Ca^{2+}$ gives white $CaC_2O_4$ and a brick-red flame.
  • $Mg^{2+}$ gives a blue lake with magneson; $Cu^{2+}$ gives a blue-green flame.
  • $Pb^{2+}$ appears in both Groups I and II, because $PbCl_2$ is partly soluble.

$Cu^{2+} + 4NH_3 \rightarrow [Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$ Deep blue complex (test for copper)

$4Fe^{3+} + 3[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} \rightarrow Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$ Prussian blue (test for $Fe^{3+}$)

$Ni^{2+} + 2\,dmgH \rightarrow [Ni(dmg)_2] + 2H^+$ Rosy-red nickel dimethylglyoximate

$Mg^{2+} + HPO_4^{2-} + NH_3 \rightarrow MgNH_4PO_4$ White precipitate (test for $Mg^{2+}$)

NEET tip: NEET most often asks the group reagent of an ion, the colour of a precipitate or complex, and the role of $NH_4Cl$ or $HCl$ in group separation.

Qualitative salt analysis: anions CO3 2-, S2-, SO4 2-, NO3-, NO2-, Cl-, Br-, I-

Dilute $H_2SO_4$ group: $CO_3^{2-}$ gives brisk effervescence of $CO_2$, which turns lime water milky. $S^{2-}$ gives $H_2S$ (rotten-egg smell), which blackens lead acetate paper. It also gives a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside. $NO_2^-$ gives brown $NO_2$ fumes; it also turns $KI$-starch blue and gives a brown ring with dilute acid. Concentrated $H_2SO_4$ group: $Cl^-$ gives $HCl$, which forms white fumes with an $NH_3$ rod. It is confirmed by the chromyl chloride test: orange-red $CrO_2Cl_2$ vapours are passed into $NaOH$ to form yellow $Na_2CrO_4$. This solution, acidified with acetic acid, gives a yellow $PbCrO_4$ precipitate with lead acetate. $Br^-$ gives reddish-brown $Br_2$ vapours, and $I^-$ gives violet $I_2$ vapours. $NO_3^-$ gives brown fumes with Cu turnings. It is confirmed by the brown ring test with fresh $FeSO_4$ and conc. $H_2SO_4$. Independent group: $SO_4^{2-}$ gives white $BaSO_4$ with $BaCl_2$, insoluble in conc. acids. Halides are confirmed with $AgNO_3$ and by the layer test with $Cl_2$ water + $CCl_4$: an orange-brown layer for $Br_2$ and a violet layer for $I_2$.

  • $CO_3^{2-}$, $S^{2-}$ and $NO_2^-$ react with dilute $H_2SO_4$; $Cl^-$, $Br^-$, $I^-$ and $NO_3^-$ need conc. $H_2SO_4$.
  • The brown ring is $[Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2+}$, in which iron is +1 and NO is $NO^+$.
  • The chromyl chloride test is given by $Cl^-$ only; bromides and iodides do not form $CrO_2X_2$.
  • AgCl is white and soluble in $NH_4OH$; AgBr is pale yellow and partly soluble; AgI is yellow and insoluble.
  • $BaSO_4$ is insoluble in conc. $HCl$, which distinguishes it from $BaCO_3$ and $BaSO_3$.
  • $NO_2^-$ interferes with the nitrate brown ring test and is removed with sulphamic acid.

$K_2Cr_2O_7 + 4NaCl + 6H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2CrO_2Cl_2 + 2KHSO_4 + 4NaHSO_4 + 3H_2O$ Chromyl chloride test for $Cl^-$

$[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+} + NO \rightarrow [Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2+} + H_2O$ Brown ring test for nitrate or nitrite

$Ba^{2+} + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow BaSO_4$ White precipitate (test for sulphate)

$Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O$ Lime water turns milky (test for $CO_2$ from carbonate)

NEET tip: NEET asks the composition and oxidation state of the brown ring complex, the chromyl chloride test, and the colours and solubility of silver halides.

Enthalpy of solution of CuSO4

Enthalpy of solution is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of solute dissolves in a large excess of solvent. A known mass of $CuSO_4$ is dissolved in a known volume of water in a calorimeter of known water equivalent. The temperature change is recorded and the heat change is calculated. Anhydrous $CuSO_4$ dissolves exothermically (about $-66.5$ kJ/mol), because the large hydration energy outweighs the lattice energy. Hydrated $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$ dissolves slightly endothermically (about $+11.7$ kJ/mol), because its ions are already partly hydrated. The difference between the two gives the enthalpy of hydration of $CuSO_4$ by 5 water molecules (about $-78.2$ kJ/mol), an application of Hess's law.

  • A temperature rise means an exothermic process ($\Delta H$ negative); a temperature fall means an endothermic one.
  • The calorimeter's water equivalent is found first, by the method of mixtures.
  • Anhydrous $CuSO_4$ is white and dissolves with heat release; $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$ is blue and absorbs heat.
  • $\Delta_{hyd}H = \Delta_{sol}H(anhydrous) - \Delta_{sol}H(hydrated)$.
  • The solution's density and specific heat are taken as those of water (1 g/mL and 4.18 J/g/K).

$q = (m + W)\,s\,\Delta T$ Heat exchanged; $W$ is the water equivalent of the calorimeter

$\Delta_{sol}H = -\frac{q \times M}{w}$ Molar enthalpy of solution for mass $w$ of a solute of molar mass $M$ (sign follows the temperature change)

$CuSO_4(s) + 5H_2O(l) \rightarrow CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O(s)$ Hydration reaction, whose $\Delta H$ is obtained by Hess's law

NEET tip: NEET checks the sign of $\Delta H$ for anhydrous versus hydrated salt and Hess's-law calculation of the hydration enthalpy.

Enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid and a strong base

Enthalpy of neutralisation is the enthalpy change when 1 g-equivalent of an acid is neutralised by 1 g-equivalent of a base in dilute solution. For any strong acid with any strong base it is almost constant at about $-57.1$ kJ/mol (13.7 kcal), because both are fully ionised. The only net reaction is therefore $H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O$. In the lab, equal volumes of, for example, 1 M $HCl$ and 1 M $NaOH$ at the same initial temperature are mixed in a calorimeter. The rise in temperature is noted, and the heat released is divided by the moles of water formed. With a weak acid or weak base the value is numerically smaller, because part of the heat is used to ionise the weak electrolyte.

  • Strong acid with strong base gives $\Delta_{neut}H \approx -57.1$ kJ/mol, independent of which strong acid or base is used.
  • With $CH_3COOH$ or $NH_4OH$ the magnitude is smaller, because energy is spent on ionisation.
  • The heat released depends on the moles of water formed, which are set by the limiting reagent.
  • The acid and base solutions must start at the same temperature.
  • For $HF$ the magnitude exceeds 57.1 kJ/mol because of the high hydration enthalpy of $F^-$.

$H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$, $\Delta H = -57.1$ kJ/mol Net neutralisation for a strong acid and a strong base

$\Delta_{neut}H = -\frac{(m + W)\,s\,\Delta T}{n_{H_2O}}$ Enthalpy of neutralisation from calorimetric data

$|\Delta_{neut}H_{weak}| = 57.1 - \Delta_{ion}H$ Neutralisation involving a weak electrolyte (kJ/mol)

NEET tip: NEET asks the heat released when given volumes and molarities are mixed (find the limiting moles of water), or why the value is lower for weak acids.

Preparation of lyophilic and lyophobic sols

Lyophilic sols, such as those of starch, gum, gelatin and egg albumin, are made directly by warming the substance with water. For starch, a paste in cold water is poured into boiling water with stirring. These sols are reversible, highly stable because the particles are solvated, and not easily coagulated. Lyophobic sols, such as those of metals, $Fe(OH)_3$, $Al(OH)_3$ and $As_2S_3$, must be prepared by special methods and need a stabilising ion. Ferric hydroxide sol (red-brown, positively charged) is formed by hydrolysis when $FeCl_3$ solution is added dropwise to boiling water. Aluminium hydroxide sol is made in the same way. Arsenious sulphide sol (yellow, negatively charged) is formed by double decomposition when $H_2S$ is passed into a dilute solution of $As_2O_3$. Excess electrolyte is removed by dialysis. Lyophobic sols are irreversible and are coagulated by electrolytes according to the Hardy-Schulze rule.

  • Lyophilic sols are reversible, self-stabilised by solvation, and have high viscosity.
  • Lyophobic sols are irreversible, stabilised only by charge, and coagulate easily.
  • $Fe(OH)_3$ sol is positive because it adsorbs $Fe^{3+}$; $As_2S_3$ sol is negative because it adsorbs $S^{2-}$.
  • $FeCl_3$ is added to boiling water, not cold water, to make $Fe(OH)_3$ sol.
  • Dialysis removes excess electrolyte, which would otherwise coagulate the sol.
  • Hardy-Schulze rule: the higher the charge of the oppositely charged ion, the greater its coagulating power.

$FeCl_3 + 3H_2O \xrightarrow{boil} Fe(OH)_3(sol) + 3HCl$ Ferric hydroxide sol by hydrolysis

$As_2O_3 + 3H_2S \rightarrow As_2S_3(sol) + 3H_2O$ Arsenious sulphide sol by double decomposition

$Fe(OH)_3/Fe^{3+}$ Positively charged sol formed by preferential adsorption of $Fe^{3+}$

NEET tip: NEET asks to classify sols, the method and charge of $Fe(OH)_3$ or $As_2S_3$ sols, and coagulating power by the Hardy-Schulze rule.

Kinetic study of the reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide

In acid medium, hydrogen peroxide oxidises iodide to iodine. The rate is studied as an iodine clock reaction. A fixed small amount of $Na_2S_2O_3$ and starch is added to the mixture. The $I_2$ formed is immediately reduced back to $I^-$ by thiosulphate, so the solution stays colourless and $[I^-]$ remains effectively constant. When all the thiosulphate is used up, free $I_2$ appears and instantly gives a blue colour with starch. The time $t$ for the blue colour to appear corresponds to a fixed amount of $H_2O_2$ consumed, so rate $\propto \frac{1}{t}$. Varying $[I^-]$ or $[H_2O_2]$ while keeping the other constant shows that the reaction is first order in each. The same set-up can be used to study the effect of temperature.

  • Rate law: rate $= k[H_2O_2][I^-]$, overall second order.
  • Thiosulphate acts as a clock and also regenerates $I^-$.
  • The blue starch-iodine colour marks the end of the timed interval.
  • Doubling $[I^-]$ halves the time $t$ if the reaction is first order in $I^-$.
  • A higher temperature gives a shorter time and a faster rate, consistent with the Arrhenius equation.

$H_2O_2 + 2I^- + 2H^+ \rightarrow I_2 + 2H_2O$ Reaction under study

$I_2 + 2S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2I^- + S_4O_6^{2-}$ Clock reaction that consumes the $I_2$ formed

$rate = k[H_2O_2][I^-]$ Experimental rate law

$rate \propto \frac{1}{t}$ Relation between rate and the time for the blue colour to appear

NEET tip: NEET tests the role of thiosulphate and starch, the order with respect to each reactant, and the inverse relation between rate and time.

Formula sheet

$Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$ Prussian blue: N in Lassaigne's test and $Fe^{3+}$ with $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$

$Na_4[Fe(CN)_5NOS]$ Violet complex: test for sulphur or sulphide with sodium nitroprusside

$[Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$ Blood-red complex: N and S together, or $Fe^{3+}$ with $KSCN$

$[Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2+}$ Brown ring complex (Fe in +1 state)

$CrO_2Cl_2$ Orange-red chromyl chloride vapours, specific to $Cl^-$

$FeSO_4\cdot(NH_4)_2SO_4\cdot6H_2O$ Mohr's salt, M = 392, n-factor 1 with $KMnO_4$

$K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot24H_2O$ Potash alum; $K^+:SO_4^{2-} = 1:2$

$n_1M_1V_1 = n_2M_2V_2$ General titration equation

$2MnO_4^- + 5C_2O_4^{2-} + 16H^+ \rightarrow 2Mn^{2+} + 10CO_2 + 8H_2O$ Permanganate-oxalate titration, warmed to 60-70 °C

$MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O$ Permanganate-Mohr's salt titration at room temperature

$E_{KMnO_4} = 31.6$, $E_{H_2C_2O_4\cdot2H_2O} = 63$ Equivalent weights in acid medium

$RNH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \rightarrow RNC + 3KCl + 3H_2O$ Carbylamine test for primary amines

$CH_3COR + 3I_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + RCOONa + 3NaI + 3H_2O$ Iodoform reaction

$C_6H_5NH_2 + NaNO_2 + 2HCl \xrightarrow{0-5^\circ C} C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + NaCl + 2H_2O$ Diazotisation for azo dye and aniline yellow

$q = (m + W)\,s\,\Delta T$ Calorimetric heat

$\Delta_{neut}H = -57.1$ kJ/mol Strong acid with strong base

$\Delta_{hyd}H = \Delta_{sol}H(CuSO_4) - \Delta_{sol}H(CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O)$ Hydration enthalpy by Hess's law

$FeCl_3 + 3H_2O \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3 + 3HCl$ Positive lyophobic sol by hydrolysis

$As_2O_3 + 3H_2S \rightarrow As_2S_3 + 3H_2O$ Negative lyophobic sol by double decomposition

$rate = k[H_2O_2][I^-] \propto \frac{1}{t}$ Iodine clock kinetics

$\text{Phenolphthalein: } pH\ 8.2\text{-}10;\ \text{methyl orange: } pH\ 3.1\text{-}4.4$ Indicator ranges for selecting an indicator

$\text{Groups: } HCl;\ H_2S/H^+;\ NH_4OH/NH_4Cl;\ H_2S/NH_4OH;\ (NH_4)_2CO_3;\ Na_2HPO_4$ Group reagents for Groups I to VI

Common traps

  • Using equal moles of $KMnO_4$ and oxalic acid. The correct relation uses n-factors: $5M_1V_1 = 2M_2V_2$, so the mole ratio of $MnO_4^-$ to oxalate is 2:5.
  • Taking the $K^+$ to $SO_4^{2-}$ ratio in potash alum as 1:1 or 2:3. Per formula unit $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot24H_2O$ there are 2 $K^+$ and 4 $SO_4^{2-}$, so the ratio is 1:2.
  • Thinking $HCl$ can acidify $KMnO_4$ titrations. $HCl$ is oxidised to $Cl_2$ and gives high readings; only dilute $H_2SO_4$ is used.
  • Heating Mohr's salt solution before titration as is done for oxalic acid. Only oxalic acid is warmed; heating oxidises $Fe^{2+}$ by air.
  • Assuming the oxidation state of Fe in the brown ring complex is +2. In $[Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2+}$, NO is present as $NO^+$, so Fe is +1.
  • Believing $Br^-$ and $I^-$ also give the chromyl chloride test. Only chloride forms volatile $CrO_2Cl_2$.
  • Choosing phenolphthalein for a strong acid-weak base titration. Methyl orange is required, because the pH jump lies in the acidic range.
  • Taking $\Delta_{neut}H$ of acetic acid with $NaOH$ as $-57.1$ kJ/mol. It is numerically less, because some energy is used to ionise the weak acid.

Quick revision

  • Lassaigne's test results: Prussian blue means N; violet with nitroprusside means S; blood red means N + S; $AgX$ precipitate after boiling with $HNO_3$ means halogen.
  • Functional group tests: $NaHCO_3$ effervescence for $-COOH$; neutral $FeCl_3$ violet for phenol; 2,4-DNP for $C=O$; Tollens' and Fehling's for aldehydes; carbylamine for $1^\circ$ amines.
  • Mohr's salt $FeSO_4\cdot(NH_4)_2SO_4\cdot6H_2O$ is pale green; potash alum $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot24H_2O$ is colourless; dilute $H_2SO_4$ stops hydrolysis in both preparations.
  • Acetylation protects $-NH_2$ before nitration, done below 10 °C; diazotisation is done at 0-5 °C; iodoform is a yellow solid with a characteristic smell.
  • Use phenolphthalein for a weak acid with a strong base, methyl orange for a strong acid with a weak base, and either for a strong acid with a strong base.
  • In acid medium, $KMnO_4$ has n-factor 5, oxalic acid 2 and Mohr's salt 1; $KMnO_4$ is its own indicator and turns pink at the end point.
  • Group reagents: I dilute $HCl$; II $H_2S$ in acid; III $NH_4OH$ + $NH_4Cl$; IV $H_2S$ in ammonia; V $(NH_4)_2CO_3$; VI $Na_2HPO_4$. $NH_4^+$ is detected with Nessler's reagent.
  • Cation confirmatory tests: DMG gives rosy red with $Ni^{2+}$; $[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$ is deep blue; $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$ gives Prussian blue with $Fe^{3+}$; $BaCrO_4$ and $PbCrO_4$ are yellow; $CaC_2O_4$ is white.
  • Anion tests: lime water milky for $CO_3^{2-}$; lead acetate black for $S^{2-}$; brown ring for $NO_3^-$; $BaSO_4$ white for $SO_4^{2-}$; chromyl chloride only for $Cl^-$.
  • Dissolution enthalpies: anhydrous $CuSO_4$ exothermic; $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$ endothermic; strong acid with strong base $\Delta H = -57.1$ kJ/mol.
  • $Fe(OH)_3$ sol is positive (hydrolysis in boiling water); $As_2S_3$ sol is negative (double decomposition); lyophilic sols are reversible and stable.
  • Iodine clock: the blue colour appears after the thiosulphate is used up; rate $\propto 1/t$; rate $= k[H_2O_2][I^-]$.

Biology · Unit 1: Diversity in Living World

This unit covers how living organisms are recognised, named and classified, from bacteria, protists, fungi, lichens, viruses, viroids and prions to plants (algae to gymnosperms) and animals (non-chordate phyla to chordate classes). It is one of the highest-weightage, most fact-dense units in NEET Biology. Questions mostly test examples, distinguishing features, taxonomic ranks and statement-based traps taken directly from NCERT lines.

PYQs (12): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q92, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q101, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q107, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q111, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q112, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q118, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q119, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q121, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q125, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q129, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q130, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q132

What is living; biodiversity; need for classification

Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response to stimuli. Not all of these are defining properties. Growth and reproduction are not, because a sterile mule or worker bee does not reproduce, and non-living crystals and mountains also grow by external accumulation. Growth in living beings is from inside. Metabolism (the sum of all chemical reactions) and consciousness (awareness of surroundings) are defining features, and cellular organisation is the defining feature of life. Biodiversity is the number and types of organisms present on Earth, and about 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described. Because the variety is so large, organisms must be grouped by observable characters into convenient categories. This makes study easier, reveals relationships and allows universally accepted names.

  • Defining properties of life: metabolism, consciousness and cellular organisation
  • Growth and reproduction are not defining properties of life
  • Growth in living organisms is intrinsic; in non-living objects it is by surface accumulation
  • Unicellular organisms grow by cell division, so growth and reproduction are synonymous in them
  • In vitro metabolic reactions are not living but are living reactions
  • Humans are the only organisms aware of themselves (self-consciousness)
  • About 1.7 to 1.8 million species are described
  • Classification groups organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters

NEET tip: Expect assertion-type questions asking whether growth or reproduction is a defining feature of life; the answer is no.

Taxonomy and systematics

Taxonomy is the science of characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification of organisms. Characterisation means describing external and internal structure, cell structure, developmental process and ecological information. Identification means placing an organism correctly, nomenclature means giving it a correct scientific name, and classification means arranging it into groups. Early taxonomy used morphology. Modern taxonomy also uses cytology, anatomy, embryology, physiology, biochemistry and molecular data. Systematics comes from the Latin word systema, meaning systematic arrangement, and Linnaeus used the title Systema Naturae. Systematics is broader than taxonomy because it also includes evolutionary relationships between organisms.

  • Basic processes of taxonomy: characterisation, identification, nomenclature, classification
  • Systematics equals taxonomy plus evolutionary relationships
  • Systematics is derived from the Latin word systema
  • Linnaeus wrote Systema Naturae
  • Modern taxonomy uses morphology, anatomy, cytology, embryology, biochemistry and molecular data
  • Taxonomic studies of plants, animals and microbes underpin agriculture, forestry and industry

NEET tip: Asked as definition-based single-correct questions on the scope of systematics compared with taxonomy.

Concept of species and taxonomical hierarchy

A species is a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Examples are indica in Mangifera indica and tuberosum in Solanum tuberosum. Each category in classification is called a rank, and a taxonomic group at that rank is a taxon. In ascending order the obligate ranks are Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum (Division in plants) and Kingdom. A genus is a group of closely related species, a family is a group of related genera, an order is a group of related families, and so on. Moving from species to kingdom, the number of common characters decreases while the number of organisms in the group increases. Higher categories are aggregates of characters and are therefore harder to define.

  • Ascending order: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum or Division, Kingdom
  • Genus is a group of closely related species, for example Panthera includes leo, pardus and tigris
  • Family examples: Felidae (cat and leopard), Canidae (dog), Solanaceae
  • Order examples: Carnivora (Felidae plus Canidae), Polymoniales (Solanaceae plus Convolvulaceae)
  • Class Mammalia includes the orders Primata and Carnivora
  • Phylum is used for animals and Division for plants
  • Common characters decrease from species to kingdom
  • Mango: Plantae, Angiospermae (Division), Dicotyledonae (Class), Sapindales (Order), Anacardiaceae (Family), Mangifera (Genus), indica (species)
  • Man: Chordata, Mammalia, Primata, Hominidae, Homo sapiens
  • Housefly: Arthropoda, Insecta, Diptera, Muscidae, Musca domestica
  • Wheat: Angiospermae, Monocotyledonae, Poales, Poaceae, Triticum aestivum

$\text{Species} < \text{Genus} < \text{Family} < \text{Order} < \text{Class} < \text{Phylum/Division} < \text{Kingdom}$ Ascending order of taxonomic ranks, used for arrangement and match-the-rank questions

NEET tip: NEET repeatedly asks to arrange ranks in ascending order or to match mango, man, housefly and wheat ranks with their category names.

Binomial nomenclature

Binomial nomenclature was given by Carolus Linnaeus. Each scientific name has two components: the generic name, followed by the specific epithet. Names are framed according to universal rules. ICBN (International Code for Botanical Nomenclature) governs plant names and ICZN (International Code of Zoological Nomenclature) governs animal names. Scientific names are in Latin or are Latinised and are written in italics. When handwritten, the genus and species names are underlined separately. The generic name begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter. The name of the author appears after the specific epithet in abbreviated form, as in Mangifera indica Linn. Proper names avoid the confusion caused by local names.

  • Binomial system was given by Linnaeus and is used worldwide
  • First word is the genus (capital initial); second word is the specific epithet (small initial)
  • Names are printed in italics; when handwritten, the two words are underlined separately
  • Names are Latin or Latinised, irrespective of their origin
  • ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals
  • Author citation is abbreviated after the epithet, for example Linn. for Linnaeus

NEET tip: Look for statement questions on the rules of writing names, such as capitalisation, separate underlining and author citation.

Five kingdom classification

Linnaeus proposed a two-kingdom system, Plantae and Animalia. It failed to separate prokaryotes from eukaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, and photosynthetic from non-photosynthetic organisms such as fungi. R.H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification in 1969: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. His main criteria were cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. Monera are prokaryotic, while the other four kingdoms are eukaryotic. Protista are unicellular eukaryotes. Fungi are heterotrophic, absorptive and have chitin walls. Plantae are autotrophic with cellulose walls. Animalia are heterotrophic, holozoic and lack cell walls. Viruses, viroids, prions and lichens are not placed in this system.

  • Five-kingdom classification was given by R.H. Whittaker in 1969
  • Criteria: cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, phylogenetic relationship
  • Monera is the only prokaryotic kingdom; its cell wall is non-cellulosic (peptidoglycan in eubacteria)
  • Fungal cell wall contains chitin, while plants have cellulose walls
  • Animalia lack cell walls and show holozoic nutrition
  • Kingdom Protista brings together Chlamydomonas, Chlorella, Paramoecium and Amoeba
  • Viruses, viroids, prions and lichens are not included in the five kingdoms

NEET tip: Comparison-table questions ask about cell wall composition, nuclear membrane or mode of nutrition across the five kingdoms.

Monera, Protista and Fungi: salient features and classification

Monera includes bacteria, the most abundant microorganisms. By shape they are coccus (spherical), bacillus (rod), vibrium (comma) and spirillum (spiral). Archaebacteria live in harsh habitats and have a distinct cell wall; they include halophiles, thermoacidophiles and methanogens. Eubacteria have a rigid wall. They include cyanobacteria with heterocysts, chemosynthetic autotrophs and heterotrophs. Mycoplasma lack a cell wall. Protista are unicellular eukaryotes: chrysophytes, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds and protozoans. Fungi are heterotrophic, with chitin walls and hyphae forming a mycelium. Sexual reproduction occurs by plasmogamy, then karyogamy, then meiosis. Fungi are classified as Phycomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes and Deuteromycetes.

  • Methanogens live in the gut of ruminants and produce methane in biogas
  • Cyanobacteria such as Nostoc and Anabaena fix nitrogen in heterocysts and may form blooms
  • Mycoplasma lack a cell wall, are the smallest living cells and can survive without oxygen
  • Bacteria reproduce mainly by fission
  • Chrysophytes (diatoms, desmids) have silica walls forming diatomaceous earth; they are chief producers in oceans
  • Dinoflagellates have two flagella and cellulose plates; Gonyaulax causes red tides
  • Euglenoids have a protein-rich pellicle instead of a cell wall, for example Euglena
  • Slime moulds form a plasmodium; their spores have true walls and are extremely resistant
  • Protozoans: amoeboid (Amoeba, Entamoeba), flagellated (Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness), ciliated (Paramoecium), sporozoans (Plasmodium causes malaria)
  • Phycomycetes are aseptate and coenocytic, with zoospores or aplanospores and zygospores, for example Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo
  • Ascomycetes are sac fungi with conidia and ascospores in asci, for example Penicillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora, yeast
  • Basidiomycetes lack asexual spores and sex organs, and form basidiospores, for example Agaricus, Ustilago (smut), Puccinia (rust)
  • Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi) have only an asexual phase, for example Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma
  • In Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes a dikaryotic (n+n) stage intervenes between plasmogamy and karyogamy

NEET tip: Match questions pair bacterial shapes with names, fungal examples with classes, and plasmogamy, karyogamy and meiosis with their events.

Lichens

Lichens are symbiotic associations, mutually useful, between algae and fungi. The algal component is the phycobiont and the fungal component is the mycobiont. The phycobiont is autotrophic and prepares food for the fungus. The fungus provides shelter and absorbs mineral nutrients and water for the alga. The association is so close that a lichen looks like a single organism. Lichens are very good pollution indicators because they do not grow in polluted areas, especially those with high $SO_2$. Lichens differ from mycorrhiza, which is a fungus and higher plant root association, as in Pinus.

  • Lichen equals alga (phycobiont) plus fungus (mycobiont)
  • The alga makes food and the fungus provides shelter, water and minerals
  • Lichens are indicators of air pollution because they are absent in $SO_2$-polluted areas
  • Lichens are pioneers on bare rock in primary succession
  • Mycorrhiza is a fungus and plant root association, not a lichen

NEET tip: A direct one-liner is common: lichen is a fungus and alga association, with mycorrhiza or chrysophytes used as distractors.

Viruses and viroids

Viruses are non-cellular, inert outside a host and become living only inside living cells, so they are obligate parasites. Ivanowsky in 1892 found that the agent of tobacco mosaic disease was smaller than bacteria. Beijerinck called the infectious fluid contagium vivum fluidum, and W.M. Stanley showed viruses could be crystallised. A virus is a nucleoprotein with genetic material that is either RNA or DNA, never both, enclosed in a protein coat called the capsid. Capsids are made of capsomeres. Usually plant viruses have single-stranded RNA and bacteriophages have double-stranded DNA. Viroids were discovered by T.O. Diener in 1971 as the cause of potato spindle tuber disease. They are free RNA without a protein coat and of low molecular weight. Prions are abnormally folded proteins that cause mad cow disease (BSE) and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

  • TMV was the first virus studied; Ivanowsky identified it in 1892
  • Beijerinck coined the term contagium vivum fluidum; Stanley crystallised viruses
  • A virus contains either DNA or RNA, never both
  • The capsid is a protein coat made of capsomeres arranged in helical or polyhedral form
  • Viral diseases include mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza and AIDS in humans, and mosaic formation, leaf rolling, curling, yellowing and vein clearing in plants
  • Viroids are smaller than viruses, lack a protein coat and cause potato spindle tuber disease
  • Prions are infectious misfolded proteins and cause BSE (mad cow disease) and CJD

NEET tip: Disease-to-agent questions are frequent, for example mad cow disease to prions and potato spindle tuber to viroid.

Plant kingdom: algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms

Algae are simple, thalloid, autotrophic and mostly aquatic. Chlorophyceae are green algae with chlorophyll a and b, starch and a cellulose wall. Phaeophyceae are brown algae with chlorophyll a and c and fucoxanthin; they store laminarin or mannitol and have a cellulosic wall, usually covered on the outside by a gelatinous coating of algin. Rhodophyceae are red algae with chlorophyll a and d and r-phycoerythrin; they store floridean starch and have no flagella. Bryophytes are the amphibians of the plant kingdom. Their dominant gametophyte bears antheridia and archegonia, the sporophyte depends on it, and a protonema stage occurs in mosses. Pteridophytes are the first vascular land plants. The sporophyte is dominant and the prothallus is the gametophyte. Gymnosperms have naked ovules. They are heterosporous, and their male and female gametophytes stay within sporangia retained on the sporophyte.

  • Green algae examples: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara
  • Brown algae examples: Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus; zoospores are pear-shaped with two lateral flagella
  • Red algae examples: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium; agar comes from Gelidium and Gracilaria
  • Algin comes from brown algae and carrageen from red algae; Chlorella is used as a protein-rich food supplement
  • Liverworts such as Marchantia reproduce asexually by gemmae
  • Mosses include Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum; Sphagnum provides peat
  • Pteridophyte classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum)
  • Heterospory in Selaginella and Salvinia is a precursor to the seed habit
  • Gymnosperms: Cycas has coralloid roots with cyanobacteria; Pinus has mycorrhiza; Sequoia is one of the tallest tree species
  • Gymnosperms have microsporophylls and megasporophylls in strobili or cones; the seeds are naked
  • Haplontic life cycle: Volvox, Spirogyra, some Chlamydomonas
  • Diplontic life cycle: seed plants and Fucus
  • Haplo-diplontic life cycle: bryophytes, pteridophytes, Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps

NEET tip: Expect pigment and stored-food matching for algae, class identification for pteridophytes (such as Sphenopsida for Equisetum) and gymnosperm statement pairs.

Animal kingdom: non-chordates up to phyla level

Animals are classified by several bases. The first is level of organisation: cellular in Porifera, tissue in Cnidaria and Ctenophora, organ in Platyhelminthes and organ system from Aschelminthes onwards. The second is symmetry: asymmetrical, radial or bilateral. The third is germ layers: diploblastic in Porifera, Cnidaria and Ctenophora, triploblastic in the rest. The fourth is coelom: acoelomate in Platyhelminthes, pseudocoelomate in Aschelminthes and true coelom from Annelida onwards. The fifth is metamerism, first seen in Annelida. Radial symmetry means any plane through the central axis divides the body into identical halves. The non-chordate phyla are Porifera, Cnidaria, Ctenophora, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata. Each has hallmark features such as choanocytes, cnidoblasts, comb plates, flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules, radula and the water vascular system.

  • Porifera have a water canal system (ostia, spongocoel, osculum) and choanocytes, for example Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia
  • Cnidaria have cnidoblasts and polyp and medusa forms; Obelia shows metagenesis; examples are Physalia, Adamsia, Pennatula, Gorgonia, Meandrina
  • Ctenophora (sea walnuts) have eight external rows of ciliated comb plates and bioluminescence, for example Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana
  • Platyhelminthes are dorsoventrally flat with flame cells, for example Taenia, Fasciola; Planaria shows high regeneration
  • Aschelminthes are pseudocoelomate and dioecious with sexual dimorphism, for example Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma
  • Annelida are metameric with nephridia; examples are Nereis (parapodia, dioecious), Pheretima and Hirudinaria (monoecious)
  • Arthropoda is the largest phylum (about two-thirds of named species), with a chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, Malpighian tubules, book gills and book lungs
  • Arthropod examples: Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer (economic), Anopheles, Culex, Aedes (vectors), Locusta (pest), Limulus (living fossil)
  • Mollusca is the second largest phylum, with a mantle, radula and ctenidia, for example Pila, Pinctada, Sepia, Loligo, Octopus, Aplysia, Dentalium, Chaetopleura
  • Echinodermata have a water vascular system and no excretory system; adults are radial and larvae bilateral; examples are Asterias, Echinus, Antedon, Cucumaria, Ophiura
  • Hemichordata have a proboscis, collar and trunk and a stomochord, for example Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus

NEET tip: Statement questions target symmetry (echinoderm larvae are bilateral), coelom type and the correct phylum for a listed animal or excretory structure.

Animal kingdom: chordates up to classes level

Chordates have four fundamental features: a notochord, a dorsal hollow single nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits and a post-anal tail. Non-chordates differ by having a ventral solid double nerve cord, no notochord and a dorsal heart, if present. Urochordates have a notochord only in the larval tail, while cephalochordates retain it throughout life. In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column, and the heart is ventral and muscular. Cyclostomata are jawless and form the division Agnatha. Gnathostomata include Pisces (Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes) and Tetrapoda (Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia). Fishes have a two-chambered heart, amphibians and most reptiles three chambers, and crocodiles, birds and mammals four. Birds and mammals are homeothermous.

  • Urochordata: Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum; Cephalochordata: Branchiostoma (Amphioxus)
  • Cyclostomata (Petromyzon, Myxine) have a circular suctorial mouth, no scales or paired fins and 6 to 15 pairs of gill slits; they migrate to fresh water to spawn and die after spawning
  • Chondrichthyes have a cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scales, a ventral mouth, no air bladder and male claspers, for example Scoliodon, Pristis, Carcharodon, Trygon, Torpedo (electric organ)
  • Osteichthyes have an operculum, an air bladder and cycloid or ctenoid scales, for example Exocoetus, Hippocampus, Labeo, Catla, Clarias, Betta, Pterophyllum
  • Amphibia have moist scaleless skin, a tympanum, a cloaca and a three-chambered heart, for example Bufo, Rana, Hyla, Salamandra, Ichthyophis (limbless)
  • Reptilia means creeping or crawling; they have dry cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes and no external ear openings
  • Reptile examples: Chelone, Testudo, Chameleon, Calotes, Crocodilus, Alligator, Hemidactylus, Naja, Bangarus, Vipera
  • Aves have feathers, a beak, pneumatic bones, a crop and gizzard, air sacs and a four-chambered heart, for example Corvus, Columba, Psittacula, Struthio, Pavo, Aptenodytes, Neophron
  • Mammalia have mammary glands, hair, an external ear (pinna) and are mostly viviparous
  • Mammal examples: Ornithorhynchus (oviparous), Macropus, Pteropus (flies), Balaenoptera, Delphinus, Camelus, Panthera
  • Electric organ is found in Torpedo; poison sting in Trygon

NEET tip: Common angles are features that are not chordate characters, the number of heart chambers (with the crocodile exception) and class-to-example matching.

Key facts

  • Whittaker proposed five-kingdom classification in 1969.
  • Linnaeus gave binomial nomenclature and wrote Systema Naturae.
  • About 1.7 to 1.8 million species are known.
  • Mango classification: Mangifera (Genus), Anacardiaceae (Family), Sapindales (Order), Dicotyledonae (Class), Angiospermae (Division).
  • Ivanowsky (1892) studied TMV; Stanley crystallised viruses; Beijerinck coined contagium vivum fluidum.
  • T.O. Diener discovered viroids in 1971 as the cause of potato spindle tuber disease.
  • Prions cause BSE (mad cow disease) in cattle and CJD in humans.
  • Mycoplasma are the smallest living cells and lack a cell wall.
  • Methanogens in the rumen of cattle produce methane (biogas).
  • Gonyaulax, a dinoflagellate, causes red tides.
  • Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness and Plasmodium causes malaria.
  • Albugo causes white rust of mustard; Ustilago causes smut; Puccinia causes rust.
  • Neurospora is used in biochemical and genetic work; Claviceps produces ergot alkaloids.
  • Agar comes from Gelidium and Gracilaria (red algae); algin comes from brown algae; carrageen comes from red algae.
  • Sphagnum provides peat used as fuel and as a packing material.
  • Equisetum belongs to Sphenopsida, Selaginella to Lycopsida and Psilotum to Psilopsida.
  • Sequoia (redwood) is one of the tallest trees; Cycas has coralloid roots with cyanobacteria.
  • Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum and Mollusca the second largest.
  • Obelia shows metagenesis (alternation of polyp and medusa).
  • Limulus (king crab) is a living fossil.
  • Ctenophores show bioluminescence and have eight external rows of ciliated comb plates.
  • Crocodiles are the only reptiles with a four-chambered heart.
  • Ornithorhynchus (platypus) is an egg-laying mammal.
  • Ichthyophis is a limbless amphibian.
  • Pteropus (flying fox) is a flying mammal; Balaenoptera (blue whale) is the largest mammal.

Common traps

  • Thinking echinoderms are radial throughout life; adults are radial but larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.
  • Assuming all reptiles have a three-chambered heart; crocodiles have a four-chambered heart.
  • Confusing lichen with mycorrhiza; a lichen is an alga and fungus association, while mycorrhiza is a fungus and plant root association.
  • Mixing up viroids and prions; viroids are free RNA without a protein coat, while prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid.
  • Writing the ascending order wrongly, for example placing Order above Class; the correct order is Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom.
  • Believing gymnosperm gametophytes are free-living; they remain within sporangia retained on the sporophyte, and the seeds are naked.
  • Treating growth or reproduction as defining properties of life; the defining properties are metabolism, consciousness and cellular organisation.
  • Calling Hemichordata a chordate subphylum; it has a stomochord, not a true notochord, and is placed with non-chordates.

Quick revision

  • Rank order upward: Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum or Division, Kingdom.
  • Binomial names: Genus capitalised, epithet in small letters, italicised or underlined separately; ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals.
  • Five kingdoms (Whittaker 1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
  • Bacterial shapes: cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod), vibrio (comma), spirilla (spiral).
  • Fungal sexual cycle: plasmogamy, then karyogamy, then meiosis to give haploid spores.
  • Fungal classes: Phycomycetes (Rhizopus), Ascomycetes (Penicillium, yeast), Basidiomycetes (Agaricus), Deuteromycetes (Alternaria).
  • Algal pigments: green (chlorophyll a, b), brown (chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin), red (chlorophyll a, d, r-phycoerythrin).
  • Bryophytes have a dominant gametophyte; pteridophytes are the first vascular plants with a dominant sporophyte; gymnosperms have naked seeds.
  • Coelom: acoelomate (Platyhelminthes), pseudocoelomate (Aschelminthes), coelomate (Annelida onwards).
  • Hallmarks: choanocytes (Porifera), cnidoblasts (Cnidaria), comb plates (Ctenophora), flame cells (Platyhelminthes), nephridia (Annelida), Malpighian tubules (Arthropoda), radula (Mollusca), water vascular system (Echinodermata).
  • Chordate features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail.
  • Heart chambers: fishes 2; amphibians and most reptiles 3; crocodiles, birds and mammals 4.

Biology · Unit 2: Structural Organisation in Animals and Plants

This unit covers how flowering plants are built and how they vary in form: external morphology, tissues, internal anatomy, inflorescence, flowers, fruits, seeds and the diagnostic features of important families. It also covers how animal bodies are organised, from basic animal tissues to the complete body plan of the frog. NEET asks many direct, fact-based questions from here on examples, placentation, aestivation, floral formulae, tissue locations and frog organ systems, so precise NCERT-level recall scores easy marks.

PYQs (5): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q103, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q105, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q113, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q120, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q135

Morphology and modifications of flowering plants

A flowering plant has an underground root system and an aerial shoot system made of stem, leaves, flowers and fruits. Root systems are of three kinds. Dicots have a tap root, monocots such as wheat have fibrous roots, and adventitious roots arise from parts other than the radicle, as in grass, Monstera and banyan. Roots, stems and leaves are often modified for storage, support, climbing, protection, respiration or vegetative propagation. The stem bears nodes and internodes, while the root never does. Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. Venation is the arrangement of veins in the lamina. It is usually reticulate in dicots and parallel in monocots. A leaf may be simple, or compound with incisions reaching the midrib or petiole. Compound leaves are pinnate (neem) or palmate (silk cotton).

  • Root regions from tip upward: root cap, meristematic region, region of elongation, region of maturation (root hairs)
  • Storage roots: carrot (tap, conical), turnip (tap, napiform), sweet potato (adventitious, tuberous)
  • Prop roots occur in banyan; stilt roots in maize and sugarcane; pneumatophores in Rhizophora (mangrove)
  • Underground storage stems: potato (tuber), ginger and turmeric (rhizome), Colocasia and zaminkand (corm)
  • Stem tendrils (from axillary bud) occur in cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon and grapevine; stem thorns in Citrus and Bougainvillea
  • Photosynthetic stems of arid plants: flattened in Opuntia (phylloclade), fleshy cylindrical in Euphorbia
  • Subaerial stems: runner in grass and strawberry, stolon in mint and jasmine, offset in Pistia and Eichhornia, sucker in banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum
  • Leaf parts: leaf base, petiole, lamina; legumes have a swollen leaf base called pulvinus, and monocots have a sheathing leaf base
  • Phyllotaxy: alternate in China rose, mustard and sunflower; opposite in Calotropis and guava; whorled in Alstonia
  • Leaf modifications: tendrils in pea, spines in cactus, fleshy storage leaves in onion and garlic, phyllode (flattened petiole) in Australian Acacia, insect-trapping leaves in pitcher plant and Venus fly trap

NEET tip: Expect example-matching questions such as modification type versus plant, and single-word definitions like phyllotaxy or venation.

Plant tissues

Plant tissues are either meristematic (dividing) or permanent (non-dividing). Meristems are of three kinds: - Apical meristems lie at root and shoot tips and cause primary growth in length. - Intercalary meristems occur at the base of internodes, as in grasses. - Lateral meristems, namely vascular cambium and cork cambium, cause secondary growth in girth. Simple permanent tissues have one cell type: - Parenchyma is thin-walled and does storage and photosynthesis. - Collenchyma has walls thickened at the corners with cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin. It gives mechanical support to young dicot stems and petioles and is absent in monocots. - Sclerenchyma has dead, lignified cells, either fibres or sclereids. Complex permanent tissues are xylem and phloem: - Xylem conducts water and minerals. It contains tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma. - Phloem conducts food. It contains sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres. Plants have three tissue systems: epidermal, ground and vascular.

  • Tracheids, vessels and xylem fibres are dead; xylem parenchyma is the only living xylem element
  • Vessels are characteristic of angiosperms; gymnosperms lack vessels
  • Protoxylem is formed first and metaxylem later
  • Xylem is exarch in roots (protoxylem towards the periphery) and endarch in stems (protoxylem towards the centre)
  • Mature sieve tube elements lack a nucleus and have perforated end walls called sieve plates; companion cells control them
  • Gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells instead of companion cells and sieve tubes
  • Phloem parenchyma is absent in most monocots; phloem fibres (bast fibres) are the only dead phloem cells
  • Epidermal tissue system includes epidermis, cuticle, stomata, trichomes and root hairs
  • Guard cells are bean-shaped in dicots and dumb-bell shaped in grasses; nearby specialised cells are subsidiary cells
  • Root hairs are unicellular; stem hairs (trichomes) are usually multicellular
  • Vascular bundles are radial in roots and conjoint in stems and leaves; they are open (with cambium) in dicot stems and closed in monocots

NEET tip: NEET frequently asks which cells are living or dead, the components of xylem and phloem, and open versus closed or radial versus conjoint vascular bundles.

Anatomy and functions of root, stem and leaf

Roots: In a dicot root, the layers from outside inward are epiblema with root hairs, a parenchymatous cortex, and an endodermis whose cells carry suberised Casparian strips. Inside these lie the pericycle, 2 to 4 alternating xylem and phloem patches separated by conjunctive tissue, and a small pith. A monocot root has more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles and a large, well-developed pith, and it shows no secondary growth. Stems: A dicot stem has a cuticle and epidermis, a collenchymatous hypodermis, a cortex, and an endodermis that acts as a starch sheath. The pericycle bears semilunar sclerenchyma patches. Vascular bundles are conjoint, collateral, open and endarch, arranged in a ring around a large pith, with medullary rays between them. A monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis and numerous scattered vascular bundles. Each bundle is closed, enclosed in a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath and has a water-containing cavity. Leaves: Dicot leaves are dorsiventral, with palisade mesophyll on the upper (adaxial) side and spongy mesophyll below. Monocot leaves are isobilateral. Functions: roots absorb and anchor, stems conduct and support, and leaves photosynthesise and transpire.

  • Endodermis has Casparian strips of suberin, which block apoplastic water flow
  • Pericycle forms lateral roots and contributes to vascular cambium in dicot roots
  • Dicot root: diarch to tetrarch; monocot root: polyarch (more than 6)
  • Dicot stem bundles: conjoint, collateral, open, endarch, arranged in a ring
  • Monocot stem: scattered closed bundles, sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, no phloem parenchyma, peripheral bundles smaller
  • Ground tissue in monocot stem is not differentiated into cortex and pith
  • Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: more stomata on the abaxial (lower) surface
  • Isobilateral (monocot) leaf: stomata on both surfaces and undifferentiated mesophyll
  • Grass leaves have bulliform cells on the adaxial epidermis; they lose turgor in water stress and the leaf rolls to cut water loss
  • In leaves, xylem lies towards the adaxial side and phloem towards the abaxial side; bundle sheath cells surround the veins

NEET tip: Questions usually present a transverse section feature (scattered bundles, polyarch xylem, bulliform cells, Casparian strip) and ask you to identify the organ or plant group.

Inflorescence: cymose and racemose

An inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis. It is decided by whether the shoot apex turns into a flower. In racemose inflorescence, the main axis keeps growing and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession: older flowers are at the base and younger ones towards the apex. In cymose inflorescence, the main axis ends in a flower, so its growth is limited. Flowers then arise in basipetal order, with the oldest flower at the top or centre. Racemose types include raceme, spike, catkin, spadix, corymb, umbel and capitulum (head). Cymes are classified by the number of lateral branches formed below the terminal flower: monochasial (one), dichasial (two) or polychasial (many).

  • Racemose: indefinite growth of main axis, acropetal order, oldest flower at the base or periphery
  • Cymose: main axis ends in a flower, basipetal order, oldest flower at the apex or centre
  • Raceme (stalked flowers on a long axis): mustard
  • Spike (sessile flowers): Achyranthes
  • Catkin (pendulous spike of unisexual flowers): mulberry
  • Spadix (fleshy axis covered by a spathe): banana and Colocasia
  • Umbel (flowers arising from one point): coriander
  • Corymb (lower pedicels longer, flowers reach one level): candytuft (Iberis)
  • Capitulum or head (flattened receptacle with florets): sunflower and Tridax
  • Monochasial cymes are helicoid or scorpioid; dichasial cyme occurs in jasmine; polychasial cyme in Calotropis

NEET tip: NEET tests the difference in growth of the main axis and flower order (acropetal versus basipetal), and matches inflorescence types with examples.

Flower, fruit and seed

Flower: The flower is a modified shoot that carries out sexual reproduction. It has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium. - Symmetry can be actinomorphic (radial), zygomorphic (bilateral) or asymmetric. - Ovary position can be hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous (half-inferior) or epigynous (inferior ovary). - Aestivation is the arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud: valvate, twisted, imbricate or vexillary. - Placentation is the arrangement of ovules inside the ovary. Fruit: The fruit is a mature ovary formed after fertilisation. A fruit formed without fertilisation is parthenocarpic. The fruit wall (pericarp) may be differentiated into epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp. Seed: The seed is a fertilised ovule. It has a seed coat (outer testa and inner tegmen), a hilum, a micropyle and an embryo with radicle, plumule and one or two cotyledons. Seeds are endospermic or non-endospermic.

  • Actinomorphic flowers: mustard, datura, chilli; zygomorphic: pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia; asymmetric: canna
  • Hypogynous: mustard, China rose, brinjal; perigynous: plum, rose, peach; epigynous: guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower
  • Aestivation: valvate in Calotropis; twisted in China rose, lady's finger and cotton; imbricate in Cassia and gulmohur; vexillary in pea and bean
  • Stamen arrangements: epipetalous in brinjal, epiphyllous in lily, monadelphous in China rose, diadelphous in pea, polyadelphous in Citrus
  • Placentation: marginal in pea; axile in China rose, tomato and lemon; parietal in mustard and Argemone; free central in Dianthus and Primrose; basal in sunflower and marigold
  • Apocarpous gynoecium (free carpels): lotus, rose; syncarpous (fused carpels): mustard, tomato
  • Drupe: develops from a monocarpellary superior ovary and is one-seeded, as in mango and coconut
  • In mango the edible part is the fleshy mesocarp; in coconut the mesocarp is fibrous
  • Non-endospermic dicot seeds: bean, gram, pea; endospermic dicot seed: castor
  • Monocot (maize) seed is usually endospermic; it has an aleurone layer, a scutellum (single cotyledon), a coleoptile around the plumule and a coleorhiza around the radicle

NEET tip: Placentation, aestivation and ovary-position match-the-list questions with example plants are among the most repeated in this unit.

Families: Malvaceae, Cruciferae, Leguminosae, Compositae and Gramineae

Families are identified from vegetative, floral and fruit characters, summarised as floral formulae. - Malvaceae (China rose, cotton, okra): epicalyx present, twisted corolla, numerous monadelphous stamens with monothecous (reniform) anthers, superior pentacarpellary syncarpous ovary with axile placentation. - Cruciferae or Brassicaceae (mustard, radish, cabbage): cruciform corolla, tetradynamous stamens, bicarpellary ovary with parietal placentation and a false septum (replum). The fruit is a siliqua. - Leguminosae (Fabaceae in the broad sense): bears legumes. Its subfamily Papilionoideae (pea, gram) has papilionaceous corolla with vexillary aestivation, diadelphous stamens and a monocarpellary ovary with marginal placentation. - Compositae or Asteraceae (sunflower, marigold, Tridax): capitulum, pappus, syngenesious epipetalous stamens, inferior bicarpellary unilocular ovary with basal placentation. The fruit is a cypsela. - Gramineae or Poaceae (wheat, rice, maize, bamboo): spikelets, lodicules, versatile anthers, feathery stigmas. The fruit is a caryopsis.

  • Malvaceae: epicalyx, gamosepalous valvate calyx, twisted polypetalous corolla, staminal tube, axile placentation, fruit capsule or schizocarp
  • Cruciferae: racemose (corymbose raceme) inflorescence, 4 free sepals in two whorls, 4 cruciform petals
  • Cruciferae: tetradynamous stamens (2 short outer and 4 long inner), parietal placentation with replum, fruit siliqua or silicula
  • Leguminosae has three subfamilies: Papilionoideae, Caesalpinioideae and Mimosoideae
  • Papilionoideae corolla: 1 standard (vexillum), 2 wings (alae) and 2 fused keel petals (carina)
  • Papilionoideae: stamens diadelphous (9)+1; legumes have root nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria and pulvinate leaves
  • Caesalpinioideae (Cassia, Tamarindus, gulmohur): imbricate (ascending) aestivation and zygomorphic flowers
  • Mimosoideae (Mimosa, Acacia): actinomorphic flowers, valvate aestivation, numerous stamens, often head inflorescence
  • Compositae: outer ray florets are ligulate, zygomorphic and often female or neuter; inner disc florets are tubular, actinomorphic and bisexual
  • Compositae: calyx reduced to pappus (aids wind dispersal), anthers fused but filaments free (syngenesious), single ovule per ovary
  • Gramineae: hollow (fistular) internodes, leaf sheath with ligule, fibrous roots, parallel venation
  • Gramineae: each floret is enclosed by lemma and palea, perianth reduced to 2 or 3 lodicules, stamens usually 3 (6 in rice and bamboo), monocarpellary superior ovary with one basal ovule
  • Gramineae fruit is a caryopsis, in which the pericarp is fused with the seed coat

$\oplus\ Epi_{5-8}\ K_{(5)}\ C_{5}\ A_{(\infty)}\ \underline{G}_{(5)}$ Malvaceae (China rose): actinomorphic, bisexual, epicalyx, gamosepalous calyx, free petals, numerous monadelphous stamens, superior syncarpous pentacarpellary ovary

$\oplus\ K_{2+2}\ C_{4}\ A_{2+4}\ \underline{G}_{(2)}$ Cruciferae (mustard): 4 sepals in two whorls, 4 cruciform petals, tetradynamous stamens, superior bicarpellary syncarpous ovary

$\%\ K_{(5)}\ C_{1+2+(2)}\ A_{(9)+1}\ \underline{G}_{1}$ Leguminosae, Papilionoideae (pea): zygomorphic, papilionaceous corolla, diadelphous stamens, superior monocarpellary ovary

$\oplus\ K_{\text{pappus}}\ C_{(5)}\ A_{(5)}\ \overline{G}_{(2)}$ Compositae disc floret (sunflower): calyx as pappus, gamopetalous corolla, 5 epipetalous syngenesious stamens, inferior bicarpellary ovary

$P_{2-3\,(\text{lodicules})}\ A_{3}\ \underline{G}_{1}$ Gramineae (wheat): perianth reduced to lodicules, 3 stamens with versatile anthers, superior ovary with one ovule

$\underline{G}$ versus $\overline{G}$ A line below G means superior ovary (hypogynous); a line above G means inferior ovary (epigynous); brackets mean fusion

NEET tip: NEET gives statements on stamen condition, placentation, ovary position or fruit type and asks which family they fit, so learn the floral formula of each family.

Animal tissues

Animal tissues are of four basic types. 1. Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines cavities, with little intercellular matrix. Simple epithelium can be squamous, cuboidal, columnar or ciliated. Compound epithelium is multilayered and protective. Glandular epithelium may be unicellular or multicellular, and exocrine or endocrine. 2. Connective tissue links and supports other tissues. It includes loose connective tissue (areolar, adipose), dense connective tissue (regular, irregular) and specialised connective tissue (cartilage, bone, blood). Except blood, these cells secrete collagen or elastin fibres. 3. Muscle tissue can be skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (fusiform, non-striated, involuntary) or cardiac (striated, branched, involuntary, with intercalated discs). 4. Neural tissue consists of neurons, which are excitable, and neuroglia, which support and protect neurons.

  • Simple squamous epithelium: walls of blood vessels and air sacs (alveoli) of lungs
  • Simple cuboidal epithelium: ducts of glands and tubular parts of nephrons; PCT has a brush border of microvilli
  • Simple columnar epithelium: lining of stomach and intestine; it may bear microvilli
  • Ciliated epithelium: bronchioles and fallopian tubes
  • Compound epithelium: dry surface of skin, moist surface of buccal cavity and pharynx, inner lining of ducts of salivary glands and pancreatic ducts
  • Goblet cells are unicellular glands; salivary glands are multicellular; exocrine glands secrete through ducts, endocrine glands release hormones directly into fluid
  • Cell junctions: tight junctions stop leakage, adhering junctions cement cells, gap junctions allow passage of ions and small molecules
  • Adipose tissue stores fat; tendons attach muscle to bone, ligaments attach bone to bone (dense regular); skin dermis is dense irregular
  • Cartilage cells (chondrocytes) and bone cells (osteocytes) lie in lacunae; bone matrix is rich in calcium salts and collagen fibres
  • Cardiac muscle cells are joined by intercalated discs, which let them contract as a unit
  • Neuroglia make up more than one-half the volume of neural tissue

NEET tip: Expect location-of-tissue match questions (which epithelium lines what, tendon versus ligament) and statement questions on cell junctions and muscle types.

Frog: morphology, anatomy and organ systems (digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous, reproductive)

The common Indian frog is Rana tigrina, now called Hoplobatrachus tigerinus. Frogs are cold-blooded (poikilothermic) and escape extreme heat and cold by aestivation and hibernation. Their body has a head and trunk but no neck or tail. The skin is moist, mucus-covered and absorbs water, so frogs do not drink water. - Respiration: in water, frogs breathe through the skin (cutaneous respiration). On land, they use the buccal cavity, skin and lungs. - Circulation: closed, with a three-chambered heart (2 atria, 1 ventricle), plus hepatic portal and renal portal systems. - Excretion: frogs are ureotelic. - Nervous system: the brain is divided into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain, and 10 pairs of cranial nerves arise from it. - Reproduction: sexes are separate.
