Fertilisation is external in water, and development is indirect through a tadpole larva that undergoes metamorphosis.

  • Eyes have a nictitating membrane; a tympanum receives sound; frogs have no external ear
  • Forelimbs have 4 digits; hindlimbs have 5 webbed digits for swimming
  • Males have vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of each forelimb
  • Digestive system: short alimentary canal (carnivorous), bilobed tongue attached anteriorly and free posteriorly, maxillary and vomerine teeth, opening into the cloaca
  • Liver bile is stored in the gall bladder; digestion occurs in the stomach (HCl, gastric juice) and intestine; absorption through villi and microvilli
  • Lungs are a pair of elongated pink sac-like structures; during aestivation and hibernation, gas exchange is through the skin
  • Heart: sinus venosus opens into the right atrium, and the conus arteriosus arises from the ventricle on the ventral side
  • RBCs are nucleated; blood has plasma, RBCs, WBCs and platelets; a lymphatic system is present
  • Forebrain: olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon; midbrain: a pair of optic lobes; hindbrain: cerebellum and medulla oblongata
  • Sense organs: touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (simple eyes), hearing (tympanum with internal ears)
  • Endocrine glands: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads
  • Male: yellowish ovoid testes attached to the kidneys by mesorchium; 10 to 12 vasa efferentia enter the kidney and open into Bidder's canal, which joins the urinogenital duct
  • Female: ovaries have no functional connection with the kidneys; oviducts open into the cloaca; 2500 to 3000 ova are laid at a time
  • Ecological role: frogs eat insects and protect crops; frog legs are used as food in some countries

NEET tip: NEET asks direct one-liners on the mode of respiration in water versus on land, the number of cranial nerves, heart chambers, and the male versus female urinogenital arrangement.

Key facts

  • Frogs respire through the skin in water and through the buccal cavity, skin and lungs on land.
  • Frogs have 10 pairs of cranial nerves.
  • Frog heart has three chambers: two atria and one ventricle, with sinus venosus and conus arteriosus.
  • Frogs are ureotelic; in males the ureter acts as a urinogenital duct, while in females the ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca.
  • A female frog lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time; fertilisation is external.
  • Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves: alternate in China rose, opposite in Calotropis and guava, whorled in Alstonia.
  • Placentation: marginal in pea, axile in tomato and China rose, parietal in mustard and Argemone, free central in Dianthus and Primrose, basal in sunflower and marigold.
  • Twisted aestivation occurs in China rose, lady's finger and cotton; vexillary aestivation occurs in pea and bean.
  • Monadelphous stamens occur in China rose, diadelphous in pea, polyadelphous in Citrus.
  • Cruciferae has tetradynamous stamens, a siliqua fruit and a replum.
  • Compositae has syngenesious stamens, a pappus, an inferior ovary with basal placentation and a cypsela fruit.
  • Gramineae has lodicules, versatile anthers, a caryopsis fruit and hollow internodes.
  • Malvaceae has an epicalyx, monadelphous stamens and monothecous (reniform) anthers.
  • Potato is a stem tuber; sweet potato is a modified adventitious root.
  • Stilt roots occur in maize and sugarcane, prop roots in banyan, pneumatophores in Rhizophora.
  • Phylloclade occurs in Opuntia; phyllode occurs in Australian Acacia.
  • Dicot root has 2 to 4 xylem bundles (diarch to tetrarch); monocot root has more than 6 (polyarch).
  • Casparian strips in the endodermis are made of suberin.
  • Vascular bundles are open in dicot stems and closed in monocot stems, with protoxylem cavities in monocots.
  • Bulliform cells in grass leaves cause leaf rolling under water stress.
  • Collenchyma is absent in monocots; vessels are absent in gymnosperms.
  • Mature sieve tube elements lack a nucleus and are controlled by companion cells.
  • Simple squamous epithelium lines blood vessels and lung alveoli; ciliated epithelium lines bronchioles and fallopian tubes.
  • Tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments join bone to bone; both are dense regular connective tissue.
  • Intercalated discs are found only in cardiac muscle.
  • In mango the edible part is the mesocarp; in coconut the mesocarp is fibrous.
  • Castor seed is endospermic; bean, gram and pea seeds are non-endospermic.

Common traps

  • Saying frogs breathe through lungs in water. In water, respiration is cutaneous (through the skin); lungs are used on land.
  • Confusing frog cranial nerves (10 pairs) with human cranial nerves (12 pairs).
  • Treating potato, ginger and Colocasia as roots. They are underground stems because they bear nodes and buds; sweet potato and carrot are roots.
  • Mixing up parietal (Argemone, mustard) with free central (Primrose, Dianthus) placentation. Free central has ovules on a central axis without septa.
  • Confusing syngenesious stamens (anthers fused, filaments free, in Compositae) with monadelphous stamens (filaments fused into one bundle, in Malvaceae).
  • Assuming a line above G means superior ovary. A line below G means superior; a line above G means inferior, as in Compositae.
  • Thinking monocot stems have open bundles and secondary growth. Monocot bundles are closed and scattered, so there is normally no secondary growth.
  • Thinking the racemose oldest flower is at the top. In racemose, flowers are acropetal, so the oldest is at the base; in cymose the terminal flower is the oldest.

Quick revision

  • Racemose inflorescence: main axis keeps growing, acropetal order. Cymose: axis ends in a flower, basipetal order.
  • Placentation: pea marginal, tomato axile, Argemone parietal, Primrose free central, sunflower basal.
  • Aestivation: Calotropis valvate, China rose twisted, Cassia imbricate, pea vexillary.
  • Cruciferae floral formula is K 2+2, C4, A 2+4, G(2) superior; fruit siliqua.
  • Papilionoideae floral formula is K(5), C 1+2+(2), A (9)+1, G1 superior; fruit legume.
  • Malvaceae has epicalyx and monadelphous stamens; Compositae has pappus, syngenesious stamens and cypsela; Gramineae has lodicules and caryopsis.
  • Dicot root is diarch to tetrarch; monocot root is polyarch with a large pith.
  • Dicot stem bundles are in a ring, open; monocot stem bundles are scattered, closed, with a bundle sheath.
  • Dicot leaf is dorsiventral; grass leaf is isobilateral with bulliform cells.
  • Squamous epithelium lines alveoli and vessels; cuboidal lines PCT and gland ducts; columnar lines gut; ciliated lines bronchioles and fallopian tube.
  • Frog: skin breathing in water, 3-chambered heart, 10 pairs of cranial nerves, ureotelic, external fertilisation, tadpole stage.
  • Male frog has vocal sacs, a copulatory pad, and Bidder's canal linking testes to the urinogenital duct.

Biology · Unit 3: Cell Structure and Function

This unit covers the cell as the structural and functional unit of life: cell theory, prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisation, cell organelles, the chemistry of life (biomolecules and enzymes), and how cells divide (cell cycle, mitosis, meiosis). It is one of the highest-weightage units in NEET Biology. Most questions are direct, NCERT-line based, and often framed as match-the-list, statement pairs or multi-statement items.

PYQs (12): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q93, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q94, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q96, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q97, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q98, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q106, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q108, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q123, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q126, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q128, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q131, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q134

Cell theory and cell as the basic unit of life

Anton von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell. Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus. In 1838 Matthias Schleiden, a German botanist, observed that all plants are made of different kinds of cells that form tissues. In 1839 Theodore Schwann, a zoologist, studied animal cells. He reported that cells have a thin outer layer, now called the plasma membrane, and that the cell wall is unique to plant cells. Together, Schleiden and Schwann proposed the cell theory. It did not explain how new cells form. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added that new cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula). Modern cell theory states two things. First, all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells. Second, all cells arise from pre-existing cells. An organism made of one cell is unicellular, and one made of many cells is multicellular. Anything less than a complete cell cannot live independently.

  • Leeuwenhoek: first to see a live cell
  • Robert Brown: discovered the nucleus
  • Schleiden (1838, plants) and Schwann (1839, animals) formulated cell theory
  • Schwann: plasma membrane in animal cells; cell wall unique to plants
  • Virchow (1855): Omnis cellula-e cellula, which completed the theory
  • Cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of life

NEET tip: Direct name-and-contribution questions (who formulated it, who added 'cells arise from pre-existing cells') are very common.

Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; plant and animal cells

Prokaryotic cells include bacteria, blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), mycoplasma and PPLO. They lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Their genetic material is naked and circular and lies in the nucleoid. Many also carry plasmids, which are small circular extrachromosomal DNA and may confer antibiotic resistance. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of 50S and 30S subunits. Mesosomes, inclusion bodies and gas vacuoles may also be present. Eukaryotic cells occur in protists, fungi, plants and animals. They have a true nucleus with a nuclear envelope, membrane-bound organelles, 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes and a cytoskeleton. Plant cells differ from animal cells in having a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole. Animal cells have centrioles, which are absent in almost all plant cells. Cell size varies widely. Mycoplasma is the smallest cell (about $0.3\ \mu m$), bacteria are 3 to $5\ \mu m$, a human RBC is about $7\ \mu m$, and the ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell.

  • Prokaryotes: bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, PPLO; fungi are eukaryotes
  • Bacterial shapes: bacillus (rod), coccus (spherical), vibrio (comma), spirillum (spiral)
  • Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles, so no peroxisomes, mitochondria or ER
  • 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes; 80S (60S + 40S) in eukaryotes
  • Polysome (polyribosome): several ribosomes on one mRNA
  • Plant cell: cell wall, plastids, large vacuole; animal cell: centrioles
  • Smallest cell: Mycoplasma; longest cells: nerve cells; largest isolated cell: ostrich egg

$70S \neq 50S + 30S$ Svedberg units measure sedimentation rate, which depends on size and shape, so subunit S values are not additive. This applies equally to $80S$ = $60S$ + $40S$.

NEET tip: Expect multi-statement items on prokaryotic features (plasmid, mesosome, 70S ribosome) mixed with a eukaryote-only feature such as peroxisomes.

Cell envelope, cell membrane and cell wall

The bacterial cell envelope has three tightly bound layers: an outer glycocalyx, the cell wall and the plasma membrane. The glycocalyx may be a loose slime layer or a thick, tough capsule. Gram staining divides bacteria into Gram-positive (retain the stain) and Gram-negative (do not). The mesosome is formed by extension of the plasma membrane into the cell. It helps in cell wall formation, DNA replication and its distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion, and increasing membrane surface area and enzyme content. Flagella move bacteria; pili and fimbriae do not help in motility but help attachment. The eukaryotic plasma membrane mainly contains lipids (phospholipids in a bilayer) and proteins. The human RBC membrane has about 52% protein and 40% lipid. Singer and Nicolson's fluid mosaic model (1972) describes a quasi-fluid lipid bilayer that allows lateral movement of proteins. Plant cell walls contain cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins, while algal walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and calcium carbonate. The middle lamella is mainly calcium pectate.

  • Cell envelope = glycocalyx + cell wall + plasma membrane
  • Bacterial flagellum: filament, hook and basal body
  • Pili and fimbriae: attachment, not motility
  • Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson (1972)
  • Membrane proteins: peripheral (surface) and integral (buried)
  • Membrane fluidity aids growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division
  • Transport: passive (along gradient, including osmosis), active (uses ATP, e.g. $Na^+/K^+$ pump)
  • Primary wall can grow; secondary wall forms on the inner side of the primary wall
  • Plasmodesmata connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring plant cells

NEET tip: Questions ask for the fluid mosaic model's proposers, the RBC membrane protein:lipid ratio, middle lamella composition and mesosome functions.

Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi bodies, lysosomes and vacuoles

The endomembrane system consists of the ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles, because their functions are coordinated. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not included. The ER divides the cytoplasm into luminal and extraluminal compartments. Rough ER carries ribosomes, is involved in protein synthesis and secretion, and is extensive in secretory cells. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is the major site of lipid synthesis; in animals it synthesises steroidal hormones. The Golgi apparatus was first observed by Camillo Golgi in 1898. It consists of flat, disc-shaped cisternae with a convex cis (forming) face and a concave trans (maturing) face. It packages materials for intracellular targets or for secretion, and it is the site where glycoproteins and glycolipids are formed. Lysosomes bud off from the Golgi and contain acid hydrolases (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) that work best at acidic pH. Vacuoles are bounded by the tonoplast and can occupy up to 90% of a plant cell's volume.

  • Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles
  • RER: protein synthesis; SER: lipid and steroid synthesis
  • Golgi: cis face receives material from the ER; trans face releases it
  • Golgi forms glycoproteins and glycolipids and packages secretions
  • Lysosomes: acid hydrolases, optimally active at acidic pH
  • Tonoplast transports ions into the vacuole against the gradient, so sap concentration exceeds cytoplasm
  • Contractile vacuole in Amoeba: osmoregulation and excretion
  • Food vacuoles in protists are formed by engulfing food particles

NEET tip: NEET checks endomembrane membership (excluding mitochondria, plastids and peroxisomes) and SER versus RER functions.

Mitochondria, ribosomes, plastids and microbodies

Mitochondria are sausage-shaped or cylindrical organelles. They are about 0.2 to 1.0 $\mu m$ wide (average 0.5) and 1.0 to 4.1 $\mu m$ long. They have a double membrane. The inner membrane encloses the matrix and folds into cristae, which increase surface area. Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration and ATP production, the 'powerhouse of the cell'. The matrix contains circular DNA, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes and components for protein synthesis, and mitochondria divide by fission. Plastids are of three types. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carotenoids and carry out photosynthesis. Chromoplasts contain fat-soluble carotenoids such as carotene and xanthophylls, giving yellow, orange or red colours. Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids: amyloplasts store starch, elaioplasts store oils and fats, and aleuroplasts store proteins. In a chloroplast, thylakoids are flattened sacs in the stroma, stacked as grana and joined by stroma lamellae. The stroma also contains enzymes, circular DNA and 70S ribosomes. Ribosomes are non-membranous RNA-protein particles first observed by George Palade (1953). Microbodies are single-membrane vesicles with enzymes and include peroxisomes and glyoxysomes.

  • Inner mitochondrial membrane encloses the matrix; cristae are its infoldings
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous: own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
  • Chromoplast: carotene and xanthophyll pigments
  • Amyloplast: starch (e.g. potato); elaioplast: oils; aleuroplast: proteins
  • Chloroplast: about 5 to 10 $\mu m$ long, 2 to 4 $\mu m$ wide
  • Chlamydomonas has a single chloroplast; leaf mesophyll cells have 20 to 40
  • Chloroplast ribosomes are smaller (70S) than cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S)
  • Ribosomes: no membrane; discovered by Palade
  • Microbodies occur in both plant and animal cells

NEET tip: Match-list items pair cristae, cisternae, thylakoids and stroma with their locations; plastid–stored substance pairs are frequent.

Cytoskeleton, cilia, flagella and centrioles

The cytoskeleton is a network of proteinaceous filaments in the cytoplasm. It has three components: microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments. It provides mechanical support, motility and maintenance of cell shape. Cilia are small and work like oars, while flagella are longer and responsible for cell movement. Both are hair-like outgrowths of the plasma membrane. Their core, the axoneme, has nine pairs of doublet peripheral microtubules and a pair of central microtubules (9+2 arrangement). The central tubules are joined by bridges and enclosed by a central sheath. Each peripheral doublet is connected to the central sheath by a radial spoke, and adjacent doublets are joined by linkers. Cilia and flagella arise from centriole-like basal bodies. The centrosome contains two cylindrical centrioles lying perpendicular to each other, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material. Each centriole has a cartwheel organisation of nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin, each a triplet, with a central proteinaceous hub. Centrioles form the basal body of cilia and flagella and the spindle fibres of animal cells.

  • Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments
  • Axoneme of cilia and flagella: 9+2 microtubule arrangement
  • Peripheral fibrils of axoneme are doublets; of centriole are triplets
  • Centriole: 9+0 cartwheel with central hub and radial spokes
  • Two centrioles in the centrosome lie perpendicular to each other
  • Prokaryotic flagella differ structurally from eukaryotic flagella
  • Centrioles absent in almost all higher plant cells

NEET tip: Questions contrast doublets in the axoneme with triplets in the centriole, the 9+2 versus 9+0 pattern, and centriole roles.

Nucleus: nuclear membrane, chromatin and nucleolus

The nucleus was first described by Robert Brown in 1831, and Flemming named the stainable material chromatin. The interphase nucleus has loose nucleoprotein fibres (chromatin), a nuclear matrix and one or more nucleoli. The nuclear envelope has two parallel membranes separated by a 10 to 50 nm perinuclear space. The outer membrane is usually continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes. Nuclear pores allow RNA and protein to move in both directions. Normally there is one nucleus per cell. Mature mammalian RBCs and plant sieve tube cells lack a nucleus. Nucleoli are non-membrane-bound, spherical sites of active ribosomal RNA synthesis and are larger and more numerous in cells active in protein synthesis. Chromatin contains DNA, basic histone proteins, non-histone proteins and RNA. A single human cell has about 2 m of DNA in 46 chromosomes. Each chromosome has a primary constriction (centromere) bearing disc-shaped kinetochores. By centromere position, chromosomes are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric and telocentric. Some have a satellite beyond a secondary constriction.

  • Nucleus discovered by Robert Brown (1831); chromatin named by Flemming
  • Perinuclear space: 10 to 50 nm
  • Outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the ER
  • Nucleolus: rRNA synthesis, no membrane
  • Enucleate cells: mammalian RBCs, sieve tube cells
  • Metacentric: middle centromere, equal arms
  • Sub-metacentric: centromere slightly away from the middle
  • Acrocentric: centromere near the end; telocentric: terminal centromere
  • Kinetochores: disc-shaped structures on the sides of the centromere

NEET tip: Common items cover chromosome types by centromere position, nucleolus function, perinuclear space width and enucleate cells.

Biomolecules: proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids

Living tissue contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in higher proportion than the earth's crust. In the NCERT table of the human body by weight, oxygen is about 65%, carbon 18.5%, nitrogen 3.3% and hydrogen 0.5%. The actual hydrogen content is about 9.5–10%, but NCERT-based questions may use the table figure. Water is the most abundant compound in cells. Chemical analysis separates an acid-soluble pool of micromolecules (molecular weight below 1000 Da) from an acid-insoluble fraction. The acid-insoluble fraction contains proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids. Lipids are not polymers but appear here because membranes break into insoluble vesicles. Proteins are heteropolymers of 20 amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Their structure has primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary levels. Polysaccharides are chains of monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds. Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose; starch stores energy and gives a blue colour with iodine; inulin is a fructose polymer; chitin forms exoskeletons. Lipids include fatty acids, glycerides and phospholipids such as lecithin. Nucleic acids are polynucleotides linked by phosphodiester bonds. Watson–Crick B-DNA has 10 bp per turn and a pitch of 3.4 nm.

  • Human body by weight (NCERT table): O (65%) > C (18.5%) > N (3.3%) > H (0.5%); actual H is about 9.5–10%
  • Water: about 70 to 90% of cell mass
  • RuBisCO: most abundant protein in the biosphere; collagen: most abundant in the animal world
  • Protein functions: antibody (fights infection), GLUT-4 (glucose transport), receptors, hormones, enzymes
  • Concanavalin A is a lectin, a secondary metabolite
  • Amino acids exist as zwitterions; their structure changes with pH
  • Starch helix holds $I_2$ (blue colour); cellulose does not
  • Palmitic acid: 16 C including carboxyl C; arachidonic acid: 20 C
  • Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate
  • Haemoglobin: 4 subunits ($2\alpha$ + $2\beta$), quaternary structure

$A + G = T + C$ and $\frac{A}{T} = \frac{G}{C} = 1$ Chargaff's rule for double-stranded DNA; use it to find unknown base percentages.

$L = N_{bp} \times 0.34\ nm$ Length of B-DNA from the number of base pairs; one turn (10 bp) = 3.4 nm.

NEET tip: Match lists pair biomolecules with functions (starch, antibody, lectin, GLUT-4); elemental-abundance order and bond types are frequent.

Enzymes: types, properties, action, classification and nomenclature

Almost all enzymes are proteins; some nucleic acids, called ribozymes, also act as catalysts. Enzymes lower activation energy and speed up reactions. For example, carbonic anhydrase increases the rate of $CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3$ about 10 million times. Substrate binds the active site to form an enzyme–substrate complex, which is transient. The substrate then changes to a transition state and finally to products. Enzyme activity depends on temperature, pH and substrate concentration. Each enzyme shows an optimum temperature and an optimum pH. High temperature denatures enzymes, whereas low temperature only inactivates them temporarily. A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site; for example, malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase. Enzymes are named with the suffix '-ase' and grouped into six classes. Many enzymes need cofactors: prosthetic groups (haem in peroxidase and catalase), coenzymes (NAD and NADP, which contain niacin) and metal ions (zinc in carboxypeptidase). The protein part alone is the apoenzyme.

  • Six classes in order: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases
  • Hydrolases break bonds using water; ligases join two compounds
  • Lyases remove groups other than by hydrolysis, forming double bonds
  • Holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor
  • Prosthetic group is tightly bound; coenzyme binds only transiently
  • Activity at $V_{max}$ does not rise further with more substrate, because active sites are saturated
  • Competitive inhibitors are used to control bacterial pathogens
  • Enzymes from thermophilic organisms in hot springs are stable at 80 to 90 degrees C

$V = \frac{V_{max}[S]}{K_m + [S]}$ Michaelis–Menten relation; $K_m$ is the substrate concentration at which $V = \frac{V_{max}}{2}$, and a lower $K_m$ means higher affinity.

NEET tip: Expect EC class identification, cofactor examples (haem, NAD, zinc), the malonate–succinic dehydrogenase pair and effects of temperature and pH.

Cell cycle

The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and divides into two daughter cells. A typical human cell in culture divides about once every 24 hours, and yeast takes about 90 minutes. The cycle has an interphase, which takes more than 95% of the time, and an M phase lasting about an hour. In G1 the cell is metabolically active and grows, but its DNA does not replicate. In S phase DNA replication occurs, so the DNA content doubles from 2C to 4C while the chromosome number stays the same. In animal cells the centriole also duplicates in the cytoplasm during S phase. G2 continues protein synthesis in preparation for mitosis, and cell growth continues. Cells that stop dividing, such as many heart cells, exit G1 into the quiescent G0 stage. G0 cells stay metabolically active and can be triggered to divide. In animals mitosis occurs only in diploid somatic cells, whereas in plants both haploid and diploid cells can divide mitotically.

  • Correct sequence: G1 → S → G2 → M
  • Interphase (resting phase) = G1 + S + G2, more than 95% of the cycle
  • Human cell cycle about 24 h; M phase about 1 h; yeast about 90 min
  • S phase: DNA 2C → 4C, ploidy unchanged
  • Centriole duplication in animal cells: S phase
  • G0: quiescent, metabolically active, not proliferating
  • Meristematic tissues divide continuously throughout life

$2C \xrightarrow{S\ phase} 4C$ DNA content doubles in S phase while chromosome number (2n) remains constant.

NEET tip: Phase-sequence questions and DNA-content versus chromosome-number questions at G1, G2 and after division are very common.

Mitosis

Mitosis is called equational division because daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent. Karyokinesis has four stages. Prophase: chromatin condenses, the centrosome moves to opposite poles and spindle fibres form. By its end, the Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope are no longer visible. Metaphase: chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids, align at the metaphase plate. Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores. This stage is best for studying chromosome morphology. Anaphase: centromeres split, and the separated chromatids, now daughter chromosomes, move to opposite poles. Telophase: chromosomes decondense at the poles, and the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform. Cytokinesis follows. In animal cells a furrow in the plasma membrane deepens and divides the cytoplasm. In plant cells a cell plate forms in the centre and grows outward; it becomes the middle lamella. If karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, a multinucleate syncytium forms, such as the liquid endosperm of coconut. Mitosis enables growth, repair, cell replacement and maintenance of the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio.

  • Stages in order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
  • Metaphase: best stage to study chromosome morphology
  • Anaphase: centromeres split and chromatids separate
  • Animal cytokinesis: furrow; plant cytokinesis: cell plate (middle lamella)
  • Syncytium example: liquid endosperm of coconut
  • Mitosis keeps ploidy constant (2n → 2n, or n → n in plants)
  • Mitosis restores the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio

$N = 2^n$ Number of cells formed from one cell after n successive mitotic divisions.

NEET tip: NEET asks stage-specific events (kinetochore attachment, centromere splitting, nuclear envelope reappearance) and the plant versus animal cytokinesis difference.

Meiosis and its significance

Meiosis is a reductional division that produces four haploid cells from one diploid cell. It occurs during gamete formation in sexually reproducing organisms. It involves a single round of DNA replication followed by two divisions. Prophase I is long and has five sub-stages. In leptotene, chromosomes become visible. In zygotene, homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) through the synaptonemal complex, forming bivalents (tetrads). In pachytene, crossing over occurs at recombination nodules with the help of the enzyme recombinase. In diplotene, the synaptonemal complex dissolves and chiasmata appear; in oocytes this stage can last months or years. In diakinesis, chiasmata terminalise, chromosomes are fully condensed, the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down. In anaphase I, homologues separate while sister chromatids stay together. Interkinesis is short and has no DNA replication. Meiosis II resembles normal mitosis, and its anaphase II separates sister chromatids. Meiosis conserves chromosome number across generations and generates genetic variation.

  • Prophase I order: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis
  • Zygotene: synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalent
  • Pachytene: crossing over, recombination nodules, recombinase
  • Diplotene: chiasmata visible; long-lasting in oocytes
  • Diakinesis: terminalisation; chromosomes fully condensed for metaphase I
  • Anaphase I separates homologues; anaphase II separates sister chromatids
  • Meiosis II, not meiosis I, resembles mitosis
  • Significance: halves chromosome number in gametes; restores it on fertilisation; creates variation

$2n \rightarrow 4 \times n$ One meiosis yields four haploid cells; useful in counting meioses needed for a given number of gametes or seeds.

NEET tip: Statement-pair and sequence questions focus on prophase I sub-stages (synapsis, crossing over, chiasmata, terminalisation) and which division resembles mitosis.

Key facts

  • Cell theory: Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839); modified by Virchow (1855).
  • Smallest cell: Mycoplasma (about $0.3\ \mu m$); human RBC about $7\ \mu m$; bacteria 3 to $5\ \mu m$.
  • Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson, 1972.
  • Human RBC membrane: about 52% protein and 40% lipid.
  • Prokaryotic ribosome 70S (50S + 30S); eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosome 80S (60S + 40S).
  • Golgi apparatus was first observed by Camillo Golgi in 1898.
  • Ribosomes were first observed by George Palade in 1953.
  • Nucleus was discovered by Robert Brown in 1831.
  • Vacuole can occupy up to 90% of plant cell volume.
  • Middle lamella is mainly calcium pectate.
  • Mitochondria: 0.2 to 1.0 $\mu m$ diameter, 1.0 to 4.1 $\mu m$ length.
  • Chloroplasts per mesophyll cell: 20 to 40; Chlamydomonas has one.
  • Perinuclear space: 10 to 50 nm.
  • A human diploid cell contains about 2 m of DNA in 46 chromosomes.
  • Axoneme is 9+2 (doublets); centriole is 9+0 (triplets).
  • Human body by weight (NCERT table): O 65%, C 18.5%, N 3.3%, H 0.5% (actual H about 9.5–10%; NCERT-based questions may use the table figure).
  • Most abundant protein in the biosphere: RuBisCO; in animals: collagen.
  • B-DNA: 10 bp per turn, pitch 3.4 nm, 0.34 nm between adjacent base pairs.
  • Carbonic anhydrase speeds $CO_2$ hydration about 10 million times.
  • Malonate competitively inhibits succinic dehydrogenase.
  • Enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases.
  • Zinc is a cofactor of carboxypeptidase; haem is the prosthetic group of peroxidase and catalase.
  • Human cell cycle about 24 h; yeast about 90 min; M phase about 1 h.
  • Crossing over occurs in pachytene and is mediated by recombinase.
  • Liquid endosperm of coconut is a syncytium (karyokinesis without cytokinesis).
  • Chromoplasts contain carotene and xanthophylls; aleuroplasts store proteins; elaioplasts store oils.

Common traps

  • Including mitochondria, chloroplasts or peroxisomes in the endomembrane system is wrong: it comprises only the ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles.
  • Assuming S phase doubles chromosome number is wrong: DNA doubles (2C to 4C), but chromosome number stays 2n.
  • Thinking meiosis I resembles mitosis is wrong: meiosis II resembles mitosis, while meiosis I is reductional.
  • Adding Svedberg units ($50S + 30S = 80S$) is wrong: the result is 70S, because S values are not additive.
  • Calling fungi prokaryotes is wrong: fungi are eukaryotes. Prokaryotes are bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma and PPLO.
  • Assuming lipids are absent from the acid-insoluble fraction because they are not polymers is wrong: they appear there as membrane vesicles.
  • Confusing doublets and triplets is a mistake: axoneme microtubules are doublets (9+2), while centriole fibrils are triplets (9+0).
  • Placing crossing over in zygotene is wrong: zygotene is synapsis, pachytene is crossing over, and chiasmata become visible in diplotene.

Quick revision

  • Cell theory: Schleiden + Schwann; Virchow added Omnis cellula-e cellula.
  • Prokaryotes: nucleoid, plasmids, mesosome, 70S ribosomes; no membrane-bound organelles.
  • Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson; quasi-fluid lipid bilayer with proteins.
  • Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles; SER makes lipids, RER makes proteins.
  • Golgi has cis (forming) and trans (maturing) faces; it forms glycoproteins and glycolipids.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts have own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes; cristae increase surface area.
  • Leucoplasts: amyloplast (starch), elaioplast (oil), aleuroplast (protein); chromoplast contains carotenoids.
  • Cilia and flagella are 9+2; centriole is 9+0 cartwheel with triplets.
  • Chromosomes by centromere: metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric.
  • Body element order (NCERT table): O > C > N > H; B-DNA has 10 bp per turn and 3.4 nm pitch.
  • Enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases; competitive inhibitor resembles substrate.
  • Cell cycle G1 → S → G2 → M; prophase I: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis.

Biology · Unit 4: Plant Physiology

Plant Physiology explains how plants capture light energy through photosynthesis, release that energy through respiration, and grow and develop under the control of internal and external factors, including plant growth regulators. It is a high-weightage NEET unit. Questions test numbers (ATP, turns of the Calvin cycle, RQ), sites of reactions, enzymes, the C3 versus C4 comparison, growth-rate calculations and practical uses of PGRs.

PYQs (9): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q100, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q102, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q109, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q110, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q114, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q116, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q122, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q127, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q133

Photosynthesis as autotrophic nutrition; site of photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process in which green plants use light energy to make organic compounds from $CO_2$ and water. This makes them autotrophs, and nearly all life on earth depends on them for food and oxygen. Our understanding grew through a series of classic experiments. Priestley (1770) showed that air is restored by plants. Ingenhousz showed that sunlight and green parts are needed. Sachs (1854) showed that glucose is produced and stored as starch. Engelmann obtained the first action spectrum using Cladophora and aerobic bacteria. Van Niel proved that $O_2$ comes from water. Photosynthesis occurs mainly in the mesophyll cells of leaves, inside chloroplasts. The membrane system (grana and thylakoids) traps light and makes ATP and NADPH. The stroma contains the enzymes that reduce $CO_2$ to sugar.

  • Autotrophic nutrition is seen only in plants, algae and some bacteria.
  • Priestley used a bell jar, a candle, a mouse and a mint plant to show that plants restore bad air.
  • Ingenhousz showed that only the green parts of plants, in sunlight, release oxygen.
  • Sachs showed that glucose is made and is usually stored as starch.
  • Engelmann used a prism and found that bacteria gathered in blue and red light, giving the first action spectrum.
  • Van Niel, working with purple and green bacteria, showed that $O_2$ released by green plants comes from $H_2O$, not $CO_2$.
  • Chloroplasts line up along mesophyll cell walls for optimum light.
  • Thylakoids (grana) carry out the light reaction; the stroma carries out the dark (biosynthetic) reaction.

$6CO_2 + 12H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{light}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6H_2O + 6O_2$ Overall equation of photosynthesis; it shows that the oxygen released comes from water.

$2H_2A + CO_2 \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2A + CH_2O + H_2O$ Van Niel's general equation, where $H_2A$ is the oxidisable hydrogen donor.

NEET tip: NEET asks the chronological sequence of experiments: Priestley, then Ingenhousz, then Sachs, then Engelmann, then van Niel.

Photosynthetic pigments

Paper chromatography of leaf pigments separates four pigments. Chlorophyll a is bright or blue-green. Chlorophyll b is yellow-green. Xanthophylls are yellow. Carotenoids are yellow to yellow-orange. Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment and forms the reaction centre. The absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a shows peaks in the blue and red regions. The action spectrum of photosynthesis closely matches this absorption spectrum. This shows that most photosynthesis takes place in blue and red light. The other pigments are accessory pigments. They absorb a wider range of wavelengths and pass the energy to chlorophyll a. They also protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

  • Chlorophyll a is the main pigment and is present at both reaction centres, P680 and P700.
  • Accessory pigments are chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids.
  • Maximum absorption and photosynthesis occur in the blue and red regions of the spectrum.
  • Some photosynthesis also occurs in other wavelengths because accessory pigments absorb them.
  • Accessory pigments protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.
  • Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) is 400 to 700 nm.

NEET tip: Expect questions on the colour of each pigment in chromatography and on which pigment forms the P700 or P680 reaction centre (chlorophyll a).

Photochemical and biosynthetic phases of photosynthesis

Photosynthesis has two phases. The photochemical (light) phase takes place on the thylakoid membranes. It includes light absorption, splitting of water, release of oxygen, and formation of ATP and NADPH. Pigments are organised into two light harvesting complexes, PS I and PS II. Each has a reaction centre surrounded by antenna pigments. The biosynthetic phase (Calvin cycle, or C3 cycle) takes place in the stroma. It uses that ATP and NADPH to fix $CO_2$ into carbohydrate. The biosynthetic phase is not directly light-driven but depends on the products of the light phase. Melvin Calvin used radioactive $^{14}C$ in algae and found that the first stable product is 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA). The cycle has three stages. Carboxylation of RuBP is done by RuBisCO. Reduction converts PGA to triose phosphate. Regeneration rebuilds RuBP.

  • Water splitting is associated with PS II on the inner (lumen) side of the thylakoid membrane.
  • Water splitting requires $Mn^{2+}$ and $Cl^-$.
  • The Z-scheme of electron flow runs PS II, then the electron transport chain, then PS I, then $NADP^+$.
  • The $CO_2$ acceptor is RuBP (5C); the first stable product is 3-PGA (3C).
  • RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme in the world.
  • Fixing one $CO_2$ needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
  • Forming one glucose needs 6 turns of the cycle, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
  • The cycle runs in all photosynthetic plants, both C3 and C4.

$2H_2O \rightarrow 4H^+ + O_2 + 4e^-$ Photolysis of water at PS II; it supplies electrons to replace those lost by P680.

$\text{Turns} = 6 \times \text{number of glucose molecules}$ Example: 3 glucose molecules need 18 turns of the Calvin cycle.

$6CO_2 + 18ATP + 12NADPH \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6$ Energy requirement for making one glucose molecule.

NEET tip: Numerical questions on Calvin cycle turns, ATP and NADPH requirement are very common; remember 6 turns, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose.

Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation

Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light. In non-cyclic photophosphorylation, PS II and PS I work in series. Electrons flow from water through PS II and PS I to $NADP^+$. This produces ATP, NADPH and $O_2$, and it occurs in the grana thylakoids. In cyclic photophosphorylation, only PS I works. Excited electrons from P700 return to the same PS I through the electron transport chain. Only ATP is formed; no NADPH and no $O_2$ are produced. It occurs in the stroma lamellae. These lack PS II and the NADP reductase enzyme. Cyclic flow also operates when only light of wavelength beyond 680 nm is available.

  • Non-cyclic photophosphorylation uses PS II and PS I and produces ATP, NADPH and $O_2$.
  • Cyclic photophosphorylation uses PS I only and produces ATP only.
  • Stroma lamellae lack PS II and NADP reductase, so only cyclic flow occurs there.
  • The reaction centre of PS I is P700; that of PS II is P680.
  • In the Z-scheme, electrons from PS II pass down the chain to PS I.
  • The final electron acceptor in non-cyclic flow is $NADP^+$.

NEET tip: NEET often asks the site of cyclic photophosphorylation (stroma lamellae) and which products it lacks (NADPH and $O_2$).

Chemiosmotic hypothesis

Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis explains how ATP is made. A proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane drives ATP synthesis. Protons build up in the lumen in three ways. First, water splitting releases $H^+$ inside the lumen. Second, the electron carrier moves protons from the stroma into the lumen as electrons travel through the chain. Third, NADP reductase on the stroma side removes $H^+$ from the stroma while reducing $NADP^+$. The result is a high proton concentration in the lumen and a lower pH there. Protons then flow back to the stroma through the $CF_0$ channel of ATP synthase. This flow changes the shape of $CF_1$, which makes ATP on the stroma side. In mitochondria, protons instead accumulate in the intermembrane space.

  • ATP synthase has two parts: $CF_0$ is the transmembrane proton channel and $CF_1$ projects into the stroma.
  • ATP and NADPH are released into the stroma, where the Calvin cycle uses them.
  • The proton gradient is broken down by the flow of $H^+$ through $CF_0$.
  • Chemiosmosis needs a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase.
  • In mitochondria the equivalent parts of ATP synthase (Complex V) are $F_0$ and $F_1$.

NEET tip: Questions ask where protons accumulate (lumen in chloroplast, intermembrane space in mitochondria) and which part of ATP synthase forms the channel ($F_0$).

Photorespiration

RuBisCO can bind both $CO_2$ and $O_2$, and its affinity for $CO_2$ is higher. When $O_2$ concentration is high, RuBP combines with $O_2$ instead of $CO_2$. This oxygenation gives one molecule of 3-PGA and one molecule of 2-phosphoglycolate, in place of two PGA molecules. The pathway involves three organelles: chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria. It releases $CO_2$ and produces no ATP or NADPH. Instead, it consumes ATP, so it is a wasteful process that lowers C3 productivity. Photorespiration occurs in C3 plants. It is absent in C4 plants because they concentrate $CO_2$ around RuBisCO in the bundle sheath cells.

  • Photorespiration is the oxygenase activity of RuBisCO.
  • Its products are 3-PGA (3C) and phosphoglycolate (2C).
  • No sugar, ATP or NADPH is formed; $O_2$ is used and $CO_2$ is released.
  • It involves the chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria.
  • It is common in C3 plants, especially at high temperature and high $O_2$.
  • It is absent in C4 plants, which is a reason for their higher productivity.

$RuBP + O_2 \rightarrow 3\text{-PGA} + 2\text{-phosphoglycolate}$ Oxygenation reaction of RuBisCO, the first step of photorespiration.

$RuBP + CO_2 \rightarrow 2 \times 3\text{-PGA}$ Normal carboxylation reaction, given for comparison.

NEET tip: Statement-based questions test that photorespiration occurs in C3 plants, forms phosphoglycolate, and produces no ATP or NADPH.

C3 and C4 pathways

C3 plants fix $CO_2$ directly through the Calvin cycle in mesophyll cells. Their first stable product is 3-PGA, a 3-carbon compound. C4 plants, such as maize, sorghum, sugarcane and Amaranthus, are adapted to dry tropical regions. They show Kranz anatomy, in which large bundle sheath cells with many chloroplasts surround the vascular bundles. This is the Hatch and Slack pathway. In mesophyll cells, PEP (3C) accepts $CO_2$ using PEP carboxylase (PEPcase), which has no oxygenase activity. This forms oxaloacetic acid (OAA, 4C). OAA is converted to malate or aspartate, which moves to the bundle sheath. There it is decarboxylated to release $CO_2$ for the Calvin cycle. The remaining 3C molecule returns to the mesophyll and PEP is regenerated.

  • The primary $CO_2$ acceptor is RuBP in C3 plants and PEP in C4 plants.
  • The first stable product is 3-PGA in C3 plants and OAA in C4 plants.
  • Mesophyll cells of C4 plants lack RuBisCO.
  • Bundle sheath cells of C4 plants lack PEPcase.
  • Bundle sheath cells have thick walls that are impervious to gases, and no intercellular spaces.
  • The Calvin cycle occurs in the bundle sheath cells of C4 plants.
  • C4 plants tolerate higher temperatures and have a higher temperature optimum.
  • C4 plants have high productivity because they lack photorespiration.

$PEP + CO_2 \xrightarrow{\text{PEPcase}} OAA$ Primary carboxylation in C4 mesophyll cells.

NEET tip: Comparison questions are frequent: the location of RuBisCO versus PEPcase, first products, Kranz anatomy, and examples of C4 plants.

Factors affecting photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is affected by internal factors and external factors. Internal factors include the number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, and the internal $CO_2$ concentration. External factors include light, $CO_2$, temperature and water. Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905) says the following. If a chemical process depends on several factors, its rate is set by the factor nearest its minimal value. A change in that factor alone will change the rate. Light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight. $CO_2$ is the major limiting factor in nature because air contains only about 0.03 to 0.04% $CO_2$. C4 plants saturate at about 360 $\mu L/L$ $CO_2$. C3 plants keep responding to higher $CO_2$ concentrations.

  • Light is rarely limiting in nature, except for plants in shade or dense forests.
  • Very high light intensity causes chlorophyll breakdown.
  • Increasing $CO_2$ up to 0.05% raises the rate of $CO_2$ fixation.
  • Greenhouse crops such as tomato and bell pepper are grown in $CO_2$-enriched air for higher yield.
  • Dark reactions are enzymatic and therefore sensitive to temperature.
  • Water stress closes stomata and causes leaves to wilt, so it affects photosynthesis indirectly.
  • C3 plants have a lower temperature optimum than C4 plants.

NEET tip: Expect questions on Blackman's law, the main limiting factor ($CO_2$), and the $CO_2$ response of C3 versus C4 plants.

Respiration: exchange of gases

Respiration is the breakdown of C-C bonds of complex organic molecules by oxidation, which releases energy that is trapped as ATP. Plants have no specialised respiratory organs. Gas exchange occurs by diffusion through stomata and lenticels. This is enough for three reasons. Each plant part takes care of its own gas-exchange needs, with little transport between parts. Plants have a low demand for gas exchange compared with animals. The distance gases must diffuse is short, because most living cells are close to the surface. In stems the living cells form thin layers beneath the bark, with lenticels, and the inner cells are dead. Leaves also produce $O_2$ during photosynthesis, which they can use for respiration.

  • Gas exchange takes place through stomata in leaves and lenticels in stems.
  • Roots, stems and leaves respire at much lower rates than animals.
  • Loosely packed parenchyma creates an interconnected network of air spaces.
  • Glucose is the most common respiratory substrate.
  • The energy released is stored in ATP, the energy currency of the cell.

$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + \text{Energy}$ Overall equation of aerobic respiration.

NEET tip: NEET asks why plants survive without special respiratory organs; the reasons are low demand, short diffusion distance, and each part managing its own gas exchange.

Glycolysis and fermentation

Glycolysis, also called the EMP pathway after Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas, occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms. It is the only process of respiration in anaerobes. One glucose (6C) is broken into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3C). ATP is used at two steps: glucose to glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase) and fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (phosphofructokinase). ATP is formed directly at two steps: BPGA to 3-PGA and PEP to pyruvate. Two NADH are formed when PGAL is converted to BPGA. The net gain is 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose. Without $O_2$, pyruvate undergoes fermentation. In yeast, alcoholic fermentation produces ethanol and $CO_2$ using pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase. In muscle cells and some bacteria, lactate dehydrogenase forms lactic acid. Fermentation regenerates $NAD^+$ but releases less than 7% of the energy in glucose.

  • Glycolysis gives 2 pyruvate per glucose; for example, 206 glucose give 412 pyruvate.
  • Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and makes 4 ATP, a net gain of 2 ATP.
  • Sucrose is first split by invertase into glucose and fructose.
  • The reducing agent in fermentation is NADH, which is reoxidised to $NAD^+$.
  • Yeasts poison themselves when the alcohol concentration reaches about 13%.
  • Fermentation gives a net gain of only 2 ATP.

$\text{Pyruvate} = 2 \times \text{glucose molecules}$ Number of pyruvate molecules formed at the end of glycolysis.

$C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2$ Alcoholic fermentation by yeast.

NEET tip: NEET asks simple numericals on pyruvate formed, the enzymes of fermentation, and the steps where ATP is used or formed.

TCA cycle and electron transport system

Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix. There, pyruvate dehydrogenase converts it to acetyl CoA, releasing $CO_2$ and forming NADH; this needs $Mg^{2+}$, $NAD^+$ and coenzyme A. The TCA (Krebs or citric acid) cycle starts when acetyl CoA (2C) condenses with OAA (4C) and water to form citric acid (6C). This step is catalysed by citrate synthase. Each turn gives 2 $CO_2$, 3 NADH, 1 $FADH_2$ and 1 GTP or ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. The cycle turns twice per glucose. In the electron transport system (ETS) on the inner mitochondrial membrane, electrons pass through a series of complexes: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), ubiquinone, Complex III (cytochrome $bc_1$), cytochrome c, and Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). Electrons from $FADH_2$ enter through Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase). Oxygen is the final acceptor and forms water. Complex V (ATP synthase) makes ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.

  • Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; link reaction and TCA cycle in the matrix; ETS on the inner membrane.
  • The TCA cycle requires continued regeneration of OAA.
  • Cytochrome c is a small protein attached to the outer surface of the inner membrane; it carries electrons from Complex III to IV.
  • Complex IV contains cytochromes a and $a_3$ and two copper centres.
  • $F_1$ is the peripheral headpiece where ATP is made.
  • $F_0$ is the integral membrane part that forms the proton channel.
  • Oxygen acts at the end of the chain as the final hydrogen acceptor, but it drives the whole process.

$\text{Pyruvic acid} + CoA + NAD^+ \rightarrow \text{Acetyl CoA} + CO_2 + NADH + H^+$ Link reaction catalysed by pyruvate dehydrogenase.

NEET tip: Questions focus on the site of each step, the names of the complexes, the role of cytochrome c and ubiquinone, and the products per TCA turn.

Energy relations: number of ATP molecules generated

Theoretical ATP yield is calculated with these assumptions: a sequential, orderly pathway; NADH from glycolysis enters the mitochondria; no intermediates are withdrawn; only glucose is the substrate. Each NADH gives 3 ATP and each $FADH_2$ gives 2 ATP. Glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP plus 2 NADH, which equals 6 ATP. The link reaction gives 2 NADH, which equals 6 ATP. Two turns of the TCA cycle give 6 NADH (18 ATP), 2 $FADH_2$ (4 ATP) and 2 GTP or ATP. The total is 38 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration. In fermentation the net gain is only 2 ATP per glucose. In reality pathways work simultaneously and intermediates are withdrawn, so the 38 ATP figure is theoretical.

  • Aerobic respiration gives a net 38 ATP per glucose (theoretical).
  • Anaerobic respiration or fermentation gives a net 2 ATP.
  • Substrate-level ATP per glucose is 4 (glycolysis) plus 2 (TCA cycle).
  • Per glucose, 10 NADH and 2 $FADH_2$ are formed.
  • Glucose is completely oxidised to 6 $CO_2$, released at the link reaction and in the TCA cycle.

$\text{Net ATP} = 4 + 10(3) + 2(2) + 2 - 2 = 38$ The 10 NADH give 30 ATP and the 2 $FADH_2$ give 4 ATP. Adding 4 substrate-level ATP from glycolysis and 2 from the TCA cycle, and subtracting the 2 ATP used in glycolysis, gives 38.

NEET tip: NEET asks the net ATP from aerobic versus anaerobic respiration and ATP from a given number of NADH or $FADH_2$.

Amphibolic pathways

Respiration is better called an amphibolic pathway than a purely catabolic one, because it takes part in both breakdown and synthesis. Substrates other than glucose enter at different points. Fats break into glycerol, which becomes PGAL, and fatty acids, which become acetyl CoA. Proteins break into amino acids, which are deaminated and enter as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or Krebs cycle intermediates. During synthesis, intermediates are withdrawn from the pathway. For example, acetyl CoA is used to make fatty acids, and Krebs intermediates are used to make amino acids. Breakdown and synthesis are therefore linked through a common pool of intermediates.

  • Glycerol enters respiration as PGAL (3-phosphoglyceraldehyde).
  • Fatty acids enter as acetyl CoA.
  • Amino acids enter after deamination, at pyruvate, acetyl CoA or the Krebs cycle.
  • Fatty acid synthesis withdraws acetyl CoA from the respiratory pathway.
  • Amphibolic means both catabolic and anabolic.

NEET tip: Questions ask the entry point of glycerol, fatty acids or amino acids, and why respiration is called amphibolic.

Respiratory quotient

The respiratory quotient (RQ), or respiratory ratio, is the ratio of the volume of $CO_2$ evolved to the volume of $O_2$ consumed during respiration. It depends on the respiratory substrate. For carbohydrates, which are completely oxidised, RQ is 1. For fats it is less than 1, about 0.7, because fats contain little oxygen and need more $O_2$ for oxidation. For proteins it is about 0.9. Organic acids have an RQ greater than 1. In anaerobic respiration $CO_2$ is evolved but no $O_2$ is consumed, so RQ is infinite.

  • RQ is 1 for carbohydrates.
  • RQ is about 0.7 for fats; tripalmitin gives $102/145 = 0.7$.
  • RQ is about 0.9 for proteins.
  • RQ is greater than 1 for organic acids such as malic and oxalic acid.
  • RQ is infinite in anaerobic respiration.

$RQ = \frac{\text{volume of } CO_2 \text{ evolved}}{\text{volume of } O_2 \text{ consumed}}$ Used to identify the respiratory substrate.

$2C_{51}H_{98}O_6 + 145O_2 \rightarrow 102CO_2 + 98H_2O + \text{energy}$ Oxidation of tripalmitin, a fat; RQ = 0.7.

NEET tip: Expect direct RQ values for different substrates or a calculation from a given balanced equation.

Seed germination

Seed germination is the process by which the embryo resumes growth and forms a seedling. It is the first step of a plant's post-embryonic growth. Germination needs suitable conditions: water, oxygen and a favourable temperature, and light in some seeds. Imbibition of water swells the seed and activates enzymes. Stored food is broken down and respiration supplies energy. The radicle emerges first, followed by the plumule. Seeds that fail to germinate even under favourable external conditions are dormant. Dormancy is caused by endogenous factors such as a hard seed coat, chemical inhibitors like abscisic acid, or an immature embryo. Dormancy can be broken by gibberellins, chilling, scarification or changes in light and temperature.

  • Germination requires water, $O_2$ and a suitable temperature.
  • Imbibition is the first step of germination.
  • The radicle emerges before the plumule.
  • Gibberellins promote germination and break dormancy.
  • ABA induces seed dormancy and inhibits germination.
  • Ethylene promotes germination, for example in peanut seeds.
  • Dormancy is controlled internally; quiescence is due only to unfavourable external conditions.

NEET tip: NEET usually links germination to PGRs: GA and ethylene promote it, ABA inhibits it.

Phases of plant growth and plant growth rate

Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in the size of an organ, its parts or a cell. Plant growth is indeterminate, or open, because meristems keep dividing. At a root or shoot tip, growth occurs in three phases. The meristematic phase has dividing cells with dense protoplasm and large nuclei. In the elongation phase, cells enlarge, become vacuolated and lay down new walls. In the maturation phase, cells reach maximum size and differentiate. In arithmetic growth, only one daughter cell keeps dividing, which gives a linear curve. In geometric growth, both daughter cells divide, which gives a sigmoid curve with a lag phase, a log (exponential) phase and a stationary phase. Absolute growth rate is the total growth per unit time. Relative growth rate is the growth per unit time per unit of initial size.

  • Growth is measured by increase in fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume or cell number.
  • A maize root apical meristem produces more than 17,500 new cells per hour.
  • Watermelon cells may increase in size up to 350,000 times.
  • Pollen tube growth is measured by length; dorsiventral leaf growth by surface area.
  • Arithmetic growth gives a straight line; geometric growth gives a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve.
  • In the geometric formula, r is the relative growth rate, also called the efficiency index.
  • Two leaves can have the same absolute growth rate but different relative growth rates.

$L_t = L_0 + rt$ Arithmetic growth. Example: $L_0 = 20$ cm, $r = 30$ cm/day, $t = 7$ days gives $L_t = 230$ cm.

$W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}$ Geometric or exponential growth, where r is the relative growth rate and e is the base of natural logarithms.

$RGR = \frac{\text{growth in given time}}{\text{initial size}}$ Relative growth rate per unit time.

NEET tip: NEET sets direct numericals using $L_t = L_0 + rt$ and asks about the phases of the sigmoid curve.

Conditions of growth

Growth needs several essential conditions. Water keeps cells turgid for enlargement and provides the medium for enzyme activity. Oxygen is needed to release metabolic energy through respiration. Nutrients, both macro and micro essential elements, are needed to make protoplasm and act as an energy source. Each plant has an optimum temperature range for growth, and deviation from it can be harmful. Environmental signals such as light and gravity also affect certain phases or stages of growth.

  • Turgidity due to water is essential for cell extension.
  • Respiration supplies the ATP used for growth.
  • Temperature affects growth through enzyme activity.
  • Light and gravity act as environmental signals that influence growth.

NEET tip: Usually asked as a simple statement question on why water, $O_2$ and nutrients are needed for growth.

Differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation

Cells from the root apical meristem, shoot apical meristem and cambium differentiate and mature to perform specific functions. This is differentiation. For example, tracheary elements lose their protoplasm and develop strong, lignified secondary walls. Living differentiated cells that have lost the ability to divide can regain it under certain conditions; this is dedifferentiation. Interfascicular cambium and cork cambium arise from fully differentiated parenchyma cells. Cells produced by these meristems lose the ability to divide again and mature into specific types; this is redifferentiation. Examples are secondary xylem, secondary phloem and cork. Plants follow different pathways in response to environment and life phase, which is called plasticity. Heterophylly in cotton, coriander and larkspur is an example.

  • Differentiation in plants is open: cells from the same meristem can form different structures.
  • Dedifferentiation produces interfascicular cambium and cork cambium.
  • Redifferentiation produces secondary xylem, secondary phloem and cork cells.
  • Heterophylly due to developmental phase is seen in cotton, coriander and larkspur.
  • Heterophylly due to environment is seen in buttercup (aquatic versus aerial leaves).
  • Tumour or callus formation in tissue culture involves dedifferentiation.

NEET tip: Matching questions pair interfascicular cambium with dedifferentiation and secondary xylem with redifferentiation, and test heterophylly examples.

Sequence of developmental process in a plant cell

Development covers all the changes an organism goes through during its life cycle, from germination of the seed to senescence. In a plant cell the sequence is as follows. A meristematic cell divides. It undergoes plasmatic growth, meaning an increase in protoplasm. It then expands or elongates. It differentiates, matures and finally undergoes senescence and death. Development is the sum of growth and differentiation. Both intrinsic factors and extrinsic factors control it. Intrinsic factors are internal genetic factors and plant growth regulators. Extrinsic factors are light, temperature, water, oxygen and nutrition.

  • Sequence: cell division, plasmatic growth, expansion (elongation), differentiation, maturation, senescence, death.
  • Development = growth + differentiation.
  • Intrinsic control comes from genes and PGRs.
  • Extrinsic control comes from light, temperature, water, oxygen and nutrition.

NEET tip: NEET may ask the correct order of developmental events in a plant cell.

Plant growth regulators: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, ethylene and ABA

PGRs are simple molecules that act as growth promoters or inhibitors. Auxins (IAA, IBA; synthetic NAA, 2,4-D) trace to Darwin's work on canary grass phototropism and Went's isolation from oat coleoptile tips. They promote rooting, apical dominance, parthenocarpy and xylem differentiation; 2,4-D kills dicot weeds. Gibberellins (over 100 forms, GA3 most studied) were discovered by Kurosawa from Gibberella fujikuroi (bakanae disease of rice). They cause stem elongation, bolting, malting and longer grape stalks. Cytokinins, discovered as kinetin from autoclaved herring sperm DNA by Skoog and Miller, are synthesised in regions of rapid cell division, e.g. root apices, developing shoot buds and young fruits, promote cell division and delay senescence. Ethylene, a gas found by Cousins, ripens fruit and promotes senescence. ABA, a stress hormone, closes stomata and induces dormancy.

  • Auxin uses: rooting of stem cuttings; flowering in pineapple; preventing fruit and leaf drop at early stages; promoting abscission of older parts; apical dominance; parthenocarpy in tomato; 2,4-D as a dicot weedicide.
  • Removing the shoot tip (decapitation) is used in tea plantations and hedge-making to remove apical dominance.
  • GA uses: longer grape stalks; elongated, well-shaped apples; delayed senescence; faster malting in brewing.
  • GA sprayed on sugarcane increases stem length and yield by up to 20 tonnes per acre.
  • GA hastens maturity and early seed production in conifers.
  • GA causes bolting (internode elongation before flowering) in beet, cabbage and rosette plants.
  • Natural cytokinins such as zeatin come from corn kernels and coconut milk.
  • Cytokinin effects: new leaves, chloroplasts, lateral shoot and adventitious shoot growth; overcoming apical dominance; nutrient mobilisation.
  • Ethylene effects: horizontal seedling growth, axis swelling, apical hook; abscission; climacteric respiration rise during ripening.
  • Ethylene breaks seed and bud dormancy (peanut seeds, potato tubers) and elongates petioles and internodes in deep-water rice.
  • Ethylene induces flowering in mango, induces female flowers in cucumber, and promotes root hair formation.
  • Ethephon, which releases ethylene, is the most widely used source of ethylene.
  • ABA is also known as inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin.
  • ABA closes stomata, induces seed dormancy, increases stress tolerance and antagonises GA.

NEET tip: Very high-yield: match each PGR with its discoverer, source or practical use, such as 2,4-D herbicide, GA bolting in cabbage, ethephon ripening, and ABA stomatal closure.

Key facts

  • Reaction centre of PS I is P700 and of PS II is P680; both are chlorophyll a.
  • Water splitting occurs at PS II on the lumen side and needs $Mn^{2+}$ and $Cl^-$.
  • Cyclic photophosphorylation occurs in the stroma lamellae and produces only ATP.
  • One glucose needs 6 Calvin cycle turns, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH; 3 glucose need 18 turns.
  • Fixing one $CO_2$ in the Calvin cycle needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
  • First stable product: 3-PGA in C3 plants and OAA in C4 plants.
  • C4 examples: maize, sorghum, sugarcane, Amaranthus.
  • RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme on earth.
  • Photorespiration forms phosphoglycolate and uses chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondria.
  • Light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight.
  • C4 plants are $CO_2$-saturated at about 360 $\mu L/L$.
  • Glycolysis was worked out by Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas; it gives net 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate per glucose.
  • Yeast alcoholic fermentation uses pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase; yeast dies at about 13% alcohol.
  • Citrate synthase condenses acetyl CoA (2C) and OAA (4C) to form citric acid (6C).
  • Each TCA turn gives 3 NADH, 1 $FADH_2$, 1 GTP and 2 $CO_2$.
  • Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, contains cytochromes a and $a_3$ and two copper centres.
  • Aerobic respiration gives a net 38 ATP per glucose (theoretical); fermentation gives 2 ATP.
  • RQ: carbohydrate 1, fat 0.7, protein 0.9, anaerobic respiration infinite.
  • Arithmetic growth follows $L_t = L_0 + rt$; geometric growth follows $W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}$.
  • The sigmoid growth curve has lag, log and stationary phases.
  • Kinetin is a modified adenine (purine) discovered by Skoog and Miller.
  • Gibberellin was discovered by E. Kurosawa from Gibberella fujikuroi, which causes bakanae disease of rice.
  • Auxin was first isolated by F.W. Went from oat coleoptile tips; Darwin worked on canary grass.
  • 2,4-D is a selective weedicide that kills dicot weeds.
  • Ethephon is the most widely used source of ethylene; ethylene induces female flowers in cucumber.
  • Sugarcane sprayed with GA yields up to 20 tonnes more per acre.
  • ABA closes stomata and is called the stress hormone.

Common traps

  • Thinking the oxygen in photosynthesis comes from $CO_2$. It comes from photolysis of water.
  • Believing photorespiration produces ATP. It actually consumes ATP and produces neither ATP nor NADPH, and it releases $CO_2$.
  • Saying the Calvin cycle is absent in C4 plants. It occurs in their bundle sheath cells; only the mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO.
  • Counting pyruvate as equal to glucose. Each glucose gives 2 pyruvate, so n glucose give 2n pyruvate.
  • Confusing turns per glucose. One turn fixes one $CO_2$, so one glucose needs 6 turns, not 1.
  • Putting ATP synthase $CF_1$ in the lumen. $CF_1$ faces the stroma, and protons accumulate in the lumen.
  • Taking dedifferentiation as forming secondary xylem. Secondary xylem is redifferentiation; interfascicular and cork cambium arise by dedifferentiation.
  • Assuming RQ of fat is greater than 1. Fats need more $O_2$, so their RQ is about 0.7.

Quick revision

  • Chloroplast: grana carry out the light reaction; the stroma carries out the Calvin cycle.
  • Non-cyclic flow (PS II plus PS I) gives ATP, NADPH and $O_2$; cyclic flow (PS I only) gives ATP only.
  • Chemiosmosis: protons accumulate in the lumen and ATP is made as they flow out through $CF_0$-$CF_1$.
  • Calvin cycle: carboxylation, reduction, regeneration; 6 turns, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose.
  • C4 pathway: PEPcase in mesophyll forms OAA, which goes as malate to the bundle sheath, where RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle work; there is no photorespiration.
  • Photorespiration: RuBP plus $O_2$ gives PGA plus phosphoglycolate and wastes energy.
  • Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and gives net 2 ATP; the TCA cycle occurs in the matrix; ETS is on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
  • NADH gives 3 ATP and $FADH_2$ gives 2 ATP; aerobic respiration gives 38 ATP and fermentation gives 2 ATP.
  • RQ is 1 for carbohydrates, 0.7 for fats, 0.9 for proteins and infinite for anaerobic respiration.
  • Growth equations: $L_t = L_0 + rt$ (arithmetic) and $W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}$ (geometric, sigmoid curve).
  • Cell development: division, plasmatic growth, expansion, differentiation, maturation, senescence.
  • PGR roles: auxin for rooting and apical dominance, GA for bolting and malting, cytokinin for cell division, ethylene for ripening, ABA for dormancy and stomatal closure.

Biology · Unit 5: Human Physiology

Human Physiology covers how the body breathes, circulates blood, excretes wastes, moves, and coordinates its activities through nerves and hormones. It is one of the highest-weightage units in NEET Biology. Questions are mostly direct recall of NCERT facts such as numbers, names, sequences and functions, along with match-the-column and multi-statement items built on NCERT lines.

PYQs (14): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q91, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q95, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q99, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q104, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q115, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q117, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q124, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q140, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q148, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q149, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q150, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q152, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q157, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q158

Breathing: respiratory organs and the human respiratory system

Respiratory organs vary with habitat and level of organisation. Sponges, coelenterates and flatworms exchange $O_2$ and $CO_2$ by simple diffusion over the entire body surface. Earthworms use their moist cuticle and insects use a network of tracheal tubes. Most aquatic arthropods and molluscs use gills (branchial respiration). Fishes use gills, amphibians use moist skin (cutaneous respiration) as well as lungs, and reptiles, birds and mammals use lungs (pulmonary respiration). In humans the air pathway runs: external nostrils, nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx (cartilaginous sound box), trachea, primary bronchi, secondary and tertiary bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles and finally the thin, vascularised alveoli. The part from the nostrils to the terminal bronchioles is the conducting part. The alveoli and their ducts form the respiratory or exchange part. The lungs lie in an air-tight thoracic chamber and are covered by a double-layered pleura containing pleural fluid, which reduces friction.

  • Pharynx is the common passage for food and air
  • Epiglottis, a cartilaginous flap, covers the glottis during swallowing
  • Trachea divides into right and left primary bronchi at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra
  • Trachea, primary, secondary and tertiary bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings
  • Thoracic chamber is formed by the vertebral column dorsally, the sternum ventrally, the ribs laterally and the dome-shaped diaphragm below
  • Conducting part: filters, humidifies and brings air to body temperature
  • Steps of respiration: breathing, alveolar diffusion, transport by blood, tissue diffusion and cellular respiration

NEET tip: Expect matching of animals to respiratory structures, such as sponges with body-surface diffusion and insects with tracheae, and questions on the sequence of the human air passage.

Mechanism of breathing and its regulation

Breathing consists of inspiration and expiration, driven by a pressure gradient between the lungs and the atmosphere. In inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and enlarges the thorax in the antero-posterior axis. At the same time the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs and sternum and enlarging the thorax in the dorso-ventral axis. Pulmonary volume increases, intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air rushes in. Normal expiration is passive. The diaphragm and intercostals relax, thoracic and pulmonary volumes fall, intra-pulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air is expelled. Abdominal muscles can increase the force of breathing. A healthy human breathes 12 to 16 times per minute. Regulation depends on several centres and receptors. The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla sets the rhythm. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons moderates it by shortening inspiration and altering the rate. A chemosensitive area beside the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to $CO_2$ and $H^+$. Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery also detect these changes. Oxygen has an insignificant role in regulation.

  • Inspiration is active and involves contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles
  • Normal expiration is passive, through relaxation of the same muscles
  • Inspiration occurs when intra-pulmonary pressure is below atmospheric pressure
  • Expiration occurs when intra-pulmonary pressure is above atmospheric pressure
  • Spirometer is used to measure respiratory volumes
  • Respiratory rhythm centre is in the medulla oblongata
  • Pneumotaxic centre is in the pons
  • Increased $CO_2$ and $H^+$ raise the rate and depth of breathing

$V_{min} = TV \times f \approx 500\,mL \times 12\text{-}16 = 6000\text{-}8000\,mL/min$ Minute ventilation: the volume of air a healthy person inspires or expires per minute

NEET tip: NEET asks which muscles contract in inspiration, the location of the rhythm and pneumotaxic centres, and which chemical (CO2 or H+, not O2) drives regulation.

Exchange and transport of gases; respiratory volumes

Alveoli are the primary site of gas exchange; exchange also occurs between blood and tissues. Both take place by simple diffusion along partial pressure gradients. Diffusion depends on the pressure gradient, the solubility of the gas and the thickness of the membrane. $CO_2$ is 20 to 25 times more soluble than $O_2$. The diffusion membrane has three layers: alveolar squamous epithelium, capillary endothelium and the basement substance between them. Its total thickness is much less than a millimetre. About 97% of $O_2$ is carried by RBCs as oxyhaemoglobin and about 3% is dissolved in plasma. Each haemoglobin molecule binds up to four $O_2$ molecules, which gives a sigmoid oxygen dissociation curve. High $pO_2$, low $pCO_2$, low $H^+$ and lower temperature (conditions in the alveoli) favour oxyhaemoglobin formation, while the reverse conditions in tissues favour dissociation. $CO_2$ is transported about 20 to 25% as carbamino-haemoglobin, about 70% as bicarbonate (formed with the help of carbonic anhydrase) and about 7% dissolved in plasma.

  • Atmospheric air: $pO_2$ 159 and $pCO_2$ 0.3 mm Hg
  • Alveoli: $pO_2$ 104 and $pCO_2$ 40 mm Hg
  • Deoxygenated blood: $pO_2$ 40 and $pCO_2$ 45 mm Hg
  • Oxygenated blood: $pO_2$ 95 and $pCO_2$ 40 mm Hg
  • Tissues: $pO_2$ 40 and $pCO_2$ 45 mm Hg
  • Every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of $O_2$ to tissues
  • Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of $CO_2$ to the alveoli
  • Tidal volume (TV) is about 500 mL
  • Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) is 2500 to 3000 mL
  • Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is 1000 to 1100 mL
  • Residual volume (RV) is 1100 to 1200 mL and can never be expelled, even by forcible expiration

$IC = TV + IRV$ Inspiratory capacity: total air inspired after a normal expiration

$EC = TV + ERV$ Expiratory capacity: total air expired after a normal inspiration

$FRC = ERV + RV$ Functional residual capacity: air left in the lungs after a normal expiration

$VC = IRV + TV + ERV$ Vital capacity: maximum air breathed out after a forced inspiration

$TLC = VC + RV$ Total lung capacity: total air in the lungs after a forced inspiration

$CO_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3 \rightleftharpoons HCO_3^- + H^+$ Reaction catalysed by carbonic anhydrase; runs forward at tissues and in reverse at alveoli

NEET tip: Numerical questions on capacities, such as VC or FRC from given volumes, and the percentages of O2 and CO2 transport modes are frequent.

Respiratory disorders: asthma, emphysema, occupational disorders

Asthma is difficulty in breathing that causes wheezing. It results from inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles. Emphysema is a chronic disorder in which the alveolar walls are damaged, so the respiratory surface area decreases; cigarette smoking is a major cause. Occupational respiratory disorders arise in industries involving grinding or stone-breaking, which produce so much dust that the body's defence mechanisms cannot cope. Long exposure causes inflammation that leads to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissue) and serious lung damage. Workers in such industries should wear protective masks. Common examples are silicosis from silica dust and asbestosis from asbestos fibres.

  • Asthma: inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles, causing wheezing
  • Emphysema: damaged alveolar walls and reduced respiratory surface
  • Major cause of emphysema is smoking
  • Occupational disorders: dust inhalation leads to inflammation and then fibrosis
  • Prevention of occupational disorders: protective masks

NEET tip: Usually tested through matching a disorder to its cause or symptom, for example emphysema with alveolar wall damage.

Blood composition, blood groups and coagulation

Blood is a special fluid connective tissue made of plasma (about 55%) and formed elements (about 45%). Plasma is 90 to 92% water and 6 to 8% proteins. The main plasma proteins are fibrinogen (clotting), globulins (defence) and albumins (osmotic balance). Plasma without clotting factors is called serum. RBCs are the most abundant cells.
