They are biconcave and lack a nucleus in most mammals. They are formed in red bone marrow, live about 120 days and are destroyed in the spleen. WBCs are nucleated and are of two kinds: granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes). Platelets are cell fragments of megakaryocytes. ABO blood groups depend on the A and B antigens on RBCs and the antibodies in plasma. The Rh antigen is present in about 80% of humans. Coagulation is a cascade. Injury activates platelets and plasma factors to form thrombokinase, which converts prothrombin into thrombin. Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap formed elements to form a clot. $Ca^{2+}$ ions are essential for clotting.

  • RBC count: 5 to 5.5 million per $mm^3$
  • Haemoglobin: 12 to 16 g per 100 mL of blood
  • WBC count: 6000 to 8000 per $mm^3$
  • Platelet count: 1.5 to 3.5 lakh per $mm^3$
  • Neutrophils make up 60 to 65% of WBCs and are phagocytic
  • Eosinophils make up 2 to 3% and are linked to allergy
  • Basophils make up 0.5 to 1% and secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin
  • Lymphocytes make up 20 to 25% (B and T cells, immunity)
  • Monocytes make up 6 to 8% and are phagocytic
  • Group A has antigen A and anti-B antibody
  • Group B has antigen B and anti-A antibody
  • Group AB has both antigens and no antibodies; it is the universal recipient
  • Group O has no antigens and both antibodies; it is the universal donor
  • Erythroblastosis foetalis can occur in the second pregnancy of an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive foetus
  • It is prevented by giving anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the first delivery

$\text{Prothrombin} \xrightarrow{\text{thrombokinase},\ Ca^{2+}} \text{Thrombin}$ First key step of the clotting cascade

$\text{Fibrinogen} \xrightarrow{\text{thrombin}} \text{Fibrin}$ Soluble plasma protein converted into insoluble clot threads

NEET tip: Watch for reversed statements such as 'fibrinogen is produced from fibrin', and for questions on the most and least abundant WBC and on the donor/recipient logic of blood groups.

Lymph: composition and function

As blood passes through capillaries, some water and small water-soluble substances move out into the spaces between cells. Larger proteins and most formed elements stay in the vessels. This fluid is called interstitial or tissue fluid, and its mineral distribution is similar to that of plasma. Nutrients and gases are exchanged between blood and cells through this fluid. An elaborate network of lymphatic vessels collects the fluid, now called lymph, and drains it back into the major veins. Lymph is a colourless fluid containing specialised lymphocytes, which are responsible for immune responses. Lymph is also an important carrier of nutrients and hormones. Fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals present in the intestinal villi.

  • Lymph is colourless because it lacks RBCs
  • Lymph contains lymphocytes, which provide immunity
  • Lymph has fewer proteins than plasma
  • Lymph returns tissue fluid to the major veins
  • Lacteals in intestinal villi absorb fats into lymph
  • Lymph carries nutrients and hormones

NEET tip: Asked as statements comparing lymph with plasma (no RBCs, fewer proteins, has lymphocytes) and on the role of lacteals in fat absorption.

Human heart and blood vessels

The human heart is mesodermal in origin. It lies in the thoracic cavity between the two lungs, slightly tilted to the left, and is about the size of a clenched fist. It is enclosed in a double-walled membranous pericardium containing pericardial fluid. It has four chambers: two thin-walled atria and two thick-walled ventricles. A thin muscular interatrial septum separates the atria, and a thick interventricular septum separates the ventricles. The tricuspid valve guards the opening between the right atrium and right ventricle. The bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle. Semilunar valves guard the exits into the pulmonary artery and the aorta. Nodal tissue conducts the heart's impulses: the SA node lies in the right upper corner of the right atrium, and the AV node lies in the lower left corner of the right atrium near the AV septum. The AV bundle (bundle of His) divides into right and left bundles that give rise to Purkinje fibres. The SA node is the pacemaker. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, and capillaries allow exchange.

  • Fishes have a 2-chambered heart
  • Amphibians and most reptiles have a 3-chambered heart
  • Crocodiles, birds and mammals have a 4-chambered heart
  • Open circulation occurs in arthropods and molluscs
  • Closed circulation occurs in annelids and chordates
  • Atrioventricular septum is made of thick fibrous tissue
  • Valves allow one-way flow of blood
  • SA node generates 70 to 75 action potentials per minute
  • Artery and vein walls have three layers: tunica intima, tunica media and tunica externa
  • Veins have valves and thinner walls than arteries
  • Capillary walls are one cell thick (endothelium only)
  • Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood

NEET tip: Valve positions, the location of the SA and AV nodes, the SA node rate (70-75 per min) and the pericardium enclosing the heart are favourite one-liners.

Cardiac cycle, cardiac output and ECG

The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in one heartbeat. It begins with joint diastole, when all chambers are relaxed. The tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open and blood flows from the pulmonary veins and venae cavae into the ventricles through the atria, while the semilunar valves stay closed. The SA node then fires and causes atrial systole, which increases flow into the ventricles by about 30%. The impulse passes through the AV node and AV bundle to cause ventricular systole. The AV valves close, producing the first heart sound 'lub', and rising pressure opens the semilunar valves so blood enters the aorta and pulmonary artery. The ventricles then relax. The semilunar valves close, producing the second heart sound 'dub', and the AV valves reopen as ventricular pressure falls. One cycle lasts 0.8 s at 72 beats per minute. Each ventricle pumps about 70 mL per beat (stroke volume), giving a cardiac output of about 5 L per minute. The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart: the P wave, QRS complex and T wave.

  • P wave: atrial depolarisation, leading to atrial contraction
  • QRS complex: ventricular depolarisation, initiating ventricular systole
  • T wave: ventricular repolarisation; the end of T marks the end of systole
  • Counting QRS complexes over a given time gives the heart rate
  • First heart sound 'lub' is caused by AV valve closure
  • Second heart sound 'dub' is caused by semilunar valve closure
  • Athletes have a higher cardiac output than non-athletes

$CO = SV \times HR \approx 70\,mL \times 72 \approx 5040\,mL/min$ Cardiac output: volume pumped by each ventricle per minute

$T_{cycle} = \frac{60}{72} \approx 0.8\,s$ Duration of one cardiac cycle at a heart rate of 72 per minute

NEET tip: Expect ECG wave–event matching, the cause of the lub and dub sounds, and cardiac output calculations.

Double circulation and regulation of cardiac activity

In double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit. In pulmonary circulation, the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. In systemic circulation, the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta, then through arteries, arterioles and capillaries to the tissues. Deoxygenated blood returns through veins and the venae cavae to the right atrium. The hepatic portal system carries blood from the intestine to the liver through the hepatic portal vein before it enters systemic circulation. The coronary system supplies the cardiac musculature. Heart activity is auto-regulated by nodal tissue, so the heart is myogenic. A cardiac centre in the medulla oblongata can moderate this activity through the autonomic nervous system. Sympathetic nerves increase heart rate, the strength of ventricular contraction and cardiac output. Parasympathetic nerves decrease heart rate, the speed of conduction and cardiac output. Adrenal medullary hormones also increase cardiac output.

  • Pulmonary circuit: right ventricle to lungs to left atrium
  • Systemic circuit: left ventricle to body to right atrium
  • Hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver
  • Coronary vessels supply the heart muscle itself
  • Human heart is myogenic
  • Neural moderation of heart activity is by the medulla oblongata through the ANS
  • Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate and output
  • Parasympathetic stimulation decreases heart rate and output

NEET tip: Usually tested as the effect of sympathetic versus parasympathetic stimulation and as the correct sequence of pulmonary or systemic circulation.

Circulatory disorders: hypertension, coronary artery disease, angina pectoris, heart failure

Normal blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg (systolic/diastolic). Repeated readings of 140/90 mm Hg or higher indicate hypertension, which leads to heart disease and also affects vital organs such as the brain and kidney. Coronary artery disease, also called atherosclerosis, affects the vessels that supply the heart muscle. Deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue narrow the lumen of these vessels. Angina pectoris is acute chest pain that occurs when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle. It can occur at any age in men and women but is more common in the middle-aged and elderly. Heart failure is the state in which the heart cannot pump blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs. It is also called congestive heart failure because congestion of the lungs is a main symptom. Heart failure differs from cardiac arrest, where the heart stops beating, and from a heart attack, where heart muscle is suddenly damaged by an inadequate blood supply.

  • Hypertension: blood pressure of 140/90 or above
  • CAD deposits: calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue
  • Angina: chest pain due to insufficient $O_2$ reaching the heart muscle
  • Heart failure: congestion of the lungs is the main symptom
  • Cardiac arrest is not the same as heart attack or heart failure

$BP_{normal} = \frac{120}{80}\,mm\,Hg$ Systolic over diastolic pressure; 140/90 or above indicates hypertension

NEET tip: Matching each disorder to its definition, and distinguishing heart failure from cardiac arrest and heart attack, is a common angle.

Modes of excretion: ammonotelism, ureotelism and uricotelism

Animals excrete nitrogen in three main forms, depending on water availability. Ammonia is the most toxic form and needs the most water for elimination. Ammonotelic animals include many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects. They excrete ammonia as $NH_4^+$ ions by diffusion across body surfaces or fish gills, and the kidneys play no significant role. Terrestrial animals convert ammonia in the liver into less toxic urea, which needs less water. Ureotelic animals include mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes, and some animals retain urea in the kidney matrix to maintain osmolarity. Uricotelic animals, such as reptiles, birds, land snails and insects, excrete uric acid as a pellet or paste with minimum water loss. Excretory structures also vary across animals. Protonephridia (flame cells) occur in flatworms, rotifers, some annelids and Amphioxus. Nephridia occur in earthworms, Malpighian tubules in insects, antennal or green glands in prawns and other crustaceans, and kidneys in vertebrates.

  • Toxicity and water needed: ammonia > urea > uric acid
  • Ammonotelic: bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects
  • Ureotelic: mammals, terrestrial amphibians, marine fishes
  • Uricotelic: reptiles, birds, land snails, insects
  • Protonephridia function mainly in osmoregulation
  • Cockroach excretes through Malpighian tubules

$2NH_3 + CO_2 \rightarrow CO(NH_2)_2 + H_2O$ Simplified net conversion of ammonia to urea in the liver (ornithine cycle)

NEET tip: Classic match-the-column: animal to excretory product, or animal to excretory structure.

Human excretory system and urine formation

The human excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra. The kidneys are bean-shaped and lie between the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae. Each kidney has an outer cortex and an inner medulla made of medullary pyramids, and it contains about one million nephrons. A nephron has a glomerulus and a renal tubule. The tubule runs from Bowman's capsule to the PCT, Henle's loop, the DCT and finally the collecting duct. Urine forms in three steps: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and tubular secretion. Filtration occurs through glomerular endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes of Bowman's capsule, and almost all plasma constituents except proteins pass into the lumen of Bowman's capsule. The PCT reabsorbs nearly all nutrients and 70 to 80% of electrolytes and water. The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water, while the ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes. The collecting duct reabsorbs much water to concentrate urine. A counter-current mechanism involving Henle's loop and the vasa recta concentrates urine. Micturition begins when stretch receptors in the bladder wall signal the CNS.

  • Each kidney is 10 to 12 cm long, 5 to 7 cm wide, 2 to 3 cm thick and weighs 120 to 170 g
  • Hilum: the notch where the ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter or leave the kidney
  • Columns of Bertini: extensions of the cortex between the medullary pyramids
  • Malpighian body (renal corpuscle) = glomerulus + Bowman's capsule
  • Malpighian body, PCT and DCT lie in the cortex
  • Cortical nephrons have short loops, and their vasa recta is absent or highly reduced
  • Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops dipping deep into the medulla
  • Medullary osmolarity gradient: 300 to 1200 mOsmol per L, maintained by NaCl and urea
  • Urine can become nearly four times as concentrated as the initial filtrate
  • PCT has simple cuboidal brush-border epithelium
  • PCT secretes $H^+$, $NH_3$ and $K^+$, helping maintain pH
  • DCT carries out conditional reabsorption of $Na^+$ and water, and reabsorbs $HCO_3^-$
  • Micturition: bladder smooth muscle contracts and the urethral sphincter relaxes
  • Daily urine output is 1 to 1.5 L, containing 25 to 30 g of urea
  • Urine is slightly acidic, with a pH of about 6
  • Glucose (glycosuria) or ketone bodies (ketonuria) in urine indicate diabetes mellitus

$GFR \approx 125\,mL/min \approx 180\,L/day$ Normal glomerular filtration rate of a healthy individual

$\frac{180 - 1.5}{180} \times 100 \approx 99\%$ Percentage of filtrate reabsorbed by the renal tubules

NEET tip: Statements on the permeability of the two limbs of Henle's loop, the functions of PCT and DCT, and numbers such as GFR and the osmolarity gradient are repeatedly tested.

Osmoregulation and regulation of kidney function: renin-angiotensin, ANF, ADH, diabetes insipidus

Kidney function is regulated by hormonal feedback involving the hypothalamus, the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) and, to some extent, the heart. Osmoreceptors respond to changes in blood volume, body fluid volume and ionic concentration. When excess fluid is lost, the hypothalamus triggers release of ADH (vasopressin) from the neurohypophysis. ADH increases water reabsorption from the later parts of the tubule, preventing diuresis. ADH also constricts blood vessels, which raises blood pressure and GFR. When GFR or blood pressure falls, JG cells release renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, which is further converted into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor and raises glomerular blood pressure and GFR. It also stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which promotes reabsorption of $Na^+$ and water from distal tubule parts. This pathway is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Increased blood flow to the atria triggers release of atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), which causes vasodilation, lowers blood pressure and acts as a check on RAAS. Diabetes insipidus results from defective ADH synthesis or release and causes water loss and dehydration.

  • ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary
  • ADH promotes water reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct
  • Increased body fluid volume switches off osmoreceptors and suppresses ADH release
  • JGA is a sensitive region formed where the DCT and afferent arteriole come in contact
  • Aldosterone causes $Na^+$ and water reabsorption
  • ANF opposes RAAS by causing vasodilation and lowering blood pressure
  • Diabetes insipidus produces large volumes of dilute urine

$\text{Angiotensinogen} \xrightarrow{\text{renin}} \text{Angiotensin I} \rightarrow \text{Angiotensin II}$ RAAS sequence triggered by a fall in GFR or blood pressure

NEET tip: Expect sequence or statement questions on RAAS, the opposing roles of ANF and RAAS, and the cause of diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency).

Role of other organs in excretion

Besides the kidneys, several other organs help in excretion. The lungs remove large amounts of $CO_2$, about 200 mL per minute, along with significant quantities of water. The liver, the largest gland, secretes bile containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs; most of these leave the body with digestive wastes. The skin has two types of glands with excretory roles. Sweat glands produce sweat, a watery fluid containing NaCl, small amounts of urea and lactic acid; the primary function of sweat is to cool the body. Sebaceous glands eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes through sebum, which also forms a protective oily covering on the skin. Small amounts of nitrogenous wastes are also eliminated through saliva.

  • Lungs remove about 200 mL of $CO_2$ per minute
  • Liver excretes bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin) and cholesterol
  • Sweat contains NaCl, urea and lactic acid
  • Sebum contains sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes
  • Saliva removes small amounts of nitrogenous waste

NEET tip: Usually asked as matching an organ to the substance it excretes, such as sebaceous glands with sterols and waxes.

Excretory disorders, dialysis and artificial kidney

When the kidneys malfunction, urea accumulates in the blood, a condition called uremia. Uremia is highly harmful and may lead to kidney failure. In such patients urea is removed by haemodialysis. Blood is drained from a convenient artery, mixed with an anticoagulant such as heparin and pumped into a dialysing unit. The unit contains a coiled cellophane tube bathed in dialysing fluid that has the same composition as plasma except for nitrogenous wastes. Because of the concentration gradient, nitrogenous wastes diffuse out through the porous membrane. The cleared blood is mixed with anti-heparin and returned to the body through a vein. Kidney transplantation is the ultimate treatment for acute renal failure, and a donor who is a close relative is preferred to minimise immune rejection. Renal calculi are stones or insoluble masses of crystallised salts such as oxalates that form within the kidney. Glomerulonephritis is inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney.

  • Uremia: excess urea in the blood
  • Heparin is the anticoagulant added before dialysis
  • Anti-heparin is added before blood is returned to the body
  • Dialysing fluid matches plasma minus nitrogenous wastes
  • Kidney transplantation is the ultimate treatment for acute renal failure
  • Renal calculi: kidney stones of crystallised salts such as oxalates
  • Glomerulonephritis: inflammation of the glomeruli

NEET tip: Questions focus on the dialysis principle (diffusion along a concentration gradient) and on defining uremia, renal calculi and glomerulonephritis.

Types of movement: ciliary, flagellar and muscular

Movement is a significant feature of living beings. Amoeboid movement occurs in macrophages and leucocytes by means of pseudopodia formed by streaming protoplasm, with microfilaments involved. Ciliary movement occurs in internal tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium. Coordinated beating of cilia in the trachea removes inhaled dust and foreign particles, and cilia in the female reproductive tract help ova pass along it. Flagellar movement is whip-like beating of flagella. It drives swimming of spermatozoa, maintains the water current in the canal system of sponges and moves protists such as Euglena. Muscular movement is used for movement of the limbs, jaws and tongue. Muscle is mesodermal in origin and makes up about 40 to 50% of adult body weight. Muscles show excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary. Visceral (smooth) muscle is non-striated and involuntary and lines hollow visceral organs. Cardiac muscle is striated, branched and involuntary.

  • Sperm motility is due to flagellar movement
  • Ciliary movement clears the trachea and moves ova through the oviduct
  • Leucocytes and macrophages show amoeboid movement
  • Skeletal muscle: striated and voluntary
  • Visceral muscle: smooth and involuntary
  • Cardiac muscle: striated, branched and involuntary
  • Locomotion requires coordinated activity of the muscular, skeletal and neural systems

NEET tip: Direct match questions link a cell or organ to its type of movement, for example sperm with flagellar movement or the trachea with ciliary movement.

Skeletal muscle: contractile proteins and muscle contraction

A skeletal muscle is made of fascicles, or muscle bundles, held together by connective tissue called fascia. Each muscle fibre is a syncytium enclosed by the sarcolemma, and its sarcoplasmic reticulum stores $Ca^{2+}$. Myofibrils show alternating light I bands, containing actin, and dark A bands, containing myosin. A Z line bisects each I band, and an M line lies in the middle of the A band. The sarcomere, the segment between two successive Z lines, is the functional unit of contraction. Contraction follows the sliding filament theory. A motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, generating an action potential that causes $Ca^{2+}$ release. $Ca^{2+}$ binds troponin and unmasks the myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads, using energy from ATP hydrolysis, bind actin to form cross bridges and pull the thin filaments towards the centre of the A band. The sarcomere shortens: I bands narrow while A bands keep their length. Binding of fresh ATP breaks the cross bridge, and the cycle repeats until $Ca^{2+}$ is pumped back.

  • Each actin filament has two F-actin strands made of G-actin monomers
  • Tropomyosin runs along the actin filament
  • Troponin masks the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest
  • Each myosin monomer is a meromyosin with a head and short arm (HMM) and a tail (LMM)
  • Myosin head acts as an ATPase and has active sites for both ATP and actin
  • H zone: central part of the A band not overlapped by thin filaments
  • Motor unit: one motor neuron together with the muscle fibres it supplies
  • Muscle fatigue is due to lactic acid accumulation from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen
  • Red fibres: rich in myoglobin and mitochondria; aerobic
  • White fibres: less myoglobin and more sarcoplasmic reticulum; anaerobic

$ATP \xrightarrow{\text{myosin ATPase}} ADP + P_i + \text{energy}$ Energy for cross-bridge formation and the power stroke

NEET tip: Expect questions on the role of Ca2+ and troponin, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, and which bands shorten during contraction (I band and H zone, not A band).

Skeletal system and joints

The adult human skeleton has 206 bones and a few cartilages. The axial skeleton (80 bones) includes the skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs. The skull has 22 bones (8 cranial and 14 facial), plus the U-shaped hyoid and three ear ossicles in each ear. It joins the vertebral column through two occipital condyles, making it dicondylic. The vertebral column has 26 vertebrae arranged from head to toe as 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacral (fused) and 1 coccygeal (fused). There are 12 pairs of bicephalic ribs: 7 pairs of true ribs, 3 pairs of vertebrochondral ribs and 2 pairs of floating ribs. The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) comprises the limbs and girdles, with 30 bones in each limb. Joints are of three types. Fibrous joints, such as the skull sutures, allow no movement. Cartilaginous joints, such as those between vertebrae, allow limited movement. Synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and allow considerable movement.

  • Forelimb: humerus, radius and ulna, carpals (8), metacarpals (5), phalanges (14)
  • Hindlimb: femur (the longest bone), patella, tibia and fibula, tarsals (7), metatarsals (5), phalanges (14)
  • Patella is the cup-shaped knee cap covering the knee ventrally
  • Pectoral girdle: clavicle and scapula
  • Glenoid cavity of the scapula forms the shoulder joint with the humerus
  • Pelvic girdle: two coxal bones, each formed by fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis
  • Acetabulum receives the femur
  • Pubic symphysis contains fibrous cartilage
  • First vertebra (atlas) articulates with the occipital condyles
  • Ball and socket joint: humerus with the pectoral girdle
  • Hinge joint: knee
  • Pivot joint: atlas and axis
  • Gliding joint: between carpals
  • Saddle joint: carpal and metacarpal of the thumb

$206 = 80_{axial} + 126_{appendicular}$ Distribution of bones in the adult human skeleton

$26 = 7 + 12 + 5 + 1 + 1$ Cervical + thoracic + lumbar + sacral + coccygeal vertebrae

NEET tip: Counting questions (vertebrae, ribs, limb bones), the head-to-toe order of vertebrae and the sequence of lower limb bones are frequently asked.

Muscular and skeletal disorders: myasthenia gravis, tetany, muscular dystrophy, arthritis, osteoporosis, gout

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction. It causes fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle. Muscular dystrophy is progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a genetic disorder. Tetany is rapid spasms, or wild contractions, of muscle caused by low $Ca^{2+}$ in body fluids. Arthritis is inflammation of the joints. Osteoporosis is an age-related disorder marked by decreased bone mass and an increased chance of fractures; decreased estrogen is a common cause. Gout is inflammation of the joints caused by accumulation of uric acid crystals.

  • Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction
  • Muscular dystrophy: genetic, progressive degeneration of muscle
  • Tetany: caused by low blood $Ca^{2+}$
  • Osteoporosis: reduced bone mass, linked to low estrogen
  • Gout: uric acid crystals deposited in joints
  • Arthritis: inflammation of joints

NEET tip: Almost always a match-the-column of disorder and cause; remember that tetany means low (not high) Ca2+ and that myasthenia gravis is autoimmune.

Neuron and nerves

The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the neural system. It has three parts: a cell body, dendrites and an axon. The cell body contains cytoplasm with typical organelles and Nissl's granules. Dendrites are short, repeatedly branched fibres that also contain Nissl's granules and carry impulses towards the cell body. The axon is a long fibre whose branched end terminates in bulb-like synaptic knobs containing synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitters; it carries impulses away from the cell body. Neurons are classified by structure. Multipolar neurons, with one axon and two or more dendrites, occur in the cerebral cortex. Bipolar neurons, with one axon and one dendrite, occur in the retina. Unipolar neurons, with a cell body and one axon only, occur in the embryonic stage. Myelinated fibres are wrapped by Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath, with gaps called nodes of Ranvier; they occur in spinal and cranial nerves. Unmyelinated fibres are enclosed by Schwann cells without a myelin sheath and occur in autonomous and somatic neural systems. Nerves are bundles of such fibres.

  • Nissl's granules are present in the cell body and dendrites, absent from the axon
  • Dendrites carry impulses towards the cell body; axons carry them away
  • Multipolar neurons occur in the cerebral cortex
  • Bipolar neurons occur in the retina
  • Unipolar neurons occur in the embryonic stage
  • Schwann cells form the myelin sheath in the PNS
  • Nodes of Ranvier are gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths

NEET tip: Neuron-type location matching (bipolar in the retina, multipolar in the cortex) and the presence or absence of Nissl's granules are typical items.

Human nervous system: central, peripheral and visceral

The human neural system has two divisions. The central neural system (CNS), made of the brain and spinal cord, is the site of information processing and control. The peripheral neural system (PNS) consists of all nerves associated with the CNS. Afferent fibres carry impulses from organs to the CNS, and efferent fibres carry impulses from the CNS to effectors. The PNS has a somatic division, supplying skeletal muscles, and an autonomic division, supplying involuntary organs and smooth muscles. The autonomic division is further divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic parts. The visceral nervous system comprises the nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses connecting the CNS with the viscera. The brain is protected by the skull and three cranial meninges: the outer dura mater, the very thin middle arachnoid and the inner pia mater. The forebrain consists of the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus. The midbrain has the corpora quadrigemina and the cerebral aqueduct. The hindbrain consists of the pons, cerebellum and medulla. The midbrain, pons and medulla together form the brain stem.

  • Corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres
  • Cerebral cortex is grey matter; the inner tracts form white matter
  • Association areas handle intersensory associations, memory and communication
  • Thalamus is the major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling
  • Hypothalamus controls body temperature, eating and drinking, and secretes hormones
  • Limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus) controls sexual behaviour, emotions and motivation
  • Cerebellum is highly convoluted to accommodate more neurons
  • Medulla contains centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretion
  • Pericardium surrounds the heart and is not part of the CNS

NEET tip: Meninges order, the parts of each brain region, the functions of the hypothalamus, medulla and limbic system, and odd-one-out questions such as pericardium are common.

Generation and conduction of nerve impulse

Neurons are excitable because their membranes are polarised. At rest, the axonal membrane is more permeable to $K^+$, nearly impermeable to $Na^+$ and impermeable to the negatively charged proteins in the axoplasm. The axoplasm is high in $K^+$ and negative proteins and low in $Na^+$, while the outside fluid is the reverse. The sodium-potassium pump maintains these gradients by moving 3 $Na^+$ out for every 2 $K^+$ moved in. The outer surface is therefore positive and the inner surface negative; this potential difference is the resting potential. A stimulus makes the membrane freely permeable to $Na^+$, and rapid $Na^+$ influx reverses the polarity. This reversal is depolarisation, and the resulting action potential is the nerve impulse. Local currents depolarise the adjacent site, so the impulse travels along the axon. A rise in $K^+$ permeability then lets $K^+$ diffuse out, restoring the resting state (repolarisation). At synapses, transmission is either electrical (fast, rare) or chemical, where neurotransmitters cross the synaptic cleft and bind receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.

  • Resting state: outside positive, inside negative
  • Depolarisation is caused by $Na^+$ influx
  • Repolarisation is caused by $K^+$ efflux
  • Electrical synapse: membranes in very close contact; faster than chemical
  • Chemical synapse: synaptic cleft and neurotransmitters
  • Neurotransmitters open ion channels on the post-synaptic membrane
  • The new potential produced can be excitatory or inhibitory

$3Na^+_{out} : 2K^+_{in}$ Stoichiometry of the sodium-potassium pump that maintains the resting potential

NEET tip: Statement questions test ion movements during depolarisation and repolarisation, the pump ratio, and differences between electrical and chemical synapses.

Endocrine glands and hormones: hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas, gonads

Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals produced in trace amounts that act as intercellular messengers, mostly from ductless endocrine glands. The hypothalamus secretes releasing hormones such as GnRH and inhibiting hormones such as somatostatin, which reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophysial portal system. The pituitary lies in the sella turcica and has two parts. The adenohypophysis consists of the pars distalis, which secretes GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH, and the pars intermedia, which secretes MSH. The neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin, both made in the hypothalamus. The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which regulates diurnal rhythms. The thyroid secretes $T_4$, $T_3$ and thyrocalcitonin. The parathyroids secrete PTH, which raises blood $Ca^{2+}$. The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline, the fight-or-flight hormones. The adrenal cortex secretes glucocorticoids such as cortisol and mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone. In the pancreatic islets, alpha cells secrete glucagon and beta cells secrete insulin. The testes secrete androgens, and the ovaries secrete estrogen and progesterone.

  • LH: stimulates androgen secretion in males; causes ovulation and maintains the corpus luteum in females
  • FSH: stimulates follicle growth in females; with androgens, regulates spermatogenesis in males
  • Oxytocin: contraction of the uterus during childbirth and milk ejection
  • Vasopressin (ADH): reabsorption of water and electrolytes in the kidney
  • Thyroid hormones regulate basal metabolic rate and support RBC formation
  • Thyrocalcitonin lowers blood $Ca^{2+}$
  • Adrenal cortex has three layers: zona glomerulosa (outer), fasciculata (middle) and reticularis (inner)
  • Cortisol: stimulates gluconeogenesis, is anti-inflammatory and suppresses immunity
  • Aldosterone: promotes $Na^+$ reabsorption and excretion of $K^+$ and phosphate
  • Glucagon is hyperglycemic and stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
  • Insulin is hypoglycemic and promotes glucose uptake and glycogenesis
  • Leydig cells secrete testosterone
  • Corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which supports pregnancy

NEET tip: Heavily tested via match-the-column of hormone to source or action and multi-statements on pituitary parts and pancreatic cells.

Mechanism of hormone action; hormones as messengers and regulators

Hormones act by binding to specific receptor proteins present only in their target tissues. Each receptor is specific to one hormone, and binding forms a hormone-receptor complex. Receptors are of two kinds: membrane-bound and intracellular (mostly nuclear). By chemical nature, hormones fall into four groups. Peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones include insulin, glucagon and the pituitary and hypothalamic hormones. Steroids include cortisol, testosterone, estradiol and progesterone. Iodothyronines are the thyroid hormones, and amino-acid derivatives include epinephrine. Hormones that bind membrane receptors usually do not enter the cell. Instead they generate second messengers such as cAMP, $IP_3$ and $Ca^{2+}$, which regulate cellular metabolism. Steroid and thyroid hormones bind intracellular receptors and regulate gene expression or chromosome function. Hormones are also secreted by non-endocrine tissues. The GI tract secretes gastrin, secretin, CCK and GIP. The heart secretes ANF, and the kidney secretes erythropoietin. Hormone levels are commonly controlled by negative feedback.

  • Gastrin: stimulates secretion of HCl and pepsinogen
  • Secretin: stimulates release of water and bicarbonate from the exocrine pancreas
  • CCK: stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and bile release from the gall bladder
  • GIP: inhibits gastric secretion and motility
  • Erythropoietin from the JG cells of the kidney stimulates RBC formation
  • Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble and act on intracellular receptors
  • Protein hormones use second messengers

NEET tip: Asked as which hormones use second messengers versus intracellular receptors, and through matching GI hormones to their actions.

Hormonal disorders: dwarfism, acromegaly, cretinism, goitre, exophthalmic goitre, diabetes, Addison's disease

Hyposecretion of GH in childhood causes stunted growth, called pituitary dwarfism; excess GH in childhood causes gigantism. Excess GH in adults, especially in middle age, causes acromegaly. Acromegaly produces severe disfigurement, especially of the face, often goes undetected for years and can lead to premature death. Hypothyroidism during pregnancy leads to cretinism in the baby, with stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism. In adult women, hypothyroidism causes irregular menstrual cycles. Iodine deficiency in the diet causes hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid, called goitre. Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism. It causes thyroid enlargement, protruding eyeballs, increased BMR and weight loss. Diabetes mellitus involves prolonged hyperglycemia with loss of glucose in urine and formation of harmful ketone bodies, and it is treated with insulin therapy. Addison's disease results from underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones. It alters carbohydrate metabolism and causes acute weakness and fatigue.

  • Dwarfism: low GH in childhood
  • Gigantism: high GH in childhood
  • Acromegaly: high GH in adults
  • Cretinism: hypothyroidism in the developing baby
  • Simple goitre: iodine deficiency
  • Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease): hyperthyroidism with bulging eyes
  • Diabetes mellitus: insulin deficiency or failure, with glycosuria and ketonuria
  • Addison's disease: adrenal cortex hypofunction
  • Diabetes insipidus is due to ADH deficiency and is not related to insulin

NEET tip: Match disorder with hormone and gland, and distinguish acromegaly from gigantism by age of onset.

Key facts

  • Human vertebral column has 26 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum and 1 coccyx
  • Adult human skeleton has 206 bones: 80 axial and 126 appendicular
  • Each limb has 30 bones; the femur is the longest bone
  • Ribs: 7 pairs true, 3 pairs vertebrochondral (false), 2 pairs floating
  • Skull: 8 cranial + 14 facial bones; the full count with hyoid and 6 ear ossicles is 29
  • SA node generates 70 to 75 action potentials per minute; the cardiac cycle lasts 0.8 s
  • Stroke volume is about 70 mL; cardiac output is about 5 L per minute
  • Normal BP is 120/80 mm Hg; 140/90 or above is hypertension
  • Tidal volume is about 500 mL; residual volume is 1100 to 1200 mL; healthy breathing rate is 12 to 16 per minute
  • About 97% of $O_2$ is carried as oxyhaemoglobin
  • About 70% of $CO_2$ is carried as bicarbonate, 20 to 25% as carbamino-haemoglobin and 7% dissolved
  • $CO_2$ is 20 to 25 times more soluble than $O_2$
  • GFR is about 125 mL per minute (180 L per day); about 99% of filtrate is reabsorbed
  • Each kidney has about one million nephrons; medullary osmolarity rises from 300 to 1200 mOsmol per L
  • RBC count is 5 to 5.5 million per $mm^3$ and RBC lifespan is 120 days
  • WBC count is 6000 to 8000 per $mm^3$; neutrophils are the most abundant WBC and basophils the least
  • About 80% of humans are Rh positive
  • Sodium-potassium pump moves 3 $Na^+$ out for every 2 $K^+$ in
  • Pars intermedia secretes only MSH
  • Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised in the hypothalamus and released from the neurohypophysis
  • Pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon and beta cells secrete insulin
  • Pancreatic islets number 1 to 2 million and form 1 to 2% of pancreatic tissue
  • Cranial meninges from outer to inner: dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater
  • Sarcomere lies between two Z lines; the A band length stays constant during contraction
  • Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction
  • Pneumotaxic centre is in the pons; the respiratory rhythm centre is in the medulla

Common traps

  • Thinking fibrinogen is produced from fibrin: thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, and serum is plasma without clotting factors.
  • Assuming the posterior pituitary synthesises oxytocin and ADH: it only stores and releases them, and they are made by hypothalamic neurosecretory cells.
  • Mixing up the limbs of Henle's loop: the descending limb is permeable to water but nearly impermeable to electrolytes, while the ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes.
  • Believing the A band shortens during contraction: only the I band and H zone shorten, while the A band length is constant.
  • Treating pericardium as a brain covering: the meninges are dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater, and the pericardium surrounds the heart.
  • Assuming arteries always carry oxygenated blood: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.
  • Linking tetany to excess calcium: tetany is due to low $Ca^{2+}$, and gout, not arthritis in general, is specifically due to uric acid crystals.
  • Confusing diabetes insipidus with diabetes mellitus: insipidus is ADH deficiency causing water loss, while mellitus is an insulin problem causing hyperglycemia.

Quick revision

  • Air path: nostrils, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli; trachea divides at T5
  • Inspiration is active (diaphragm and external intercostals contract); normal expiration is passive
  • $VC = IRV + TV + ERV$, $TLC = VC + RV$, $FRC = ERV + RV$
  • Clotting cascade: prothrombin to thrombin, then fibrinogen to fibrin, with $Ca^{2+}$ essential
  • ECG: P is atrial depolarisation, QRS is ventricular depolarisation, T is ventricular repolarisation
  • Lub is caused by AV valve closure; dub by semilunar valve closure
  • Valves: tricuspid between right atrium and right ventricle; bicuspid between left atrium and left ventricle
  • Toxicity order: ammonia > urea > uric acid; bony fish are ammonotelic, mammals ureotelic, birds uricotelic
  • RAAS raises BP; ANF lowers BP; ADH conserves water, and its deficiency causes diabetes insipidus
  • Contraction: ACh, action potential, $Ca^{2+}$ binds troponin, cross bridges form, sarcomere shortens
  • Vertebrae (26): 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum, 1 coccyx; lower limb sequence: femur, patella, tibia, tarsals
  • Hormonal disorders: GH excess in children causes gigantism, in adults acromegaly; iodine deficiency causes goitre; low adrenal cortex hormones cause Addison's disease

Biology · Unit 6: Reproduction

Unit 6 covers sexual reproduction in flowering plants, human reproduction and reproductive health. It runs from flower structure, gametophytes, pollination, double fertilization and seed formation to human gametogenesis, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, contraception, STIs and assisted reproductive technologies. NEET asks about 8-10 questions from this unit every year, almost all line-based from NCERT, so precise facts, examples and sequences score directly.

PYQs (10): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q139, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q142, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q143, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q145, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q151, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q154, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q155, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q156, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q166, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q173

Flower structure

The flower is the site of sexual reproduction in angiosperms. The androecium is the whorl of stamens, and each stamen has a filament and an anther. A typical anther is bilobed and dithecous, meaning each lobe has two thecae. In transverse section it is tetragonal with four microsporangia, one at each corner, which develop into pollen sacs. The gynoecium is the female whorl. It may be monocarpellary or multicarpellary, and multicarpellary gynoecia are either syncarpous (fused carpels, as in Papaver) or apocarpous (free carpels, as in Michelia). Each pistil has a stigma (landing platform for pollen), a style and a basal swollen ovary. The ovarian cavity (locule) holds ovules attached to the placenta. The number of ovules ranges from one (wheat, paddy, mango) to many (papaya, watermelon, orchids).

  • Anther is bilobed and dithecous, with 4 microsporangia (tetrasporangiate)
  • Filament is attached to the thalamus or to a petal
  • Pistil consists of stigma, style and ovary
  • Syncarpous gynoecium: Papaver; apocarpous gynoecium: Michelia
  • Single ovule: wheat, paddy, mango; many ovules: papaya, watermelon, orchids

$\text{Microsporangia per anther} = 2 \text{ lobes} \times 2 \text{ thecae} = 4$ Counting thecae or microsporangia in a typical anther

NEET tip: NEET asks counting questions (thecae per lobe = 2, microsporangia per anther = 4) and examples of single or multi-ovuled ovaries.

Development of male and female gametophytes

Microsporogenesis: the wall of a microsporangium has four layers, from outside inward the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum. The outer three layers protect the sporangium and help dehiscence. The tapetum nourishes the developing pollen; its cells have dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus. Sporogenous tissue forms microspore mother cells, which undergo meiosis to give microspore tetrads, which mature into pollen grains. The exine is made of sporopollenin, the most resistant organic material known, and has germ pores where sporopollenin is absent. The intine is made of cellulose and pectin. A mature pollen grain has a large vegetative cell and a small generative cell; the generative cell later divides to form two male gametes. Megasporogenesis: inside the ovule, a megaspore mother cell in the micropylar region of the nucellus divides by meiosis to give four megaspores. Three degenerate, so development is monosporic. The surviving functional megaspore undergoes three free-nuclear mitoses, giving an 8-nucleate, 7-celled embryo sac.

  • Microsporangium wall from outside: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum (innermost, nutritive)
  • Exine is sporopollenin, which resists high temperature, strong acids, alkalis and enzymes
  • Over 60% of angiosperms shed pollen at the 2-celled stage; the rest shed it at the 3-celled stage
  • Pollen viability is about 30 minutes in rice and wheat but months in Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae
  • Pollen can be stored in liquid nitrogen at $-196^\circ C$ in pollen banks
  • Ovule parts: funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus, embryo sac
  • Embryo sac: egg apparatus (2 synergids plus 1 egg) at the micropylar end, 3 antipodals at the chalazal end, and a central cell with 2 polar nuclei
  • Synergids carry the filiform apparatus, which guides the pollen tube
  • Pollen of Parthenium (carrot grass) causes allergy

$\text{Meioses needed} = \frac{\text{number of pollen grains}}{4}$ One microspore mother cell gives 4 pollen grains

$\text{Meioses needed} = \text{number of embryo sacs}$ One megaspore mother cell gives only 1 functional megaspore, so 1 meiosis per embryo sac

$\text{Mitoses to form embryo sac} = 3 \;(1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 8 \text{ nuclei})$ Free-nuclear divisions of the functional megaspore

NEET tip: Expect questions on the role of the synergids and filiform apparatus, the composition of exine, the tapetum, and the 8-nucleate 7-celled embryo sac.

Pollination: types, agencies and examples

Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains to the stigma. There are three types. Autogamy uses pollen from the same flower. Geitonogamy uses pollen from another flower of the same plant; it is functionally cross-pollination but genetically similar to autogamy. Xenogamy uses pollen from a different plant and is the only type that brings genetically different pollen. Chasmogamous flowers have exposed anthers and stigma. Cleistogamous flowers never open, so they are invariably autogamous and assure seed set; examples are Viola, Oxalis and Commelina. Abiotic agents are wind and water. Biotic agents are animals, mainly insects (especially bees), as well as birds, bats, rodents and lizards. Wind-pollinated flowers produce light, non-sticky pollen, have well-exposed stamens, large feathery stigmas and often a single ovule; examples are grasses and maize. Water pollination occurs in about 30 genera, mostly monocots.

  • Wind pollination: grasses, maize (tassels are the stigma and style)
  • Water pollination: Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera (marine seagrass)
  • In Vallisneria, pollen is released on the water surface and the long-stalked female flowers reach the surface
  • In seagrasses, the long ribbon-like pollen grains are carried inside the water
  • Water hyacinth and water lily are aquatic but are pollinated by insects or wind
  • Insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and nectar-rich
  • Amorphophallus has a flower about 6 feet tall
  • Yucca and a moth species are mutually dependent; the moth lays eggs in the locule
  • Floral rewards are nectar and pollen; bees are the dominant biotic pollinators
  • Some insects, called pollen or nectar robbers, take rewards without pollinating

NEET tip: Match-the-column questions on agent versus example (Vallisneria, Zostera, maize, Yucca, Amorphophallus) and on cleistogamy are very frequent.

Outbreeding devices and pollen-pistil interaction

Continuous self-pollination causes inbreeding depression, so plants have outbreeding devices. In some species pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised. In others the anther and stigma are placed at different positions. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules, by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil. Unisexual flowers also help. In monoecious plants such as castor and maize, autogamy is prevented but geitonogamy is not. In dioecious plants such as papaya, both autogamy and geitonogamy are prevented. Pollen-pistil interaction is the dynamic process by which the pistil recognises compatible pollen through chemical components of the pollen and the pistil. Compatible pollen germinates, and the pollen tube grows through a germ pore, down the stigma and style, and enters the ovule through the micropyle. It then enters one synergid through the filiform apparatus. Plant breeders use artificial hybridization, which involves emasculation (removing anthers from bisexual flowers before dehiscence) followed by bagging.

  • Outbreeding devices: non-synchrony of pollen release and stigma receptivity, different positioning, self-incompatibility, unisexuality
  • Monoecious plants (castor, maize) prevent autogamy only
  • Dioecious plants (papaya) prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy
  • Pollen tube enters a synergid via the filiform apparatus
  • Emasculation is needed only for bisexual flowers; unisexual female flowers are only bagged
  • Rebagging is done after dusting pollen on the stigma

NEET tip: NEET often asks which plant prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy (papaya) and the steps of an artificial hybridization programme.

Double fertilization

The pollen tube releases two male gametes into the cytoplasm of a synergid. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell; this is syngamy and forms a diploid zygote. The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell; this is triple fusion and forms a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN). The central cell then becomes the primary endosperm cell. Because two fusions occur in one embryo sac, the process is called double fertilization, and it is unique to angiosperms. The zygote develops into the embryo and the PEN develops into the endosperm.

  • Syngamy: male gamete plus egg gives the zygote ($2n$)
  • Triple fusion: male gamete plus 2 polar nuclei gives the PEN ($3n$)
  • Double fertilization is a characteristic feature of angiosperms
  • Each ovule needs one pollen grain, which carries 2 male gametes

$\text{Endosperm} = n_{\text{male}} + 2n_{\text{polar}} = 3n$ If $2n = 36$, then $n = 18$ and the endosperm has $3n = 54$ chromosomes

$\text{Male gametes required} = 2 \times \text{number of seeds}$ Each fertilized ovule uses two male gametes

NEET tip: Chromosome number calculations for the endosperm, zygote, egg and nucellus, and the products of syngamy versus triple fusion, are asked repeatedly.

Post-fertilization events: endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit

Endosperm development always precedes embryo development. The PEN usually undergoes free-nuclear divisions first and cellularisation later. In coconut, the water is free-nuclear endosperm with thousands of nuclei, and the white kernel is cellular endosperm. The endosperm may be fully consumed before seed maturity, as in pea, groundnut and beans, giving non-albuminous (exalbuminous) seeds. It may instead persist, as in wheat, maize, barley, castor and coconut, giving albuminous seeds. In a dicot, the embryo develops through proembryo, globular and heart-shaped stages to maturity. It has two cotyledons and an embryonal axis made of the epicotyl (ending in the plumule) and the hypocotyl (ending in the radicle and root cap). A monocot embryo has one cotyledon, the scutellum. Its radicle is enclosed in the coleorhiza and its plumule in the coleoptile. After fertilization the ovule becomes the seed, the integuments become the seed coats, and the ovary becomes the fruit, whose wall is the pericarp. In seeds the micropyle persists as a pore for entry of oxygen and water.

  • Persistent nucellus is called perisperm: black pepper, beet
  • Mature seeds have about 10-15% moisture and may enter dormancy
  • False fruits develop from the thalamus: apple, strawberry, cashew
  • True fruits develop from the ovary only
  • Lupinus arcticus seed germinated after about 10,000 years
  • Phoenix dactylifera (date palm) seed was about 2000 years old, recovered from King Herod's palace near the Dead Sea
  • Orchids produce tiny, numerous seeds; Orobanche and Striga are parasites with many tiny seeds
  • Monocot embryo parts: scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza

$\text{Seed coat (maternal, } 2n), \; \text{embryo } (2n), \; \text{endosperm } (3n), \; \text{perisperm } (2n)$ Ploidy of the parts of a seed

NEET tip: Albuminous versus non-albuminous examples, perisperm, coconut endosperm and monocot embryo parts are standard one-liners.

Apomixis, parthenocarpy and polyembryony

Apomixis is the production of seeds without fertilization, so it is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction. It occurs in some Asteraceae and in grasses. In one route, a diploid egg cell forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilization. In another route, nucellus or integument cells divide and protrude into the embryo sac to form embryos. Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, often from nucellar cells; examples are Citrus and mango. Apomixis is valuable because hybrid seed has to be bought fresh every year, since hybrid characters segregate in the next generation; apomictic hybrids would not segregate. Parthenocarpy is the formation of a fruit without fertilization, giving seedless fruits. Banana is the classic example, and parthenocarpy can be induced by applying growth hormones.

  • Apomixis gives seeds without fertilization, and the offspring are clones
  • Apomixis occurs in Asteraceae and grasses
  • Polyembryony: Citrus, mango (nucellar embryos)
  • Parthenocarpy gives fruits without fertilization: banana
  • Introducing apomictic genes into hybrids is a goal of crop scientists

NEET tip: NEET contrasts apomixis (seed without fertilization) with parthenocarpy (fruit without fertilization) and asks for polyembryony examples.

Male and female reproductive systems

The male reproductive system lies in the pelvis. The testes are housed in the scrotum, which keeps them 2-2.5 degrees C below body temperature, as needed for spermatogenesis. Each testis is about 4-5 cm long and 2-3 cm wide and has about 250 testicular lobules, each with 1-3 seminiferous tubules. The duct pathway is seminiferous tubules, then rete testis, then vasa efferentia, then epididymis, then vas deferens, then ejaculatory duct, then urethra, which opens at the urethral meatus. The accessory glands are the paired seminal vesicles, the single prostate and the paired bulbourethral glands. Their secretions form seminal plasma, which is rich in fructose, calcium and enzymes; bulbourethral secretion helps lubricate the penis. The penis has an enlarged tip called the glans penis, covered by the foreskin. The female system has paired ovaries (2-4 cm), oviducts, uterus, cervix, vagina and external genitalia, together with the mammary glands. The oviduct is 10-12 cm long and has three parts: the infundibulum with its fimbriae, the ampulla and the isthmus. The uterine wall has three layers: the perimetrium, the myometrium and the endometrium.

  • Infundibulum, ampulla and isthmus are parts of the oviduct, not the male system
  • Male duct sequence: rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra
  • Myometrium shows strong contractions during parturition
  • Endometrium undergoes cyclical changes in the menstrual cycle
  • External female genitalia: mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen, clitoris
  • Mammary gland duct sequence: 15-20 mammary lobes with alveoli, then mammary tubules, mammary duct, mammary ampulla, lactiferous duct

NEET tip: Questions ask whether a structure belongs to the male or female system, the correct duct sequence, and the layers of the uterus.

Microscopic anatomy of testis and ovary

In the testis, each seminiferous tubule is lined on its inside by two types of cells. Male germ cells (spermatogonia) undergo meiosis to form sperm. Sertoli cells nourish the germ cells. The interstitial spaces outside the tubules contain small blood vessels, immunocompetent cells and Leydig (interstitial) cells, which synthesise and secrete androgens such as testosterone. In the ovary, the stroma is divided into a peripheral cortex and an inner medulla. Follicles develop in stages. A primary follicle is a primary oocyte surrounded by granulosa cells. A secondary follicle has more granulosa layers and a new theca. A tertiary follicle has a fluid-filled antrum, and its theca is organised into theca interna and theca externa. The mature Graafian follicle holds a secondary oocyte surrounded by the zona pellucida. After ovulation, the follicle remnants form the corpus luteum.

  • Leydig cells secrete androgens; Sertoli cells nourish germ cells
  • Oocytes are surrounded by granulosa cells
  • The antrum first appears in the tertiary follicle
  • Zona pellucida is the covering around the secondary oocyte in the Graafian follicle and at ovulation
  • Many follicles degenerate by follicular atresia

NEET tip: Identifying cell function (Leydig versus Sertoli) and follicle stages from diagram-based or statement-based questions is common.

Gametogenesis: spermatogenesis and oogenesis

Spermatogenesis begins at puberty. Spermatogonia ($2n = 46$) multiply by mitosis, and some become primary spermatocytes. Meiosis I gives two secondary spermatocytes ($n = 23$). Meiosis II gives four haploid spermatids. Spermatids transform into spermatozoa by spermiogenesis, and the sperm are released from the tubules by spermiation. The process is controlled by hormones: GnRH increases release of LH and FSH. LH acts on Leydig cells to stimulate androgens, and FSH acts on Sertoli cells to promote factors that aid spermiogenesis. A sperm has a head (nucleus and acrosome, which helps fertilization), a neck, a middle piece packed with mitochondria (energy for motility) and a tail. Oogenesis begins during foetal life. Oogonia form primary oocytes, which start meiosis but remain arrested in prophase I. No oogonia are added after birth. At puberty only 60,000-80,000 primary follicles remain in each ovary. The primary oocyte completes meiosis I in the tertiary follicle, giving a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body. Meiosis II is completed only when a sperm enters, giving the ovum and a second polar body.

  • Spermatogenesis starts at puberty; oogenesis starts in the foetus
  • Spermiogenesis converts spermatids into sperm; spermiation releases sperm
  • A normal ejaculate has 200-300 million sperm
  • For normal fertility, at least 60% of sperm should have normal shape and at least 40% should show vigorous motility
  • Primary oocyte remains arrested in prophase I until puberty
  • Unequal cytokinesis in oogenesis produces polar bodies
  • The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II only after sperm entry

$1 \text{ primary spermatocyte} \rightarrow 4 \text{ sperms}$ Calculating sperm number from spermatocyte number

$1 \text{ primary oocyte} \rightarrow 1 \text{ ovum} + \text{polar bodies}$ Calculating ova number; only one functional gamete forms

$\text{Spermatogonia, primary spermatocyte} = 2n; \; \text{secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, sperm} = n$ Ploidy at each stage

NEET tip: NEET tests the ploidy of each stage, the targets of LH and FSH in the male, and the stage at which oocyte meiosis is arrested and completed.

Menstrual cycle

The menstrual cycle is the reproductive cycle of female primates. It averages about 28/29 days, begins at menarche at puberty and stops at menopause, around 50 years. The menstrual phase lasts 3-5 days, when the endometrium breaks down because the ovum was not fertilized. In the follicular (proliferative) phase, rising FSH and LH drive follicle growth, and the follicle secretes estrogen, which regenerates the endometrium. LH and FSH peak around mid-cycle, about day 14, and this LH surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle, which is ovulation. In the luteal (secretory) phase, the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone, which maintains the endometrium for implantation. If no fertilization occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and menstruation follows. Pregnancy stops the cycle.

  • Phases: menstrual, follicular (proliferative), ovulatory, luteal (secretory)
  • LH surge causes ovulation around day 14
  • Corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone, which maintains the endometrium
  • Estrogen peaks before ovulation
  • Lack of menstruation may indicate pregnancy, stress or poor health

$\text{Ovulation day} \approx \text{cycle length} - 14$ Luteal phase is roughly constant at 14 days

NEET tip: Statement-type questions check that the LH surge causes ovulation and that the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, not mainly estrogen.

Fertilisation, embryo development up to blastocyst and implantation

Fertilisation occurs at the ampullary-isthmic junction of the oviduct. When a sperm contacts the zona pellucida, changes in the membrane block entry of additional sperm. Acrosomal enzymes help the sperm enter the cytoplasm of the secondary oocyte, which then completes meiosis II, giving the ovum and a second polar body. The haploid nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote. Sex is decided by the sperm: an X sperm gives a female (XX) and a Y sperm gives a male (XY). The zygote undergoes mitotic cleavage as it moves toward the uterus, forming blastomeres. The 8-16 cell embryo is the morula. The morula becomes a blastocyst with an outer trophoblast and an inner cell mass. The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium, the uterine cells cover the blastocyst, and the blastocyst becomes embedded. This embedding is implantation, and it leads to pregnancy.

  • Site of fertilisation: ampullary-isthmic junction
  • Only one sperm fertilises an ovum because of the block to polyspermy
  • Morula: 8-16 blastomeres
  • Blastocyst: trophoblast (outer) plus inner cell mass
  • Inner cell mass contains stem cells that give rise to all tissues and organs
  • Implantation occurs in the endometrium of the uterus

NEET tip: NEET asks the site of fertilisation, the morula cell count, the fate of the trophoblast versus the inner cell mass, and the role of the father in sex determination.

Pregnancy, placenta formation, parturition and lactation

After implantation, finger-like chorionic villi grow from the trophoblast and interdigitate with uterine tissue to form the placenta. The placenta supplies oxygen and nutrients to the embryo, removes carbon dioxide and wastes, and is connected to the embryo by the umbilical cord. It acts as an endocrine tissue, secreting hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens. Relaxin is secreted by the ovary in later pregnancy. Placental hormones together with raised maternal hormones support pregnancy. The inner cell mass differentiates into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Human gestation lasts about 9 months. Parturition starts with the foetal ejection reflex, which comes from the fully developed foetus and placenta. This triggers oxytocin release, causing stronger uterine contractions in a positive feedback loop. Lactation begins toward the end of pregnancy. The first milk, colostrum, contains IgA antibodies that give passive immunity to the newborn.

  • Hormones of pregnancy only: hCG, hPL, relaxin
  • LH and FSH are not placental hormones
  • Development timeline: heart forms after 1 month; limbs and digits by the end of month 2
  • By the end of 12 weeks (first trimester), most organ systems, limbs and external genitalia have formed
  • First foetal movements and hair on the head appear in the 5th month
  • By the end of 24 weeks, the body has fine hair, the eyelids separate and eyelashes form
  • Oxytocin acts on the uterine myometrium during parturition
  • Colostrum is rich in IgA antibodies

NEET tip: Common questions: which hormone is not placental (LH, FSH), the foetal development timeline, and the role of oxytocin and colostrum.

Reproductive health and prevention of STDs

The WHO describes reproductive health as total well-being in the physical, emotional, behavioural and social aspects of reproduction. India was among the first countries to start a national family planning programme, in 1951. These efforts were later expanded as Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs), also called venereal or reproductive tract infections, include gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis B and HIV/AIDS. Hepatitis B and HIV are also spread by sharing needles, transfusion of infected blood and from mother to foetus. Except for hepatitis B, genital herpes and HIV, the others are completely curable if detected early. They are most common in the 15-24 years age group. Untreated STIs can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancy, infertility and cancer of the reproductive tract. Prevention includes avoiding sex with unknown or multiple partners, always using condoms, and seeking early medical help.

  • Tuberculosis, typhoid and cholera are not STIs
  • Not completely curable: hepatitis B, genital herpes, HIV
  • Highest STI incidence is in persons aged 15-24 years
  • Population was about 350 million in 1947, about 1 billion in 2000 and about 1.2 billion in 2011
  • Statutory marriageable age is 18 years for females and 21 years for males
  • Reduced MMR and IMR, and increased life expectancy, contributed to population growth

NEET tip: NEET frequently asks which disease is not an STD, or which STDs are incurable.

Birth control: methods, contraception and MTP

An ideal contraceptive is user-friendly, easily available, effective, reversible and has no or few side effects. Natural methods include periodic abstinence (avoiding coitus on days 10-17 of the cycle), withdrawal (coitus interruptus) and lactational amenorrhea, which is effective for up to 6 months after parturition. Barrier methods are condoms (Nirodh for males, and female condoms), diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults, often used with spermicidal creams. IUDs are of three kinds: non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper-releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375), which suppress sperm motility, and hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20), which make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperm. Oral pills contain progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations, taken for 21 days starting within the first five days of the cycle. They inhibit ovulation and implantation. Saheli, a once-a-week pill, was developed at CDRI Lucknow. Emergency contraception (pills, IUD) is effective within 72 hours of coitus. Surgical sterilisation is vasectomy in males and tubectomy in females. MTP is safe in the first trimester. Under the MTP (Amendment) Act 2017, termination within 12 weeks needs the opinion of one registered medical practitioner, and termination between 12 and 24 weeks needs two.

  • Copper IUDs suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity
  • Hormonal IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperm
  • Saheli is a non-steroidal, once-a-week pill from CDRI Lucknow
  • Vasectomy removes or ties a small part of the vas deferens; tubectomy does the same to the fallopian tube
  • Surgical methods have very poor reversibility
  • About 45-50 million MTPs occur worldwide each year, about one-fifth of all pregnancies
  • IUDs are ideal for females who want to delay pregnancy or space children

NEET tip: Matching contraceptives to their type or mode of action, Saheli facts, the emergency window and MTP time limits are very frequently tested.

Amniocentesis

Amniocentesis is a prenatal diagnostic technique. A small sample of amniotic fluid surrounding the developing foetus is withdrawn, and the foetal cells and dissolved substances in it are analysed. It detects chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome and some genetic or metabolic disorders. Because the karyotype also reveals the sex of the foetus, it has been misused for sex determination, which led to female foeticide. Its use for sex determination is therefore legally banned in India. Its legitimate use is to identify serious foetal disorders, so that informed decisions, including MTP under the legal framework, can be made.

  • Analyses foetal cells in amniotic fluid
  • Detects chromosomal and genetic abnormalities
  • Use for sex determination is legally banned in India
  • Misuse is linked to female foeticide

NEET tip: NEET asks what amniocentesis detects and why its misuse for sex determination is banned.

Infertility and assisted reproductive technologies: IVF, ZIFT, GIFT

Infertility is the inability to conceive despite unprotected cohabitation. It may arise from physical, congenital, immunological, psychological or drug-related causes, in either the male or the female partner. Assisted reproductive technologies (ART) help such couples. In IVF-ET (in vitro fertilisation followed by embryo transfer, the test tube baby method), gametes are fused outside the body and the embryo is transferred into the woman. In ZIFT, a zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube. In IUT, an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus. Embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation can also be transferred. In GIFT, an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and development. In ICSI, a sperm is injected directly into the ovum. Artificial insemination (AI), including intra-uterine insemination (IUI), is used when the male has a low sperm count or cannot inseminate.

  • ZIFT: embryo with up to 8 blastomeres placed in the fallopian tube
  • IUT: embryo with more than 8 blastomeres placed in the uterus
  • GIFT: ovum, not zygote, is transferred into the fallopian tube
  • ICSI: sperm injected directly into the ovum
  • AI or IUI: semen from the husband or a donor introduced into the vagina or uterus
  • ART is costly and needs specialised professionals; emotional, religious and social factors limit its use, and legal adoption is an alternative

$\le 8 \text{ blastomeres} \rightarrow \text{ZIFT}; \; > 8 \text{ blastomeres} \rightarrow \text{IUT}$ Deciding the transfer site from the embryo stage

NEET tip: NEET asks which technique matches which description, such as ICSI for direct sperm injection, GIFT for ovum transfer, and ZIFT versus IUT by blastomere count.

Key facts

  • A typical anther is bilobed and dithecous, with 4 microsporangia
  • Sporopollenin in the exine is the most resistant organic material known
  • Over 60% of angiosperms shed pollen at the 2-celled stage
  • Pollen viability is about 30 minutes in rice and wheat
  • Pollen is stored in liquid nitrogen at $-196^\circ C$
  • The embryo sac is 8-nucleate and 7-celled, with monosporic development
  • The filiform apparatus of the synergids guides the pollen tube
  • Cleistogamous flowers: Viola, Oxalis, Commelina
  • Water pollination: Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera
  • Papaya is dioecious and prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy
  • Endosperm is triploid ($3n$); if $2n = 36$, the endosperm has 54 chromosomes
  • Non-albuminous seeds: pea, groundnut, beans; albuminous seeds: wheat, maize, barley, castor, coconut
  • Perisperm is found in black pepper and beet
  • False fruits: apple, strawberry, cashew; parthenocarpic fruit: banana
  • Polyembryony occurs in Citrus and mango; apomixis occurs in Asteraceae and grasses
  • The testes lie in the scrotum at 2-2.5 degrees C below body temperature, with about 250 lobules per testis
  • Leydig cells secrete androgens; Sertoli cells nourish germ cells
  • Each ovary has 60,000-80,000 primary follicles at puberty
  • The LH surge around day 14 causes ovulation; the corpus luteum secretes progesterone
  • Fertilisation occurs at the ampullary-isthmic junction
  • The morula is the 8-16 cell stage
  • Placental hormones: hCG, hPL, estrogens, progestogens; relaxin comes from the ovary in pregnancy
  • Colostrum contains IgA antibodies
  • Saheli is a once-weekly non-steroidal pill developed at CDRI Lucknow
  • Emergency contraception is effective within 72 hours of coitus
  • MTP needs one registered medical practitioner up to 12 weeks and two between 12 and 24 weeks
  • Copper IUDs: CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375; hormonal IUDs: Progestasert, LNG-20; non-medicated IUD: Lippes loop
  • STIs that are not completely curable: hepatitis B, genital herpes, HIV
  • India started its family planning programme in 1951
  • ZIFT transfers embryos with up to 8 blastomeres; IUT transfers embryos with more than 8 blastomeres

Common traps

  • Thinking the corpus luteum mainly secretes estrogen; it secretes large amounts of progesterone.
  • Thinking geitonogamy is genetic cross-pollination; it is genetically similar to autogamy because the pollen comes from the same plant.
  • Assuming every aquatic plant is water-pollinated; water hyacinth and water lily are pollinated by insects or wind.
  • Thinking monoecious plants such as maize and castor prevent geitonogamy; they prevent only autogamy, while dioecious papaya prevents both.
  • Confusing GIFT with ZIFT; GIFT transfers an ovum, while ZIFT transfers a zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres.
  • Listing LH or FSH as placental hormones; the placenta secretes hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens.
  • Believing meiosis in the oocyte is completed before ovulation; meiosis II is completed only after sperm entry.
  • Taking the endosperm as diploid; it is triploid, formed from one male gamete plus two polar nuclei.

Quick revision

  • Anther: 2 lobes x 2 thecae = 4 microsporangia; the innermost wall layer, the tapetum, is nutritive
  • Embryo sac: 1 meiosis plus 3 mitoses gives 8 nuclei in 7 cells; synergids with filiform apparatus guide the pollen tube
  • Double fertilization: syngamy gives the $2n$ zygote and triple fusion gives the $3n$ PEN
  • Cleistogamy: Viola, Oxalis, Commelina; water pollination: Vallisneria, Zostera; Yucca is pollinated by a moth
  • Albuminous: cereals, castor, coconut; non-albuminous: pea, groundnut, beans; perisperm: black pepper, beet
  • Apomixis gives seed without fertilization; parthenocarpy gives fruit without fertilization (banana); polyembryony: Citrus, mango
  • Male duct path: rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra
  • Oogenesis starts in the foetus and arrests at prophase I; the secondary oocyte at ovulation is covered by the zona pellucida
  • Cycle: menstrual (3-5 days), follicular (estrogen), LH surge and ovulation (about day 14), luteal (progesterone)
  • Fertilisation at the ampullary-isthmic junction; morula is 8-16 cells; blastocyst has trophoblast plus inner cell mass
  • Parturition: foetal ejection reflex leads to oxytocin release; colostrum carries IgA
  • ART: ICSI injects sperm into the ovum; GIFT transfers an ovum; ZIFT for up to 8 blastomeres; IUT for more than 8 blastomeres

Biology · Unit 7: Genetics and Evolution

Genetics and Evolution covers how traits pass from parents to offspring, from Mendel's laws to the molecular basis of inheritance (DNA, replication, transcription, translation, gene regulation). It also covers how populations change over time, from the origin of life to human evolution. It is one of the highest-weightage Biology units in NEET, regularly giving 15-20 questions, mostly direct NCERT statements, crosses, numerical problems and match-the-following items.

PYQs (11): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q138, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q141, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q147, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q153, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q159, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q160, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q164, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q167, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q169, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q170, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q175

Mendelian inheritance

Gregor Mendel worked on garden pea (Pisum sativum) from 1856 to 1863. He chose 7 pairs of contrasting traits and used true-breeding lines and large samples, then analysed results statistically. He called the inherited units factors; these are now called genes, and their alternative forms are alleles. In a monohybrid cross (tall TT x dwarf tt) all F1 plants are tall (Tt). F2 gives 3:1 phenotypically and 1:2:1 genotypically. His three principles are dominance, segregation and independent assortment. Segregation means alleles separate during gamete formation, so gametes are always pure. Independent assortment means a dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1 in F2. A test cross is a cross with the homozygous recessive and reveals the genotype of a dominant-looking plant. Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900 by de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak.

  • 7 contrasting traits: stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape, seed colour
  • Monohybrid F2: phenotype 3:1, genotype 1:2:1
