  • Dihybrid F2: phenotype 9:3:3:1, with 4 phenotypic classes (2 parental and 2 recombinant types) and 9 genotypic classes ($3^2$), arising from independent assortment
  • Monohybrid test cross gives 1:1; dihybrid test cross gives 1:1:1:1
  • Law of segregation is universal; independent assortment applies only to unlinked genes
  • Punnett square was developed by Reginald C. Punnett
  • Dominance is a property of an allele pair and depends on the product each allele makes, not on the allele alone

$2^n$ Number of gamete types, or F2 phenotypes under complete dominance, for n heterozygous gene pairs

$3^n$ Number of F2 genotypes for n heterozygous gene pairs

$4^n$ Number of F2 combinations (boxes in the Punnett square) for n gene pairs

NEET tip: Expect ratio-based crosses, test cross outcomes and assertion-reason items on why F1 shows only the dominant trait.

Deviations from Mendelism: incomplete dominance, co-dominance, multiple alleles, blood groups, pleiotropy

Incomplete dominance occurs when the F1 heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype. In snapdragon (Antirrhinum), red RR x white rr gives pink Rr. The F2 phenotypic ratio then equals the genotypic ratio, 1:2:1. In co-dominance both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote; the ABO blood group $I^AI^B$ shows both A and B sugars. Multiple alleles means more than two alleles exist for one gene in a population, although any individual carries only two. Gene I has three alleles: $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$. $I^A$ and $I^B$ are co-dominant to each other and both are dominant over $i$. This gives 6 genotypes and 4 blood groups. Pleiotropy means a single gene shows multiple phenotypic effects. One example is phenylketonuria, where a single gene mutation causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation. Another is the starch synthesis gene in pea, which affects both starch grain size and seed shape.

  • Incomplete dominance: F2 phenotype and genotype ratios are both 1:2:1
  • Blood group A = $I^AI^A$ or $I^Ai$; B = $I^BI^B$ or $I^Bi$; AB = $I^AI^B$; O = $ii$
  • The ABO gene codes for a sugar polymer on the RBC plasma membrane; $i$ adds no sugar
  • Pea starch gene: BB gives large grains and round seeds; bb gives small grains and wrinkled seeds; Bb gives round seeds with intermediate grains
  • So seed shape shows dominance while grain size shows incomplete dominance; dominance depends on the phenotype chosen
  • An O-group child needs both parents to carry $i$; an $I^AI^B$ parent cannot have an O child

$\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ Number of possible genotypes for n multiple alleles of a gene (n = 3 gives 6)

NEET tip: Blood group parentage questions, such as which parental genotypes cannot produce an O child, and pea starch grain pleiotropy are favourites.

Polygenic inheritance (elementary idea)

In polygenic inheritance, a trait is controlled by three or more genes whose alleles act additively, and the environment also influences the trait. Such traits show continuous variation and a bell-shaped distribution rather than discrete classes. Human skin colour and height are classic examples. Consider skin colour controlled by three genes A, B and C, where each dominant allele adds one unit of pigment. The genotype AABBCC is darkest, aabbcc is lightest, and AaBbCc is intermediate. Phenotype depends on the number of dominant alleles present, not on which particular alleles they are. An F2 from AaBbCc x AaBbCc gives 7 phenotypic classes in the ratio 1:6:15:20:15:6:1. Polygenic inheritance is quantitative, unlike Mendel's qualitative traits.

  • Multiple genes with additive (cumulative) effect
  • Continuous variation; graph is bell-shaped
  • Environment also modifies the phenotype
  • Examples: human skin colour, height
  • Polygenic (many genes, one trait) is the opposite of pleiotropy (one gene, many traits)

$2n+1$ Number of phenotypic classes in F2 for n polygenes (n = 3 gives 7)

$\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^n$ Fraction of F2 showing one particular extreme phenotype, darkest or lightest (n = 3 gives 1/64 each); both extremes together make up $2 \times \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^n$

NEET tip: Usually asked as an identification of the example (skin colour) or as a count of phenotypic classes for a given number of genes.

Chromosome theory of inheritance; chromosomes and genes

Mendel's work stayed unrecognised for decades. Reasons include poor communication, a mathematical approach unfamiliar to biologists, and the absence of physical proof for his factors. By 1900, microscopy showed that chromosomes occur in pairs, segregate at meiosis and assort independently, exactly as Mendel's factors did. Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri (1902) united chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles in the chromosome theory of inheritance. The theory states that genes are located on chromosomes and that chromosome behaviour during meiosis explains segregation and independent assortment. Thomas Hunt Morgan provided experimental verification using the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. Drosophila is a convenient model because it can be grown on simple synthetic medium and completes its life cycle in about two weeks. A single mating produces many progeny, the sexes are clearly distinguishable, and it shows many hereditary variations visible under a low-power microscope.

  • Genes lie on chromosomes in linear order
  • Homologous chromosomes pair and separate at anaphase I, which explains segregation
  • Non-homologous chromosome pairs orient independently at metaphase I, which explains independent assortment
  • Proposed by Sutton and Boveri, 1902; verified by T.H. Morgan using Drosophila
  • Both chromosomes and genes occur in pairs in diploid cells, and gametes receive one of each pair

NEET tip: Questions ask who proposed the theory versus who verified it, and why Drosophila is a suitable organism.

Sex determination in humans, birds and honey bee

Henking (1891) observed a nuclear structure he named the X body in some insects; it was later called the X chromosome. In XO types such as grasshopper, females are XX and males have a single X. Humans follow the XX-XY type, where the male is heterogametic: half the sperms carry X and half carry Y, while all eggs carry X. The sex of the child therefore depends on the sperm, so the father determines sex. Birds follow the ZW-ZZ type: females are ZW (heterogametic) and males are ZZ, so the mother determines sex. The honey bee shows haplodiploid sex determination. A fertilised egg (2n = 32) develops into a female, either a queen or a worker. An unfertilised egg develops by parthenogenesis into a haploid male drone (n = 16). Drones produce sperms by mitosis, have no father and cannot have sons, but they do have a grandfather.

  • Humans: 22 pairs of autosomes plus XX (female) or XY (male); male heterogamety
  • Probability of a male child is 50% in every pregnancy
  • Birds: female ZW heterogametic, male ZZ
  • Grasshopper and many insects: XO type; males have one chromosome fewer
  • Honey bee: female 2n = 32, male drone n = 16; drone sperms form by mitosis
  • Queen and worker are both diploid; their difference is nutritional (royal jelly), not genetic

NEET tip: Match-the-following items on which sex is heterogametic in which organism, and honey bee drone facts, are common.

Linkage and crossing over

Morgan carried out dihybrid crosses in Drosophila involving X-linked genes, such as yellow body with white eyes crossed to brown body with red eyes. He found that F2 ratios deviated strongly from 9:3:3:1 and that parental combinations far outnumbered recombinants. He concluded that genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, and he coined the term linkage for this physical association. He used recombination for the generation of non-parental combinations, which arise by crossing over between non-sister chromatids at pachytene of prophase I. Tightly linked genes show low recombination, while loosely linked genes show high recombination. Alfred Sturtevant, Morgan's student, used recombination frequency as a measure of the distance between genes. With this he constructed the first chromosome maps.

  • Yellow-white genes: 1.3% recombination (tightly linked)
  • White-miniature genes: 37.2% recombination (loosely linked)
  • Recombination frequency is proportional to the distance between genes
  • 1% recombination = 1 map unit (centiMorgan)
  • Crossing over occurs at pachytene, mediated by the enzyme recombinase
  • Complete linkage gives only parental types in a test cross

$RF = \frac{\text{number of recombinants}}{\text{total progeny}} \times 100$ Percentage recombination, which equals map distance in cM

NEET tip: Questions focus on Morgan's percentages (1.3 and 37.2) and on the relation between recombination frequency and gene distance.

Sex-linked inheritance: haemophilia and colour blindness

Sex-linked traits are controlled by genes on the X chromosome. Males are hemizygous, so a single recessive X-linked allele expresses in them, while females usually remain heterozygous carriers. Haemophilia is X-linked recessive. A single protein in the cascade of proteins involved in blood clotting is affected, so a simple cut can cause non-stop bleeding. A carrier female transmits it to half her sons. A haemophilic female is very rare, because her mother must be at least a carrier and her father must be haemophilic; such females often do not survive to later stages of life. Queen Victoria was a carrier, and several of her descendants were haemophilic. Colour blindness is also X-linked recessive and involves defects in red or green cones of the eye. It occurs in about 8% of males but only about 0.4% of females. A daughter is colour blind only if her father is colour blind and her mother is at least a carrier.

  • Criss-cross inheritance: a trait passes from an affected father through a carrier daughter to her son
  • Sons inherit their X from the mother, so an affected father never passes an X-linked trait to his son
  • Carrier mother x normal father gives 50% of sons affected and 50% of daughters carriers
  • Affected father x normal mother gives all daughters carriers and all sons normal
  • Pedigree symbols: square = male, circle = female, shaded = affected, double line = consanguineous mating

NEET tip: NEET tests probability calculations for children of carrier mothers and the incidence figures of colour blindness.

Mendelian disorders: thalassemia

Mendelian disorders are caused by alteration or mutation of a single gene and follow Mendelian inheritance; pedigree analysis helps trace them. They may be dominant or recessive, and autosomal or sex-linked. Examples include haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria and thalassemia. Thalassemia is an autosomal recessive blood disease transmitted when both parents are unaffected carriers. A mutation or deletion reduces the synthesis of one of the globin chains of haemoglobin, producing abnormal haemoglobin and anaemia. Alpha thalassemia involves two closely linked genes, HBA1 and HBA2, on chromosome 16 of each parent. Mutation or deletion of one or more of these four genes reduces alpha chain production; the more genes affected, the less alpha globin is made. Beta thalassemia involves the single gene HBB on chromosome 11 of each parent, where mutation of one or both genes reduces beta chain production.

  • Thalassemia is quantitative: too few globin chains are synthesised
  • Sickle-cell anaemia is qualitative: an incorrectly functioning globin is made
  • Sickle-cell: Glu replaced by Val at the 6th position of the beta chain (GAG becomes GUG); autosomal recessive
  • Phenylketonuria: autosomal recessive; missing enzyme converting phenylalanine to tyrosine
  • Alpha thalassemia: chromosome 16, four genes in total; beta thalassemia: chromosome 11, two genes in total
  • Two carrier parents have a 25% chance of an affected child

NEET tip: Expect chromosome-number matching (16 for alpha, 11 for beta) and the quantitative versus qualitative contrast with sickle-cell.

Chromosomal disorders: Down's, Turner's and Klinefelter's syndromes

Chromosomal disorders are caused by the absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes. Failure of chromatids to segregate during cell division causes aneuploidy, the gain or loss of a chromosome. Failure of cytokinesis after telophase causes polyploidy, which is common in plants. Down's syndrome is trisomy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes), first described by Langdon Down in 1866. Affected persons are short with a small round head, a furrowed tongue and a partially open mouth, a characteristic palm crease, and retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development. Klinefelter's syndrome is 47, XXY: the person has an overall masculine development with some feminine features such as gynaecomastia, and is sterile. Turner's syndrome is 45, XO, caused by the absence of one X chromosome. Affected females are sterile because the ovaries are rudimentary, and they lack other secondary sexual characters.

  • Down's: autosomal trisomy 21; 47 chromosomes; occurs in both sexes
  • Klinefelter's: 44 + XXY; male; sterile; gynaecomastia
  • Turner's: 44 + XO; female; sterile; rudimentary ovaries
  • Turner's is a monosomy, not an extra-chromosome condition
  • Aneuploidy is caused by non-disjunction; polyploidy by failure of cytokinesis

NEET tip: Statement-based questions swap the causes (extra copy versus missing X), so memorise the exact karyotype of each syndrome.

Search for genetic material; DNA as genetic material

Frederick Griffith (1928) worked with Streptococcus pneumoniae and mice. The S strain has a mucous capsule and is virulent, while the R strain is non-virulent. Heat-killed S strain mixed with live R strain killed the mice, and live S bacteria were recovered from them. Griffith called this transformation, caused by a transforming principle, but did not identify it. Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty (1933-44) purified the components and showed that the transforming principle is DNA. Proteases and RNases did not stop transformation, but DNase did. Hershey and Chase (1952) grew bacteriophages with radioactive $^{32}P$ (labels DNA) or $^{35}S$ (labels protein). After infection and blending, only $^{32}P$ was found inside the bacteria, proving that DNA is the genetic material. A genetic material must replicate, be chemically and structurally stable, allow slow mutation, and express itself as Mendelian characters.

  • Griffith: transformation discovered, nature of the principle unknown
  • Avery, MacLeod and McCarty: biochemical proof that DNA is the transforming principle
  • Hershey-Chase: unequivocal proof using phage; $^{32}P$ for DNA, $^{35}S$ for protein
  • Protein has no phosphorus; DNA has no sulphur
  • RNA was the first genetic material, giving an RNA world
  • DNA is more stable than RNA because it lacks the 2'-OH group and has thymine instead of uracil
  • RNA is catalytic and mutates faster, which suits RNA viruses

NEET tip: Match scientists with experiments, and know which isotope labels which molecule in the Hershey-Chase experiment.

Structure of DNA and RNA; DNA packaging

A nucleotide has three parts: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate. A base joined to a sugar by an N-glycosidic linkage forms a nucleoside. Adding phosphate by a phosphoester linkage forms a nucleotide, and nucleotides join by 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds. Purines are A and G; pyrimidines are C, T (in DNA) and U (in RNA). Watson and Crick (1953) proposed the double helix using X-ray diffraction data from Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin. In this model, two antiparallel polynucleotide chains form a right-handed helix with sugar-phosphate backbones outside and bases inside. A pairs with T through 2 hydrogen bonds, and G pairs with C through 3. The pitch is 3.4 nm, with about 10 bp per turn and 0.34 nm between base pairs. Chargaff's rule states A = T and G = C. In eukaryotes, negatively charged DNA wraps around a positively charged histone octamer (rich in lysine and arginine) to form nucleosomes of about 200 bp. These appear as beads-on-string and coil further into chromatin fibres.

  • Human DNA: $6.6 \times 10^9$ bp, about 2.2 m long
  • E. coli: $4.6 \times 10^6$ bp; phi X174: 5386 nucleotides; lambda phage: 48502 bp
  • Prokaryotic DNA is held in a nucleoid by positively charged proteins
  • Histone octamer: two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4; H1 is the linker histone
  • Non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins are needed for higher-order packaging
  • Euchromatin is loosely packed, light-staining and transcriptionally active; heterochromatin is densely packed, dark-staining and inactive
  • RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and uracil, and occurs as mRNA, tRNA and rRNA

$A + G = T + C$, i.e. $\frac{A+G}{T+C} = 1$ Chargaff's rule for double-stranded DNA; used to find the percentage of other bases

$L = \text{bp} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}\,m$ Length of a DNA double helix from its number of base pairs

NEET tip: Numericals on base percentage and DNA length, plus histone and nucleosome facts, are frequently asked.

DNA replication

Watson and Crick proposed that DNA replication is semiconservative: each daughter duplex contains one parental and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl (1958) proved this in E. coli. They grew cells in $^{15}NH_4Cl$, transferred them to $^{14}N$ medium, and analysed the DNA by CsCl density gradient centrifugation. After 20 minutes (one generation) all DNA was hybrid. After 40 minutes, hybrid and light DNA were present in equal amounts. Taylor showed the same in Vicia faba using radioactive thymidine. Replication starts at a definite origin and proceeds through a replication fork. DNA-dependent DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the $5' \rightarrow 3'$ direction. Synthesis is therefore continuous on the leading strand (template $3' \rightarrow 5'$). On the lagging strand it is discontinuous, producing Okazaki fragments that DNA ligase joins. Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates act both as substrates and as the energy source. In eukaryotes, replication occurs in the S phase.

  • E. coli replicates $4.6 \times 10^6$ bp in about 18 minutes, roughly 2000 bp per second
  • DNA polymerase cannot initiate replication on its own and works only $5' \rightarrow 3'$
  • Unwinding of the helix opens a replication fork
  • Lagging strand: discontinuous synthesis, Okazaki fragments, joined by DNA ligase
  • Failure of cell division after replication results in polyploidy
  • After n generations in $^{14}N$, hybrid DNA = 2 molecules out of $2^n$

$\frac{2}{2^n}$ Fraction of hybrid ($^{15}N$-$^{14}N$) DNA after n generations in light medium (Meselson-Stahl)

NEET tip: Meselson-Stahl generation fractions and leading versus lagging strand features are standard questions.

Central dogma, transcription, genetic code and translation

Crick's central dogma states that genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein. In retroviruses, reverse transcription (RNA to DNA) also occurs. A transcription unit has a promoter (towards the 5' end of the coding strand), a structural gene and a terminator. The template strand has $3' \rightarrow 5'$ polarity. The coding strand has the same sequence as the RNA except that T is replaced by U. Bacteria have one RNA polymerase, which uses the sigma factor for initiation and the rho factor for termination. Eukaryotes have three nuclear RNA polymerases. They have split genes: hnRNA undergoes splicing (introns removed), capping (methyl guanosine triphosphate added at the 5' end) and tailing (200-300 adenylates added at the 3' end). The genetic code is triplet, with 64 codons: 61 code for amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons. AUG codes for methionine and is the start codon. The code is unambiguous, degenerate, comma-less and nearly universal. During translation, tRNA carries amino acids to the ribosome, where rRNA catalyses peptide bonds.

  • RNA polymerase I makes rRNAs 28S, 18S and 5.8S; RNA polymerase II makes hnRNA (precursor mRNA); RNA polymerase III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs
  • Prokaryotic transcription and translation are coupled because mRNA needs no processing
  • George Gamow proposed the triplet code; Khorana synthesised RNA with defined base combinations; Nirenberg used a cell-free system; Severo Ochoa's enzyme polynucleotide phosphorylase polymerises RNA without a template
  • UUU codes for phenylalanine
  • tRNA is the adapter molecule: cloverleaf in 2D, inverted L in 3D, with an anticodon loop
  • Charging (aminoacylation) of tRNA uses ATP
  • 23S rRNA in bacteria acts as a ribozyme (peptidyl transferase)
  • UTRs lie before the start codon and after the stop codon; a release factor binds the stop codon

$4^3 = 64$ Total number of triplet codons

NEET tip: Questions ask which RNA polymerase makes which RNA, the properties of the code, and the scientists behind deciphering it.

Gene expression and regulation: lac operon

Gene expression can be regulated at transcription, processing or splicing, transport of mRNA, and translation; in prokaryotes, control of transcription initiation is predominant. The lac operon of E. coli was described by Francois Jacob and Jacques Monod. It has a regulator gene i, which codes for a repressor and is constitutively expressed from its own promoter. It also has a promoter, an operator, and three structural genes. Gene z codes for beta-galactosidase, which hydrolyses lactose into galactose and glucose. Gene y codes for permease, which increases cell permeability to lactose. Gene a codes for transacetylase. When lactose is absent, the repressor binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. When lactose (the inducer) is present, it binds the repressor and inactivates it, so RNA polymerase transcribes z, y and a as one polycistronic mRNA. This is negative regulation. A very low level of operon expression always exists so that some lactose can enter the cell.

  • Lactose (or allolactose) is the inducer; it inactivates the repressor, it does not activate it
  • The i gene is not part of the z, y, a transcription unit and has its own promoter
  • z, y and a share a single promoter and form a polycistronic mRNA
  • Galactose and glucose are products, not inducers
  • The operon is switched off again once lactose is used up
  • The lac operon is an inducible operon under negative control by the repressor

NEET tip: Statement items check whether the i gene is constitutive, what the inducer is, and which genes share a promoter.

Genome, Human Genome Project and DNA fingerprinting

The genome is the complete DNA content of an organism. The Human Genome Project (HGP) was launched in 1990 and completed in 2003, coordinated by the US Department of Energy and NIH with the Wellcome Trust (UK). It used two approaches: Expressed Sequence Tags, which identify genes expressed as RNA, and sequence annotation, which sequences the whole genome and then assigns functions. DNA fragments were cloned in BAC and YAC vectors and sequenced on automated sequencers based on Sanger's method. DNA fingerprinting was developed by Alec Jeffreys. It uses Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTRs), a type of satellite DNA that shows high polymorphism. The steps are DNA isolation, digestion with restriction endonucleases, gel electrophoresis, Southern blotting, hybridisation with a labelled VNTR probe, and autoradiography. Its main uses are forensics and paternity testing.

  • Human genome: about $3 \times 10^9$ bp (3164.7 million nucleotide bases)
  • Average gene: 3000 bases; largest is dystrophin at 2.4 million bases
  • About 30,000 genes; 99.9% of bases are identical among all humans
  • Less than 2% of the genome codes for proteins; repeated sequences form a large portion
  • Functions of over 50% of discovered genes are unknown
  • Chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and Y the fewest (231)
  • About 1.4 million SNPs identified
  • VNTR size ranges from 0.1 to 20 kb; PCR amplifies DNA from tiny samples

NEET tip: Expect HGP statistics and the correct sequence of DNA fingerprinting steps.

Origin of life

According to the Big Bang theory, the universe originated about 20 billion years ago, and Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. Life appeared roughly 500 million years later. Early theories included special creation and spontaneous generation; Louis Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation with swan-neck flask experiments. The panspermia idea held that spores reached Earth from outer space. Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed chemical evolution: the first life formed from pre-existing non-living organic molecules under a reducing early atmosphere. In 1953 Stanley Miller created electric discharge in a closed flask containing $CH_4$, $H_2$, $NH_3$ and water vapour at 800 degrees C, and he obtained amino acids. The first non-cellular forms of life probably arose about 3 billion years ago. The first cellular forms appeared about 2000 million years ago.

  • Early atmosphere was reducing: $CH_4$, $NH_3$, $H_2$, water vapour; free $O_2$ absent
  • Miller's experiment gave amino acids; others observed sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats
  • Pasteur: life comes only from pre-existing life
  • Oparin-Haldane theory: chemical evolution preceded biological evolution
  • The first life forms were probably giant molecules such as RNA, proteins and polysaccharides that could reproduce

NEET tip: Questions target the gases used and the temperature in Miller's experiment, and who proposed which theory.

Evidences for biological evolution

Paleontological evidence comes from fossils in sedimentary rock layers, which show that life forms changed over time. Comparative anatomy provides two kinds of evidence. Homologous organs share the same structure and origin but perform different functions; examples are the forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah and human, and Bougainvillea thorns compared with Cucurbita tendrils. These indicate divergent evolution. Analogous organs perform similar functions but differ in structure and origin; examples are the wings of butterfly and bird, the eyes of octopus and mammals, the flippers of penguin and dolphin, and sweet potato (a root) compared with potato (a stem). These indicate convergent evolution. Ernst Haeckel proposed embryological support, citing vestigial gill slits in all vertebrate embryos. Karl Ernst von Baer disapproved this, noting that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals. Biochemical similarities in proteins and genes also support common ancestry.

  • Homology indicates divergent evolution; analogy indicates convergent evolution
  • Heart and brain of vertebrates are also homologous
  • Industrial melanism in the peppered moth Biston betularia, England: before industrialisation white moths outnumbered dark ones; after it the reverse
  • Lichens are industrial pollution indicators
  • Antibiotic, herbicide and pesticide resistance are evolution through anthropogenic action
  • Haeckel's embryological evidence is the version NCERT treats as disapproved

NEET tip: Classify examples as homologous or analogous, and remember that Haeckel's embryological evidence was disapproved by von Baer.

Darwin's contribution and modern synthetic theory

Lamarck proposed evolution through the use and disuse of organs and the inheritance of acquired characters, illustrated by the giraffe's long neck; this view is now rejected. Charles Darwin sailed around the world on HMS Beagle and studied fauna such as the Galapagos finches. He concluded that existing living forms share similarities with each other and with forms that existed millions of years ago. His theory has two key concepts, branching descent and natural selection. Fitness means reproductive fitness: the fitter individuals leave more progeny. Alfred Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago, reached similar conclusions. Darwin was influenced by Malthus's ideas on population. Hugo de Vries, working on evening primrose (Oenothera lamarckiana), proposed that mutation causes evolution. He described saltation as large, single-step mutations, whereas Darwin's variations were small and directional. The modern synthetic theory combines Darwinian selection with genetics.

  • Darwin: variation, overproduction, struggle for existence, survival of the fittest, natural selection
  • Darwinian variations are small and directional; mutations are random and directionless
  • de Vries: mutation theory, saltation, Oenothera lamarckiana
  • Synthetic theory factors: gene mutation, recombination, gene flow, genetic drift, natural selection
  • Darwin could not explain the source of variation; genetics later supplied it

NEET tip: Match the scientist with the plant, animal or concept: de Vries with evening primrose, Lamarck with giraffe, Darwin with finches.

Mechanism of evolution: variation and natural selection; types of natural selection

Evolution is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutations in organisms. Variation arises through mutation, recombination during gametogenesis, and gene flow. Natural selection acts on heritable variation: individuals that are better fitted leave more offspring, so their alleles increase over generations. Selection on a continuously varying trait can produce three outcomes. Stabilising selection favours individuals with the average value, so the peak becomes higher and narrower. Directional selection favours one extreme, so the peak shifts in one direction. Disruptive selection favours both extremes over the mean, producing two peaks. Lederberg's replica plating showed that mutations pre-exist in a population and are not induced by the environment. Bacteria grown on antibiotic medium reveal pre-existing resistant forms within days, which shows evolution on a short timescale.

  • Stabilising: more individuals acquire the mean character value; variation decreases
  • Directional: more individuals acquire a value other than the mean, at one extreme
  • Disruptive: more individuals acquire peripheral values at both ends; two peaks
  • Genetic drift is a chance change in allele frequency and is not a type of natural selection
  • Natural selection is the main driving force of adaptive change

NEET tip: Match graphs with the type of selection, and note that drift is not an outcome of natural selection.

Gene flow, genetic drift and Hardy-Weinberg principle

The Hardy-Weinberg principle states that allele and genotype frequencies in a population stay constant from generation to generation when no evolutionary force acts. The total of all genes and alleles in a population is the gene pool, and its stability is called genetic equilibrium. With two alleles of frequencies p and q, $p + q = 1$, and the genotype frequencies are $p^2$ (AA), $2pq$ (Aa) and $q^2$ (aa). Five factors disturb this equilibrium: gene migration (gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection. Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations when individuals migrate. Genetic drift is a chance change in allele frequency and is strongest in small populations. In the founder effect, a small group that colonises a new area becomes genetically different from the original population and may become a new species. A disturbed equilibrium indicates evolution.

  • Equilibrium conditions: large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, no selection
  • Founder effect: the colonisers are called founders
  • Bottleneck effect: a drastic reduction in population size, also a form of drift
  • If $q^2$ is known, take its square root to get q
  • Carrier (heterozygote) frequency is $2pq$

$p + q = 1$ Allele frequencies for two alleles

$p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$ Genotype frequencies of AA, Aa and aa at equilibrium

NEET tip: Numericals give p, q or $q^2$ and ask for a genotype frequency; for example, p = 0.1 gives AA = 0.01.

Adaptive radiation

Adaptive radiation is the evolution of different species in a geographical area, starting from one point and radiating into other habitats. Darwin's finches on the Galapagos Islands are the classic example. A seed-eating ancestral finch gave rise to many forms with altered beaks, including insectivorous and vegetarian types. Australian marsupials are another example: many different marsupials evolved from a common ancestral stock within the Australian island continent. Both are examples of divergent evolution. When more than one adaptive radiation appears to have occurred in an isolated geographical area, representing different habitats, the result can be called convergent evolution. Australian placental mammals show adaptive radiation into forms that each resemble a corresponding marsupial. Examples include the placental wolf and the Tasmanian wolf, and the flying squirrel and the flying phalanger.

  • Adaptive radiation from a single ancestor is divergent evolution
  • Similarity between placental mammals and marsupials in Australia is convergent evolution
  • Pairs: placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf; flying squirrel and flying phalanger; mole and marsupial mole; anteater and numbat; lemur and spotted cuscus; bobcat and Tasmanian tiger cat
  • Darwin's finches show variation in beak type according to food habit

NEET tip: NEET asks whether a given radiation example is divergent or convergent evolution.

Human evolution

About 15 million years ago, Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus existed. They were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees; Ramapithecus was more man-like and Dryopithecus more ape-like. About 2 million years ago, australopithecines probably lived in East African grasslands. They hunted with stone weapons but essentially ate fruit. Homo habilis, the first human-like being, had a brain capacity of 650-800 cc and probably did not eat meat. Homo erectus, about 1.5 million years ago, had a brain of 900 cc and probably ate meat; its fossils were discovered in Java in 1891. Neanderthal man, with a brain of 1400 cc, lived in the Near East and Central Asia between 1,00,000 and 40,000 years ago. Neanderthals used hides to protect the body and buried their dead. Homo sapiens arose in Africa and moved across continents. During the ice age, between 75,000 and 10,000 years ago, modern Homo sapiens arose.

  • Sequence: Dryopithecus/Ramapithecus, then Australopithecus, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthal and Homo sapiens
  • Brain capacity: H. habilis 650-800 cc; H. erectus 900 cc; Neanderthal 1400 cc
  • Prehistoric cave art developed about 18,000 years ago (Bhimbetka, Madhya Pradesh)
  • Agriculture began about 10,000 years ago, along with human settlements
  • Homo sapiens originated in Africa, not Australia or Asia

NEET tip: Statement items test the place of origin (Africa), the 75,000-10,000 years window and brain capacities.

Key facts

  • Mendel studied 7 pairs of contrasting characters in garden pea between 1856 and 1863.
  • Mendel's laws were rediscovered in 1900 by de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak.
  • ABO blood group has 3 alleles, 6 genotypes and 4 phenotypes; $I^A$ and $I^B$ are co-dominant.
  • Morgan's Drosophila data: yellow-white recombination 1.3%, white-miniature 37.2%.
  • Honey bee: female 2n = 32, male drone n = 16, and the drone has no father.
  • Colour blindness occurs in about 8% of males and about 0.4% of females.
  • Alpha thalassemia genes HBA1 and HBA2 lie on chromosome 16; the beta thalassemia gene HBB lies on chromosome 11.
  • Down's syndrome is trisomy 21 (Langdon Down, 1866); Klinefelter's is 47, XXY; Turner's is 45, XO.
  • Hershey and Chase used $^{32}P$ to label DNA and $^{35}S$ to label protein in bacteriophage.
  • DNA double helix: pitch 3.4 nm, 10 bp per turn, 0.34 nm between base pairs.
  • Human haploid genome is $3 \times 10^9$ bp; diploid DNA is $6.6 \times 10^9$ bp and about 2.2 m long.
  • A nucleosome contains about 200 bp of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer.
  • Meselson and Stahl (1958) used $^{15}N$ and CsCl density gradient centrifugation; E. coli divides every 20 minutes.
  • E. coli replicates $4.6 \times 10^6$ bp in about 18 minutes, roughly 2000 bp per second.
  • RNA polymerase I makes rRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S); II makes hnRNA; III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNA.
  • Of 64 codons, 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA. AUG is the start codon.
  • Lac operon structural genes: z (beta-galactosidase), y (permease), a (transacetylase).
  • HGP ran from 1990 to 2003; about 30,000 genes; dystrophin is the largest gene at 2.4 million bases.
  • Chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and the Y chromosome the fewest (231).
  • DNA fingerprinting was developed by Alec Jeffreys using VNTR probes.
  • Miller (1953) used $CH_4$, $NH_3$, $H_2$ and water vapour at 800 degrees C with electric discharge.
  • Earth is about 4.5 billion years old; the universe is about 20 billion years old.
  • Industrial melanism was seen in the peppered moth Biston betularia in England.
  • Hugo de Vries worked on Oenothera lamarckiana and proposed saltation.
  • Homo erectus fossils were found in Java in 1891; brain capacity 900 cc.
  • Modern Homo sapiens arose in Africa during the ice age, between 75,000 and 10,000 years ago.

Common traps

  • Thinking lactose activates the repressor: the inducer actually inactivates the repressor, which frees the operator for transcription.
  • Assuming the i gene shares the z, y, a promoter: the i gene has its own promoter and is constitutively expressed.
  • Calling Turner's syndrome trisomic or Down's syndrome an X-chromosome defect: Turner's is 45, XO (missing X) and Down's is autosomal trisomy 21.
  • Listing genetic drift as an outcome of natural selection: natural selection is stabilising, directional or disruptive, while drift is a separate chance process.
  • Writing 2p or $p^2$ for the heterozygote: in Hardy-Weinberg, AA = $p^2$, Aa = $2pq$ and aa = $q^2$.
  • Treating Australian placental-marsupial similarity as divergent evolution: radiation within one lineage is divergent, but the placental-marsupial resemblance is convergent.
  • Assuming an affected father passes an X-linked trait to his son: sons get their X from the mother, so the father passes it only to daughters.
  • Considering Haeckel's embryological evidence valid: NCERT states it was disapproved by Karl Ernst von Baer.

Quick revision

  • Monohybrid F2 is 3:1 (1:2:1 genotype); dihybrid F2 is 9:3:3:1; incomplete dominance F2 is 1:2:1 for both.
  • ABO blood group shows co-dominance and multiple alleles; pleiotropy is seen in phenylketonuria and pea starch grains.
  • Polygenic traits give $2n+1$ phenotypes and a bell-shaped curve; skin colour is the standard example.
  • Sutton and Boveri proposed the chromosome theory; Morgan verified it, coined linkage, and Sturtevant made gene maps.
  • Heterogametic sex: male in humans (XY), female in birds (ZW); honey bee drones are haploid.
  • Haemophilia and colour blindness are X-linked recessive; thalassemia and sickle-cell are autosomal recessive.
  • Down's is 47 (+21); Klinefelter's is 47, XXY (sterile male); Turner's is 45, XO (sterile female).
  • Griffith showed transformation, Avery's group identified DNA, and Hershey-Chase proved it using $^{32}P$.
  • Replication is semiconservative and polymerase works $5' \rightarrow 3'$; Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand are joined by ligase.
  • RNA polymerase II makes hnRNA, which is capped, tailed and spliced; the genetic code is degenerate, unambiguous and nearly universal.
  • Lac operon: lactose is the inducer, the repressor comes from the i gene, and z, y, a form one polycistronic mRNA.
  • Hardy-Weinberg: $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$; disturbed by gene flow, drift, mutation, recombination and selection; Homo sapiens arose in Africa.

Biology · Unit 8: Biology and Human Welfare

This unit applies biology to human welfare. It covers how diseases are caused and spread, how the immune system defends the body, cancer, AIDS and substance abuse, and how microbes are used in food, industry, sewage treatment, energy generation and agriculture. NEET reliably draws 4-6 questions from it. Most are direct, NCERT-based factual questions on pathogen and disease pairs, immunity types, drug sources and microbe-product pairs, so precise recall gives quick marks.

PYQs (5): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q136, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q165, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q171, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q177, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q179

Health and disease; pathogens and parasites

Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease. It depends on genetic factors, infections, lifestyle (food, water, rest, exercise, habits) and a balanced mind. Diseases are infectious if they pass from one person to another, such as typhoid, malaria and AIDS. They are non-infectious if they do not, such as cancer. Pathogens are disease-causing organisms: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans and helminths. Most are parasites, living in or on the host and harming it. A pathogen must enter the body, multiply and interfere with normal function, and it must adapt to the host environment (for example, intestinal pathogens resist stomach acid and digestive enzymes). Spread occurs through contaminated food and water, air (droplets), direct contact or vectors such as mosquitoes and houseflies.

  • Health = physical + mental + social well-being.
  • Infectious diseases spread between people; non-infectious diseases such as cancer do not.
  • Cancer is a major non-infectious cause of death.
  • Pathogen groups: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, helminths.
  • Most pathogens are parasites that harm the host.
  • Modes of transmission: air, water, food, contact and vectors.
  • Good health is maintained by a balanced diet, personal hygiene, sanitation, vaccination and vector control.

NEET tip: NEET asks you to classify diseases as infectious or non-infectious and to identify the pathogen group (bacterial, viral, protozoan, fungal or helminth).

Human diseases: malaria, filariasis, ascariasis, typhoid, pneumonia, common cold, amoebiasis, ringworm, dengue, chikungunya

Malaria is caused by Plasmodium (P. vivax, P. malariae, P. falciparum; falciparum causes the most serious, malignant form). Sporozoites enter through the bite of a female Anopheles mosquito. They multiply asexually first in liver cells and then in RBCs. Rupture of RBCs releases the toxin haemozoin, which causes chills and high fever recurring every 3-4 days. Gametocytes form in RBCs. Fertilisation and development occur in the mosquito gut, and sporozoites are stored in the mosquito's salivary glands. Filariasis (elephantiasis) is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi, transmitted by female mosquitoes, and causes chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs and genitals. Ascariasis is caused by Ascaris and spreads through contaminated food and water. Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi and is confirmed by the Widal test. Pneumonia is caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Common cold is caused by rhinoviruses. Amoebiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, with houseflies as mechanical carriers. Ringworm is caused by Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton. Dengue and chikungunya are viral and spread by Aedes mosquitoes.

  • Malaria: Plasmodium is a protozoan; the female Anopheles is the vector and the definitive host.
  • Humans are the intermediate host of Plasmodium; asexual reproduction occurs in liver cells and RBCs.
  • Haemozoin causes the cyclic chills and fever of malaria.
  • Filariasis: Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi; the worms live in lymphatic vessels and cause elephantiasis of the limbs and genitals.
  • Ascariasis: internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage; eggs pass out in faeces.
  • Typhoid: sustained high fever of 39-40 degrees C, weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite.
  • Typhoid can cause intestinal perforation and death; it is diagnosed by the Widal test.
  • Mary Mallon (Typhoid Mary) was a symptomless carrier of typhoid.
  • Pneumonia infects the alveoli, which fill with fluid; lips and fingernails may turn grey to bluish.
  • Pneumonia spreads by droplets and by sharing glasses or utensils.
  • Common cold: rhinoviruses infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs; it lasts 3-7 days.
  • Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery): Entamoeba histolytica lives in the large intestine.
  • Amoebiasis symptoms: constipation, abdominal pain, cramps, and stools with excess mucus and blood clots.
  • Ringworm: dry, scaly, itchy lesions on skin, nails and scalp; heat and moisture favour it, especially in groin and skin folds.
  • Dengue and chikungunya: viral diseases with fever and joint pain, spread by Aedes; control by eliminating stagnant water.

NEET tip: Expect pathogen-disease-vector matching and malaria life-cycle statements, such as where sexual and asexual stages occur.

Basic concepts of immunology and vaccines

Immunity is the ability of the host to fight pathogens. Innate immunity is non-specific and present at birth. It has four types of barrier: physical (skin, mucus), physiological (stomach acid, saliva, tears), cellular (neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, NK cells) and cytokine (interferons protect uninfected cells from viruses). Acquired immunity is pathogen-specific and has memory. The first encounter produces a low-intensity primary response; a later encounter produces a stronger, faster secondary (anamnestic) response. B-lymphocytes produce antibodies, giving humoral immunity. T-lymphocytes give cell-mediated immunity (CMI), which is responsible for graft rejection. An antibody is a Y-shaped molecule of two heavy and two light chains. Active immunity is slow and comes from the body's own response to antigens (infection or vaccine). Passive immunity is quick and comes from ready-made antibodies (colostrum IgA, placental IgG, antitoxin and antivenom). Vaccines work by creating memory B and T cells. Allergy is an exaggerated IgE response with release of histamine and serotonin from mast cells. Autoimmunity, such as rheumatoid arthritis, is an attack on self cells.

  • Antibody types: IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG and IgM.
  • IgG crosses the placenta; IgA is abundant in colostrum; IgE mediates allergy; IgM is the largest antibody (pentamer).
  • Primary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus, where lymphocytes form and mature.
  • Secondary lymphoid organs: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix and MALT.
  • MALT makes up about 50 percent of the body's lymphoid tissue.
  • The thymus is large at birth and shrinks with age.
  • The spleen is a large bean-shaped organ that filters blood and acts as a reservoir of erythrocytes.
  • Recombinant DNA technology produces hepatitis B vaccine in yeast.
  • Allergens include dust mites, pollen and animal dander; allergy is treated with antihistamines, adrenalin and steroids.
  • Snakebite is treated with antivenom containing preformed antibodies, which gives passive immunity.

$H_2L_2$ Antibody structure: two heavy and two light polypeptide chains forming a Y shape.

NEET tip: NEET favours questions on antibody types and locations, primary versus secondary lymphoid organs, active versus passive immunity, and innate barrier examples.

Cancer

Normal cells show contact inhibition: they stop dividing when they touch other cells. Cancer cells lose this property and divide uncontrollably to form tumours. Benign tumours stay localised and cause little damage. Malignant tumours invade surrounding tissue, and cells that reach distant sites through the blood start new tumours there, a process called metastasis. Cancer-causing agents (carcinogens) include ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays), non-ionising UV radiation, chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, and oncogenic viruses. Cellular oncogenes (c-onc), or proto-oncogenes, can become activated and transform cells. Cancer is detected by biopsy and histopathological study, by blood and bone marrow tests (for leukaemia), and by imaging: radiography, CT and MRI. Monoclonal antibodies against cancer-specific antigens are also used. Treatment combines surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

  • Cancer cells have lost contact inhibition.
  • Benign tumours are non-invasive; malignant tumours are invasive and metastasise.
  • Ionising carcinogens: X-rays and gamma rays; non-ionising: UV radiation.
  • Oncogenic viruses carry viral oncogenes.
  • MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation.
  • CT uses X-rays to produce 3-D images.
  • Biological response modifiers such as alpha-interferon activate the immune system against tumours.
  • Chemotherapy has side effects such as hair loss and anaemia.

NEET tip: NEET asks about carcinogen types, the meaning of metastasis, detection techniques (especially MRI versus CT) and alpha-interferon therapy.

HIV and AIDS

AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) was first reported in 1981. It is caused by HIV, a retrovirus with an RNA genome inside an envelope. HIV spreads through sexual contact with an infected person, transfusion of contaminated blood, sharing of infected needles (common among intravenous drug users), and from an infected mother to her child through the placenta. After entry, the virus infects macrophages. Its reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA into DNA, which integrates into the host DNA, so the macrophage becomes an 'HIV factory'. HIV then enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH cells), replicates and destroys them, progressively lowering the TH count. The patient becomes immunodeficient and suffers opportunistic infections such as Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and Toxoplasma. The period between infection and AIDS symptoms is 5-10 years. Diagnosis is by ELISA. Antiretroviral drugs prolong life but do not cure the disease. Prevention relies on safe blood, disposable needles, condoms and awareness.

  • HIV is a retrovirus; its genetic information flows from RNA to DNA via reverse transcriptase.
  • Macrophages act as the HIV factory; helper T cells are the main cells killed.
  • The incubation period is 5-10 years.
  • ELISA is the standard diagnostic test.
  • HIV does not spread by touch or physical contact; it spreads only through body fluids.
  • NACO (National AIDS Control Organisation) leads AIDS prevention efforts in India.
  • World AIDS Day is observed on 1 December.

$RNA \xrightarrow{reverse\ transcriptase} DNA$ How HIV converts its RNA genome into DNA that integrates into the host genome.

NEET tip: Typical questions cover the sequence of HIV infection (macrophage, then TH cell), the role of reverse transcriptase and the ELISA test.

Adolescence; drug, alcohol and tobacco abuse

Adolescence, roughly 12-18 years, is the period of physical and psychological transition from childhood to maturity. Curiosity, peer pressure and stress make adolescents vulnerable to drugs, alcohol and tobacco. Opioids bind opioid receptors in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract. Heroin (smack, diacetylmorphine) is a white, bitter powder made by acetylation of morphine, which comes from the latex of the poppy Papaver somniferum. Heroin is a depressant that slows body functions. Morphine is a strong sedative and painkiller used after surgery. Cannabinoids (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja) come from Cannabis sativa, act on cannabinoid receptors in the brain and affect the cardiovascular system. Cocaine (coke, crack) comes from Erythroxylum coca, interferes with dopamine transport and is a stimulant causing euphoria and increased energy. Atropa belladonna and Datura are hallucinogenic plants. Tobacco nicotine stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and noradrenaline, raising blood pressure and heart rate. Smoking raises blood carbon monoxide, which reduces oxygen carried by haemoglobin. It is linked to lung, bladder and throat cancer, bronchitis, emphysema and coronary heart disease. Chronic alcohol use damages the nervous system and the liver, causing cirrhosis.

  • Heroin is made from morphine; morphine comes from the poppy Papaver somniferum.
  • Cocaine comes from Erythroxylum coca and acts on dopamine transport, stimulating the CNS.
  • Cannabinoids come from Cannabis sativa; they are usually smoked or taken orally.
  • Barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and LSD have medical uses for depression and insomnia but are often misused.
  • Tobacco is smoked, chewed or used as snuff; chewing increases the risk of oral cancer.
  • Withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating.
  • Anabolic steroids in females: masculinisation, aggressiveness, mood swings and abnormal menstrual cycles.
  • Anabolic steroids in females also cause excess hair growth, enlarged clitoris and a deeper voice.
  • Anabolic steroids in males: acne, reduced testicle size, reduced sperm, kidney and liver problems, breast enlargement and premature baldness.
  • Prevention: avoid undue peer pressure, education and counselling, help from parents and peers, and attention to danger signs.

NEET tip: Plant-source to drug matching, the receptor or action of each drug, and the effect of nicotine on adrenaline are favourite questions.

Microbes in household food processing and industrial production

Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) such as Lactobacillus convert milk into curd by producing acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins. LAB also increase vitamin B12 and check disease-causing microbes in the stomach. Dough for bread is leavened by baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, whose CO2 makes it puff up. Dosa and idli batters are fermented by bacteria. Toddy is made by fermenting palm sap. Swiss cheese has large holes because Propionibacterium sharmanii produces a lot of CO2. Roquefort cheese is ripened by a specific fungus. In industry, microbes are grown in large vessels called fermenters. Brewer's yeast (S. cerevisiae) ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to make wine and beer without distillation, and whisky, brandy and rum with distillation. Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the mould Penicillium notatum, which inhibited Staphylococci. Chain and Florey established it as an effective antibiotic, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize. Microbes also produce organic acids, enzymes and bioactive molecules.

  • Citric acid is produced by Aspergillus niger (fungus).
  • Acetic acid is produced by Acetobacter aceti (bacterium).
  • Butyric acid is produced by Clostridium butylicum (bacterium).
  • Lactic acid is produced by Lactobacillus (bacterium).
  • Ethanol is produced commercially by Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
  • Lipases are added to detergents to remove oily stains.
  • Pectinases and proteases are used to clarify bottled fruit juices.
  • Streptokinase, from Streptococcus and genetically modified, is a clot buster for myocardial infarction.
  • Cyclosporin A, from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum, is an immunosuppressant used in organ transplants.
  • Statins, from the yeast Monascus purpureus, lower blood cholesterol.
  • Statins work by competitively inhibiting the enzyme for cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase).

$C_6H_{12}O_6 \rightarrow 2C_2H_5OH + 2CO_2$ Alcoholic fermentation by yeast; the $CO_2$ leavens dough and the ethanol forms the basis of beverages.

NEET tip: Microbe-product-use matching (streptokinase, cyclosporin A, statins and organic acids) appears almost every year.

Microbes in sewage treatment and energy generation

Sewage is municipal waste water. It is treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) in two stages. Primary treatment is physical: debris is removed by sequential filtration, and grit is removed by sedimentation. Settled solids form the primary sludge, and the supernatant is the effluent. Secondary (biological) treatment takes place in aeration tanks. Vigorous aeration lets aerobic microbes grow as flocs, which are masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments in mesh-like structures. The flocs consume organic matter and greatly reduce BOD (biochemical oxygen demand). BOD measures the oxygen microbes need to oxidise the organic matter in one litre of water, so higher BOD means more pollution. The effluent then passes to a settling tank, where the flocs sediment as activated sludge. A small part is returned to the aeration tank as inoculum. The rest goes to anaerobic sludge digesters, where anaerobic bacteria digest it and produce biogas (methane, H2S and CO2). The treated effluent is released into rivers and streams. Biogas is also produced from cattle dung (gobar) by methanogens such as Methanobacterium, which are also found in the cattle rumen and help digest cellulose.

  • Primary treatment is physical: filtration and sedimentation.
  • Secondary treatment is biological: aerobic flocs in aeration tanks reduce BOD.
  • Activated sludge is partly recycled as inoculum and partly sent to anaerobic digesters.
  • BOD is an index of organic pollution; greater BOD means greater polluting potential.
  • The Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan were launched by the Ministry of Environment and Forests to treat sewage before it reaches rivers.
  • Biogas contains mainly methane, with $CO_2$, $H_2S$ and $H_2$.
  • A biogas plant has a 10-15 feet deep concrete tank fed with slurry of dung and a floating cover that rises as gas accumulates.
  • Biogas technology in India was developed mainly by IARI and KVIC.

$CH_4 + CO_2 + H_2S + H_2$ Approximate composition of biogas, which is mostly methane; used as fuel for cooking and lighting.

NEET tip: NEET tests the sequence of sewage treatment steps, what flocs and activated sludge are, the meaning of BOD and methanogen examples.

Microbes as biocontrol agents and biofertilizers

Biocontrol is the use of biological methods instead of chemical pesticides to control plant diseases and pests. It supports organic farming and integrated pest management (IPM). Ladybirds control aphids, and dragonflies control mosquitoes. Spores of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) are sprayed on plants and eaten by butterfly caterpillars. A toxin released in the larval gut kills the larvae while leaving other insects unharmed. Bt toxin genes have been introduced into plants such as Bt cotton. The free-living fungus Trichoderma, common in root ecosystems, controls many plant pathogens. Baculoviruses, mainly the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus, attack insects and arthropods. They are species-specific and narrow-spectrum, so they do not harm non-target organisms and suit IPM in ecologically sensitive areas. Biofertilizers are organisms that enrich soil nutrients. They include bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria.

  • Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes (symbiotic).
  • Azospirillum and Azotobacter are free-living soil nitrogen fixers.
  • Mycorrhiza (for example Glomus) helps the plant absorb phosphorus from soil.
  • Mycorrhizal plants also show resistance to root-borne pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought.
  • Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria fix atmospheric nitrogen.
  • Cyanobacteria are important biofertilizers in paddy fields and also add organic matter to the soil.
  • Biocontrol reduces dependence on toxic chemicals and protects non-target organisms.

$N_2 \rightarrow NH_3$ Biological nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium, Azotobacter and cyanobacteria, which enriches soil nitrogen.

NEET tip: Questions match organisms to roles, such as Bt for caterpillars, Trichoderma as a fungal biocontrol, Glomus for phosphorus and Anabaena in paddy fields.

Key facts

  • Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant malaria; haemozoin causes the recurring chills and fever every 3-4 days.
  • The female Anopheles is the vector and definitive host of Plasmodium; fertilisation occurs in the mosquito gut.
  • Plasmodium sporozoites are stored in the mosquito's salivary glands.
  • Filariasis is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi and leads to elephantiasis.
  • Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi and confirmed by the Widal test.
  • Mary Mallon, nicknamed Typhoid Mary, was a carrier of typhoid.
  • Pneumonia is caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.
  • Common cold is caused by rhinoviruses and does not affect the lungs.
  • Ringworm fungi: Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton.
  • Houseflies are mechanical carriers of Entamoeba histolytica.
  • Dengue and chikungunya are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.
  • Interferons are the cytokine barrier of innate immunity.
  • IgA is abundant in colostrum; IgG crosses the placenta; IgE is involved in allergy.
  • Bone marrow and thymus are primary lymphoid organs; spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils are secondary.
  • Peyer's patches and the appendix are also secondary lymphoid organs.
  • MALT forms about 50 percent of the body's lymphoid tissue.
  • Hepatitis B vaccine is produced in yeast by recombinant DNA technology.
  • Alpha-interferon is used in cancer immunotherapy.
  • HIV infects macrophages first (the HIV factory) and then destroys helper T cells.
  • The incubation period of AIDS is 5-10 years; it is diagnosed by ELISA.
  • Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is made by acetylation of morphine from Papaver somniferum.
  • Cocaine comes from Erythroxylum coca and interferes with dopamine transport.
  • Nicotine stimulates the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline and noradrenaline.
  • Propionibacterium sharmanii produces the large holes in Swiss cheese.
  • Penicillin was discovered by Fleming from Penicillium notatum; Fleming, Chain and Florey shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.
  • Streptokinase comes from Streptococcus; cyclosporin A from Trichoderma polysporum; statins from Monascus purpureus.
  • Citric acid comes from Aspergillus niger; acetic acid from Acetobacter aceti; butyric acid from Clostridium butylicum.
  • Methanobacterium is a methanogen that produces biogas from dung and is also found in the cattle rumen.
  • Baculoviruses of the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus are species-specific biocontrol agents.
  • Glomus (mycorrhiza) aids phosphorus uptake; Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria are nitrogen-fixing biofertilizers in paddy fields.

Common traps

  • Thinking Plasmodium reproduces sexually in human RBCs or liver. In humans it reproduces only asexually; gametocytes form in RBCs, but fertilisation occurs in the mosquito gut.
  • Calling the thymus or bone marrow a secondary lymphoid organ. They are primary; spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches and MALT are secondary.
  • Assuming colostrum gives active immunity. It provides ready-made IgA, so the immunity is passive; vaccination gives active immunity.
  • Confusing the sources of Trichoderma products. Trichoderma polysporum gives cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant), while Trichoderma as a free-living fungus is a biocontrol agent; statins come from Monascus purpureus.
  • Believing that wine and beer are distilled. They are not distilled; whisky, brandy and rum are distilled.
  • Thinking HIV first infects helper T cells. It first multiplies in macrophages, which act as the HIV factory, and then enters and destroys TH cells.
  • Assuming low BOD means polluted water. High BOD indicates high organic pollution; secondary treatment aims to reduce BOD.
  • Calling heroin a stimulant. Heroin and other opioids are depressants; cocaine is the stimulant.

Quick revision

  • Malaria: Plasmodium and female Anopheles; asexual in human liver and RBCs, sexual in mosquito gut; haemozoin causes fever.
  • Other diseases: typhoid (Salmonella typhi, Widal); pneumonia (Streptococcus, Haemophilus); common cold (rhinovirus); ringworm (Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton).
  • Innate barriers: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine (interferons); acquired immunity is specific and has memory.
  • Antibody = $H_2L_2$; IgA in colostrum, IgG crosses placenta, IgE in allergy.
  • Lymphoid organs: primary = bone marrow and thymus; secondary = spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, MALT.
  • Cancer: loss of contact inhibition, metastasis; detected by biopsy, CT and MRI; treated by surgery, radiation, chemotherapy and alpha-interferon.
  • HIV: retrovirus with reverse transcriptase; macrophage then TH cells; 5-10 year incubation; ELISA.
  • Drugs: heroin and morphine from poppy (depressant); cocaine from Erythroxylum (stimulant, dopamine); cannabinoids from Cannabis sativa.
  • Food microbes: LAB make curd (vitamin B12); Saccharomyces leavens bread and brews beverages; Propionibacterium makes Swiss cheese holes.
  • Microbial medicines: streptokinase is a clot buster, cyclosporin A an immunosuppressant, statins lower cholesterol.
  • Sewage: primary (physical) then secondary (flocs, lower BOD), then activated sludge and anaerobic digesters producing biogas ($CH_4$, $CO_2$, $H_2S$).
  • Biocontrol: Bt kills caterpillars, Trichoderma controls plant pathogens, Nucleopolyhedrovirus suits IPM; biofertilizers include Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Glomus and Anabaena.

Biology · Unit 9: Biotechnology and Its Applications

This unit covers how genes are cut, joined, cloned and expressed using recombinant DNA technology, and how these tools are applied in medicine (insulin, vaccines, gene therapy), agriculture (Bt crops, RNAi) and animal biotechnology, along with the ethical and legal issues they raise. NEET asks 3-5 questions from it every year. Most are direct NCERT-based items on enzymes, vectors, PCR steps, Bt toxin, ADA gene therapy, transgenic animals and biopiracy.

PYQs (5): NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q137, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q162, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q163, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q168, NEET (UG) 2026 · Code 50 · Q180

Principles and process of biotechnology: recombinant DNA technology

Biotechnology rests on two core techniques. Genetic engineering alters the chemistry of the genetic material. Bioprocess engineering maintains a sterile, contamination-free environment for large-scale culture. Cohen and Boyer made the first recombinant DNA in 1972 by linking a gene encoding antibiotic resistance with a native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium. The basic steps are: isolate DNA, cut it with a restriction enzyme, amplify the gene of interest by PCR, ligate it into a vector, transfer it into a host, culture the host and recover the product. Restriction endonucleases recognise palindromic sequences and leave sticky ends that DNA ligase joins. A vector needs three features: an ori, a selectable marker and cloning sites. Recombinants are identified by insertional inactivation, either of an antibiotic resistance gene or of lacZ (blue-white screening). Hosts are made competent with $Ca^{2+}$ and heat shock, or the DNA is delivered by microinjection or a gene gun. The product is then made in bioreactors and purified by downstream processing.

  • Restriction enzymes are molecular scissors. Hind II was the first isolated. Endonucleases cut within DNA, while exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends.
  • EcoRI is named from Escherichia coli strain RY13 and recognises the palindrome GAATTC, cutting between G and A to leave sticky ends.
  • Cell disruption depends on the cell wall: lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plants, chitinase for fungi.
  • During DNA isolation, RNase removes RNA and protease removes proteins. Chilled ethanol then precipitates DNA as fine threads, which are spooled out.
  • In agarose gel electrophoresis, the agarose comes from seaweed. DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the anode. Smaller fragments move farther.
  • DNA bands are stained with ethidium bromide and seen as orange bands under UV light. Cutting a band out and extracting its DNA is called elution.
  • PCR has three steps: denaturation at about $94^\circ C$, annealing of primers, and extension by thermostable Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus at about $72^\circ C$.
  • pBR322 carries ori, rop, $amp^R$ and $tet^R$. It has a BamHI site in $tet^R$ and PstI and PvuI sites in $amp^R$.
  • Insertion at BamHI inactivates $tet^R$, so recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline.
  • In blue-white selection, an insert in lacZ inactivates $\beta$-galactosidase. Recombinant colonies stay colourless (white) on a chromogenic substrate, while non-recombinants turn blue.
  • Natural vectors include the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens, which is disarmed to deliver genes to plants, and disarmed retroviruses for animal cells.
  • Transformation methods include $CaCl_2$ treatment with heat shock (ice, then $42^\circ C$, then ice), microinjection into the nucleus, biolistics using gold or tungsten particles, and disarmed pathogen vectors.
  • Stirred-tank bioreactors (typically 100 to 1000 L) control temperature, pH, foam, oxygen and sampling. Downstream processing (separation, purification, formulation, preservatives) and clinical trials follow.

$N = N_0 \times 2^n$ Number of DNA copies after n PCR cycles, starting from $N_0$ double-stranded molecules, assuming ideal doubling each cycle.

$\text{Probability of a site} = \frac{1}{4^n}$ Expected frequency of a specific n-bp restriction site in random DNA. A 6-bp site such as GAATTC occurs about once every $4^6 = 4096$ bp.

NEET tip: Expect PCR step identification, enzyme to cell-wall matching, pBR322 sites and insertional inactivation, the direction of DNA movement in a gel, and matching vector features (ori, selectable marker, cloning site) to their functions.

Human insulin and vaccine production

Insulin used to be extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs, which caused allergic reactions in some patients. Mature human insulin has two polypeptide chains, A (21 amino acids) and B (30 amino acids), joined by disulphide bridges. In the body it is made as pro-insulin, which carries an extra C-peptide that is removed during maturation. In 1983 Eli Lilly, an American company, prepared DNA sequences for the A and B chains and introduced them into plasmids of E. coli. The two chains were produced separately, extracted, and combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin (Humulin), which avoids the need to process the C-peptide. Recombinant DNA technology also enables recombinant vaccines. Here a gene for a pathogen's antigenic protein is expressed in a host to give a safe subunit vaccine. The hepatitis B vaccine is the standard NCERT example: it uses the surface antigen produced in yeast.

  • Human insulin consists of an A chain of 21 amino acids and a B chain of 30 amino acids, linked by disulphide bridges.
  • Pro-insulin contains an extra C-peptide that is removed to give mature insulin.
  • Eli Lilly produced recombinant human insulin in 1983 by expressing the A and B chains separately in E. coli.
  • The C-peptide is not part of the final recombinant product.
  • Animal-derived insulin could trigger allergy or immune reactions, which recombinant human insulin avoids.
  • Recombinant vaccines express only an antigenic protein of the pathogen, so they cannot cause the disease.
  • Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine uses the surface antigen (HBsAg) produced in yeast.
  • Other recombinant therapeutics are approved worldwide, and around 12 of them are marketed in India.

NEET tip: NEET asks for the amino acid numbers in the A and B chains, the fate of the C-peptide, Eli Lilly with 1983, E. coli as the host, and yeast as the host for the hepatitis B vaccine.

Gene therapy

Gene therapy corrects a hereditary defect by delivering a normal gene into a person's cells or tissues, where it compensates for the non-functional gene. The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. ADA is crucial for the immune system, and its absence causes severe immunodeficiency. Her lymphocytes were grown in culture outside the body. A functional ADA cDNA was introduced into them using a retroviral vector, and the cells were returned to her. Because lymphocytes are not immortal, the infusion has to be repeated periodically. A permanent cure is possible only if the ADA gene, isolated from marrow cells, is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages. Alternatives for ADA deficiency are bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy, in which functional ADA is injected.

  • The first clinical gene therapy, in 1990, treated ADA deficiency in a 4-year-old girl.
  • ADA stands for adenosine deaminase. A deletion in the ADA gene causes immunodeficiency.
  • The procedure was ex vivo: lymphocytes were cultured, given functional ADA cDNA through a retroviral vector, and reinfused.
  • The treatment is not permanent because genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so periodic infusions are needed.
  • A permanent cure requires introducing the ADA gene, isolated from marrow cells, into cells at early embryonic stages.
  • Non-gene options are bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy (injection of functional ADA).
  • Retroviruses are used because they integrate their genetic material into the host genome. They are first disarmed so they do not cause disease.

NEET tip: Typical questions ask which disease was first treated (ADA deficiency), which vector was used (retrovirus), which cells were used (lymphocytes), why the therapy is not permanent, and what a permanent cure would require.

Genetically modified organisms: Bt crops

Genetically modified (GM) organisms carry genes altered by manipulation. GM plants have made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses, reduced reliance on chemical pesticides, cut post-harvest losses, improved mineral use efficiency and raised nutritional value, as in Golden rice rich in vitamin A. Bt crops carry cry genes from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. Bt toxin is formed as inactive protoxin crystals, which is why the bacterium is not harmed. When an insect eats them, the alkaline pH of its gut solubilises the crystals and activates the toxin. The active toxin binds to midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, causing swelling, lysis and death. NCERT also describes pest resistance through RNA interference (RNAi). Nematode-specific genes are introduced into tobacco through Agrobacterium vectors, producing sense and anti-sense RNA. These form dsRNA, which silences the parasite's mRNA so that Meloidogyne incognita cannot survive in the transgenic host.

  • Bt toxin protein is called Insecticidal Crystal Protein (ICP) and is encoded by cry genes.
  • The toxin exists as inactive protoxin and is activated by the alkaline pH of the insect gut.
  • Active toxin binds midgut epithelial cells and forms pores, leading to cell swelling, lysis and insect death.
  • Bt toxin targets lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).
  • cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, while cryIAb controls corn borer.
  • Bt cotton is the prominent Bt crop grown in India.
  • In RNAi, dsRNA silences a specific mRNA. It is used against the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita in tobacco roots.
  • In the RNAi method, Agrobacterium vectors introduce nematode-specific genes into the host plant, producing both sense and anti-sense RNA.
  • Golden rice is a GM rice rich in vitamin A.

NEET tip: Be ready for why the protoxin is activated (alkaline pH), matching cry genes to pests, which insect orders are affected, and the RNAi mechanism with the nematode name.

Transgenic animals

Transgenic animals carry and express an extra foreign gene in their DNA. Rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been made transgenic, but over 95 percent of existing transgenic animals are mice. They are used for five main purposes. First, they help study how genes regulate normal physiology and development, for example insulin-like growth factor. Second, they serve as disease models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease. Third, they produce useful biological products, such as alpha-1-antitrypsin for treating emphysema. Fourth, they test vaccine safety, as with transgenic mice used for polio vaccine before human trials. Fifth, they test chemical safety, because animals carrying sensitive genes respond faster to toxic chemicals. In 1997 Rosie, the first transgenic cow, produced milk enriched with human protein (2.4 g per litre) containing human alpha-lactalbumin. This milk is nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk.

  • Over 95 percent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.
  • Rosie (1997) was the first transgenic cow. Her milk contained 2.4 g per litre of human protein, including human alpha-lactalbumin.
  • Alpha-1-antitrypsin produced by transgenic animals is used to treat emphysema.
  • Transgenic animals are being developed to make products for phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis.
  • Transgenic mice are used to test the safety of polio vaccine.
  • Toxicity testing in transgenic animals gives faster results because the animals carry genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances.
  • Transgenic animal models are used to study cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease.

NEET tip: NEET usually asks about Rosie (year, protein, amount), alpha-1-antitrypsin for emphysema, polio vaccine testing in mice, and the 95 percent mouse figure.

Biosafety issues, biopiracy and patents

Genetic modification raises ethical and safety concerns, including unpredictable effects when GM organisms enter ecosystems. In India the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) judges whether GM research is valid and whether introducing GM organisms for public services is safe. A patent is a right granted by a government that stops others from commercially using an invention. Biopiracy is the use of bio-resources or traditional knowledge by multinational companies or organisations without proper authorisation or compensation to the countries and people concerned. In 1997 an American company obtained patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office. The rice had been derived from Indian farmers' varieties crossed with semi-dwarf varieties. India has about 200,000 varieties of rice, of which 27 documented varieties are Basmati. Attempts have also been made to patent uses of turmeric and neem. Developing nations demand fair benefit-sharing, and India amended its Patents Bill to address patent terms, emergency provisions and research and development initiatives.

  • GEAC (Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee) is the Indian body that regulates GM research and the release of GM organisms.
  • Biopiracy is the unauthorised use of bio-resources or traditional knowledge without compensation.
  • A patent on Basmati rice was granted to an American company in 1997.
  • India has about 200,000 rice varieties, of which 27 are documented Basmati varieties.
  • Turmeric and neem are other Indian examples where patent attempts were made on traditional knowledge.
  • Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, whereas developing nations are rich in both.
  • The Indian Parliament cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill to address these issues.

NEET tip: Questions focus on the full form and role of GEAC, the definition of biopiracy, and the Basmati facts (1997, 27 varieties, 200,000 rice varieties).

Key facts

  • Cohen and Boyer constructed the first recombinant DNA in 1972 using a Salmonella typhimurium plasmid.
  • Hind II was the first restriction endonuclease isolated, and it always cuts at a specific 6-bp sequence.
  • EcoRI recognises GAATTC and is named from Escherichia coli strain RY13.
